en: Preface to the *Fozu gangmu*:

This unworthy writer has drifted in and out of the historical archives for nearly fifty years, and I have found that among all matters of antiquity and the present, none is more difficult than history.
This holds true not only for the orthodox histories (*zhengshi*), but even for partial records and minor chronicles; it is no less so for the unofficial annals (*baishi*). Even [the latter]...

It is difficult even to compile a miscellaneous collection of trivial sayings; how much more so when advancing to the histories of heaven and earth, and further advancing to the histories of the immortals and the Buddha?

Unless one regards the mountains and rivers as the Dharma-body and takes humans and devas as one’s own hands and eyes, there has never been anyone capable of grasping their essentials and synthesizing them into a whole.
The Layman Xin Kong, with thirty years of diligent effort, has compiled [this work].

Thus, the *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) provides a comprehensive grasp of the Brahma-net precepts, records for the various Dharma gates, a source and stream for the religious teachings, and a critical examination of their decline and flourishing.
Taken together, it may be said that this is a grand history of the one vehicle since the time of the Seven Buddhas.
During the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty, Wang Jian compiled the *Qizhi* (Seven Monographs), wherein he merely appended Buddhist texts to the section on maps and genealogies.

At the end of the Liu Song dynasty and the beginning of the Liang, Emperor Wu ordered Ren Fang and others to catalog the various books in Wende Hall and to separately compile the Buddhist scriptures in Hualin Garden.
Subsequently, Ruan Xiaoxu extensively gathered from the classics and histories, yet he uniquely honored only the Buddhist records;

however, even beyond his "Seven Records," his efforts did no more than provide a basis for broad learning and display extraordinary eccentricity. From the Tang and Song dynasties onward, the study of the [Buddhist] schools flourished.

Flourishing, the branches and leaves each diverged. From the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp from the Jingde Era) onward, successive compilers continued the lineage until they were consolidated into the "Five Lamps.
Thus, after Caoxi, the lineages split again under Huineng and Shenhui; since Mazu, the five schools have each manifested their distinctiveness.

Reaching the Song dynasty monk Fapian, he established a separate doctrinal school, taking the *Lotus Sūtra* as its scripture, Tiantai as its system, and *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) as its gateway.

This is the origin from which the *Fozu Tongji* (The Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) was produced. Reaching into the Yuan dynasty, the monk Zhichang further composed the *Tongzai* (Comprehensive Records), which followed the name of the *Tongji* but established different precedents.
He first employed the annalistic method of historians; his intention was to take the [Buddhist] schools as primary and the teachings as secondary.

Consequently, it encompasses everything without exception—pure practices, supernatural powers, the nature and characteristics of phenomena, and the contemplation of their meanings—and its scope is vast.

Those who have scrutinized its errors and omissions find them beyond the reach of refutation; such is the difficulty inherent in historical records. The Layman [Zhao Mengfu] possessed a clear and lucid mind from his past lives, considering himself a reincarnation of Mingjiao Huihong.

Consequently, he was solemn and earnest regarding the great principles of the "Establishment of the Patriarchs" and the "True Lineage. He identified the major frameworks and minute details with exquisite precision.

Yet, when it came to summarizing the traces of his spiritual transformation and emphasizing the conditions of karmic encounter (*nidāna*), he integrated these with the essential teachings of the school.

Returning to the Pure Land, he further provided skillful and subtle guidance, nothing but blending water and milk and blowing upon the bright transmission of the lamp, so that the principle of "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha" might be understood directly by everyone as they open a scroll.

Thus, his vow to manifest for the sake of the layman and repay his kindness was fulfilled. How could it ever come to such a state as the petty disciples and disputants who recklessly divide the orthodox from the heterodox? False...
Dividing North from South, one begins by investigating history, yet it becomes a spear and shield for religious factions. Alas! Wei Zhao relied on orthodoxy and his writings fell into the pit;

Cui Hao offended against taboos and his clan suffered a mass extermination. Consequently, upright ministers and men of integrity were forced to silently mark the texts of Zhang Yan and privately preserve the manuscripts of Sun Sheng.
With the halls of the Imperial Academy and the Golden Horse Gate filled with pitfalls and latrines, how could this be?
Like the side of a sandalwood forest where one may stroll and compose, the shores of the Great Perfect Ocean are free from the winds and waves of external phenomena.

Humans, ghosts, devas, and nāgas all contribute to the refinement of the brush. With the city-gates and Deer Park serving as my private quarters, I shoulder the historian’s responsibility like a lay devotee;
who would say that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is no station for the brush-tip or no person to hold the pen?
Also. On an auspicious day in the second month of autumn in the year Jiashu of the Great Ming Chongzhen era.

By Imperial Decree, conferred the rank of Jinshi (Presented Scholar), Grand Master for the Cultivation of Virtue (Zizheng Dafu), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Taizi Taibao), Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Libu Shangshu) concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlin Xueshi), and Director of the Court of Imperial Scholars (Zhangshifu).
Preface to the *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), composed by Dong Qichang, Vice Director of the Shilu (Veritable Records).
In compiling this work, I harbor a profound aspiration. As the Sūtra says: "One who seeks to deliver others before one has oneself attained deliverance is a Bodhisattva."

To resolve the mind (*cittotpāda*) and, having perfected one’s own awakening, to be able to awaken others—this is the Tathāgata appearing in the world. It is said that resolving the mind is precisely to seek one’s own awakening;
it is said that appearing in the world is precisely to fulfill that original resolve. Before the mind has taken form, it is profound and obscure.
"To not see a single thing—neither Buddha, nor Patriarch, nor纲 (the guiding line), nor 目 (the eyes)—is because not even a speck of dust can be established within this nature.
When the mind has already manifested, it is vast and expansive, leaving nothing out;

that there is Buddha, Patriarch, guiding line, and eyes is because the myriad dharmas are luminously clear within this nature. Therefore, it is said: one cannot seek with a mind possessed of intentional thought."
It is attained through the mindless; it cannot be constructed through language, nor can it be communicated through silence. It transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
It is like planting flowers in the sky, or treading upon the moon in the midst of waves. There is no place for you to settle, no place for you to deliberate. Ultimately, how is it?
By using the Buddhas and Patriarchs to dispatch the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and by using the essential principles to seize the essential principles—it is divine.
Its elucidation depends solely upon the individual. This work was first drafted in the *gengxu* year of the Wanli era (1610) and completed in the *xinwei* year of the Chongzhen era (1631).

Having devoted his heart and withered his beard over twenty-one years, he finally produced the *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Patriarchs and Buddhas) in forty-one fascicles. At that time, the practitioners of the Lotus Society...
I entrusted the planning to the carvers to create this "Eye for the Human and Heavenly Beings. Thereupon, I was filled with joy and exultation, and spoke these verses:
I have composed this book Not for the sake of fame, But so that both principle and phenomena are complete, And both the provisional and the ultimate are practiced together.
I hope that those who observe will understand as clearly as a bright mirror; that upon opening this scroll and reading it, they will give rise to the unsurpassed mind.

I do not wish for the sons of the Buddha to be attached to the flavor of the words; I only wish that they would look back within themselves, realizing that right here and now is where the roots of entanglement are severed and the tree of ignorance is felled.
I do not wish for the sons of the Buddha to give rise to even a fleeting intellectual understanding.
I only wish that you would exhaust the source and sweep away all strangeness; returning home with empty hands, may every dust mote be free from obstruction.

I do not wish for the Buddha’s disciples to be arrogant and conceited; I only wish they would recognize their errors, so that the numinous light may manifest—where even the Buddhas have no power and the demonic armies scatter of their own accord. I do not wish for the Buddha’s disciples to treat the *vinaya* with negligence.
I only wish that through the nature-precepts, there be neither transgression nor observance; That from this mass of red flesh, the *maṇi* jewel should emerge.
I do not wish for the children of the Buddha to sink into emptiness and sit in withered stillness; I only wish they would clarify the mind, so as to be free from falling back.
What matters is the meditation cushion—whether it is worn out or not. I do not wish for the children of the Buddha to let their time pass in vain.
I only wish that you would be diligent, holding fast to the teachings with earnest devotion; may you maintain a single thought for ten thousand years, even as the great earth sinks away.

I do not wish for the Buddha’s disciples to be muddled and superficial; I only wish they would attain thorough awakening, shatter the mass of doubt, advance beyond the tip of the staff, and kick through the bottom of the bucket.
I do not wish for the Buddha’s disciples to be preoccupied with superficial adornments or external protections.
I only wish that with a sincere heart, I may perfectly cultivate the six perfections; The ocean of Dharma is boundless, Yet I shall traverse it in a single instant.

May all Buddhas bear witness to this verse I have composed: Though the vast ocean may be exhausted And Mount Sumeru may crumble, This power of my vow shall endure forever, Coexisting eternally with the Buddhas.
Appended is the original memorial.
I, a commoner of this vast world, reflect upon my meager fortune and wisdom. For over forty years, I have spent my time in vain.
Having received the education of my parents in my youth, I humbly cherished the bequeathed words of the Sage Confucius. Subsequently, my mother passed away first, whereupon I came to admire...
When Buddhist scriptures followed the footsteps of Confucianism, they nearly imitated its forms while attacking Buddhism;
yet when they took refuge in Buddhism, they disparaged Confucianism because they had tasted its excellence.

Both instances arose from a failure to merge with the profound source of the Great Sage, which led them to conform to the tracks of common worldly customs. In the previous year, the Wanyili dingsi era, it was precisely at this time...

At the age of forty-four, he gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve and diligently sought the wondrous Way. Morning and evening he visited and consulted [his master], never daring to be negligent or idle. Even in his dreams, he silently received the seal of approval.

Only then did he come to believe that the Dharma-way of a thousand ages is not obtained from others; that the wondrous functions of the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind.
Saving sentient beings is the urgent priority—why restrict this to either monastics or laypeople? It is only the ignorant who are deluded and falsely make such distinctions.
Regarding Confucianism and Buddhism: Originally, when the World-Honored One preached the twelve divisions of the sūtras, humans and devas looked up to him in reverence;

when Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, rebellious ministers and treacherous sons were struck with fear. If these works can open the eyes of the world, how could one begrudge even a single hair or inch of one’s own skin?
Now, I, En, daringly reflect upon myself and wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness by compiling [this work] according to the chronological reign titles of successive dynasties.

I have compiled the *Fozu Gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), intending to emulate Confucius and adopting the same title as that of Ziyang (Zhu Xi). This will likely require ten years before it can be completed.

Yet, even though Confucius was a sage, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* still pertains to worldly conventions (*saṃvṛti-satya*); at that time, he even risked the reproach of being accused of "excessive self-praise.
How much more so for me—what person am I? What I have here recorded in chronological order are all those who are the God among Gods, the Sage among Sages.
O Holy One! You are not merely a manifestation of an ancient Buddha, but a Bodhisattva who rescues the world.
From the celestial Māras and non-Buddhist heretics above, down to the narrow-minded Confucian scholars below, none can disturb or trouble you, nor do they frequently slander or revile you.

For this reason, I cast myself in sincere devotion, earnestly entreating the Buddhas of the three periods, the Great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and other protectors of the Dharma: may you be covered by immeasurable...
Through supernatural power, you have protected and sustained this work in manifold ways. Relying upon your vast spiritual penetration, you have graciously bestowed skillful means.
With diligent mental exertion, wisdom flowed forth in a continuous stream; with all-out effort in collation and proofreading, your spirit remained radiant and ever-vigilant.

Whether it be rare books or ancient scrolls, or fragmented manuscripts and incomplete fragments, there was nothing sought that could not be obtained. At times you provided the funds for carving the blocks, and at others you opened the way [for publication].

This compendium of the works of the Great Sage, gathered over several years, is no different from a single moment; though comprising a thousand leaves of verse, they appear as if breathed from a single breath.

Once the volumes are completed, the sublime regulations of Vulture Peak seem as if they have not yet dispersed; when fully unfolded, the auspicious assembly of the Dragon Flower is already grasped before one’s eyes.
Let it be said that even if there were subsequent authors, their succession would remain uninterrupted, transforming this work into something inexhaustible.
This lamp—those who now possess the resolve for *dhyāna* will understand it at a single glance without omission; wherever the eye falls, it is the path to Bodhi.
May the Illustrious Ruler enshrine it within the canon for universal circulation, enduring as long as heaven and earth; may spirits and deities never forget this bequest and provide their protection.

It is like the jade tablets and golden caskets; the celestial Māras and heterodox practitioners will fold their hands in submission, and the narrow-minded scholars and pedants will turn their hearts toward the Way.
Were it not for great compassion and great power, how could this beginning and end be accomplished? I shall now resolve to compile and collect [these teachings].

From the very beginning, my prayers have not been answered, despite the utmost sincerity. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the Gengxu year of the Wanli era, the disciple Zhu Shien respectfully submits this memorial.
Having already made these great vows before the image of the Tathāgata, I have repeatedly obtained auspicious dreams, not just once.
It is sufficient. Or, one may dream of a sage from after the Three Teachings who privately feels moved by it and wears it as private mourning attire.
Or, one may dream that Chan Master Mingjiao Song has returned as a sage from after the [Three] Teachings; what is recorded in this book is precisely the transformative traces of such former sages.
Those who are inspired upon reading this book are all sages from after the Three Teachings. "Privately" means they are neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs. Because...

I am but an ordinary layman who has compiled this "Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs" (*Fozu Gangmu*). This is what Confucius meant when he said, "As for its underlying principle, I have privately appropriated it.
Though it is public, it is also private. Those who are moved by it will, through this book, clarify their minds and realize their nature;
they should naturally feel a gratitude that they never forget. Those who apply it will, through this book, sever their delusions.
Adhering to emptiness, you should naturally embrace it with tireless devotion. Mingjiao is a "returner";
formerly, as a bhikṣu, he authored the *Zhuanfa Zhengzong Ji*, and now, as a layman (jūshì), he has authored the *Fozu Gangmu*.

From beginning to end, he appears as if one and the same person. From this, one knows that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have bestowed their grace upon me. Although my research and compilation are not yet complete...
The profound essence that has not been transmitted by the thousand sages and which transcends language and writing is, as it were, both contained within and breathed forth from this book.
As an ancient worthy said: "To offer this deep resolve to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness."
General Principles of the *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):
A Buddha is so named because they are fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, and have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
A Patriarch is so named because they clarify the mind-source of the Buddha, such that their practice and realization are in accord. The fourth Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa is titled Śākyamuni.
Śākyamuni ruled this Sahā world of the five turbidities. Śākyamuni transmitted [the Dharma] to Kāśyapa; twenty-eight transmissions later reached Bodhidharma.
These are known as the Twenty-eight Patriarchs of the Western Heaven. Bodhidharma transmitted it to Huike; six transmissions later reached Huineng.
These are known as the Six Patriarchs of the Eastern Land. Thereafter, the five schools flourished in succession, with each dharma being transmitted to the next, without failing its mandate.

The Patriarchal Lineages: Within the gates of the teachings, there are the Yogācāra school, the Nanshan school, the Tiantai school, the Ci'en school, and the Xianshou school. The Structural Framework and its Details:

"Gang" (framework) refers to the great framework; "mu" (details) refers to the fine details. The *Spring and Autumn Annals with its Annals and Memorials* (*Chunqiu Zuozhuan*) serves as a model for worldly dharmas.
Both good and evil are set forth to serve as a basis for the Dharma-precepts; thus, there is both praise and censure.

The *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) is a teaching of the supramundane Dharma specifically intended to entrust oneself to those Buddhas and Patriarchs who have already attained realization, thereby manifesting the Buddha and Patriarch of one’s own intrinsic nature.
Therefore, there is neither praise nor censure.

Regarding the volumes: when the Tathāgata manifested his birth in India and the Great Teaching gradually spread to China, the compositions of this land were invariably centered upon Śākyamuni as their primary subject.
Now, regardless of the number of fascicles, they are categorized by a single sexagenary cycle.

It consists of one volume. Beginning from the second year of King Kang of the Zhou dynasty, the Jiazi year, and ending in the Guihai year of the sixteenth year of Hongwu, it covers a total of forty-one sexagenary cycles (*jiǎzǐ*).
This results in forty-one volumes, which have been assigned character codes for the convenience of reference and examination.
Regarding the era names: the Western lands and the Eastern lands differ in their worldly laws, and their methods of the Path likewise differ.
Therefore, at the beginning of the outline for each fascicle, I have first recorded the era names of this land within the sexagenary cycle (*jiǎzǐ*).
Only then do I specifically record the karmic encounters and transformative traces of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so that they may not become confused.
The Five Periods: The Tathāgata manifests five periods. First, his descent from heaven; second, his renunciation of the household life;

third, his attainment of enlightenment; fourth, his preaching of the Dharma; and fifth, his entry into nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma also comprises five periods: first, the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the *Āgama* (or *Aranyaka*);
third, the *Vaipulya*; fourth, the *Prajñāpāramitā*; and fifth, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Regarding the "Opportune Conditions" (jīyuán) as the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings": from the moment one first emerges from the mother’s womb, they have already been revealed.

Why wait for the "Picking of the Flower" incident to serve as a formal record? That the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* exclusively records these opportune conditions after the Buddha’s passing possesses a profound underlying meaning. For those of superior capacity, this is truly so.
If one can find a point of vulnerability here, the seventeen hundred public cases will not require even a single squeeze.
As for miraculous traces and supernatural transformations, even Buddhas and Patriarchs must sometimes rely upon them to subdue demons and heretics;
yet in truth, the True Dharma does not depend on these. Take, for example, Guishan and Yunmen—their Way filled the world, yet we have never heard it said that—
Because the kings of the three periods lost their supernormal powers, the spirit of their lineage was somewhat diminished;
thus, while the *Gangmu* does not erase their traces of transformation, it likewise does not become mired in those traces.
"Jiao" (Teaching) refers to the Buddha’s words; "Zong" (Principle) refers to the Buddha’s mind. One need only worry that the mind does not become Buddha;
one need not worry that the Buddha cannot understand one's speech. However, if one understands the Principle but not the Teaching, every word they utter will be confused and erroneous.
Therefore, this book takes the transmission of the True Principle of the Dharma as its primary focus, while the Teaching is secondary; it must certainly be read.
Pure Land: The Buddha opened the single gate of the Pure Land as a truly efficacious remedy for saving the world and a swift shortcut for the practice of Chan.
Before Bodhidharma arrived, Master Huiyuan first established the Lotus Society, teaching people to recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
Its ultimate goal is not even a hair’s breadth different from the direct pointing and single transmission. In recent times, Master Yunqi Hongwu... [text continues]
The Buddha returns once more. He stands as resolute as Deshan and Linji, yet he does not employ the staff or the shout; instead, he single-mindedly upholds the *nianfo* (Buddha-remembrance) *huatou*.
This may be called skillfully emulating Liu Xiahui—learning from him without following his outward traces. Those who read the *Tongjian Gangmu* must surely recognize this meaning.
*Zongjing lu*, Section on Names and Titles, Volume Thirty-one. Under the lineages of Mazu and Shitou, there were two individuals named Daowu who must be distinguished.
One Daowu was a successor of Shitou; he was the son of the Zhang family of Dongyang.
He first studied under Guoyi and later visited Shitou, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment. He resided at Tiantai Monastery to the east of the city of Jingzhou. His disciples numbered three.
Ren, Yi-hui, Zhen, Yi-wen, Ben, Yi-you, and Xian. Fu Zai composed the stele inscription for Xie-lü.
Yi-dao-wu succeeded Mazu; he was the son of the Cui family of Zhugong. Initially, he visited Shitou but did not find resonance; next, he visited National Teacher Zhong;

later, he visited Mazu and attained great enlightenment upon hearing a single word. Mazu bestowed a prediction upon him, and he returned to Jingmen. The regional commander [honored him] as Tianwang...
[The author] rebukes [the error]. He established Tiantong Temple to the west of the capital to serve his master. His disciple was Longtan Chongxin.
The inscription was composed by Qiu Xuansu, the Regional Inspector of Jingnan. According to this, it is beyond doubt that Longtan succeeded Tianwang, and Tianwang succeeded Mazu.
It is only the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) that erroneously lists him within the lineage of Shitou. Furthermore, Song Jing...
The Postscript on Protecting the Dharma by Zhu Xi follows this as well. Why is this?

Furthermore, the "Stele for Nanyue" by the Tang figure Wenren Guide, Guifeng’s "Reply to Minister Pei on the Essential Tenets," and Quan Deyu’s "Epitaph for Mazu’s Stupa" all regard the Heavenly King as the successor to the Dharma of Mazu.
Moreover, Foguo Bai, Da, Guan Ying, Lü Xiaqing, and Zhang Wujin likewise [hold this view].
The *Biànzhèng chuánténg* contains errors which have been verified and corrected one by one through the *Gāngmù*.

*Biàné*: Volume 34 of the Tēng edition. In the Gēnyòu gēngxū year, the King of Wuyue offered a vegetarian feast for monks on his birthday and asked Yongming, "Are there any true monks appearing now? He replied, "There is the 'Long-Eared Monk'."
He was, in fact, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. When the King hurriedly approached his carriage to pay his respects, he addressed him as "Dīpaṃkara Appearing in the World.
Chang-er (Long-ear) merely replied, "Yongming is too talkative," and then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

He was posthumously titled Yongming; both Yongming and Chang-er were dharma heirs of Xuefeng. Initially, he resided at Cuiyan Tianfu. In the year of Dingyou, the King invited him to reside at Longce. This is...
Regarding the Yongming you have inquired about: in the Jiǎyín year of the Xiǎndé era, the King first established Yongming Temple and invited Dàoqián to reside there.
In the Xīnyǒu year of the Sòng Jianlóng era, when Dàoqián passed away, the King then invited Yǎnshòu to dwell at Yongming.
Counting back from that Xīnyǒu year to the Gēngxū year, it was a total of eleven years; at that time, Yǎnshòu had not yet appeared in the world at Yongming.
The temple had not yet been built; how, then, can it be said that the Yongming mentioned by the King was the same Yongming as that of Chanyue?

There are many such instances within Buddhist scriptures, and the omissions are likewise numerous. We shall wait for scholars of broad learning to provide a detailed revision before continuing further.
Preface: Regarding the opening of the *Outline and Details* (*Gangmu*), with the exception of my own statement of aspiration and the original preface, I have recorded only two pieces:

the preface by Song Jingliao to the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Dharma Transmission* (*Zhengfa Zhengzong Ji*) and the postscript to the *Compilation for Protecting the Teachings* (*Hujiao Bian*).
Furthermore, I did not dare to beg for writings from famous gentlemen to serve as embellishments.

This book had already been carved for printing in the Guiyou year. Then, in the autumn of the Jiayou year, Master Si retired from official service and returned south; upon seeing it, he was delighted and wished to provide a preface that would be vast, profound, and essential, thereby serving as the crown of this work. Thus, he composed this.

although the Western Sage is the Teacher of the Great Thousandfold World System, in reality...

Following the sexagenary cycle of the emperors of the Eastern Land, I have compiled the chronology and titles, arranging them from the preface through to the list of donors' surnames at the end of the final fascicle into forty-one sections, totaling twelve volumes in all. Herein concludes the postscript.

Once the *Fozu gangmu yuanxing ke fendeng lu* (The Annotated Genealogy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, with Prefaces and Excerpts from the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) was completed, the seeds of past lives within all faithful practitioners were already awakened and stirred.
Nevertheless, the Master Xin Kong’s vast vows and profound compassion continued to increase without end; indeed, he devoted his entire life’s energy to this endeavor.

The *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) is a work that compiles the essentials and probes the profound mysteries of the entire Tripitaka, arranged according to a chronological method.
It takes Śākyamuni as the primary teacher; it regards the various patriarchs of India and China—the "One Flower and Five Leaves"—as the orthodox lineage;
and it treats the scriptural teachings, doctrinal meanings, contemplative practices, pure conduct, and supernormal powers as auxiliary wings. This includes, furthermore, officials and lay elders.

There are no virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who are not encompassed herein. Although this work follows the precedent of the *Tongzai* (Comprehensive Records), it eliminates all seven types of errors found therein;

by selecting and collating [the sources], its merit is doubled while its labor is redoubled. It may truly be called a great raft for the *piṭaka* and a golden probe for the seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), enabling students to cultivate their practice within it without needing to peruse the entirety of the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings.
In my heart, I knew that the apertures of my eyes had opened all at once. It was like a thirsty man drinking celestial nectar, or a hungry man feasting on the cuisine of a king;

it was as if one who had been dazed by the Eastern Sea suddenly found himself wandering through the Land of Fragrance. Bearing this frail child and leaning upon my staff, I entered the marketplace of a hundred medicines.
Their leaping joy and exultation are, moreover, beyond measure. The work consists of forty fascicles, which have been compiled into twelve volumes.
These shall be entrusted to twelve individuals possessing great spiritual power to circulate and propagate them. There are those who will take sole responsibility for this task.
This humble servant says: In this degenerate age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), all people throughout the world have become deluded regarding that which transcends the mundane.

Rather than being a solitary gentleman, it is better to share one's goodness with others. Thus, there has arisen this collective fundraising for the printing of the canon, following entirely the regulations of Mount Jing.
May each person’s name be engraved at the end of the scrolls, so that the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—may be universally moistened by a single rain.
Is this not immediately the merit of the half and the full? Are they not, for a moment, equal and non-dual?
Do not say that the Layman Mind-Empty has intentionally cast a vast net across the heavens to capture the phoenix and ensnare the dragon.
April, the fifth year of Chongzhen (Ren-shen), Written on the Buddha’s Birthday by Huang Tinggu (Dan-zhi-fu) as a preface to the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma*,

There were thirty-seven rulers in total, spanning eight hundred and sixty-seven years. The World-Honored One [Śākyamuni] lived during the twenty-sixth year of the fourth ruler, King Zhao.
To manifest his birth. Therefore, the present calculation begins from the *jiayin* year of King Zhao.

At the time of the World-Honored One’s birth, the rivers and streams in this land overflowed, springs and wells surged forth, the earth shook violently, and light of five colors pierced through the Taiwei Palace.
The King questioned his ministers: "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer Suyao replied: "In the west..."
"A Sage has been born. The King asked, "What of this? Daoxuan replied, "At present there is nothing else;
however, after one thousand years, his teachings and influence will reach here. The King ordered that it be engraved upon stone and buried at the Southern Suburb, inscribing upon it: [as recorded].
(Jia-yin) Śākyamuni Buddha’s Manifestation of Birth.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. Under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he was the Sage of Good Wisdom (Kalyāṇaprajña).
Once, he purchased lotus flowers to offer to the Buddha. Seeing that the ground was damp, he stripped off his clothes, spread them upon the earth, and untied his hair to cover it.

The Buddha prophesied to Śubhavyūha: "After an incalculable number of kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), in this world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni—the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was the Bodhisattva Roca; at the end of his life there, he departed for...
He was born in the Tuṣita Heaven as the Lord of the Devas, where he taught the practices of the stage of succession.
He also manifested various bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions, preaching the Dharma to all sentient beings according to their needs.

When the time for his attainment of Buddhahood drew near, he observed that all the sentient beings here in Jambudvīpa were those whom he had matured since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, and were thus capable of receiving [the teaching].
The Sublime Dharma does not arise in other lands or border regions; it must arise in this world. Among all places, Kapilavastu is the most central.
All Buddhas of antiquity who appeared in the world were born here. Of all lineages and clans, the Kṣatriya is the foremost.
"Descendant of the Gautama lineage, heir of the noble kings, King Śuddhodana possesses the karmic conditions from the past and is fully endowed with pure nature and conduct;
his wife is truly authentic, worthy of being my parents. Having made this observation, he then assembled the sons of the gods and addressed them, saying:
"It will not be long before I leave this celestial palace and take birth in Jambudvīpa.

There, I shall renounce the world to study the Path, realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), and convene a great Dharma assembly to extensively benefit humans and devas. You, too, should partake together in the food of the Dharma.

The sons of the gods were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, each thinking to themselves: "Before long, the Bodhisattva shall attain Perfect Enlightenment. At that time, the Bodhisattva mounted [his vehicle].
The six-tusked white elephant departed from the Tuṣita heaven and descended into the womb of his mother.

During her waking or sleeping state, Queen Māyā, the consort of King Śuddhodana, saw the Bodhisattva come through the air and enter her right side; yet he appeared clearly on the outside as well, like one standing within lapis lazuli.
She beheld her own body as if illuminated by the sun and moon. While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, in the early morning, for the sake of the devas of the Form Realm...
He preached the Dharma. At midday, he preached the Dharma for the devas of the desire realm; at the hour of *prahara*, he preached the Dharma for the various spirits and ghosts;

and during the three periods of the night, he did likewise. Thus, he brought immeasurable sentient beings to maturity. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jia-Yin, at the first appearance of the sun, Queen Māyā reached out her hand to grasp a branch of an *aśoka* tree, and the Bodhisattva emerged from her right side. At that time, he was born beneath the tree.
There were seven stalks of lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems. The Bodhisattva descended onto the lotus flowers and walked seven paces by himself.
Raising his right hand, he said: "In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored. My immeasurable births and deaths are now ended. This life shall benefit all devas and humans.
Having spoken these words, the Four Heavenly Kings received him and placed him upon a jeweled stand; the Dragon King then emitted [water].

Pure water was poured over the Prince’s body. Because of the various auspicious omens that had occurred at the time of the Prince’s birth, the King named him Sarvārthasiddha (meaning "Accomplished in All Aims").
At that time, there was a brahmin seer on Mount Gandhamādana named Asita, who possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Able to sever all doubts, he arrived through the air by means of his supernormal powers. Having observed the Prince, he suddenly wept with grief.
The King asked him in astonishment for the reason, and the seer replied: "The Prince possesses the thirty-two marks; at nineteen years of age, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
If he leaves the household life, he will achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). However, it is certain that the Prince will achieve this."
[He attained] all-knowledge and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. This year I am one hundred and twenty years old; my life will soon end, and I shall be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought.
There I shall not behold the arising of a Buddha, nor hear the sutras and the Dharma; therefore, I grieve for myself. Seven days after the Prince was born, [the prophecy was made].
When Māyā passed away, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The King entrusted her sister, Prajāpatī, with the upbringing of the Prince.
At his birth, the Prince uttered the words "I am the Sole Honored One," after which he fell silent like any other infant. At the age of seven, the King had him study writing;
he sought out the foremost wise Brahmin in the kingdom, named Kātyāyana, to serve as the Prince’s tutor. The Brahmin—
The Brahmin taught him the Brahmī script and the Kharoṣṭhī script. The Prince asked, "How many kinds of scripts are there in Jambudvīpa?
The teacher remained silent. He asked again, "What is the meaning of the letter 'A'? The teacher remained silent once more.
Thereupon, he rose from his seat and asked, "When you were first born, you declared yourself to be the most honored and supreme among gods and humans; these words are not false. I pray only that—"

He asked, "How many kinds of scripts are there in Jambudvīpa? The Prince replied, "In Jambudvīpa, there are the Brāhmī script, the Kharoṣṭhī script, the Gaurī script, the Drāviḍī script, the Nāga-script, the Yakṣa-script, the Asura-script, the Mṛgākṣara script, the Devamātṛkā script, the Gaṇanā script, the Akṣiparivarta script, the Śūnyatādṛṣṭi script, the Saṃgraha script; these comprise all those of heaven and earth."
There are sixty-four such types of sounds, including those of the eight classes of beings, the four continents, birds, beasts, and various scriptures.
Furthermore, the syllable *A* is the sound of the Brahma-voice; the meaning of this syllable is indestructible, and it is also the meaning of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Such meanings are immeasurable and boundless. The Brahmin said to the King: "The Prince is a celestial being."
"The foremost of teachers—how could he wish for me to instruct him? Furthermore, he has commanded the Deva Kṣānti to teach the prince the art of war;
yet the prince is already capable of mastering it himself. Thus, the Deva Kṣānti has instead shown disrespect toward the prince."

Jiazi (beginning in the thirty-sixth year of King Zhao of Zhou); Gengchen (the first year of King Mu of Zhou); Guihai (ending in the forty-fourth year of King Mu of Zhou).
In the year *Ren-shen* (792 BCE), at the age of seventeen, Śākyamuni Buddha manifested his renunciation of the household life.
The King took Yaśodharā, a daughter of a brāhmaṇa, as the Crown Prince’s consort, and further added two other consorts:
the first named Gopī and the second named Mṛgajā. Although the Crown Prince had these three consorts, in the stillness of the night...
He practiced meditative contemplation alone. One day, he informed the King that he wished to go out for an excursion.

As he first emerged from the eastern gate, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as an old man with white hair and a hunched back, leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps. The Prince then reflected: "The sun and moon flow on;
seasons change and years pass. Old age arrives like a flash of lightning. How can this body be relied upon? Though I am wealthy and noble, how could I alone escape it? What is this world?"
Undaunted by fear, he proceeded further to the southern gate. There, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a sick man, supported on both sides by two attendants, standing by the roadside.
The Prince spoke again: "Such a body is a great mass of suffering; why is it that the people of the world do not realize this?
When the King heard this, he sternly rebuked his ministers. There was a son of a Brahmin named Udāyin, who was wise and...
His eloquence was peerless. The King ordered him to befriend the Prince and instructed him to describe the pleasures of the world in detail, intending to stir the Prince’s heart.

When the Prince again went out through the western gate, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven first manifested old age and sickness according to their previous thoughts, so that the entire multitude could see them;
this caused the King to reprove him in anger. [The devas] then manifested death, appearing only to the Prince and Udāyin, and immediately transformed it into a corpse.
Four men carried him on a litter. The members of his household, both great and small, wailed and wept as they escorted him. The Prince and Udāyin were the only two who saw him;
the Prince asked, "Who is this man? Udāyin, having previously received the King’s command, remained silent and did not answer.
When the question was asked three times in this manner, through the majestic spiritual power of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, he involuntarily replied, "This is a dead man."

What is meant by death? The answer is: Death is when the "sword-wind" (kṛtānta-vāyu) dissolves the physical form and the consciousness departs. The four limbs and the various sense faculties no longer possess any cognition.
While this person was in the world, they were greedily attached to the five desires and did not recognize impermanence; suddenly, they abandon them and die.
Furthermore, though they were cherished by their parents and relatives, after the end of life, such feelings of affection and preferences no longer persist.
[The King] replied, "It is truly lamentable. He asked, "If this one person dies, would it not be the same for all others?
He answered, "All people in the world must be like this; there is no one, whether noble or lowly, who can escape it.
The Prince said, "In this world, such suffering exists; how can one act with negligence amidst it? Then he went out through the northern gate and reached that garden, where he rested.

Beneath a tree, he dismissed his attendants and sat upright in contemplation. At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a bhikṣu, wearing dharma robes and holding an alms bowl, with a *khakkhara* staff in hand;
looking at the ground, he walked slowly. The Prince stepped forward and asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa. "What is meant by 'śramaṇa'? [The deva] replied, "The triple world is in turmoil; the six realms of existence are shrouded in darkness. The mind of consciousness..."
"Having reached the fundamental source, one is therefore called a śramaṇa. He further said, "All things are impermanent;

only the Noble Path I have cultivated leads to the eternal attainment of the unconditioned and the reaching of the shore of liberation. Having finished speaking, he ascended into the air and departed.
The Prince rejoiced, saying, "Among gods and humans, this alone is supreme. I shall resolutely cultivate and study this Path. The Prince was nineteen years of age.
Knowing that the time for his renunciation had arrived, he went to the king and said: "O Father King, where there is a gathering born of affection, there must inevitably be separation.
I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and study the Way, so that all sentient beings may be liberated from the suffering of separation from those they love."
The king wept and said, "You should now desist from this intention. The kingdom has no heir, yet you would abandon me without a single thought of concern.

The prince then returned. At that time, a physiognomist informed the king, "If the prince does not renounce the world, after seven days have passed, he will certainly attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin). The king immediately went to inform the prince, "I have heard the words of Asita."
"You surely do not wish to remain in this world. I only pray that you will bear me a son; thereafter, I shall no longer oppose you.
The Prince replied, "As you command," and immediately pointed with his left hand toward his consort’s womb. Yaśodharā then perceived that she was pregnant.
On the seventh day of the second month, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed the Prince, saying: "Having practiced cultivation for immeasurable kalpas, now..."
[The fruits] were ripening perfectly. The Prince said, "As you say, [the fruits are ripe], yet I am strictly guarded both inside and out;
I wish to depart, but have no way to do so. The devas replied, "We shall devise a skillful means ourselves. Then, by their supernatural power, they caused everyone to fall into a deep sleep.
When the latter part of the night arrived, the devas filled the void of space and spoke with one voice: "Now is the very time for your renunciation, O Prince!"
He went to where Chandaka was and said to him, "Bring me Kanthaka. Kanthaka was the name of the horse ridden by the Prince.

Chandaka wept and asked, "In the middle of the night, where do you wish to go? The Prince replied, "I now wish to subdue the afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings; you must not disobey me. Chandaka wailed and cried out.
He caused the royal palace to remain unaware through the power of the devas, so that [the king] remained in a deep sleep as before.

Thereupon, the devas supported the four hooves of the horse and took hold of Chandaka; Śakra held the parasol, and they exited through the northern gate, which opened of its own accord without a sound.
The Prince spoke again: "If I do not sever the eight sufferings, I shall never return to the palace. If I do not attain Anuttara..."
I shall not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor shall I turn the wheel of Dharma, nor shall I ever again meet with my father, the King.
If I do not exhaust my feelings of affection, I shall never again see Māyādevī and Yaśodharā.
He traveled until dawn; having already gone three *yojanas*, the gods vanished and disappeared. When the Prince reached the secluded forest, he immediately...
He then dismounted from his horse, stroked Kaṇṭhaka’s back, and said, "The task that was difficult to accomplish has now been completed by you. He further addressed Chandaka:

"When people in this world possess wealth and status, they vie with one another to follow and serve them. Yet since I abandoned my kingdom and came here, you alone have been able to follow me; this is truly rare.
Now that I have arrived at my destination, both you and Kaṇṭhaka may return to the palace. Chandaka was filled with grief.
Unable to restrain himself, Kaṇṭhaka knelt down and licked his feet, tears falling like rain. The Prince then approached Chandaka and took a sword of the seven precious gems;
he shaved off his own beard and hair, making this vow: "May I, together with all beings, sever afflictions as well as all habitual obscurations.
A deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens further manifested as a hunter, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe. The Prince said joyfully, "What you have..."
"This garment is the raiment of tranquility. I now give these precious robes to you in exchange for my own.
These robes are intended to gather and rescue all sentient beings and sever their afflictions. He replied, "Excellent," and so he removed his precious robes and traded them.
The Prince proceeded forward; Chandaka immediately returned. The Prince entered Mount Tāḍaka to practice the Way, beginning there...
He stayed at the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma for three years, and again at the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra for three years.

Then he went to Mount Gayāśīrṣa, where by the side of the Nairañjanā River, he sat in quiet meditation and reflected that he should practice austerities for six years in order to deliver sentient beings.
The heavens offered him wild hemp and rice. With a pure mind, he maintained his precepts; sometimes eating but once a day, sometimes eating but once every seven days.
He did not avoid wind or rain, nor did he rise to perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Even when magpies' nests defiled him with their droppings, he did not remove them.
(Geimei) Śākyamuni Buddha manifested the attainment of enlightenment.
He showed himself practicing austerities for six years, then thought to himself: "This is not the true liberation. I shall partake of food and thereafter attain Buddhahood."
He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River; the gods bent down the trees so that he might pull himself out.
At that time, outside the grove, there were two cowherd girls, one named Nandā and the other named Nandabalā, who saw a thousand-petaled lotus flower growing from the earth.
Above was some milk-rice; he took it and offered it to the Bodhisattva, who then accepted and ate it.
He further recalled that past Buddhas had used grass as a seat to achieve the Unsurpassed Way. Śakra, having transformed himself into an ordinary man, held some pure, soft grass.
The Bodhisattva asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Śrī. The Bodhisattva said joyfully, "I shall destroy inauspiciousness and thereby achieve auspiciousness. Thereupon...
Having accepted the grass, he proceeded toward the foot of the Bodhi tree to attain perfect enlightenment.

While the Bodhisattva sat beneath the Jambu tree for forty-eight days, observing and contemplating, the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows eclipsed the palace of Māra. King Māra Pāpīyān was struck with terror.
He summoned his various demons and, while the Way was not yet perfected, went to disturb it. His eldest son, the merchant leader, wept and remonstrated with him, but he would not listen;
he then led the hosts to create difficulties, manifesting all manner of terrifying and seductive scenes. At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body and mind remained tranquil and unmoved.
He pressed the earth with his finger, and the earth shook violently. The demons heard this and were struck with fear; they returned to their original palace. Then, on the day of Gui...

On the evening of the seventh day of the second month, he entered the samādhi of right concentration. At the time when the morning star appeared on the eighth day of the second month, he attained great enlightenment and realized perfect, equal awakening.
He sighed and said: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet, because of their deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it."
Regarding Śākyamuni Buddha’s manifestation of preaching the Dharma:

from the eighth day of the second month when he attained enlightenment, until the ninth through the twenty-ninth day, he remained at the site of awakening (Bodhimaṇḍa) as the wisdom that realizes the equality of the three periods of time.
His body pervades all worlds, and his voice universally accords with the ten directions.

In that land, there were immeasurable and boundless *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas, such as Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Maitreya, as well as those whose roots had matured over past lives, including the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, all surrounding him at once like clouds enveloping the moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the body of Vairocana and preached the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. When twenty-one days had passed, part two.
On the thirtieth day of the month, he rose from his seat at the site of enlightenment and proceeded toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Having traveled until he reached the banks of the river Ajapālā, he stayed there for the night as evening fell and entered into meditative concentration. A great wind and rain burst forth;
a great nāga king named Mucilinda, with his massive body, encircled him in seven folds. The dragon had seven heads, which he spread over the Buddha like a canopy.
There was an obscuration. On the sixth day of the third month, when the four weeks had been completed, the rain ceased and he emerged from meditative absorption.

The Dragon King transformed himself into a young Brahmin, prostrated, and inquired after his well-being; [the Buddha] accepted the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. Among all beings of the animal realm, he was the very first to see the Buddha.
On the seventh day of the third month, he accepted the food offering of the elder Trapusa. On the eighth day of the third month, he arrived at the Deer Park. First...
The World-Honored One, having attained enlightenment, sat beneath the tree in contemplation: "All sentient beings dwell in an age of five turbidities, shrouded by the three poisons;
they possess meager merit and dull faculties, lacking wisdom. How could they understand the Dharma I have realized?

If I were now to turn the wheel of Dharma, they would surely not believe it; they would give rise to a mind of slander and fall into the evil realms, undergoing immeasurable suffering. I would rather—"
He did not speak, but entered into *nirvāṇa*. At that time, Mahābrahmā Devarāja felt deep sorrow and distress, thinking: "Sentient beings have for a long night been submerged in birth and death;
I must now go and entreat him to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. The six heavens of the desire realm likewise offered this exhortation.
The World-Honored One accepted their request by remaining silent. He subsequently established the teaching in five periods: first, the period of the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the period of the Deer Park.
At that time, there was the period of the Three Samyak-saṃbuddhas; fourth, the period of Prajñā; fifth, the period of the Lotus Sūtra and Nirvāṇa.
When the World-Honored One arrived at the Deer Park, the five—Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāma, Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, and Bhadrika—saw the Buddha and their hearts were filled with great joy.
They requested the Buddha for ordination, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained Arhatship.
Arhat. Thus, for the first time in this world, the Three Jewels appeared: the Tathāgata is the Buddha Jewel; the Four Noble Truths are the Dharma Jewel;
and the Arhat is the Saṅgha Jewel. There was a son of an elder named Yaśas. During the middle watch of the night, he awoke from sleep and saw that his female attendants were impure.
He conceived a sense of weary detachment, yet amidst that impurity he had previously maintained the notion of purity. Suddenly, he beheld the sky.
Seeing the radiance, he followed the light and proceeded toward the Deer Park. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the state of an Arhat.
At dawn, Yaśas’s father, searching for his son, arrived at the place where the Buddha was. The Buddha received him into the Three Refuges, making him the very first Upāsaka.
Furthermore, fifty of Yaśas’s companions went together to the Buddha’s presence, and all became Śramaṇas. [At] Kapilavastu...
In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a son of a brāhmaṇa named Pūrṇa, who was fully proficient in the Vedas and other treatises. He was born on the same day as the Buddha.

By nature, he felt a sense of weary detachment toward the world; seeing that the Buddha had left the household life, he immediately joined thirty friends and went to the Snowy Mountains to study the Way with single-minded devotion.
There, he attained the four dhyānas and the five supernatural powers. With his divine eye, he saw from afar that the World-Honored One was at the Deer Park.
He preached the Dharma in a forest garden. Eventually, together with thirty others, he came to where the Buddha was and requested ordination and liberation.
Among those who preach the Dharma, he is the foremost. In South India there was a Brahmin of the Mahākātyāyana clan; his second son was named Nārada.
His father ordered him to study the Vedas and various treatises, which he mastered in no long time. His eldest brother, however, was envious.
He intended to take his life. His father sent him to the hermit Asita, where he thoroughly mastered all treatises and attained the four dhyānas and five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
When the hermit passed away, Nārada became greedy for worldly gain and ceased to have faith in the Triple Gem.
There were two dragon kings, Elāpattra and Śaṅkha, who spoke to the yakṣa Kiñjika, saying: "In that city there was previously a verse:"
It was asked: "In what does sovereignty reside? What is called 'defilement'? How is one purified?
Why is one called 'deluded'? For what reason is a person deluded? What makes one a wise person? And what constitutes the meeting and parting that is called the 'exhaustion of causal conditions'?
The Dragon King went to the presence of the Seer Nārada and inquired about the meaning of these verses, but Nārada was unable to understand or explain them.
He then went to the Buddha. The Buddha explained the Dharma for him, teaching various doctrines. He conceived great joy and subsequently sought to leave the household life.
Based on his ancestral lineage and original clan name, he was called Mahākātyāyana; he was foremost in debate.

In the kingdom of Magadha, there were three brothers, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his two younger brothers, who practiced the path of the ancient seers. Kings and ministers placed their faith in them. The Buddha went to visit them.
At that dwelling place, he manifested various supernatural powers and tamed beings in manifold ways. First, he converted Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa along with five hundred disciples;
he then converted Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, each having two hundred and fifty disciples, all of whom together realized arhatship. He also had a nephew, a brahmin with matted hair named Upasena.
On Mount Āsuriya, together with two hundred and fifty disciples, he practiced the way of the rishis; he too then went forth under the Buddha and became an arhat.
When King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha saw the three Kāśyapas as disciples of the Buddha, he sighed and said:
"Alas! The Tathāgata possesses great supernormal power; his wisdom is profound and far-reaching, inconceivable. Thus it was.
The Buddha was able to subdue such a person and take him as a disciple. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*).
The King commanded his ministers to construct various halls and residences within the Bamboo Grove (*Veṇuvana*) and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to reside there.
Among the kings who had seen the Buddha, King Bimbisāra was the foremost. The Bamboo Grove was the first of all the monasteries (*saṃghārāma*). [This occurred] in the city of Rājagṛha.
There were two brahmins possessed of great wisdom: one named Śāriputra and the other named Maudgalyāyana. Each had a hundred disciples.
They went to the Bamboo Grove, where the Buddha preached the Dharma for them; they attained the state of Arhat.
Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom, and Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernormal powers. In the kingdom of Magadha, there was a brahmin named...
He replied, "Kāśyapa possesses great wisdom; he has recited the four Vedas and diligently sought the unsurpassed Dharma day and night.
Having subsequently left the household life, he practices the dhūta austerities. At that time, a deity in the sky announced to him:

'A Buddha has appeared in the world; you should go and take him as your teacher. Kāśyapa then proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove. Knowing that he was coming, the Buddha went out in person to welcome him. When they arrived at the [Bamboo] Grove...
They met before the stupa of the Elder. Kāśyapa joined his palms and said, “The World-Honored One is truly the All-Knowing One;

he is truly compassionate in rescuing sentient beings; he is truly the refuge for all. He then prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, you are my Great Teacher; I am your disciple. Thus he spoke three times. The Buddha said, “So it is.”

Kāśyapa, I am your teacher; you are my disciple. If anyone who is not truly possessed of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) were to wish to accept you as a disciple, their head would split into seven pieces.
Furthermore, I have taught the Dharma for you, so that you have become an Arhat.
Because of this, Kāśyapa possesses great majestic power and is honored by gods and men; therefore, he is named Mahākāśyapa. [Thus spoke] King Śuddhodana.
Having heard that the Buddha had attained the Way six years prior, he desired to see him once. He sent the brahmin Udāyin to invite the Buddha to return to his kingdom.
Upon meeting the Buddha, Udāyin saw that the various devas, Śakra, and Brahmā had all been converted; he too wished to become a śramaṇa.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the path of an arhat. The Buddha then dispatched Udāyin to first manifest supernatural transformations in order to inspire the aspiration for the Way.
Thereupon, by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he flew through the air and traveled to his native land. There he manifested the eighteen transformations and announced:
"Seven days from now, the Buddha shall descend here. The king went forty *li* out to welcome the Buddha;

seeing the Buddha, he was filled with great joy and selected five hundred members of his own clan to become śramaṇas to attend upon the Buddha’s left and right. Of the two sons of King Droṇodana, one was named Ma...
Mahānāma—also known as Aniruddha—said, "Many of the Śākyas have left the household life, yet in our own family alone there has been none.
Let one person manage the household affairs and one person leave the home.

Then Aniruddha and the Śākya Vatsa, finding domestic matters to be tedious and trivial, each petitioned their mothers to earnestly seek ordination. After seven days had passed, these eight Śākya sons...
They departed from the city of Kapilavastu, divested themselves of their precious robes, elephants, and horses, and entrusted them to the messenger Upāli, instructing him to return them.
Upāli reflected: "A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter. Even those of the highest nobility have all renounced worldly glory."

"My body is lowly and base; what is there for me to crave or delight in? He then hung his precious robes and other belongings upon a tree and proceeded together with [the others] to the place where the Buddha was.
He addressed him, saying, "My parents have already granted their permission; I pray that you will allow me to go forth from the household life. I beg that Upāli be ordained first."
In order to eliminate our prideful minds, the World-Honored One first ordained Upāli, followed by Nanda, Aniruddha, and others.
As for the World-Honored One’s cousin Ānanda, he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; therefore, he was named Ānanda (which in this language means "Joy").

The entire nation celebrated with great joy, so he was also called "Celebration of Joy. He left home to become a monk at the age of eight and became the foremost among the disciples in erudition. At that age...
31. The Buddha commanded him to serve as his attendant. Ānanda said, "I wish for the Tathāgata to grant me three vows:
first, that I shall not accept the Tathāgata’s old robes; second, that I shall not follow the Tathāgata when he accepts special invitations;
third, that I am permitted to enter and leave at any time. The Buddha said, "Excellent! You possess complete wisdom and have foreseen potential censure. Why is this? If..."
Some people say: "You [the Buddha] have been provided with food and clothing; therefore, you do not accept old clothes, nor do you accept separate invitations.
Since your coming and going are restricted by fixed times, you cannot extensively benefit the various assemblies. Thus, I seek for you the freedom to come and go at any time.
For my sake, Ānanda, these three matters were opened up. As for the Buddha’s son Rāhula, who was already nine years of age, the Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana.
He went to the city of Kapilavastu and informed his father and Yaśodharā that he wished to release Rāhula so that he might leave the household life and cultivate the Noble Path.
Maudgalyāyana received the command and went there; although he instructed Yaśodharā with various skillful means, she would not consent.
At that time, the Buddha manifested a transformed person who spoke from mid-air, saying: "Yaśodharā, do you perhaps remember a time in a former life?"

"Is this not the fulfillment of my vow? At that time, while practicing the path of a bodhisattva, I purchased five stalks of lotuses from you for five hundred silver coins and offered them to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Then you requested of me that we be husband and wife in every lifetime we were born into.
I did not wish to accept this, and I said to you: 'I am a bodhisattva; throughout successive kalpas, I shall practice vows and bestow all things in charity.'"
"Generosity! Do not oppose another's will. If you can do so, I grant you permission to be my wife. Make this vow:

'In every life into which we are born—whether in kingdoms, cities, as wives, or children, and including my own person—I shall follow whatever you bestow upon others, vowing never to harbor a heart of regret.
Now, for what reason do you cherish Rāhula and prevent him from leaving the household life to study the Noble Path? Having heard this, Yaśodharā was suddenly restored to her senses.
He recalled the causes and conditions of his past karma; everything became clear to him. Knowing what he had seen yesterday, his affection for his son naturally subsided.
Then King Śuddhodana immediately assembled the prominent clans of the kingdom and sent one son from each, totaling fifty men, who followed him into the homeless life.
The Buddha sent Ānanda to shave his head, while Śāriputra served as his preceptor and Maudgalyāyana as his...
Ācārya: Regarding the method for bestowing the ten precepts, one becomes a śrāmaṇera. At that time, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī had a great minister named Sudatta.
His family was immensely wealthy, and he relieved the poor and destitute; thus, he was popularly known as "The Provider of the Orphaned and Solitary.
Now, wishing to take a wife for his son, he went in person to the home of the minister Ghoṣila in the city of Rājagṛha. Having arrived, he saw his house...
Inside, he spread out a great array of offerings. Sudatta asked for the reason, and [Nāgārjuna] replied, "I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Sudatta asked, "What is meant by 'Buddha' and what is meant by 'Saṃgha'? Nāgamitra fully explained the reasons therefor. Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s hair stood on end all over his body.
He soon arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs, which surpassed those described by Pūrṇa; his heart was filled with great joy.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Sudatta wished to build a vihāra and invited the Buddha to descend upon the kingdom of Śrāvastī to deliver its sentient beings.
The Buddha granted his permission. He took leave of the Buddha and returned home. The Buddha then commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to Śrāvastī.
He traveled throughout the kingdom inspecting various sites until he found that Prince Jeta alone possessed a garden in a perfectly suitable location.

Sudatta then addressed the prince, but the prince was unwilling to sell. Sudatta entreated him earnestly two or three times, whereupon the prince said, "If you can cover the ground with gold coins so that no space remains uncovered, I shall grant it to you. He replied, "So be it," and then dispatched his men on elephants.
They carried gold, and within eighty *qǐng* of land, it was almost full, lacking only a small portion.

The Prince thought to himself, "The Buddha must possess great virtue, for he can cause these people to regard such treasure as so light. He then ordered them to stop and no longer bring out more gold, saying, "The garden grounds belong to you;
the trees belong to me. Together we shall establish a vihāra. Thus, Sudatta and Śāriputra traversed the site together.
When it was finished, he rose and established a vihāra. He informed the King and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said, "Sudatta purchased the grove, but the trees belong to Jeta; it may be named the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma.
When the Buddha returned once more to the kingdom of Kapilavastu, the King asked, "How should one practice to attain the Way of all Buddhas? The Buddha replied, "All sentient beings..."
"All these are indeed Buddhas. Father King, you should keep in mind Amitābha Buddha of the western world-realm;
by constantly practicing with diligent vigor, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha. The King asked, "How can all sentient beings be Buddhas?

The Buddha said, "All dharmas are unarisen, unmoving, without taking or abandoning, without characteristics, and without intrinsic nature. You, O King, should [abide] within this Dharma of the Buddhas."

He established his mind in tranquility and did not rely on others. When the King and seventy thousand Śākyas heard this teaching, they believed, understood, and rejoiced, realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the first Buddha returned to his kingdom, his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī (also known as Gautamī) requested permission from the Buddha to go forth [into the religious life].
Though she petitioned three times, he did not grant it. When the Buddha returned to his kingdom for a second time, she requested again as before; yet the Buddha still did not grant it.
After the Buddha had departed from the country, Mahāprajāpatī and the other elderly women followed him and halted by a riverbank.
They again requested ordination, but this too was not granted. Retreating to stand outside the gate, they wept with sobs. Ānanda returned from outside and asked for the reason;
she replied, "Because I am a woman, I have been unable to receive ordination; it is for this that I grieve. Ānanda then addressed [the Buddha].
The Buddha [was approached]. Mahāprajāpatī, with a sincere heart, desired to receive the laws and precepts, and wished for the Buddha to grant her permission.

The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! If you permit women to go forth, it will cause the True Dharma not to abide for long. Ānanda spoke again, saying, "The Buddhas of the past all possessed the fourfold assembly;
does the Tathāgata alone not possess them? The Buddha said, "If Mahāprajāpatī cultivates the Eight Weighty Rules..."

The Dharma is to be practiced for the duration of one's life; thus one may enter the Law and Discipline. Ānanda went out and informed Mahāprajāpatī, who then received the full precepts and became a bhikṣuṇī, subsequently attaining arhatship.
○ The Bodhisattva Ruci requested the establishment of a precept platform (sīmāmaṇḍala) for the purpose of binding the bhikṣus with precepts and administering ordination.
Thereupon, three platforms were established: to the east of the gate of the Buddha Hall, the one named "Binding Precepts for Bhikṣus" was designated for the Buddha.
The Ordination Platform (*śīlakaṇḍa*). To the west of the gate of the Buddha Hall, the Buddha established the ordination platform for bhikṣuṇīs.

To the south of the eastern gate of the outer enclosure, he established the ordination platform for monks (*bhikṣu*) to receive the precepts. The ordination platform rises from the ground and is characterized by three tiers to symbolize the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*), serving as the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Śakra Devendra offered a covered cauldron and placed it upon the platform; Mahābrahmā... [continued].
The King offered a priceless precious jewel and placed it atop the inverted cauldron to enshrine the śarīra; this constitutes the fifth layer.

This represents the time when the dharma-body altar of the *vibhajya-dharmakāya* was established. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions, immeasurable bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas all gathered like clouds.

The Buddhas ascended it and together deliberated upon the characteristics of the gravity of the precepts, their observance and violation, as well as the ordination of bhikṣuṇīs and the extinction of the True Dharma.
Regarding the characteristics of the Dharma, the Buddhas collectively deliberated, saying: "In antiquity there were four assemblies; why is it that now only one is absent?

Although the True Dharma was initially reduced by half, because the nuns now practice the Eight Observances of Respect, they shall likewise abide for a thousand years. Therefore, these two ordination platforms are those upon which only a Buddha may ascend, as they jointly measure the Buddha's work.
As for the outer enclosure ordination platform, this is the platform where the Sangha bestows the precepts upon the fourfold assembly."
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Two;
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Three (marked with the character "Xuan").
Jiazi (starting from the 45th year of King Mu of Zhou). Yihai (the first year of King Gong). Dinghai (the first year of King Yi). Renzi (the first year of King Xiao). Gui...

In the year Hai (the twelfth year of King Xiao of Zhou), at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a violent wind suddenly arose in this land, damaging houses and breaking trees; the earth shook and the shadows of trees quivered.
From the west, twelve white rainbows appeared, penetrating from south to north, not fading throughout the night. King Mu marveled at this.
He questioned his ministers. The Grand Astrologer Hutu replied, "This is merely the sign of the parinirvāṇa of a sage from the West.

(Xinwei) Śākyamuni Buddha transmitted the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, who preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in two locations and three assemblies: first at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, then ascending into the void, and finally returning once more.
Returning to Mount Ling, there was a Great Brahma King who offered golden *pāra* flowers to the Buddha and requested him to preach the Dharma.

When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, he held up a flower to show the assembly; among the hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, none could fathom his meaning, yet only Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the true mark which is markless."
"This subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate is entrusted to you. You must protect, uphold, and circulate it so that it does not come to an end.
Listen to my verse: 'The Dharma is fundamentally no-Dharma; No-Dharma is also Dharma. Now, when the no-Dharma is transmitted, How has any dharma ever been a dharma?
Having spoken this verse, he further addressed Kāśyapa: 'I shall now transmit to you my golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe.'"
“You, transmit this to Maitreya, the successor in the position of regent, so that it shall not perish. Furthermore, command Ānanda to act as his deputy in the propagation of the teaching.
Kāśyapa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to him, “Excellent, excellent! I shall comply with these instructions out of my reverence for the Buddha.”
On the full moon of the eleventh month of the *xinwei* year (the *renshen* year), Śākyamuni Buddha manifested his *nirvāṇa*.
Recalling that the fourfold assembly was indolent, he did not take a personal attendant;

in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm, he went alone to the Nandana Grove in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There he entered the three-month *varṣā* retreat. The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: “Go to...”
[The Buddha] said, "My mother is here on the way. When Māyā arrived, the Buddha said, "Throughout the course of one's life, one experiences both suffering and pleasure;
you should cultivate the path to Nirvāṇa, which is forever free from suffering and pleasure. Upon hearing this teaching, Māyā attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
At that time, it had been a long while since people in the human world had seen the Buddha. King Udayana and others went to Ānanda and asked where the Buddha was. Ānanda replied:
He replied, "I do not know either. At that time, King Udayana, thirsting with longing for the Tathāgata, issued an edict to skilled craftsmen to create an image of the Tathāgata.
The deva Viśvakarman manifested as a craftsman and completed it in no time.
As the three months were drawing to a close, the Buddha commanded Kumāra to announce throughout Jambudvīpa: "The Tathāgata is about to descend; he intends to enter parinirvāṇa. Thereupon—
The Buddha manifested jeweled stairs that descended from heaven. King Udayana carried the image to welcome him and prostrated before the Buddha.
The Buddha called out three times and received three responses, whereupon he said: "The true Buddha of non-action truly resides within my own body.

He further spoke to the image, saying: "In future ages, you shall perform great buddha-work. When the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, she addressed the assembly, saying:
"I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One enter *nirvāṇa*. Thereupon, she and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs addressed the Buddha. The Buddha silently consented.
Mahāprajāpatī then returned to the vihāra, where they each manifested their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and simultaneously entered *parinirvāṇa*.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana could not bear to see the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, so they entered extinction first; seventy thousand arhats did likewise.

At that time, he entered parinirvāṇa. The fourfold assembly was in a state of panic and confusion. By his supernatural power, the Buddha manifested two disciples standing at his left and right, and the assembly gradually regained its composure.

On the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of *rénshēn*, while the Buddha was at the city of Kuśinagara, on the banks of the Hiranyavatī River—the birthplace of the Mallas—amidst the twin *śāla* trees, as he approached the time of his parinirvāṇa, he preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and addressed the Great [Assembly].
