The assembly said: "By means of the profound Prajñā, I have observed the triple world everywhere; its fundamental nature is detached, ultimately quiescent, identical to the characteristics of empty space, and utterly non-existent.
Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Those who know this are called world-transcending people."

Not knowing this matter is called the beginning of birth and death. At that time, the bhikṣus entreated the Tathāgata, saying, "We only pray that you will remain for a long time and not enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha said, "You should not speak such words.
All my unsurpassed, true Dharma has now been entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. This Kāśyapa shall act as a great [teacher] for you all."
Regarding his reliance [on the Buddha], it was just as with the Tathāgata. Again, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "Ānanda has served me for more than twenty years.
He has heard the Dharma and received it into his keeping, like pouring water into a vessel. Now I wish to have him receive and uphold this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Since he is being tormented by various Māras, you should hold this great *dhāraṇī* and protect Ānanda. Having received it, Mañjuśrī [acted accordingly].
He went to where Ānanda was. Upon hearing the incantation, the Māra immediately released Ānanda, who returned to the Buddha’s presence.

Thereupon, the Buddha entered meditative absorption three times and emerged from it three times, declaring: "By these causes and conditions, I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence, which is named Great Nirvāṇa.
He then lay upon his right side on a jeweled couch. During the middle watch of the night, all was silent and still.
Upon hearing the news, Kāśyapa came from afar to announce the passing. The golden coffin opened of its own accord, and two feet emerged from outside it.
After the assembly had prostrated at the feet, they returned to the coffin, which then rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees.

It traveled back and forth through the air and manifested the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-transformation samādhi); in an instant, ashes were produced, and eight *droṇas* of *śarīra* (relics) were obtained.
A *śarāva* measure [of relics]. The various kings vied with one another to seize them. There was a Brahmin who, using a stone jar smeared with honey, immediately divided them into three portions:
one portion for the various devas, one portion for the Dragon Kings, and one portion for the eight kingdoms. Regarding the four stupas in the heavens:

in the Eastern Garden of Illumination in the city of Trāyastriṃśa, there is the Stupa of the Buddha’s Hair; in the Southern Garden of Roughness, the Stupa of the Buddha’s Robe; and in the Western Garden of Joy, the Stupa of the Buddha’s Alms Bowl.
The Stūpa. To the north of the city is the Garden of the Charioteer (Jārandhara). The Tooth Relic Stūpa. These are the four stūpas among those of human beings.
The Birthplace Stūpa is located within the Lumbinī Garden in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. The Enlightenment Stūpa is located beneath the Aśvattha tree in the kingdom of Magadha.
The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma Stūpa is located within the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. The Nirvāṇa Stūpa is located in the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
Between the twin trees of the magnificent grove in the birthplace of the Mallas.

After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, when the Venerable Ānanda was compiling the Tripiṭaka, the various heavenly kings and others addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "The city of the Dharma is about to collapse; the banner of the Dharma is about to fall."
"One should establish the Buddha-dharma through great compassion. Kāśyapa accepted the invitation and went to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where he struck the great gong.
All the noble disciples who possessed supernormal powers gathered there. Kāśyapa addressed them, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is about to perish."
"Beings are to be pitied; wait until the compilation is finished, and then enter parinirvāṇa according to your wish.

All the noble assembly who had gathered remained in the Veṇuvana Cave (Piṇḍola Cave) having received these instructions. Kāśyapa, observing with his divine eye, saw that only Ānanda’s afflictions were not yet exhausted.
He then led Ānanda out from among the great assembly, saying, "Your fetters are not yet severed; you should not remain here. Ānanda wept bitterly.
He said to Kāśyapa, "I possess the power to have attained the Way long ago;
however, because I was to serve the Buddha, and because one who is an Arhat cannot provide such service, I have left behind residual fetters and have not severed them completely.
Kāśyapa then said to Ānanda, "You have six kinds of offenses that you must repent before the Saṃgha. At that time, Ānanda knelt with his palms joined and, in accordance with the six...
Having confessed his various transgressions, and once the confession was complete, Kāśyapa led Ānanda out and said to him, "You have exhausted your outflows; you may come in.
Having spoken, he closed the door of the cave. Ānanda wept with tears of sorrow, seeking to sever his fetters and delusions with the utmost sincerity.
When the latter part of the night arrived, he lay down exhausted to rest. Before his head had even reached the pillow, he attained awakening with radiant clarity;
having realized the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, he became a great Arhat. He went back to the cave and knocked on the door, saying, "My outflows are exhausted.

Kāśyapa said, "If your outflows are indeed exhausted, you may employ your supernormal powers to enter through the keyhole of the door. Ānanda leaped into the air and entered, whereupon he prostrated himself in worship.
The assembly was satisfied. Kāśyapa placed his hand upon Ānanda’s head and addressed him, saying, "I wish to cause you to attain the Way;
do not harbor resentment. Then the great assembly requested Ānanda to ascend the seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.

Once Ānanda had ascended the seat, before he had yet spoken, he manifested physical marks and signs of excellence identical to those of the Buddha. At that time, the great assembly was filled with doubt.
The Buddha rose once more. Some wondered if a Buddha from another direction had come; others wondered if Ānanda had attained Buddhahood. Then, as he uttered the words, "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was staying in such-and-such a place, together with such-and-such an assembly," these three doubts were all dispelled.

**The Circumstances of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Enlightenment:** When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and the other toward earth, took seven steps around, and gazed in the four directions, saying:

"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the Honored One. **The World-Honored One Ascends the Seat:** One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat, and the great assembly gathered.

[The assembly] was settled in meditation. Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, “Contemplate carefully the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat.
○ On one occasion, the World-Honored One ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, “I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, “In this assembly there are two bhikṣus who have violated the monastic discipline. Therefore, I shall not preach the Dharma.”
The World-Honored One found it difficult to perceive those bhikṣus with his knowledge of others' minds and consequently sent them away.
The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again: "Just now, because two bhikṣus had violated the Vinaya, those two bhikṣus have already been sent away.
Why does the World-Honored One not preach the Dharma? The World-Honored One said, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the two vehicles, such as the śrāvakas. Thereupon, he descended.

[The Master] ascends the seat. One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma," and then descended from the seat.
[The Master] showed a multicolored mani-jewel to the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions and asked, "What color is this jewel?"

At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the five directions each spoke of different colors regarding the World-Honored One’s hidden pearl. The World-Honored One then raised his hand and asked, "What color is this pearl?
The Heavenly Kings replied, "There is no pearl in the Buddha's hand; how can there be any color? The World-Honored One said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
I have presented you with a worldly pearl, yet you insist on claiming it has blue, yellow, red, or white colors. The World-Honored One then...
He showed them pearls, yet none of them understood at all. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all realized the Way on their own.
Later, when the Brahmin Kāla offered a cluster of *aśoka* flowers, the World-Honored One called out to the Rishi, "Put it down.
The Brahmin put down one flower with his left hand. The Buddha called to the Rishi again, "Put it down. The Brahmin then put it down [again].
In his right hand he held a single flower. The Buddha again called to the immortal, saying, "Put it down.
The Brahmacārin replied, "Now both my hands are empty; what more do you command me to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not commanding you to discard that flower.

You should discard the six external objects (*viṣaya*), the six internal faculties (*indriya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) in between—all at once. When there is nothing left to discard, that is it."
"This is the place where you shall relinquish your body and life. At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because the World-Honored One wished for the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) to see Samantabhadra, yet could not find him, he entered meditative concentration three times in succession.
He surveyed the trichiliocosm in its entirety, but though he sought Samantabhadra, he could not find him. He then came and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "You need only..."
Within the samādhi of stillness, a single thought arises, and one immediately beholds Samantabhadra.
Thus, as soon as Puyan (Universal Eye) gives rise to a single thought, he beholds Samantabhadra riding upon a six-tusked white elephant in mid-air. A seer with the five supernormal powers asked:
"The World-Honored One possesses the six supernormal powers, while I possess only five; what is this one power? The Buddha called out to the seer with the five supernormal powers, and the seer—
He assented to the Buddha, saying, "Which one? You ask me... One day, the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda:
"The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda assented. The World-Honored One said:
"Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked: "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas? The World-Honored One—
He summoned Ānanda. Ānanda responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go. Because of a question from a bhikṣu, [the bhikṣu] said:
"Within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, I see that there is a place of abiding, yet the place of realization is not yet attained. What will the World-Honored One show me?"
The World-Honored One said, "Bhikṣu so-and-so, what should be shown to him? This is your question.
Because Jīvaka was skilled at distinguishing sounds, the World-Honored One went to a cemetery and saw five skulls. He then struck one skull and asked Jīvaka, "Where was this person born?
Jīvaka replied, "This person was born into the human realm. He struck another and asked, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "This..."
He was reborn in the heavenly realms. Furthermore, the World-Honored One asked Jīvaka separately, "Where has this person been reborn? Jīvaka did not know where they had been reborn.
Once, when the Seven Virtuous Women were wandering through the Śītavana cemetery, one woman pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is right here."
"Where has the person gone? One woman said, "How? How? Sisters, observe closely! Each of them attained realization.
Moved by this, Śakra Devendra scattered flowers and said, "I pray only that you, Noble Sister, may have whatever you require; I shall provide for you for the rest of my life."
The woman said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided. I require only three things: first, a single trunk of a rootless tree;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists; and third, a mountain valley that does not echo when one calls.
Śakra said, "Of everything you need, I have it all. As for these three things, I truly do not possess them."
The woman said, "If you do not possess this, how can you understand how to save others? Śakra was at a loss for what to do, so he went with her to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my disciples, the great Arhats, do not understand this meaning; only the great Bodhisattvas understand it.
[The Buddha continued: "When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara."
The Buddha, having seen the place where Dīpaṃkara had spread his hair, withdrew the assembly. He then pointed to the ground and said, "In this spot, it is fitting to establish a Brahma-monastery.
At that time, there was among the assembly an elder named Bhadra who took a staff and inserted it into the pointed spot, saying:
When the construction of the Brahma-shrine was completed, the various devas scattered flowers and praised it in unison.
Once, while the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, they came upon the stupa of an ancient Buddha. The World-Honored One paid his respects, whereupon Ānanda asked, "Whose stupa is this?
The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stupa of past Buddhas. Ānanda then asked, "Of whom were those past Buddhas the disciples?"
The World-Honored One said, "This is my disciple. Ānanda said, "It ought to be so...
On the day of the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of seeking admonition), Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places. Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him;

as soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs. Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the gavel. The World-Honored One then questioned Kāśyapa...
“Kāśyapa, which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa had no reply. To the east of the city there was an old woman who had been born at the same time as the Buddha.
She did not wish to see the Buddha; whenever she saw him approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him.
Nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha. She then covered her face with her hand, yet even within the palms of her ten fingers, it was all the Buddha.

When this Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to depart from the place where the Buddhas had assembled because Mañjuśrī had arrived, he encountered the various Buddhas each returning to their own abodes.
There was only one woman remaining near the Buddha’s seat, having entered into *samādhi*. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why is it that this person may approach the Buddha while I am not permitted to do so? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "You need only awaken this woman and cause her to arise."
He arose from samādhi. "Ask her yourself," [the Buddha] said. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times, snapped his fingers once, and then attempted to lift her up as far as the Brahma Heaven;
yet, despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her out. The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs..."
Nor can anyone else emerge this woman from her samādhi. Forty-two Ganges-sands of worlds below, there is the Bodhisattva Wangming (Vimalakīrti), who is able to emerge this woman from her samādhi.
In an instant, the Mahāsattva Wangming surged forth from the earth.
He prostrated before the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One commanded Wangming to go out. Wangming returned to the woman and snapped his fingers once;
thereupon, the woman emerged from her meditative concentration. Aṅgulimāla, carrying his alms bowl, arrived at the gate of a certain elder’s house.
At that moment, the elder’s wife was in the throes of difficult labor. The elder said, "Disciple of Gautama, you have come here for this reason?"
"Venerable One, what dharma is there that can deliver one from the perils of childbirth? Aṅgulimāla said to the householder, "I have only recently entered the Path and do not know this dharma.
Wait while I return to ask the World-Honored One, and I shall come back to inform you. Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla, "Go quickly and tell him: 'Since I followed the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, I have never killed a living being. Aṅgulimāla departed.
"Obeying the Buddha’s words, she went quickly to inform him. When her wife heard this, she gave birth at that very moment.
One day, the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate and said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter the gate?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I do not see a single dharma outside the gate; how can you tell me to enter? [The Bodhisattva] Anantagātra...

Śakra took a bamboo staff and measured the crown of the World-Honored One’s head; it reached sixteen feet, then another sixteen feet, and continued until he reached the Brahma Heaven, yet he could not see the limit of the World-Honored One’s crown.
He then cast down the bamboo staff, joined his palms, and spoke this verse: "Space has no boundaries, And the Buddha’s merit is likewise.
Were there one who could measure it, Even through kalpas, it could not be exhausted. [The World-Honored One, because of the Gandharva...]
The king presented music. At that time, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all produced the sound of a lute.
Kāśyapa rose and performed a dance. The king asked Kāśyapa, "Are you not an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? Why do you still have residual habits?
The Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma. The king again stroked the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise [responded] three times.
[The Buddha] performed a dance. The King said, "Kāśyapa, performing a dance—is this not practicing [the arts]? The Buddha said, "In truth, I have never performed a dance.

The King said, "World-Honored One, how can you speak falsely? The Buddha said, "It is no falsehood. When you play the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all wood and stone produce the sound of the lute;
is this not so? The King said, "It is. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa is also like this. Regarding that which...
Since [the deity] had never actually performed a dance, the King then accepted this with faith.

While the World-Honored One was in the Sixth Heaven preaching the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, he commanded all the fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands, this world, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble together.

Having received the Buddha’s entrustment, they shall protect the True Dharma. Should there be any who do not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings of the Gates shall pursue them with flying wheels of glowing iron to compel their assembly.
Once assembled, there shall be none who do not comply with the Buddha’s command, and each shall give rise to a great vow.
He protected the True Dharma. There was only one Māra King who said to the World-Honored One:

"Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the realm of sentient beings is emptied and the very name 'sentient being' no longer exists; only then will I resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Because Devadatta had slandered the Buddha and entered the hells in his physical body, the World-Honored One then had Ānanda ask him: "Are you there?"
[Devadatta asked: "How is it within hell? [The Buddha replied: "Though I am in hell, it is like the bliss of the Third Dhyāna Heaven.

The Buddha then commanded him to ask again: "Do you still seek to leave? [Devadatta replied: "I shall leave as soon as the World-Honored One arrives. Ānanda said: "The Buddha is the Guide of the Three Realms;
how could he have a portion [of karma] that leads him into hell? Devadatta said: "Since the Buddha has no portion that leads him into hell, how could I..."
There is the "Departure from Hell" chapter. The World-Honored One, because of Mañjuśrī, suddenly gave rise to a vision of the Dharma;

he saw [beings] being gathered by the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual power and led toward the two Iron Ring Mountains. The World-Honored One, because of the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, [addressed] five thousand bhikṣus.
They had attained the four dhyāna-concentrations and were endowed with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet they had not yet attained the patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), each of them saw themselves having killed their own fathers and mothers and committed various grave offenses.

Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to enter into the profound Dharma. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, took up a sharp sword in his hand and approached them.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, then said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop, stop! You should not commit an act of rebellion. Do not harm me.
If I am to be harmed, it is for the sake of goodness that I am harmed. Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning, there has been no self or person."
It was merely because they perceived a self and a person within their own minds that, when such thoughts arose, they felt as though they were being harmed;
thus, it was designated as "harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized their own fundamental minds to be like dreams and illusions.
Within these dreams and illusions, there is no self or person, not even the parents who give birth to us. Then, the five hundred bhikṣus together praised him, saying:
The Great Sage Mañjuśrī, who has profoundly penetrated the very source of the Dharma, personally grasped a sharp sword and pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata.
As the sword is so, the Buddha is likewise; they are of one single mark and not two. Being without marks and without arising, how could there be killing therein?
[O] The World-Honored One, when asked by a non-Buddhist, neither spoke of existence nor spoke of non-existence. After the World-Honored One had remained silent for a long while, the outsider...

Dao Tan said, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; he has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way]. He prostrated himself and departed. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "By what principle did this non-Buddhist practitioner gain such praise before departing? The World-Honored One replied, "It is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, immediately gallops forward. The World-Honored One, due to a question from King Prasenajit regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), said: [The verse continues: "If one can see the shadow of the whip... and so forth. The King asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of this verse? The Buddha replied, "O King, the shadow of the whip refers to the teachings of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. If a person can perceive these teachings, they will immediately awaken to the Dharma and attain liberation. The King further asked, "World-Honored One, how does one perceive the shadow of the whip? The Buddha replied, "O King, when a person hears the teachings of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, they should contemplate them deeply and practice accordingly. This is called perceiving the shadow of the whip. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'perceiving the shadow of the whip'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one encounters the teachings of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, one should not merely listen with the ears, but should contemplate them with the mind and practice them with the body. This is called perceiving the shadow of the whip. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'immediately awakening to the Dharma'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one perceives the shadow of the whip, one immediately realizes the nature of the mind and attains the path of liberation. This is called immediately awakening to the Dharma. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'attaining liberation'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one attains the path of liberation, one transcends all suffering and afflictions, and dwells in eternal bliss. This is called attaining liberation. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'dwelling in eternal bliss'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one dwells in eternal bliss, one is free from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is never again subject to the cycle of rebirth. This is called dwelling in eternal bliss. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'never again subject to the cycle of rebirth'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one is no longer subject to the cycle of rebirth, one has severed the roots of craving and ignorance, and has attained the state of Nirvāṇa. This is called never again being subject to the cycle of rebirth. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'attaining the state of Nirvāṇa'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one attains the state of Nirvāṇa, one is eternally extinguished of all suffering and afflictions, and dwells in the supreme peace and joy. This is called attaining the state of Nirvāṇa. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'supreme peace and joy'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one dwells in supreme peace and joy, one is free from all worldly concerns and attachments, and experiences the ultimate liberation of the mind. This is called supreme peace and joy. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'ultimate liberation of the mind'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one attains ultimate liberation of the mind, one has realized the true nature of all phenomena and is no longer bound by any conceptual constructs. This is called ultimate liberation of the mind. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'realizing the true nature of all phenomena'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one realizes the true nature of all phenomena, one understands that all things are empty, signless, and wishless. This is called realizing the true nature of all phenomena. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'understanding that all things are empty, signless, and wishless'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one understands that all things are empty, signless, and wishless, one has transcended all dualistic views and attachments. This is called understanding that all things are empty, signless, and wishless. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'transcending all dualistic views and attachments'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one transcends all dualistic views and attachments, one dwells in the state of non-duality and non-attachment. This is called transcending all dualistic views and attachments. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'dwelling in the state of non-duality and non-attachment'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one dwells in the state of non-duality and non-attachment, one is free from all conceptualization and discrimination, and experiences the ultimate reality of the Dharma. This is called dwelling in the state of non-duality and non-attachment. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'experiencing the ultimate reality of the Dharma'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one experiences the ultimate reality of the Dharma, one realizes that the Dharma is neither born nor destroyed, neither coming nor going, and is beyond all verbal expression. This is called experiencing the ultimate reality of the Dharma. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'realizing that the Dharma is neither born nor destroyed, neither coming nor going, and beyond all verbal expression'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one realizes that the Dharma is neither born nor destroyed, neither coming nor going, and beyond all verbal expression, one has attained the wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. This is called realizing that the Dharma is neither born nor destroyed, neither coming nor going, and beyond all verbal expression. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'attaining the wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one attains the wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, one is able to manifest various forms and teach sentient beings according to their capacities, leading them all to the path of liberation. This is called attaining the wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'being able to manifest various forms and teach sentient beings according to their capacities, leading them all to the path of liberation'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one is able to manifest various forms and teach sentient beings according to their capacities, leading them all to the path of liberation, one has fulfilled the great vow of a Bodhisattva. This is called being able to manifest various forms and teach sentient beings according to their capacities, leading them all to the path of liberation. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'fulfilling the great vow of a Bodhisattva'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one fulfills the great vow of a Bodhisattva, one has perfected all the paramitas and attained the stage of Buddhahood. This is called fulfilling the great vow of a Bodhisattva. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'perfecting all the paramitas and attaining the stage of Buddhahood'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one perfects all the paramitas and attains the stage of Buddhahood, one is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This is called perfecting all the paramitas and attaining the stage of Buddhahood. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'being endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha'? The Buddha replied, "O King, it means that when one is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma and liberate all sentient beings. This is called being endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The King then asked, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'being able to turn the wheel of the Dharma and liberate all sentient beings'? The Buddha replied, "O King,
"Is there a conventional truth? If you say there is not, then wisdom should not be twofold. If you say there is, then wisdom should not be single.
What is the meaning of this oneness and twoness? The Buddha said, "Great King, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Dragon Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this meaning.
Now I do not speak; now you do not listen. This absence of speaking and absence of listening—this is the meaning of oneness and twoness."
Yi: Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma did you teach yesterday? the World-Honored One replied, "I taught the Dharma of certainty.
The non-Buddhist asked, "What Dharma do you teach today? He replied, "The Dharma of uncertainty. The non-Buddhist said, "Yesterday you taught the Dharma of certainty;
why do you teach the Dharma of uncertainty today? The World-Honored One said, "Yesterday was certain; today is uncertain. [End of] the World-Honored One’s discourse.
A certain heterodox teacher asked, "Are all phenomena permanent? The World-Honored One did not answer. He asked again, "Are all phenomena impermanent?
The World-Honored One likewise did not answer. The heterodox teacher said, "The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom; why do you not answer me?
The World-Honored One replied, "What you ask concerns nothing but frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Once, the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a Nyagrodha tree.
Regarding the sequence of events: Two merchants asked the World-Honored One, "Did you see the carriage pass by?

He replied, "I did not see it. "Did you hear it? He replied, "I did not hear it. "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration. "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep.

The merchants then sighed in admiration, saying, "Excellent, excellent! The World-Honored One is truly awake, yet sees nothing... [The text continues: "...The World-Honored One, because of [the monk] Chang..."
The brahmin Cūḍapanthaka sought to debate on the meaning of the Dharma, making a prior agreement: "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my head to apologize.
The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? The brahmin replied, "I take 'non-acceptance of all things' as my fundamental tenet. The World-Honored One said:
"Is this view accepted or not? Zhi shook his sleeves and departed. As he traveled along the road, he attained a realization and sighed, saying:
"In my interpretation, I have fallen into error in two respects. If this view is accepted, the point of failure is coarse; if this view is not accepted, the point of failure is subtle."
All humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles do not know where my meaning falls; only the World-Honored One and the great bodhisattvas know where my meaning falls.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My meaning has fallen into two points of defeat; therefore, I shall behead myself as an apology.
The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing. You should turn your mind toward the Way. Thereupon—
Together with five hundred followers, they all at once threw themselves before the Buddha and left the household life, attaining the state of Arhat.
One day, while the World-Honored One was sitting, he saw two men carrying a pig past him and asked, "What is this? They replied, "The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom;
yet you do not even recognize a piglet. The World-Honored One said, "I must ask you about it as well. When the World-Honored One was about to enter Nirvana...
The Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more. The World-Honored One exclaimed, "Mañjuśrī!
In the forty-nine years I have dwelt in this world, I have never spoken a single word. You ask me to turn the Wheel of Dharma again—is it that I have ever turned the Wheel of Dharma?
At the assembly of the Nirvāṇa, the World-Honored One rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying, "You all should well..."
"Behold my body, the color of purple-polished gold; gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you later feel regret.
If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciple; if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you are likewise not my disciple.
The World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly: "I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter nirvāṇa. He then proceeded to the Śāla grove.
Beneath the twin trees, he entered parinirvāṇa with serene composure. He then rose from his coffin and preached the Dharma for his mother, reciting the verse on impermanence:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.

At that time, the disciples hurriedly gathered fragrant wood and vied with one another to cremate him. After the embers were spent, the golden coffin remained as it was. The great assembly then [approached] the Buddha...

He then praised him with a verse, saying: "How could the fierce and blazing fires of the common world burn this body? I pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi shall cremate this golden-hued body.
At that moment, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees, moving back and forth through the air.
Through the transformative fire of samādhi, ashes were produced in an instant, and eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* relics were obtained.
Regarding the karmic conditions of the various Bodhisattvas and Arhats:
One day, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva instructed Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs, saying, "Bring back whatever is not a medicine.
Sudhana surveyed the entire earth and found that there was nothing that was not medicine. He returned and reported, "There is nothing that is not medicine. Mañjuśrī said:
"Bring this medicine. Sudhana then picked up a blade of grass from the ground and handed it to Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī received it and showed it to the assembly, saying: "This medicine can both kill people and bring them to life.
Mañjuśrī asked the lady Āmrapālī: "What is the meaning of 'birth'? The lady replied: "The meaning of birth is that which is born through non-birth."
[The Master] asked, "What is the meaning of 'birth through non-birth' as the definition of birth?

The woman replied, "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never attained self-existence and yet are able to harmonize according to what is appropriate—this is the meaning of birth.
[The Master] asked, "What is the meaning of death? The woman replied, "Death takes 'not dying by means of death' as the meaning of death. [The Master] said, "As for..."

"What is the meaning of 'death' when one dies by means of non-death? The woman replied, "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never themselves experienced separation, yet can accord with what is appropriate for each, this is the meaning of death.
The woman Ātreyī asked Mañjuśrī, "If one clearly understands the principle that birth is non-birth, why then..."
They are carried away by the currents of birth and death. Mañjuśrī said: "Their power has not yet been fully developed. Mañjuśrī once said to the Devaputra Susthitamati:
"If you were now able to turn your back on all Buddhas and slander the Dharma and the Saṃgha, I would immediately practice such a holy life together with you.
The Devaputra asked: "Great Being, for what reason do you speak thus again? Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra..."
"Son, according to your understanding, what do you take to be the Buddha? The Devaputra replied, "The suchness of the dharma-realm;
I say that is the Buddha. Suśīma said, "Devaputra, what do you think? Can the suchness of the dharma-realm be stained or attached to? He replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said, "For this reason, I have spoken thus. If you can now turn your back on and reject the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, I shall practice this holy life together with you.

The Devaputra Sunirmita said to Mañjuśrī, "We may go together to the place of the Tathāgata to inquire about and receive that which we have not yet heard, and likewise to pose questions according to the Dharma at this very time. Mañjuśrī said, "Do not make distinctions."
"Do not separately grasp or cling to the Tathāgata. The Devaputra asked, "Where is the Tathāgata now, that I should not cling to him?
Viśeṣacintin replied, "He is right before your eyes. The Devaputra said, "If it is thus, why do I not see him?
Viśeṣacintin replied, "If you do not see anything at all, this is called truly seeing the Tathāgata. The Devaputra said, "If he is seen before me, why do you admonish me [not to see him]?"
"Do not grasp at the Tathāgata. Vimalakīrti said, "What do you see before you now? The devaputra replied, "I see the realm of empty space.
Vimalakīrti said, "The Tathāgata is the realm of empty space; therefore, the realm of empty space is itself the Tathāgata.
Within this, there is not a single thing that can be conceptually distinguished. [In the assembly of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, thirty-two bodhisattvas each spoke...]
Regarding the Gate of Non-duality, Mañjuśrī said: "In all dharmas, I have no speech and no discourse; there is no indication and no cognition.
To be free from all questioning and answering—this is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-duality.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again asked Vimalakīrti: "Virtuous one, you should speak: what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-duality? Vimalakīrti remained silent. Mañjuśrī—
The special praise says: "Even to the point where there are no words or letters—this is the Bodhisattva’s true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
When Sudhana visited fifty-three spiritual friends and finally arrived before the pavilion of Maitreya, he saw that the door of the pavilion was closed.
He gazed up at it in admiration and offered praise. Then, seeing Maitreya coming from another direction, Sudhana prostrated himself and said: "I pray..."
The doors of the pavilions opened, allowing me to enter. Maitreya soon arrived before Sudhana and snapped his fingers once;
the doors of the pavilions opened. Sudhana had already entered the pavilions, and the doors closed immediately.

He saw hundreds of thousands of millions of pavilions, and in each pavilion stood a Maitreya leading his retinue, with a Sudhana standing before him. ○ [End of section] 須 (xu) [Note: This character appears to be a scribal mark or error].
The Venerable Bodhidharma was sitting in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave when the devas rained down flowers and offered praise.
A man asked, "Who is it raining flowers from the sky to praise? For what reason are they praising? The deva replied, "I am Brahmā.

I respectfully honor the Venerable One’s excellent exposition of Prajñāpāramitā. The Venerable One said, "Regarding Prajñāpāramitā, I have never spoken so much as a single word. Why do you offer praise?"
The deva said, "In this way, O Venerable One, there is no speaking, and thus I have heard nothing. This absence of speaking and hearing is the true teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
One day, while Subhūti was preaching the Dharma, Śakra rained down flowers. Subhūti asked, "From where did these flowers come?

Thereupon, they made a vow together, saying: "May we two be husband and wife without marriage throughout all our lives.

Due to these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were entirely golden in color. In this present life, as well, he and the nun Jālinīprabhā (Purple-Gold Light) again became husband and wife.

The Dharma-piṭaka was compiled so that it would not be allowed to perish. Once the compilation was complete, Kāśyapa reflected upon his own old age and decrepitude, thinking it appropriate to enter meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya. He then summoned Ānanda and said, "I shall not remain much longer in this world."
"I now entrust the True Dharma to you; you must protect and uphold it. Listen to my verse: 'Every phenomenon is originally the Dharma; there is neither non-Dharma nor anything contrary to Dharma.
Why, within a single phenomenon, would there be both Dharma and non-Dharma? Having spoken this verse, Kāśyapa thought: 'The Tathāgata’s relics are all with the various devas.
I shall travel through the air to reach every stūpa. Ānanda prostrated himself and received his command. Kāśyapa then ascended into the void and traveled everywhere to the stūpas.
After the temple rites were completed, he returned and once again took his leave of King Ajātaśatru according to their prior agreement.
He then vanished into Mount Kukkuṭapāda, where he sat upon a grass mat. He thought to himself:

"Now, clad in robes of discarded rags and wearing my saṃghāṭī, I shall remain here for five hundred and seventy koṭis and sixty hundred thousand years until Maitreya appears in the world; throughout this time, my body shall never decay."
He then said to the mountain, "If King Ajātaśatru and Ānanda come, you should open for them; once they have departed, close again.
When King Ajātaśatru learned that Kāśyapa had already entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda, he invited Ānanda to go together with him.

The mountain indeed opened for them, and they saw Kāśyapa seated in meditative absorption, solemn and majestic. After the king had paid his respects, he wished to perform the cremation using fragrant wood.
Ānanda said, "It must not yet be cremated. Mahākāśyapa is currently sustaining his body through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), awaiting the descent of Maitreya before entering parinirvāṇa.
When the king heard this, he marveled in astonishment; he paid his respects to Ānanda and took his leave. The mountain closed back up as it was before.

The second patriarch Ānanda transmitted the Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin.
Ānanda was a native of Rājagṛha; his clan was Kṣatriya. His father was King Droṇodana, who was indeed the younger cousin of the Buddha.
He was widely learned and profoundly insightful, possessing unimpeded wisdom; the World-Honored One regarded him as foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī* and had frequently praised him.
Furthermore, due to his great merit from past lives, he had received and upheld the Dharma-treasury like water being passed from one vessel to another.

Consequently, the Buddha appointed him as his attendant. One day, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today, upon entering the city, I witnessed a most extraordinary event. The Buddha asked: "What extraordinary thing did you see?"
"A rare occurrence," Ānanda said. "Upon entering the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; upon leaving the city, I saw nothing but impermanence.
The Buddha said, "Yesterday, when I entered the city, I too saw a rare occurrence. Ānanda asked, "I do not know what rare occurrence you saw.
The Buddha said, "When I entered the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, it was likewise."

Seeing a musician performing a dance, Ānanda one day asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe that the World-Honored One transmitted to you, what else did he transmit? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said:
"Knock down the banner-pole in front of the gate! One day, Ānanda entered the Bamboo Grove and heard a bhikṣu reciting a verse:
"If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not see an old crane by the water, it is not as good as living for a single day and beholding one."

Ānanda corrected him, saying, "Not so. The Buddha said: "If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the pivot of the Buddhas' teachings, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining such understanding. Thereupon, the bhikṣu reported this to his teacher.
His teacher said, "Ānanda has grown old and is senile; what I have said is correct. On another day, Ānanda was passing through the Bamboo Grove and saw...
The bhikṣu recited the verses as before. Ānanda questioned him and learned the reason;
reflecting that this foolish person was difficult to transform, he entered *samādhi* and sought a noble sage to bear witness for him. Thereupon the earth shook and a sudden radiance burst forth.
Immediately, a holy elder (*sthavira*) manifested himself and spoke a verse for him, saying: "That one who recites and chants the verses is truly not [an ordinary being]."

The Buddha’s intention was this: "Now that you have encountered the Honored One of Joy, you may rely upon him for full understanding. The master and his disciple were filled with reverent awe and soon attained the second fruit [of the path].
Later, King Ajātaśatru addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata and the Honored Kāśyapa—these two supreme masters—have both entered parinirvāṇa.
Due to my many affairs, I was unable to behold them all. When you, O Venerable One, enter parinirvāṇa, I pray that you will deign to grant me a parting word."
He did not grant the request. Later, he thought to himself: "My body is fragile and brittle, like a mass of foam; how much more so now that it is worn by old age—how could it endure for long?
He further reflected: "King Ajātaśatru has made a pact with me. Thereupon, he went to the royal palace and said to him:
"I wish to enter *nirvāṇa*; therefore, I have come to bid you farewell. The gatekeeper said, "The King is sleeping; he cannot hear you.

Ānanda said, "Wait until the King awakens, and I shall speak for you. At that time, the King saw in a dream a precious parasol, adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions who gazed up at it in reverence. Suddenly, a violent wind and rain arose, blowing and breaking its handle. The treasure—
His precious necklaces all fell to the ground. His heart was filled with great wonder and alarm. Upon waking, the gatekeeper reported the matter in full to the king.
Having heard these words, the king wailed aloud in grief, his lamentation moving both heaven and earth.
He immediately proceeded to the city of Vaiśālī and saw Ānanda sitting cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River. The king then paid homage and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Three..."
"O Honored One of the World, you have abandoned us and come here; for a time, rely upon the power of your compassionate vow and do not yet enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the King of Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank and spoke again in verse: "O Venerable One, why so quickly return to the field of quiescent extinction?"
"I pray that you will remain for a brief moment and accept this offering. At that time, Ānanda, seeing the two kings both coming to entreat him, spoke these verses:
"O Two Kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve with sorrowful longing. Nirvāṇa is my purity, for it is free from all states of existence.
He further reflected: "If I were to enter parinirvāṇa in one kingdom, the other kingdoms would contend [for my remains]."
"It is impossible that [the Dharma] should perish. One ought to deliver all sentient beings through equanimity.

Within the Snowy Mountains, five hundred rishis beheld this auspicious omen and flew through the air to arrive. They prostrated at Ānanda’s feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and said: "I shall, within..."
