The Origin of King Aśoka’s Construction of Stūpas:
The king of the city of Pāṭaliputra was named Bindusāra. He had a son named Aśoka (translated here as "Sorrowless"), whose body was coarse and unrefined, and whom the king did not like to behold.
Later, when the frontier kingdom of Siṃhala rebelled, [the king] alone commanded Aśoka among all his sons...
Aśoka went forth to wage war, accompanied by only a few dozen worn-out and blunt weapons.

His followers found this difficult to accept, but Aśoka said, "If I am destined to rule as king, there will naturally be those who come to support me. As he spoke these words, military equipment suddenly surged forth from the earth.
He then set out with them to invade that kingdom. Suddenly, a voice was heard proclaiming from the air: "Prince Aśoka shall reign as king here!"
"O you all, do not harbor rebellious intentions against the realm. Thus, all the kingdoms were pacified, extending as far as the shores of the ocean.
Just then, the King fell ill; his ministers supported him together, and Aśoka brought him to his bedside, intending to establish him as king. Upon hearing this, the King was displeased.
Even as his life was ending, King Aśoka thought to himself: "If I am destined to be king, may the devas spontaneously pour water upon my head and bind a white silk cloth around my brow.
As soon as he had finished speaking, an iron wheel descended from the sky. He became the king of Jambudvīpa, ruling over the entire world.

King Aśoka performed the funeral rites for his father according to the Dharma and was immediately installed on the throne. He appointed Āṭavika as his chief minister. At that time, the various ministers...
Holding the whip, he established his merit; yet, conceiving a haughty mind, he became arrogant and contemptuous.

The King, perceiving his intent, issued a decree to all his ministers to cut down the trees bearing flowers and fruit and to plant thorny brambles instead. When the ministers did not comply with this third command, the King took up a sharp sword and slew them with his own hand.
Rāvaṇa then advised the King that he ought to appoint a man who was a butcher. At that time, there was a fierce and wicked son of Jīrṇa who boasted of himself...
"It can," [the king replied]. Thereupon, the king had a building constructed for him, with only a single door opened. Inside, he established various methods of punishment that resembled a hell.
A cruel man informed the king, "If one enters this place, they shall not emerge again. The king granted his permission.
At that time, there was the son of a merchant leader who, weary of the sufferings of the world, left the household life to study the Way. He traveled through various kingdoms, and next—
While begging for alms, he mistakenly entered a slaughterhouse. From afar, he saw within the house chariots of fire, glowing coals, and other such horrors;
his hair stood on end with terror, and he wished to leave through the door. A cruel master came forward and seized the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu felt deep remorse and grief, his eyes filling with tears.
He begged for a month’s delay, but was not granted it. Thus, the time was gradually reduced until it reached seven days, at which point permission was finally given. The bhikṣu—

With courageous diligence, he sat in meditation to quiet his mind. On the seventh day, just as the king was about to send a palace maiden to the executioner, the executioner seized her and pounded her in a mortar with a pestle until she was reduced to fine powder in an instant. When the bhikṣu saw this, [he was moved].
He felt extreme revulsion, thinking, "My own body shall likewise become like this before long; I must sever all fetters and become an Arhat.
The executioner said to the bhikṣu, "The time limit has expired. The bhikṣu replied, "My mind has attained liberation; I have severed all existence.
Now, regarding this physical carcass, I have no further attachment or regret. The executioner then seized the bhikṣu and placed him upon the iron [grill].
In the boiling oil, the messenger lit a fire, yet it could not heat it; when he approached, the fire ignited spontaneously and became fierce and intense.
Having opened the lid of the cauldron, he saw that bhikṣu sitting upon a lotus flower. Struck with wonder, he immediately informed the king.
The king then prepared his carriage and led his retinue to come and look. The bhikṣu’s body rose into the air like a king of geese, manifesting various [miraculous displays].

Manifesting a transformation, he addressed the king with a verse, saying: "I am a disciple of the Buddha; having reached the state where all outflows are exhausted, I have now completely escaped the great terrors of birth and death.
Upon hearing this, King Aśoka conceived a profound sense of reverence and faith toward the Buddha’s Dharma.
He addressed the bhikṣu, saying, "Before the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, what did he prophesy? The bhikṣu replied, "The Buddha prophesied:
'Great King, one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, in the city of Pāṭaliputra, there will be three hundred million households. In that kingdom, there will be a king.'"
"He shall be named Aśoka and will rule this Jambudvīpa as a Cakravartin king, governing by means of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, he shall distribute my relics throughout Jambudvīpa and erect eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Since the King has now constructed this great hell and slaughtered immeasurable beings, he ought to honor the Buddha’s prophecy and practice according to the Dharma. Thus spoke King Aśoka.
With palms joined in reverence, he said: "I have committed a great transgression. I pray only that the Son of the Buddha will accept my confession; do not further reproach me, a fool.
After the bhikṣu had delivered King Aśoka, he ascended into the air and vanished. At that time, the king wished to depart, but the executioner detained him.
The king said, "Do you wish to kill me? He replied, "It is so. The king said, "Who entered this place first? He replied, "I am he.
The king said, "If that is the case, you should die first. He then commanded his attendants, "Take the perpetrator and place him in a lacquer house; burn him with fire.
Furthermore, he commanded that this hell be demolished and given to sentient beings for their security. Thus did the King.
He arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and took the relics from within the Buddha’s stūpa.

He fashioned eighty-four thousand caskets of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and likewise fashioned eighty-four thousand vases made of the four precious substances. He commanded the various spirits and deities to construct eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Then, the Venerable Yaśas extended his fingers and emitted eighty-four thousand rays of light, commanding the swift-moving spirits to [proceed] to Jambudvīpa.
In the cities, towns, and villages of Jambudvīpa where there were a full one hundred million households, a stūpa was erected in each.

In the land of Zhendan (China), there were nineteen such sites. At first, when the World-Honored One was traveling through the villages with his bhikṣus, there were two boys—one named Jayanta and the other named Vijaya—who were playing together in the sand. From afar, they saw the World-Honored One.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks. Jayanta thought to himself, "I shall offer parched barley meal to the Buddha.
He then took fine sand in his hands and placed it into the World-Honored One’s bowl. Viśākha also joined his palms in sympathetic joy. At that time, the youth made a vow, saying:
"By the merit and roots of goodness from this gift, may I become a king of a single world-system under one parasol. Immediately—
Having been born in this place, he shall make offerings to the Buddhas. The World-Honored One smiled and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this boy shall rule over a single world-system in the city of Pāṭaliputra as a Cakravartin King of the Maurya clan named Aśoka.
He shall govern by the True Dharma and further distribute my relics, constructing eighty-four thousand [stūpas]."
"Four thousand stūpas. Ānanda, you may take this sand offered into this bowl and place it where the Tathāgata used to walk.
Ānanda, he followed these instructions and carried them out."
When King Aśoka paid his respects to Upagupta at Pāṭaliputra, there was a senior elder named Yaśas.

King Aśoka conceived a deep sense of reverence for him and established the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery, inviting Yaśas to preside over it. Upon arriving at the Kukkuṭārāma, he addressed Yaśas, saying: "Furthermore..."
"Bhikṣu, will the one prophesied by the Buddha perform the work of a Buddha? I shall go to him to offer worship and respect.
Yaśas replied, "When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā and said to Ānanda:
'One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a son of a householder named Upagupta who will renounce the world.'"
He practiced the Way and was titled the Buddha of Formlessness (*Nirnimitta-buddha*). The King asked, "Has he now appeared in the world?
He replied, "He has already appeared in the world; he resides in Mount Urumuṇḍa. Upon hearing this, the King wished to go there and sent a messenger to inform him.
Guptaka reflected, "If the King comes, his countless attendants will kill and harm minute insects. He said to the messenger, "I shall go myself..."

He went to the king’s presence. Guptaka eventually arrived at the kingdom, and the king was greatly delighted. He approached the Venerable One, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and said:
"I now govern this Jambudvīpa and hold the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, yet I do not consider this a cause for joy.
Now that I behold the Venerable One, it is as if I were beholding the Buddha; my exultation is immeasurable. Truly, you are a disciple of the Tathāgata."
"It is possible," [the Buddha] replied. Again, [the king] said, "The Venerable One’s countenance is upright and handsome, whereas my own physical form is ugly.
Why is this? Kuvinda spoke a verse, saying: "When I practiced giving, My mind was pure and my wealth excellent; Yet it was not equal to the King's giving, Who offered sand to the Buddha.
The King further addressed him, saying, "I pray that the Venerable One will show me the places where the Buddha preached the Dharma and where he traveled."
He also mentioned the places where the Buddha had prophesied that the stupas of the great disciples should be venerated and offered to. Kūṭadanta said, "Excellent, excellent!
He then led the king to those locations, pointing each one out for him as they made offerings. When they reached the stupa of Ānanda, he said:

"This person is the Buddha’s attendant; foremost among those of great learning, he has compiled the Buddha’s scriptures. The king then relinquished ten billion precious treasures to make offerings to this stūpa.
He addressed his ministers, saying: "The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, whose nature is pure.

He is able to uphold it all in its entirety; therefore, my offering is supreme. May the lamp of the Dharma remain forever in the world to extinguish the darkness of this ignorance. All [were thus enlightened].

Since Sāgara came from that place, he therefore made offerings with superior intent. The King then proceeded once more beneath the Bodhi tree, holding an incense burner in his hand and prostrating toward the four directions, vowing:
"May the Tathāgata’s noble and holy disciples who dwell in all quarters come together in this assembly.
At that time, thirty thousand great Arhats were present; seeing that the first seat was unoccupied, the King asked for the reason. Sāgarabuddhi said:
The Venerable One said, "This is the seat of Piṇḍola; this person has personally seen the Buddha come.
The King asked, "Where is he now? Samudramati replied, "Wait but a moment. Having spoken, Piṇḍola descended from the sky.
The King invited him to take his seat and paid him homage, but Piṇḍola paid no heed. The King then asked, "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha come—is this so?"
"No," [the King] replied. Piṇḍola raised his eyebrows with his hand and asked, "Do you understand? The King said, "I do not understand.
Piṇḍola said, "The Nāga King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal; at that time, I was also included among the number."
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Five; *Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Six (marked with the character "Zhou"):
Jiazi (beginning in the fifth year of King You of Zhou), Xinwei (the first year of King Ping), Wangxu (the first year of King Huan), and Guihai (ending in the second year of King Huan of Zhou).
(庚子) The Fourth Patriarch, Upagupta, transmitted the Dharma to Tiṣya.
Upagupta was a native of the country of Cīnabhukti (one name is Upagupta; another is Upagupta). His clan was Śūdra; his father was Sumati.

At seventeen he left the household life; at twenty he realized the fruit [of Arhatship]. He traveled through various regions to convert and transform others, arriving at the kingdom of Mathurā, where those who attained deliverance were exceedingly numerous.
Consequently, the palace of Māra shook, and Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear. He then exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma.
Kuvula (Gupta) immediately entered samādhi to observe the cause of this occurrence. Pāpīyān, finding no other means, secretly took a jeweled necklace.
He bound Māra’s neck with a ball of thread. When Māra emerged from his meditative absorption, [the Buddha] took three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands.
Speaking with gentle words, he exhorted Pāpīyān, saying: "This necklace of yours is truly exquisite; let me offer these flower garlands of mine in exchange.
Pāpīyān was greatly delighted and stretched out his neck to receive them. Immediately, they transformed into three kinds of putrid corpses, rotting with maggots.
It was rotten. Pāpīyān loathed it and was filled with great distress and anguish. He exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not move it.
Thereupon, he ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various lords of the gods; he also went to the Brahmā King to seek deliverance from it.

They each replied, "The miraculous transformations performed by the disciples of the One of Ten Powers—how could we, who are vulgar and lowly, be able to remove them? Pāpīyān said, "If that is so, then what can be done?"
"What? the Brahma King asked. "If you can direct your mind toward the Venerable One, it will immediately be severed," he said, and then spoke a verse to guide him in his dedication of merit:
"If one falls upon the ground, one must rise from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.
Having received these instructions, Pāpīyān descended from the celestial palace to the place where Guptaka was. He prostrated at his feet and offered a sorrowful confession. Guptaka said: "You..."
"From this day forward, will you no longer cause harm to the True Dharma of the Tathāgata? Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn toward the Buddha-way and forever sever all unwholesome deeds.
Kuvinda said, "If that is so, you may yourself proclaim with your own mouth: 'I take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Pāpīyān joined his palms and recited it three times; his flower garlands were all cast off, and he then leaped for joy and spoke this verse:
He said: "I prostrate to the Honored One of the Three Realms and to the noble disciples of the Ten Powers. I now dedicate my merit, praying that no weakness may arise.
Having spoken this verse, he paid his respects and departed. One day, Kumāralāta went to visit an elderly bhikṣuṇī.
As soon as he entered the gate, he bumped and knocked over the alms bowl. The bhikṣuṇī said, "When the Buddha was alive, the group of six bhikṣus were extremely coarse in their conduct;
though they came to my house frequently, they were never like this. How can you, a venerable one who succeeds to the ancestral seat, act with such coarseness? Thereupon, Kūṭadanta withdrew.
During his lifetime, Kūṭadanta guided and transformed beings, leading many to realize the fruits of the path. Every time he delivered one...
Each person placed a tally inside a stone chamber; the chamber was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide, until it was filled to capacity.
Finally, there was the son of an elder named Gandhamādana, who came to pay homage to Kūṭadanta and requested ordination.
Kūṭadanta asked him, "Do you seek ordination with your body, or do you seek ordination with your mind? He replied, "I have come for ordination, not for the sake of my body."
“Mind,” said Kumārajīva. “If it is neither body nor mind, who then has left the household life? He replied, “One who leaves the household life does so because there is no self and no ‘mine.
Because there is no self and no ‘mine,’ the mind is neither born nor extinguished. That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is the eternal Way. Even the Buddhas are eternal;
their minds have no form or appearance, and their essence is likewise so. Kumārajīva said, “You shall attain great enlightenment; the mind itself—”

Having attained thorough penetration, he said, "You should rely upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and continue the noble lineage. He then shaved his hair and conferred upon him the full precepts (upasaṃpadā).
Furthermore, he addressed him, saying: "Your father once dreamed of a golden sun at your birth; you may therefore be named Tiṭṭhaka. He spoke again, saying:
The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in successive order until it reached me; I now, in turn, entrust it to you. Listen to my verse:
"The mind is itself the primordial mind; The primordial mind is not a dharma that exists. If there were dharmas that existed, there would be a primordial mind;

But since it is neither mind nor a fundamental dharma, [it is beyond all categories]. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, he leaped into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations, then returned to his original seat and sat cross-legged.

He passed away while sitting cross-legged; he was then called the Buddha Without Marks. Dhitika used the counting sticks from his room to cremate the master’s body, collected the relics, and erected a stupa.
This occurred in the thirtieth year of King Ping of the Zhou dynasty, the *gengzi* year.
There was one who held the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and sought ordination from Guptaka. Guptaka said, "The method for seeking ordination requires that you believe my words."
"Do not disobey my instruction. The man said, "Since I have come to seek refuge with you, Master, I shall certainly obey your command.

Guptaka then transformed a precipitous cliff where tall trees grew, commanding him to climb the tree. He further manifested a great pit beneath the tree, a thousand cubits deep and wide, and commanded him to let go of his feet.
The man followed the instruction and immediately let go of both feet. When he was told to let go of one hand, he let it go as well.
He held him by one hand and commanded him to let go. The man replied, "If I let go, I will fall into the pit and die.
Kuṭadanta said, "Previously you agreed to receive my instruction; why do you now disobey me? At that moment, the man's attachment to his body was extinguished.
He let go and fell, yet he did not see the tree or the pit; he immediately realized the fruit of the Path.
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Six; *Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Seven (Hong Character Series).
Jiazi (Third year of King Huan of Zhou); Yibyou (First year of King Zhuang); Gengzi (First year of King Xi); Yisi (First year of King Hui); Guihai.
(Ending in the nineteenth year of King Hui of Zhou) On the fifth day of the fifth month in the summer of the tenth year of King Zhuang of Zhou, the year Jiawu, the fixed stars did not appear,
and stars fell like rain. Then, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of the West manifested at the Snow Mountains and transformed five hundred rishis.
He returned to his native country, where the radiance [of his presence] eclipsed the fixed stars so that they no longer appeared.
(Jichou year) The Fifth Patriarch, Diṭāka, transmitted the Dharma to Miñjaka.
Diṭāka—translated as "Measure of Penetrating Truth"—was a native of Magadha. His original name was Gandhaja. At that time, his father dreamed of gold...
The sun emerged from his house, illuminating heaven and earth. Before him was a great mountain, adorned with various jewels;
springs gushed from its peak, flowing forth in torrents in all directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Kuddāla, who explained it for him, saying:
"The jewel mountain is my own body. The gushing springs represent the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. The sun emerging from the house is the sign that you have now entered the Path."
"That which illuminates heaven and earth is your transcendent wisdom. For this reason, I shall change your name.
Having heard the verse, Tiṭṭibha leaped for joy and recited a verse in response: "The towering mountain of the seven jewels constantly yields a spring of wisdom;
it transforms into the flavor of the true Dharma, able to deliver all who have the karmic affinity. Guptaka also spoke a verse, saying: "I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall now manifest it."
One of great wisdom, he emerged from his dwelling on this golden day, illuminating heaven and earth. When Tiṭṭhika heard the verse, he prostrated and took it up with devotion.
Later, he traveled to Central India. In that country, there were eight thousand great seers, headed by Mucilinda.
Hearing that Tiṭṭhika had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage. They said to Tiṭṭhika, "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven."
"I encountered the seer Asita, who bestowed upon me the methods of the seers. My teacher met a disciple of the One of Ten Powers and practiced *dhyāna*.
Since then, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths for six kalpas. Tīraka said, "That you have drifted apart for so many kalpas is indeed not in vain.
Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, thereby entering the Buddha-vehicle. Mecaka said, "In the past, Asita..."
"O Rishi, you granted me this prediction: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of non-outflow.
That we have met now—is this not due to past affinities? I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation.

Tīrthika then ordained him as a monk and commanded the holy ones to bestow the precepts upon him. The remaining assembly of rishis then began to give rise to pride; Tīrthika manifested his great [powers] to them.
They attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Thereupon, they both gave rise to the bodhicitta and left the household life at the same time. Then, Dīrghanakha addressed Miśraka, saying:
"In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye (*mahādharmanetra*) to Kāśyapa;

it was transmitted in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse: "Thoroughly penetrating the fundamental Dharma, the mind is without..."
The Dharma is non-existent; the realization of what is not the Dharma is the same as the non-existence of the unrealized.

The mind, too, has no dharma. Having spoken this verse, he leaped into the void and performed eighteen transformations. Entering the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
Mucilinda and eight thousand bhikṣus together collected the relics and erected a stūpa for offerings on Mount Paṇḍava. This was during the reign of King Zhuang of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
The fifth year, the year of Jichou (1089).
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Seven;
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Eight (Huang character series).

Jiazi (starting from the 20th year of King Hui of Zhou) | Gengwu (the 1st year of King Xiang) | Jimao (the 1st year of King Qing) | Jiyou (the 1st year of King Kuang) | Yimao (the 1st year of King Ding) | Ji hai (ending in the 9th year of King Ding of Zhou) [Jia Shen] | The Sixth Patriarch Micaka transmitted the Dharma to Vasumitra.
Mecaka was a man from Central India. Having received the Dharma from Dhitika, he traveled to the kingdom of Northern India to propagate the teachings.
There, seeing auspicious golden clouds above the city walls, he sighed and said, "This is the breath of a person of the Way;
there must be a Great Being who shall be my successor in the Dharma. He then entered the city, and amidst the crowds in the marketplace, he saw a man holding a vessel of wine in his hand.
The man approached him and asked, "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go?
Mīṣaka replied, "I have come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere. The man said, "Do you recognize this object in my hand?
Mīṣaka replied, "This is a vessel for contact, yet it is carried by one who maintains purity. The man said, "Do you recognize me, Master? Mīṣaka replied, "I do not recognize you."
"Consciousness is not the self. He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and clan; I shall subsequently reveal your original cause.
He replied with a verse: "From immeasurable kalpas until my birth in this land, my original clan was Bharadvāja."
His name was Vasumitra. Miśraka said, "My teacher, Diṅnāga, told me that when the World-Honored One was formerly traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'In this country, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man.'"
His clan name was Pārāśarya and his personal name was Vasumitra. Among the patriarchs of the dhyāna lineage, he was destined to be the seventh.
The World-Honored One had prophesied to him, "You should leave the household life. Thereupon, he set down his vessel, performed a prostration, stood to one side, and said:
"I recall that in a past kalpa, I once acted as a donor (dānapati) and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha prophesied to me, saying: 'In this Bhadrakalpa, under Śākyamuni...'"
Within the Dharma, he proclaimed the ultimate teaching. Now, in accordance with the Master’s instruction, I pray that you grant me deliverance.
Mīzhējiā immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts. He then addressed him, saying: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you;
do not let it be severed. He then spoke this verse: "No mind exists that can be attained; What is spoken of cannot be called the Dharma. If one realizes that the mind is no-mind,"
Having first explained the mind and mental factors, Mīḍhaka spoke these verses and entered the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*.

He leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed himself into fire to consume his own body. Vāsūmitra collected his sacred relics and placed them in a casket of the seven precious gems;
he erected a stupa and enshrined them on its upper level. This occurred during the fifteenth year of King Xiang of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
The year was Gengshen (Dingsi).
In the third year of King Ding of the Zhou dynasty,
on the fourteenth day of the ninth month, Laozi was born in Kuxian, Chen Commandery, the state of Chu, within the land of Zhendan.
He hailed from the village of Renshi in Laiyang. His surname was Li, his given name was Er, and his courtesy name was Boyang; he was posthumously titled Dān.

He remained in his mother’s womb for eighty-one years before being born by a caesarean section on her left side. Upon birth, he was already radiant white, and thus he was called Lǎozi (the Old Master).

Because he was born beneath a plum tree (*liùshù*), his surname became Li. He was of a yellowish complexion with beautiful eyebrows, long ears, and large eyes; his nose had two columns, and his ears had three openings.
Within the assembly of Śākyamuni, Laozi was the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa. A sutra states: "Kāśyapa shall be born in Zhendan (China), manifesting the name Laozi.
He shall establish the teaching of 'no external' [non-action] to govern the state, and employ the arts of the immortals to cultivate the self.
From the Buddha's parinirvāṇa until the birth of Laozi, exactly three hundred and forty-six years elapsed.
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Eight; *Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Nine (marked with the character 日).
Jiazi (starting from the tenth year of King Ding of Zhou); Bingzi (the first year of King Jian); Gengyin (the first year of King Ling); Dingsi (the first year of King Jing); Guihai.
(Stops in the seventh year of King Jing of Zhou) (Xinwei).
The Seventh Patriarch, Vāsumitra, transmitted the Dharma to Buddhanandi.
Vāsumitra was a native of Northern India; his family name was Bharadvāja. He constantly wore pure garments and traveled about carrying a wine vessel.
He traveled through the villages and hamlets, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people called him mad. Upon meeting Mīchaka, he proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past records.
Reflecting on his own prior karmic conditions, he cast aside his worldly vessel and left the household life. Having received the Dharma, he went forth to transform others.
Arriving at the kingdom of Kāmala, he extensively promoted Buddhist activities. Before the Dharma seat, there suddenly appeared a man of wisdom who declared, "My name is Buddhānandi. Now...
He engaged in a debate with his teacher. Vasumitra said, "O worthy one, if you debate, it is not the True Dharma; if it is the True Dharma, there is no debate.

If you intend to debate the True Dharma, in the end it will not be a discourse on the True Dharma. Nandi understood that Vasumitra’s meaning was superior, and with a heart of deep admiration, he said, "I wish to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the Ambrosia.
Vasumitra then granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts upon him, further instructing him:
He said: "The Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye, I now entrust to you; you should protect and uphold it. Then he spoke this verse:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It reveals dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes empty space, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is'."
The verse ended, Vasumitra immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together, paid their respects, and spoke this verse: "O Patriarch of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position.
Venerable One, have compassion for us and please proclaim the stage of the Buddha. Vasumitra arose from samādhi and said to the assembly: "What I..."

He attained the Dharma, yet it was not something that exists as a substantial entity. Having declared that the stage of Buddhahood transcends both existence and non-existence, he returned to samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa.
At that very seat, Nandi immediately caused a stupa made of the seven precious jewels to arise, wherein his entire body was enshrined.
This occurred in the seventeenth year of King Zhou Ding’s reign, the year of Xinwei.
(Gengxu) In the land of Zhendan, Kong Qiu was born as the son of Shang Emperor Yi’s son, Weizi.
His lineage first received the fief of Song. In the thirteenth generation, Kong Fangshu moved his residence to Pingxiang in Zouyi, Lu State.
Fangshu’s son was Boxia; Boxia’s son was Shiliang He. He had previously married [the daughter of] Zou...
The Lady gave birth to a son named Mengpi, who was not talented. Later, she married a woman of the Yan clan named Zheng.

While praying at Mount Niqiu, she gave birth to Confucius; he was thus named Qiu and styled Zhongni. On the evening of his birth, two dragons circled the room and five elders descended into the courtyard.
Within the chamber of the Yan lady, the music of the Heavenly Court was heard. His height was nine chi and six cun, and his waistband [was ten...]

His arms hung down past his knees; his temples were like the moon and his nose like the sun; his eyes were like the River and his mouth like the Sea. His countenance was like a dragon’s with a square forehead and a majestic brow like a phoenix’s;
he had a chin like a swallow’s, spiraled whiskers, and a gaze like a tiger’s. His eyebrows possessed twelve colors, and his eyes contained sixty-four veins.
It was the fourth day of the eleventh month in the twenty-first year of King Ling of Zhou, which was the twenty-second year of Duke Xiang of Lu. This was the assembly of Śākyamuni.
Among them, Confucius was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Rutong), and Yan Hui was the Bodhisattva Candraprabha (Yu Guang). A sutra states:

"Within the realm of Jambudvīpa, there is the land of Zhendan (China). I have dispatched three sages to transform and guide those within it; its people are compassionate and their rites and righteousness are complete.
From the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the birth of Confucius, four hundred years passed.

Jiazi (beginning in the eighth year of King Jing of Zhou), Renwu (the first year of King Jing), and Guihai (ending in the forty-first year of King Jing of Zhou).
(Bingyin) The Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi, transmitted the Dharma to Vajramitra.
Buddhanandi was a native of the country of Kamarupa; his clan name was Gautama. He had a fleshly protuberance upon his crown and possessed swift, unimpeded eloquence.
Having first encountered Vasumitra, he received the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. Subsequently, leading a group of disciples, he traveled to propagate the teaching and arrived at the country of Tika.
At the house of the Vaiśya Śreṣṭhin, a white light was seen ascending from the roof.

He said to his disciples, "There is a holy man in this house who does not speak with his mouth; he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk through the four crossroads, knowing that contact is defiling.
Having finished speaking, the elder came out to pay his respects and asked, "What do you require? Nandika replied, "I seek an attendant. The elder said, "I have one..."
He had an only son named Puṇyamitra, who was already fifty years old; he had never spoken with his mouth nor ever stepped with his feet.
Nandika said, "As you have described him, he is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Puṇyamitra rose immediately and paid obeisance.
And he spoke in verse: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the supreme Way?
Buddhatrāta then answered him in verse: "What you say regarding intimacy with the mind cannot be compared to parents.
Your practice accords with the Way; the mind of all Buddhas is precisely this. To seek externally for a Buddha with form is to [separate] from you..."
"It is not so. I wish to know your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated. Having heard this verse, Vālmīka took seven steps.
Nanda then said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great.
Fearing that his parents’ affection would make him difficult to relinquish, he neither spoke nor stepped forward. The elder then released him to let him go forth into homelessness. Nanda...
He immediately conferred full ordination upon him and further addressed him, saying: "I now entrust to you the treasury of the Tathāgata’s eye of the True Dharma;
do not allow it to be severed. He then spoke this verse: "Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so.
If one realizes the nature of space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā). Vajramitra, having received the entrustment from Nanda, immediately transcended...
His body vanished into space like the void, scattering myriad jeweled flowers. He praised him in verse, saying: "Among the patriarchs of our school, you shall be the eighth.

Your Dharma transformation will reach immeasurable multitudes, all of whom shall attain Arhatship. At that time, Nanda suddenly rose from his seat, manifested great supernormal transformations, and then returned to his original seat, solemnly entering parinirvāṇa. The assembly immediately erected a jeweled stupa at that place to enshrine him.
The year his entire body [was enshrined] was the tenth year of King Zhou Jing of this land, the *bingyin* year.
(In the *renwu* year,) Li Er of the kingdom of Zhendan entered the Western Desert.
In the fourth year of King Zhou Jian, Li Er served the Zhou court as the Archivist (*shoucang li*). In the thirteenth year, he was promoted to the position of Pillar-Beneath-the-Horse (*zhuxia*).
Shi. From that time on, for fifty-four years, he did not change his single post. People of the era called him an "official recluse" (lìyǐn).
In the first year of King Jing’s reign, at the age of eighty-six, because the House of Zhou was in decline, he departed from the capital and traveled west through the Hangu Pass.
When Yin Xi, the Commandant of the Pass, saw purple clouds moving westward, he knew a man of the Way was about to cross over; he accordingly welcomed him and prepared the rites. Thereupon, Shi...
He composed a commentary on the *Dàodé jīng* in five thousand words and, together with Yin Xi, subsequently traveled west into the shifting sands.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he beheld a Buddha image; grieving that he had not lived in time to meet the Buddha, he recited a verse before the image, saying:
"Why was my birth so late? Why did the Buddha appear so early? Not seeing Śākyamuni, my heart is constantly filled with distress. Thereafter, nothing was known of his final end.
(甲寅) The Ninth Patriarch, Buddhabhadra, who transmitted the Dharma to Upagupta:
Buddhabhadra was a native of the country of Tiqia. His secular surname was Viśāla. Having received the entrustment of Buddhadeva, he...

Later, he traveled to teach and convert others, arriving in Central India. There was an elder named Gandhaka who brought a son with him and paid his respects, saying, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years;

therefore, he is named Duṣprasāha (Difficult to Be Born). He had also once met a seer who said that this boy’s skeletal features were extraordinary and that he would surely become a vessel for the Dharma.
"Now that you have encountered the Venerable One," he said, "you may give him up so that he may leave the household life. Vimalamitra then accepted him.
At the time of the *karmavācanā* ceremony for his tonsure, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and he further experienced the appearance before him of twenty-one *śarīra* relics.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Before long, Vajramitra said to him, "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you;
you must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke this verse: "The True Principle is originally nameless, Yet through names the True Principle is revealed. [Receive...]"
He attained the True Dharma, which is neither true nor false. Having entrusted the Dharma to Maitreya, he immediately entered the samādhi of cessation and passed into parinirvāṇa.
The assembly cremated his remains with fragrant oils and sandalwood, collected the relics, and erected a stūpa at Nālandā Monastery.
This was in the thirty-third year of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin.
(Renxu) In the land of Zhendan, Kong Qiu entered nirvana.
At the age of seventeen, Confucius visited Zhou to inquire about the rites from Laozi and to seek instruction on music from Chang Hong.

Upon returning from Zhou to Lu, in the nineteenth year of King Jing of Zhou, he served as the governor of Zhongdu in Lu, establishing the regulations for the care of the living and the funeral rites for the dead. He... [continued]
Infants were given different foods; those of differing strengths and weaknesses were assigned different duties. Within one year, the feudal lords of the four quarters took this as their model.

Duke Ding of Lu asked, "How would it be to govern Lu according to these laws? Yanzi replied, "Even the whole world could be so governed. In his twenty-first year, he served as the Minister of Works for Lu.
He established the characteristics of the five types of soil, ensuring that each object obtained what was most suitable for its growth. In his twenty-second year, [he served] Lu...

Duke Ding met with Duke Jing of Qi at Jiaju. Confucius acted as the presiding minister (*xiangshi*), and the people of Qi returned the territories they had seized by way of apology for their transgression.
When Confucius served as Grand Minister of Justice (*Da Sikou*), within seven days he executed Shao Zhengmao and demolished the walls of the three strongholds (*sandu*).

He strengthened the public house (*gongshi*) and weakened the private houses (*sishi*), honoring the sovereign and humbling his ministers; thus, the transformative influence of his governance flourished, and within three months it was widespread.
The administration was orderly. Those who sold lambs and piglets did not embellish their prices. Men and women traveled on separate paths. Lost articles were not picked up.

Guests from the four quarters arriving at the town did not have to seek out officials. When Duke Ding accepted the music of the women of Qi, he did not attend to government affairs for three days, nor did he offer the sacrificial meat to the suburban altar.
Confucius then set out and went to Wei. Twenty-three years later, Confucius departed from Wei and traveled to...
When Chen passed by Kuang, the people of Kuang—because they thought Confucius resembled Yang Huo—surrounded him.
Once he had escaped, he went to Song and practiced the rites with his disciples beneath a great tree. Sima Huan-tui wished to harm him and uprooted the tree. This was the thirty-second year.

When Confucius reached Chen, it was the thirty-fifth year [after his departure from Lu]. Chu attacked Chen; while Confucius was in Chen, his provisions were exhausted. He left Chen again and returned to Wei.

In the thirty-sixth year, Confucius returned to Lu from Wei, where he edited the *Shi* and *Shu*, standardized the *Li* and *Yue*, appended the explanations to the *Zhou Yi*, and composed the *Chunqiu*.
Among the group of seventy disciples, they gathered together what Confucius had spoken and compiled it as the *Lunyu*. (3)
In the nineteenth year (the fourteenth year of Duke Ai of Lu), while hunting in the west, Duke Ai of Lu captured a qilin.
Confucius lamented that the qilin had appeared at an improper time; he then ceased his brush at the Spring and Autumn Annals.

On the day Jichou of the fourth month in the forty-first year, Confucius rose early, leaning on his staff with his hand, strolling leisurely by the gate and singing: "Will Mount Tai crumble? Will the ridgepole decay?"
"The Sage is withering away! When Zi Gong heard this, he said, "The Master must be seriously ill. He hurried in.
Confucius said, "Last night I dreamed that I was being laid out between the two pillars. Since the enlightened kings do not arise, who in the world can honor me as their master?
I am likely to die. He lay ill for seven days and passed away at the age of seventy.
12. He was buried on the banks of the Si River north of the city of Lu. His disciples all observed a period of mourning for three years according to their hearts' sincerity.
When the mourning was over, they took their leave of one another and departed. Only Zigong lived in a hut by the tomb for six years.

Among the disciples and the people of Lu, there were more than a hundred households who settled near the tomb; consequently, it was named Kongli (the Village of Confucius). Of his three thousand disciples, those who were thoroughly proficient in the Six Arts...
There were seventy-two disciples. Confucius fathered Li, whose courtesy name was Boyu. Li fathered Ji, whose courtesy name was Zisi. Ji studied under Zengzi and composed the *Zhongyong*.
Later there was Meng Ke (Mencius), who further received instruction from the disciples of Zisi. Altogether, they were in profound accord with the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
thus they are titled the "Sages of the Confucian School. Initially, the Grand Chancellor Pi of the Shang dynasty questioned Confucius.
The Master said: "Is the Master a sage? [The disciple] replied: "I, Qiu, am merely one who has studied extensively and possesses a strong memory;

I am not a sage. "Are the Three Kings sages? He replied: "The Three Kings were skilled at employing wisdom and courage; as for being sages, that is beyond what I know. "Are the Five Emperors sages? He replied:

"The Five Emperors were skilled at employing benevolence and trustworthiness; as for being sages, that is beyond what I know. "Are the Three Sovereigns sages? He replied: "The Three Sovereigns were skilled at..."
"Regarding current administration, the Sage is not something I know. The Grand Chancellor was greatly startled and asked, "In that case, do you consider yourself a sage?
The Master’s expression changed for a moment, and he replied, "I have heard that in the West there is a Great Sage who governs without governing and yet remains orderly;
who commands confidence without speaking; and who brings about transformation without acting. How vast and boundless he is—no one is able to give him a name!"

The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Pārśva, transmitted the Dharma to Punyayaśas.
Venerable Pārśva was a native of Central India; his original name was Duṣprasaha. He remained in the womb for sixty years. On the eve of his birth—
In her mother’s dream, a white elephant carrying a precious throne entered through the gate; upon the throne sat a single bright pearl. Upon waking, she was born.
At birth, auspicious light illuminated the chamber, and her body emitted a wondrous fragrance. Although she grew up eating grain-based food, she remained entirely free of any bodily impurities.
Later, he encountered Puṇyamitra and attended upon him at his side. He never slept, so much so that it was said his ribs never touched his mat;
consequently, he was called the Venerable Pārśva. When he first arrived in the city of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, declaring to the assembly:
"When this ground turns golden in color, a holy person shall enter this assembly. As soon as he finished speaking, the ground immediately turned golden. At that time...
There was a son of a householder named Pūrṇayaśas. Standing before Vīra with palms joined, he asked, "From where have you come?
Vīra replied, "My mind does not go. Vīra asked, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not abide. Vīra asked, "Are you then not settled?
He replied, "The Buddhas are likewise. Vīra said, "You are not the Buddhas. He replied, "The Buddhas are also..."
It was not Pārśva. He spoke a verse, saying: "This ground has turned the color of gold; it is known in advance that a Sage is arriving.

He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and having perfected the awakening flower, he will attain enlightenment. Yaśas then spoke a verse: "The Teacher sits upon the golden ground and constantly speaks the meaning of reality.
Turning his light back, he shines upon me; now he enters samādhi. Pārśva understood his intention and immediately ordained him as a renunciant.
Furthermore, having completed the chapter on the precepts, he addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you. You must protect and keep it in mind.
He then spoke this verse: "The true body is spontaneous; the true cause is the true teaching. If one understands it through principle, there is neither true nor false dharma.
Even practice has no cessation. Having thus transmitted the Dharma, Hui-xi manifested supernatural transformations and entered nirvana, transforming into fire.

The śarīra spontaneously ignited and descended from the sky in numbers beyond counting. The fourfold assembly gathered them in their robes and constructed stupas at various locations to offer worship.
This occurred in the twenty-seventh year of King Zhen Ding of the Zhou dynasty in this land, the year of Jihai (459 CE).
In North India there was Asaṅga, who widely propagated the teachings of the religion; his younger brother, Vasubandhu, initially adhered to the Hīnayāna and composed five treatises.
Vasubandhu. Asaṅga, perceiving that his faculties and conditions were about to ripen, feigned illness and summoned him back.
When they were but one station away, he dispatched a disciple to go and meet him. That night they stayed together in the same lodging. The disciple recited a verse, saying:

"If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all is created by mind alone. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu was suddenly enlightened.

He attained enlightenment and repented of his past transgressions of slander, realizing they were all due to his faculty of the tongue. He immediately rose from his bed, took up a sharp blade, and intended to cut out his own tongue.
Asanga perceived this from afar, reached out his arm, and seized him, admonishing him, saying: "You have now awakened to the Mahāyāna."
"Truly, the time has come. Formerly you disparaged me with your tongue; now you ought to praise me with your tongue. If you were to cut out your tongue and remain silent, what benefit would there be?
Vasubandhu then desisted. He traveled by night under the stars until he could visit Asaṅga.

There, he listened attentively to the instructions of Maitreya and subsequently composed five hundred Mahāyāna treatises, earning him the title "The Master of a Thousand Treatises. One day, while Asaṅga entered the *dharmaprakāśa-samādhi*, [Vasubandhu beheld the Buddha Amitābha].
At night, he ascended to Tuṣita Heaven and inquired about the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from Maitreya Bodhisattva. Maitreya spoke eighty verses;
Asaṅga composed a commentary in two fascicles based on eighteen topical sections. Vasubandhu composed a commentary in three fascicles based on the severing of twenty-seven doubts.
Furthermore, while Vasubandhu was lecturing on the *Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra* for the assembly, the meaning of what he taught in a single day—namely...
He composed a single verse to summarize it and circulated it throughout various countries; however, the masters and teachers were unable to understand it.
Consequently, he himself composed a prose commentary on the verse (which is the present *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*). One day, when Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Asaṅga asked him:
"Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for those gods. In a single session, Maitreya..."

Five hundred billion devaputras attained the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). [The interlocutor] asked, "I do not yet know what Dharma was preached.
Vasubandhu replied, "It was precisely this very Dharma that was preached; it was merely that the Sanskrit sounds were elegant and refined, making it a joy for people to hear."

Hài (ending in the eleventh year of King Xian of Zhou, Year Wùxū):
The Eleventh Patriarch, Pūrṇāśa, transmits the Dharma to Aśvaghoṣa.
Pūrṇāśa was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; his secular surname was Gautama. His father was Ratnagātra, who had seven sons. [The eldest was] Rātra...

Upasena was the youngest [of the brothers]. From his youth, his inclinations differed from those of his elder brothers. He once said, "If I should encounter a Great Being seated in a place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I shall go there to attend upon him and rejoice in his merit.
When he met the Venerable Pārśva, the latter subsequently transmitted the Dharma to him.
Among those taught by Upasena who attained the fruits [of the path], there were already five hundred. Later, when he arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was an elder who came...
He went to that assembly. Upagupta said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātr̥ceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Mātr̥ceṭa paid his respects and asked, "I wish to know the Buddha; which one is he?
Upagupta replied, "If you wish to know the Buddha, it is he whom you do not recognize. Mātr̥ceṭa said, "Since the Buddha cannot be recognized..."
"How do you know it is this? Vasubandhu asked. Yaśas said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not? Aśvaghoṣa said, "This is the meaning of the saw.
Yaśas said, "That is the meaning of the wood. He then asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? [Aśvaghoṣa] replied, "It emerges level with the teacher."
Aśvaghoṣa then asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? [The master] replied, "You have been liberated by me. Aśvaghoṣa was suddenly enlightened and subsequently requested ordination.
Nāgasena said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly the King of Viśālī.
Because there was a class of naked people in his kingdom who were like horses in their exposure, the King exercised his supernatural powers and divided his body into silkworms for them."
He then obtained his robes. Later, he was reborn in Central India. Because the horse-man had wept with longing and sorrow, he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry).

The Tathāgata had previously made a prophecy: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa shall, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, subdue those of heterodox paths and continue my transmission of the Dharma.
Now is precisely that time. He then addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now..."
He entrusted it to you, and spoke this verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are never separate.

Now I entrust to you this dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two. Having completed the transmission of the dharma, he immediately manifested spiritual transformations and entered profound, perfect stillness (parinirvāṇa).
The assembly erected a precious stupa to enshrine his entire body. This was in the nineteenth year of King Zhou'an of this land, the Wuxu year.
The *Zongjing lu* states: On Mount Vindhya in the Western Heavens, there was an arhat named Pūrṇa.
Aśvaghoṣa went to visit him and found him sitting upright in the forest, his spirit so vast and profound that he seemed unfathomable.
Aśvaghoṣa said to him, "If you, śramaṇa, speak, I dare to clarify my own views; I must certainly humble you. If I do not prevail, I shall cut my own throat to apologize. The arhat...
Han remained silent; his expression showed neither signs of defeat nor of victory. Though he was questioned four or five times, he never responded in accordance with the spirit of the inquiry.
Ming withdrew and reflected to himself: "I am defeated; he has won. He remains peaceful and speechless, thus there is nothing by which he can be humbled.
It is because I rely on words that, despite my speaking, I might be humbled. As long as I cannot avoid words, I am truly to be pitied. Thereupon, he threw [himself down].
[He] left the household life. This account differs from that in the *Chuanteng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp); both should be noted.

[Jiamu] The twelfth patriarch, Aśvaghoṣa, transmitted the Dharma to Kātyāyanīputra.
The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa was a native of Vārāṇasī; he was also named Kāśyapa because his cultivated and unconditioned merits were most preeminent.
Having received the seal of the mind from Yaśas, he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and refuted all heterodox arguments.
Once, a non-Buddhist came to seek a debate on doctrine, and the king, his ministers, and the fourfold assembly were all assembled together.
At the assembly for debate, Aśvaghoṣa asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? [The opponent] replied, "Whatever is spoken, I am able to refute it all.
Aśvaghoṣa then pointed to the king and said, "The land is currently peaceful and prosperous, and Your Majesty enjoys long life;
I request that you refute this. The non-Buddhist was thus subdued. Subsequently, at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma. Suddenly, an old man appeared before his seat.
He prostrated himself on the ground. Aśvaghoṣa said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be extraordinary signs. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Suddenly, a golden man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. Pointing her right hand toward Aśvaghoṣa, she spoke this verse:
"I bow my head to the Venerable Elder; You shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this very ground, you shall proclaim and spread [the Dharma]."
After he had finished reciting the verse on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he suddenly vanished from sight. Aśvaghoṣa said, "A māra is about to come to contend with me for strength.
After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently, and heaven and earth became dark and gloomy. Aśvaghoṣa said, "It is certain that the māra has come;
I shall eliminate him. He then pointed toward the sky, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power and shaking the mountains and peaks.
As Aśvaghoṣa sat solemnly upon his seat, the demonic activities subsided accordingly. After seven days, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, concealing its form beneath the seat.
Aśvaghoṣa took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation produced by Māra."
They were merely eavesdropping on my Dharma; thus, I released them and let them depart. Yet the Māras could not move [him]. Aśvaghoṣa addressed them, saying:
"If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers. Thereupon, they resumed their original forms, prostrated, and repented.
Aśvaghoṣa asked: "What are your names? How many are your retinues? They replied: "My name is Kambalāśvatara. I have three thousand followers."

[The disciple] belonged [to him]. Maming asked, "Exerting the full power of your spiritual transformations, what can you create? He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat.
Maming said, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*)? He asked, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'? "I have never known it," he replied.

Maming then explained the ocean of nature for him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth all depend upon it for their establishment. The three samādhis and the six supernormal powers arise from it..."
Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra was inspired with faith; he and his three thousand followers together sought ordination.

Aśvaghoṣa then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon them. He further addressed them, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata shall now be entrusted to you.
Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma; light and darkness are originally [one]...'"

"Non-dual. Now I entrust to you the Dharma of realization, which is neither grasped nor abandoned. Having thus entrusted [the teaching], he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*nāgavikrīḍita-samādhi*).
His body rose into the air like the orb of the sun, and then he manifested his passing into extinction.

The Thirteenth Patriarch, Kāpimāra, transmitted the Dharma to Nāgārjuna.
Kāpimāra was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Initially, he was a non-Buddhist practitioner with three thousand followers; he was well-versed in all heterodox doctrines.
Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his disciples to Western India.
There was a crown prince there named Meghasvabhāva who, hearing the name of Upamanyu, invited him to the palace to provide offerings.
Upamanyu said, "The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not draw near kings, ministers, or families of great power. Meghasvabhāva replied, "In my country now..."
To the north of the city was a great mountain. Within the mountain was a stone cave. "Could you practice dhyāna in silence here? he asked.
Māra replied, "Yes," and immediately entered that mountain. After traveling several *li*, he encountered a large python.
Māra walked straight forward, paying no heed, as the serpent coiled itself around his body. Māra then conferred the Three Refuges upon it; once the serpent had heard them, it departed. Māra...

As they were about to reach the stone cave, another elderly man emerged dressed in plain garments. He joined his palms in greeting and inquired after their well-being. Māra asked, "Where do you reside?
He replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude. However, novice bhikṣus frequently came to seek my instruction;
I grew weary of responding to them and gave rise to thoughts of anger and resentment. Consequently, at the end of my life, I fell into this state as a python."
"I have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years. Having just encountered you, Venerable Sir, I was able to hear the Dharma of the precepts; thus I have come to express my gratitude.
Māra asked, "Are there any other inhabitants dwelling on this mountain? He replied, "Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree."

It provides shade for five hundred great dragons; this king of trees is named Nāgavṛkṣa (Dragon Tree). He has frequently preached the Dharma for the dragon hosts, and I too have heard and received it from him.
Māra then went with his followers to that place. Nāgavṛkṣa came out to meet them and said, "This deep mountain is solitary and desolate."
"This is the dwelling of dragons and pythons. Great Virtue and Supreme One, why do you deign to travel here on foot? Nāgārjuna replied, "I am not a supreme one;
I have come to visit a worthy sage. Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself: "Has this master attained the nature of certainty? Does he possess the clear eye of the Way?

Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle? Māra said, "Though you speak only with your mind, I already know it by my own mind. Simply prepare for your renunciation; what need is there to worry about me?"
[The dragon] did not realize he was a sage. Upon hearing this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. Māra immediately granted him liberation;

together with five hundred dragon followers, they all received full ordination (*upasampadā*). He further addressed them, saying: "I now entrust the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye to you."
Listen attentively to these verses: "The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

One who awakens to this dharma of the hidden and the manifest is neither a fool nor a wise man. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and used fire to cremate his body.
Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored relics and erected a stupa there; this was in the forty-sixth year of King Nan Wang of the Zhou dynasty, the *Renchen* year.
Nāgārjuna was also known as Nāgasena. A native of South India, while still a nursing infant, he heard the Brahmins reciting the four Vedas, totaling forty thousand verses;
he mastered both the words and their meanings. As he grew up, he became proficient in all arts, including astronomy, geography, astrology, and cartography, mastering them all without exception.
Later, having encountered misfortune due to his mastery of these arts, he realized that desire is the root of suffering.
Having left the household life, he entered a stone cave where he dwelt with Nāgārjuna and became a refuge for the assembly of nāgas. There he encountered Māra, who entrusted him with the Dharma.

Over the course of ninety days, he recited and mastered all the sūtras and treatises existing in Jambudvīpa. He further reflected: "Although the Buddha’s sūtras in this world are sublime, their phrasing and meaning are not yet exhaustive.
I shall further expound upon them to enlighten future students. Then the Great Dragon Bodhisattva, by means of his supernatural power...
[He] entered the dragon palace by means of his supernatural power. [The dragon] opened a casket of seven treasures and gave him various Vaipulya sūtras.

Within ninety days, he had thoroughly mastered a great many. The dragon asked, "As you read these scriptures now, have you finished them all? Shu replied, "Your scriptures are immeasurable; they cannot be exhausted.
What I have read today alone exceeds ten times that of Jambudvīpa. The dragon said, "In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are..."
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, exceeding this by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, he dwelt in the palace of the nāgas to practice, deeply penetrating the non-arising [of phenomena].

The nāgas escorted him out of the palace; thereafter, he greatly propagated the Buddha-dharma and composed treatises such as the *Mahā-Abhayamati*, totaling several hundred thousand verses (the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is one chapter of this, as is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa*).
The Sūtra says: 'After the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there shall be in a future age one from Southern India...'"
The Bhikṣu Zhú, whose title was Nāgārjuna, was able to refute the doctrines of existence and non-existence and manifest our Mahāyāna Dharma.

He attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy, and was reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Nāgārjuna entered the Dragon Palace and examined the treasury; there he saw the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in three versions:
the Upper Version, consisting of verses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen worlds and chapters as numerous as the atoms in four world-systems (*cāturdvīpaka*).

The middle version consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters. The abbreviated version consists of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.
The expanded version is such that none but a Buddha can know it; the middle version can only be known by Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Consequently, [the Master] recorded the abbreviated version and returned to the Western Land (India). It was transmitted from the Western Land to China in eighty fascicles.
The Sūtra consists of thirty-nine chapters, which are divided into seven locations and nine assemblies. First Assembly: At the Bodhimaṇḍa; six chapters in eleven fascicles.
Samantabhadra is the presiding host. Second Assembly: In the Hall of Universal Radiance; six chapters in four fascicles. Mañjuśrī is the presiding host.
Third Assembly: In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; six chapters in three fascicles. Dharmamati is the presiding host. Fourth [Assembly]...

The fifth assembly was held in the Yāma Heaven; four sections in three fascicles were spoken, with Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha as the presiding master of the assembly. The sixth assembly was held in the Tuṣita Heaven;
three sections in twelve fascicles were spoken, with Vajradhvaja as the presiding master of the assembly. The seventh assembly was held in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; one section was spoken.
Vajragarbha serves as the presiding master of the assembly. In the seventh assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*), eleven chapters in thirteen fascicles are taught;

therein, the "Universal Worthy Chapter" (*Samantabhadra-parivarta*) discusses the cause of equality, while the "Tathāgata’s Manifestation Chapter" (*Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava-parivarta*) discusses the fruit of equality.
In the eighth assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance, one chapter in seven fascicles is taught, also by Universal Worthy. In the ninth assembly at Jetavana...
The Forest (Lín) speaks of one chapter in twenty-one fascicles; this is the Tathāgata acting as a virtuous friend.
This is the lower version of the first division, consisting of thirty-six thousand verses, with sixty-four thousand verses still remaining. The nine chapters exist in the Western Land.

(己丑) The Fourteenth Patriarch, Nāgārjuna, transmits the Dharma to Kāṇadeva.
Having already received the Dharma from Māra, Nāgārjuna later traveled to South India. The people of that country mostly believed in the efficacy of meritorious deeds (*puṇya-karman*).
When Nāgārjuna preached the Dharma for them, they said to one another, "If a person possesses meritorious deeds, they are foremost in the world; it is all in vain to speak otherwise."
"Buddha-nature—who can perceive it? The tree said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride.
The man asked, "Is Buddha-nature large or small? The tree said, "It is neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow; without merit and without retribution; neither dying nor being born.
Hearing these superior principles, they all returned to their original resolve. The tree then manifested its sovereign body from its seat.
It was like the full moon disk; all the assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and did not perceive the appearance of the tree.
Among that assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who said to the assembly, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never seen such a thing with our eyes."
"How can one distinguish them? Deva replied, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essential form and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us.
How do we know this? It is because through the signless samādhi, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.
As he finished speaking, the wheel-marked hands vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The body manifests as the full moon,"
The marks manifest the essence of all Buddhas; the preaching of the Dharma has no form, and its function distinguishes that which is neither sound nor color.

When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly realized non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life in their quest for liberation. The tree then shaved their hair and commanded the sages to confer the full ordination upon them.
At that time, there were five thousand non-Buddhist practitioners from South India who employed great magical illusions; the King and the people of the land were [overwhelmed by them].

However, he followed him without knowing that it was the Buddha. The tree was moved by this sentiment and changed its demeanor; clothed in white and holding a banner, it would always wait for the king’s departure and hasten before him, appearing and disappearing at intervals. This continued for seven years. One day, the king suddenly noticed this and asked, "Who are you that precedes my procession? I cannot catch up with you, yet even when I let you go, you do not leave. The tree replied: [The tree replied: "I am a tree spirit. Because I have long admired your majesty's virtue and wished to follow you, I transformed myself into this form. I have been waiting for your departure for seven years now. The king then asked, "What is your wish? The tree said, "I wish to become a human being. The king said, "If you truly desire to become a human, you must first undergo the tonsure and don the saffron robes. The tree immediately shed its bark and leaves, and its body became that of a young monk. The king then took him as his attendant. Later, the king went out on a journey. The young monk, following behind, saw a woman by the roadside who was weeping bitterly. He asked her why she was crying. She said, "My husband has gone abroad to trade. It has been three years since he left, and I have heard no news of him. I fear he may have perished, and thus I weep. The young monk said, "Do not worry. I shall go with you to find him. They traveled together for several days until they reached a mountain pass. There, the young monk suddenly vanished. The woman looked back and saw him sitting atop a tree, smiling down at her. She realized then that he was a tree spirit. She returned home and told her family. Her parents went to the mountain and searched for him, but could not find him. They returned and reported this to the king. The king sent messengers to summon the young monk, but he did not appear. The king then went to the mountain himself. When he reached the foot of the tree, the young monk emerged from the tree and bowed to the king. The king asked, "Why did you vanish? The young monk replied, "I am a tree spirit. Because I saw the woman weeping, I felt compassion for her and wished to comfort her, so I manifested myself. Now that I have fulfilled my purpose, I shall return to my original form. The king said, "You have already become a human being; why do you still wish to return to a tree? The young monk said, "A human life is fleeting and full of suffering. I wish to cultivate the Way and seek liberation. Therefore, I do not desire to remain a human. The king then permitted him to return to his original state. The young monk ascended the tree and resumed his form as a tree. The king sighed and said, "How extraordinary! A mere tree spirit can possess such wisdom and resolve. How much more so those who are capable of self-cultivation! Thus, he honored the tree as a field of merit. From that time on, the tree flourished and grew large, eventually becoming a great banyan tree. To this day, people call it the "King’s Tree" (Rājavṛkṣa). It is located in the kingdom of Sāvatthī. Those who visit it and offer incense and flowers will often see the tree spirit manifesting in various forms to protect and benefit sentient beings. This is the power of the Buddha’s transformative influence. Thus ends the story of the King’s Tree.
He said, "I am a wise man; I know all dharmas. The king asked, "Do you know what the devas are doing now?
The tree said, "The devas are currently at war with the asuras. The king asked, "How can this be known? The tree said, "It will be evident shortly."
Suddenly, spears, halberds, hands, and feet descended from the sky in a chaotic swirl. The King then conceived great faith and reverence;

he commanded all the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) to prostrate themselves before the tree, but the tree transformed them all, causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. Later, he said to his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva:
"The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata shall now be entrusted to you. He then recited this verse for him: "To clarify..."

Having taught the Dharma of concealment and manifestation, he then expounded the principle of liberation. Regarding this Dharma, his mind did not grasp at realization; he was without anger and without joy.

Having entrusted the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*) and extensively manifested supernatural transformations. He then returned to his original seat and entered stillness.

On the seventh day, as rain fell and śarīra were showered down, a tree grew back upon his seat. Pointing to the sky, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In the past, the younger brother of Kāśyapa Buddha..."

"Son, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had three vows: first, when he was a Buddha, whenever a holy person was transformed and delivered by him, the heavens would send down rain, and his body would entirely become śarīras;
second, everything produced upon the great earth would be fit to serve as medicine to heal the illnesses of sentient beings;
third, all who possess wisdom would attain the subtle and profound knowledge that allows them to penetrate past lives. Now it rains."
"Śāriputra, this is the supernatural power of Mahākāśyapa. Having said this, he became silent once more. Kanadeva and the assembly erected a stūpa and enshrined his entire body therein.
This was in the thirty-fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin, the year of Jichou.
