(Geng-chen) The Fifteenth Patriarch, Kanadeva, transmitted the Dharma to Rāhulata.
Kanadeva was a native of South India, of the Viśvāmitra clan. Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while also delighting in philosophical debate.
Later, he went to visit Nāgārjuna. As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, knowing him to be a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant to place a bowl filled with water before his seat.
When Āryadeva saw this, he immediately threw a single needle into it and proceeded inside. They were delighted by their mutual accord. Nāgārjuna then preached the Dharma for him;
without rising from his seat, he manifested the form of a lunar disc. Having thus received the Dharma, Āryadeva...
His fame resounded throughout the Five Indies. Yet he remained concerned that people did not place trust in his words.

At that time, there was a great Īśvara deity in India, whose body was of true golden color and stood twenty feet tall; whatever anyone requested of him, it was always fulfilled according to their wishes.
Deva visited the temple and saw it; ten thousand people followed him inside. The image indeed blinked its eyes as if in anger.
Deva said, "It is a deity, indeed, but how small it is! It ought to move people through its majestic spirit and transform beings through its wisdom and virtue.
To use gold for its body and glass for its eyes to deceive the world—this is not what I expected. He then climbed upon its shoulder and chiseled the eyes out.
As for his eyes, onlookers marveled, saying, "How could Maheśvara be so humbled and distressed by a mere minor brāhmaṇa?
Deva said, "The deity is vast and remote; therefore, he tested me with a mundane matter. Since I have won his heart, I dared to act thus.
Thereupon, he prepared an offering. That night, Maheśvara descended to receive it and said, "You have attained..."
"My heart! People obtain my body; you offer me your heart, while others present me with their physical substance.
It is you who know me and revere me; it is those people who, out of fear, slander me. Yet your offering is most excellent; it simply lacks what I desire.
Deva asked, "What does the deity require? Mahādeva said, "I am missing my left eye. Can you bestow it upon me? Deva laughed.
He immediately drew forth his own eyes and gave them to him; the more he gave, the more they were inexhaustible.
From dawn until dusk, he produced tens of thousands of eyeballs. Shen Zan said, "Excellent, Mahāmaṇavaka! This is truly a supreme gift. What do you seek? Deva replied:
I have received this illumination within my own mind; it does not depend on external things. Later, I arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was an elder there named Brahmāyuśas. One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden, like fungi, and their flavor was most exquisite.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhula, took them and ate them. As soon as they were taken, they grew back again; once exhausted, they sprouted anew. As for the rest...
None of his relatives were able to see him. Deva, knowing the cause from their past lives, went to their home.
When the elder asked the reason for this, Deva said, "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu. However, that bhikṣu’s insight into the Path was not yet clear;

he consumed the faithful offerings in vain, and thus his retribution was to become a wooden fungus. It is only because you and your son have made offerings with diligent devotion that you are able to see it."
"Only those who have attained [realization] may enjoy it; others may not. He asked again, "How old are you, Elder?
He replied, "I am seventy-nine. Deva then spoke this verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, One returns to this body to consume the faithful offerings.
At eighty-one years of age, This tree shall no longer grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was deeply moved by his admiration and submission, saying, "Disciple..."
He was aged and infirm, unable to serve his teacher. He wished to relinquish his second son so that he might follow the teacher and leave the household life.
Deva said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. That we have met now is surely in accord with our past causes.
He then shaved the boy's hair and they went to the city of Pāṭaliputra. There, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma, and he devised a plan for it.
After some time, Deva took up a long banner and entered into their midst. They asked him, "Why do you not go before us?
Deva replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You appear to be a lowly person. Deva said, "You appear to be a noble person. They asked, "What Dharma do you understand?
Deva said, "You do not understand even a hundred things. They said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. Deva [replied]...
Deva said, "I have clearly attained Buddhahood. The other replied, "It is not fitting for you to have attained it. Deva said, "Originally I claimed I had attained it; you truly have not attained it.
The other asked, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? Deva replied, "Because you harbor the notion of a self."
"Therefore, it cannot be attained; for I am without self, and I myself shall attain it. When his argument was thus defeated, he asked Deva, "What is your name?
Deva replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Since he had long heard of Deva's reputation, he repented his error and offered his apologies.
At that time, those in the assembly continued to raise various challenges and difficulties, which Deva refuted with unimpeded eloquence.
Thereupon, they submitted and took refuge. He then informed his senior disciple, Rāhulabhadra, and entrusted him with the Dharma-eye, saying in verse:
"I have explained the principle of liberation To you, the person who transmits the Dharma; In truth, there is no realization of the Dharma, Neither end nor beginning.

Having spoken this verse, he entered the Samādhi of Vigorous Prowess (*vejayanta-samādhi*), emitted eight rays of light from his body, and returned to nirvāṇa. The assembly of disciples erected a stūpa and made offerings. At that time...

This was the *gengchen* year, the nineteenth year of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty. In the second year of the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu of the Han, the General of the Flying Cavalry, Huo Qubing, campaigned against the Xiongnu.

The sixteenth patriarch, Rāhulata, transmitted the Dharma to Saṃghanandin.
Rāhulata was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī. There was a river there named...
The water was golden and its flavor exceptionally exquisite. In the middle of the stream, the reflections of the five Buddhas appeared once more.
Rāhulabhadra addressed the assembly, saying, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells the noble Saṃghanandin.
The Buddha prophesied that one thousand years hence, he shall succeed to the holy position. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream until they reached [the source].
He saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption. Rāhulabhadra and the assembly waited for him for twenty-one days before he finally arose from his concentration.
Rāhulabhadra asked, "Is your body in concentration, or is your mind in concentration? Saṃghanandin replied, "Both my body and my mind are in concentration.
Rāhulabhadra said, "If both body and mind are in concentration, how can there be entering or emerging [from it]? Saṃghanandin replied:
"Though there is coming and going, the characteristic of concentration is not lost; it is like gold in a well—the essence of the gold remains eternally still.

Rādhagupta said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself is neither moving nor still. What is it that comes and goes? Nandika said, "If one speaks of the movement or stillness of the gold, what is it that comes and goes?
If one speaks of the coming and going of the gold, the gold itself is neither moving nor still. Rādhagupta said, "If the gold is in..."
[The Buddha said: "Well. What is that which comes out? If gold comes out of the well, what remains inside? Nanda replied: 'If gold comes out of the well, what remains is not gold;
if gold remains in the well, what comes out is not [gold]. Rādha said: 'This meaning is not so. Nanda said: 'That meaning is not tenable.
Rādha said: 'This meaning must fall away. Nanda said: 'This meaning is not established.'"
Rādhagupta said: "Your thesis is not established; my thesis is established. Nandika said: "Although my thesis is established, the Dharma is not 'I'. Rādhagupta said:
"My thesis is already established, because 'I' does not exist. Nandika said: "Because 'I' does not exist..."
"What further meaning does this establish? Rādhagupta replied, "Because there is no self for me, your proposition is thereby established.

Nandika asked, "Venerable sir, who was your teacher from whom you attained this realization of non-self? Rādhagupta replied, "My teacher was Kāṇadeva; it was he who realized this non-self. Nandika then praised him with a verse:
"I bow my head to the teacher Kāṇadeva, From whom you yourself have emerged. Since you, O venerable one, are free of self, [So too is he]."
"I wish to take you, O virtuous one, as my teacher. Rādha replied in verse: "Since I am already without a self, you must perceive my self;
if you would take me as your teacher, know that my self is not a self. Nandika’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought liberation.

Rādha said, "Your mind is sovereign; it is not bound by me. Having spoken, he immediately took up the golden bowl with his right hand and raised it to the Brahma palace, where he took that fragrant food to provide for the great assembly. Suddenly, the members of the assembly felt a sense of revulsion.
Rādha said, "This is not my fault; it is the result of your own karma. He then commanded Nanda to share his seat and eat with him. The assembly was again astonished by this.
Rādha said, "That you were unable to eat was entirely due to this reason. You should know that he who shared his seat with me was the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifested his traces here; you all have likewise adorned yourselves [for the same purpose]."

Within the kalpa, [Nandika] had already attained the third fruit but had not yet realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our teacher is indeed credible.
However, as for his claim regarding the Buddhas of the past, they harbored secret doubts. Nandika, perceiving the arrogance of the sentient beings, said:
During the time when the World-Honored One was present, the world was level and even; there were no hills, rivers, ditches, or moats. All water was sweet and delicious;

plants and trees flourished, and the lands were abundant. There were no eight kinds of suffering, and people practiced the ten wholesome deeds. Since he manifested his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees, more than eight hundred years have passed.
The world has become desolate, plants and trees are withered and parched, people lack profound faith, and their right mindfulness is slight and feeble.
He had faith in *tathatā* (Suchness) and cherished only the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*).

Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the *vajra*-wheel, where he took up nectar-water in a lapis lazuli vessel and brought it to the assembly. When the great multitude saw this, they immediately felt deep admiration;
repenting their faults, they prostrated themselves. Thereupon, Rādhagupta charged Nandimitra with the Dharma-eye, saying in verse: Regarding the Dharma...
In reality, there is no realization; there is neither grasping nor abandoning. Phenomena possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence. How, then, could they arise internally or externally?

Having heard these instructions, Nandi respectfully and diligently attended to them. He then spoke a verse of praise, saying: "Excellent, O Great Sage! Your mind’s clarity surpasses that of the sun and moon.
A single ray of light illuminates the world, and the darkness of Māra is not left unextracted. After Rāhulabhadra had finished transmitting the Dharma, he sat peacefully.
He returned to quiescence. The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for him; this was the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Han Wudi of this land, the *wuchen* year (30 B.C.).
(Dingwei) The Seventeenth Patriarch, Saṃghanandin, transmitted the Dharma to Gayāśata.
Saṃghanandin was a native of Śrāvastī, the son of King Ratnavyuha. He was able to speak from birth and constantly...
He performed acts of praising the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my Flesh-and-Blood Mother. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me.

His parents tried to dissuade him firmly, but he subsequently refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the home-life while remaining at home, giving him the name Saṃghanandin. They further commanded him—
The śramaṇa Śāṇavāsa served as his teacher for nineteen years without ever feeling weary or discouraged. He often thought to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life?
One night, as a divine light shone down from above, he saw a path that was level and smooth. Without realizing it, he began to walk slowly along it.
After about ten li, he arrived before a great cliff where there was a stone cave; he then entered its midst to dwell in quiet seclusion.
Once the father had lost his son, he immediately banished Śāṇakavāsin and departed the country to search for him, but did not know where he was.
Ten years passed. After Saṃghanandin encountered Rāhulabhadra, received the Dharma, and obtained a prediction, he traveled to propagate the teaching in the kingdom of Mathurā.
Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and comfort to both body and mind; yet they did not know how it came to be. Difficult...
Tandi said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue. Surely a sage shall appear in the world to continue the ancestral lamp.
Having spoken, he used his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly on a journey through the mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.
He pointed to the assembly and said, "At the summit of this peak, there is purple cloud like a canopy; a sage dwells here. He then led the assembly to wander about.
After a long time, he saw a mountain cottage where a young boy was holding a round mirror and walking straight toward Nandī.
Nandī asked, "How old are you? The boy replied, "One hundred years. Nandī said, "You are still a child; why do you say you are one hundred years old?
The boy said, "I do not understand the principle; I am truly one hundred years old. Nandī asked, "Are you skilled in wit? The boy said, "The Buddha said: 'If a person is born...'"
"One who lives for a hundred years without comprehending the pivot of the Buddhas is not equal to one who lives for a single day and attains definitive realization.
Nandika asked, "What does that which is in your hand symbolize? The youth replied, "It is the great perfect mirror of all Buddhas, without flaw or obscuration within or without."
The two of them both saw [the light], and their mental vision was identical. When his parents heard their son’s words, they immediately allowed him to leave the household life.
Nandika escorted him to his original dwelling; once he had received full ordination, he was named Gayāśīrṣa.
Later, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, Nandika asked, "Is it the bells that ring, or is it the wind? Śīrṣa replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells."
"Śāṇakavāsin said, 'It is my mind that resounds. Nandi said, 'And who is this mind? Śāṇakavāsin said, 'Because all is utterly tranquil.
Nandi said, 'Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way? He then transmitted the Dharma-eye, saying in verse:"
The mind-ground is fundamentally without birth; the ground of practice arises from conditions. Conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another; it is the same for flowers and fruits.

Once Saṃghanandin had transmitted the Dharma, he passed away while grasping the tree with his right hand. The assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree;
shall its shade provide shelter for future generations? They then decided to enshrine his entire body on a high plateau and erect a stūpa. The assembly...
They were unable to lift it with their strength. When they pulled it with the strength of many elephants, it still would not move. They then set fire to it beneath the tree;
when his body was consumed, the tree became even more lush and verdant. This occurred in the thirteenth year of Emperor Zhao of the Han dynasty, the year of Dingwei.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Seventeen; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Eighteen (Lai series).

Wu-yin (the Yongguang era was inaugurated); Gui-wei (the Jianzhao era was inaugurated); Wu-zhi (the Jingning era was inaugurated); Ji-chou (the first year of Emperor Cheng’s Jianshi era);

(Ren'yin, the third year of Yuanshi of Emperor Ping of the Han dynasty; ceased.

The second year of Hongjia: Liu Xiang, Grand Master for Imperial Entertainments, compiled the *Biographies of Transcendents* (*Shenxian zhuan*), stating that from the time of the Yellow Emperor down to the present, one hundred and forty-nine individuals had attained the Way of the Transcendents; of these, seventy-four—
The person replied, "I have already seen Buddhist scriptures. Furthermore, I have observed that when extensively examining the classical texts, Buddhist scriptures are frequently encountered.
In the year Jiwu (138 CE), during the first year of the Yuanshou era, Emperor Jing sent an envoy to the country of Da Yuezhi; upon his return, he obtained the *Futu jing* (Buddhist scriptures).
At that time, there was no one who recognized him.
(Wu-shen) The eighteenth patriarch, Gayasata, transmitted the Dharma to Kumāralāta.
Gayasata was a native of the country of Mathura; his secular surname was Uttara, his father was Deva-śaila, and his mother was Bhadra-āryā. He once...
The Great Deity appeared in a dream holding a mirror; consequently, she conceived. After seven days, she gave birth; her body was as translucent as lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).

She never required bathing or washing, for she was naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, she delighted in seclusion and her speech was extraordinary. As a child, she would go out to play while holding a mirror.
After meeting with the Venerable Saṃghanandin and receiving the Dharma-transmission, he led his disciples to the kingdom of Mahācīna.
There he perceived an extraordinary fragrance emanating from a Brahmin’s house; he frequently entered that house. The master of the house, Kumāralata, asked him:
"What kind of assembly is this? Śāta replied, "They are the disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his spirit was suddenly stirred;
he immediately closed the door. After a long while, Śāta knocked on the door. Rāta said, "There is no one in this house. Śāta said:
When asked, "Who is there who does not exist? Rādhagupta heard these words and, recognizing that it was someone else, hurriedly opened the door to welcome him.
Śreṣṭha pointed to the place beneath the eaves of the house where his dog used to sleep and said to Rādhagupta, "Your father buried gold here; now the dog guards it.
He then dug the ground and indeed found the gold. Śreṣṭha further said to Rādhagupta, "In the past, the World-Honored One made this prophecy..."
He said, "One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, there will appear a Great Being in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Yuezhi) who shall propagate and flourish the profound transformation.
Now you have encountered me; you should respond to this auspicious destiny. Thereupon, Rādhagupta awakened to the wisdom of his past lives and, with sincere devotion, entered the monastic order.

Śāradvatīputra transmitted it to Gayāśata. Having conferred the full precepts upon him, he entrusted him with the Dharma-eye, speaking this verse: "There is the seed and the field of the mind; Through causes and conditions, they can bring forth illumination.
When there is no obstruction among conditions, Birth after birth, there is non-arising. Having thus completed the transmission of the Dharma to Gayāśata, [Śāradvatīputra passed away].
He leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations. Entering the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
The multitude erected a stūpa for his relics; this was during the twentieth year of Chengdi’s reign in this land of China, the year Wushen.
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle 18;
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle 19 (Shu character series).

The first year of the founding of the state (Jian’guo): Jiashu (newly changed to Tianfeng); Gengchen (newly changed to Dihuang); Guiwei (the first year of the Han Gengshi era); Yiyou (the first year of Jianwu of Emperor Guangwu of Eastern Han);

[Renwu]—the nineteenth patriarch, Kumāralāta, transmitted the Dharma to Jayanta.

Kumāralāta was the son of a brāhmaṇa from the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi. Formerly, while he was a lord among the devas of the six heavens of the desire realm, he beheld the jeweled necklace of a bodhisattva and suddenly gave rise to a mind of attachment. Consequently, he fell and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There, he heard Kausika preach the Prajñāpāramitā; because the Dharma is supreme, he ascended to the Brahmā Heaven, and because his faculties were sharp, he excelled at expounding the Dharma.
It was essential that the various heavenly beings take him as their guide. As the time had come for him to succeed to his ancestral lineage, he subsequently descended upon the country of the Yuezhi.
Having received the Dharma, he later traveled to the kingdom of Central India. There was a Mahāsattva named Jayata who asked him:

"In my family, our parents have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illnesses. Whatever we undertake is never as we intend. However, in the house of my neighbor..."

For a long time he has practiced the deeds of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body remains ever vigorous and healthy, and all his undertakings are successful. How fortunate is he, and what crime have I committed?
Kumāralāta said: "Why do you doubt this? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time.

Ordinary people, seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, then claim that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty."
One does not realize that cause and effect follow one another without the slightest deviation; even if a hundred thousand million kalpas were to pass, they would never perish.
When Śāṇakavāsin heard these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled. Kumāralāta said:

"Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists dependent upon consciousness, and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (avidyā). Non-awakening...
"Rely on the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
It is profoundly still and luminously aware. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas. All that is good or evil, conditioned or unconditioned, is like a dream or an illusion.
Śāṇakavāsin received these words and grasped their meaning; he immediately awakened his latent wisdom and made a fervent vow.
He requested to leave the household life. Kumāralāta asked, "What country are you from? You must inform your parents before you may become a renunciant.
Nyatā replied, "My country is North India; it is three thousand *li* from here. However, I possess a minor skill by which traveling back and forth is easy.
He then performed that skill, and together with Kumāralāta, they arrived there in an instant. Once Nyatā had informed his father...
The Mother. Rāhula then conferred full ordination upon him. Later, he told him: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived;

you should succeed me in carrying out the traces of my transformative work. He then entrusted him with the verse of the Dharma-eye: "In the nature of phenomena, there is originally no arising; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it.

Since nothing at all can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved? He further said: "This is the seeing of the nature of purity by the Tathāgata Sublime Sound."

"This is the phrase of purity. You should propagate it for future students. Having spoken these words, he immediately, while seated upon his throne, used his fingernails to gash his face until it opened like a red lotus, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly before entering parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsin erected a stūpa to enshrine his entire body; this was in the fourteenth year of the Xinmang era, the Renwu year (502 CE). [The Han Yongping era follows.]

In the fourth year [of the reign], Emperor Ming had a dream at night of a golden man over ten feet tall, with a sun disc encircling his neck and a svastika inscribed upon his chest, flying through the palace courtyard and radiating brilliant light.
In the morning, he questioned his ministers. The Grand Astrologer Fu Yi submitted this report:

"According to my examination of the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou), on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin, the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao’s reign, at the break of dawn—"

A strange wind suddenly arose, and the palaces and houses all shook violently. There was a five-colored radiance that pierced through the Taiwei constellation and spread in all four directions, appearing entirely in shades of blue and red.
The King questioned the Grand Astrologer Suyao, asking, "What auspicious omen is this?"
He replied, "A Great Sage has been born in the West. The King asked, "What of this? He replied, "At present there is nothing else;
however, after one thousand years, his teachings will reach here. The King then ordered that it be inscribed upon stone before the celestial shrine at the southern suburb.
Calculating by the number of years, from then until the present year of Xinyou, one thousand one hundred years have passed. "What Your Majesty dreamed must surely be this," [the monk said].

The Emperor believed him deeply and consequently dispatched eighteen men, including the General of the Household Cai Yin, the Doctors Wang Zun and Qin Jing, to the Western Regions to seek out that Way. The Buddha knew that the sentient beings of this land of Zhendan...

When the conditions ripened, he was brought forth to be transformed and taught. Lord Zitrong once said: "By the retribution of my past karma, I became a dragon of Qiongchi, confined beneath vast waters.
For years there have been cruel droughts, and the water has turned to mud. My body is so immense that there is no hole large enough to contain it.
As the blazing sun descends upon me, I suffer the torment of heat both inside and out. Within each of my scales, small insects have grown, biting and gnawing at me."
In my distress, one morning at the cool of dawn, the light suddenly broke through the sky. Five-colored clouds drifted past, shimmering with radiance; within them appeared an auspicious sign:
dark blue hair coiled in spirals, a golden countenance as bright as the moon. The mountain spirits and the River Lord, along with a multitude of beings, bowed their heads in prostration.
Their voices of praise and joy shook heaven and earth. Celestial incense swirled about, bringing the fragrance of spring wherever it reached. I then looked upward and wailed in lamentation.
"I pray that you deign to deliver all spirits. The various sages all said to me, "This is the Great Sage of the West, the World-Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Now that his teachings are circulating in the Eastern Land, he will manifest a transformation body to go to the Middle Kingdom.
Since you have encountered him, your past karma may be liberated. Thereupon, my body leaped up in joy and entered into the celestial radiance.
He fully recounted the principles of karmic retribution from the past. The World-Honored One replied, "Excellent, O Prince! You have been filial toward your family and loyal toward your state;
furthermore, you have felt compassion for the world and developed a mind of protection. Yet, as cause and effect were not yet complete, enemies came to contend with one another."
Because of the perception of a self and others, I gave rein to cruelty and transferred my anger onto other beings. Now that the karmic debt must be repaid, I repent once more and desire liberation.
At this time, do you still harbor thoughts of enmity or kinship, or the notions of hatred, anger, and delusion?
Having heard the ultimate truth, my mind has become clear and enlightened; internally and externally all is empty and still, abiding like space. Looking back upon myself—
His body was extinguished in accordance with his recollection, and he was again born as a man who attained the wisdom of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
I take refuge in him. *Fozu gangmu*, Volume Nineteen;
*Fozu gangmu*, Volume Twenty (Wang character series).

Jiazi (the seventh year of Emperor Ming of Han’s Yongping era); Bingzi (the first year of Emperor Zhang’s Jianchu era); Jia Shen (the era was changed to Yuanhe); Dinghai (the era was changed to Zhanghe);

Jichou (the first year of Emperor He’s Yongyuan era); Yisi (the era was changed to Yuanxing); Bingwu (the first year of Emperor Shang’s Yanping era); Dingwei (the first year of Emperor An’s Yongchu era);
Jiayin (the era was changed to Yuanchu); Gengshen (the era was changed to Yongning); Xinyou (the era was changed to Jianguang); Renxu (the era was changed to Yanguang); Guihai (Hanjian).
In the second year of Emperor [An] Lian-guang’s reign (the Ding-mao year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han), Buddhism first entered Zhendan.
In that same Ding-mao year, the Indian śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna arrived in Luoyang.

In the tenth year of the Yongping era, Cai Yin and others from the eastern lands reached the kingdom of Yuezhi, a neighbor to India, where they encountered the two Indian monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
These two monks intended to bring scriptures and images to this land of Zhendan; consequently, they returned together to the east. In the tenth year of Yongping, they arrived.
Upon arriving in Luoyang, Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the palace to present scriptures and images. The Emperor was greatly pleased and housed them at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì).

An Shìgāo also arrived later, traveling by circuitous routes. In the fourteenth year of Yongping, the year Jǐsī (57 CE), Emperor Ming issued an edict to establish a separate monastery outside the Yōng Gate to the west of Luoyang for them to reside in;
because they had come with the scriptures carried on white horses, it was consequently named Baima Si (The White Horse Monastery).
The Baima Monastery. The Emperor visited the monastery and asked Kāśyapa Mātanga: "After the Buddha appeared in the world, why did his transformation [of sentient beings] not reach this place?
Mātanga replied: "In India, the kingdom of Kapilavastu is where the Buddhas of the three periods appear throughout the trichiliocosm—the ten billion suns and moons.
Among the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all those who possess the power of aspiration [are gathered there]."

Those born therein receive transformation and awaken to the Way. Although Buddhas do not personally travel to other regions, wherever their radiant marks reach—whether for a thousand or five hundred years—there are always sages who transmit the Buddha’s voice and teachings to transform those who come.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. Kaśyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna stepped forward and said, "What building is that to the east of the temple?
The Emperor replied, "In the past, there was a mound that rose up without cause; when it was leveled, it appeared again as before. At night..."
A strange light appeared, and the common people called it a "sage’s tomb," subsequently offering sacrifices to it; they suspected it was the spirit of Luoyang.

Dharmakṣema said, “According to the records in the *Indic Golden Treasury* (*Tianzhu Jinzang*), King Aśoka enshrined the relics of the Tathāgata throughout the world in eighty-four thousand locations.
Within the borders of China today, there are nineteen such sites, and this is one of them. The Emperor was greatly astonished and immediately set out in his carriage.

He had the good fortune to pay his respects there when, suddenly, a circular halo appeared above the tomb. Within the light, the three bodies of the Buddha manifested. The attendants cried out, "Ten thousand years!

The Emperor said with joy, "Had I not met these two Great Beings, how could I have known of the lingering blessings of the Supreme Sage? He issued an edict to build a stupa over the site. Under the guidance of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, the construction was undertaken;
the stupa was completed in nine stories, reaching a height of two hundred feet. The following year, the light appeared once more, and gold... [was revealed].
A hand emerged from the top of the stupa, about one chi in height, appearing like lapis lazuli; within it, celestial incense was seen wafting fragrantly.

When the Emperor went in person to pay his respects, the light circled around him in accordance with his footsteps. It remained until the hour of Shen (3–5 p.m. before it vanished. The Emperor held the Buddha-dharma in profound reverence and faith.
In the fourteenth year of Yongping, the Daoist practitioners of the Five Peaks, including Chu Shanxin and Fei Shucaī, became envious of it.

They spoke out in condemnation, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is false and deceptive. Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna addressed the Emperor, saying, "Our Buddha’s Dharma of the world-transcending way cannot be destroyed by water or fire.

We request to verify this with the Daoist masters. The Emperor commanded Shenxin and others to bring forth all their marvelous scriptures and secret manuals to be placed alongside the Sanskrit manuscripts held by the śramaṇas.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, an altar was constructed for a fire-ordeal test. The fire was lit.
The Daoist scriptures were all consumed by the flames, while only the Buddhist sutras and images remained intact. The Daoists and their followers were filled with shame and died;
the entire assembly of Daoists bowed their heads in humble submission. Among the great multitude, Falan then sang this verse: "The fox is not of the lion’s kind;
A lamp does not possess the brilliance of the sun and moon. A pond does not have the capacity of the rivers and seas; A mound lacks the majesty of the mountains and peaks. [The Dharma-cloud...]
The world was brought to maturity; the sprouts of the seeds of goodness were able to unfurl. He manifested and propagated the rare Dharma, transforming sentient beings everywhere.
From this point on, the Emperor was increasingly struck with wonder and marvel. Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna mastered the Chinese language; after a long time, they translated five scriptures:

the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, the *Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika*), the *Severing the Bonds*, the *Buddha’s Previous Births* (*Jātakamālā*), and the *Treasury of the Dharma Ocean* (*Dharmasāgaragarbha*), as well as the *Buddha’s Original Deeds*. In the sixteenth year of Yongping, Śramaṇa...
Teng entered nirvana. Zhu Falan personally translated five scriptures in thirteen fascicles.
(Jiaxu) The twentieth patriarch, Jayata, transmitted the Dharma to Vaśu-pāṇḍu Jayata.
He was a native of Northern India, possessed of profound and deep wisdom, and converted immeasurable beings. Later, he arrived at Rājagṛha.
In that city, he propagated the sudden teaching (sudden enlightenment). Among the assembly of disciples there, they valued debate above all else.

Their leader was named Vāsula (translated here as *Biànxíng*, "Universal Practice"), who constantly ate only one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day.
Pure and free from desire, he was a refuge for the multitude. That night, [the Buddha] intended to deliver him; first, he asked the assembly, "Can this ascetic Vāsula practice the Brahma-faring?"
"By practicing in this way, can one attain the Buddha-way? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent; why should it not be possible?
Yan-duo said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for aeons as numerous as dust motes, it would all be the root of falsehood. The assembly asked:
"Venerable sir, what virtues do you possess that you would disparage my teacher? Yāmadhara replied: "I do not seek the Path, yet I am not deluded.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat at improper times. I am not contented, yet I am free from greed. My mind has no expectations; this is what I call [the practice]."
At that time, having heard this, Sarvakāmin attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and with great joy, he offered praise.
Nyagrodha then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? The reason I acted thus was because his resolve for the Way was so earnest. Now, if a string is too tight, it snaps;
therefore, I did not praise him, so as to cause him to abide in a state of peace and happiness and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas. He then addressed Sarvakāmin again, saying:
"I have just been humiliated before the assembly; might this not cause distress in your heart, O Benevolent One?

Viśvāmitra replied, "I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Happiness under the teacher Jñānacandraprabha. He prophesied that before long I would realize the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, a Bodhisattva named Mahāprabha appeared in the world. Because I was old, I leaned upon a staff to pay my respects."

I went to pay my respects. The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor your son while slighting your father—how vulgar this is! At that time, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to show me where I had erred.
The Master said, "When you prostrated before the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, you leaned your staff against the wall and drew upon the Buddha’s face.

Because of this arrogance, you subsequently lost the two fruits of the path. Since I have taken responsibility for my own conduct and repented my transgressions, even when I hear various harsh words, they are like the wind passing by."
"It is like an echo; how much more so now that you have obtained the drink of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality—how could you instead give rise to feverish affliction?

'In a single word, one accords with the unborn, Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand it thus, One will penetrate both phenomena and principle.'"
When the night had ended and Yanadu had finished transmitting the Dharma, he inverted his head and planted it into the branches of a *śāla* tree upon his seat, whereupon he passed away suddenly.

When the Venerable Vāṣpa was fifteen years old, he paid homage to the Arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life. He was moved by the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣā...

He replied, "In that place, three Buddhas have appeared in the world; now, in Your Majesty’s kingdom, two masters provide guidance. The king said:

"Who are these two masters? He replied, "The Buddha prophesied that during the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two great beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life and succeed the Sage.
One is the King’s second son, Maṇḍara; though my virtue is meager, I shall be the other."
Formerly, in the kingdom of Nādi, there was a malevolent elephant that caused great harm. Since Nāla was born and the elephant’s depredations ceased, thirty years have passed.
People still did not know why the harm had ceased. Just as the King was conversing with Paṇḍu at their shared table, a messenger suddenly reported:
"A massive elephant is approaching the city. The King was filled with anxiety. Paṇḍu said, "If Nāla goes out, the calamity will be resolved. The King then tested him by ordering [Nāla to go].
Nāla emerged. Nāla then went out of the southern city gate and, facing the elephants, struck his belly and let out a great roar.
The city shook, the herd of elephants fell prostrate, and in a short while they all fled in dispersal. At this, people finally realized that their thirty years of peace were due to Nāla.
The Great King, filled with profound reverence and faith, commanded Nāla to go forth under Paṇḍaka; Paṇḍaka immediately conferred the full ordination upon him and entrusted him [with the teachings].
The Dharma verse says: "Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why do you not realize this? To penetrate the Dharma within them is neither of this age nor of antiquity.
Having thus transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the air to a height of half a *yojana* and remained there, standing firm. The fourfold assembly addressed him, saying:

Along with various miscellaneous treasures, they were used to establish a legal foundation for constructing a stūpa, so that [the spirit] might be reborn in a good realm.

One day, at a place where the king practiced his path, a stupa suddenly appeared, one chi and four cun in height and a deep azure color;

Its four sides display various scenes: on the front is King Śibi cutting his own thigh to feed a hawk and save a dove; on the back is King Maitrībala gouging out his flesh to light a lamp;
on the left is Prince Sattva leaping from a cliff to feed a tigress; and on the right is Candraprabha..."
The King relinquished his precious head. [The deity said: "In all four directions are the traces of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s cultivation of the Way in past lives;

The King asked, "What are these three substances and seven things? He replied, "The three substances to be eliminated are greed, hatred, and delusion.

The seven things to be possessed are great compassion, joy, non-self, valor, benefiting others, subduing demons, and non-attainment. It is because of these that people are either enlightened or unenlightened."
He understood it by means of this very ear. Having heard this, the King said, "A truly holy one is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.

this is the fragrance of his arrival. The king and Ratnākara both turned westward and paid homage. Mañjuśrīmitra also extended his hand toward the east and made three dots.
He answered him on the ground and immediately took his leave to receive ordination. Together with his attendants, he traveled through the air.

because he sat there and consumed food indiscriminately, his retribution was rebirth as a winged creature. Because of the karmic affinity between master and disciple from former lives, they now follow one another.
Ratnacūḍa asked: "By what skillful means can he be brought to liberation? Nālada replied: "I possess a supreme Dharma."
"Ba, you should listen and receive this. To transform those of future ages, he spoke these verses: 'The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound.

Nāla immediately leaped into the air and displayed the eighteen transformations. Returning to his seat, he pointed to the ground, causing a divine spring to gush forth.
He then spoke a verse: "The spring of the pure mind-ground can moisten all things; Surging up from the earth, it fills the limits of the ten directions.
Having finished the verse, he entered a state of serene extinction. Ratnākara and King Ratnamudrā erected a stūpa to enshrine his remains in their entirety.

Rising to look into the jar, five-colored rays flashed forth. He cried out, "It is truly as I wished! At dawn, he presented it to Zhi Quan. Zhi Quan...
He gathered with the high officials and nobles to observe it, and sighed, saying, "This is an auspicious omen rarely seen in the world.
