In the Buddha-dharma, one diligently cultivates *prajñā*. Who would not speak thus, yet instead contradict the Buddha’s teaching? To those who abandon appearances, it is said:

"The Buddha-dharma is fully endowed with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and its pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is stainless; how could this be abandoning appearances? To those who cling to appearances, it is said:
"The Buddha-lands are pure, sovereign, and unattached; why then do you cling to appearances? To those who speak of knowledge and vision, it is said: "This is the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas."
"Because there is nothing to be attained, this Dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is beyond the reach of cognition or hearing. Being unconditioned and signless, how can it be known or seen?
The fourfold assembly was all in agreement, but only the meditation master Dharmada remained unconvinced by their arguments.

Incensed and indignant, he arrived. The Master said: 'Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration; why have you come here? Now that you have arrived, why do you say you are practicing [concentration]? "
[The monk] said, "Though I have come here, my mind is not distracted. Concentration follows one's practice; how could it depend on a location?
The Lion said, "Since you, O worthy one, have arrived, your practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on one's practice? The other replied:
"It is because the person practices concentration, not that concentration practices the person. When I come here, it is because I am constantly practicing that concentration.
Śāriputra said, "It is not that concentration practices the person; rather, it is because the person practices concentration that [the concentration] comes of its own accord when the time arrives.

When that concentration is practiced by him, what is it like? He replied, "It is like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurations inside or out. If concentration is fully realized, it must necessarily be like this. Śāriputra said, "If concentration is fully realized..."
"It resembles a bright pearl. Now that I see you, O Virtuous One, you are no mere pearl. He said, "That pearl is transparent and clear; it is settled both inside and out.
My mind is undisturbed, just as this [pearl] is pure. Siṃha said, "That pearl has neither inside nor outside; how could you, Virtuous One, be 'settled'?
Impure things do not waver; this 'settling' is not purity. Having heard this, Dharmadatta then composed [a verse].
Lǐ said, “In my study of the Way, I have been nothing but exhausted in vain. May the Venerable One deign to instruct me. He entreated him with earnest and compassionate persistence.
Sīzi replied, “The dhyāna-concentration of all Buddhas has nothing that can be attained; the awakening-way of all Buddhas has nothing that can be realized.”

There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; this is true liberation. While worldly karmic retribution involves repaying causes and answering effects, within this Dharma, it is entirely not thus.
When Dharmada received the awakening of his mind from Śiṃha, his heart-ground became radiant and clear.
Once Śiṃha had gathered the fivefold assembly, his fame spread far and wide, and he was then seeking a dharma heir. He encountered an elder who led his son forward and asked:
"This boy’s name is Sthavira. At birth, he clenched his left hand in a fist; even now that he is twenty years old, he has never been able to open it.
I pray that the Venerable One will reveal the cause from his past lives. When Siṃha saw this, he reached out his hand and said, "Give me back my pearl.
The boy immediately opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. Siṃha said, "In my previous life, I was a monk. There was a child..."
"Your name is Vasiṣṭha. Once, when I went to the Western Sea for a vegetarian feast, I received a pearl as an offering which I entrusted to you.
Now, you must return my pearl; this is but natural. The Elder then caused him to leave the household life. Among the assembly of holy ones at Siṃhala, he was ordained with full precepts.
Because of his previous connection, he was named Vasiṣṭhasena. Siṃhala then said to him, "My teacher had a secret prophecy that you would encounter hardship."
"It will not be long. The Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma Eye shall now be entrusted to you. You must protect it so that it may universally moisten all beings until the end of time.

The verse says: "When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is expounded, both knowledge and vision are the mind; when the mind is realized, that is knowledge and vision; knowledge and vision are right here and now.
After Śimha had spoken this verse, he secretly entrusted his saṃghāṭī robe to Sthavira, commanding him to go to another country.

The transmission evolved through successive generations, and many received the teachings. [Bodhidharma] proceeded directly to South India. Śrī (師子) said, "It is impossible to evade destiny. He remained alone in Kaśmīra.
Dharmadatta regretted that Śrī had not allowed him to succeed to the Patriarchate. One day, while crossing a stream, he saw a woman washing her feet, which were exposed;
he thought to himself, "How exceptionally white and lustrous these shanks are! Just then, Śrī suddenly arrived and said:
"Can the mind of this day succeed to that of the patriarchs?
(Ji-mao). On the twenty-fourth day, the Venerable Siṃha entered nirvana.
While Siṃha was residing in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners: one named Māmuta and the other named Tu... [text fragment].
Rāhula and his companions hid in the mountains and studied various magical arts, intending to plot a rebellion together.

They subsequently changed their followers, all of whom assumed the appearance of monks, and secretly entered the royal palace. When they failed to carry out their plan, they were captured by the state. King Mīlinda was greatly incensed and said:
"I have always held the Buddha in high esteem; why would I commit such a great act of rebellion? He then issued an edict to execute the śramaṇas and destroy the Buddhist temples.

The king himself took up a sword and went before the Lion (the master), asking, "Have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates? The master replied, "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates. The king said:
"Have you transcended birth and death? He replied, "I have already transcended birth and death. The king said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head.
He said, "The body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The king then brandished his blade and severed the Lion’s head.
White milk gushed forth, rising several feet high. The king’s right arm also fell to the ground at that moment. Seven days later, he passed away. Crown Prince Prabhāvatī wept and said:

"Why did my father bring this calamity upon himself? he asked, as he led the assembly in repentance. At that time, there was a seer on Mount Elephant-White who clearly understood cause and effect, saying:
"Sīha and Roga were both laymen in a previous life; because they envied those whose Dharma was superior," so it was said.

The demon Yin (Yin) had previously harmed him at Mount Qie; now he has received his retribution. The multitude subsequently used a lion’s body to replace his own. A stupa was erected at the site where he was killed.
This occurred in the fourth year of the Ganlu era of the Wei dynasty in this land, the Jimao year.
In the year *Yǐyǒu* (253), the Tripiṭaka monk Senghui remonstrated with Sun Hao, the ruler of Wu, regarding the destruction of Buddhist temples.
Sun Hao issued an edict to destroy all shrines to deities throughout the realm, and this reached even the monasteries of the Buddha.

The assembled ministers remonstrated, saying, "The former emperors established these temples in response to auspicious omens; they must not be destroyed. Sun Hao then summoned Kang Senghui and asked him, "The Buddha spoke of good and evil—"
"May I hear about retribution? Huì said, "When a sagacious ruler governs the world with filial piety and compassion, vermilion phoenixes soar and elderly sages appear.
When he nurtures all things with benevolence and virtue, sweet springs become clear and auspicious grain flourishes.
Since goodness has its response, so too does evil. Thus, if one commits evil in secret, ghosts will find and punish them; if one commits evil in public,"
People may catch and execute them. The *I Ching* proclaims that accumulated goodness brings forth blessings, and the *Odes* praise seeking fortune without turning back from righteousness.

Though these are the maxims of the Confucian classics, they are in fact the clear instructions of Buddhism. Huì said, "If that is so, then since the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are already clear, what need is there for Buddhism?
Hào replied, "The Duke of Zhou and Confucius did not wish to speak of things in depth, and thus they merely indicated their outward traces. Buddhism does not stop at shallow words."

Therefore, I have detailed these essentials; all of them are for the sake of goodness. The Sage only feared that goodness was not sufficient, yet Your Majesty considers it a source of suspicion—why is this?
Emperor Hao had no reply and consequently rescinded the order to destroy the monasteries.

When the Indian physician Jīvaka first arrived in Jiǎoguǎng, he manifested many miraculous signs. Upon reaching Luoyang, he saw that the bhikṣus’ robes were sumptuous and elegant, whereupon he remarked: "Great..."
"To violate the precepts is not the intention of the Buddha. Upon seeing the imperial palaces, he remarked, "In general, they resemble the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
yet humans and devas are fundamentally distinct. To exhaust the labor of the common people to construct and carve such things—is this not excessive?

In the first year of the Dà'ān era, knowing that Luoyang was about to fall into chaos, he took his leave to return to India. A monk requested a word from him as a memento, so Faxie ordered the assembly to gather.
Ascending the seat, he said: "Guard the mouth, restrain the body and mind; be careful not to commit any evil. Practice all forms of goodness;
in this way, one attains transcendence of the world. Having finished speaking, he remained silent. Thereupon, several hundred people each invited him to their homes for a meal.
Lokakṣema consented to go to them all. The next day, Lokakṣema manifested his body in five hundred places, receiving food in every house.
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Twenty-three; *Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Twenty-four (Imperial Catalogue Number).
Jiazi (Beginning with the first year of Yongxing of Emperor Hui of Jin); Bingyin (changed to Guangxi); Dingmao (First year of Yongjia of Emperor Huai); Guiyou (Jianxing of Emperor Min).
First Year) Dingchou (First year of Jianwu of Emperor Yuan of Eastern Jin); Wuyin (changed to Daxing); Renwu; Guiwei (First year of Taining of Emperor Ming);
Bingxu (First year of Xianhe of Emperor Cheng); Yiwei (changed to Xiankang); Guimao (First year of Jianyuan of Emperor Kang); Yisi (First year of Yonghe of Emperor Mu); Dingyi (changed to Shengping);
Renxu (First year of Longhe of Emperor Ai); Guihai (First year of Xingning of Emperor Ai of Jin—ends here).
(Gengwu) Fotudeng of India arrived in Luoyang.
Fotudeng was a man from India whose secular surname was Bo. He arrived in Luoyang in the fourth year of the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty. He claimed to be over one hundred years old.
He sustained himself by ingesting qi and could go for many days without eating. He was skilled at reciting divine spells and could command ghosts and spirits. His abdomen...
There was a hole on his side which he plugged with cotton wool. At night, he would pull the cotton out of the hole to illuminate himself.

Whenever he approached a stream, he would draw his intestines and stomach out through the hole to wash them, then return them to his belly. He wished to establish a monastery in Luoyang to propagate the Great Dharma.
Encountering the chaos of Liu Yao’s invasions, his plan was ultimately not realized. At that time, Shi Le was stationed at Gepo and was committing many acts of slaughter.
A senior general under him, Guo Helü, had long been a devotee of the Dharma; Daorong [Tancheng] immediately took up his staff and sought out Helü, who then received the five precepts from him.

Later, whenever Helü went on military expeditions, Daorong would invariably predict victory or defeat in advance. Suspecting this, Shi Le questioned Helü, who replied, "There is a śramaṇa whose wisdom and arts..."
"Extraordinary! General Yun shall surely govern the lands of the Central States; he ought already to be my teacher. All that I have reported to you previously was his very own words.
Shi Le said with joy, "This is a gift from Heaven! He then summoned Fotudeng and asked, "What spiritual efficacy does the Way of the Buddha possess?
Knowing that Shi Le did not understand profound principles and could only be moved by signs of supernatural power, Fotudeng took a bowl, filled it with water, and burned incense.
He cast a spell over it, and in a short while, a blue lotus flower sprouted from it. Fu Le was thereby convinced and gained faith.
Daozheng then advised him, saying, "When a ruler's virtuous transformation pervades the realm, then the four auspicious creatures manifest their omens. Fu Le was greatly pleased by this.

Later, however, Fu Le became enraged and intended to harm the various Daoist practitioners, wishing also to persecute Daozheng. Daozheng then fled; Fu Le sent men to search for him, but they could not find him. They returned and reported this to Fu Le.
Shi Le said in alarm, "I had intended to turn toward the Sage, but the Sage has abandoned me. He did not sleep all night, longing to see Fotudeng.
Fotudeng, knowing that Shi Le’s heart was filled with regret, visited him the following morning. Shi Le asked, "What were you doing last night?
He replied, "Your Majesty harbored a mind of anger; therefore, I temporarily avoided you. Now that you have changed your mind, I have ventured to come. Shi Le laughed heartily.
(Year of the Earth-Ox, 25th Patriarch) Bodhidharma transmits the Dharma to Praśāntasena.
Praśāntasena was a native of Kaśmīra; his family name was Brāhmaṇa. His father was Śānticara, and his mother was Nityasukha.

Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently conceived. Upon his birth, his left hand remained in a fist. He met with the Venerable Siṃha, who [revealed]... [the truth].
He activated his past causes and secretly received the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*). Later, he traveled to South India and reached Central India.

There, the king was named Kalyāṇa, who offered him hospitality and veneration. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner known as Nirātman-guru, who had previously been held in high esteem by the king.
Envious of Śrīmitra’s great success, he then engaged in a debate before the king, saying to Śrīmitra: "I understand the art of silent debate; it requires no words."
Sudhana said, "Who knows who will win or lose? He replied, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I seek only the meaning. Sudhana asked, "What do you take to be the meaning?
He replied, "A mindless state is the meaning. Sudhana said, "Since you have no mind, how can you obtain the meaning?
He replied, "When I speak of 'no-mind,' it is designated as such, but it is not itself a meaning. Sudhana said, "You speak of 'no-mind'..."

"If the name does not correspond to the meaning, I say it is not the mind. If the meaning does not correspond to the name, he says: 'If the meaning does not correspond to the name, who is able to discern the meaning?

Sthavira said: 'If your name does not correspond to the meaning, what is this name called? He replied: 'It is for the sake of discerning that which is not the meaning; thus, this name is a nameless name. Sthavira said:
'Since the name is already not a name, and the meaning is also not a meaning, who is it that discerns? It must be discerned.'"
"What is this? he asked. Thus they went back and forth fifty-nine times until the non-Buddhists were silenced and submitted in faith.

At that moment, a strange fragrance suddenly filled the royal palace, and Sthiramati was struck with solemn awe. Facing north with palms joined, he sighed deeply and said, "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, has encountered peril today;
how tragic! He then took his leave of the king, who said, "Venerable One, please stay for a short while; allow me—"
[The questioner] asked: "In this garden there is a spring that is so hot it cannot be touched; I pray you resolve this for me. Sthavira said:
"This is a hot spring, caused by three conditions. The first is the karma of a deity; the second is the karma of a ghost; the third is hot stones.

As for the hot stones, their color is like gold and their nature is eternally fiery; therefore, when they emerge as a spring, it is like boiling water. As for the karma of a ghost, it refers to its..."
The demon from the land of Ghosts emerged from the place of punishment and wandered among humans. By the power of his residual karma, he boiled and scorched this spring to repay his ancient debts.
As for those who practice sorcery, it means that such spirits do not uphold the Way, but instead arbitrarily create calamities and blessings to obtain offerings.

Their evil karma has reached its full measure; they ought to be punished with forced labor and made to boil and scorch this spring as well, to repay for their sacrilegious sacrifices. The King said, "Fortunately..."
The Venerable One examined this. Among the three conditions, he asked, "By which of these was this fruit brought about? Sūrata replied, "It was brought about by the karma of this spirit.
He then commanded that incense be burned and they approach the water to perform repentance for its sake. After a short while, a tall man appeared on the riverbank.
Śrīmitra bowed before him and said, "I have received a small measure of merit in that I encountered the Venerable One and was immediately reborn among humans;
therefore, I have come to offer my thanks. Having spoken, he then vanished. Seven days later, the water of that spring became clear and cool once more, just like an ordinary spring.
Śrīmitra took his leave of the king, who personally led his retinue and escorted him as far as South India. There, he went into seclusion within a mountain valley. At that time, in that country...
The king’s name was Devaśrī. He welcomed [the sage] and made offerings to him. The king had two sons:
the elder was named Guṇasena, who was fierce and violent yet possessed of great physical vigor; the younger was named Amṛtodana, who was gentle and mild but constantly afflicted by illness.

The king questioned Sthavira on this matter, and Sthavira explained the law of cause and effect for him. The king received it with reverence and faith. Sixty years later, Guṇasena succeeded to the throne.

He placed his faith in the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), which led him to pose many difficult challenges to Sthavira. Rather than [the king’s] excessive [hostility], Sthavira offered counsel, and was consequently imprisoned.

The King suddenly questioned Sthavira, saying: "In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive doctrines have long been absent. As for that which you have transmitted, Master, to what school does it belong? Sthavira replied:
"In Your Majesty's kingdom, there has indeed been no false dharma from ancient times. That which I have attained is precisely the Buddhist school. The King said:

"It has been one thousand two hundred years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. From whom did you receive [this teaching], Master? Sthiramati replied, "The Mahāsattva Kāśyapa personally received the seal of the Buddha;
through successive transmission it reached my twenty-fourth-generation teacher, the Venerable Siṃha. From him I received it. The King said:
"I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution; how, then, could he transmit the Dharma to future generations?
Sthavira said, "Before my teacher’s ordeal had arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the Dharma verses to manifest the lineage of succession. The King said:
"Where is that robe? Sthavira then took the robe out from the bag and showed it to the king. The king ordered it to be burned;

though the five colors were vividly bright, it remained as it was even when the fuel was exhausted. The king immediately felt remorse and paid his respects. Since it was now clear that Siṃha was the true successor, he pardoned Guptamitra.
Guptamitra then requested to leave the household life. Sthavira asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you seek to do so?"
He said, "If I leave the household life, I shall not engage in those affairs. Sudatta asked, "What affairs will you not engage in? He replied, "I shall not engage in worldly affairs.
Sudatta asked, "What affairs will you then engage in? He replied, "I shall engage in the Buddha’s work. Sudatta said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as the heavens;

surely the various sages have descended in his form. He then granted him permission to leave the household life. For six years he served him, and subsequently, within the royal palace, he received [instruction].
[The assembly] was present. At the moment of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), the great earth shook violently, and many miraculous phenomena occurred.

Sengduo then addressed him, saying: "I am already decrepit and worn out; how can I remain for long? You must well protect the treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakṣus*) and universally deliver all sentient beings.
Listen to my verse: "The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision; Within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now awakened to the original nature; There is no path."
This is also illogical. After Madhyāntika had received the verse, he asked, "May this robe be transmitted? [Madhyāntika] replied, "This robe was for those who face hardships;

it was used as a means of authentication. Your person faces no such hardships, so why rely upon this robe? Its transformation shall cover the ten directions, and people will naturally have faith and turn toward it.

Thereupon, Madhyāntika manifested supernatural transformations: he transformed his body into the fire of samādhi and burned himself to death on level ground. His *śarīra* were over one chi in height. His virtue—
He enshrined it within a stupa of a superior king and kept it secret. This was during the year of Yiyou (157) of Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty in this land.
(In the year Wushen [324]), the Venerable Fotudeng entered nirvana and Shi Le passed away.
His younger brother, Shi Hu, succeeded to the throne and devoted himself even more earnestly to serving Fotudeng. Fotudeng said to Hu: "O Emperor..."
To serve the Buddha means to abide in reverence, frugality, compassion, and patience; to manifest and praise the Way of the Dharma; and not to commit acts of cruelty or harm the innocent.

If there are among the people those who do evil and do not reform despite being exhorted, how can they not be punished? However, executions must not be indiscriminate, and one must not fail to show compassion.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Yonghe era, Fotudeng said to his disciples: "The House of Shi shall perish."

"I have reached this point before the world fell into chaos; it is already too late. He then sent a messenger to take leave of the tiger. The tiger was startled and said, "Great Monk, why do you suddenly abandon my kingdom?
Is there some danger? He immediately went to the temple to console Fǎchéng. Fǎchéng said, "To emerge from life and enter into death is the constant way of the Path.
Longevity and brevity are determined by destiny; there is no means to increase or diminish them. What I regret is that the state has set its heart upon the Buddha-Dharma and established..."

Those who ordain monks in a temple ought to receive blessings; however, if one governs with cruelty and employs punishments excessively and indiscriminately, they will specifically contravene the sacred scriptures and ultimately receive no fortune or protection.
Only by being able to disseminate benevolent governance might one’s reign be prolonged. Hu wailed and sobbed in grief, knowing that [the Master] would surely pass away;
he immediately excavated a pit and prepared a tomb. On the eighth day, [the Master] sat upright and passed away, at the age of one hundred and seventy.
He entered the Way one hundred and nine years ago. He did not drink wine beyond his teeth’s reach, nor did he eat past midday.
There was nothing he would undertake that did not conform to the precepts. He established eight hundred and ninety-three temples and ordained more than seven thousand disciples.

Wherever Fotudeng resided, no one among the local people dared to spit, sneeze, or relieve themselves in that direction. They constantly cautioned one another, saying: "Do not give rise to evil thoughts toward the Great Monk."
I know. Since your Great Teaching came to the East, it has flourished since the time of Fotucheng. Later, there was a monk who came from Yongzhou;
seeing that Fotucheng had entered the Guanzhong region to the west, he reported this to Shi Hu. Hu ordered the tomb to be opened, but only a block of stone remained.

Zhu Fotu had long been a disciple of Fotucheng and resided at Changshan Temple for many years. At times he would divide his body to appear elsewhere, and at other times he would enter the mountains for months or years, carrying only dried provisions.
He would eat several pecks of rice, yet upon his return there was always a surplus. A monk followed Huizhao on a mountain journey; encountering snow, Huizhao entered a tiger’s cave to stay the night.

When the tiger returned, it lay down to sleep with him. Later, Huizhao determined the date of his own death, and people from near and far all gathered there. Huizhao said, "The human body is impermanent."
He was able to concentrate his mind on the true purity; though their physical forms were separated by time, they were surely united in the same realization.

Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. His disciples entered the mountains and saw Tiao sitting upon a rock. The assembly prostrated themselves and asked, "Is the Master still here? Tiao replied, "I am always here; it is simply that you do not see me.
Thereupon, the assembly together opened the coffin, and found nothing there but his robes and shoes.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Twenty-four; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle Twenty-five (Intercalary Year Designation).
Jiazi (Beginning in the second year of Xingning of Emperor Ai of Jin); Bingyin (The first year of Tahe of Emperor Yi); Xinwei (The first year of Xian’an of Emperor Jianwen); Guiyou (Emperor Xiaowu).
(Ningkang Year 1) Bingzi (revised to Taiyuan); Dingyou (Emperor An’s Long’an Year 1); Rentyin (revised to Yuanxing); Yisi (revised to Yixi);
Jiwu (Gongdi’s Yuangxi Year 1); Gengshen (Emperor Gaozu of Song’s Yongchu Year 1); Guihai (Emperor Wen of Song’s Jingping Year 1, ending). Southern and Northern Dynasties:
Song. Surname Liu. Eight rulers. A total of sixty years. Wei. Surname Tuoba. Ten [rulers].
The two rulers together reigned for one hundred and forty-nine years, during which time the empire was divided into Eastern Wei and Western Wei.
(Dingmao year) Dharma Master Zhi Dun retired to Mount Shan. His courtesy name was Daolin.
He entered the monastic order in his prime; in the second year of the Xingning era, he arrived at the capital to lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states: Xie An, Wang Yizhi, Yin Hao, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Xu Xun, He Chong, Wang Tanzhi, and others all entered into a relationship of "square friendship" with him.
In the second year of the Taihe era, he retired to live in seclusion at Mount Shan. He once composed an inscription to exhort the multitude, which said:
"Be diligent, be diligent! The Ultimate Way is not far off. Yet within the vast and boundless Three Realms, one remains in a state of long and aimless bondage. Guard it carefully..."
He was clear-sighted regarding prohibitions and set his will upon non-action (*wuwei*). When someone presented him with a horse, he kept it, saying, "I cherish its divine spirit and magnificent form.
When someone presented him with a crane, he released it, saying, "A creature capable of soaring to the heavens—how could it be a mere object for the ears and eyes to play with?

Later, he moved to Shicheng Mountain, where he lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams. He subsequently went to Shanyin and lectured on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, with Xu Xun serving as the assistant lecturer (*dougjiang*). Those who listened...

He was one whom [the people of] Qinfu admired. Huìyǒng was the son of the Pán family of Nèi Jiāng. He and Huìyuǎn studied under the same teacher, Dào'ān, and they pledged to build a hermitage together on Mount Luófú.
When Huìyuǎn was detained by Dào'ān, Huìyǒng arrived there first. Táo Fàn, the Regional Inspector (Cìshī) of Xún-yáng, [honored him].
He remained to rest at the Lu-shan residence, which was provided for him by Xi-lin. He established a thatched hut on a mountain peak;
once, a tiger would crouch submissively nearby. Anyone who entered his hut would invariably perceive a wondrous fragrance, and thus it was named Xiang-gu (Fragrant Valley).
(Ji-mao) Dharma Master Dao’an arrived in Chang’an.

Dao’an was the son of the Wei family of Changshan; his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. At the age of eleven, he left home to enter the monastic life and took Fotudeng as his teacher.

He could read ten thousand words a day from memory; his talent and eloquence were unrivaled. He was intelligent by nature but ugly in appearance. People of the time said, "The lacquer-clad ascetic startles his neighbors.
After Sengcheng passed away, he led his disciples to rely on Mount Luhun. In the first year of the Ningkang era, he went to Xiangyang and established Tanxi Temple.
At that time, there was a man of high character named Xi Zuochi, who visited Dao'an and introduced himself, saying, "I am the Xi of the Four Seas."
Zuochi asked. Dao’an replied immediately: “I am Shi Dao’an, who covers the heavens. In the fourth year of the Taiyuan era, Fu Jian, the ruler of Qin, attacked and captured Xiangyang.
Upon obtaining Dao’an, he was delighted and said to his attendants: "It was with an army of one hundred thousand that I took Xiangyang."
"Only one person and a half have been obtained. His attendants asked who they were. He replied, "Master Daoan is one person; Xi Zuochi is half a person.
When Daoan arrived in Chang'an, he extensively propagated the Dharma and its transformation.
(Cengxu) Dharma Master Huiyuan resided at Mount Lu.
He was a native of the Jia family from Yanmen. From his youth, he was fond of learning; he extensively mastered the Six Classics and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*.

Among the veteran scholars and senior practitioners, none failed to admire the profundity of his insights. At the age of twenty-one, together with his younger brother Huichi, he went to seek the Dharma Master Dao’an.

Dao’an heard the teachings of the supramundane Dharma and, being delighted by them, sighed and said, "The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are merely chaff and husks. He subsequently left the household life.
At that time, his disciples numbered in the thousands; Yuan resided as the foremost seat. Dao’an once said to the assembly, "He who shall cause the Way to flow to the Eastern lands must be Yuan.
When the region of Guanzhong fell into turmoil, Dao’an dispersed his disciples, each following their own destination. Yuan... [was not among those who remained].

He did not instruct or admonish him repeatedly; Huiyuan alone remained far removed from hearing a single word. [Huiyuan’s disciple] asked him about this in astonishment, and Huian said, "As for someone like you, what more could I possibly say?
He then departed from Jingzhou for Mount Luofu. Upon reaching Xunyang, he beheld Mount Lu and took a liking to it, so he established a vihāra there.
However, as it was still some distance from water, he struck the ground with his staff and said, "If this place is fit to dwell in, [may the water appear]."

He said, "Let this decaying soil draw forth a spring. As soon as he finished speaking, a clear stream gushed out. His disciples gradually increased in number, and he became concerned that the site was too cramped and not a place for propagating the Way.
That night, a mountain deity suddenly appeared in a dream and said, "This mountain is sufficient for you to dwell; I pray you do not go elsewhere.
One night there was a great thunderstorm, and at dawn the next day, the forest foot was cleared wide open, with white sand spread across the ground and *pien* and *nan* trees [appearing].

The wood was of the finest *wénzǐ* (sandalwood) species, which covered the ground. The Provincial Governor was deeply moved and consequently established a monastery for it. On the day of Bingxū, the construction was completed;

he named its hall "Divine Transport" (*Shényùn*) and titled the monastery "Eastern Grove" (*Dōnglín*). Previously, while Táo Kǎn was serving as the Governor of Guangzhou, fishermen saw a divine light in the sea;
they cast their nets and caught a golden statue of Mañjuśrī. Later, merchants obtained another one from the eastern seas.
The halo was held so that it resembled the image itself, as if it were sewn to it. Hui-k'an sent it to Hanxi Temple in Wuchang.
When Hui-k'an transferred his command to Jiangzhou, he went to welcome the image back; however, upon reaching the boat, it sank.

When the temple was completed, Hui-yuan went to the riverbank and prayed with devotion. Suddenly, the image floated out. He then welcomed it into the Shen-yun Hall and constructed a multi-storied pavilion to enshrine it.
(25th year, Wuzi) The twenty-sixth patriarch, Rāhulamitra, received the Dharma from Prajñātāra.
Rāhulamitra was of the Kṣatriya caste and was the second son of the King of South India. Having received the Dharma from Vaseṣṭha, he later traveled to East India to propagate the teachings.
There, the king’s name was Sthira, and he followed the teachers of non-Buddhist paths.
When the Brahmin Nakhin and Mātanga were about to arrive, the King and the Brahmin both beheld a white vapor piercing through from above to below.
The King asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin replied, "This is merely a sign that Māra is approaching; what auspiciousness could there be in it?
He then immediately gathered his followers and deliberated, saying, "It would be better not to let Mātanga enter the capital city. Who is capable of defeating him? A disciple said:
"We each possess incantations capable of shaking heaven and earth and entering fire and water; what need have we to worry?

When Maitreya arrived, he saw black vapors over the palace walls and said, "This is but a minor difficulty. He proceeded directly to the king's presence. The king asked, "For what purpose has the Master come?
He replied, "To deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what method do you deliver them? He replied, "I deliver them each according to their own kind. At that time—
Upon hearing these words, the brahmin could not contain his rage. He immediately employed his illusory powers to conjure a massive mountain atop Maitreya’s head.
Maitreya pointed at it, and the conjured mountain suddenly shifted, pressing down upon the brahmin’s head. He then pressed his hand against the earth, causing the ground to tremble.
None of the five hundred non-Buddhists were able to establish their positions. The Brahmin was terrified and prostrated himself in repentance before Maitreya.

Maitreya again pressed down upon the earth, and the ground became still; he pointed toward the mountain, and the mountain vanished. On another day, the King prepared a great feast and gathered all the non-Buddhists, earnestly requesting that Maitreya join the assembly.
Maitreya initially did not wish to go, but knowing that the site of the gathering was about to collapse, he went nonetheless. The King said with joy:

"Will the Master truly come? Maitreya replied, "I am not one who accepts offerings; I have come only to save you from death. This place has already become a dragon's lair; in a moment it will sink down.
The King was greatly terrified and, together with his retinue, fled to high ground. Looking back at the site, he saw that the earth had indeed collapsed.

It had already become a deep, secluded pool. King [Śīlāditya] grew increasingly respectful and faithful. Guṇamati then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the king, leading him toward the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*).
He further declared, "In the king’s kingdom there shall be a sage who will succeed to my Dharma.

Previously, in East India, there was the son of a Brahmin, twenty years of age, who had lost his mother at an early age; his name and lineage were unknown, and he sometimes referred to himself as "The Man with the Necklace" (*Muktāhāra*).
He was thus named the Youth Maṇicūḍa. As he went about begging in the streets and villages, if anyone asked him why he walked so hurriedly, he would reply, "Why do you walk so slowly?
If asked what his clan name was, he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one could fathom this.
One day, King [Śubhavyūha] and Maitrakanyaka were traveling out together in a carriage. Maṇicūḍa prostrated himself before them, and Maitrakanyaka said, "Do you remember past events?"
He replied, "I recall that in a past kalpa, I lived together with this master. He expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I expounded the profound *Sūtras*.
Today’s events are surely in accord with our past causes. Maitreya said to the king, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Two others will appear hereafter: one shall transform South India, and the other’s affinity lies in China (Zhèn)."
In the ninth year, he returned to this land. Consequently, based on their past causes, he named the youth Prajñātāra and entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
He spoke in verse: "The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither beginning nor end.

Responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called 'Wisdom' (Jñāna). Once the Dharma had been entrusted, Prajñātāra took his leave of the King, saying: "My work of transformation is now complete."
In the end, he returned to the state of quiescent extinction. He exhorted the King, saying, "I pray that you will not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle.

He then returned to his original seat, manifesting a form like the sun. After a short while, he again displayed eighteen transformations; he emitted the fire of samādhi to cremate himself, raining down golden śarīras.
The King enshrined them within a golden stūpa. This was during the *wuzi* year of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty in this land.

(Ji-chou) In the fourteenth year of the Taiyuan era, on the twenty-seventh day of the first month, Dharma Master Dao’an entered nirvana. While Dao’an was alive, he saw a strange monk entering and exiting through the lattice of a window.
When Dao’an asked him where his place of birth was, the strange monk pointed toward the northwest with his hand. Immediately, the clouds parted, and a multi-storied pavilion became visible.
He appeared as if emerging from an illusion; it was said that he had come from Tuṣita Heaven. On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

Da’an frequently annotated the meanings of the sutras, always seeking scriptural corroboration. One day, he was moved by the descent of an elder with a bushy beard; when Da’an presented his own compositions to him, they were found to be remarkably similar.
The Venerable One praised him with admiration, considering that he had fully accorded with the Buddha’s mind; he further granted his secret assistance in the propagation of the teachings.
Dao’an recognized him as Piṇḍola, and consequently established a daily offering for him. Among his disciples who mastered the practice were several dozen people.
There was one named Fayu, who transmitted the teachings to Changsha. Among his several hundred followers, there was once a man who drank wine in private; Fayu let it pass without reprimand.

Hui'an knew of this and immediately sealed the *jing* plant and sent it to him. Upon receiving the *jing*, Huiyuan wept, saying, "Dongzhong has acted improperly and has brought great distress upon my teacher from afar.
Thereupon, he prostrated himself to accept his reprimand. On Hui'an’s left arm there was a fleshy protuberance, raised like a seal.
He could roll his hands up and down without them leaving his wrists; at that time, he was called the Bodhisattva of the Sealed Hand.
(Gengyin) Dharma Master Huiyuan established the Lotus Society.
During the decline of the Jin dynasty, many men of extraordinary talent and world-transcending character lived in seclusion and did not serve in office; they came to join Huiyuan.
Huiyuan said, "Gentlemen, if you have the aspiration to journey to the Pure Land, you should exert yourselves with diligence.

Thereupon, he led the assembly to form the Lotus Society, where they single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land. He commissioned Liu Chengzhi to compose the *Vow Text*.
Furthermore, Wang Qiao and others composed poems on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) to manifest their aspirations.

Yuan’s preface states: "What is *nianfo sanmei*? It refers to the concentration of thought and the stillness of visualization. When thought is concentrated, the will becomes single-minded and undisturbed;

when visualization is still, the vital energy (*qi*) becomes empty and the spirit becomes lucid. When the vital energy is empty, wisdom shines with tranquil clarity; when the spirit is lucid, there is no depth of mystery it does not penetrate. These two—"

This is indeed the profound tally of spontaneity; it unifies all things to bring forth their utility. Therefore, by maintaining tranquility and reverence within the inner chamber, one moves others through resonance;

by attaining spiritual penetration and governing the mind, one aligns with the correct and enters the subtle. This is achieved by relying on cultivation to concentrate the spirit and through accumulated practice to transform one's nature.

If such results can be obtained even in this manner, how much more so for one who dwells like a corpse in "sitting-forgetfulness" (zuowang), whose contemplation merges with the ultimate, and whose intellect transcends the mundane realm?

He traverses the cosmos and secretly treads upon the Great Way. Let me speak of its beginning: when the Bodhisattva first ascends to the stage of the Way, he has just caught a glimpse of the Mysterious Gate.

His essence is quiescent and non-active, yet there is nothing he does not do. When his spiritual transformations manifest, they cause the long and the short to adjust their constant measures, and the great and the small to become mutually discordant.
The three luminaries turn their reflections to shift their illumination; heaven and earth are rolled up and brought within his breast.
Furthermore, the names of various samādhis are exceedingly numerous; yet among them, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is foremost for its high merit and ease of progress.

It exhausts the profound mystery and reaches the ultimate subtlety, for the Honored One is called the Tathāgata. His divine body merges with all transformations, responding without fixed form. Therefore, those who enter this concentration become oblivious and forget their cognitive awareness;
they take that which is perceived as the means to achieve clear vision. When this vision is bright, internal illumination reflects one another, and forms and images arise.

It is not something reached by the ears or eyes, yet hearing and seeing function therein. Thus, when one beholds the body of the profound, coagulated, empty mirror, one awakens to the numinous marks—serene, unified, and luminously clear.
Naturally, one perceives the resonance of the mysterious sound; when the mind listens, the accumulation of defilements is constantly dissolved and obstructed emotions melt into clarity.
Were it not for the ultimate subtlety of all under heaven, who could participate in this? By means of...
Observing this, we see that the impact of a single encounter can dispel the deep obscurations of long-standing habituation and clear away the heavy delusions of ignorant practice.
This is like the collective focus of many individuals; therefore, it is evident that one cannot judge its relative superiority or inferiority.
For this reason, I exhort all worthy sages to contemplate the resonance of this singular principle and to fear the wasting of every passing moment, lest future provisions be lacking.

Hoping that through the power of sincere devotion he might fulfill the aspiration for the Three Vehicles, he sought to ferry others across the ford and proceed together with the nine schools;

Mountain spirits manifested in all manner of forms, yet all vanished as soon as they were transformed by Huiwei’s spiritual power.

The waters of the ocean may be exhausted; Mount Sumeru may be toppled. Yet that superior man maintains a firm and steadfast resolve.
(Xinchou) Dharma Master Kumārajīva arrived in Chang’an.
Kumārajīva (translated as "Child Longevity") was a native of Central India. His father’s name was Kumārayāna, and his family had served as prime ministers for generations.

Renouncing his glory, he went forth to travel. The King of Kucha gave him his younger sister as a wife, and from her was born Kumārajīva. From birth, Kumārajīva possessed divine intelligence. At the age of seven, he accompanied his mother to a temple;
there he saw an iron almsbowl and attempted to lift it onto his neck. Suddenly, he thought, "This bowl is extremely heavy; how can I possibly lift it?

He immediately found that he could not bear its weight, whereupon he attained the realization that all phenomena are but the mind. He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory such that no one could equal him.
When Kumārajīva was twenty years old, his mother took leave of the King and departed for India. She said to him, "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya are inconceivable.
To transmit them to the Eastern Lands depends solely upon your strength; however, this will bring you no personal benefit. What can be done? Kumārajīva replied:

He resolved that he must cause the Great Transformation to flow abroad; though it was suffering, he harbored no regret. His mother reached India, where she perfected the Way and attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
When Fu Jian occupied Qin and attacked Xiangyang, he captured Dao’an. Dao’an subsequently urged Fu Jian to welcome Kumārajīva from the Western Regions.

Just then, the Grand Historian reported: "A star of virtue has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to the Western Regions; there must be a man of great wisdom who shall enter to assist the Central Kingdom.

Yao Xing said, "I have heard that in Kucha there is one named Kumārajīva. Could this not be him? He dispatched General Lü Guang and addressed him, saying, "It is not that I covet territory that I am raising an army.
I have heard that Kumārajīva possesses a profound understanding of the characteristics of dharmas and is a master for later students. If you are victorious..."
Regarding Kucha: he should have immediately dispatched an express courier to send Kumārajīva back. When Kucha was conquered, Kumārajīva was sent home;
however, on the way, he heard that Yao Xuan had already been killed by Yao Chang, so he stopped and did not return. Consequently, Kumārajīva never reached Qin.

Later, Yao Chang also heard of Kumārajīva’s reputation and issued an invitation, but Sengguang did not grant permission. After Yao Chang died, his son Yao Xing again requested his presence, but [Sengguang] still did not grant it, and subsequently sent troops to invade.
Guang was defeated and surrendered. Only then was Kumārajīva able to be welcomed back. In the twelfth month, Kumārajīva arrived in Cháng'ān.

The ruler of Qin commanded Kumārajīva to translate scriptures in the Xiāoyáo Garden within the Western Palace. Kumārajīva examined the existing translations and found that many were erroneous and did not correspond with the Sanskrit originals (*bāṇ-běn*).
He then assembled śramaṇas such as Sēngzhào and Sēngruì to retranslate them. As for Sēngzhào, he himself served as a śramaṇa...

His reputation resounded throughout the Three Fu regions. While Kumārajīva was at Guzang, Sengzhao went there to rely upon him. When Kumārajīva spoke with him, he was astonished and said, "He is a dragon-elephant within the Dharma.

Upon returning to Guanzhong, Sengzhao assisted Kumārajīva in carefully determining the scriptures and treatises. Following the translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he composed the *Prajñā-aprajñā-śāstra*.
When Kumārajīva read it, he marveled at its excellence and circulated the treatise. When it reached Mount Lu, Huiyuan praised it deeply.
[Tan] Sengrui was a native of Jizhou. Initially, he traveled to various regions to study; later, he entered Guanzhong to follow Kumārajīva.

He lectured on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, whereupon Kumārajīva sighed in admiration, saying: "You possess truly refined discernment; you are one who appreciates the nuances of translation. What regrets could I have?"
Dharma Master Huiyuan composed the *Faxing deng lun* (Treatise on the Equality of Dharmas).
Residing at Mount Lu, he extensively propagated the Way of the Dharma. Upon hearing that Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong, he sent a letter to establish friendly relations with him.
Kumārajīva’s reply, in brief, stated: "The Sūtra says that at the end of time, in the East, there shall be Bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma.
Be diligent, O benevolent one, and propagate this matter well! He also sent a verse, which said: "Since you have already abandoned the pleasures of defilement, has your mind attained perfect mastery?
If it does not scatter toward external objects, has it deeply entered the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)? Within the empty nature of diverse realms, is your mind without [attachment]?"
"Joy! If one delights in the wisdom of dhyāna, this dharmatā is without illumination. It is empty, deceptive, and so forth, lacking reality and not being a place for the mind to rest.
O Benevolent One, regarding the Dharma you have attained, I pray that you will show me its essential point. Yuanfu replied with a verse: "From where does the original source ultimately come?

Its arising and ceasing lie beyond the boundaries of existence and non-existence. When a single atom enters the realm of movement, it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. Delusive conceptions further..."

They interact with one another; when touching upon the principle, obstructions arise spontaneously. Although causes and conditions have no master, the opening of the path has not occurred in a single lifetime.
Since there is currently no enlightened master to serve as a guide, who will grasp the profound seal? My inquiries thus remain lingering and distant; let us together look forward to the final years.

Originally, in China, there was no teaching regarding the eternal abiding of *nirvāṇa*; it was only said that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching. Daoyuan said: "The Buddha is the ultimate."

When one reaches the ultimate, there is no change. How could the principle of non-change ever be exhausted? He then composed the *Dharmatā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Nature of Dharmas) in fourteen chapters, of which a brief summary states:
"The ultimate takes non-change as its nature; attaining this nature takes the realization of the ultimate as its core principle.

Upon seeing this treatise, Kumārajīva sighed in admiration and said: "In these frontier regions, we have not yet seen the scriptures, yet you have darkly harmonized with the underlying principle. Is this not marvelous?"
(Bingwu year) Buddhabhadra of India arrived at Guanzhong;
Buddhabhadra (translated as Jue Xian) received the True Dharma from Buddhadasa.
Buddhadasa had studied together with Dharmatrāta under the twenty-seventh patriarch, Buddhabhadra. After receiving the Dharma, he traveled to Kaśmīra, where he resided for many years.
While he was sitting in meditation, the Qin śramaṇas Zhìyán and others traveled west to Jibin to welcome Guṇabhadra to the Pass.
Kumārajīva turned his shoes upside down in haste to welcome him, regretting that they had met so late. They engaged in much discussion, which served as a medicinal cure for one another’s views.
Prince Yao Hong of Qin invited him to the Eastern Palace, where he debated the Dharma with Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva asked, "How is it that dharmas are empty? Guṇabhadra replied, "The various atoms..."

Form is established as such. Since form has no intrinsic nature, form is itself emptiness. Again, he asked: "If you have already refuted form as being empty by means of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), how then do you refute the single atom?
Bodhidharma replied: "Because of the single atom, the multitude of atoms is empty; because of the multitude of atoms, the single atom is empty.
The śramaṇa Baoyun did not understand his meaning and all claimed that the *paramāṇus* reckoned by Bodhidharma were eternal. Furthermore...
He submitted this request. Kumārajīva said, "Dharmas do not arise of themselves; they arise because conditions meet. Because of a single atom, there are many atoms.
Since atoms have no self-nature, they are empty. How could one say that a single atom is not destroyed?

At that time, several thousand śramaṇas who were devoted to the profound transformation of the Dharma frequented the imperial palace. Guṇabhadra remained composed and indifferent. One day, he happened to say:

The disciple said, "Yesterday I saw five ships from India depart together; they should have arrived by now. Furthermore, his followers claimed for themselves that they had attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Master Sengzheng said, "The Buddha did not permit one to speak of the Dharma attained by oneself. As for these claims regarding the five ships, what is there to be refuted?
Your disciple’s light words are deceptive and delusive according to the Vinaya, and they constitute a violation of the meaning of the teachings. They are not to be shared with others."
He then crossed the Yangtze River and entered Mount Kuanglu, where he met Huiyuan to discuss the meaning of the teachings.

Huiyuan held him in high esteem and requested that he translate various sutras on meditation and numerical categories (*śāstra*), so as to examine the purport of the distinct transmissions and their origins. Before long, five ships arrived together.
(Dingwei) The Indian Buddhayaśas arrived in Guanzhong while Kumārajīva was in the Qin state.
He once lectured on a sūtra at Caotang Temple; Yao Xing, the ruler of the Qin, along with several thousand court officials and śramaṇas, listened with solemn countenances.
One day, Xing said to Jīva, "The Great Master is brilliant and possesses great eloquence."
"He is peerless within the realm. How can we allow the lineage of the Dharma to fail its succession? He then coerced ten palace women into taking him as their husband.
From that time on, Kumārajīva no longer resided in the monks' quarters but established a separate residence for himself.
When some among the monks wished to emulate his example, Kumārajīva gathered a bowl full of needles and said to them, "If you can emulate this by eating these, then you may do so."

He merely kept a room for storing [his requisites]. Consequently, he presented seven needles at once, as if they were his regular meal. The monks were filled with shame and submission, and [the practice] ceased.

Buddhabhadra (translated as "Awakened Clarity") from India arrived at Guzang. Hearing that Kumārajīva had accepted palace women from the Qin court, he sighed and said, "Kumārajīva is like fine cotton;
how could one allow him to enter thorny brambles? When Kumārajīva heard that Buddhabhadra had come from afar for his sake, he urged the Qin ruler to welcome him.

When the messenger arrived there, Yaśas said, "Since Your Excellency has deigned to send such a far-reaching command, I shall immediately set out by relay carriage to repay the donor’s diligent hospitality toward a guest.
However, if you intend to treat me as you did Kumārajīva, then this poor monk shall remain on the northern mountain. The messenger returned [with this message].

Xingfu respectfully invited him, and Guṇavarman consequently arrived. The Ruler of Qin went out to the suburbs to welcome him and established a separate vihāra for his residence, providing offerings befitting a king;
yet Guṇavarman accepted nothing at all. When the time came for almsround, he would take but a single meal.
The Layman Tao Qian visited Master Huiyuan.
Huiyuan resided at Donglin Monastery; below it lay Tiger Creek. Whenever Huiyuan saw off guests, he invariably used Tiger Creek as the boundary.
In the third year of the Yixi era, the Daoist Lu Xiujing accompanied Tao Qian into the mountains to see Huiyuan. As Huiyuan saw them off, he took their hands in his.

As they conversed, they unconsciously passed beyond Tiger Creek. The tiger then let out a roar, and the three men looked at one another and laughed heartily; this is what the world has traditionally known as the "Three Laughs.

At that time, Huiqian was living in seclusion at Chaisang, near Mount Lu, and frequently visited Huiyuan. Huiyuan, admiring his expansive and untrammeled spirit, sent a letter inviting him to join the community.
Huiqian’s nature was a fondness for wine, and he said that if he were permitted to drink, he would come. Huiyuan granted him this permission, and so he went to visit him. After a long time...
Because there was no wine, he knit his brows and departed. Qian’s courtesy name was Yuanliang; his original name was Yuanming. He once served as Magistrate of Pengze during the Jin dynasty.
After the fall of the Jin, he changed his name to Qian. He was commonly known as Master Jingjie.
(Gengxu) Liu Chengzhi, a retired layman from the common people, Manifests Birth in the Pure Land.

Liu Chengzhi, styled Zhongsi, was a native of Pengcheng. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned. He initially served as a military aide (*canjun*) to the regional governor, but immediately withdrew into seclusion.
Although Huan Xuan and Liu Yiqing both recommended him repeatedly, he did not accept their offers. He subsequently went to Mount Lu to rely upon Huiyuan.
Huiyuan said, "Official emoluments are lofty and grand; why not pursue them? Chengzhi replied, "Ruler and subject suspect one another; those with flaws undermine one another.
The Jin house lacks the stability of a bedrock foundation, and the sentiments of the people face a peril like a stack of eggs. What could I possibly do? Huiyuan agreed with his words.
He highly esteemed Chengzhi’s magnanimity and integrity, and the court, recognizing that his will could not be swayed, honored him with the title "The Recluse" (Yi).

The people established the Lotus Society at Yuanchuang, commissioning Cheng to compose a vow-text. Its summary states: "The Divine can be reached through resonance, yet cannot be sought through traces.
If there is a substance to this resonance, then the dark path is but a few inches away; if one seeks it without a proper method, how can one find the ford in such vast obscurity?
Now, fortunately, we have resonated without prior consultation, our collective hearts directed toward the Western Realm; this is indeed a manifestation of the cosmic mechanism."
I have been deeply moved by our shared dreams and joyful visions; that you have come as my son is a cause for great rejoicing.

How could I not cultivate my heart and sharpen my mindfulness, concentrating my thoughts with redoubled vigor and layered reflection? Yet, as our lifespans differ and our merits vary, though we share the same morning aspirations, our evening returns are separated.
This is truly lamentable for the deep affection between us, teacher and friend. Therefore, I have sighed and summoned you here together.
Adjusting their collars in the Dharma Hall, they shared a single mind, harboring aspirations for the profound and ultimate, vowing to join with others to travel together to the transcendent realm.

Among them, those who were world-renowned and peerless, the first to ascend to the divine sphere, did not seek solitary perfection upon the cloud-capped peaks nor forget the value of refined gold in secluded valleys.

As the seniors advanced and the juniors followed in ascent, they encouraged one another to contemplate the way of collective progress; only then did they contemplate the subtle observations of the Great Rites and open [the Way].

As his mind shone with true illumination, his consciousness awakened to the new. His physical form was transformed through spiritual refinement. Cheng then composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Shi* (Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) to manifest his single-minded resolve.
Within half a year, while in meditative concentration, he beheld the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, all of which turned the color of gold.
After fifteen years, he again saw Amitābha Buddha; the light from his jade-like brow shone forth as he lowered his hand to comfort and welcome him. Cheng...
He made this earnest plea: "How may the Tathāgata stroke my head and cover me with his robe? Suddenly, the Buddha stroked his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him.
On the following day, as he was recollecting the Buddha, he again saw himself entering a precious pond where blue and white lotuses bloomed.
The water was limpid and clear. A man with a halo upon his head and the *svastika* mark (*śrīvatsa*) appearing on his chest pointed to the pond water and said, "This is water of eight virtues;
you may drink from it. Cheng drank the water, which was sweet and delicious. Even after he woke up, he still felt its effects, and a fragrance emanated from his pores.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The karmic conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have reached their fulfillment. Facing the image, he burned incense and prostrated twice, praying:
"By virtue of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that Amitābha Buddha exists. This incense is offered to Śākyamuni Tathāgata."
Next, he made offerings to Amitābha Buddha and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, vowing that all sentient beings might be born together in the Pure Land.

Having finished speaking, he faced west, joined his palms, and passed away. A rare fragrance filled the air, which subsided after seven days. This was during the sixth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty.
Zhou Xuzhi, style name Daozu, was a native of Yanmen. In his youth, he was thoroughly versed in the Five Classics and the Five Wai (the five supplementary classics), and was thus known as...
The youth Shi Jing lived in seclusion to cultivate his aspirations. Although high officials repeatedly summoned him, he declined to serve in all instances. Huiyuan joined the Lotus Society.

When Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty ascended the throne, he summoned Huiyuan for an audience to engage in debate and analysis; the Emperor was greatly pleased. Someone asked: "It is said that one who serves as a retired scholar (*chushi*) should not frequent the royal court.
Is this permissible? He replied: "Those whose hearts race toward the gates of Wei regard the rivers and lakes as shackles; those whose sentiments [are detached]..."

For one who has forgotten both [worldly and transcendental], even a marketplace or a court is but a mountain cave. He was known in his time as Master Tongyin (The Penetrating Hermit). Later, he resided on Mount Zhong, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
he grew increasingly steadfast in his practice as he aged. One day, facing the sky, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and with palms joined, he passed away.

Zhang Ye, style name Xinmin, lived in Xunyang. He was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit literature and was particularly skilled in composing prose. He was nominated for the position of *Mocaicai* (Man of Outstanding Talent).
He was repeatedly summoned to serve as an Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sanqichangshi), but he declined both times. He entered the Lotus Society at Mount Lu to cultivate the practice of purity.

In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he bid farewell to his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away. Zhang Quan, style name Xiushi, was a descendant of Zhang Ye. He was lofty and reclusive, yet fond of learning;
even amidst his plowing and weeding, he never laid down his scroll. Though repeatedly summoned, he did not accept. Jinyue [praised him] for this.
Because he was poor, he was appointed as the Magistrate of Xunyang. He laughed and said, "The ancients considered even a space that could accommodate one's knees to be sufficient for peace.

To bend one's will for the sake of official emolument—what glory is there in that? Thereupon, he entered Mount Lu and relied upon the Lotus Society (*liánshè*), where he investigated the inner scriptures (*nèidiǎn*) with great depth and attained many insights.
In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while lying peacefully in bed without illness. Lei Cizong, style name Zhonglun, entered Mount Lu.
The Lotus Society established its hall beside Donglin. When Huiyuan was about to pass away, he wrote in a letter to his nephews and nieces, saying:

"At the age of twenty, I entered Mount Lu to serve Master Shi. At that time, our teachers and friends were a profound source of learning; we were dedicated to propagating the sacred Way and contemplating the principles of the Buddha, day and night.
We took such joy in this that we forgot our sorrows for over twenty years. Now that our master of deep wisdom has passed and our virtuous friends have likewise departed..."
Upon his father’s death, he returned with you all to farm on the slopes of the mountains. Ten years passed; he has surpassed the age of fifty.
Now that he is old yet not yet senile, he can still exert his will to become a bridge for those seeking to return to the West.
From this day forward, let no matter of household affairs, great or small, concern you—this is the teaching of Zi Ping, which may serve as a model. [Omission of Gongze’s entry into Mount Lu].
After the Master of the Lotus Society passed away, a friend performed a memorial service for him at night within the Baima Monastery in Luoyang.
Suddenly, all the trees, forests, halls, and buildings were transformed into gold. A voice resounded from the air, saying, "I am Gongshe Queze.
I prayed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī, and now I have attained rebirth there. Having finished speaking, nothing was seen.
(Renzzi) Dharma Master Huichi entered nirvana.
Huichi was the younger brother of Huiyuan. At the age of eighteen, he served with Huiyuan under Dao’an and resided at Mount Lu.

In the second year of the Long’an era, he took leave of Huiyuan to enter Shu. Huiyuan detained him, saying: “In human life, one cherishes gathering together; why do you alone delight in separation? Huichi—

He said, "Those whose emotions are stagnant and who cling to worldly attachments should not have left the household life. Now that I have severed my desires to seek the Way, I shall take the Western Land as my destination.
He then took his leave and went to Chengdu, where he propagated the Buddha-dharma extensively. Those who entered his hall were all hailed as having "ascended the Dragon Gate.
In the eighth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, after delivering his final admonitions to his disciples, he entered meditative absorption beneath a tree at Longkan (Dragon Cave).
(Guichou) Dharma Master Kumārajīva passed away.
Kumārajīva had always been fond of the Mahāyāna and was intent upon its propagation. He often sighed, saying:
"If I were to take up my pen and compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra. Now that those with deep understanding are so few, what shall I do?
Treatise: He composed the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the True Mark) in two fascicles solely for Yao Xing.

In the fourth month of the fifteenth year of Hongshi during the Later Qin, he manifested signs of illness and then orally recited three sets of divine mantras, instructing his foreign disciples to chant them so that he might save himself.
Before he had yet applied himself fully, his illness became critical. He then assembled the congregation and said: "We have met because of the Dharma, yet we have not exhausted our hearts' efforts.
As we face the world beyond, my grief is beyond words. Considering my own ignorance and shortcomings, I have mistakenly served as a translator; I pray that this work may be transmitted to posterity."
May this be circulated by all in the world. Now, before this assembly, I make a sincere and truthful vow:

if what I have transmitted is without error and its meaning accords with the Buddha’s mind, may my tongue not be scorched or decayed after my self-immolation. Having finished speaking, he passed away.

When the funeral pyre was extinguished and his body consumed, his tongue-organ remained unimpaired, the color of a red lotus. He lived to the age of seventy. Previously, Kumārajīva had once visited the Great [Teacher] with his mother.
The Venerable of the Northern Mountains in the country of Yuezhi said to his mother, "Guard this śrāmaṇera well;
at thirty-five years of age, he will be without flaw in the Vinaya and will save people just as Upagupta did.

When Beidu was in Pengcheng, he heard that Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong and sighed, saying, "I and this youth parted in play more than three hundred years ago; our meeting now is so remote that it cannot be expected."

[The results will only appear] in a future life. After Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, his disciples numbered more than a thousand; Sheng, Zhao, Rong, and Rui were known as the "Four Sages of Kumārajīva’s School. The sutras and śāstras he translated totaled more than three hundred and ninety fascicles. *Śramaṇa Daosheng:* [He was born in] the second year of the Taichu era of Emperor Wu of Jin (353 CE). His secular surname was He, and his courtesy name was Lingyu. His ancestors were from Wuxing; his great-grandfather had served as the Governor of Donghai. His father, Daohui, was a man of refined character who lived in seclusion in the mountains. At age seven, Daosheng lost his mother and was raised by his paternal uncle, Daohuan. From a young age, he possessed a sharp intellect and a profound capacity for learning. He studied the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* under Master Huiguan and attained a deep understanding of its subtle meanings. At age twelve, he received the ten precepts from Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu. He then traveled to Chang’an to study under Kumārajīva. During the Tianjian era of the Liu Song dynasty, he resided at the Jianchu Monastery in Jiankang. He was renowned for his eloquence and his ability to penetrate the profound mysteries of the Dharma. He frequently lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. He was particularly skilled at expounding the doctrine of the "sudden awakening" (*dunwu*). He once remarked: "If one does not suddenly awaken to the Buddha-nature, one cannot attain Buddhahood. This view conflicted with the established teachings of the time, leading to heated debates. He subsequently composed the *Niepan wusheng fashi lun* (Treatise on the Doctrine that Nirvāṇa is Unborn) and the *Fahua youyi* (Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra). Because his views were unconventional, he was expelled from the monastic community. Later, he returned to Mount Lu, where he died at the age of forty-one. His remains were interred at the foot of Mount Lu. He authored over twenty works, totaling more than two hundred fascicles. His disciples included Zhizang, Huiguan, and others. He was posthumously honored as the "Great Master of the True Dharma" (*Zhengfa Dashi*). His legacy has continued to this day. *Śramaṇa Daosheng:* [He was born in] the second year of the Taichu era of Emperor Wu of Jin (353 CE).

His secular surname was He, and his courtesy name was Lingyu. His ancestors were from Wuxing; his great-grandfather had served as the Governor of Donghai. His father, Daohui, was a man of refined character who lived in seclusion in the mountains. At age seven, Daosheng lost his mother and was raised by his paternal uncle, Daohuan. He was renowned for his eloquence and his ability to penetrate the profound mysteries of the Dharma. He frequently lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. He was particularly skilled at expounding the doctrine of the "sudden awakening" (*dunwu*). He once remarked: "If one does not suddenly awaken to the Buddha-nature, one cannot attain Buddhahood. This view conflicted with the established teachings of the time, leading to heated debates. He subsequently composed the *Niepan wusheng fashi lun* (Treatise on the Doctrine that Nirvāṇa is Unborn) and the *Fahua youyi* (Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra). His remains were interred at the foot of Mount Lu. He authored over twenty works, totaling more than two hundred fascicles. His disciples included Zhizang, Huiguan, and others. He was posthumously honored as the "Great Master of the True Dharma" (*Zhengfa Dashi*). His legacy has continued to this day.

His surname was Wei. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent and did not delight in the clamor of the secular world. Having shaved his head and received the precepts, he first entered Mount Lu, where he lived in seclusion for seven years.
Later, he traveled to Guanzhong, where he studied under Kumārajīva. The monastic community of Guanzhong held him in such deep reverence that they regarded him as a deity.
(Jia-yin) Dharma Master Huiyong’s Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Huiyong resided at Xilin for thirty years, severing his will from worldly clamor and single-mindedly directing his heart toward An-yang (Sukhāvatī).

When He Wujì, General Who Pacifies the South, arrived at Huxi, Huìyuǎn was accompanied by several hundred disciples; their lofty discourse and elegant arguments were such that their deportment was exemplary.

Huiyong was observing [the assembly] when, with his monastic robe reaching only halfway down his calves, he arrived amidst the pine trees carrying his staff and alms bowl, his spirit composed and serene.
Huiji sighed and said, "Master Yong’s style of pure detachment exceeds even that of Master Yuan. In the tenth year of the Yixi era, he manifested slight illness;
suddenly, he adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and asked for his sandals, wishing to rise as if seeing something. The entire assembly was struck with amazement.
Wen Yong asked, "The Buddha has come to welcome me. Having spoken these words, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for seven days before it ceased.
(Bingchen) Dharma Master Huiyuan manifested birth in the Pure Land.
He resided at Mount Lu for thirty years, never venturing beyond its borders. His resolve was fixed upon the Western Realm. For the first eleven years...

On three occasions he beheld the marks of a sage; he remained solemn and did not speak. Nineteen years later, on the evening of the final day of the seventh month in the year of Bingchen of the Yixi era, while at the front of the Prajñā Terrace, he was just arising from meditative concentration when he saw Amitābha Buddha’s body filling the void of space.
Within his circular halo were various transformation Buddhas, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance on his left and right. He also saw flowing water and radiant light.
[The river] divided into fourteen tributaries, flowing upward and downward, as he expounded the wondrous Dharma. The Buddha told Huiyuan: "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you.
Seven days hence, you shall be born in my land. Furthermore, he saw Buddhabhadra, Huichi, Huiyong, and Liu Yimin standing by the Buddha's side.
They stepped forward and bowed to Huiyuan, saying: "Master, your aspirations were formed long ago; why have you come now?"
"Is it not late? Huiyuan then said to his disciples, "When I first resided here, I beheld the holy form three times;
now I have seen it once more. It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. On the sixth day of the eighth month, Huiyuan sat upright and entered nirvana at the age of eighty-four.
Sengji followed Huiyuan as a disciple; Huiyuan once said, "The upholding and flourishing of the Great Dharma rests upon you."
Later, when his illness became grave, he sincerely aspired for the Pure Land. He sent a candle from afar, saying, "You should settle your mind on An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Ji held the candle and leaned against the couch, maintaining his visualization without distraction. Furthermore, he gathered the assembly to chant various sutras concerning the Pure Land.

At the fifth watch, Ji passed the candle to his disciple, Yuanbi, instructing him to join the assembly in their devotional practice. After a short while, he felt himself holding a candle and ascending into the air.
As he walked, he saw Amitābha Buddha, who took him up in his palm and traveled throughout the ten directions. Suddenly he awoke, feeling both sorrowful and comforted;
he examined his four limbs and found them entirely free from illness or pain. At dawn the following evening, he suddenly rose and stood, gazing upward into the void.
Just as he had seen, he lay down again for a moment with a joyful countenance and said to those beside him, "I am going. He then passed away lying on his right side.
At that time, it was the height of summer, yet after three days his body remained unchanged, pervaded by a pervasive and wondrous fragrance. — Daojing.
He was a native of Langya. His grandfather, Ningzhi, served as the Prefect of Jiangzhou, and [Huiyuan] followed him to become a monk under Huiyuan.

He was widely learned in the sutras and śāstras and was devoted to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. In the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he said to the assembly, "My former master has summoned me;
it is time for me to depart. Sitting upright, he chanted the name of the Buddha and passed away. The assembly saw a radiance fill the room, which did not vanish until a long time had passed.
*Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Twenty-Five; *Fozu gangmu*, Scroll Twenty-Six (Supplementary Volume).

Jiazi (Beginning with the first year of Yuanjia of Emperor Wen of the Song Dynasty). Jiamu (The first year of Xiaojian of Emperor Xiaowu). Dingyou (The year the era was changed to Daming). Yisi (The Taishi era of Emperor Ming).
First Year: *Renzi* (reigned as Tāiyù); *Guichou* (the first year of Emperor Yuandi’s Yuánhuī era); *Dingsi* (the first year of Emperor Shundi’s Shèngmíng era);
