*Jiwei* (the first year of the Qi Taizu’s Jiànyuán era); *Guīhài* (the first year of the Qi Wǔdì’s Yǒngmíng era).
Qi: surnamed Xiāo. Seven sovereigns. A total of twenty-four years.
(Yichou) Dharma Master Tanshun Attains Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Tanshun was a native of Huanglong. He studied the sutras under Kumārajīva, who marveled, saying, "This youth is a vessel of extraordinary talent."

Later, he followed Huiyuan and cultivated the practice of Pure Land. In the second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty (525 CE), he passed away while seated separately from the assembly, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
(Bingyin) Venerable Beidu entered nirvana.

Initially, he manifested his presence in Jizhou; his appearance was quite haggard and poor, yet he would often cross waters riding upon a wooden bowl. His spiritual transformations were beyond measure.
Cè did not cultivate refined conduct. Sometimes he bathed by striking the ice; sometimes he climbed mountains wearing wooden clogs; and sometimes he entered the marketplace barefoot.

He carried only a single reed basket and possessed nothing else. Once, when he arrived at Guangling, he encountered the Li family of a village house who were in the midst of providing a meal for monks.
Dù placed his reed basket in the middle of the courtyard and walked straight into the dining hall to sit down, while the assembly stared at him with wide eyes.
As he crossed, it remained as it was. At that time, several people saw the reed basket obstructing the path and exerted all their strength to move it, but they could not budge it.
After Sengdu finished his meal, he simply picked it up and departed, saying with a smile, "The Four Heavenly Kings.
Later, when Li’s young son peered inside the basket, he saw four small children, each several inches tall, with features like those of a painting. Thereupon, Li knew that [Sengdu] was extraordinary.
Fadu invited Huizhi to his home, where he provided him with offerings for a long time. Suddenly, Fadu asked for his *kāṣāya*.
Before Li could prepare it, Fadu said he was going out briefly; by evening he had not returned. The entire district smelled a wondrous fragrance.

Following its source, they suddenly saw Fadu beneath the northern cliff, sitting peacefully and silently upon a worn-out *kāṣāya* spread on the ground. From his head to his feet, lotus flowers had grown, fresh and fragrant.

He was pressing others for alms. One night he withered away. Several days after his burial, someone coming from the north reported that he had seen Sengdu carrying a reed basket across [the river] and heading toward Pengcheng.
Upon opening the coffin, only his leather sandals remained. In Pengcheng there was a man named Huang Xin who had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma;
seeing Sengdu, he invited him to return to his home. His family was extremely poor, possessing nothing but barley gruel.

He crossed over it as if it were sweet as molasses. Later, he traveled east to Wu Commandery. Seeing a fisherman, he begged him for his fishing net, but the fisherman grew angry and would not give it to him.
Zhi Du then picked up two small stones and threw them into the water; suddenly, two oxen appeared and fought over the net until it was shattered.
The oxen then vanished. A resident of Wu Commandery named Zhu Lingqi was returning from Goryeo when a wind carried him to an island, where he saw a...
At Baosi, the monks prepared a meal. [Bodhidharma] then prostrated to the monks and requested to return to his home country quickly.

One of the monks asked, "Do you know the practitioner Beidu? He replied, "I know him. The monk then pointed to a bag on the northern wall where a monk’s staff and alms bowl were hanging and said: [This is he.]
“This Beidu now entrusts his bowl to you. He has also written a letter and placed it inside this box; furthermore, he gives you this green bamboo staff to set before the boat.
In three days, you will arrive at Shitou. Suddenly, Beidu arrived. Opening the letter, he laughed heartily, took the bowl, and tossed it into the air.
Catching it as it fell, he said, “I have not seen this bowl for four thousand years. It was the ninth month of the third year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
He manifested his passing into extinction. After his death, people still occasionally saw him. He once composed a song for a bowl, saying:
"Loud clamor and incessant noise, all are but the idle forging of shackles. Like one who eats salt when hungry, it only increases their thirst;
they waste a lifetime with heads bowed low. In the end, they cannot know the beginning or the end. Casting aside this corpse, where will you escape? I urge you to exert yourself!"
Strive with all your might for liberation. When idle matters reach their end, you must bring them to a conclusion. When fire falls upon your body, you must immediately brush it away;
do not wait until the last moment to cry out for the Bodhisattva. A man of spirit must speak with clarity and resolve; do not imitate the foolish who allow themselves to be patted and fondled.

Seize the opportunity to wrap yourself in practice and learn to shake off delusions. Sometimes you act with gentleness, sometimes with coarseness; sometimes you shave your head, sometimes you wear coarse cloth. And so it goes.
I study the way of ordinary people to live their lives. I speak plainly to you, yet you do not understand. Let me sing once more a long song of the single alms-bowl.
Song of the Alms-Bowl: Within the many, there is one; within the one, there are many. Do not laugh at this rustic man’s song of the alms-bowl;
with this single bowl, I have crossed through the Sahā world. The vast blue sky, the moon rises high; at this moment, its reflection in the void contains ten thousand images. Wherever it floats...
Giving rise to self-righteousness and judgment; the single source is pure, with no coming or going. Do not further use the mind to create bubbles of illusion. Who taught the hundred hairs to bleed?
It is better to sit in stillness upon the ground of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Let the magpies build their nests atop your head.
The Prince of the Golden Wheel for ten thousand generations—this very numinous awakening of True Suchness is he. Beneath the Bodhi tree, he delivers all sentient beings.
Having delivered all sentient beings, one neither dies nor is born; neither born nor dead, such is the true man. Formless and signless, he is the Great Vairocana;
with afflictions extinguished, he is the True Thusness. A single, perfectly luminous, priceless jewel—neither seen by the eye nor heard by the ear.
Not seeing and not hearing is true seeing and hearing. From of old, there has been but this one word beyond speech; today, a thousand words are but forced elaborations.
This is for the sake of distinction. You must listen attentively: every person possesses the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is just like gold within ore;

as it is smelted again and again, the essence of the gold becomes pure. The true is false, and the false is true. If one were to remove both the true and the false, there would be no person remaining.
Do not needlessly give rise to afflictions regarding the true mind. Wear fine clothes or coarse ones as the times require to sustain the physical body. Whether it be good or bad, wear them all. One.
Do not harbor any thoughts, nor be stained by attachment. There is neither good nor evil; it is the level and equal path of the two limits.
Whether coarse or subtle, eat them both. Do not follow the common folk in observing appearances. There is neither coarse nor subtle;
in the Fragrant Accumulation above, there is no root or stem. Sitting is walking, and walking is sitting; beneath the tree of birth and death lies the fruit of Bodhi. Furthermore, there is nothing.
Even sitting, there is no walking. Since there is no birth, what use is there in seeking non-birth? Birth is attained and death is also attained;
everywhere one shall come to see Maitreya. Yet there is neither birth nor death; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are all thus. To leave is to be attached, and to be attached is to leave.
Within the gateway of illusion, there is no real meaning. There is nothing to leave and nothing to be attached to—where else could one seek it?
The medicine for the absence of illness: speaking when silent and remaining silent when speaking; speech and silence are free-flowing and without fixed location.
There is neither speech nor silence. Do not call east and west by the names of south and north. Anger is joy, and joy is anger. I myself subdue the Māras and turn the Wheel of Dharma;
yet there is neither anger nor joy. Water does not depart from its waves; the waves are themselves water. When stingy, one gives; when giving, one is stingy.
Avarice does not depart from the internal, the external, or that which lies between; there is neither avarice nor renunciation. It is silent and vast, with nothing to grasp.
When there is suffering, there is joy; when there is joy, there is suffering. This very practice cuts off all gateways; there is neither suffering nor joy.
Originally free and without ropes; defilement is itself purity, and purity is itself defilement. In both extremes, there is ultimately no before or after; there is neither defilement nor purity.
The great trichiliocosm is of one single nature of *tathatā*. Medicine is the illness, and illness is the medicine; in the end, both must be cast aside.
There is neither medicine nor illness—this is precisely the numinous, awakened nature of *tathatā*. Māra.
The Buddha becomes a demon, and the demon becomes a Buddha; like seeking a form within a mirror or ripples upon water. There is neither demon nor Buddha;

throughout the three periods of time, there has never been a single thing. The ordinary is the sacred, and the sacred is the ordinary; like blue pigment in the lacquer or salt in the water. There is neither ordinary nor sacred;
all practices are held together as not a single practice. Within the true there is the false, and within the false there is the true; this is simply the ordinary.
When delusory dust arises, there is neither true nor false. If one does not call out, how can there be a response? Originally, there is no surname and no name;
simply wander aimlessly, walking wherever the feet lead. Sometimes in the marketplace or at a butcher’s stall, a single red lotus blooms upon the fire.
I have also once leaned on my staff to roam through the capitals of Jing and Luo; my body was like a drifting cloud, with no fixed dwelling. Illusion.
Transformation has always been like a temporary lodging; in other houses, every place is even more pure and void. If you seek precepts, when will the sores of the three poisons ever heal?
If you seek Chan, I simply sleep at ease, rolling about as I please—most pitiable, yet not mad.
He is the one in the world, the one beyond the world, the God among gods. People of this age do not understand the meaning herein: strike the south, and the north moves.
If you seek the Dharma, ask Kāśyapa on Mount Kukkuṭapāda; the Great Being holds his robe within it—originally, there was no need to seek it with such single-minded intensity.
If you seek the Sūtras, the true source of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is beyond hearing. If you seek the Vinaya, the impoverished son has no need for instruction to run away.
If you seek cultivation, where can the eighty-four thousand stūpas be found? One simply knows that yellow leaves were used only to stop a child's crying.
I weep; I am unaware that black clouds have obscured the sun. Do not take my mad words as lacking order: the sieve gradually moves from the coarse to the fine.
Yet even this "coarse and fine" does not exist; it is the perfectly luminous, true reality (*tattva*).

This true reality is fundamentally not "true"; it is merely a name, and names are themselves dust. If one seeks to understand true reality within the midst of dust, that is precisely the majestic, unimpeded state.
One who has transcended the world does not engage in conditioned activity. Walking alone and stepping forth, solitary and empty, there is neither birth nor death, nor is there nirvana.
From the beginning, birth and death have never been involved with one another; there is no right or wrong, no movement or stillness. Do not vainly cast your body into the empty well.
There is neither good nor evil, neither coming nor going, nor is there a bright mirror hung upon a high terrace. Such is the understanding of this mountain monk.
It is simply this. Do not fail to believe it; otherwise, you will create the ashes of a kalpa.
(Xinwei year) Guṇavarman of India arrived in Jinling.

Guṇavarman (translated as "Armor of Merit") had originally renounced the throne to enter the monastic life. He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and was highly esteemed by the kings of various neighboring states.
All received his refuge and precepts. He traveled to the kingdom of Śrīvijaya, where its king desired to leave the household life and serve him as a disciple.

However, the ministers adamantly petitioned against it, and the king consequently issued a decree throughout the land, saying: "If all within the realm will uphold the Upādhyāya’s refuge and precepts, then I shall grant your request.

Thereupon, the officials and citizens of that country bowed their heads and complied with the command. At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty heard of his fame and dispatched an envoy.

He welcomed him. Buddhabhadra joyfully boarded the ship and arrived at Guangzhou. On his way, he passed through Shixing; finding that its mountains resembled Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he stayed there for one year.

He painted images of Dīpaṃkara offering his hair and other figures upon the temple walls. At night, they would frequently emit light. Once, he remained in meditative concentration for several days without emerging.
A monk from the temple sent a novice to check on him; suddenly, he saw a white lioness looking up and treading upon [the wall].

He leaned against a pillar and played; the entire sky was filled with blue lotus flowers. The novice monk fled in alarm, crying out loudly, and the temple monks rushed forward in a scramble, but there was nothing at all to be seen.

In the eighth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked him, "I have long desired to observe the fast and refrain from killing, yet as I am bound to respond to worldly affairs, I have not been able to fulfill this wish.
I pray that you, Master, will instruct me. Mo said, "The Way lies in the mind; it does not lie in..."
Matters of principle depend on oneself, not on others. Furthermore, what a sovereign cultivates differs from that of an ordinary man.
If an ordinary man cannot overcome his own selfishness and undergo rigorous self-discipline, how can he be of use? A sovereign takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children.

When he utters a single virtuous word, scholars and commoners alike rejoice; when he implements a single benevolent policy, spirits and humans are brought into harmony, and punishments do not cause untimely death.
If labor does not exhaust one’s strength, then wind and rain will be timely, cold and heat will follow their seasons, the hundred grains will flourish, and the mulberry and oak trees will grow lush.
To observe the fast for this reason is a great fast; to refrain from killing for this reason brings great benefit.
Why must one first cease eating for half a day and spare the life of a single bird before it can be considered a vast salvation? The Emperor struck his armrest and sighed in admiration.

It was said: "The laity are deluded regarding the distant principle, while the monastics are stalled by proximate teachings. As the Master says, we may now discuss the boundary between heaven and humanity.

(Ren-shen) When Dharma Master Daosheng arrived in Jinling, he first saw the initial portion of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which stated: "With the exception of the icchantikas, all possess Buddha-nature. Thereupon, he declared:
"How can it be that icchantikas alone lack the Buddha-nature? This scripture has not yet reached its conclusion. Thereupon, he proclaimed that all icchantikas shall surely attain Buddhahood.
At once, the masters of letters collectively denounced this as a heterodox teaching and declared that, according to the Vinaya, he should be expelled.
Daosheng then made a vow, saying: "If what I have said does not accord with the meaning of the scriptures, I pray that I may receive the retribution for my evil deeds in this very lifetime. If...
He truly conformed to the Buddha-mind. He vowed that at the time of his passing, he would sit upon a lion throne, then shake out his robes and enter Tiger Hill (Huqiu).

There, he felt a sudden, clear resonance with the enlightened mind. Consequently, he took up residence at Qingyuan Temple. Once, while sitting alone beneath a tall pine tree, he gathered stones to serve as his disciples.
One day, while lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when he reached the passage concerning icchantikas, he declared that they possess the Buddha-nature, saying: "As for me..."
When he asked, "Does the meaning of what I have preached accord with the Buddha's mind? all the stones nodded their heads. That summer, thunder shook the Buddha hall at Qingyuan Temple;
suddenly, a dragon was seen leaping up, emitting a celestial light that cast its shadow upon the western wall. Consequently, the name of the temple was changed to Longguang (Dragon Light).
People of the time sighed and said, "Since the dragon has departed, the Master must surely depart as well. After several days, he indeed returned to Mount Lu, leaving behind...
One of his shadow-images fell among the crags and grottoes of Tiger Hill (Húqiū), where the monastic community all paid their respects.

When Daosheng heard that Dharmakṣema had retranslated the latter chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which stated that even those with "definitive disbelief" (*icchantika*), though they have severed their roots of goodness, still possess Buddha-nature, he was filled with great joy and consolation.
In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled to Jinling; not long after, he returned once more to Mount Lu.
(Jiaxu) Dharma Master Daosheng entered nirvana.

While residing at the Lu Shan Monastery, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. In the eleventh month of the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, as he ascended the Dharma seat and engaged in several rounds of doctrinal debate, all who observed and listened were filled with joy. Suddenly, they saw his fly-whisk fall down in a flurry.

He sat upright on the ground, composed his appearance, leaned against a small table, and passed away. He was eighty years old. He had written commentaries during his lifetime, which the world all treasures.
(Yihai) Dharma Master Daobing’s Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Daobing was a native of Yingchuan. From childhood, he served as a disciple of Huiyuan. He thoroughly mastered the Tripiṭaka, and his words were in accord with his conduct. His mindfulness...
The Buddha’s Samādhi. He investigated the mind without interruption. In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he gathered the assembly for the practice of Buddha-recollection;
while seated, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the room. His age was seventy-one.
(Ji-mao) Dharma Master Sengrui’s Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Sengrui initially studied the meaning of the scriptures under Kumārajīva. Later, he joined the Lotus Society at Mount Lu and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

In the Ji-mao year of the Yuanjia era, he suddenly gathered his assembly and took his leave, saying, "I am about to depart. He then ordered that preparations for a ritual bath be made and incense to be burned.
After burning incense and prostrating, he returned to his seat facing west; with palms joined, he passed away.
The assembly saw a single golden lotus flower suddenly vanish before Hui’s couch, while five-colored fragrant smoke issued forth from his room.
In the year Jiashen, Dharma Master Xuangao entered nirvana.
Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty, having heard the slanderous accusations of Cui Hao, imprisoned his crown prince, Huang. Huang then sought mercy from Xuangao.

Gao performed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual for the Emperor. The Emperor dreamed that his late ancestor Letian said to him, "You ought not to have harbored suspicions against the Crown Prince due to slander.
Upon waking, he spoke of this to his ministers, and all the ministers declared that the Crown Prince was without fault; they treated him as before.
Hao, fearing that the Crown Prince would bring harm to himself, told the Emperor, "The Crown Prince actually did plot [against you] previously; furthermore, he has formed a bond with Xuangong..."
"Xiao Gao used his arts to bring about the former Emperor; I fear he will do the same to Your Majesty. If you do not eliminate him early, he will surely cause great harm.
The Emperor was enraged and had Xiao Gao and Hui-chong arrested and strangled. Xiao Gao’s disciple, Xuan-chang, arrived in haste from afar.

Gao suddenly opened his eyes and said: "The Great Dharma responds to conditions; it flourishes or declines according to those conditions. Flourishing and decline reside in its outward manifestations, while its underlying principle remains eternally serene. I only regret that you..."
"Practice the Way as I have done. Only Xuanchang shall cross southward. After you have passed away, the Dharma shall flourish once more.

Cultivate your own minds well; do not let yourselves regret it midway. Having finished speaking, he immediately transformed and vanished. The śramaṇa Fajin cried out, "The Sage has departed from this world; what use is there for me to live?
At that sound, [the Master] appeared high in the air and said to Jin, "Do not forget anything. How could..."
"Am I alone being abandoned by you? Jingjin asked. Daokao replied, "As for Master Heshang and Master Chong, where have they both been reborn?

I am going to an evil realm to rescue and protect sentient beings, while Chong has returned to An-yang. Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight. Initially, Daokao had resided at Maiji Mountain.
Hearing that Dharmapriya had arrived in Liang, he went there to serve as his disciple; within ten days, he attained realization, leading Dharmapriya to exclaim that he surpassed himself.
Emperor Wu of Wei sent an envoy to welcome Sengao to serve as the preceptor for the Crown Prince. Among Sengao’s disciples who had mastered the Dharma, there were many;
one, named Sengyin, claimed to have attained the fruit of an Arhat. At that time, while he was observing the summer retreat, Sengao [confronted him] by means of a pretext...

By means of his supernormal powers, he caused himself to see, within meditative concentration, the infinite worlds of the ten directions and heard the various teachings expounded by the Buddhas, each of which was different.
Within a single summer retreat, he sought out what he had seen and found that it could not be exhausted; thereupon, he felt shame and regret.
(Year of the Earth-Dragon, 27th Patriarch) The Transmission of the Dharma by Prajñātāra to Bodhidharma.
Prajñātāra was a native of Eastern India who received the Dharma from Rāhulamitra.
Once, while he was invited to a vegetarian feast by the King of Eastern India, the king asked: "Everyone here is reciting the sutras; why alone do you not recite? Prajñātāra replied: [text continues]
He said, "This poor monk’s exhalation does not involve external conditions, and his inhalation does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates.

He constantly recites this sutra hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times, not merely one or two scrolls. Later, while traveling to convert others in South India, he arrived at the kingdom of King Gandhāra.
The king respected and made offerings to him beyond compare with others, and further bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had..."
He had three sons: the first was named Candravairocana, the second Guṇavairocana, and the third Bodhivairocana; the youngest was a bodhisattva.
Prajñātāra wished to test what they had attained, so he took the pearl he had been given and asked the three princes, "This pearl is perfectly round and luminous;
is there anyone who can equal it? Candravairocana and Guṇavairocana said, "This pearl is [seven]..."
"Among treasures, it is most honored; indeed, nothing surpasses it. Bodhi said: "This is a worldly treasure; it is not yet supreme.
Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This is a worldly light; it is not yet supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly clarity; it is not yet supreme. Among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. As for this jewel..."
Light cannot illuminate itself; it requires the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a pearl.
Once it is known to be a pearl, its value as a treasure is realized. If its value as a treasure were inherent, the treasure would not be a treasure by itself;

if the pearl were discerned by itself, the pearl would not be a pearl by itself. That the pearl is not a pearl by itself means that it requires the "wisdom-pearl" to discern the worldly pearl as a treasure.
Regarding those who do not treasure themselves: they must rely upon the treasure of wisdom to illuminate the treasure of the Dharma. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that treasure manifests;
when sentient beings possess the Way, the treasure of their minds is likewise so. Tāra praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what is signless? He replied, "Among all things, non-arising is signless. Again he asked, "Among all Buddhas, which is the highest?
He replied, "Among all things, the person-self (pudgala-ātman) is the highest. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. Tārā understood this Dharma.

[The Master] said: "Since the time has not yet arrived, remain silent for now and blend in with the crowd. When the incense reached the place where the King had passed away, the multitude all wailed and fainted.
Bodhidharma alone entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) before the coffin; after seven days had passed, he emerged and requested ordination from Tāla.
Once he had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), Tāla said: "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery. As for *Dharma*, it is thorough penetration."
"This is the meaning of 'Great. You should be named Dharma. He then changed his name accordingly. Later, he told him:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse:
'From the mind-ground arise all seeds; Based on the mind, they again take root. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; When the flower blooms, the world [is revealed].'"
The Dharma realm arose. Having entrusted the Dharma, he immediately rose from his seat and extended his left and right hands, each emitting twenty-seven streams of light, brilliant with five colors.
He then leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and consumed himself by fire through transformation.
Śarīra relics fell like rain from the sky; the great assembly erected a stūpa to collect and offer them. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty in this land.
The first year of the Ming dynasty was the year of Dingyou (547).
(Wuxu) In the twenty-eighth generation, Bodhidharma preached the Dharma in South India, while Prajñātāra entered parinirvāṇa.
Bodhidharma subsequently propagated the teachings in his own country. At that time, there were two masters.
The first was named Buddhadasa; the second was named Buddhasanta. Originally, they had studied the small-vehicle (*hīnayāna*) meditative contemplations together with Māra.
Buddhadasa encountered Prajñātāra, and both he and Māra received the True Dharma from him. However, Buddhasanta further divided his followers into six schools:

first, the School of Characteristics (*sākāravāda*); second, the School of Non-characteristics (*nirākāravāda*); third, the School of Samādhi and Wisdom (*samādhiprajñā*); fourth, the School of Precepts...
The School of Practice, the School of Non-attainment, and the School of Quiescence—each adhering to their own understanding and separately expanding the source of their conversion.
He sighed deeply and lamented: "If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so when they have fragmented into six schools?

If I do not eliminate this, it will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken thus, he subtly manifested his supernatural power and went to the place of the School of Characteristics, where he asked:
"Regarding all dharmas, what is called their 'true mark' (bhūtalakṣaṇa)? A senior elder named Sarvāla among that assembly replied:
"Among all marks, the non-interchangeability of marks is called the true mark. [He asked: "If all marks are not interchangeable, by what are they determined?
[He replied: "Among all marks, there is truly no fixed determination. If marks were fixed, how could they be called [marks]?"
[The interlocutor] said: "It is real. [Subhūti] replied: "Because all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are indeterminate, they are called the 'characteristic of reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

You are now indeterminate; how then can you attain it? [The interlocutor] said: "When I say 'indeterminate,' I do not speak of characteristics. It is precisely when speaking of characteristics that their meaning is likewise [indeterminate]. [Subhūti] said:

"If what you call 'indeterminate' were to constitute the characteristic of reality, then because it is both determinate and indeterminate, it would not be the characteristic of reality. [The interlocutor] said: "Since the determinate is itself indeterminate, it is not [the characteristic of reality]."
"True Reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is known because it is not the self; it is neither fixed nor unchanging. [The interlocutor asks: "If you are now unchanging, why is it called True Reality?
That which has already changed and passed away is likewise so. [He replies: "Unchanging would mean 'to abide. Because of the presence or absence [of abiding], change is indeed True Reality."

To determine its meaning, [the Master] said: "The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is unchanging; that which changes is not the true mark. Within existence and non-existence, what can be called the true mark?
Śāvala understood that the Holy Teacher had attained profound liberation and reached a deep realization beyond the senses. He then pointed his finger at empty space and said:
"This is the world of conditioned marks (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), yet it is also capable of being empty. Can my body become like this? [The Master] replied: "If you understand..."
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the seeing of non-marks. If one realizes non-marks, then form (*rūpa*) is likewise so.
Within form, one does not lose the essence of form; within non-marks, one is not obstructed by existence. If one can understand it thus, this is called the true mark.

Having heard this, the assembly’s minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it in faith. In a flash, [the teacher] vanished from sight and went to the abode of the School of Non-Mark (*alakṣaṇavāda*).
Question: You speak of "signlessness" (animitta). How should this be realized? Among that assembly was one named Pratītya, who replied: "I am called signless because the mind does not manifest.
He asked: "If your mind does not manifest, how do you clarify it? He replied: "I clarify signlessness by neither grasping nor rejecting with the mind.
At the time of such clarification, there is also no one who clarifies. He asked: "Regarding all that exists and does not exist, the mind..."
There is neither grasping nor abandoning, and furthermore, there is no one who acts as such, because all forms of clarity (*vidyā*) are absent. This is called entering the Buddha-samādhi.

Since even that which is attained is non-existent, how much more so can one seek to know the signless (*animitta*)? It is said: "Since the sign itself is not known, who can speak of existence or non-existence?

Since even that which is attained is non-existent, what is it that is named 'samādhi'? It is said: "I speak of non-realization; realization is that wherein nothing is realized, for it is not [ordinary] samādhi. Thus I speak.
"Samādhi," he said, "is that which is called 'non-samādhi. How then could it be named? Since you have not yet realized it, what realization can there be in non-realization?
Having heard this, Pratibhānu immediately awakened to his original mind. He prostrated in gratitude to Māra and repented of his past errors.

Māra recorded, saying: "You shall attain the fruit; before long, you will realize it for yourself. There is a demon in this land; you shall subdue him before long. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished.
Xian went to the monastery of the Zong of Samādhi and Prajñā and asked, "In your study of samādhi and prajñā, are they one or two?

Among the assembly was one named Bharadvāja, who replied, "This samādhi and prajñā of ours are neither one nor two. Xian said, "If they are neither one nor two, why are they called 'samādhi' and 'prajñā'?
He replied, "Abiding in samādhi, it is not samādhi; dwelling in prajñā, it is not prajñā. One is not one, and two is also not two."
[The Master] said: "It should be one, yet not one; it should be two, yet not two. Since it is neither fixed concentration nor wisdom, by what means could it be defined as concentration or wisdom?

[The Monk] asked: "If it is neither one nor two, who is in concentration and who is in wisdom? Who is wisdom and who is concentration? [The Master] said: "Wisdom is not concentration; how then can it be known?

That it is neither one nor two—who is in concentration and who is in wisdom? It is the same for that which is neither concentration nor wisdom. When Póluán tuó heard this, his doubts were completely dispelled like ice melting away.
Upon arriving at the fourth hall, the Hall of the Essential Principles of Preceptual Practice, he asked: "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? What is called 'practice' (caryā)?
Are these precept and practice one or two? Are they both produced from that [source]? Among the assembly was a worthy man who replied: "'One and two,' and 'two and one'—all are produced from that.
To rely on the teaching without defilement is what is called 'preceptual practice'. He said: "Your statement that one relies on the teaching implies there is still defilement. "One."

Both [positions] are refuted. How can you say that [the precepts] rely on the teachings? These two are contradictory and do not reach the level of practice; being neither internal nor external clarity, how can they be called "precepts"?
He replied: "I have both the internal and the external. Once he has fully understood this and attained thorough penetration, it constitutes the practice of the precepts.

"If you say they are contradictory, then both 'is' and 'is not' apply; yet you speak of purity, which is itself both precept and practice. If both 'is' and 'is not' apply, how can you speak of purity?
Since this has been made clear, why discuss internal and external? Upon hearing this, the worthy one felt ashamed and submitted. He went to the abode of the Master of Non-Attainment and asked:
"You speak of non-attainment. What is attained through non-attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained..."

Nor is there an attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was one named Baojing (Jewel-Quiescence), who replied: "I say there is no attainment; it is not that there is an attainment of non-attainment.
One should speak of the attainment of attainment: non-attainment is itself attainment. [The other] asked: "If attainment is already non-attainment, then attainment is also non-attainment.

Since you speak of the 'attainment of attainment,' what is attained by this attainment of attainment? [Baojing] replied: "To see attainment as non-attainment—that non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called..."

[The interlocutor] asked: "Is it for the sake of attaining attainment? [The Master] replied: "Since 'attainment' is itself non-attainment, the 'attainment of attainment' is non-attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, what could possibly be attained through attainment?

Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt. He went to the abode of Jijing and asked: "What is meant by 'quiescence'? Within this Dharma, what is quiescent and what is tranquil?
There was a venerable elder there who answered: "This mind is unmoving; this is what is called..."
[The Master] said: "To be unstained by phenomena is called 'quiescence' (*śānti*). [The Disciple] asked: 'If the original mind is not quiescent, one must rely on the practice of stillness.

Since it is originally quiescent, what need is there for stillness? [The Master] replied: 'All phenomena are fundamentally empty. Because they are empty even of emptiness, they are named "sublime stillness" (*praśānta*).
[The Disciple] asked: 'If even emptiness is already empty, all phenomena are likewise so. Being quiescent and signless, what is there to be stilled and what is there to be made quiescent?'"
Upon hearing this instruction, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Thereupon, the six assemblies all vowed to take refuge in Baozhi.
A native of Jinling, he was originally the child of Zhu, a woman from Dongyang; she heard a child crying in an eagle’s nest, climbed the tree to retrieve him, and raised him as her own son.

At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order under the monk Jian at Mount Zhongshan and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation. It was at this point that his spiritual manifestations became manifest.
He hung a pair of scissors, a ruler, and a whisk from the tip of his staff and traveled carrying it on his back. When he passed through villages, children would clamor and chase after him;
sometimes he begged for a little wine, and at other times he went for days without food. Once, he encountered someone eating sliced raw fish and followed them to beg for some.
The eater shared some with him, but with a frivolous and contemptuous mind, he spat it into the water. It all became live fish. He traveled back and forth between Mount Wan.
Beneath the Jian River, he shaves his hair and goes barefoot, wearing a brocade robe. His face is square and as clear and translucent as a mirror;
his hands and feet all have bird-claws. From time to time he composes poems, which at first seem unintelligible, but later all prove to be verified.
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle Twenty-Six;
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle Twenty-Seven (Character Code: Cheng).

Jiazi (Beginning in the second year of Yongming of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty); Jiaxu (The first year of Jianwu of Emperor Ming); Xinsi (The first year of Zhongxing); Renwu (The [first] year of Tianjian of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty).
Jiān 1 (Gēnzǐ; changed to Pǔtōng); Dīngwèi (changed to Dàtōng); Jǐyǒu (changed to Zhōngdàtōng); Yǐmǎo (changed to Dàtóng);
Guǐhài (ended in the ninth year of the Dàtóng era of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng).
Liáng: surnamed Xiāo. Four rulers. A total of fifty-six years.
(Renwu year) The Great Master Baozhi was preaching the Dharma within the royal palace.
Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty initially became enraged that Baozhi was deluding the masses and had him arrested and imprisoned in Jiankang.

On this day, people saw Baozhi wandering through the markets and streets, yet when they searched for him, he was still inside the prison. That evening, he said to his attendants, "Outside the gate, there are two carriages."
She ate from a golden bowl filled with rice; you may take it. Subsequently, when Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling sent offerings that reached Jiankang, the Emperor was informed of this.
He expressed regret and apologized, then invited her into the inner palace. Shortly thereafter, while the Emperor was holding a banquet for the ladies of the harem, Zhi temporarily went out.
Yet, she was still seen walking in meditation at the Xianyang Hall. Startled, the Emperor dispatched an official to inquire about her whereabouts. The official reported that Zhi—

He had been away from the capital for a long time. The Emperor’s divine reverence for him increased further after Hui-zhi used his supernatural powers to show the Emperor how the High Ancestor was undergoing the suffering of being pricked with awls and knives in the underworld.
From that time on, the use of awls and knives was abolished forever. When Wang Zhong-xiong asked him what position he would attain in official service, Hui-zhi did not answer;
instead, he untied the left-hand cord from the end of his staff and gave it to him. Later, Wang Zhong-xiong indeed reached the rank of Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs. Xu...
When Ling was a child, his father took him to visit Daoshi. Daoshi rubbed the top of his head and said, "This child is a stone qilin from the heavens.
Later, he indeed became renowned in the world. In the year Renwu, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty ascended the throne, he summoned Daoshi to the palace.

One day, the Emperor dressed in full ceremonial attire and asked, "I, your disciple, am still plagued by afflictions and delusions; how may they be cured? Daoshi replied, "In twelve [years]. When the Emperor asked for the meaning of this, it was as follows:

"What? he asked. [Zhiyi] replied, "It is within the time-measures of the written characters. The Emperor was even more perplexed. He asked again, "When may my disciple obtain a tranquil mind to practice cultivation?
[Zhiyi] replied, "At the beginning of the *Anle jin* (The Prohibition of Killing). Previously, Emperor Wu had dreamed that a divine monk told him:

"The six realms and four modes of birth are undergoing great suffering and affliction. Why do you not perform the Great Water-Land Feast (*shuilu daizhai*) to rescue and deliver them? Thereupon, the Emperor...

He visited the śramaṇa Sengzhi, who urged the Emperor to seek out the Buddhist scriptures, saying that there must surely be a karmic cause for this. The Emperor then took up the Buddhist sutras and personally examined them;
he then composed the liturgical texts, which were completed after three years. One night, holding the manuscript while the candles were extinguished, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the principles of these writings accord with those of the sages and the common people, I pray that when I rise from my prostrations, this lamp will light itself. If the rituals are not yet detailed," [the lamp would remain dark].
The darkness remained as before. Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself on the ground; as he rose from his first bow, the lamps and candles were all brightly illuminated.

On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Tianjian era, he performed the ritual according to the prescribed rites at Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang. Daoshi had also once availed himself of the Emperor’s supernatural power.
He caused them to see the suffering of the hells and asked how they might be saved from it. [The Master] replied, "The fixed karma of past lives cannot be extinguished all at once;

however, upon hearing the sound of a bell, their suffering may briefly cease. Thereupon, he issued an edict for all temples throughout the empire to strike bells, instructing that the sound be drawn out slowly.
The Emperor once summoned the painter Zhang Sengyou to paint an image of Master Zhi. Whenever Sengyou set his brush to the canvas, [the image would not take form].
He resolved to do so himself. Huizhi then used his finger to scratch his face, revealing the form of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, appearing sometimes compassionate and sometimes majestic;
however, he was ultimately unable to paint it. Huizhi said, "Vipaśyin Buddha applied his mind to this long ago, yet until now I have not attained its perfection.
On another day, while the Emperor and he were gazing out over the river, an object floated upstream. Huizhi pointed at it with his staff.
He was summoned; [the statue] followed the staff as it arrived. It was made of purple sandalwood, which was immediately entrusted to an attendant official to have the image carved.
It was completed in an instant, its divine spirit appearing as if alive.
(Jia-ma) The Great Being Baozhi passed away.

Having manifested for over forty years, in the winter of the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era, he suddenly informed the assembly of monks to move the statue of the Vajra Deity from the temple and place it outside.
He then spoke secretly to someone, saying, "The Bodhisattva is about to depart. Thereupon, he went to...
In the inner palace, he took his final leave of Emperor Wu. The Emperor was greatly startled and asked, "How long will my life last? Zhi did not answer;
instead, he pointed with his finger to his throat and then out toward the mountain. He lit a single candle on the mountain and entrusted it to Wu Qing, an attendant of the rear palace.
Qing reported the matter to the Emperor, who sighed and said, "The Great Master will not remain with us any longer. Will this lamp now illuminate me regarding his final affairs?
On the sixth day of the twelfth month, he passed away without illness; his entire body was fragrant and supple. He was ninety-two years of age.
The Emperor erected a stupa for him on Dulong Peak at Mount Zhong and commanded Lu Chui to compose an inscription, while Wang Yun set up the stele. This was preceded by...
Sengzhi accompanied the Emperor up Mount Zhong. Pointing to the ridge of Dulonggang before them, he said, "This shall serve as a burial site; it will ensure the prosperity of your lineage.
The Emperor asked, "Who shall obtain this place? Sengzhi replied, "He who comes first shall have it. That year, Sengzhi passed away.
The Emperor then paid two hundred thousand *jin* of gold to purchase the land, erected a five-storied pagoda, enshrined within it an invaluable precious pearl, and interred him there.
On that day, the imperial carriage arrived in person. Suddenly, Daoshi appeared amidst the clouds; the myriad people cheered, their voices shaking the mountains and valleys.
Daoshi had once given these instructions: "Throughout the entire day, one picks up incense and selects firewood, yet remains unaware that the body itself is the site of enlightenment (dharma-śāla).
He also said: "The vast expanse of the capital and Ye-du is itself the Great Path of Bodhi. Furthermore, he said: "As my own body is empty, so all dharmas are empty."
"The thousand species and myriad classes are all identical. Furthermore, he once asked a Brahman monk: "I have heard that you, Venerable Sir, called me a butcher.

Have you ever seen me kill a living being? The monk replied, "I have seen it. He asked again, "Is there a seeing of seeing? Is there a non-seeing of seeing? Is there a neither-existence-nor-non-existence of seeing?

If there is a seeing of seeing, that is the vision of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). If there is a non-seeing of seeing, that is the vision of a Śrāvaka. If there is a neither-existence-nor-non-existence..."

"Non-viewing—this is the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). I do not yet understand what kind of view you, Venerable Sir, hold. The Indian monk said, "Do you have such views as these? Zhi then ceased speaking.
He once composed the *Song of the Twelve Hours*, which says: "At dawn, the hour of *yin*: Within the workings of madness lies the person of the Way.
Having endured suffering and hardship for immeasurable kalpas, one still does not believe in constantly holding the wish-fulfilling jewel. If one grasps at objects..."
Entering the ford of delusion: even the slightest trace is but dust. Do not dwell upon former appearances; seeking a teacher outside is not the truth.

At the hour of the sun rising in the morning (Mao), in your practice there is no need for clever artifice. Even if the divine light illuminates existence and non-existence, the moment you give rise to a thought, you will be beset by demonic affairs.
If you exert effort, you will never reach completion; day and night you will be tormented by others and the self.
Twisted! No need for contrivance; simply follow along as it is. When has affliction ever arisen in the mind? At the hour of eating, ignorance is itself the body of Śākyamuni.
Sitting or reclining, one does not know that this is fundamentally the Way. Thus one busily undergoes suffering and toil.
Recognizing sounds and forms, one seeks out the distant and the near; such a person is merely defiled by the world. If you intend to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, ask!
Grasping at emptiness is the beginning of emerging from the dust. At the hour of Youzhong (9–11 a.m.), those who have not yet attained understanding will find that the teaching does not reach them.

Even if you should master the words of the Patriarchs, do not settle upon "resolved meaning" within your own mind. Simply maintain the profound mystery beyond words; yet if you recognize it as such, you remain, as before, in error.
For a moment, if you spontaneously consent and cease seeking, for kalpas on end you shall not be driven by demonic realms. At the hour of Rimmianwu (noon).
Within the body of the four elements lies a priceless jewel; one refuses to cast away the mirage and the flowers in the sky. Cultivating practice with deliberate effort only increases hardship;
since there has never been delusion, do not seek awakening. No matter how many times the morning sun turns to evening, within this body of form dwells the formless body;
upon the road of ignorance lies the path of non-arising. Before the sun has set, why has the mind-ground ever attained the ultimate meaning? His house—

In words there is neither intimacy nor estrangement; do not use the mind to seek their underlying meaning. Let them run freely in all directions, free from all taboos. It abides among people but does not dwell in the world.
Its application never departs from the midst of sound and form. Through kalpas it has never been abandoned for even a moment.
[The hour of] *búshí* (the seventh watch). To study the Way, one must first not loathe poverty. Having form is originally but a provisional accumulation; what use is there for that which is formless?
Seeking the truth is demanding; performing pure deeds merely exhausts the spirit. Suddenly recognizing ignorance as one's neighbor, one does not seek a place of non-existence beneath these words.
For a brief moment, one is called a renunciant. When the sun enters the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), illusory sounds do not endure for long.
One does not even partake of the rare delicacies of the joy of dhyāna; who then could ever drink the wine of ignorance?

It is neither to be cast away nor to be guarded; vast and carefree, it has never existed. Even if you possess great learning and mastery of past and present, you are still a deluded madman wandering outside.
At the hour of dusk, the night-watch, the frantic child exerts effort and enters a dark room. Even if the mind were to penetrate through immeasurable time, across kalpas...
How has it ever been different from today? To attempt to deliberate upon it is merely to chatter; it only serves to make the heart as black as lacquer.

Day and night, the light shines forth, illuminating both existence and non-existence; yet fools call this the *pāramitā*. At the hour of *rātri* (midnight), even those who are courageous and diligent fall into indolence;
they do not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study. Within the light of formlessness, one is eternally sovereign, transcending Śākyamuni and surpassing [all others].

The Patriarchs of old: if the mind harbors even a speck of dust, it remains subject to obstruction; if one is dissolute, one remains forever like a dull-witted fool. His own house naturally has those who understand and love him.
At the hour of midnight, if the mind abides in non-arising, that is itself birth-and-death; yet how could birth-and-death ever belong to existence or non-existence?

When used, it is used; there are no words. The Patriarch spoke of that which lies beyond. Recognize it when it arises, yet it is not that very thing. If you seek it with deliberate intent, truly there is no trace.
When the demons of birth and death come, let them test you as they will. At the hour of the Cock (1–3 a.m.): A single round light has shone for a long time.
Searching within and without, nothing at all can be found. Yet, in the midst of worldly activity, it is perfectly present. It is not seen.
The head has no hands; when heaven and earth perish, it does not decay. Listen to a single word from one who has not yet attained understanding:
who is it that moves their mouth right now? Zhi also composed ten verses in praise of the Mahāyāna and fourteen sections of fourteen verses.
(Jihai) Dharma Master Huiyue expounded the precepts in the royal palace.

Huiyue’s surname was Lou. From his youth, he possessed a refined character and virtue. His clan ancestor, Lou Youyu, who served as a Secretariat Drafter, would invariably rise to pay his respects whenever he saw Huiyue.
Someone once asked, "This man belongs to the lower stratum of your clan; why do you show him such reverence? Youyu replied, "He is a Bodhisattva."

He entered the world and was soon to be a teacher to all under heaven; how could it be that I, an old man, would merely pay him respect? Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited him to reside within the palace.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era, the Emperor received the Bodhisattva precepts and further established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*amogha-mahā-pariṣad*).
On this day, heavenly nectar (*amṛta*) suddenly descended upon the courtyard, and three-legged crows and two peacocks appeared in succession.

The deer tamed themselves and submitted. In total, forty-eight thousand people—including princes, dukes, high officials, monastics, and laypeople—who followed [the Master] and received the precepts, were present.
Consequently, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.

(Gengzi) On the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, Master Fu retired to live in seclusion at Shuanglin. Master Fu was born on the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty to Fu Xuanci in Yiwu County, Wuzhou;
his name was Xi, and his courtesy name was Xuānfēng. At the age of sixteen, he married a woman of the Liu clan named Miaoguang, and they had a son.
Pu Jian achieved universal success at the age of twenty-four. While fishing upstream at the foot of Jieting Pond, he caught some fish;
having finished his catch, he lowered his net into the water and said, "Those that leave may go as they please; those that stay shall remain.

People called him foolish, but there happened to be the Indian monk Śramaṇa Sengqiu (Saṃghadatta), who said to him, "In the past, you and I made a vow before the Buddha Vipaśyin to deliver sentient beings."

"When will you return to the Tuṣita Palace? he asked. He then commanded him to look at his reflection in the water; seeing the circular halo and the jeweled canopy, he immediately realized his former cause.
The gentleman smiled and said, "In a forge there are many pieces of dull iron; at the gate of a skilled physician there are many patients."
"Saving sentient beings is my urgent task; what leisure have I to contemplate the pleasures of the celestial palaces? Thereupon, he discarded his fishing gear and returned home with his belongings.
He then asked for a place to cultivate the Way. Huisong pointed to the twin *tao* trees on Mount Song and said, "This will suffice.
He subsequently built a hermitage and styled himself the "Future Liberated Mahāsattva of Good Wisdom Beneath the Twin Trees. He planted fruits and vegetables there for...
He worked as a hired laborer together with his wife, Miaoguang. He would work by day and return home at night to expound the Buddha-dharma.
(Gengzi) The twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma, arrived in the land of Zhendan (the Eastern Land).
Bodhidharma was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India; his clan name was Kṣatriya. Originally...
His name was Bodhidhara. Upon encountering Prajñātāra and receiving the transmission of the Dharma, he changed his name to Daruma.
Daruma asked Tāra, "To which country should I go to perform the work of a Buddha? He replied, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay in Southern India for now;
wait sixty-seven years after my passing, and you shall go to China to administer the great medicine of the Dharma and directly guide those of superior capacity."
"Root, be careful not to travel too hastily; you will decline under the sun. Is there a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) capable of serving as a vessel for the Dharma?
Will there be obstacles for a thousand years to come? He replied, "In the regions you shall convert, those who attain Bodhi will be beyond counting.
More than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, that land will face a calamity. Water will spread like cloth across the land; you must personally subdue it with goodness."
When you reach the South, do not remain there. They value only conditioned achievements and do not perceive the principle of the Buddha.
Even if you should go there, you must not stay for long. Listen to my verse: Traveling on the road, crossing water, one again meets sheep; Alone and weary, one crosses the dark river at night.
At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses; Two young cassia trees have long flourished in prosperity. He asked again.
"What further events will there be after this? He replied, "One hundred and fifty years from now, there will be minor difficulties.

Listen to my prophecy. He spoke in verse: "Though auspicious within the mind, it is ominous without; A monastic dwelling by the river, its name ill-fated. Because of encountering a venomous dragon, a martial son shall be born;
Suddenly meeting a small mouse, there will be endless stillness. He asked again, "What will happen after this? He replied, "On the contrary..."
Two hundred and twenty years hence, you shall see a person beneath these trees who will attain the fruit of the Way. Listen to my prophecy:
"Though China is vast, there is no other path; it must be traversed by the feet of one's own descendants. When the golden cock releases a single grain of millet,"
He made offerings to the assembly of Arhats throughout the ten directions and further recited various verses, all of which were prophetic premonitions of the rise and fall of the Buddha’s teachings.

He studied and received the doctrines and meanings of the Dharma, serving with diligence for forty years. Upon the passing of Master Multāra, he subdued the six heterodox sects, and his transformation of beings spread throughout Southern India.
After sixty years had passed, he had delivered immeasurable multitudes of beings. Later, he encountered King Harsa (Molu), his uncle, who held heterodox views and sought to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
Mulu felt compassion for him and wished to dispel his ignorance. The six disciples also each reflected that the Buddha-dharma was facing peril and wondered how their teacher would provide succor.
Mulu perceived the thoughts of the assembly from afar and responded by snapping his fingers; all six disciples heard it and said, "This is the sound of our teacher’s faith."

They all went to the place where the Śramaṇa was. The Śramaṇa said, "A single film obscures the sky; who is able to brush it away? [The Master] replied, "The preceding school of Non-characteristic (Animitta) is superior in doctrine, yet I desire to practice.

The Śramaṇa said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete. Furthermore, you have no karmic affinity with the King. [The Master] took his leave of the Śramaṇa.
He eventually arrived at the king’s location and extensively expounded upon the essentials of the Dharma. The king asked, "Regarding what you have now understood, where does that Dharma reside?
Zongsheng replied, "Just as Your Majesty governs and transforms the realm, it should accord with the Way. The king asked, "Where does the Way possessed by Your Majesty reside?

The king replied, "The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings; as for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue? At this, Mo did not rise from his seat, yet he knew [the king's intent] beforehand.
When Zongsheng fell into defeat, he summoned Boluoti and said, "Zongsheng did not follow my instructions; he has been defeated in debate with the King. You must go quickly to rescue him.

Boluoti replied, "I pray you grant me your supernatural power. As soon as he had spoken, clouds rose from beneath his feet. When he arrived before the King, the King was in the midst of questioning Zongsheng;
seeing him suddenly, he was struck with amazement and forgot what he was asking or answering, exclaiming, "One who comes through the air!"
"Is this right or wrong? Ti replied, "I am neither wrong nor right; I come to rectify both right and wrong. If Your Majesty’s mind is upright, I shall have neither wrong nor right.
Although the King was struck with wonder, his arrogance was still burning fiercely; he immediately expelled Zongsheng.
Ti said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you expel a śramaṇa? Though I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me a question. The King asked angrily:

"What is it that constitutes a Buddha? He replied, "To see one's nature is to be a Buddha. He asked, "Does the Master see your nature? He replied, "I see my Buddha-nature. He asked, "Where does this nature reside?
He replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. He asked, "What is this functioning? I do not perceive it now.

He replied, "It is functioning right now; it is simply that you, O King, do not see it. He asked, "Does it exist within me as well? He replied, "If you were to function, there would be nothing that is not [the Buddha-nature]."
"It is so. If Your Majesty does not employ it, its substance is likewise difficult to perceive. [The King] asked: "When it is employed, in how many places does it manifest?
[The Master] replied: "When it manifests, there are eight instances. [The King] said: "Please explain to me these eight manifestations. Vasubandhu then spoke in verse: "In the womb, it is the body;
dwelling in the world, it is the person. In the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing. In the nose, it discerns..."

Fragrance is in the mouth when speaking, in the hand when grasping, and in the feet when running; it manifests everywhere, encompassing all lands as numerous as grains of sand, yet can be withdrawn and gathered within a single minute atom.
Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*jīva*).
Upon hearing these verses, the King’s mind was immediately enlightened; he repented his former errors and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. The King asked again: "Who is your teacher?"

"Who is he? [the king] asked. "It is none other than Your Majesty’s uncle, Bodhidharma," they replied. Upon hearing this, the king was struck with alarm and immediately commanded his attendants to escort Bodhidharma to the royal palace.
There, Bodhidharma performed repentance for the king’s past transgressions. Hearing this, the king wept and apologized, then issued an edict to recall Zongsheng to the kingdom.
An attendant remarked, "When Zongsheng was exiled, he already cast himself from a cliff and gave up his life. Bodhidharma said, "Sheng is still alive."
When summoned, he was due to arrive. Initially, when Śaṅkara had received the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), he felt ashamed that he could not rectify the King.

He then threw himself from a perilous cliff. Suddenly, a divine being appeared, catching him with his hands and placing him upon a rock above. Śaṅkara said: "I am a śramaṇa by merit and ought to be the master of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Yet I have been unable to suppress the King's transgressions; for this reason, I cast away my body to reproach myself. What assistance has the deity provided? I pray that you will show me [the way]."
For this reason, the divine person then spoke these verses: "The Master lived for a hundred years; at eighty, he committed transgressions.
Because he drew near to the Most Honored One, he cultivated his practice and entered the Path. Although he possessed a modicum of wisdom, he harbored much sense of self and other.

Toward the various worthies he encountered, he never once gave rise to reverence. For twenty years of meritorious effort, his mind remained neither tranquil nor serene. [The text continues: "He was clever..."
"Because I was negligent and disrespectful, I have come to this state. Those who fail to show respect to a king shall experience such karmic results.
From now on, I shall no longer be lax; before long, I will achieve extraordinary wisdom. All the sages keep this in mind, and the Tathāgata does likewise.
Hearing these verses, Vararuci was delighted and subsequently sat in meditation within a mountain cave. At that time, the king sent a messenger to summon him. Vararuci said to the king:

He asked, "Has Sheng arrived? He replied, "I do not yet know. [The Master] said, "He will come only after being summoned a second time. When the messenger reached the mountain, Sheng declined; indeed, he only arrived upon being summoned a second time.
Mo Nian reflected that his conditions in China were ripe and the time for his transformative teaching had come. He then took leave of the ancestral stupa and bid farewell to his fellow students.
Later, he went to the King's residence and comforted him, saying, "Diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem. My departure is not..."
In the evening, on the nineteenth day, he returned. He traversed the vast deep for three full cycles of winter and summer before reaching the South Sea.

When Bodhidharma arrived at Jinling, and later reached the South Sea, Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu. The Emperor then dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree.
He was invited and arrived in Jinling in the eleventh month of the first year of the Putong era.

The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. What merit do these deeds possess? He replied, "They possess no merit. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?
He replied, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas; they are causes tainted by outflows (*āsrava*). They follow one like a shadow follows a form."
[The Emperor] said, "Although these are not real, what then constitutes true merit? [Huineng] replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;

its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? [Huineng] replied, "Vast emptiness—therein no 'sage' exists.
The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? [Huineng] replied, "I do not know. The Emperor could not fathom the profound principle.
The Monk Baozhang of One Thousand Years’ Age visited Bodhidharma. Baozhang was a native of Central India.

From the moment he descended as an incarnation and received his physical form, his left hand remained clenched in a fist; it was only when he was seven years old and had undergone tonsure that the fist opened.
For this reason, he was named Baozhang (Precious Hand). During the Wei and Jin dynasties, he traveled east to this land, entered Shu, and paid homage to Samantabhadra. He was constantly...

He ate [only once] per day and recited over a thousand scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras daily. One day he said to the assembly, "I have a vow to remain in this world for a thousand years;
now six hundred and twenty-six have passed. Therefore, people call me 'The One of a Thousand Years.

During the Daming era of the Song dynasty, he traveled to Mount Wutai, then southward through Mount Heng, Huangmei, and Mount Lu. He subsequently entered Jianye, where he met Bodhidharma as he arrived.

He went to Liang, where he inquired after and requested the profound essence [of the Dharma], thereby awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Emperor Wu, holding him in high esteem for his seniority in the monastic order, invited him to provide offerings within the inner court.
Before long, he traveled to Wu, where he composed a verse: "In the city of Liang I met the Teacher; through Zen practice I realized the ground of the mind.

Drifting and wandering, I have traveled through the Three Zhe regions, fully exhausting their finest mountains and waters. Thereupon, he extensively explored the famous mountains of the two Zhe provinces.
The First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, arrived at Shaolin.
Knowing that Emperor Wu’s spiritual capacity was not in accord with his own, on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, he secretly returned north of the Yangtze River.
On the twenty-third day, he arrived at Luoyang and stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the entire day;
no one could fathom him, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin."
(Jiachen) The First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, transmitted the Dharma to Huike.
Huike was the son of Lady Ji of Wulao. Because his father had no sons, he prayed for a long time; one night, an extraordinary light illuminated the room, and his mother subsequently became pregnant.
Thus, when he was born, they named him Guang. From childhood, his aspirations were unlike those of his peers. He studied extensively...

He exhausted the depths of the written records and was especially refined in the profound principles (*xuanli*). He did not concern himself with family property and delighted in roaming among mountains and waters. Later, upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a state of transcendence and self-realization.
He left the household life to receive full ordination and wandered through lecture halls, studying extensively the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

At the age of thirty-two, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he sat in meditative repose all day long. After another eight years, while in a state of silent stillness, he suddenly beheld a divine being.
He said, "You are about to receive the fruit of your practice; why linger here? The Great Way is not far off; you should go south. On the following day, he felt a headache as if pierced by needles.
When he sought treatment, a voice from the air said, "This is the transformation of your bones. Go to see your original teacher.
His original teacher examined the crown of his skull, which rose up like five peaks of a mountain. Because of this divine anomaly, he changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).
He further said to him, "Your marks are auspicious; you shall surely attain realization. As for the divine command that you go south, there is the Great Being Bodhidharma at Shaolin;
he will certainly be your teacher. Huiguan received these instructions and subsequently traveled to Shaolin to visit Bodhidharma.

Bodhidharma sat facing a wall in silence, and no instruction or encouragement was heard. Huiguan reflected to himself, "Those of old who sought the Way would break their bones to extract their marrow and pierce..."
They saved those starving with their own blood; they spread their hair to cover the mud; they threw themselves from cliffs to feed tigers. If the ancients were already like this, what person am I?

When there was a great snowfall, Daoguang stood in attendance throughout the night. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees, yet he stood even more reverently. Sengmo looked back at him and felt pity for him.

A questioner asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what do you seek? Guang replied with tears of sorrow, "I only pray that the Upādhyāya will, out of compassion, open the gate of the nectar of immortality and extensively deliver all classes of beings.
Mo said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort over vast eons;
one must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How could it be sought with a small virtue or small wisdom, or with a frivolous mind or a conceited mind?"

Hoping for the True Vehicle, he had labored in vain through diligent hardship. Bodhidharma heard of his earnest exhortations; secretly taking a sharp blade, he severed his own left arm and placed it before the grinding wheel.
Knowing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, Bodhidharma said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking may indeed be granted. Thereupon, he changed his name to Huìkě (Huike). Bodhidharma said:
"Can the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas be heard? He replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from others.

[The monk] said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. He said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace. [The monk] said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable."
He said, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
(Wu-shen) Master Fu held a great assembly. Master Fu resided at Shuanglin for seven years.
One day, while on his way practicing the Way, he was moved by the appearance of the Seven Buddhas following him, with Śākyamuni leading the way.
He led from the front while Vimalakīrti followed behind; Śākyamuni alone frequently looked back at him, saying, "I shall speak with him as my successor.
On another day, he saw the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Kanakamuni, and Dīpaṃkara—emitting light that enveloped his body.
The Master then said, "I have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. From this, his disciples increased even more. In the second year of the Datong era, the Master desired to guide all classes of beings.
He then transformed his wife and children to sell themselves, assisting in the establishment of a great assembly.
The First Patriarch, Bodhidharma (the twenty-eighth patriarch in India), manifested his passing while residing at Shaolin.
There he taught the Dharma to Huike, instructing him solely to externally cease all conditions and internally remain free from the panting of the mind.
"A mind like a wall can enter the Way; one may speak in various ways of the nature of the mind, yet it has never truly accorded with principle.
Maghi refuted his error and did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind to him. One day, he suddenly said, "I have already stilled all conditions."

Damo said, "Is it not that you have attained the cessation of extinction? He replied, "I have not attained the cessation of extinction. Damo said, "This is the essence of mind transmitted by all Buddhas;
do not harbor further doubts. In the second year of the Yong’an era of the Wei dynasty, he suddenly said to his disciples, "The time has arrived."

"You all should speak of what you have attained. Dao Fu said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters, for they serve as the functioning of the Way.
Daomeng said, "You have attained my skin. The nun Zongchi said, "As for what I now understand—"
It was as when Ānanda saw the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; having seen it once, he never saw it again. Mo said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist. In the place where I see, not a single dharma can be apprehended."
Sengmo said, "You have attained my bones. Finally, Huik'e performed three prostrations and stood in his place. Sengmo said, "You have attained my marrow.
He then turned to Huik'e and said, "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to the Great Being Kāśyapa."

It has been transmitted from one to another through successive entrustments until it reached me; I now transmit it to you. You must protect and uphold it. Furthermore, I bestow upon you this *kāṣāya* as a token of the Dharma.

Each of these items symbolizes something specific, which you should understand. [The disciple] said, "I pray that the Master will explain them. [The Master] said, "Internally, the transmission of the Dharma-seal serves to verify the mind through realization;
externally, the conferral of the *kāṣāya* serves to establish the fundamental tenets. In future generations, when people become corrupt and thin in virtue, they will harbor doubts."
He feared that disputes would arise, saying: "I am a man from the Western Heaven; you are a son of this land. On what basis did you receive the Dharma? By what do you realize it?
You have now received this robe and the Dharma; in the future, difficulties will arise. Simply produce this robe along with my verse of the Dharma."

This is used to demonstrate that his transformation is unimpeded. Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the transmission of the robe shall cease, while the Dharma shall pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra.
Those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few; those who expound the principles will be many, but those who penetrate the principles will be few.

There will be more than ten million who secretly accord with and secretly realize [the truth]. You must propagate this; do not look down upon those who have not yet awakened. A single thought that turns back the mechanism [of delusion], and one immediately—
"It is the same as the original attainment. Listen to my verse: 'I have come to this land / To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings.
/ One flower opens into five petals; / The fruiting occurs naturally. Furthermore, I have four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which I also entrust to you."
This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter it.
Since I first arrived here, I have been poisoned five times. I once tested this by placing a stone upon it; the stone shattered.

This was because I originally departed from South India to come to this Eastern Land, where I beheld the grand atmosphere of the Mahāyāna in the land of China, and thus crossed the seas and traversed...
The desert. For the sake of the Dharma, I have sought a successor; yet our fates had not yet harmonized, and I remained as if ignorant and mute.
Now that I have obtained you to transmit the teachings, my intentions are fulfilled. Having said this, he went with his disciples to Yumen, where they stayed for three days.
