There was Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng, who had long admired the Buddha-vehicle. He asked Daomoluo: "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the masters are revered as patriarchs. Their Way is such that..."
"What? he asked. [The Master] replied, "One who clarifies the essence of the Buddha-mind and whose practice accords with understanding is called an Ancestor (Patriarch).

He asked again, "Beyond this, what is required? [The Master] replied, "One must clarify the minds of others and know both the present and the past; one must not weary of existence or non-existence, nor have any grasping toward phenomena.

One is neither virtuous nor foolish, neither deluded nor awakened. If one can understand in this way, they are therefore called an Ancestor. He further said, "My disciple has taken refuge in the Three..."

"Venerable One, it has been many years since I entered the Way, yet my wisdom remains clouded and dull, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle. Having just heard your words, I do not know how to proceed.
I pray that you, out of compassion, will reveal the essential tenets. He then spoke with utmost sincerity, and [the Master] immediately spoke a verse, saying:
"Neither seeing evil does one give rise to aversion; Nor observing good does one strive to practice it. Neither abandoning wisdom does one draw near to folly; Nor..."
Without casting aside delusion to seek enlightenment, he attained the Great Way beyond measure and penetrated the Buddha-mind through transcendence.
Not entangled with either the mundane or the holy, he was loftily named a Patriarch. Upon hearing this verse, Xuanzhi was overcome by a mixture of sorrow and joy, saying:

"I pray that you, Master, will remain long in this world to transform and guide all sentient beings. [The Master] replied: "I shall depart immediately; I cannot remain for long. [Such was his] capacity and nature.

[The Master] replied, "There are ten thousand differences. I often encounter the difficulties posed by the ignorant. [The disciple] asked, "I do not know who this person is. May your disciple act as master to eliminate them?
[The Master] said, "I have transmitted the Buddha’s secrets to benefit those on the path of delusion. To harm another for my own peace is certainly contrary to reason.

[The disciple] said, "If you, Master, do not speak, how can it manifest the power of your transformative contemplation? Being unable to resist his persistence, [the Master] then offered a cryptic prediction (*chan*), saying: "A raft on the river."
The jade waves were divided; the torches of the pipes opened the golden locks. Five mouths traveled together, and for ninety days there was no sense of "self" or "other.
Xuanzhi could not fathom this and took his leave with ritual courtesy. At that time, the Wei dynasty honored the Śākya teachings, and eminent Chan masters were as numerous as a forest.

Dharma Master Daoguang and Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha were like phoenixes among the clergy, yet their opinions often conflicted with those of Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva’s profound influence, however, resounded far and wide.
All who possessed discernment turned to him in devotion, yet his disciples became envious and repeatedly administered poisons, none of which could harm him.
When he reached the sixth instance, as his work of transformation was completed, he sat upright and passed away; this was the fifth day of the tenth month in the year of Jǐyǒu.

He was buried at Xióng'ěr Mountain, and a stupa was erected at Dìnglín Monastery. That same year, the Wei envoy Sòng Yún was returning from the Western Regions when he encountered [the Master] at Mócōng.
At Ling, he saw [Hui]neng carrying a single shoe, walking gracefully and alone. Yun asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven.

Yun returned and reported the matter in detail to the Emperor. The Emperor ordered the tomb to be opened; only the single shoe remained. By imperial decree, the remaining shoe was taken from Shaolin Temple for veneration.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, in his remembrance of him, personally composed an inscription for a stele, which was carved at Mount Zhong. Its conclusion reads: [The text continues with the inscription.]
Alas! To see and yet not see; to encounter and yet not encounter; to meet and yet not meet—whether in the present or the past, one can only regret and lament it.
Although I am but a single, ordinary man, I venture to take him as my teacher from this day forward.
(Guichou) Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty Consults Dashi Fu Daoshi.
In the first month of the Guichou year, Dashi Fu Daoshi dispatched his disciple Fu Yang to the imperial palace to present a letter to Emperor Wu of the Liang.

The Emperor issued an edict summoning him to the palace. He asked the Master from whom he had received his teachings. The Master replied: "I have followed none; I have no teacher to follow. I have served nothing;
I have no object of service. The Emperor asked again: "Why do you not discuss the principles of doctrine? The Master replied:
"That which Bodhidharma taught is neither long nor short, neither broad nor narrow, neither finite nor infinite. It is the suchness of the true principle. What further words could there be?"
(Yimao) In the ninth month of the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyue entered nirvana.
When Huiyue manifested a slight illness, Emperor Wu issued an imperial decree dispatching a palace attendant to inquire after his health.
Huiyue said, "Tonight I shall depart. At the fifth watch, a wondrous fragrance filled the room; those around him were struck with solemn reverence. He then exhorted his disciples.
He said, "Birth and death are the natural, constant law. Diligently cultivate mindfulness and wisdom; do not give rise to distracted thoughts.
Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away. His usual mount, a blue ox, bellowed with tears that would not cease.
A pair of white cranes began circling the stupa they had built themselves, wailing with a most piteous sound. Three days later, they suddenly departed.

(Jihwei) In the fifth year of the Datong era, when the Dharma Master Fu was preaching in the royal palace, he entered the capital once more. Emperor Wu received him with courtesy and asked, "What constitutes the ultimate truth?"
He said, "It ceases but is not extinguished. He said, "It ceases but is not extinguished. This, then, is form. Because there is form, it is dull.
If this is so, the householder has not yet escaped the common world. He said, "In the face of wealth, do not seek gain by dishonest means;

in the face of hardship, do not seek escape by dishonest means. He said, "The householder greatly understands propriety. He said, "All dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. All forms within the great trichiliocosm—"

"Nothing that has form is not entirely empty. Just as the hundred rivers flow together and do not exceed the sea, so too the immeasurable and wondrous Dharma does not transcend True Suchness (*tathatā*).
For what reason, O Tathāgata, do you alone surpass all others within the ninety-six paths of the triple world?
You regard all sentient beings as if they were your own infant children. In the world, there is no peace without the Way, and no joy without propriety. The Emperor remained silent for a moment. I.

The Japanese Emperor invited the Master to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As soon as the Master ascended the seat, he struck the desk once with his ruler and immediately descended.
The Emperor was astonished. A monk asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not. The monk said, "The Great Being has finished lecturing on the sūtra."
(Renxu) Dharma Master Tanyuan’s Rebirth in the Pure Land:
During the Eastern Wei dynasty, Tanyuan left the household life with the aspiration to prolong his lifespan and subsequently practice the Buddha-dharma.

Hearing that the reclusive scholar Tao Hongjing of Jiangnan possessed the arts of the immortals, he traveled to the Liang court to visit him. Tao Hongjing joyfully bestowed upon him ten scrolls of alchemical formulas. Furthermore—
Returning to Wei and arriving at Luo, he met Bodhiruci and asked whether there was a method for longevity and immortality within the Buddha-dharma.

Bodhiruci replied, "What kind of talk is this? Where has there ever been a method for longevity in this land? Even if one were to attain a brief period of non-death, one would ultimately continue to transmigrate.
He then bestowed upon him the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, saying, "This is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Relying on it—

He practiced accordingly and was forever liberated from birth and death. Daoluan then burned his Daoist scriptures and devoted himself to the cultivation of the Pure Land. The Wei ruler titled him "Divine Luan.
In the fourth year of the Xinghe era, he saw incense, flowers, banners, and music coming to welcome him, and he passed away suddenly.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 27; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 28 (marked with the character “Sui”).
Jiazi (beginning in the tenth year of the Datong era of Emperor Wu of Liang);
Bingyin (the era name Zhongdatong was changed); Dingmao (the era name Taiching was changed); Gengwu (the first year of the Dabao era of Emperor Jianwen).
Ren-shen (the first year of Emperor Yuan’s Chengsheng era); Yi-hai (the first year of Emperor Jing’s Shaotai era); Bing-zi (the era was changed to Taiping);

Ding-chu (the first year of Chen Gaozu’s Yongding era); Geng-chen (the first year of Shizu’s Tianjia era); Bing-xu (the Chen dynasty changed the era to Tiankang); Ding-hai (the first year of Chen Linhaiwang’s Guangda era); Ji-chou (the first year of Chen Xuandi’s Taijian era);
Xin-chou (the first year of Sui Gaozu Wendi’s Kaishuang era); Gui-mao (the first year of Chen Houzhu’s Zhide era); Ding-wei (the Chen dynasty changed [the era]).
Zhenming (the year Xinyou was changed by the Sui to Renshou; it ended in the third year of Renshou under Emperor Wen of the Sui).
Northern Dynasties: Zhou, surnamed Yuwen; five rulers for a total of twenty-six years. Qi, surnamed Gao;
six rulers for a total of twenty-eight years.
Southern Dynasties: Later Liang. Surname Xiao. Three rulers. A total of thirty-three years. Chen. Surname Chen. Five rulers.
A total of thirty-three years. Sui. Surname Yang. Three rulers. A total of thirty-eight years.

(Jiazi) On the occasion of the Great Dharma Assembly convened by Master Fu, Master Fu once composed the *Inscription on the Mind-King*, which says: "Contemplate the mind-king as empty, profound and wondrous, difficult to fathom.

Formless and signless, it possesses great supernormal power. It can extinguish a thousand calamities and bring to fulfillment ten thousand virtues. Although its essential nature is empty, it is able to bestow the Dharma."
Thus, when observed it has no form; when called upon it has sound. It acts as the general of the Great Dharma, transmitting the sutras through the mind-precepts.

Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of lacquer-blue within its color, it is certainly present, yet its form is not seen. The sovereign mind is likewise: it dwells within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face.
Responding to objects according to circumstances, it is free and unimpeded; all that it does is accomplished. Thus one realizes the fundamental consciousness.

Mind. With the conscious mind one perceives the Buddha; this Buddha is the mind, and this mind is the Buddha. In every thought-moment there is the Buddha-mind, and the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.

If you wish to achieve success quickly, restrain yourself with the precepts. Purify the precepts and purify the mind; the mind itself is the Buddha. Apart from this sovereign mind-king, there is no other Buddha.
If you seek to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing. Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger—
Truly, upon entering this Dharma-gate, one sits upright and attains Buddhahood. Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*.
The true seeker of the Way observes their own mind and knows that the Buddha is within; they do not seek outwardly. Mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind.

When the mind clearly recognizes objects, it understands and awakens to the nature of consciousness. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind. There is no non-Buddha... [text ends]... do not.

To speculate is to be incapable of true responsibility; to cling to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence is to drift and sink within this state. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind herein.
The Great Beings who have clarified their minds awaken to this profound resonance: the nature of body and mind is wondrous, and its function undergoes no alteration.

Therefore, the wise let go of the mind with ease and spontaneity. Do not say that the Mind-King is empty and devoid of a substantial essence, for it is capable of causing the physical body to act either rightly or wrongly.

It is correct. It is neither existent nor non-existent; its manifestation and concealment are indeterminate. The nature of the mind transcends emptiness, yet it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely.
Therefore, I exhort you: take care to guard yourself with vigilance. A single moment of action may lead once again to drifting and sinking.

The pure mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind. The unconditioned jewel of the Dharma is neither shallow nor deep—the Bodhi of all Buddhas.

Sā. One who thoroughly understands this original mind and encounters its conditions is neither of the past, future, nor present. Furthermore, a verse says: Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep;
morning after morning one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, we always follow one another; whether speaking or silent, we dwell together. Not even a hair’s breadth separates us.
Like a shadow following a body, if you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech. Furthermore, there is a verse: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth;
formless, it is fundamentally serene and solitary. It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons.

In the tenth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, Master [Huisi] established a great Dharma assembly for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they might repent and extinguish the suffering of their transgressions, swiftly attaining liberation.
Furthermore, as Buddhist scripture catalogs were numerous and some individuals could not read them all, he established a Wheel Treasury (Lun-zang) and made this vow:
"May those who enter the gate of my treasury never lose their human form throughout birth after birth; and may those who give rise to the bodhicitta [attain enlightenment]."

He was able to push the Wheel-Treasury (Cakravāḍa). His merit was no different from that of those who uphold and recite various sutras. Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty, Xiao Yan, possessed extraordinary features:

a sun-mark on his forehead and the countenance of a dragon; a halo encircled his neck, and his body did not cast a shadow when in the sun. The room where he resided was often filled with cloud-like vapors.
From his youth, he was fond of learning, ranging from the *Shi* and *Shu* classics to the arts of Yin-Yang, the celestial portents (*weishi*), and the divination of omens and prognostication.
He was thoroughly proficient in both the calligraphy of cursive script and the arts of archery and horsemanship. Although he had ascended the great throne, he still never laid down his books.
Later in life, he embraced the Buddhist path and restricted himself to a single meal per day. He did not perform music except for ancestral sacrifices, feasts, or grand assemblies.

When sentencing a prisoner to death, he would invariably shed tears. He was diligent in state affairs; even during the winter months, he would take up his pen and attend to business past the hour of midnight.

His hands were cracked and weathered. By nature he was upright and square. Even when staying in a dark room, he would invariably adjust his robes and cap. During the months of summer, he never once bared his arms.
Even when encountering eunuchs or minor attendants, he treated them as if they were solemn guests. In the third year of the Taiqing era, Hou Jing breached the Tai City.
He took five hundred armored soldiers with him for his own protection and entered the hall wearing his sword. The Emperor’s countenance remained unmoved;

he gestured for him toward the seat reserved for the Three Ducal Ministers and said, "You have served in the military for a long time; will it not be wearisome? Jing was so struck with fear and trepidation that he could not respond.
Xiao Chuzhi said to those around him, "Whenever I have mounted my horse to face the enemy, even as arrows and stones rained down upon me, I felt no fear at all.
Now, seeing Lord Xiao, he makes one feel awestruck and cowed. Is this not because his celestial majesty is difficult to approach? I shall not see him again.

As his illness worsened, he recited the name of the Buddha day and night without ceasing. When he reached the final stage and could no longer take food, after a long time his mouth became bitter and he asked for honey.
Raising his hand, he exclaimed, "He-he! and subsequently passed away in the Jingju Hall at the age of eighty-six (Gengwu year).

Regarding Dharma Master Huimeng of the Northern Qi, whose name was Huimeng and whose secular surname was Gao: while reading Nāgārjuna’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he attained a sudden and profound enlightenment. Thereupon...
From afar, he took Nāgārjuna as his teacher.
(Jiaxu) During the third year of the Chengsheng era, Dashi Fu again donated his family wealth to provide offerings to the Triple Gem for the sake of sentient beings. He spoke in verse:
He relinquished everything for the sake of all beings, making offerings to the God among Gods. He looked upward in prayer for the rain of ambrosia, which fell in boundless streams.
○ Huisi visited Master Huiwen.

Huisi was the son of the Li family of Wujin. He possessed a fleshly protuberance on his crown; his gait was like that of an ox and his gaze like that of an elephant. From his youth, he was renowned among his neighbors for his compassion and forbearance.
He once dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life; he then took leave of his parents to shave his head and don the robes of a monk. Upon receiving full ordination, he...

He ate but one meal a day and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* a thousand times. In the third year of the Chengsheng era of the Liang dynasty, he heard that Huiren of Northern Qi had several hundred disciples;
he went there to receive the Dharma, concentrating his mind day and night without his side ever touching the mat. He sat through the summer retreat for twenty-one days.

He attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Immediately thereafter, an obstruction arose: his four limbs became limp and weak, and he was unable to walk.
He thought to himself: "Illness arises from karma; karma arises from the mind. Since the source of the mind is without arising, what form can external objects have?

Illness, karma, and the body are all like clouds and shadows. Having made this contemplation, he regained his former lightness and ease. When the summer retreat concluded, he still had no realization and felt deep shame.
Feeling ashamed, he relaxed his body and leaned against the wall; before his back had even touched it, he attained sudden and profound awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
○ Lu Fahe, in his youth, lived in seclusion at Mount Qingxi in Jiangling, where he served the śramaṇas with the etiquette of a disciple. Upon reaching adulthood, he traveled abroad.
Because his conduct was peerless, he was held in high esteem by Xiao Gang, Prince of Xiangdong. When Hou Jing first surrendered, He knew that he would surely rebel;
he spoke of this to Zhu Yuan Ying, but Yuan Ying did not grasp his meaning. Not long after, Hou Jing besieged the capital.
Yuan Ying sought a strategy, and He said, "To gather fruit, one must wait for it to ripen. When Hou Jing dispatched his general Ren Yue to attack the Prince of Xiangdong, He requested troops.

He opposed them. They drew up their lines opposite each other at Chisha Lake. The rebels took advantage of the wind to set fire to the huts. He [Zhu He] brandished a white-feathered fan to ward off the wind, and the wind immediately reversed its direction.

From then on, his illness gradually improved. After serving him for two years, Huik'e was told:

"You must protect this so that it does not become extinct. Listen to my verse: 'Originally there was the ground of conditions;

Depart well and act with virtue, awaiting the time for the transmission of the *saṃnāha* (the armor of resolve). [The Master’s] surname was Sengna.
Lady Ma was brilliant and gifted from her youth and had mastered the classical scriptures. At the age of twenty-one, she lectured on the *Book of Rites* and the *Book of Changes* in Donghai;
her audience gathered like a marketplace. When she later traveled south to the region of Xiangbu, her circle of students followed her there.

He used a single alms bowl, sat in one posture, and observed the dhūta practices. Having served Huiké for a long time, he later said to his disciple Huiman:
"The mind-seal of the Patriarchs does not consist solely in asceticism; asceticism merely assists the Way. If one accords with the fundamental mind,"
If you activate the function of the true light of spontaneous intention (*yathā-saṃjñā*), then ascetic practice is like grasping soil and turning it into gold.

However, if you merely devote yourself to asceticism without clarifying the fundamental mind, and remain bound by hatred and attachment, then ascetic practice is like walking upon a perilous path in the darkness of a black moon night.

If you wish to clarify the fundamental mind, you must examine and investigate with thorough discernment: when encountering forms or sounds, before the arising of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).

At that time, where does the mind go? Is it non-existent? Is it existent? Since it does not fall into the realms of existence or non-existence, the jewel of the mind shines alone and clearly, constantly illuminating the world without so much as a speck of dust’s worth of interval. "How deeply lamentable! I now entrust this to you; you should guard and uphold it well. Be cautious not to transmit it to non-humans.

Having thus given his final instructions, he departed to wander through various lands, and no one knew his end. As for the lay practitioner [Hui-]xiang, he dwelt in seclusion among the forests and wilds, eating from the trees and drinking from the mountain streams.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi dynasty, hearing that Huike was flourishing in his propagation of the Dharma, he sent a letter to establish friendly relations, saying:
"Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To dally with shadows is to weary the form; yet one does not realize that the form is the root of the shadow. To raise a sound is to produce an echo;

yet one does not know that the sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions in pursuit of nirvana is like discarding the form to seek the shadow, or departing from sentient beings [to find the Buddha]."

Yet they seek the fruit of Buddhahood; it is like seeking an echo while remaining silent. Thus we know that delusion and awakening follow one and the same path, and that the ignorant and the wise are not distinct.
Where there is no name, names are created; because of these names, right and wrong arise. Where there is no principle, principles are fabricated; because of these principles, disputes break out.
Illusions and transformations are not real—whose is right and whose is wrong? They are empty fabrications without substance—what is void and what exists?
I understand that there is nothing gained in what is gained, and nothing lost in what is lost. Before I have had the opportunity to pay you a formal visit, I have briefly set forth these thoughts;

I humbly hope for your reply. He commanded his scribe to respond as follows: "I have carefully examined the purport of your letter, and it is entirely in accordance with reality. The principle of the truly profound is ultimately no different [from my own].
Originally, I mistook the *maṇi* jewel for a mere pebble, but now, with sudden awakening, I realize it is a genuine pearl. Thus, ignorance and wisdom—"
They are equal and without distinction; one should know that all phenomena are thusness. Out of compassion for those who hold these two views, I have set forth my brush to compose this work.
When one observes that the body and the Buddha are no different, what need is there to seek that which is beyond remainder?
The lay practitioner [Wuzhuo] received and read the Patriarch’s verse, whereupon he prostrated himself, received the seal of transmission, and respectfully accepted it.
(Wuzi) Great Master Huisi resided at Mount Nanyue. While staying at Dasu, he addressed the assembly:
"The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not remote. Seek it only within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere. If you seek it, you will not find it;
even if you were to find it, it would not be real. He spoke in verse: "Suddenly awakening to the source of the mind opens the treasure storehouse."
Hidden and manifest, spiritually penetrating, he reveals the true reality. Walking alone and sitting alone, he is ever majestic. His billions of emanations are beyond measure;
though they should fill and pervade all of empty space, when one looks for them, not even a particle of form can be seen. This laughable thing has no comparison;
from his mouth he spits forth bright pearls, their light shimmering and dazzling. What is commonly seen and spoken of as inconceivable is, in a single word, given its name.
When Huisi was about to ascend the seat to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he was poisoned by rival masters of various treatises.
Huisi focused his mind single-mindedly on the *Prajñā*, and the poison was immediately neutralized. He then instructed his disciple Zhiyi to take his place in lecturing.

When Zhiyi reached the passage, "Single-mindedness encompasses the ten thousand practices," he suddenly encountered a point of doubt and requested his master to resolve it. Huisi said, "As for your doubt, it is precisely..."
This is merely the sequential meaning of the *śāstra* chapters; it is not yet the perfect and sudden (*yuantun*) purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

In the past, during the summer retreat, I suddenly awakened in a single thought-moment, and all dharmas manifested before me. Having personally realized this, there is no need for you to harbor doubts. Guanding asked, "Is what you have realized that of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*)?

He replied, "In one lifetime, I hoped to enter the Bronze Wheel [Stage] (the tenth *vihāra* of the Perfect Teaching). Because I led disciples too early, I sacrificed myself for the benefit of others."

He [Hui]si did so, yet he resided only under the Iron Wheel [Kingdom]. (The Ten Faiths of the *Enshōkyō*) Si once held a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) in his hand and pointed to Huiji among the assembly, saying, "One may truly say that the Dharma has been entrusted to a Dharma-minister;
the Dharma-King has nothing further to do. At that time, Dasu was warned by a portent, and the disciples were unsettled.
Si then said to Ji, "I have long admired Mount Nanyue, yet I regretted having no one to whom the Dharma could be entrusted. You must transmit the lamp."
"Do not become one who severs the lineage of the Buddhas at its end. You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen; you should go there to bring benefit.
Having received this command, he traveled to Chen and resided at Waguan Monastery. There, he expounded upon the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

On the sixteenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Guangda era, he led more than forty monks and proceeded directly to Mount Nanyue. Upon ascending Mount Zhurong, he encountered the deity of the mountain playing chess.
The deity asked, "Master, why have you come here? He replied, "I seek from the patron a space the size of a single sitting mat.

The deity said, "So be it," and immediately flew with his monk's staff to demarcate the site (which is now Fuyan Temple). The mountain deity requested the precepts, and Hui si intended to preach the Dharma for him.
Consequently, he said, "I shall reside on this mountain for only ten years; thereafter, I must travel far. In a previous life, I once walked these very grounds, traveling as far as Hengyang."
Upon reaching a particularly excellent grove of forest and springs, he said, "This is an ancient temple where I once resided; order it excavated. The foundations still remained.
He then pointed toward the base of a cliff and said, "It was here that I sat in meditation when a bandit severed my head. Thereupon, they discovered a set of skeletal remains.
From then on, his spiritual transformation flourished even more widely, and the ruler of the Chen dynasty bestowed upon him the title "Great Chan Master."
(Ji-chou) The Great Master Fudashi of Shanhui Passes into Nirvana. The Great Master Fudashi was an emanation of Maitreya.
Residing at the Twin Trees, he performed great Buddha-works. He once spoke a verse: "Empty-handed, I grasp a hoe;

During the persecution of the Dharma by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, Sengcan deeply concealed his identity and lived without a fixed residence for more than ten years; no one was able to recognize him.

When the morning star appeared, the divine monk praised him, saying: "To overcome and conquer one's enemies may be called valor; but to be able to surmount such a hardship as this—none is like you.

(Xinchou) The first year of the Kaihuang era: Buddhism was revived after being suppressed by Emperor Wu of the Zhou. Xinchou:

At the time of his birth, a crimson light illuminated the chamber and a purple vapor filled the courtyard. Beside his residence stood a convent for bhikṣuṇīs; one nun named Zhixian was popularly known as the "Divine Nun."

During a period of intense heat, his mother fanned him; yet he was so cold that he nearly died. A *bhikṣuṇī* arrived from outside and said to the father, "This child is protected by the Buddha and the gods;
his body is like a *śarīra*, indestructible. She then named the boy Nārāyaṇa. She further said, "The origins of this child are beyond the ordinary;
a secular home is defiling. You should take him to the monastery to raise him. The father then entrusted him to the *bhikṣuṇī*.
One day, while the nun was away, the mother came to embrace the child. Suddenly she saw that the child had transformed into a dragon, its scales and horns already fully formed.

The Dharma was exactly as the bhikṣuṇī had said. After he ascended the throne, he would frequently look toward his ministers and reminisce about his *ācārya*, making it a constant topic of conversation.

(Guichou year) Grand Master Guanding received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Furthermore, at the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, he discoursed on the Unsurpassed Way, and those who listened gathered like a forest.

At that time, Dharma Master Bianhe was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the temple; when his disciples heard that [Hui]kan was expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away from him. Bian...
Unable to contain his indignation, Hebu slandered the district magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan, by falsely accusing him. [Huiyuan] could remain serene and submit to his fate;
those who understood him called this "repaying a debt. This occurred on the sixteenth day of the third month of the Gui-chou year.
He was one hundred and seven years old. He was buried seventy li northeast of Fuyang County in Cizhou.
○ Regarding the Great Master Zhixi Preaching the Dharma at Yuyuan:
Zhixi went to Yuyuan in Jingzhou and entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within a large tree. One day, a giant python over ten *zhang* long appeared, its mouth gaping inward;
demonic forces (*māra*) drew up their ranks, raining down slings and arrows like rain. This continued for seven days, yet Zhixi remained undisturbed.
Terrified, he took pity on him and said, "What you have done are the karmic deeds of birth and death; yet you cling to residual blessings and do not feel sorrow or repentance.
Having spoken these words, the various demons all vanished. That evening, the clouds parted and the moon shone bright; two men were seen, their majestic bearing like that of kings.
He bowed respectfully and said, "I am Guan Yu. During the chaos at the end of the Han dynasty, the nine provinces were split like melon seeds;

Cao Cao was unrighteous, and Sun Quan sought only self-preservation. I, a loyal minister of Shu-Han, vowed to restore the imperial house. However, the times were adverse and my ambitions remained unfulfilled.
My death leaves behind a lingering brilliance, and I have found this mountain as my domain. Great Virtuous Holy Master, why do you deign to trouble your divine feet here? He replied, "I wish to..."
"This site is established as a *bodhimaṇḍa* solely by virtue of my body born of retribution (*vipākaja-kāya*). I pray that you will take pity on my folly and graciously accept me.
One *śāyana* from here, there is a mountain shaped like an overturned boat; its soil is deep and rich. Your disciple shall level it with you to build a temple and provide offerings.
I pray that you remain in meditative absorption for seven days to await its completion. Once he emerged from *samādhi*, he saw a pond.
The thousand-fathom deep pool was transformed into level ground, and the buildings were magnificent and brilliant, their exquisite craftsmanship surpassing the eye’s capacity for appreciation.
Huiji then led the assembly to reside there and expounded the Dharma for one day. A spirit addressed Huiji, saying, “Today, your disciple has been fortunate enough to hear the supramundane Dharma.

I pray that you will cleanse my heart and transform my thoughts, so that I may seek to receive the precepts of taking refuge, forever establishing the foundation for Bodhi. Huiji then conferred upon him the five precepts.
On the day of Ding-si, in the eleventh month, Master Zhiyi entered nirvana.
The Prince of Jin dispatched an envoy to welcome Zhiyi. As he was about to depart, Zhiyi said to his disciples:
"I shall go forth and not return. You all should complete the construction of Fulong South Temple.
He further said, "This was prepared by the royal family; you shall see it, but I shall not. Arriving before the Hundred-Foot Stone Image at Shicheng Temple in eastern Shan, he stopped.
Looking back at his attendant, he said, "I know my destiny lies here; I will not proceed further. Thereupon, he set down his chisel and ceased [his work].
The strings were tuned this very day. Having finished chanting the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he spoke again: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land with lotus ponds and jeweled trees;
yet, though it is easy to go there, no one does so. Even those for whom the signs of the fiery chariot have appeared can still attain rebirth if they repent for a single thought.
How much more so for those who cultivate the holy path through the power of precepts and meditative concentration—their merit shall not be in vain. At that time...
The stone Buddha emitted a great radiance that filled and overspread the mountains and valleys. A disciple asked, "I do not know at what stage of attainment or in what rebirth the Master will be.

He replied, "I shall not lead a multitude; I must purify my six sense faculties. By sacrificing myself to benefit others, I shall merely attain the fifth stage. As for your question regarding my rebirth:
my teachers and friends are all waiting for me to follow Avalokiteśvara, and they have all come to welcome me. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
(Gengshen) The Third Patriarch Sengcan transmitted the Dharma to Daoxin.

Daoxin relied upon the Third Patriarch to realize the Way and served him with diligent labor for nine years. Later, he received full ordination in Jizhou and attended upon him with even greater reverence.
Sengcan repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle matters; knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he then entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma, saying in verse: Flower...
Although seeds depend upon the earth, flowers grow from the earth because of the seeds; yet if no one sows the seeds, neither flowers nor earth will ever produce anything.
During the Sui dynasty, Lady Gudu, though dwelling in the royal palace, felt a profound distaste for her female nature and focused her mind single-mindedly on the Buddha.
In the *xin-you* year of the Renshou era, when she passed away, various kinds of music spontaneously resounded to the north of Yong'an Palace, and a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber.
They arrived from the void. Sīna of India reached the capital, and the Emperor asked, "What auspicious omen is this?
He replied, "In the Pure Land there is a Buddha named Amitābha. Because the Empress’s karma is sublime, she has transcended to that land; therefore, this auspicious sign has appeared."
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle Twenty-eight;
*The Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs*, Fascicle Twenty-nine (Lü-zì-hào).

Jiazi (Beginning in the fourth year of Renshou of Emperor Wen of the Sui Dynasty); Yichu (the first year of Daye of Emperor Yang); Dingchu (the first year of Yining of Emperor Gong); Wuyin (the [first year of] Gaozu of the Tang Dynasty).
Dinghai (the first year of Emperor Taizong’s Zhenguan era); Gengxu (the first year of Emperor Gaozong’s Yonghui era); Bingchen (the year Xianqing was adopted); Xinyou (the year Longshuo was adopted);
Guihai (ending in the third year of Emperor Gaozong’s Longshuo era).
The Tang dynasty: surnamed Li. Began in the first year of Gaozu’s Wude era, Wuyin; ended in the second year of Emperor Zhaozong’s Tianyou era.
The year was Yi-chou (605). There were twenty-one patriarchs in total for two hundred and ninety years.
(Jia-zhi) The Third Patriarch, Sengcan, lived in seclusion on Mount Luofu.
After the Third Patriarch Sengcan had transmitted the Dharma to Daoxin, he told him: "In the past, Master Ke transmitted it to me..."
After the Dharma [had been established], he went to the capital of Ye. He practiced his teachings for thirty years before passing away. Now that I have found you, why do you linger here?

In the fourth year of the Renshou era, he traveled to Mount Luofu. He once composed the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind), which says: "The Supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing.
Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear. A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. If you wish to attain...
When [the mind] manifests before you, do not harbor notions of compliance or resistance. For compliance and resistance to contend with one another is the sickness of the mind.

Failing to recognize the profound essence, you labor in vain by merely contemplating stillness. Perfectly identical to the great void, it lacks nothing and has no surplus. It falls short only because of grasping and rejecting;

therefore, do not pursue conditioned objects, nor dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of even-mindedness, all is extinguished of its own accord. Cease movement and return to stillness; yet, if you fixate on stillness, it will further...
It moves excessively; it merely stagnates at the two extremes. How can one know that there is but "one kind"? If this one kind is not penetrated, both sides will fail in their function.

To dismiss existence while clinging to existence, or to follow emptiness while turning one's back on emptiness—much talk and much deliberation only result in further lack of correspondence. When words are cut off and deliberations cease, there is nowhere that does not penetrate.

Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; yet following illumination, one loses the source. A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the previous emptiness. That previous emptiness...
All transformations arise from deluded views. Do not seek the Truth; simply cease these views. When the two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.

As soon as right and wrong arise, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. Since the two arise from the one, do not cling even to that one. When the One Mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Where there is no fault, there are no dharmas; where there is no arising, there is no mind. If you can cause the objects of perception to cease through this, then the objects will follow suit.

The capacity to sink arises from the object; the object arises from the capacity for the object, and the capacity arises from the object. If you wish to understand these two segments, know that they originally constitute a single emptiness.

This single emptiness encompasses both, equally containing the myriad phenomena. When neither the subtle nor the coarse is perceived, how could there be partiality? The substance of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult.
With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly frantic and increasingly slow. To cling to it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path; let it go.

Spontaneity. Its essence has neither going nor staying. To follow its nature is to accord with the Way; to roam at ease is to be free from affliction. To fixate one's thoughts is to deviate from the truth;
to be muddled and heavy is not good. It is not good to weary the spirit; what use is there for intimacy or estrangement? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects.

If the six sense-objects are not loathed, they are identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise act without contrivance; the ignorant bind themselves. In the Dharma there is no separate dharma; it is through delusion that one [creates distinctions].
Attachment! To direct the mind with the mind—how could this not be a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes.

All dualistic extremes are truly a matter of one’s own discernment. Dreaming, illusions, and flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them? Success and failure, right and wrong—let them all be cast aside at once.
If the eye does not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord. If the mind does not vary, the myriad dharmas are as one. One suchness.
The essence is profound and mysterious; in a state of stillness, one forgets all conditions. One contemplates the myriad dharmas as equal and returns to the natural state.

That which causes [this state] to cease is itself obliterated, beyond any comparison. In stillness there is no stillness; in movement there is no movement. Since duality cannot be established, how can there be unity? Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or patterns remain.
The mind accords with equality, and all conditioned activity comes to rest. Doubts are completely purified, and right faith arises.
It is straightened and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty luminosity illuminates itself spontaneously, requiring no exertion of mind or effort.

It is not a place of discursive thought, difficult for consciousness and emotion to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither "other" nor "self. One must urgently seek resonance with it; it is simply called "non-duality.
Non-duality is universal sameness, encompassing all without exception. The wise of the ten directions all enter this school (*zong*). This school is not...

Extending and contracting: a single thought-moment is ten thousand years; there is neither being nor non-being. The ten directions are before one’s eyes. The most minute is identical to the vast, as all boundaries and realms are forgotten and severed.
The most vast is identical to the minute, with no visible limits or surfaces. Being is precisely non-being; non-being is precisely being.
If it were not thus, one would certainly have no need to maintain [this state]. One is precisely all; all is precisely one. If one can simply act in this way, what need is there for concern?
It was not yet finished. His faith was non-dual; his non-dual faith transcended the path of words and speech. It was neither past, future, nor present.
○ Zhishun entered Mount Lu and followed the pure practices of Huiyuan. At the beginning of the Daye era, after he had finished lecturing on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he manifested illness.
He saw parrots and peacocks reciting the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds. He told his disciples, "Today I am departing."
He was born. Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully.
(Bingyin) The Third Patriarch, Sengcan, entered nirvana.
Sengcan had preached the Dharma for over thirty years, yet he never spoke of his surname, lineage, hometown, or village. He once said to Dao...
Xin said, "If anyone asks about me, do not say that you received the Dharma from my place. In the fourth year of the Renshou era, he traveled to Mount Luofu, where he stayed at leisure for two years.
In the second year of the Daye era, he returned to Shuzhou to Guishan Valley Temple. Within a month, the local officials and commoners flocked there and prepared a grand offering of alms.
Huichan extensively proclaimed the essentials of the mind for the fourfold assembly; when the dharma assembly concluded, it was as if a great tree had been planted.
He passed away while standing with his palms joined in *añjali*. This was on the fifteenth day of the tenth month of that year.
During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Li Chang, the Governor of Henan, opened Chan’s tomb and performed cremation. Three hundred grains of five-colored *śarīra* were obtained;
he used one hundred grains from his own salary to build a stupa, gave one hundred grains to Heze, and kept one hundred grains with him.
(4th year of Jiashen) The Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin, began his propagation of the Dharma at Mount Poutou.
In the Dingchou year, Daoxin led his disciples to Jizhou. There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city; for seventy days the siege did not break.

The multitude was filled with terror, but Daoxin took pity on them and instructed the entire city to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, from within the crenels of the city walls, the rebel host gazed out.
There were divine soldiers who said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within this city," and so they departed.
In the second year of the Wude era, he preached the Dharma at Luochuan. In the seventh year, he returned to Qizhou and resided at Poutou Mountain, where disciples gathered like clouds.
(Wuzi) Dharma Master Daocuo’s Rebirth in the Pure Land: Daocuo was a native of Bingzhou.
He left the household life to study the sutras and treatises; later, he served under Chan Master Zan to study meditation. Furthermore, he was deeply devoted to the Pure Land.
A monk once saw Daocuo’s prayer beads in his meditative state as a great mountain of the seven treasures. In his daily life, he lectured for the assembly.

They recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* nearly two hundred times; each person counted their beads while chanting the Buddha’s name aloud. At times, the sound dispersed through the assembly, resonating throughout the forests and valleys.

They performed prostrations during the six periods of the day without ever failing or neglecting them. Each day, they set a limit of seventy thousand recitations for the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he entered nirvana. Those who heard of this and came to the mountain temple filled its halls;

they beheld a transformation Buddha dwelling in the void as celestial flowers descended and scattered. Sengxuan was a native of Bingzhou. Initially, he recited the name of Maitreya, vowing to be reborn in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven).
At the age of ninety, he met Daochuo, whereupon he first turned his mind toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name. He performed one thousand prostrations daily with single-minded devotion.
Later, when he fell ill, he told his disciples: "Amitābha Buddha has bestowed upon me fragrant robes; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have shown me their jeweled hands.
It is time for me to depart. Having finished speaking, he passed away. For seven days, a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate.
At that time, there were two Dharma masters, Qifang and Yuango, who witnessed this event firsthand; they subsequently gathered together at Wuzhen Temple and each broke off a willow branch.
Within the hand of Avalokiteśvara, she made a vow: "If I have a karmic affinity for the Pure Land, these flowers shall not wither for seven days.

When the period arrived, they grew even more luxuriant; she rejoiced in the fragrant blossoms. Day and night she contemplated the Buddha without ceasing, until she suddenly perceived herself at a pond of the seven treasures.
Entering a great jeweled canopy, she saw the Buddha and the two Great Beings seated upon a precious lotus throne, their radiance shining brilliantly. She paid homage with the fragrant flowers.
The Buddha said: "Those who recite my name shall all be born in my land. Furthermore, he heard Śākyamuni Buddha and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praising the Pure Land with Brahma-sounds.
He also saw three jeweled stairways: the first was for laypeople, the second for a mixture of monastics and laity, and the third was for monks alone.
It was said that those who have recited the Buddha's name with a sincere mind attain birth upon these.
He passed away. Five days later, he suddenly heard the sound of a bell and said, "The sound of the bell is our business.
He and his companions all passed away at once. Mingzhan lived in seclusion at Zhiju Temple on Mount Taiyi. In his later years, he resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

In the tenth month of the second year of the Zhenguan era, knowing his life was coming to an end, he entered the capital to attend a vegetarian feast at Xingshan Temple, where he took leave of both the clergy and the laity. At that time—
The Vice-Presidents Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui were both present at this time. He then returned to Zhiju Temple, where he adjusted his dignified demeanor and recited the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he said, "Amitābha Buddha is coming! The two Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) have also arrived. Rising on tiptoe with palms joined, he passed away.
(Gengyin) The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin transmitted the Dharma to Farong.
Farong was the son of the Wei family from Yanling; at the age of nineteen, his mastery of the classics and histories was thorough. He subsequently read through the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtras.
Having thoroughly realized the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one day he sighed and said: "The classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma;
the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he entered the monastic order under a master and shaved his head.

Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou, where there was a marvel of hundreds of birds offering him flowers. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, Daoxin observed him from afar.
Xuanchang sensed that there was an extraordinary person on that mountain and went there in person to seek him out. He questioned the temple monks, asking, "Is there any man of the Way in this place?
They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, who is not a man of the Way? Xuanchang asked, "Which one, then, is the true man of the Way? The monks were at a loss for an answer.
Another monk said, "About ten li from here into the mountains, there is one named Lanrong; he does not rise when he sees people."

He also did not join his palms. [Dao]xin thought, "This cannot be a man of the Way," and so he entered the mountains. There he saw Daorong sitting upright and composed, seemingly unconcerned with anything.
Xin asked, "What are you doing here? Daorong replied, "I am contemplating the mind. Xin asked, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind?"
Tong was without a rival. He immediately rose, prostrated himself, and said, "Virtuous One, where do you dwell in seclusion?
He replied, "I have not decided where to stay; sometimes east, sometimes west. Tong asked, "Do you still know the Great Master Daoxin? He asked, "Why do you ask about him?

Tong said, "I have long admired his virtue and hoped to pay my respects to him once. He replied, "I am that very person. Tong asked, "For what reason have you descended here? He replied, "Specifically..."
He came to visit him and asked, "Is there perhaps another place for rest? Nengrong pointed behind him and said, "There is a separate small hermitage.
He then led Xinxin to the site of the hermitage; as they circled it, they saw only tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
Xinxin then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. Nengrong said, "There is still this one remaining. Xinxin asked, "What is this? Nengrong had no reply. After a short while...
Huishin, however, sat in meditation upon a rock and wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛). When Huiri saw it, he was struck with awe. Huishin said, "There is still this remaining.
Huiri did not yet understand, so he prostrated himself and requested an exposition of the essential teaching of the mind. Huishin replied, "Among the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates..."
They all return to the single square inch of the mind. The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind.
All gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and inherently complete;

they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are originally empty and still. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no Bodhi to seek.
Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma you have now attained; there is nothing lacking. How is this different from the Buddha? There is no other dharma apart from this.

You need only allow the mind to be free and at ease. Do not perform contemplative practices, nor do you need to clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger, and harbor no sorrow or anxiety. Be vast and unconfined.

Unobstructed, moving freely in all directions, neither performing any good nor committing any evil, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—whatever meets the eye and whatever encounters the conditions—is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha.
Joyful and free from sorrow, it is therefore called "Buddha. He asked: "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha and what is the mind?
He replied: "It is not that the mind does not inquire about the Buddha; it is not that inquiring about the Buddha is not the mind."
[The questioner] asked: "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplative visualization (*vipaśyanā*), how does one apply an antidote when objects arise?

[The Master] replied: "Objects and conditions have neither beauty nor ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly assign names, from where would deluded sentiments arise?

Since deluded sentiments no longer arise, the true mind functions freely in universal cognition. You need only follow the mind with ease and freedom; there will be no further need for antidotes—this is what is called 'abiding eternally'."
The Dharma-body is without change or variation. I have received the sudden teaching of the Great Master Can; I now entrust it to you.
You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain on this very mountain. Hereafter, there shall be five men who attain realization and will carry forward your profound transformation.
Having thus completed the transmission of the Dharma, he returned to Shuangfeng (i.e., Póutóu Mountain). While Daoxin was residing among the mountains at Shuangfeng, there...
There was an old monk who spent his days solely planting pine trees; people called him the "Pine-Planting Wayfarer. He said to Xinxing, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma?
Xinxing replied, "You are already advanced in years. Even if you were to hear it, would you be able to propagate it widely? If you could come again..."
"I can still wait for you," the Wayman replied, and he then departed from the mountain.
Upon reaching Zhuogang in Huangmei County, he saw a woman washing clothes and bowed to her, asking, "May I stay the night? She said, "I have parents; you may go and ask them."
He said, "Will you grant me your consent? She replied, "I do. The Master returned to the mountain and sat in a precarious posture until he passed away.

The woman was the youngest daughter of the Zhou family; as soon as she married, she became pregnant. Her parents detested her and cast her out. Having nowhere else to go, she worked as a hired spinner in the village.
After some time, she gave birth to a son. Thinking him an ill omen, she threw him into the water. The next day, she saw him sitting cross-legged amidst the waves.

He traveled upstream against the current and was subsequently raised until he reached the age of a youth. At seven years old, he followed his mother on alms rounds, traveling back and forth along the road through Huangmei.
One day, while Xuanshi was heading toward Huangmei, he encountered the boy playing by the roadside and asked, "What is your surname? The boy replied, "I do have a surname."
He asked, "Is this not a common surname? He replied, "It is the Buddha-nature. He asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "Because the nature is empty, it has none.
Xin knew that he was not deluded, so he immediately sent an attendant to his mother’s place to request permission for him to leave the household life.
Because of past karmic conditions, the mother consented to let him become her disciple. Xin performed the tonsure for him and named him Hongren.
(1532) The *Guanjing Fashi* Reborn in the Pure Land (Tiantai School).
Guanzheng resided at Tiantai. He once composed the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Xuanyi* in two volumes and its commentary in twenty volumes.

At Anzhou on the southern side of Le’an Ridge in Xianju, it was said that the mountain stream flowed with such violent rapids that people were frequently drowned each year. Guanzheng made a vow, saying: "If this stream..."
The ground became level and smooth. He was to preach the sutra there, and within ten days, white sand surged forth everywhere until it was as level as a jade mirror.

He then preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sutra) and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (Golden Light Sutra) in response to this spiritual grace. Whenever he sat in meditative seclusion, celestial flowers would drift down and fall by his side.

On the eighth month of the Renchen year, he manifested illness; a rare fragrance filled his chamber. As he approached his end, he instructed his disciples, saying: "The sutra says that the World-Honored One enters..."

He passed away. He burned many incense sticks of excellent fragrance, the smoke of which rose like clouds. "You should now burn much incense; I am about to depart," he said, leaving this final instruction.
Suddenly rising, he joined his palms, invoked the names of Amitābha Buddha and the two Great Beings (Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra), and vanished in an instant.

Xuanzang was a native of Goushi, surnamed Chen. He entered the monastic order in his youth; at the age of eleven, he could recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, standing out as preeminent.

He was self-reliant and did not conform to the currents of his time. He lectured on the *Śataśāstra* twenty-one times without examining the textual characteristics [of the commentary], and his exposition flowed forth inexhaustibly;

he was thus called a "divine man" (*shénrén*) of his era. In the winter of the third year of the Zhenguan period, he submitted a memorial requesting to travel to the Western Regions to retrieve Buddhist scriptures, but Emperor Taizong did not grant his request.

He then secretly departed through the Jade Pass (Yumenguan) and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There he followed the master Saṃgha to resolve his doubts regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Hetuvidyā*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and other treatises.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Mahāvana, where he studied the *Mādhyamaka-śāstra* and the scriptures of heterodox paths under a Brahmin.
At that time, the Brahmin was over seven hundred years old. He then traveled to the kingdom of Puṇḍravardhana, where he studied the *Abhidharma* under the Dharma Master Pūrṇavasu.
He studied treatises such as the *Dharmaguptaka-nikāya-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* at the country of Cīnabhukti under the master Candrāvatī;
he studied the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* at the country of Roruka under the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta;
and he studied the *Sautrāntika-vibhāṣā*, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, and other treatises at the country of Kucha under Viśeṣamitra.
He was a master of the Tripiṭaka and had studied both types of *Vibhāṣā*. The king possessed a superior army of one hundred thousand men and was preeminent among the kingdoms of the Western Regions.

Xuanzang entered with about eighty Hu merchants and, having crossed the Gaṅgā River, arrived in Central India. There he met a Mahāyāna layman (*upāsaka*), who expounded for him the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. He then proceeded to Rājagṛha.
Having heard in advance of Xuanzang’s arrival, the king prepared full honors and went out to welcome him from the suburbs; there Xuanzang beheld him.
The Master of Śāstras Śīlabhadra was already one hundred and six years old at that time. After Xuanzang had paid his respects, Śīlabhadra invited him to sit and asked from where he had come.
He replied, "I have come from the land of China, wishing to study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises.

Thereupon, Śīlabhadra called out to his disciple Guṇabhadra, pointed toward Xuanzang, and said to him, "My disciple, how did my previous dream turn out? The disciple then said to Xuanzang, "O Upādhyāya..."
Three years ago, he fell gravely ill, as if someone had cut open his abdomen with a blade. He intended to fast to death, but one night he dreamed of a man with a golden body who said to him:
"Do not loathe your own body. In the past, when you were a high-ranking official, you took many lives.
You ought to repent and reproach yourself; what benefit is there in ending your own life? A monk from the land of China has come here to study the Dharma. [He has already arrived.]
"He is on his way; he shall arrive in three years. By bestowing the Dharma upon him, he will in turn propagate it, and your transgressions will naturally be extinguished.
I am Mañjuśrī; therefore, I have come to inform you. The Upādhyāya had been ill for three years, and now the Ācārya had indeed arrived.
Thereupon, they were filled with a mingling of comfort and joy, as if they shared a long-standing bond of intimacy.
(Wuxu) The Sixth Patriarch Huineng was born. His surname was Lu;

he was a native of Xinzhou in Nanhai. His mother was Li. She dreamed that white flowers blossomed in competition before her courtyard, two white cranes flew together, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Upon waking, she conceived. She carried the child for six years. This was the Wuxu year of the Zhenguan era. II.
On the eighth day of the month, he was born. A radiance from his brow ascended into the sky, and a fragrant aroma wafted through the air.
At dawn, two monks came to visit Huineng’s father and said, "A son has been born during the night; he may be named Huineng. 'Hui' means to benefit sentient beings with the Dharma;
'Neng' means to be able to perform the work of a Buddha. Having spoken, they vanished without a trace. At the age of three, his father passed away, and his mother raised him.
(Gengzi) Dharma Master Fashun passed away. His surname was Du.
It was traditionally said that he was an incarnation of Mañjuśrī who had descended as a spirit in Wannian, Yongzhou. Whenever someone was ill, they had to sit upright and face him;

they would then immediately recover. There were those suffering from deafness; when Fashun called out to them, their hearing would instantly become clear. There were those suffering from... [text fragment ends]

To those who were mute, he would converse with them in accordance with their condition, and they were immediately able to speak. There was one suffering from insanity; when Shun sat in meditation facing him, the man immediately bowed in thanks and departed.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty summoned him and said, "I am suffering from the heat of exhaustion. By what means can Your Reverence’s spiritual power dispel it?

He replied, "Simply issue a general amnesty, and Your Majesty’s person will naturally find peace. The Emperor followed his advice, and his illness was subsequently cured. Consequently, [the Emperor] bestowed [a reward upon him].

He was titled Dixin (Heart of the Emperor). He was once invited into the imperial palace, where he extensively propagated the principles of the *Avataṃsaka*’s sudden and perfect teaching and established the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.
The whole world took him as their master. He once composed a verse on the Dharmakāya, which says: "In Jiazhou, an ox eats the grain; in Yizhou, a horse’s belly swells.
The world seeks a physician, yet he applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. He passed away in the fifth month of the Gengzi year. [Huemian.]
A man of the Zhang family from Yongyang was a monk who succeeded Sena in the Dharma. He upheld the dhūta practices, keeping only two needles;

he would beg for thread to mend them in winter and discard them in summer. His mind was free from fear, and he slept without dreaming. He constantly practiced begging for food, and at whichever monastery he arrived, he would split firewood and make sandals himself.
He never stayed more than one night. In the *Renyin* year of the Zhenguan era, he was at Shanhui Monastery in Luoyang.
Beside the temple, he stayed overnight in an ancient tomb. When a great snowfall occurred, he entered the temple at dawn to see Tan-kuang.

Kuang marveled at where he had come from. Man said, "Does the Dharma have a place from which it comes? Kuang sent someone to search for his point of entry; on all four sides, the snow was piled about five feet high.

Subsequently, news spread that there was an official registration of monks, and the various monastics fled and hid themselves. Man, however, took up his alms bowl and traveled through the villages, meeting no obstruction whatsoever. Following...

He attained a state of detached wandering. Whenever he sought out quietude, if there were those who invited him for a vegetarian feast, Daobian would say, "Only when there are no monks in the world will I accept such an invitation.

He also once told people: "The Buddhas taught that the mind is to be understood as having illusory characteristics; now, to further add to these mental characteristics is a profound violation of the Buddha’s intent.
Moreover, to increase the proliferation of discursive arguments is utterly contrary to the Great Principle. He constantly carried the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* with him.
In four fascicles, he took this as his essential practice. Later, amidst the forging of metal, he passed away while sitting in meditation without illness (Gui-mao year).
Chan Master Farong transmitted the Dharma to Zhiyan and Zhian of Zhishan.
A native of the Hua family in Qu’a, he possessed exceptional wisdom and courage from his youth. He stood seven chi and six cun tall. Sui dynasty.
During the Daye era, he served as a *langjiang* (colonel). At the age of forty, he left the household life and entered Mount Wangong, where he became a disciple of Bao Yue.

Later, while sitting in meditation one day, he beheld a strange monk over ten feet tall, whose spiritual bearing was exceptionally noble and whose speech was clear and resonant. The monk said to Yan, "You have left the household life at eighty years of age;

you ought to increase your diligent practice. Having finished speaking, he vanished. He once... [was] in... (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary, ending abruptly with "甞在" [once in...]). I have translated the extant portion as requested.)
While Yan was absorbed in meditative concentration in the valley, the mountain waters surged in a torrential flood. Yet, Yan remained unmoved; the waters receded of their own accord.

A hunter encountered him there and, as a result, reformed his ways and cultivated virtue. Furthermore, two men who had previously served with him in the military heard that Yan had retired into seclusion.

Thereupon, they entered the mountains together. Having searched for him and found him, they said to Yan, "Are you mad, General? Why do you dwell here? He replied, "My madness desires to awaken, while yours is now fully manifest.
Those who indulge in lustful sights and lewd sounds, and who covet glory and overstep their station, will transmigrate through birth and death; by what means can they emerge from this on their own?
The two men were moved to realization, sighed in lamentation, and departed. In the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era, he returned to establish [the monastery].
Daoye entered Mount Niutou and paid his respects to Farong, seeking clarification on the Great Matter. Farong said, "I have received the true instructions of Master Xinxin;
that which I have attained has entirely vanished. Even if there were a single dharma superior to *nirvāṇa*, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.
A single speck of dust flying can obscure the heavens; a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth. You have now already transcended such views; as for me, I too..."
The Master asked, "The transformation and guidance of the mountain gate shall be entrusted to you. Yuanyan then received this command and became the Second Patriarch.
(Jiachen year) The Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin, transmitted the Dharma to Hongren.
Emperor Taizong once issued an imperial decree summoning Daoxin to the palace. The messenger went three times, but Daoxin remained firmly reclining and did not rise. On the fourth occasion...

The Emperor commanded the messenger, saying, "If he does not rise, bring his head here. When the messenger arrived at the mountain and delivered the imperial decree, Hui-xin then extended his neck toward the blade;
his expression remained serene. The messenger was struck with wonder and returned to report this. The Emperor’s admiration and longing for him grew even deeper.

At this point, Hui-xin said to Hong-ren, "In the past, the Tathāgata transmitted the Eye of the True Dharma, which has been passed down through successive generations until it reached me. I now entrust it to you."
"You, together with your robes and bowl, listen to my verse: 'The nature of the lotus seed exists; because of the ground, the lotus grows.
When the great conditions unite with its nature, what should grow is non-growing. He then entrusted his disciples to him. One day, Xìn addressed the assembly, saying:
'During the Wǔdé era, I traveled to Mount Lúshān and ascended its summit. Looking toward Mount Pòtóu, I saw purple clouds like a canopy.'"
"Below there are white vapors, divided horizontally into six paths. Do you all understand? The assembly remained silent.
Zhenren said, "Could this not be the Dharma-branch that the Master will produce crosswise in the future? Xinxing replied, "Excellent."
In the winter of the Jiachen year, Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions.
On the second month of the Yi-si year, he had an audience with the Emperor at the Yiluan Hall.

The Emperor comforted and commended him repeatedly, and subsequently inquired about the products and customs west of the Snow Mountains, as well as the ancient sites of the Eight Kings and the Seven Buddhas.

Regarding these traces left behind, Xuanzang answered each question with systematic coherence. The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "The Master has traveled through more than one hundred kingdoms;
you may compile a record of their mountains, rivers, and customs to compose the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* for the benefit of future generations."
Is this not truly magnificent? As Xuanzang was about to conclude his service upon receiving the imperial decree, the Emperor said to his attendants:

"In the past, Fu Jian praised Dao’an as a 'divine vessel,' and the entire nation held him in reverence. When I observe the Master’s refined and elegant speech and his upright, austere integrity, he does not merely live up to the ancients;
he far surpasses them. At that time, the imperial carriage was about to set out on a punitive expedition against Goguryeo, and [the Emperor] heard of Xuanzang...
Regarding the date of his return, [the Emperor] briefly summoned him for an audience and engaged him in conversation; before he realized it, the sun had already set.

Xuanzang then submitted a memorial stating that he had obtained a total of six hundred and fifty-seven Sanskrit texts of sutras and śāstras from the Western Regions, and requested permission to translate them for the sake of the state at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song.
The Emperor said, "I have recently established Hongfu Monastery for the late Empress Dowager Mu; it is extremely secluded and tranquil. You may proceed there."

Regarding the translations required, all matters were deliberated with Xuánlíng. Xuanzang then submitted a memorial, saying: "When the common people see that I have returned from afar, they will indiscreetly gaze upon me;

this will not only hinder and disrupt my religious duties, but I also fear it may lead to unforeseen calamities. I pray that an official in charge of the gate may be assigned to prevent any such breaches.
The Emperor granted his request. The Emperor further regarded Xuanzang’s virtue and learning as profound and vast, and his physical presence as peerless.

Lun wished to have me renounce the monastic life so that we might together manage the affairs of state. Xuanzang replied at length, explaining that the peace and order of the empire are entirely due to Your Majesty’s sagely virtue and do not depend on others.

Even if talent were required, there are currently many such as Yi Yin and Lü Shang; as for the humble and mediocre person that I am, Xuanzang— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Xuanzang yonglou," which translates to "the humble and mediocre person that I am, Xuanzang.")
"How could I be worthy to participate in this? As for observing the precepts within the monastic community and propagating the bequeathed Dharma—this is my sincere aspiration.

I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s compassionate grace will not revoke it until the end. The Emperor said, "If you, Master, wish to propagate the wondrous Way, I shall not obstinately oppose your lofty ambition.
He then asked, "What sutra have you been translating recently? [He] replied, "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. [The Emperor] asked, "What principles does it elucidate? [He] replied, "This..."
It was composed by the Great Being Maitreya and elucidates the meaning of the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*). The Emperor sent a messenger to retrieve the treatise and bring it into the palace;

it consisted of one hundred fascicles. After the Emperor had examined it in detail, he said to his attendants: "When I observed the newly translated sūtras and śāstras of the Dharma Master, they were like gazing at the heavens or looking out over the ocean—their height and depth are beyond measure.
Recently, as military and state affairs have been burdensome, I have not had the leisure for a thorough investigation. From this day forward..."

Realizing that the source of our tradition was profound and vast, he looked upon the Confucian and Daoist schools and the nine currents of thought as being like small marshes and streams compared to the great ocean.

Consequently, he issued an edict to the relevant authorities to select nine scribes from the Secretariat to hand-copy nine newly translated scriptures and treatises each, which were then bestowed as gifts upon the Governors-General of the Nine Provinces.
It was circulated and spread far and wide, in the hope that throughout the entire realm, all would together receive this Dharma never before heard.

When the Emperor returned from his campaign against Liaodong, he harbored anxieties regarding the state of the world; however, upon meeting Xuanzang, he turned his attention to the Great Teaching and his condition gradually recovered.

He then asked: "In wishing to plant the benefits of the Dharma-gate, what should take precedence? [Xuanzang] replied: "Sentient beings sleep in delusion; there is nothing other than wisdom [that can awaken them]."
"Qī: 'The sprouts of wisdom must be planted, and the Dharma serves as their nourishment. To propagate the Dharma, one requires people; thus, the ordination of monks is paramount.
The Emperor was pleased and issued an edict that every monastery in all the provinces of the realm should ordain five monks."
(Jiyou) Master Shandao Expounds the Dharma Gate of the Pure Land.
Shandao’s place of origin is unknown. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he visited the Nine Grades Practice Hall of Daochuo in the Western Capital.

He lectured on and recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, exclaiming with great joy, "This is truly the essential ford for entering the Buddha-way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish;
only this dharma-gate allows for swift transcendence of birth and death. Thereupon, he performed prostrations and recitations day and night, inspiring the fourfold assembly.

Every time he entered his room, he knelt in the *hu* posture and recited the Buddha’s name; he would not cease until his strength was exhausted. Even when the weather was cold and freezing, he would perspire profusely.
Upon leaving, he would expound the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land for others. For over thirty years, he did not sleep for even a moment.

He practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, performed prostrations according to the *Vaipulya* sutras, and upheld the precepts without violating even the slightest detail. When fine food was sent to the kitchen, he would eat only coarse and poor-quality fare.
