He did not personally consume milk, curd, or clarified butter (ghṛta). Whatever offerings he received, he used to transcribe one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and to paint three hundred wall murals depicting the transformations of the Pure Land.
Wherever there were ruined temples or dilapidated stupas, he repaired and restored them; he lit lamps to maintain perpetual illumination, never allowing them to cease throughout the year.
He would not have anyone carry his three robes or alms bowl, nor would he travel with the multitude, fearing that they might engage in idle talk.
Regarding worldly affairs, there have been countless individuals from the Chang'an Daozu clan who transmitted the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Someone asked, "Does reciting the Buddha's name lead to rebirth in the Pure Land? He replied, "It shall be according to what you recite; it will fulfill your aspirations.

Thereupon, he himself recited a single invocation, and a ray of light issued from his mouth; as he recited up to ten and then a hundred times, the light did likewise. His verse for exhorting the world says:
Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair turns white like a crane; look at how one’s gait grows unsteady and frail.
Even if gold and jade fill one’s halls, how can one escape the suffering of decay and illness? No matter how many kinds of joy one may have, impermanence will inevitably arrive.
There is only the path of direct cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
(Gengxu) Vinaya Master Daoxuan returned to Zhongnan Mountain.
He was the son of the Qian family of Jingzhao; his father served as the Minister of the Ministry of Personnel. His mother dreamed that a lunar disc pierced her womb and she became pregnant.
She further dreamed of a foreign monk who said to her, "The one you carry in your womb is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty. Once he was born, he gradually...
He was extensively read in a vast array of books. At the age of sixteen, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, mastering it in twenty days. He shaved his head to receive the monastic precepts;

his three robes were made solely of plain cloth, and he often practiced the discipline of eating only once a day. In the seventh year of the Wude era, he moved his residence to Zhuma on Mount Zhongnan.

He once practiced the *Prajñāpāramitā-samādhi*, moving the dragon deities to change their forms to listen to the Dharma. During the Zhenguan era, he collaborated with Xuanzang in translating the scriptures.
He was appointed as the chief scribe and editor for the texts. In the first year of the Yonghui era (Xin Hai), he again resided at Zhuma.
The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin entered nirvana;
having succeeded to the patriarchal position, he had maintained his concentration of mind without sleep for sixty years, such that his ribs never touched his mat. In the Yonghui era...
On the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month of the second year, he suddenly issued an admonition to his disciples, saying:
"All dharmas are entirely liberation. You each must protect and mind yourselves, and propagate this teaching for the sake of the future. Having spoken these words, he sat upright and passed away.

He was seventy-two years of age. His stupa was erected at his native mountain. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord without cause; his physical features remained as they were.
After he passed away, his disciples did not dare to close the door again.
(Renzi year) Chan Master Farong lectured on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra while residing at Mount Niutou.
His dharma assembly flourished greatly. During the Yonghui era, his followers ran short of provisions; Farong went to Dan...

Yangyuanhua lived eighty *li* from the mountains. He personally carried eighteen *dou* of rice, traveling there in the morning and returning by evening, providing for three hundred monks without fail at the two meal times.
For three years, the district magistrate Xiao Yuanshan invited him to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at Jianchu Monastery.
Listeners gathered like clouds; when they reached the "Chapter on Cessation and Tranquility," the earth shook. After the lecture concluded, he returned home.
Shan: "When an object-condition arises from form, you do not say that it arises by depending on form.
How can one know that it depends [on conditions], yet you wish to cease its arising? Answer: "When the objective realm first arises, both the nature of form and the nature of the realm are empty.

Fundamentally, there is no knower of conditions; the measure of the mind is identical to knowing. When illumination is based on the fundamental, there is no arising. At that time, arising ceases of itself. [He] embraced the darkness.
The conditions for the arising of cognition do not follow the mind at the moment it arises. As for the time before birth, form and mind are not yet nurtured;

from emptiness there is originally no thought. Perception, feeling, and speech arise from thought; their activation has never truly occurred—how could they require the instructions of the Buddha? Question:
When one closes the eyes and does not see forms, mental objects and deliberations nevertheless abound. Since forms do not concern the mind, from where do these objects arise? Answer:

With eyes closed, no forms are seen; yet the inner mind stirs with manifold anxieties. Illusory consciousness arises through provisional conditions; though names are given, they ultimately do not transcend [reality].
Knowing that form does not concern the mind, and the mind likewise does not concern the person, as one acts, appearances shift like a bird flying away into the true emptiness of space.

Question: When an object arises, it has no fixed location; the Pratyekabuddha understands this as its birth. When the object passes away, awareness returns and turns back; awareness then transforms into an object.
If one uses the mind to drag the mind, it is again what is perceived by awareness. Following it, following it as it goes, one does not depart from the boundary of arising and ceasing. Answer:

Within the preceding, succeeding, and middle moments of form and mind, there is in reality no object of dependent origination. In a single thought-moment, self-doubt is forgotten; who then could calculate [the nature of things]?
In movement and stillness, this knowing is itself without knowing; the knower and the known do not meet. You should examine your own fundamental form;
why seek it beyond the realm? The preceding object does not change or pass away, and the subsequent thought does not come from the present.
To seek the mind’s original nature is like looking at a dream, or like ice in the sixth month—present everywhere.
It is like this: avoiding emptiness, one will never be liberated; seeking emptiness, it likewise cannot be attained. I ask you of the image in a mirror: from where does the mind arise?
When asked, "Precisely when the mind is being employed, how can there be peace and ease? the answer is: "Precisely when the mind is being employed, precisely there is no employment of the mind.
To speak in circuitous ways of names and forms is wearisome; to speak directly, there is no redundancy. When there is no mind, precisely there is its employment. Always...

In its ultimate application, there is nothing at all. Now, when we speak of the state of no-mind, it is not different from the state of having a mind. Question: When the wise cite sublime words, they should accord with the nature of the mind;
yet these words differ from the path of the mind. If one unites them, they will be ten thousand times more discordant. Answer:

Sublime words are taught as skillful means to break through the illnesses of sentient beings; they do not concern the discourse on the original nature. They arise from the transformations of emptiness; non-thought is the truth.
Constantly, one shall ultimately sever the path of the mind; detached from thought, its nature is unmoving. Birth and cessation are without contradiction or error.

As the echo in the valley possesses sound, and the reflection in the mirror can look back, [the questioner asks: "If the essence of the practitioner exists within the object, then upon awakening, the object is forgotten.

There are three minds: the preceding awakening, the subsequent awakening, and the object itself. [The answer is: "The function of the object is not its essence. Once awakening has ceased, there should be no further deliberation. Because of awakening..."
When one knows that objects have vanished, objects do not arise during the state of awakening. The prior awakening, the subsequent awakening, and the object—these three are delayed.
Question: Abiding in meditative concentration, neither [awakening nor object] shifts; this is taken to be the true samādhi, such that no karmas can pull one away.

Yet one does not realize that subtle ignorance gradually follows upon its heels. Answer: Furthermore, I have heard of others who falsely grasp at mental constructs (*cittamātra*); thus, among these three, the objective reality is not established.

Not turning back from falsehood, the mind is bound by right reception (*samādhi*). It creates karmic obstacles for the sake of purity; though it is but one ten-thousandth part of the mind’s dust, failing to comprehend this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Subtle habitual causes arise, and gradually the marks of phenomena (*nimitta*) appear; like wind coming and waves rolling.
When one desires stillness, the waters return to their level flow. Yet, if one wishes further to speak of the path ahead, I fear the subsequent mind will be startled.

The great beast of non-conceptualization roars; the emptiness of nature lets fall frost and hail. The stars scatter and the weeds of defilement are crushed; birds fall down in disarray from all sides. Within the five realms of existence, all is surely in turmoil.
The four māras cannot advance or retreat before it; it is like a fierce fire blazing, and yet like a sharp sword cutting.

Question: Relying on awakening and knowledge, one faces the myriad dharmas; yet the myriad dharmas are originally thus. If one relies on the mind of illumination, one only obtains the mind of illumination; it does not correspond to the affairs within the mind. Answer:

Relying on awakening and knowledge, one faces the myriad dharmas; yet the myriad dharmas ultimately have nothing to rely upon. If one relies on the mind of illumination, it should not reside [within the mind].

Regarding "Outside of Mind": Question: When following along with whatever arises without discrimination, the clarity of mind does not manifest; furthermore, fearing that the mind is dark and dull, one applies effort while remaining within the mind.
Thus, the obstacles of ignorance become difficult to remove. Answer: This [effort] should not exist; this [object] should not be sought.

Non-discrimination is itself true discernment. By attaining this, the dark mind emerges as the luminous mind. As for "fearing," it refers to the mind being obscure and dull; to maintain the mind and entrust oneself to effortful practice—what is the point?

The treatise discusses the difficulty of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It is only upon reaching Buddhahood that this becomes an illness. Regarding the inquiry into the intermediate message of "breaking through" (*zhézhōng*), it is indeed difficult to find rest.

Unless one is a practitioner who applies these methods, this difficulty will ultimately remain unresolved. Answer: As for the desire to receive the intermediate message, the message itself is neither difficult nor easy.
First, observe the mind within the locus of the mind; next, infer the wisdom within wisdom. Third, illuminate that which infers; fourth, penetrate the non-dual.
Record. The fifth is the name of liberation; the sixth is the equalizing of the true and the false. The seventh is knowing the source of phenomena; the eighth is the unconditioned compassion.

The ninth is pervading the aggregates within emptiness; the tenth is the covering by clouds and rain. Most exhaustively ending that which is without perception, the ignorance-born gives rise to fundamental wisdom.

Like reflections appearing in the three karmas, like illusory people manifesting at the crossroads, one does not abide in the limit of emptiness, but should illuminate that which exists within existence.

There is nothing that does not emerge from within emptiness and existence; it has not yet been brought together as both emptiness and existence. This is termed "the Middle Way. The Middle Way is beyond verbal expression;
it finds no place of rest to settle upon. How can its application and function be determined? Question: Is there not a distinct class of people who are well-versed in emptiness and signlessness?

They claim that stillness and distraction are one and the same, and further maintain that while existing within existence, they are non-existent. They testify to the same realization, remaining eternally quiescent in their functioning. Their awareness is itself quiescence.

Constantly employing the mind to realize the True Principle, one further speaks of "employing the non-employing. Wisdom and skillful means are manifold; though words may seem chaotic, they accord with the Principle.
Suchness and the Principle are as they are; they are not realized through the conscious mind. Since one knows that realization by the mind is erroneous, mind after mind is further extinguished.
Such a Dharma difficult to know cannot be known even throughout eternal kalpas. For those who employ their minds in this same way, the Dharma is not [attained].

[The interlocutor] asks: "Is there one who can transform [others]? [The Master] answers: There is indeed one who realizes emptiness; this is discussed further in the preceding verse: "Practicing emptiness while guarding at peace, Consciousness and views are momentarily overturned.

To realize that truth is the measure of the mind, Yet in the end, one knows it is not yet the original source. Furthermore, it is said: "When the functions of the mind are stilled, Much wisdom may still resemble doubt.
This is truly because the nature is not clear; Seeking emptiness merely exhausts oneself. For kalpas on end, one dwells in obscure consciousness, Clinging to marks."

He knows nothing at all. When light is emitted, the earth immediately shakes; what could he possibly do with that? To the aforementioned questioner regarding the observer of the mind, there is further the difficulty of the "gauze screen.

The answer is: if the observer of the mind has a gauze screen, why wait for an observer when the illusory mind itself is present? Moreover, for one who has no illusory mind, what need is there for an observer?
It is difficult to bring [the mind] down with ease. Question: For a long time there has been a great foundation; yet, amidst the divergences of the mental path, one perceives subtle obstacles.
One then reaches the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Unless one is a skillful teacher, none can resolve this principle.

I look up to our Great Master to open for us the essential gate, to guide those who apply their minds, and not to let them lose the right path. Answer: The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally...
The foundational karma and dream-like perceptions differ and conflict; regarding the subtle body of true reality (*dharmatā*), one is perpetually unaware of both form and mind.
Suddenly encountering a man of primordial chaos (*hundun*), who pities and takes compassion for all living beings, he entrusts his doubts and poses questions at length.

Embracing principle within, he is ever-illuminated; having penetrated the dark paths of birth and death, his mind is undisturbed by praise or blame. The wild elder provides a clear and distinct response; the Dharma-nature feels ashamed of such a grand arrival. Thus, the multitude are enlightened.
Regarding the production of medicine, it is as with the nature of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
(Gui-chou) Great Master Huìkuān passed away.
Huìkuān was the son of the Yang family of Yizhou; his father, Yuǎnwěi, was a Daoist practitioner known as Sāndòng Xiānshēng. His elder sister was Xìnxiàng.
From birth, Dao was known for his wisdom. Throughout the day, he remained in meditative stillness. When he was five or six years old, he would daily discuss with Xinxin;

their conversations were entirely devoid of worldly matters, such that no one who heard them could understand a single word. His family had followed the Way for generations, yet Dao alone took no pleasure in it.

His father scolded and reviled him, ordering him to bow before the Celestial Venerable. Reluctantly, Dao bowed; the iron image suddenly toppled over and shattered. The entire clan was struck with wonder and marvel. Consequently—

A record of the words he spoke in discussion: Previously, the Chan Master Tanshang of Longhuai Monastery said to his disciple Hui at the time of his death, "My karmic conditions dictate that I shall be reborn in the family of the Yangs on a mountain peak in Mianzhu, Guanghan.

Seven years hence, you shall come to see me. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Subsequently, Hui dreamed that Tanshang reproached him for breaching their agreement. Startled awake, Hui then proceeded to...
Fengding knocked on the door. Huian asked, "Who is knocking at the door? Hui said, "I am your disciple, Hui. Huian smiled and said, "How do you know me, that you call yourself my disciple?
Hui replied, "I have perceived the Master's voice; it is just as it was in the past. They then met face to face.
His father brought out the records he had compiled of the discussions he had held with Huixin and showed them to him; these were treatises such as the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*.

Hui then respectfully submitted to Daoquan. He returned once more to Longhuai Temple to undergo the tonsure ceremony; at that time he was thirteen years old. Hui revered him as if he were a divine dragon.

While the assembly numbered three thousand, all of whom performed manual labor with their own hands, Daoquan alone remained leisurely and at ease. When people commented on this, Hui said: [The text provided ends here.]

"This was my former master. He then related the circumstances in detail. From that time on, his spiritual wonders became increasingly manifest, and the common people called him "The Holy Monk" (Sheng Heshang).
His sister, Xinsiang, also followed him into the monastic life. At Jinghui Temple, there was an extraordinary monk who entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) throughout the entire monastery;
red flames blazed continuously, yet no one recognized him. Xinsiang said, "This is the Venerable Agnidatta entering the 'Blazing Fire' (*tejodhātu*) samādhi."

She entered samādhi and extinguished it with water; thus she was able to enter [the fire]. She then practiced the visualization of water (*āp-aṃśa-bhāvanā*), until the entire room became serene, and seeing only water, her physical form could no longer be perceived.
A monk of extraordinary character marveled at this and considered her to have attained the fruits of the path. At that time, she was also called the "Holy Nun.
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Yonghui era, Huikuan passed away. Those of the time said she was an emanation body of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
(Jia-yin) Kuiji Dharma Master participated in the translation of sutras and śāstras.
Kuiji’s secular surname was Wei-chi; he was a native of Dai Commandery. He was the nephew of Duke Jing-de of Eguo and the son of General of the Jinwu Guard, Jing-zong.
His mother dreamed of a lunar disc in her palm, which she swallowed and thereby conceived him. On the evening of his birth, divine light filled the room. Six...
Each year he was able to compose a book. Initially, when Xuanzang had obtained a young boy in the Western Regions who possessed peerless intelligence and insight, he brought him to see Daorong.
Daorong called Ji out to pay his respects to Xuanzang and then had him recite several thousand words from the military treatises he had composed.
Xuanzang counted the number of characters. Once the boy and Ji had finished reciting them, he deceived him by saying, "This is merely an ancient book.

He then ordered a boy from the Western Regions to recite it over again, and not a single character was in error. Zong was greatly enraged, believing that Ji had stolen an ancient book to deceive him, and intended to kill him.
Xuanzang approached him to request ordination. Ji said, "If you agree to let me consume meat for my evening meals, then it may be so; otherwise, I would rather submit to the sword and die.
Xuanzang granted this, and consequently followed him into the Way. He became proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. In the fifth year of the Yonghui era, Emperor Gaozong issued a special edict.

Xuanzhi became a *bhikṣu* and entered the Great Ci'en Monastery to participate in the correct translation of the scriptures. There, he followed Xuanzang to receive the essential tenets of the *Yogācāra-vijñaptimātra* school.
He authored approximately one hundred treatises, earning him the contemporary title of "Master of the Hundred Treatises. However, his character was grand and ostentatious;
whenever he went out, he invariably prepared three carriages, for which reason he was also called the "Dharma Master of the Three Carriages."
(Dingsi year) Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou entered nirvana. (The fourth patriarch Xinxing’s collateral successor.
Farong resided at Mount Niutou and widely propagated the Way of the Dharma. The local magistrate, Xiao Yuanshan, invited Farong to reside at Jianchu Monastery;
he declined, being unable to accept. Thereupon, he charged his disciple Zhiran with the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), ordering him to transmit it in succession. He was about to—
He descended the mountain and said to the assembly, "I shall not tread upon this mountain again. At that time, the birds and beasts wailed in grief, continuing for more than a month without ceasing.
Before the hermitage stood four large paulownia trees; in the middle month of summer, they suddenly withered and fell.
On the twenty-third day of the intercalary first month of the third year of the Xianqing era, he passed away without illness.
The Passing of National Teacher Baoguang (A Dharma Heir of the First Patriarch Bodhidharma): Baoguang resided late in his life at Baoyan on Pujiang Mountain.
He was close friends with Xuānlǎng; whenever they exchanged greetings, Baoguang would dispatch a white dog to deliver his letter, while Xuānlǎng would send back a green monkey as a messenger.
On the first day of the first month of the second year of the Xiǎnqìng era, Baoguang personally molded a clay image of himself. Upon its completion...

On the ninth day, he completed [his preparations]. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble? Yun replied, "It is no different from the Master himself. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus position.
He said to Yun, "I have remained in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years.
Now I am about to depart from the world. Listen to my verse: "Originally there is neither birth nor death; Now I likewise manifest birth and death. I have attained the freedom of going and staying."
He said, "My mind shall be reborn elsewhere, yet it will return here again. He further instructed them, saying, "Sixty years after my passing, there will be a monk who comes to take my bones;
do not refuse him. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Forty-four years after his parinirvāṇa, the Elder Tiṣya came from Yunmen to the site of the stupa.
He prostrated and prayed, "I hope the stupa will open wide. After a short while, the door of the stupa indeed opened, and his bones were found linked together like a chain.
If it was gold, he immediately took it to Mount Qinwang and constructed a stūpa to enshrine it.

From the *dingmao* year of the Zhou dynasty to the *dingsi* year of the Tang dynasty, exactly one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years elapsed; thus, it remained in this land for over four hundred years.
(Xin-you) The Fifth Patriarch Hongren transmitted the Dharma to Huineng.
Huineng’s family was poor; he gathered firewood to support his mother. One day, while carrying wood through the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Startled, he asked the guest, "What dharma is this? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*. He learned it from Huangmei...
Master Neng suddenly informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma and traveled directly to Shaozhou.
There he met Liu Zhilüe, a man of noble conduct from the local area, with whom he formed a friendship. A nun named Wujinzang was Zhilüe’s paternal aunt;
she had once read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and was able to explain its meaning. When the nun took up the scroll and asked about the characters, Neng said:
He did not recognize the characters, yet he inquired about their meaning. The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend their meaning?

Huineng replied, "The wondrous principle of the Buddhas has nothing to do with written words. The nun was struck with wonder and amazement; she announced this throughout the fourfold assembly and invited him to reside at Baolin Temple.
One day, he suddenly thought to himself, "I have sought the Great Dharma; what am I doing staying here? He then abandoned his post. (Longshuo era)
In the first year [of the Kaiyuan era], he traveled to Huangmei to attend upon Hongren. Ren asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan. Ren asked, "What do you seek to do?
He replied, "I seek only to become a Buddha. Ren said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha?

He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but Buddha-nature has neither north nor south. Ren knew that he was extraordinary, and thus rebuked him, saying, "Go work in the fodder shed! Huineng—
Having prostrated at his feet, he withdrew and entered the millhouse, where he performed manual labor with the pestle and mortar for eight months.
Knowing that the time had come to transmit the Dharma, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be merely memorized.

I shall speak, and you each must spontaneously compose a verse according to your own inclination. If the words and meaning accord perfectly, then both the robe and the Dharma shall be transmitted. At that time, there were over seven hundred members in the assembly.
Shenxiu occupied the first seat; his learning was thorough in both Buddhist and secular traditions, and he was revered by the assembly.

Shenxiu, too, was self-important, believing there was no one who surpassed him, and thus ceased further reflection. He then inscribed a verse upon a wall in the corridor, saying: "The body is the Bodhi tree."
"The mind is like a bright mirror-stand; at all times one must diligently wipe it clean, lest it be defiled by dust.

When Hui-neng saw this verse while walking for exercise, he knew in his heart it was composed by Shenxiu and praised it, saying, "Those of future generations who rely on this to practice will likewise attain supreme fruition.
When the assembly heard these words, each person began to recite it. While at the rice-hulling shed, Hui-neng heard the verse and asked his fellow students, "Who composed this?"
[Dao]xuan said: "The Master was about to transmit the Dharma and had each of them compose a verse; this was the work of the Venerable Xiu.
Huineng said, 'It is beautiful, but it is not yet complete. His fellow students did not answer, but looked at one another and laughed.
That night, Huineng secretly informed a young boy, who led him to the corridor. Huineng held a candle himself and instructed the boy to stand beside the verse of the Venerable Xiu."
He wrote a verse, saying: "Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is also not a stand. Originally there is not a single thing;
Where could dust and grime settle? Huineng asked, "Who wrote this? You have still not seen your nature. When the assembly heard Huineng’s words, they paid him no further heed.
Huineng then went to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet? He replied, "It is white, but it has not been sifted."

Rin struck the pestle three times with his staff; it immediately sounded three times, and he entered the room. Rin used his *kāṣāya* robe to screen the entrance so that no one could see him, and said:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is for the sake of the One Great Matter. According to the capacities of beings—whether great or small—they are guided accordingly.

Thus, there are the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the Sudden, the Gradual, and so forth, which serve as the gateways of instruction. However, [it is] by means of the unsurpassed, subtle, and profound..."
This secret, perfect, luminous, and true Eye of the Dharma-treasury has been transmitted from Kāśyapa down through successive generations until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you, along with the robe that has been passed down; you must protect and uphold it well so that it is never severed.
Listen to my verse: "When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises according to the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, They likewise lack the nature [of rebirth]."

Wusheng was able to receive it in its entirety. He then asked, "The Dharma has now been transmitted; to whom shall the robe be given? [Huineng] replied, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet know or believe him.

Therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with your person and no longer be passed on.
For the time being, you should remain hidden and wait for the right time to go forth and transform others. This is what is called "receiving" [the robe].
The man who had been given the robe said, "My life is like a thread hanging from a string. Where should I hide? He replied, "When you encounter a place of sincerity, stop there;

when you meet with an opportunity, conceal yourself. Once he had prostrated at his feet, the man took the robe and departed. That night he traveled south, and none of the assembly knew of it. For three days thereafter, Hui-ning did not ascend the hall.
The assembly marveled at this and asked Hui-ning, "Our Way has gone forth. They asked again, "Who received the robe and the Dharma?"
He replied, "The one capable will obtain it. Thereupon, the assembly deliberated; since the name of the ascetic Lu was "Neng" (Capable), they immediately pursued him again.
Neng traveled south until he reached Mount Dayu, where there was a monk named Daoming, who had formerly served as a Fourth-Rank General and was accompanied by several hundred men.
When Neng came intending to seize his robe and bowl, Huiming reached him first. Neng was able to cast the robe and bowl onto a rock and said, "This robe represents the seal of faith;
can it be contended for by force? Huiming lifted the robe and bowl, but could not move them. Thereupon he said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of the robe.
Neng then said, "Since you have come for the sake of the Dharma, you should set aside all external conditions and not give rise to a single thought. I shall [act] for you..."
[Zhaozhou] spoke. After a long silence, Nanquan said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, at that very moment, what is the original face of Master Ming?
At these words, Ming attained great enlightenment. He then asked, "Beyond the secret words and secret meanings mentioned above..."
"Is there yet another hidden meaning? Huineng replied, "What I have told you is not secret. If you reflect back upon yourself, the secret is right within you.
Huineng said, "Although I was at Huangmei, I truly did not realize my own original face.
Now that I have received your instruction, it is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. The one walking here is now my teacher. Huineng said, "You..."
"If it is so, I and you share the same teacher at Huangmei. Guard and uphold this well. Ming then asked, "Where shall I go now?
Neng said, "When you meet Yuan, stop; when you encounter Meng, dwell. Ming bowed and took his leave.

Upon reaching the foot of the ridge, he said to the assembly, "I have just ascended the steep heights, yet there was no trace of him. We must seek him by another path. Thereupon, the assembly dispersed.
Later, Ming resided at Mount Meng in Yuanzhou; his surname was Chen.
(Renxu year) Master Shandao manifested birth in the Pure Land.
Master Shandao specialized in converting people through the Pure Land teachings. In the second year of the Longshuo era, he suddenly said to others: "This body is loathsome."
"I shall return to the West. He then climbed a willow tree and, facing west, made this vow: "May the Buddha receive me;
may the Bodhisattvas assist me, so that I may not lose right mindfulness and attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. Having spoken these words, he threw himself down and passed away.

Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, knowing that his recitation of the Buddha’s name had produced light from his mouth and that his self-sacrifice was of the utmost sincerity, bestowed upon the temple a plaque inscribed with the name "Guangming" (Radiance).
The monk Huigan resided at Qianfu Temple in Chang’an. He entered the念佛法門 (nianfo daochang) of Shandao, but for twenty-one days he did not behold any spiritual omens.

Lamenting his own deep karmic obstructions, he wished to fast unto death; however, Shandao would not permit it, instead exhorting him only to practice with utmost sincerity. For three years, Huigan followed these instructions.
Subsequently, he beheld the Buddha’s golden body and jade-like *ūrṇā-kośa*, and attained the *nien-fo san-mei* (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). [He then] composed...
*Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts), seven fascicles. At the time of his death, he joined his palms and said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," whereupon he passed away.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 29; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 30 (Lü character series).
Jiazi (the first year of Linde under Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty); Bingyin (changed to Qianfeng); Wuchen (changed to Zongzhang); Gengwu (changed to Xianheng);

Jiashu (changed to Shangyuan); Bingzi (changed to Yifeng); Jimao (changed to Diaolu); Gengchen (changed to Yonglong); Xinsi (changed to Kaiyao); Renwu (changed to Yongchun); Guiwei (changed to Hongdao);
Jia Shen (the first year of Zhongzong’s Sisheng era, also the first year of Empress Wu’s Guangzhai era); Yi You (Empress Wu).

The first year of Chuigong (Jichou; the Empress Wu changed the era to Yongchang); the second year (Gengyin; the Empress Wu changed the era to Tianshou and the state name to Zhou); the fourth year (Renchen; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Ruyi, then to Changshou);

the sixth year (Jiamu; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Yanchai); the seventh year (Yiwu; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Zhengsheng, then to Tiance Wanshou); the eighth year (Bingshen; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Wansui Dengfeng, then to Tongtian Wansui); the ninth year (Dingyou; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Shengong);

the tenth year (Wuxu; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Shengli); the twelfth year (Gengzi; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Jiushi); the thirteenth year (Xinchou; the Zhou dynasty changed the era to Dadeng, then to Chang'an); the seventeenth year (Yi...).
[When Zhongzong was restored to the throne and changed the era name to Shenlong (Shenlong 1–2),] Dingwei (changed to Jinglong), Gengxu (the first year of Ruizong’s Jingyun era),
Renzi (the first year of Xuanzong’s Xuantian era), Guichou (changed to Kaiyuan), Guihai (ending in the eleventh year of Tang Xuanzong’s Kaiyuan era),
[and] Jiazi: Chan Master Huian went into seclusion at Mount Zhongnan.
Hui’an was the son of the Wei family of Jingzhou. He left the household life and received full ordination, practicing the dhūta austerities.

During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled to Huangmei to visit Hongren, from whom he attained the essential points of the Dharma. In the first year of the Linde era, he lived in seclusion at Shibi Cliff in Zhongnan.
Fachih was the son of the Zhang family of Jiangning. He studied under Hongren, and upon hearing the Dharma, his mind was opened. On another occasion, Hongren said to his disciples:
"Those who shall later transmit my Dharma will number ten; Jinling Fachih is one of them.
Furthermore, he encountered Niutou Huifang, who granted him formal authorization, and thus he succeeded to the lineage of the mountain gate.

When Xuanzang was bedridden with illness, he commanded his disciple Dasheng Guang to record the scriptures and treatises he had translated, totaling seventy-five works in one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles. He then composed—
There were ten *koṭi* of Maitreya statues. When his illness became critical, he commanded those around him to chant together three times:
"Namo to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya! May I swiftly behold the compassionate countenance of all sentient beings.

Namo to the inner courtyard where the Tathāgata Maitreya dwells! May I, upon casting off this life, surely be reborn therein. Thereupon, he lay down on his right side and passed away. At that time, the Qilin...

It was the fifth day of the second month in the first year of the Tianji era. That evening, four white rainbows appeared, stretching from north to south and piercing the *Jin* mansion and the pagoda of Ci’en Temple.
Suddenly, a strange monk arrived carrying powdered sandalwood incense and requested that it be used to anoint the Master’s body according to the Indian rites.
Dàchéngguāng and others, fearing that the sarcophagus had been closed for too long, were reluctant to open it. The monk said, "I have brought another [offering]..."

The Emperor’s decree stated: "Should you refuse to comply, I shall submit a memorial and then open the sarcophagus. When the coffin was opened, the countenance appeared as if he were still alive, and a fragrant aroma wafted forth.
After the monk had finished applying the lacquer, he suddenly vanished from sight.
(Dingmao year) Vinaya Master Daoxuan entered nirvana.

Daoxuan was so deeply moved by his observance of the Vinaya that deities provided him with offerings and served as his guardians. Once, while walking along a path at night, he approached a stone step and stumbled.
A youth in armor appeared and shielded him, preventing him from falling. Daoxuan asked who he was, and the youth replied, "I am your disciple, King Pāñcika."

Zi Zhang was named Qiong. Because of his teacher’s virtuous precepts, he had come to serve as a guardian. He inquired about matters concerning the World-Honored One while he was in the world and after his parinirvāṇa;
Qiong recounted each of these things for him. Thereafter, his manifestations were not limited to a single occasion. In the spring of the second year of the Qiánfēng era, Heaven announced to Xuán:
"Your karmic conditions are nearing their end; you shall be reborn in the inner palace of Maitreya. On the thirtieth day of the tenth month, the assembly witnessed [his passing].
In the air, banners and flowers were arrayed in succession; extraordinary fragrances and celestial music arose, and with one voice they requested that he proclaim his return to visit Maitreya.
(Jisi year) The Great Being Saṃgha manifested himself at Sizhou.
Originally from Kucha, he traveled through Xiliang and, in the second year of the Zongzhang era, appeared to convert the people in Luoyang, holding in his hand—

Yangzhi mingled with the ranks of the black-robed monks. Someone asked the Master what his surname was; he replied, "My surname is He. When asked what country he was from, he said, "I am from the land of He.

Subsequently, on the banks of the Si River, he wished to construct a monastery. Because the local resident of Suzhou, a member of the Heba clan, offered up his own dwelling, the Master said, "This was originally a Buddhist temple.
He ordered the ground to be excavated, and indeed an ancient stele was found which stated that it was the "Fragrant Accumulation" (Gandhakuṭī) Hall.
In the temple, he further obtained a golden image and said, "This is King Universal Radiance Buddha (Puguangwang Fo). Consequently, this was adopted as the name of the temple.
(Guiyou year) Wan-hui manifested himself in the royal palace.

Wan-hui was the son of the Zhang family of Wenxiang. From his youth, he lived with a carefree air, feigning madness, such that his fellow villagers could not fathom him. He had an elder brother, Wan...
For many years, he campaigned in Liaodong on the left. His mother, longing for news of him, asked, "How easy would that be? He then informed his mother that he was going; by evening he had returned.
When he brought back the letter, the neighbors were struck with wonder, and thus he was called "Wanhui" (Ten-Thousand Returns).
Wanhui was close with the śramaṇa Daming of Longxing Temple, frequently visiting his quarters. It happened that Ming Chongyan, an official of the Palace Remonstrance Bureau, passed by at night.

At the temple, he saw Huí surrounded on all sides by divine soldiers acting as his guard. Huí was greatly alarmed. One day, Huí ordered his family members to sweep and sprinkle the grounds, saying, "An eminent guest is coming.

On that very day, Xuánzàng returned from the Western Regions and visited Huí. Huí questioned him about the customs and landscapes of India, and [Xuánzàng’s] descriptions were exactly as he had seen them.
Xuánzàng prostrated himself, circumambulated him, and praised him as a Bodhisattva. In the fourth year of the Xiánhéng era, Emperor Gāozōng...
By imperial decree, he was admitted into the palace and ordained as a śramaṇa. At that time, there was a monk from Fufeng named Senghong who had previously been within the palace.
He used to say daily, "He will return, he will return. When Daohui finally returned, Hong said, "The replacement has arrived; it is time for me to go. Ten days later, Hong passed away.
(Jiaxu) Zhizhi of the Tiantai school resided at Xuanyuan Temple.

He was the son of the Jiang family of Jingyun. At the age of eighteen, he served as the head of the local academy. While returning home to take a wife, he encountered a foreign monk on the road who asked, "Young man, what is your intention?
Do you wish to violate the solemn vows of your past life? Thereupon, the monk revealed his former incarnation to him.

On behalf of Xu Ling, he personally made five vows before the Venerable Zhi (Zhiyi). Having heard the majestic reputation [of the Master], he no longer returned home but went directly to Tiantai, where he became a disciple of Zhang’an as his teacher.

He realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra. In the first year of the Shangyuan era, he flew through the air with his staff and reached Mount Xuan-yuan Lian-dan, where he eventually resided. Disciples flocked to him from all directions.
(Wuyi, the second year of the Shangyuan era): The Fifth Patriarch Hongren passed away.
In the second year of Shangyuan, Hongren suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now complete; it is time for me to depart. He then entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.
He was seventy-four years old. A stupa was erected for him on East Mountain at Huangmei.
(丙子) The Sixth Patriarch Huineng manifested his appearance in the world.
He returned south and lived in seclusion among a band of hunters at Sihui for fifteen years, occasionally associating with them.

He preached the Dharma according to what was appropriate. A hunter had him guard his nets, whereupon he would release living beings. One day, he suddenly thought, "The time has come for me to preach the Dharma. He then traveled to Faxing Monastery in Guangzhou.
On the eighth day of the first month in the first year of the Yifeng era, he encountered the monk Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At night, the wind blew and the banners fluttered; two monks engaged in debate over this, one saying it was the wind that moved, and the other saying it was the banner.

The wind was blowing. It continued to blow back and forth without ceasing. Huineng said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is the mind of the worthy one that moves. The entire assembly was struck with awe.
Mazu Zongyan invited him to the seat of honor and interrogated him on the profound meaning of the Dharma.

Seeing that Huineng’s words were concise and his principles correct, and that they did not rely on written texts, Mazu said, "I have long heard that the robe and Dharma of Huangmei have come southward; could you be the practitioner? He replied, "Yes. Mazu [said], "Indeed."

He then performed the rites of a disciple and requested his robe and bowl, presenting them to the great assembly. He asked again, "How did you receive the instructions regarding the entrustment at Huangmei?
He replied, "There were no specific instructions; we spoke only of seeing one's nature, not of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or liberation (*vimokṣa*.
He asked, "Why do you not speak of meditative concentration and liberation? He replied, "Because these two are dualistic dharmas; they are not the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha-dharma is non-duality."*

The Master said: "What is the non-dual dharma of the Buddha-dharma? He replied: "When a Dharma Master lectures on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and elucidates the Buddha-nature, this is the non-dual dharma of the Buddha-dharma.
For example, as when the noble King Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Even one who has committed the four grave offenses...'"
"If those who commit the five heinous crimes, as well as icchantikas and others, sever their roots of goodness, do they also sever their Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said: "There are two kinds of roots of goodness: first, the permanent; second, the impermanent. The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore, it is not severed."
This is called "non-duality. First is the wholesome; second is the unwholesome. Buddha-nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called non-duality.
As for the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*), ordinary people perceive them as two, but the wise understand that their nature is non-dual.
This nature of non-duality is itself Buddha-nature. Zongwen was filled with joy and, joining his palms, exclaimed: "The person who lectures on the sutras is like..."
Debris. "O Benevolent One, your discourse on the Dharma is like pure gold. Thereupon, he assembled those of renown and virtue, and they conferred upon him the tonsure and full ordination.
On the following day, Wei Ju, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, invited Huineng to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"All of you, with pure minds, recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. 'Mahā' means great. The capacity of the mind is vast and great, just like empty space."
It is empty. It has no boundaries; it is neither square nor round, neither large nor small. It is not blue, yellow, red, or white.
It has no up or down, no long or short. It is without anger and without joy; it is without right and without wrong, without good and without evil. It has neither beginning nor end.
The wondrous nature of worldly beings is fundamentally empty; not a single dharma can be apprehended. The self-nature of true emptiness is likewise so.
This self-nature is capable of containing all dharmas; it is the Great All-Dharmas existing within the persons of all people.
If one perceives the evil and the good of all people, yet neither grasps nor rejects them, and remains unstained by them, with a mind like space—this is called [the state of liberation].

It is great; therefore, it is called *mahā*. "Prajñā" means wisdom. To be free from delusion in every place and at all times, moment after moment, and to constantly practice wisdom—this is the practice of *prajñā*. A single thought of delusion severs *prajñā*;
a single thought of wisdom gives rise to *prajñā*. *Prajñā* has no form or appearance; the mind of wisdom is itself it. If one acts in this manner...

"Understanding" is precisely what is called *prajñā* (wisdom). As for "pāramitā," it means "reaching the other shore. The meaning of understanding is to be free from arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
When one is attached to objects, arising and ceasing occur, like waves upon water; these waves are then termed "this shore. When one is free from objects, there is no arising or ceasing;
like water constantly flowing through, this is termed the "other shore. Therefore, it is called *pāramitā*. Ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas; afflictions...
This is itself bodhi. The preceding thought in delusion is the ordinary person; the succeeding thought in awakening is the Buddha. The preceding thought attached to objects is affliction;
the succeeding thought detached from objects is bodhi. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is most honored, most supreme, and foremost.
It is without abiding, without going, and without coming. From within it, the Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge. Furthermore, it says: "If one wishes..."

Cultivation can be practiced even by those living at home; it does not depend on residing in a monastery. If one practices in reliance upon the signless (*animitta*), one is always dwelling with me without distinction.
If one does not practice in reliance upon the signless, what benefit is there for the Way, even if one has shaved one's head and left the household life? — Shenxiu.

When Huineng arrived at Baolin Monastery at Caoxi, he saw that the halls and buildings were cramped and insufficient to accommodate the assembly.
Wishing to expand them, he went to visit Chen Yaxian, a local resident, and requested a plot of land the size of a sitting mat as a donor. Yaxian...
The immortal replied, "Yes, indeed. I can spread my sitting mat once to cover the entire four borders of Caoxi.
The immortal fulfilled his vow and donated it to become a monastery; thus, thirteen *ārāmas* were established.
(Wuyin) Chan Master Zhiran entered nirvana. (The second patriarch of Niutou Mountain and successor to Farong.
Zhiran entrusted the True Dharma to Huifang and resided at both Baima and Qixuan Temples. He later moved to reside at Shitou City.
On a day in the first month of the third year of the Yifeng era, he passed away; his countenance did not change, and he could bend and stretch as if alive. Within his chamber...
A rare fragrance lingered for ten days without ceasing. His final instruction was to be buried in water. He was seventy-eight years of age and thirty-nine years of *lǎ* (seniority).

On the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Yonglong era, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture; a wondrous fragrance did not cease for seven days.
(Renwu) Biography of Chan Master Hui’an. Yuan-gui, to whom Hui’an transmitted the Dharma, was born into the Li clan of Ique.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and received full ordination during the Yongchun era. He was registered at Xianju Monastery and studied the Vinaya.
Upon visiting Hui’an, he attained sudden enlightenment into the profound essence of the teachings. He subsequently built a hermitage at Pangwu on Mount Song.
In the first year of the Yongchun era, Kuiji passed away. Kuiji was of robust and imposing appearance, standing eight chi tall; his spirit overwhelmed ten thousand men.

He possessed a jade pillow upon which his ten fingers left imprints with spiraling patterns like seals; those who saw him were struck with awe and submission. Nevertheless, his heart was kind and compassionate, and he instructed others through teaching.

In his later years, he prayed to be reborn in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven), observing the precepts with ever-increasing rigor. Initially, Daoxuan had propagated the Vinaya and experienced the descent of celestial cuisine.

(Cengxu) Chan Master Huifang Returns to Maoshan (Third Generation of the Oxhead School, Dharma Heir of Zhiyan).
Huifang was the son of the Pu clan from Runzhou. Having left the household life and received full ordination, he thoroughly mastered the sutras and śāstras. Later, he entered Mount Niutou.
He went to visit Zhiyan, who showed him the method of the Mind-Seal (cinyin). He attained sudden and thorough enlightenment.

Thereafter, he did not leave the forest retreats for more than ten years, during which time scholars from all quarters gathered like clouds. One day, he said to the assembly, "I wish to travel elsewhere to benefit sentient beings according to their capacities;
you should remain at peace. He then entrusted the True Dharma to Fahchi, who subsequently returned to Maoshan.
(Dinghai) Chan Master Huairang’s Ordination:
Huairang was the son of the Du family from Jinzhou. He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Guiyou year of the Xianheng era.

Six tracks of white vapor were perceived piercing the heavens, and the Grand Astrologer reported this to the Emperor. Gaozong asked, "What auspicious omen is this? He replied, "A Dharma-treasure for the nation."
Unstained by worldly glory, Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, also submitted a memorial. The Emperor issued an edict ordering Jie to personally visit and offer condolences to his family.
Among the three sons, Rangju was the youngest; his nature was characterized solely by kindness and yielding, hence he was named Huairang.

In the third year of the Chuigong era, at the age of fifteen, he once silently observed still water. Looking at his reflection, his physical form appeared dignified, as if perfectly present within a mirror.
Three times he manifested such signs as when he first awakened his mind; he alone attained the method. As he was returning, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying:

"The bridge and raft of the Buddha-dharma awaits you to make it great. Since you have been entrusted with this mandate, you must exert yourself. Thereupon, he took leave of his parents and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu to renounce the household life.
(17th year of Renchen) Chan Master Renjian preached the Dharma in the royal palace. (A collateral line descending from Wuzu, the successor of Hui’an. Renjian was none other than Master Teng-teng.
In the fourth month of the Renchen year, Empress Wu issued an imperial decree inviting him into the palace.

Renjian gazed at the Empress Dowager for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? She replied, "I do not understand. He said, "This old monk observes the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed.

He presented nineteen short poems (*ge*), one of which said: "In the Way of cultivation, there is no Way to cultivate; In the Dharma of inquiry, there is no Dharma to inquire about. The deluded person does not understand that form is emptiness;

The awakened one fundamentally knows there is neither opposition nor compliance. Of the eighty-four thousand gates of Dharma, The ultimate principle is not separate from the square inch of the heart-mind.
Recognize the city and prefecture of your own house; Do not vainly seek other provinces and districts. There is no need for extensive learning."
Much learning does not require eloquence or brilliance; one need not know the length of the months, nor concern oneself with the intercalary days of the year.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; pure flowers grow from mud and filth. When people come to ask me how it is, I am unable to engage them in discourse.
At dawn, I satisfy my hunger with congee; at the time of the midday meal, I eat another portion. Today, I proceed according to the natural flow.
Vigorous! Tomorrow, remain vigorous and spontaneous; with the mind clearly aware of all things, simply act as if feigning ignorance and dullness.

Yan. Zang attended Yan for a long time and fully mastered his teachings. After Yan passed away, Zang preached the Dharma wearing a headcloth and cap. Empress Wu granted him the tonsure and ordained him as a monk.

In the year Yiwu (695), she issued an edict for Zang to expound upon the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Just as he was about to introduce the title of the scripture, a brilliant white light shone forth.
It issued from his mouth and, in an instant, formed a canopy suspended in the air. Later, the Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title "Worthy Head" (Xianshou).
