"Is it simply this state of being undefiled that is what all Buddhas protect and keep in mind? Since you are thus, I am also thus."
"From this day forward, the Buddha-dharma shall proceed from you. In India, Prajñātāra prophesied of you: 'A colt shall emerge from beneath your feet and trample the people of the world to death.
This must reside within your own mind; there is no need to speak of it hastily. Upon hearing this, Huo suddenly attained great enlightenment.

(Xin-chou) When the Venerable Fazang lectured on the new translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Empress Wu issued an edict for Fazang to lecture on the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Foshouji Temple. The earth shook violently, and it subsided only after some time had passed.
That same day, he was summoned to the Changsheng Hall, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the ten layers of profound gates of the Imperial Net (*diwang*). Fazang expounded upon them.
There was a thread [of connection]; the profound purport was thoroughly integrated. When the Empress heard this, she was struck with wonder.

Zang pointed to the golden lion in the corner of the hall to provide an illustration for Xiaoxiao, leading her from the lion at the tip of a single hair to the lions at the tips of ten billion hairs. Thereupon, the Empress attained sudden enlightenment and her practice and contemplation became clear.
The son of the Liu family of Jizhou left home to become a monk at a young age. Whenever he sat in a group discussing the Way, he would remain silent in contemplation.

Later, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch and asked, "What should I devote myself to so as not to fall into stages? The Master replied, "What have you been doing? He said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths.
The Master asked, "Then in what stage do you fall? He replied, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stage could there be?"

The Patriarch [Nanyue Huairang] held him in high esteem and appointed him as the head of the assembly. Xuánjué (Huineng), whose secular surname was Dài, was a native of Yǒngjiā. From his youth, he possessed innate understanding; his learning required no further reflection.
He entered the monastic order at an early age and became widely versed in the Tripiṭaka. He specialized in the Tiantai teachings on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
While reading the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he attained enlightenment regarding the nature of the mind. Later, he met Zuòxī who exhorted him to join Xuánce in studying under the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch [Nanyue Huairang] first arrived, shaking his staff and circumambulating the Patriarch [Mañjuśrī] three times, then standing upright.
The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is endowed with three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Virtue, from where have you come, giving rise to such great arrogance?

He replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, "Why do you not realize the state of no-birth, which is beyond swiftness? He replied, "I realize it..."
"It is precisely non-arising. Jiao said, "To realize that it is fundamentally non-existent is swift. Mazu replied, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the great assembly was not without astonishment.
Jiao then assumed his proper dignified demeanor and prostrated himself; after a short while, he took his leave. Mazu said, "Is your return too swift?

Jiao replied, "Since it is fundamentally motionless from the start, how could there be swiftness? Mazu asked, "Who knows it is not moving? Jiao replied, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to such discrimination. Mazu said, "As for you—"
He had profoundly grasped the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). [The Master] asked, "Does 'non-arising' have any intention? He replied, "If there is no intention, who would be able to discern?
[The Master] said, "Discernment, too, is not intention. He replied, "Excellent! Please stay for one night. Because of this, he was called "Awakened in One Night" (*Ekāgrarātra-bodhi*).
(Nényin) Chan Master Fachih of Niushan entered nirvana. (Huimengfa was the successor of the fourth generation of Niutou.
Fachih entrusted the mountain gate to Zhiwei. On a day in the ninth month of Nényin, he passed away.

His final instructions were that his remains be exposed beneath the pines to feed the birds and beasts, and that his body be carried out into the sky at sunrise. A divine banner came from the west and circled the mountain several times.
The bamboo grove surrounding his former residence turned white and remained so for seven days.

(Yisi) The Sixth Patriarch Huineng was preaching the Dharma while Shenxiu had previously memorialized Empress Wu, requesting that Huineng be invited to the imperial court. Huineng firmly declined. Shenxiu then composed a letter himself to urge him once more.
He was invited. Huineng said to the messenger, "My appearance is short and unrefined; if those of this land were to see me, I fear they would not respect my Dharma.

Furthermore, my late master stated that I have a karmic affinity with the South, and I cannot go against that. In the first year of the Shenglong era, Emperor Zhongzong again dispatched the envoy Xue Jian to welcome Huineng.
Huineng declined on the grounds of illness, wishing to spend his final years at the foot of the forested hills. Xue Jian replied, "The virtuous Chan masters of the capital city..."

Everyone said, "If one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice dhyāna and cultivate meditative concentration. Hui Neng replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'To say that the Tathāgata sits or lies down is to walk a deviant path. Why is this so? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
there is neither birth nor extinction—this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. All dharmas are empty and quiescent."
"This is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting; it is ultimately without realization, let alone 'sitting. [The Master] said:
'I pray that you, O Teacher, out of compassion, will point out the essentials of the mind so they may be presented to the two palaces. It is like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps;

those in darkness all become bright, and this brightness is inexhaustible. [The Master] said: 'The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of succession. That brightness is inexhaustible is also..."
"This has an end. [The Master] said: "Light is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means can one transcend birth and death? [The disciple] asked: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi.
If one uses wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, this is the view of the Two Vehicles. Those of superior wisdom and great capacity do not act in this way. If you wish..."

Know the essential point: simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever, and you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Having been briefly instructed, I suddenly attained awakening.
(Bingwu) Chan Master Shenxiu Enters Nirvana (A Dharma Heir of the Fifth Patriarch Huineng). Shenxiu resided in the Eastern Capital.
The world hailed him as the "Dharma Lord of the Two Capitals and the Preceptor at the Gates of Three Emperors.

On a day in the second month of the second year of the Shenglong era, he entered nirvana. His posthumous title was Datong. Born at the end of the Sui dynasty, he lived for over one hundred years. He never... [ever claimed to have attained realization].
Thus it was said; therefore, no one knew his number. Pujì was the son of the Mã family of Hedōn. He served Shénxiù as his teacher for six years.
Shénxiù marveled at him and transmitted the Way to him in its entirety. When Shénxiù entered *nirvāṇa*, students vied with one another to serve Jì as their teacher.
Zhìwēi was the son of the Chén family of Jiāngníng. At the age of four, he already desired to leave the household life. One day, he suddenly disappeared from his home; no one—
He knew where [his parents] had gone. When his parents went to search for him, they learned that he had already left home to become a monk.

Later, hearing that Fahai was propagating the world-transcending Dharma, he went to pay his respects and received the transmission of the True Dharma. A monk named Huizhong arrived at the mountain; as soon as Wei saw him, he said, "The master of the mountain has come.

Huizhong once went out to visit the monastery, where he noticed a *lingxiao* vine growing through the courtyard that had withered completely during the height of summer. His attendants wished to cut it down.
Dawe said, "It must not be so. Once Zhong returns, [the tree] will surely flourish again. When Zhong returned, it was indeed as predicted. One day, Dawe showed him a verse, saying:
"Do not bind yourself with thoughts; they form the river of birth and death. You circle through the sea of the six realms, seeing no way out from these long waves.
Zhong said: "Thoughts and perceptions have always been illusions; the nature itself has no beginning or end. If one grasps this meaning within, the long waves shall [subside]."
Zizhi stopped. Weiyi further showed him a verse, saying: "My original nature is void and non-existent; through delusive conditions, the notions of self and other arise.
How can one still these delusive emotions? Return to sit in the place of emptiness. Zhong said: "If voidness and non-existence are the true reality, why must there be self and other?
There is no need to still delusive emotions; one simply boards the boat of Prajñā. Weiyi, knowing that he had attained realization, then entrusted him with the mountain gate.
Shenhui was the son of the Gao family of Xiangyang. At the age of fourteen, he became a śrāmaṇera and went to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch.

The Patriarch said, "My good friend, you have come from afar with great hardship; have you brought your original nature with you? If you possess this original nature, you ought to recognize its master. Try to explain it to me."
[The Master] said, "Take non-abiding as the foundation. To see is itself the master. [The monk] said, "How can this śrāmaṇera speak so casually?
[The Master] asked, "When you, Preceptor, sit in meditation, do you see or not? The Patriarch struck him three times with his staff and said, "When I strike you, is it painful or not?
[The monk] replied, "It is both painful and not painful. [The Master] said, "I also both see and do not see. Huì asked, "What is..."
"Both seeing and not seeing. He said, "That which I see is that I constantly observe my own faults and transgressions, while I do not observe the right or wrong, the good or bad, of others.
For this reason, it is both seeing and not seeing. As for your statement, 'both painful and not painful':
if you were not in pain, you would be the same as wood or stone; if you were in pain, you would be the same as an ordinary person who immediately gives rise to resentment. You previously saw..."
He did not perceive these two extremes; that which is painful or not painful is birth and cessation. You have not even seen your own nature, yet you dare to mock others.
Huihui prostrated himself. One day, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a thing that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no face.
Do you all recognize it? Huihui stepped forward and said, "It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas."
Regarding Shenhui’s view of Buddha-nature, [the Master] said: "I told you that it has no name and no character; yet you immediately call it 'original source Buddha-nature.
In the future, even if you have a thatched roof over your head, you will merely become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding."
(Dingwei) Chan Master Yuangui Preaches the Dharma for the Spirit of Songshan (A collateral line descending from Wuzu, successor to Hui’an).
Yuangui resided at Mount Song. During the Jinglong era, a divine being led a multitude of followers to visit him.
Observing that his appearance was extraordinary, Yuangui said, "Welcome, O benevolent one; for what purpose have you come? [The spirit] replied, "Do you not recognize me, Master?"
He said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye—how could I make such distinctions? The spirit replied, "I am a mountain deity of this peak.
I can bring people to life or kill them. How can you, Master, view me with a single eye? The Master said, "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you kill me?
I view my body as equal to empty space, and I view myself as equal to you. Can you destroy empty space or yourself?"
"If you were truly able to do so, I would be neither born nor extinguished. How much less could you, being unable to do so, cause me to undergo birth and death?
The spirit bowed his head and said, "I am also intelligent and more upright than other spirits; how could I have known that you, Master, possess such vast wisdom and eloquence?
I pray that you will bestow upon me the rules of the True Precepts, so that I may cross over the world. [The Master] said, "You shall receive the request for the precepts. Thus it was done.
"Observe the precepts! Why is this so? Because there is no precept outside of the precepts themselves; what further precept could there be? He said, "This is the principle.

What I have heard is obscure and vast; I seek only the Master’s instruction on the precepts. As a disciple, I [the author] immediately prepared a seat, took up the incense burner, and set the desk upright, saying:
"I confer upon you the Five Precepts. If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'No'. He replied, "I shall do so with utmost care."
He received the instruction. [The Master] asked, "Are you able to refrain from sexual misconduct? He replied, "I am married. [The Master] said, "That is not what I mean.
I mean that you must have no lustful desire. He replied, "I can. [The Master] asked, "Are you able to refrain from stealing? He replied, "What lack do I have? How could I ever steal anything?"
[The Master] said: "I do not mean this. I mean that blessings follow the licentious when they offer feasts, while calamities befall the virtuous when they fail to provide offerings.
[The Official] said: "I can. [The Master] said: "Can you refrain from killing? [The Official] said: "I truly hold the authority over it; how could I refrain from killing?

[The Master] said: "I do not mean this. I mean that there may be excesses, errors, doubts, or confusions. [The Official] said: "I can. [The Master] said: "Can you refrain from being arbitrary? [The Official] said: "I am upright and honest; how could I be arbitrary?"

He said, "I do not mean this. I mean that their actions before and after do not accord with the Will of Heaven. [The other] said, "I can. He asked, "Have you never been ruined by wine? [He] said, "I can.
He said, "As described above, these constitute the Buddha’s precepts. Furthermore, he said: 'Maintain them with a conscious mind, yet remain free from the attachment of a clinging mind;
act for the sake of others with a conscious mind, yet remain free from thoughts of one's own body. If one can be thus, one precedes Heaven."
Born from the earth, it does not become vital essence; when heaven and earth perish later, it does not become old age.
Throughout the day it undergoes transformation without becoming movement; it reaches ultimate stillness and silence without becoming cessation or awakening.

This is to marry without being a wife, to feast without taking, to hold the handle without wielding power, to act without artifice, and to be intoxicated without being muddled. If one can thus be without mind—

Regarding all things: not harboring desire is non-lust; not seeking blessings for the licentious or bringing calamity upon the virtuous is non-theft; not being reckless, erring, suspicious, or confused is non-killing;

not violating the Way of Heaven through prior or subsequent acts is non-falsehood; and not being muddled, deluded, or inverted is non-intoxication. This is called "no-mind. Where there is no mind, there is no separate precept;
where there is no precept, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor [me].
"There is no self. Who, then, would observe the precepts? He replied, "My supernatural powers are second only to the Buddha's. [The Buddha] said, "Your supernatural powers consist of ten items:

five abilities and five incapacities. The Buddha’s, however, consists of ten items: seven abilities and three incapacities. Shen [the deity] was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat; kneeling, he addressed him, saying:
"May I hear it? [The Buddha] said: "Can you cause the Supreme Deity (Shangdi) to turn back, making the eastern heavens travel westward while the seven luminaries move eastward?
He replied: "I cannot. [The Buddha] said: "Can you seize the Earth-Spirit (Diqu), melting the Five Sacred Peaks and binding the Four Seas?

He replied: "I cannot. [The Buddha] said: "These are called the five impossibilities. The Buddha can empty all phenomena (lakṣaṇa) and realize the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish [suffering]."

Fixed karma. The Buddha can know the natures of all beings and exhaustively understand events across billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform or guide those who lack the necessary conditions (*apratyaya*).

The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*). These are called the three "incapacities. Furthermore, fixed karma is not eternal;
the lack of conditions is likewise but a single occasion; and the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease. Moreover, there is no...
"One person can preside over the Dharma; yet there is a Dharma that has no presider—this is called the 'Dharma-less. That which is Dharma-less and without a presider is called 'mindlessness.
As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, there is likewise no supernatural power (*abhijñā*). It is simply by means of mindlessness that one penetrates all dharmas as they truly are.
He said, "I am indeed shallow and ignorant, and have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The precepts bestowed upon me by the Master, I shall faithfully practice. Now..."
"I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by manifesting what I am capable of. [The Master] said, "I observe that my body is nothing and that all phenomena are impermanent;

being but a lump of flesh, what further desire could I have? [The monk] said, "Master, you must surely command me to perform a worldly task so that I may display a small measure of my spiritual power, causing those among the five classes of people—those who have already resolved for enlightenment, those who have first resolved, those who have not yet resolved, those who do not believe, and those who will certainly come to believe—to behold my divine efficacy with their own eyes."
I know that there are Buddhas and spirits; there is that which can and that which cannot; there is the spontaneous and that which is not spontaneous.

It is said that non-action (*wuwei*) is right, and it is said that the Buddha also employs spirits to protect the Dharma. "Master, I pray you will deign to instruct me as you wish. Guī, having no choice, spoke:
"The landscape surrounding Dongyan Temple is vast and treeless. While there are trees on the northern peak, its slope does not form a protective screen behind the temple."
"Can you move the tree from the north to the eastern ridge? He replied, "I have received your command. However, there will surely be much commotion during the night;

I hope the Master will not be alarmed. He then prostrated himself and departed. Dao-gui saw him off at the gate and observed that his ceremonial retinue was drawn out in long procession, appearing like a sovereign.
That evening, indeed, a violent wind arose with thundering peals of lightning, and the buildings shook and swayed. At dawn, the weather cleared and brightened. Then—
The pines and cypresses of the northern crags were all moved to the eastern ridge, where they stood in dense rows. Guī cautioned his disciples, saying, "Do not let outsiders know;
people will regard me as a sorcerer. Huì'ān took his leave from within the palace and returned to Mount Song.
One day, he suddenly instructed his gatekeepers, saying, "When I die, place my corpse in the forest and wait for a wild fire to consume it. On the eighth day of the seventh month, [the time arrived].
Hù Yǎn passed away in silence at the age of one hundred and twenty-eight. His disciples carried his remains to the forest, where a wild fire spontaneously broke out to cremate them.
Eighty *śarīra* relics were obtained; five of these were exceptionally large and purple-red in color, their radiance dazzling to the eye.
As for Pòzào Duò, his name and lineage are not recorded. Having attained the Dharma through Huì'ān, he lived in seclusion on Mount Sōng. At the mountain...

The wu had a temple that was extremely efficacious. In the hall there was only a single hearth, yet offerings were made from near and far without ceasing, and the slaughter of living beings for cooking was immense.
One day, Huo led his disciples into the temple, struck the hearth three times with his staff, and said: "Tsk! You hearth!"
"It is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the 'sage' come? From where does the 'spirit' arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings.
He struck three more blows, and the hearth collapsed and fell apart. In a moment, a person appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap;

bowing before the fallen ruins, he said, "I am originally the hearth god of this temple. Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have been fortunate enough to hear the Master preach the Dharma of Emptiness."

"A being born by way of dharma has attained liberation from this place and been reborn among the devas; he has come specifically to express his gratitude. The deity said, "This is your own inherent nature;
it is not my forced words. The spirit bowed twice and vanished. After a short while, the attendant monks asked, "We have long served the Master, yet we have not received any instruction.
By what path or principle did the hearth-deity obtain such that he was able to be reborn in heaven? He replied, "I simply..."
He said to him, "This is merely composed of clay and tiles; there is no other principle. Because the attendant monk remained silent, [Zhaozhou] said, "Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not understand. [Zhaozhou] asked, "Why do you not understand the nature that is originally present? Thereupon, the attendant monk prostrated himself.

A monk asked, "When every single thing is formless, what then? Baizhang Huaiye said, "If you pay homage, it is only you and not me;
if you do not pay homage, it is only me and not you. The monk then bowed in thanks. Huaiye said, "The thing that is originally present is not a thing.

Spiritual illumination shines within this interval; the myriad phenomena manifest spontaneously through their profound essence. Since object and wisdom are not one, who can speak of coming and going?
How sublime these words! Thereupon, I closed the volume and fell asleep unconsciously. In a dream, I traveled with the Sixth Patriarch, riding upon a single tortoise as we swam within a deep pool.
Upon waking, I reflected: "The spiritual tortoise is wisdom; the deep pool is the ocean of nature."
I and the Patriarch ride together upon the numinous wisdom and roam the ocean of nature. Thus, I have composed the *Cantong qi* (The Mysterious Agreement), which says:

All objects—whether they interact or do not interact; whether they interpenetrate one another or abide according to their respective positions. Form is fundamentally distinct in its substance and appearance;

There is merit in its own right; one should speak of it when it comes to its actual application. In matters, there is the meeting of lid and box; in principle, there should be the meeting of arrow-points.

When receiving words, you must grasp the essence; do not establish your own rules. If you do not realize the Way upon encountering it before your eyes, how can you know the path as you set foot forward?
Advancing is neither far nor near, yet delusion makes mountains and rivers impassable. I respectfully address those who study the profound mystery: do not let your time pass in vain. — Guangde.

(Bingwu) Chan Master Wuzhu preached the Dharma of Non-Abiding for Du Hongjian.

A crow was cawing in the trees of the courtyard. [The Master] asked, "Did you hear it? He replied, "I heard it. After the crow had gone, he asked again, "Did you hear it? He replied, "I heard it.

○ Mazu Daoyi opened the Dharma at Zhongling.
Mazu was registered as a monk at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling. Lu Sijing, the regional commander, heard of his reputation and admired him; he personally received [the teachings].
The Essential Purpose: Scholars from the four quarters gathered like clouds beneath his seat. He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha;

this very mind is the Buddha-mind. The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle—the single mind—to cause you all to attain awakening. Furthermore, he cited passages from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to...

This seals the ground of the minds of sentient beings. Fearing that you might fall into delusion, [I teach that] you must have confidence that this Dharma of the mind exists within each and every one of you.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core principle and "no-gate" as its Dharma-gate. Now, one who seeks the Dharma should have nothing to seek.
Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not reject evil—this is purity.
Defile both sides; neither can be relied upon. Realize that the nature of offenses is empty, for from moment to moment they cannot be apprehended, as they lack intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the three realms are but mind. The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by this single Dharma. Whatever forms you perceive are all perceptions of the mind.
Mind does not exist as mind of itself; it exists because of form. You need only speak according to the occasion, such that the phenomenon and the principle are one.
There is nothing whatsoever that obstructs it. The fruit of the path to Bodhi is likewise: that which arises within the mind is immediately termed "form" (rūpa).
Because one knows that form is empty, arising is itself non-arising. If one realizes this mind, then one may, according to the occasion, put on clothes and eat food.
Nurturing the noble embryo, one passes the time spontaneously; what further matter is there? You have received my instruction; listen to this verse of mine:

"The ground of the mind is explained according to the occasion; awakening (*bodhi*) is likewise only peace. When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, that which arises is precisely non-arising."
A monk asked, "How does one cultivate the Way? He replied, "The Way does not belong to cultivation. If you say it is attained through cultivation, then once cultivated, it will again perish;

A single thought of delusion is the very root of birth and death within the triple world. If you simply have no such single thought, you eliminate the root of birth and death."

He was the son of the Wang family in Zhengzhou. From childhood, he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). He left the household life and received full ordination. Initially, he studied the Xiangbu school and investigated the *Vinaya*.

One day, while serving rice gruel to the assembly of monks, the Patriarch asked, "What is that in the bucket? He replied, "Old man, shut your mouth and stop talking like this! Thereupon, the Patriarch ceased questioning.

It was like treading upon a steep mountain path; the assembly of monastics looked at one another, none daring to step forward.
At that time, the śramaṇa Chonghui of Zhangjing Temple received an imperial decree to place a ladder of sharp blades—gleaming white as frost—among the trees in the courtyard of his own temple.

He increased the height of the Eastern Ming Pavilion’s hundred-foot ladder by this means. Chonghui ascended barefoot, stopping only when he reached the end of the ladder, and then descended again, as if walking on level ground.

On level ground, he proceeded to tread upon blazing fire, plunge into boiling oil, eat iron leaves, and chew iron nails and wire. When the monastic community witnessed this, they fled in terror, their sweat pouring down as they covered their faces with their sleeves.

The fourfold assembly praised and looked up to him, their voices like thunder and lightning. The Emperor dispatched an imperial eunuch to deliver a proclamation of consolation and reward, sighing in admiration more than twice.

He was granted purple robes and bestowed with the title "Tripitaka Master for the Protection of the Nation. Soon thereafter, he was summoned to appear before the Emperor for an audience and interrogation.
"Whom do you follow as your teacher? He replied, "The monk Fachin of Mount Jing is my teacher. As I have not yet received full ordination, I dare not accept the imperial gift of purple robes.
The Emperor specially ordered the ordination platform to be established; just as the *karmavācanā* was being performed, Huiyi manifested his body upon the altar.

Not knowing where he had gone, the Emperor was increasingly struck with wonder and awe. He subsequently honored Qin as his teacher and dispatched an inner attendant with a special imperial edict to respectfully invite him.

Upon his arrival, the Emperor personally went out to meet him and inquired about the Dharma, treating him with the etiquette due to a disciple. One day, while in the inner court, Qin saw the Emperor rise to his feet;
the Emperor asked, "Why have you risen, Master? Qin replied, "How can a *dānapati* (donor) look upon [a monk] within the context of the four dignified postures (*catur-īryāpatha*)?"
"I am but a poor monk. The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the title Guoyi (National One). Shortly thereafter, he wished to take his leave and return home.

The Emperor said, "If there are sentient beings here who are to be saved, how could those sentient beings elsewhere be any different? Zhiqin replied, "In truth, there is no dharma by which to save sentient beings.
At first, Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou. Once, while eating in the monks' hall, he beheld five-colored clouds within his alms bowl.
Within one of these Brahma-realms, to the northeast, there was a mountain ravine with a stone gate. There he again saw a monastery; its plaque was inscribed in golden letters:

"The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery" (Dàshèng Zhúlín Sì). On another day, he again saw several monasteries amidst the clouds, with ponds, terraces, and towers, where tens of thousands of bodhisattvas dwelt together.
In the third year of the Dali era, he established a five-assembly *nianfo* practice hall, which moved the heavens to manifest auspicious clouds.
It spread everywhere, covering all. Within the clouds, a multi-storied pavilion appeared, and he beheld Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, their bodies filling the void.
He further saw an old man who said to him, "You previously made a vow to pay homage to the Great Sangha in the Golden World; why do you now stop so abruptly?
Thereupon, together with his companions, he set out on his journey. In the fourth month of the fourth year, he arrived at Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai. (1)
Just as he had seen in the bowl, during the fourth watch of the night, he saw a beam of light descending from the northern mountain, shining and illuminating everything.
It suddenly entered the hall. He asked the assembly, "What auspicious light is this? A monk replied, "This is the inconceivable light of a Great Sage.
The Master then followed the light to the temple; five li to the northeast, there was indeed a great mountain. On the mountain was a ravine, and to the north of the ravine—
There was a stone gate where two youths dressed in blue stood at its entrance; one was named Sudhana and the other Nanda.
They led him through the gate, and traveling north, he saw a golden gate and a multi-storied pavilion. A golden plaque inscribed the name "Great Sage Zhulin Monastery.
The monastery was twenty *li* square and contained one hundred courtyards, each featuring golden grounds, jeweled stupas, flowered altars, and jade trees. He entered the lecture hall and saw—
Mañjuśrī was in the west and Samantabhadra was in the east; seated upon lion thrones, they preached the Dharma for the assembly.
Zhao bowed before them and asked, "As for ordinary beings in the final age, I do not yet know what dharma-gate they should cultivate. Mañjuśrī replied, "Regarding all gates of cultivation..."
"There is nothing like the recitation of the Buddha's name. The vow-power of Amitābha Buddha is inconceivable; you should fix your mindfulness upon it and resolutely seek rebirth there.
At that time, the two great beings both extended their golden arms, rubbed the crown of Zhao’s head, and conferred this prediction:

"By the power of your recitation of the Buddha's name, you shall ultimately realize unsurpassed enlightenment. They then commanded him to go to the various courtyards of the bodhisattvas. Having completed his circumambulation and worship, he returned.

Having paid his respects and taken leave, he was escorted to the gate by two green-clad attendants. As Zhao bowed once more, when he raised his head, both [the attendants] had vanished. Huizhong resided at Niutou.
Throughout his life, he never changed his single patched robe, and his only utensil was a single cauldron.

When County Magistrate Zhang Xun visited Huizhong and asked, "How many disciples do you have? Huizhong replied, "There are three or five. The Magistrate asked, "May I see them? Huizhong struck his meditation seat with his staff.
Three times he descended from his bed, and three tigers emerged, roaring. Xun retreated in terror. Later, the assembly requested that he enter the city, where he resided at Zangyan Temple.
To the east of the main hall, he separately established a Dharma Hall. There was previously an ancient tree upon which a colony of magpies had nested.
The workmen were about to fell it when Dōshō said, "A hall is to be built on this site; why do you not depart at once?
As soon as he finished speaking, the flock of magpies moved their nests to another tree. From then on, disciples gathered like clouds, and thirty-four attained the Dharma.

There is a verse on the Settled Mind (*anshin*) that says: "When both person and phenomena are purified, good and evil are forgotten; with a direct mind of true reality, this is the Bodhi-maṇḍala. Great!
In the third year of the calendar [era], a cauldron-hanging tree and a robe-hanging vine stood before the stone chamber; though it was the height of summer, they suddenly withered and died.

On a day in the sixth month of the fourth year, after the assembly of monks had completed the *poṣadha*, he ordered his attendant to shave his hair and bathe his body. That night, auspicious clouds appeared.

He covered his vihāra, and from the air, the sound of celestial music was again heard. At dawn, he sat peacefully and passed away. Suddenly, wind and rain burst forth, shaking and breaking the trees and forests.
Furthermore, a white rainbow pierced through the cliffs and valleys. When his body was cremated, the śarīras were beyond counting.
He was eighty-seven years old. Dolín was the son of the Pán family of Fuyáng. His mother dreamed that she had swallowed a ray of sunlight and [conceived him].

When she was pregnant, a wondrous fragrance filled the room at the time of her birth; thus, she was named Xiangguang (Fragrant Light). At the age of nine, she left home to become a nun, and at twenty-one, she received full ordination.
Later, she went to Chang’an to study under Master Fuli, where she studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*.

Fuli showed her the "Verses on Reality and Delusion" and instructed her to practice *dhyāna*. Lin asked: "How should one first contemplate? How should one apply the mind? Fuli [remained silent] for a long while without answering.
He said, "Lín then performed three prostrations and withdrew. It happened that Fǎqīn arrived at the palace; Lín went to pay his respects and thereby obtained the True Dharma.
(Gēngxū) When Meditation Master Fǎqīn returned to Jìngshān, he had resided in the capital for barely one year.
Every time Emperor Dàizōng bestowed upon him silks and brocades or provided imperial meals, [Fǎqīn] would not accept them.
As for his sustenance, he wore only plain clothes and ate simple vegetables; his utensils were made of clay and gourds, as if he were in ordinary times.

When the Chancellor Yang Wan saw him, he sighed and said, "This is a transcendent gentleman beyond the mundane world; it is difficult to find one worthy of such a name. Duke Cui Zhaoqun once questioned [Daoyi] Qin.
The disciples asked, "Is it possible for us to leave the household life [to become monks]? Qian replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

how could it be something that high officials or generals can achieve? The group sighed in admiration of these words. Shortly thereafter, he declined their requests with firm resolve and returned south to his former mountain retreat.

Later, the Tripitaka Master "Large-Ears" from the Western Regions arrived at the capital, claiming to have attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others. Emperor Daizong ordered him to test this against Huizhong. As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw Huizhong, [he realized the master’s state of mind].
He immediately prostrated and stood to the right. Zhong asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds?
He replied, "I dare not say so. Zhong said, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? He replied, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation;
how could he have gone to Xichuan to watch the boat races? After a long silence, Zhong asked again, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? He replied, "The Mas..."
"I am still the teacher of an entire nation. How can you be here on Tianjin Bridge, watching a monkey performance?
After a long silence, he asked again, "Where do you say the old monk is right now? Zang was at a loss. Zhong rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit!
Where is your *abhijñā* (supernormal power) of knowing others' minds? One day, Imperial Attendant Zilin came to visit. Zhong asked, "Where have you come from?"
[Zhong] said, "From where have you come? [The monk] replied, "From south of the city. [Zhong] asked, "What color is the grass south of the city? [The monk] replied, "It is yellow.

Zhong then asked the attendant boy, "What color is the grass south of the city? [The boy] replied, "It is yellow. Zhong said, "This very boy may also be granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and discourse on the profound mysteries in the presence of the Emperor.
Furthermore, he serves as an attendant who annotates the *Siyi jing* (Saṃghāṭa-sūtra). Zhong continued, "In annotating a sūtra, one must first understand it."
Fayan thought he had finally grasped the Buddha’s intent, but Fayan said, "You have not understood the Buddha’s intent; why do you strive to compose commentaries on the sutras?

Zhong then ordered his attendant to fill a bowl with water, place seven grains of rice in it, and set a single chopstick across the top of the bowl. He asked the official, "What is the meaning of this?
The official was speechless. Zhong said, "If I, an old monk, cannot even understand my own intent, how much less can you understand the Buddha’s intent?"
○ Mazu Daoyi transmitted the Dharma to Daowu.
Daowu was the son of the Cui family from Zhugong; he left home at the age of fifteen and received full ordination at twenty-three.

At thirty-three, he went to attend upon Xiqian, receiving frequent instructions, yet he had not yet attained the point of resonance. Subsequently, at the age of thirty-four, he visited Huizhong. Together with...
The attendant Zhong Yingzhen returned south to visit Daoyi. Daoyi said, "The self-mind that you recognize is originally the Buddha;

it does not belong to gradual stages, nor does it require cultivation. Its essence is spontaneously suchness, and its myriad virtues are complete. Upon hearing these words, Zhong attained great enlightenment.
Daoyi instructed him, saying, "If you take up the position of abbot, do not leave your former location. Having received this prediction of his future realization, Zhong returned to Jingzhou.
The prefecture was not far from the city walls; he constructed a thatched hut there.
(Xin-hai) Tianran went to seek the Way under Mazu.
Tianran had originally practiced the Confucian arts and was about to enter Chang’an to take the imperial examinations when he stayed overnight at an inn. Suddenly, he dreamed of a white light.

The room was filled with people. A diviner said, "This is an auspicious sign of understanding emptiness. A Chan practitioner happened to ask, "Where are you going, virtuous one? He replied, "I am going to take the official examinations.
The Chan practitioner asked, "How does taking the official examinations compare to selecting a Buddha? He asked, "If one were to select a Buddha, where would one go? The Chan practitioner replied:
"Now, the Great Master Ma has appeared in Jiangxi; it is a field for selecting Buddhas. You, O virtuous one, may go there. He then traveled to Jiangxi.
As soon as he saw Mazu, he placed his hand upon the front of Mazu’s head-wrap. Mazu looked at him for a long while and said, "Nanyue Shitou is your teacher.
He then went to Shitou and again placed his hand on the front of Shitou’s head-wrap. Shitou said, "Go to the fodder shed."
He departed. Having paid his respects, he entered the quarters of the practitioners and served as a cook according to his turn for three years.

One day, the Head (the Abbot) addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, you shall clear the weeds before the Buddha Hall. On the following day, the members of the community each prepared spades and mattocks to clear the weeds;
however, [Zhaozhou] alone took a basin of water, knelt before the Head, and remained there. The Head laughed and proceeded to shave his hair. Furthermore, for him...
While he was reciting the precepts, [the old man] covered his ears and departed. He went again to Jiangxi, where on the road he encountered an old man with a young boy.
The old man asked, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "Above is heaven; below is earth. The old man said, "What if suddenly heaven collapses and the earth opens up?"
"Furthermore, how is it? he asked. Danxia replied, "Heaven! Heaven! The boy let out a single sigh. Then Danxia said, "It is not without a father that a son is born.
Thereupon, the old man entered the mountain with the boy. Upon arriving at the Patriarch’s place, Danxia did not even pay his respects;

instead, he went straight into the Sangha hall, mounted the neck of the Sacred Monk (Śākyamuni), and sat there. The assembly was struck with astonishment and immediately informed the Patriarch, who personally entered the hall.
The Patriarch looked at him and said, "My son, Tianran. Tianran then descended from the platform and prostrated, saying, "I thank the Master for bestowing this Dharma-name.
Thus he was named Tianran. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Shitou. The Patriarch said, "The path at Shitou is slippery; did it cause you to fall?
He replied, "If I had fallen, I would not have come here. Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled to observe the various regions, later residing at Mount Danxia.
○ Zhizang was the son of the Liao family from Qianhua. He left home life to receive full ordination.
A physiognomist, observing his extraordinary features, said to him, "Your master’s bone and spirit are not ordinary; you shall become a counselor to a Dharma King.
Thereupon, he went to Foji Rock to pay respects to Mazu, becoming one of his inner disciples. One day, Mazu asked Zhizang, "Why do you not read the sutras? He replied:
"Is the Sūtra not different [from you]? He replied, "Indeed it is so; nevertheless, you must prepare yourself for the future.

Mazu said, "Zang is ill and thinks only of self-preservation; how would he dare speak of benefiting others? Mazu said, "In your final years, you will surely flourish in the world. Zang then prostrated himself in worship.
Zu was under Lu Sīgōng. When Yǎnzǔ first began teaching the Dharma, Zàng requested to return to his home district.
Yǎnzǔ gave him a *kāṣāya* robe, and later he resided at Xītáng in Qiānzhōu. As for Zhìjiān: once, while traveling with Pǔyuàn and Zhìcháng, they encountered a tiger on the road.
Each of them passed by the tiger’s side. Pǔyuàn asked Zhìcháng, "Just now, when you saw the tiger, what did it look like? Zhìcháng said, "It looked like..."
There was a cat. Chang once asked Jian, who said, "It looks like a dog. He then asked Yuan, who said, "I see it as a great tiger.
One day, while Jian was eating his meal, Yuan was gathering the leftover rice. Jian said, "Leftover? Yuan replied, "Non-arising.
Jian said, "Non-arising is still secondary. Yuan walked several paces away; Jian called out, "Elder! and Yuan turned back.
Tou asked, "What is it? Jian replied, "Do not say this is the 'end'. Later, Jian resided at Shanshan (in the *Renzi* year).
In the fifth year of the Dali era, Master Fazhao was reborn in the Pure Land.
Fazhao again traveled with fifty monks to visit the Vajra Cave, where he suddenly beheld a multitude of jewels.
In the palace, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and ten thousand bodhisattvas appeared, illuminating the quarters as they paid homage; when he raised his head, they had all vanished.
Later, in the Huayan Hall, while recollecting that the two Great Beings had prophesied his rebirth in the Pure Land, he focused his mind on the Buddha.
Suddenly, he saw Buddhatāpala, who said to him, "Your lotus pedestal has already been formed; in three years, the flower will bloom. You shall see the bamboo grove."
[He asked,] "Why do you not let all living beings know of these various temples? Zhao then ordered craftsmen to carve the figures into stone at a prominent location and built Zhulin Monastery there.
Once it was completed, he said to the assembly, "My work is finished. A few days later, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting in meditation.

"Setting aside raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes, show me your original face. [The monk] said, "I ask the Master to set aside raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes and examine me.
[The Master] said, "I have already set them aside. [The monk] said, "I have already presented it to the Master. [The Master] said, "Since you have already presented it to my mind, how is it?

[Q]: "There is no thing. [A]: "You, too, are no thing. [Q]: "Since there is no thing, that is the true thing. [A]: "The true thing cannot be apprehended.
Your mind’s perception and measurement are like this; you must guard and maintain them with great care. One day, Xuantong asked:

The Master brought it forth with his lips and said, "There is not this. [Wuye] said, "If it is so, you have merely gained entry into the gate.
(Gui-chou year) Weiyen visited Chan Master Xiqian.
Weiyen was the son of the Han family from Jangzhou; from childhood he did not associate with other children, often sitting alone as if in deep contemplation.

Like Sengsi, he left the household life and received full ordination. He became widely learned in the sutras and śāstras and strictly observed the monastic precepts. One day he sighed, saying: "A great man should seek purity through the Dharma itself;
who could deign to concern themselves with such trivialities as the meticulous handling of handkerchiefs and cloths?

He first visited Shitou and asked about the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures. [Shitou replied,] "I know them roughly. However, I have heard that in the South there is a teaching that directly points to the human mind."
"I have seen my nature and attained Buddhahood, yet I am truly not yet clear about it. I humbly hope that the Master will compassionately provide instruction.
Baizhang Tou said, "It cannot be thus, nor can it be otherwise; it cannot be both thus and otherwise. How do you understand this? Yanyue was at a loss for words.
Tou said, "Your karmic conditions do not lie here. Go instead to the place of Master Ma. Yanyue departed.
He then went to visit the Patriarch and repeated his previous question. The Patriarch said, "Sometimes I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink;
sometimes I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink. Sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are right;
sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are not. What do you say to this? Under these words, Yanyan attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said:
"What principle have you seen? he asked. Mazu then prostrated himself. Mazu said, "When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito on an iron ox.
Mazu said, "Since you are thus, protect and maintain yourself well. Tianran took his leave of Mazu and traveled to various regions.
He resided at Mount Huading on Tiantai for three years, then went to Jingshan to pay respects to Fachin, and later went to the capital to visit Huizhong. One day...
Upon seeing [the monk], he immediately spread out his sitting mat. Zhong said, "Not so, not so. Then the monk stepped back;
Zhong said, "So it is, so it is. Then the monk stepped forward again; Zhong said, "It is not so, it is not so. Thereupon, the monk circumambulated Zhong once and departed. Zhong said:

At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk and received the Mahāyāna sūtras; he could read five lines simultaneously and never forgot what he saw at a single glance.
