With feet clad in mother-born trousers, you speak much and chatter even more; from this, you have long been led astray. If you wish to deliver sentient beings, there is no way other than to deliver yourself first.
Do not slander the True Celestial Buddha; the True Buddha cannot be seen, for it is the wondrous nature and the numinous mind.
What need is there to undergo refinement through incense and fire? The mind is a mind of non-action; the face is one’s mother-born face.
Though the kalpa-stone may be moved, within this there is no change. Non-action is fundamentally without affairs; what need is there to read written words? Eradicate the root of self and other.
To secretly harmonize with the meaning within this—how many kinds of toil for one's sinews and bones! It is not as good as sleeping beneath the forest trees.

Stupefied, one raises the head and sees the sun has grown high; eating rice, one proceeds from the very beginning. To apply effort upon effort is to wander further into obscurity. If you grasp it, you do not obtain it; if you do not grasp it, you naturally penetrate it.
I have a single word: cut off deliberation and forget conditions. It cannot be skillfully explained; it is transmitted only through the mind. Furthermore...
There is a single phrase: there is no fault in giving it directly. Subtle as a fine hair-tip, vast without spatial boundaries, it is primordially perfected without the need for laborious weaving.
Worldly affairs are endless; they are not as good as a mountain peak. Green pines shade the sun; emerald ravines flow on long.
Mountain clouds serve as a curtain; the night moon serves as a hook. Lying beneath the wisteria vines, with a block of stone for a pillow, one does not attend upon the Son of Heaven—how could one?
I envy the kings and lords; having no anxiety regarding life or death, what more need I worry about? The moon in the water has no fixed form; I am always simply at peace. All phenomena are thus:
they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning. Sitting upright and free from affairs, when spring comes, the grass turns green of its own accord.
The Dharma Master Zhànrán entered nirvana (Tiantai School).
In the first year of the Xìngyuán era, as Zhànrán was about to pass away, he addressed his disciples, saying: "The Great Way has no fixed direction and no substantial form.
Whether one is born or dies, its underlying principle is one and the same. I shall leave my bones on this mountain; tonight my retribution is exhausted. I merely wish to speak with you for a moment."
They discussed the Way and took their leave. Now, a single thought devoid of marks is called Emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that no dharma is not fully present is called Provisionality (*upādāya-prajñapti*);

and that it is neither one nor different is called the Middle (*madhyama*). In the state of ordinary beings, these are the three causes; in the state of the sages, they are the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

As when burning a wick, the beginning and end share the same nature; yet as when crossing the sea, the shallow and deep follow different currents. To benefit oneself and others lies precisely in this. Having finished speaking, [he departed].
Thus he transformed others. Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy inscribed the back of his stele, praising him as one destined for the world and a "sublime sage" (ārya).
(Yichu year) Layman Pang Yun visited Chan Master Xiqian.
Pang Yun, courtesy name Daoxuan, was a native of Xiangyang. His father served as the Governor of Hengyang, and the family resided south of the city. When Yun was young...
Awakening to the nature of worldly toil, he resolved to seek the ultimate truth. He built a hermitage to the west of his residence to practice cultivation.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he first visited Xiqian, asking, "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas? Xiqian covered his mouth with his hand, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment.
One day, Xiqian asked him, "Since you came to see this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily life?"
Dafayun replied, "If you ask about the affairs of daily life, there is no place to open one's mouth. Changqing said, "I knew you were like this before I even asked you.
Dafayun then presented a verse: "In the affairs of daily life, there is nothing different; Only I myself find harmony. At every point, there is neither grasping nor rejecting;
In every place, there is no discord or strain. Who assigns the titles 'Red' and 'Purple'? Mountains and hills are free from a speck of dust. The Spirit..."

He was proficient in both [secular] affairs and subtle spiritual applications; he transported water and carried firewood. One day, Yanran asked him, "Do you follow the black [robe of the monkhood] or the white [robe of the layman]?
He replied, "I wish to follow what I admire. Thereupon, he did not shave his head or don the monastic robes.
Master Fachang of Damei was the son of the Zheng family of Xiangyang. He left home to become a monk at a young age. Initially, he visited Daoyi and asked, "What is the Buddha?"
The first [teaching] states: "The mind itself is Buddha. One is constantly and immediately awakened.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he went to the old hermitage of Mei Zizhen, seventy li south of Ning County, where he bound together thatched grass for his dwelling. He addressed the assembly, saying:

"All of you, each turn your minds back toward the source and reach the fundamental; do not pursue its branches. If you simply attain the fundamental, the branches will arrive of their own accord. If you wish to recognize the fundamental, merely understand..."
One’s own mind. This mind is fundamentally the root of all worldly and world-transcending phenomena.
Therefore, when the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. The mind merely manifests in accordance with all that is good and evil.
The myriad dharmas are fundamentally suchness, one and the same. Always let the monk ask the Master: "What did you obtain upon seeing Master Ma?"
He then remained on this mountain. [A monk] asked, "The Master told me, 'The mind itself is Buddha,' so I have been dwelling right here.
The monk said, "Lately, the Master’s understanding of the Buddha-dharma has changed again. The Master asked, "How so? The monk said, "He also says, 'Neither mind nor Buddha.
The Master said, "This old fellow is confusing people; he will never come to an end. Let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha'—I..."
"Simply take it as 'this very mind is Buddha. The monk returned and related this to Yiyuan. Yiyuan said, "The plum has ripened.
Chan Master Weiyen resided at Yaoshan.
Having personally received the transmission of the Mind-Seal, at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, while resting at Yaoshan, he sighed deeply and said, "My life is but a temporary lodging..."

"Worldly existence is like duckweed or a water lily; why then should one imitate their drifting and turning? He then cleared away the brushwood and constructed a hut, just large enough to shelter his cross-legged sitting.
When villagers brought food and drink, running to him in haste, Huyan Yan said, "I have bestowed no virtue upon others;
why should I trouble people? He declined them all and would not accept. The villagers knelt and said, "We wish to hear what provisions you require for your daily expenses. He replied, "Rice."

"One *sheng* is sufficient. From then on, he would always serve mountain vegetables as accompaniments to his meals. Once he had finished eating, he would take his seat and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtras;
day and night were as one. Several years later, the monastic community renovated the monks' quarters until the rafters and beams were arranged in orderly rows.
The number of those coming to study was beyond counting. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Patriarchs taught nothing other than protection. If..."
When greed and anger arise, you must strictly guard against them; do not allow them to provoke you. If you wish to know this, you must take up the withered wood and the stone;
truly, there are no branches or leaves to be found. Even so, you should examine yourself further; you must not cut off speech.
I am now speaking these words for you to reveal that which is beyond words. That is its original state.
They come forth without the features of ears, eyes, and so on. Furthermore, it is said: "Those who appear now are all busy people;
one cannot find a single person who is dull-witted and simple. Do not take the words from your manuals and treat them as your own realization.
Those who, knowing that others do not understand, then give rise to contempt—these types are all icchantikas and non-Buddhists."
Master Lingmo resided at Wuxie (a dharma heir of Mazu Daoyi).
Initially, he visited Daoyi; Daoyi received him, whereupon Lingmo shaved his head and received full ordination. He subsequently visited Xiqian and immediately asked:
If there was mutual accord in a single word, he would stay; if not, he would depart. When Guoqing Xian took his seat, Mo remained silent and then departed.
Xian called out to him from behind, saying, "Ajari. Mo turned his head back. Xian said, "From birth until death, it is only this very thing.
Why do you turn your head and twist your brain? At these words, Mo attained great enlightenment. He then broke his staff in two and settled there. (Zhenyuan)
At first, he entered Tiantai, stayed at Baisha, and later resided at Wuxie. A monk asked, "What thing is greater than heaven and earth?
He replied, "No one knows it. The monk asked, "Can it be carved or polished? He replied, "Try taking a hand to it and see."
(Bingyin) Mazu Daoyi transmitted the Dharma to Pangyun.
When Pangyun arrived in Jiangxi, he visited Daoyi and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?"
The first said: "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I shall tell you. He asked again:
"If water has no sinews or bones, how is it that it can support a ten-thousand-hu vessel? The first said: "In my place, there is neither water nor vessel."
"What need is there to speak of sinews and bones? Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The ten directions gather together as one;
Each and every one studies non-action (wuwei). This is the field for selecting the Buddha; With an empty mind, one returns with the highest degree.

After his awakening, he loaded his entire fleet of boats with tens of thousands of bags of treasures and sank them in Lake Dongting, to the right of the Xiang River. He donated his residence to establish a monastery; from then on, his livelihood consisted of nothing but this alone.
Yexun’s wife was Pangpo, who had a son and a daughter; the daughter was named Lingzhao. They sold bamboo utensils to provide for their daily needs.
A verse says: "Having a son, he does not marry; having a daughter, she does not wed. The whole family sits together in a circle, discussing the discourse on non-arising.
One day, while Yexun was sitting, he asked Lingzhao: "The ancients said: 'Clearly clear at the tips of the hundred grasses, clearly clear is the Patriarch...'"
"What is the Master’s meaning? Zhao asked. Yun said, "Old and decrepit as you are, why do you speak such words?
Zhao asked, "And what about you? Zhao replied, "Clearly at the tips of the hundred grasses; clearly is the meaning of the Patriarchs. Yun then laughed.
On another day, while Yun was sitting in meditation, he suddenly exclaimed, "Difficult! Difficult! Ten piculs of sesame oil spread across a tree! Pangpo took up the sound and said, "Easy!"
"Easy! When hunger comes, eat; when tiredness comes, sleep. Zhao said, "It is neither difficult nor easy. The meaning of the Patriarch is at the tips of the hundred grasses.
One day, while selling a bamboo sieve, he went down a bridge to beg for alms. Seeing him, Zhao also lay down beside him.
Dongyan said, "What are you doing? Zhao replied, "I saw my father fall to the ground and have come specifically to help him up. Dongyan said, "Fortunately, no one saw it.
One day, Lady Pang entered Lukuan Temple to offer a vegetarian feast. The *vina* (chant leader) requested the meaning of the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
Pobian stuck a comb into the back of his topknot and said, "I have turned my merit toward [the Way]," and then he went out.
Chan Master Tanzang lived in seclusion at Mount Heng.
He received the mind-seal from Mazu and later visited Shitou, where his realization became crystal clear and penetrating. In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away.

Huiyuan secluded himself on the highest peak of Mount Heng, where few people visited him. Later, due to a foot ailment, he moved to the Western Garden, where his dharma companions grew numerous each day.
One day, while he was bathing by heating the water himself, a monk asked why he did not employ a śrāmaṇera to do so. Huizang then clapped his hands three times.
He once kept a clever dog. While he was walking about at night, the dog would take his robes and hide them; when it was time to store them away, the dog would return them to him.
Furthermore, it would crouch and guard by the side of the door. One night, it suddenly barked repeatedly, leaping up and assuming the posture of a fierce bite.

At dawn the next day, there was a great python in the eastern kitchen, several *zhang* in length, with its mouth agape and fangs bared, its poisonous flames blazing intensely. An attendant requested that he avoid it.
Zang said, "Can death be avoided? They come with poison, but I receive it with compassion. Poison has no inherent nature; it becomes potent only when provoked.
If compassion is truly unconditional, then enemies and kin are one and the same. Having spoken these words, the python lowered its head and moved slowly away, vanishing in an instant.
One night, a band of thieves arrived, and the dog again bit Zang’s robe. Zang said to the thieves, "In the thatched hut there is..."
"Take whatever you desire; I shall never begrudge it. The thief was moved by these words, bowed his head, and departed.
The recluse Li Yuan visited the bhikṣu Yuanze.
Initially, when An Lushan had seized the Eastern Capital, Li Cheng, the former Minister of Works, died as the city's governor. Li Cheng’s son, Yuan, was filled with grief and indignation.
He vowed: "I shall not serve in office, I shall not marry, and I shall not eat meat. He donated his residence to establish Huelin Temple.

A monk of the temple named Yuanze was on close terms with Yuan; together they set out to travel to Mount Emei. Yuan wished to travel upstream from Jingzhou along the gorges, while Yuanze wished to take the route through the Xiyu Pass at Chang'an.
Yuan said, "I have already severed all ties to worldly affairs; how could I ever speak of returning to the capital again? Yuanze remained silent for a long time.

He said, "Whether one moves or stays is certainly not within human control. Subsequently, traveling by boat along the route from Jingzhou, he arrived at Nanpu and saw a woman wearing a brocade apron drawing water.
Daoye pointed to her and wept, saying, "The reason I did not wish to go this way was because of her. Yuan asked him about it in surprise.
Daoye said, "That woman’s surname is Wang; I am to be her son. She has been pregnant for three years, yet I have not—"
"I came, but could not obtain milk. Now that I see there is nowhere to escape, you must assist me with mantras and incantations so that I may quickly give birth.
On the third day, when the child is bathed, I pray that you will attend to me; let your smile be my sign.
Thirteen years hence, beneath the autumn moon at the outskirts of Tiantzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, I shall meet you there. I shall become a bhikṣu through three lifetimes."
While practicing meditation at Yuelu Monastery on the western slopes of Mount Heng, Huayuan heard the sound of lamentation and remorse.
By evening, the wife of a man named Ze had not nursed her child for three days. Yuan went to see him; the infant indeed smiled. Later, as promised, Yuan went to Wu to fulfill his agreement.
There he heard a cowherd by the banks of Ge Hong’s stream tapping on a cow horn and singing: "The old spirit upon the三生石 (Sānshēng Shí) stone, enjoying..."
Chanting by the moon and playing in the wind need not be discussed; a person of sincere shame has come from afar to visit me. Though this body is different, my nature remains forever.
Yuan then called out to Master Ze, asking after his health. He replied: "Master Li is truly a man of faith, yet his worldly attachments are not yet exhausted.
Be careful not to draw near him; only through diligent cultivation without falling away shall we meet again. He then sang a verse: "Affairs before the body and affairs after the body..."

Vast and boundless. I wish to speak of these causes and conditions, yet I fear it would break my heart. Having searched throughout the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue, I now turn my smoke-shrouded oars back toward Qutang Gorge.
Thereupon, he vanished from sight. Fayuan resided at the temple for over fifty years; he passed away at the age of eighty-something.
○ Liang Su, Layman, on the Completion of the Treatise on the Tiantai Practice of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Liang Su, having entered the Hanlin Academy from the position of Counselor, was profoundly learned in the teachings of the Tiantai school. He composed the "Treatise on the Tiantai Practice of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*."

In the fifth year of Jiànzhōng (the jiǎzǐ year), he first began the work of revision; after three years, in the second year of Zhēnyuán (the bǐngyīn year), his labors were completed with the composition of the *Zhíguān Tǒnglì*.
It states briefly: "What is the purpose of *zhǐguān*? It is to guide the principles of the myriad transformations and return them to the *shíjì* (the limit of reality).
What is the *shíjì*? It is the fundamental nature (*xìng*). That which things cannot [attain]..."
Furthermore, it is darkness and movement that cause this state. That which illuminates darkness is called clarity; that which halts movement is called stillness.

Clarity and stillness are the essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). In the causal stage, they are called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; in the resultant stage, they are called wisdom (*jñāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
The causal stage is called practice; the resultant stage is called realization. One who practices these is a practitioner; one who realizes these is one who has attained fruition.
Indeed. To trace the origins of this, the Sage perceived that delusion is sufficient to lose one’s will and movement is sufficient to lose one’s direction.
Thereupon, he ceased to act and observed; he remained still and clarified his vision. He enabled movement to become still and stillness to become clear.
By relying on mutual dependence, he established the Dharma; by transcending dependence, he illuminated the source. He drove the great chariot to maintain rectitude and mounted upon great affairs.
Thus, he wields all-encompassing authority, finding rest in the field of non-duality and inspiring others within the realm of the threefold teaching.
Reaching the utmost subtlety, he exhausts his nature; reaching the utmost complexity, he embodies the divine. Speaking of what is near, even a single hair’s worth of goodness can lead one through;
speaking of what is far, the gate of the double mystery can be beheld. He employs the most perfect to bring about perfection, so that no thing is left partial. He employs...
The ultimate reality is realized through reality itself; therein, things are not deceptive. The Sage sets forth his words to demonstrate, and expands their scope to inform.
He treats them with ease and gentleness so that they may seek the truth for themselves; he provides models and deliberations so that they may arrive at it spontaneously.
This is the origin of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Now, what are the Three Truths? They are simply the One. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Provisional (*prajñapti*), and...
What is this "Middle"? It is the primary category. "Emptiness" and "Provisionality" are terms for their mutual relationship; "the Middle Way" is the name for attaining unity.
This is a discourse based on conceptual thought; it is not the ultimate principle of Unity. Ultimate Unity is precisely the Three, and ultimate Three is precisely the One.
This is not so because they contain one another, nor is it so because they give rise to one another. It is not a matter of numerical logic, nor—
These are strong names [for what is ineffable]. They are the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*). To speak of them and transmit them constitutes the "traces" (*ji*).
Principle is called the "root" (*ben*); traces are called the "branch" (*mo*). The root is the ground reached by the sages; the branch is the teaching demonstrated by the sages.
By descending from the root to manifest the traces, there arise the small and the great, the common and the distinct, and the sudden and the gradual.
It is gradual; it is manifest and it is esoteric; it is provisional and it is real; it is fixed and it is unfixed.
Following the traces to return to the source, it is the One and the Great, the Perfect and the Real, Non-abiding and the Middle, the Sublime and the Ultimate Truth.
This is the synthesis of the One and the Three. That which is called "emptiness" is a term used to encompass all phenomena. It is the provisional.
"Those" refers to that which establishes the ten thousand dharmas as its discourse. "The Middle" refers to that which wondrously permeates the ten thousand dharmas as its discourse.
To shatter all delusions, nothing is more preeminent than emptiness (*śūnyatā*). To establish all dharmas, nothing is more preeminent than the provisional (*prajñapti*).

To exhaustively realize all natures, nothing is greater than the Middle. When the Middle is raised, there is no dharma that is not the Middle; when the provisional is raised, there is no dharma that is not the provisional. When the [Middle] is raised...
If it is empty, there is no phenomenon that is not empty. To accomplish this is called the Three Virtues; to cultivate this is called the Three Contemplations. To state its essentials:
is this not the teaching of the Sage who exhausts the profound, investigates the subtle, and fully realizes principle and nature?

It causes the ignorant to become enlightened and the obstructed to become unimpeded. When unimpeded, one attains awakening; when awakened, one reaches the ultimate; when reached, one is eternal; when eternal, one is perfected. When enlightened, one illuminates; when illuminated—

Thus there is transformation; transformation leads to completion; completion is unity. The Sage has a means by which he encompasses all phenomena without error and pervades all kalpas without contradiction.
He sustains them for as long as the sands of the Ganges yet does not possess them; he returns to the state of non-substantiality yet is not nothingness.
We provisionally designate him "Buddha" and arbitrarily call him "Awakened. To investigate his ultimate intent, there is no liberation or sovereignty greater than this.

How wondrously sublime is this virtue! Such indeed is the accomplishment of the Three Truths. It is further said: "Alas, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—are they not the books that save the world and clarify the Way?
Were it not for one whose great sage-wisdom is transcendent, peerless, and standing alone, who could have produced them?
Were it not for one who is intelligent, profoundly penetrating, and who has grasped the meaning while forgetting the symbols, who could understand them? As for people of the present day...
One uses specific chapters, phrases, and characters to explain them from this perspective; how, then, could there be any omissions or oversights?
More than two hundred years have passed since the World-Honored One Zhìzhě entered nirvana, yet these writings have been transmitted through five masters:
Guǎngdǐng, Jìnyún Wēi, Dōngyáng Xiǎowēi, Zuǒxī Lǎnggōng, and Jīngxī Ránɡōng. It was Zuǒxī who first propagated the exegesis.
Jingxi [Zhiyi] extensively recorded this in biographical accounts totaling hundreds of thousands of words, encompassing the remaining Dharma with such diligence and completeness.
(Wuchen year) Chan Master Mazu Daoyi passed away (he was a dharma successor of Nanyue Huairang).
Among his disciples who entered the inner chamber, there were one hundred and thirty-nine people, each becoming a patriarch in their own region and propagating the teachings.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, during his travels through the forest on Mount Shimen in Jianchang, he beheld a level valley within a cavern.
He said to his attendant, "This withered body of mine shall return to this place next month. Upon returning, he manifested a slight illness.
When the head of the monastery asked, "How is the Master’s health these days? he replied: "One. (The character *yi* [one] is a homophone for *yi* [to end]).

On the first day of the second month, the Buddha Nirmāṇaruci and the Buddha Candranirmāṇa bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and entered parinirvāṇa. His lifespan was eighty years, and his seniority as a monk was sixty years.
In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, he was posthumously titled Daji (Great Quiescence), and his stupa was named Dazhuangyan (Great Adornment).
The Biography of Chan Master Huaihaiman:

He transmitted the Dharma to Xiyun. Xiyun was a native of Min County. In his youth, he left the household life at Huangbo Mountain in his home prefecture. He stood seven chi tall, and there was a circular mole upon his forehead.
Later, while traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk on the road with whom he conversed and laughed as if they were old acquaintances; the monk gazed intently at him.

His gaze pierced people, and he possessed several extraordinary features. Daoxuan then traveled with him. When they reached a place where the mountain stream was surging with a torrential flood, the monk cast aside his hat, set down his staff, and stopped.
Daoxuan urged him to cross together, but the monk said, "If you want to cross, you must cross;

I shall cross. He immediately lifted his robes and stepped into the waves as if walking on level ground. Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! Daoxuan said, "Tsk! You self-satisfied fellow!"
"I should have known sooner that you were fabricating a falsehood; I would have cut off your shin! The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma, one whom I could not surpass.
Having spoken, he vanished. He arrived at the capital of Luoyang to beg for alms, chanting the sound of his bowl being filled.
An old woman appeared between the door panels and said, "You are truly insatiable. Yun said, "You have not yet given anything; why do you reproach me for being insatiable? The woman laughed.
He closed the door. Baizhang Yun found this strange and went forward to speak with him; the man offered many points of medicinal instruction. After a short while, he took his leave.
The old woman said to him, "You may go to Nanchang to see Master Ma. Upon arriving in Nanchang, Daoyi had already passed away. He then went to Shimen to pay respects at the stupa.
At that time, Huaihai was performing a vigil beside the stupa, so he went to visit him there. Huaihai asked, "Majestic and dignified as you are, from where have you come?"
"From where have you come? He replied, "Majestic and imposing; I have come from Lingnan. Baizhang said, "Being so majestic and imposing, what business do you have here?
He replied, "Being so majestic and imposing, I have no other business. Baizhang held him in high esteem. The next day, he took his leave of Baizhang.
Baizhang asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to pay my respects to Master Ma. Baizhang said, "Master Ma has already passed away."
[The Master] said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects. My karmic fortune is shallow and meager; I have not even had the opportunity for a single meeting.

I do not know what words or phrases you have spoken on ordinary days. I wish to hear your instruction. Daohai then recounted the circumstances of his second visit to Mazu. When Fanyun heard this, [he was moved].
Unconsciously, he stuck out his tongue. Hai said, "Will you not, in the future, become a successor to Master Ma? He replied, "Not so.
Today, because of what you have raised up, I have been able to see the great capacity and great function of Mazu; yet, I do not recognize Mazu.
If I were to succeed Mazu, then in days to come I would lose my own descendants. Hai said, "So it is, so it is. When one’s vision is equal to that of the teacher..."
"One who diminishes their teacher’s virtue cannot be entrusted with the lineage; only one whose insight surpasses that of the teacher is fit for transmission.

You now possess an insight that far exceeds your teacher's. Yun then performed a prostration. One day, Yun asked, "How do you instruct others regarding the ancestral vehicle? Hai remained silent for a long while.
Yun said, "You must not allow the teaching to be severed for future generations. Hai said, "I took you for someone of substance," and then he rose.
He entered the abbot’s quarters. Yun followed him in and said, "I have come specifically for this purpose.
Hai said, "If that is so, you must not let yourself be deceived by me hereafter. Tong remained silent; he was given this name because from childhood he had spoken little.

While he was prostrating before the Buddha, a Zen practitioner asked, "What is it that you are bowing to? Tong replied, "It is the Buddha. The practitioner then pointed to the statue and said, "This one..."
"What is this? Tong was without opposition [to the inquiry]. When evening came, he prepared his dignified demeanor and paid respects to inquire of the Chan master.

He did not yet know the meaning of the master's intent. The Chan master asked, "Master of the Tripitaka, how many years have you spent in the monastic life? Tong replied, "Ten years. The Chan master said, "Have you even left the household life yet? Tong became utterly bewildered.
The Chan master said, "If you do not understand this, what is the point of ten years of monastic life? One hundred years would be the same. Thereupon, he ordered him to stay together with him.
He went to visit Mazu. By the time he reached Jiangxi, Mazu had already passed away. He then visited Huaihaimazu, who immediately resolved his doubts.
(Jisi year) Chongxin went to visit Chan Master Tianwang Daowu.
After receiving the seal of approval from Mazu, Daowu settled in a thatched hut outside the city of Jingmen. One day, the regional military governor came to visit him.

Dao-wu did not offer him formal greetings, which caused [the official] to fly into a rage. He seized Dao-wu and threw him into the river. Upon returning, he saw that fire had broken out throughout the entire yamen;

moreover, he heard the voice of the Heavenly King from above rebuking him in anger. Thereupon, he wailed in grief and prostrated himself in worship, whereupon the smoke and flames were suddenly extinguished.
He appeared exactly as he had been at first. Thereupon, [Daosheng] went in person to Jiangbiao to welcome Sengwu. Seeing Sengwu standing in the water, his robes remained completely dry;
this caused Daosheng to respect him all the more. To the west of the prefecture, he built Tianwang Temple to provide for Sengwu’s needs.

Among those who held him in deep faith was a man originally from Zhugong who was exceptionally gifted from his youth. His family sold cakes, and he lived in the lane where the temple stood; he used to deliver ten cakes every day.
Huiwu said, "I have awakened. Huiwu accepted it. Every time a meal was finished, he would set aside one cake and say, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide protection for your descendants.
One day, Sengxin thought to himself, "The cakes were what I brought here; why has he returned them to me? Is there some hidden meaning in this?
He went to see Huiwu and asked about it. Huiwu replied, "These were what you brought; returning them to you—what fault is there in that? Upon hearing this, Sengxin felt a deep sense of realization.

Having understood the profound mystery, Chongxin consequently sought out Wuzu to leave the household life. Wuzu said, “In the past you honored and cultivated merit; now you believe my words. You may be named Chongxin (‘Venerable Faith’).
From then on, he served and exhorted those around him. One day he asked Wuzu, “Since I arrived here, I have not received the Master’s instruction on the essentials of the mind.
Wuzu replied, “From the moment you arrived, there has never been a time when I have not pointed it out to you.”
Xiao asked, "Where did you point out the essential teaching? Wuzhuo said, "When you brought me tea, I received it for you;
when you brought me food, I accepted it for you; when you bowed to me, I lowered my head. Where was the essential teaching not pointed out?"
Xin bowed his head for a long time. Wuzhu said, "If you see, then see directly; if you deliberate, you are already mistaken. Xin attained immediate understanding.
He then asked again, "How does one maintain this? Wuzhu said, "Roam freely according to your nature; relax and let go in accordance with conditions.
Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's' understanding. Later, Xin resided at Longtan and succeeded Deshan.
(Gengwu) Chan Master Zhichang Opens the Dharma at Guizong (a dharma heir of Mazu).
Zhichang resided at Guizong Temple on Mount Lu. Because he had double pupils in his eyes, he used his hands to massage them with medicinal ointment until both corners of his eyes became red;
thus, he was popularly known as "Red-Eyed Guizong. He ascended the hall and said: "The ancient worthies of old were not without knowledge."

To understand others as noble beings is not the same as following the common stream. At present, you are unable to achieve self-reliance and merely waste your time. My sons, do not misapply your minds;
there is no one who can take your place, nor is there any place for your mind to dwell.

Do not seek it from another. From the past until now, you have simply relied on the interpretations of others; thus, every word you utter is obstructed and your light does not penetrate through. This is solely because of your eyes.
There is an object before one. There is always a verse that says: "The affairs and principles of Guizong are cut off; The sun’s orb is exactly at noon.
Free and easy like a lion, He does not rely on external things. He strides alone upon the four mountain peaks; He wanders at ease along the three great paths. When he yawns, flying birds fall;
When he grunts, all the heterodox are terrified. If the trigger is set, the arrow is easily caught; If the shadow vanishes, the hand cannot cover it. Relaxing and tensing are like—"
The Art of Archery: Cutting and shaping according to the scale, Intricate carvings of myriad names— When returned to their source, they are like earth.
Speech and silence, sound and voice are cut off; The wondrous intent is beyond the reach of emotion. Discard the eye and you become deaf; Take up the ear and you become blind.
A single shaft pierces the three barriers; Clearly visible is the path behind the arrow. Pitiful, O great man! Prior to heaven, you were the Buddha and the Patriarch. — Jiang (Song)
Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of the province, once asked Chang: "In the teachings, it is said that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed; I do not doubt this.

But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—is that not mere idle talk? Chang replied: "People say you, Excellency, have read ten thousand scrolls of books; is this true? Li Bo said: "It is. Chang said:
"From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut. Where, then, are those ten thousand scrolls?"
Chuzhu Bo bowed his head and remained silent. On another day, Bo asked again, "What edge of reality does the entire Great Canon of Teachings clarify?
Chang raised his fist and showed it to him, saying, "Do you understand? Bo replied, "I do not. Chang said, "This scholar does not even recognize a fist.
Bo said, "Please, Master, give me instruction. Chang said, "When you meet someone, you shall be granted it on the road. He did not continue.
Chang was encountered while he was engaged in the worldly dissemination of the Dharma. One day, while he was weeding, a presiding master (zuozhu) came to visit him.
Suddenly seeing a snake, Chang cut it with his hoe. The presiding master said, "I have long heard of Guizong;
having come here, I see only a monk of coarse conduct. Chang replied, "You are coarse, and I am coarse. The master asked, "What is this 'coarseness'? Chang held up his hoe. The master—
[Chang] asked, "What is 'subtle'? He constantly made the gesture of slaying a snake. The Master said, "If that is so, then I shall follow it and act accordingly.
Chang said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of following and acting, where did you see me slaying a snake? The Master was speechless.
○ Chan Master Shitou Xiqian (Dharma Heir of Qingyuan Xingsi) entered nirvana.
Xiqian resided at Shitou. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The dharma-gate of my teaching was transmitted by the Buddhas of the past.

It does not concern itself with meditative concentration or diligent effort, but only with attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. 'Mind is Buddha,' and 'mind, Buddha, and sentient beings; enlightenment, bodhi, and afflictions'—these are merely names."
Though their forms differ, they are one in essence. You should know that the substance of your own spiritual mind is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence;

its nature is neither defiled nor pure. It is profoundly still and perfectly complete, identical for both ordinary beings and sages. Its applications are boundless, transcending the mind, intellect, and consciousness. The three realms and the six paths are merely manifestations of your own mind;
like the moon in water or an image in a mirror, how could they have arising or ceasing? If you can understand this, there is nothing that is not fully provided. This is the eternal truth.
On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Yuan era, he demonstrated his passing. His age was ninety-one; his years since ordination were sixty-three.
○ Tanguan Changzi Kuang first went to Caoxi to pay respects at the stupa. Upon returning, he visited Xiqian. Xiqian asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan.
Xiqian said, "At the head of Mount Dayu, there is a station for meritorious deeds. Have you completed them yet? He replied:
[Daokai] had achieved realization long ago; he simply lacked the "dotting of the eyes. Xuanzhe said, "Do you not wish for the dotting of the eyes?
Daokai replied, "I request it at once. Xuanzhe then lowered one foot. Daokai prostrated himself. Xuanzhe said, "You prostrate yourself because you see such a principle.
Daokai said, "According to what I have seen, it is like a single drop of snow upon a red-hot furnace. Later, while residing at Changzi, a monk asked him, "Not to be in vain..."
The various sages of antiquity asked: "What is the first phrase of the Long-Bearded One? He replied: "One has a mouth but cannot speak.
They asked: "Why can the mouth not speak? Kuang then offered this verse: "The stone lion and the wooden girl— The first phrase is the pivot of all Buddhas.
It cannot be spoken; how marvelous! Right here it is; do not harbor doubt. After a long silence, he said: "This is the first."
[The monk] spoke this second phrase: "Neither one nor two. Guoqing Kuang said, "To see the profit and forget the awl—there is still much left to do.
The monk bowed. Kuang picked up his tea bowl and said, "Right here, you do not fail the sages of antiquity.
The monk asked, "Regarding 'Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha'—what about that? Kuang set down the bowl and returned to his quarters.
(Xinwei) Chan Master Zhizang resided at Xitang during the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era.
In the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era, Chan Master Zhizang was residing at Xitang in Qianzhou. Once, Minister Li Ao asked a monk, "What teachings did Master Mazu have?
The monk replied, "The Master sometimes said 'this very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he said 'neither mind nor Buddha.'"
Buddha. Ao said, "Everyone, come over here. Ao then asked Zang, "What instructions did Master Ma have?
Zang called out, "Li Ao! Ao responded, "Yes? Zang said, "The drums and horns are sounding. A layman asked Zang, "Are there heavens and hells? He replied, "There are.
The man asked, "Are there the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? He replied, "There are. The man asked many more questions, and Zang answered them all.
[The monk] said, "There is. Juezhang asked, "When the Master speaks thus, are you not perhaps mistaken? Cang said, "Have you ever visited a venerable elder?
[The monk] said, "I have previously attended upon the Master of Jingshan. Cang asked, "How did he speak to you? [The monk] said, "He said that everything is entirely non-existent.
Cang asked, "Do you have a wife? [The monk] said, "I do. Cang said, "Does the Master of Jingshan have a wife?"
"No. He replied, "There is none. Zang said, "The Abbot of Jingshan may say there is none, but that is all. The scholar thanked him and departed.
(Ren-shen year) Chan Master Faqin of Jingshan passed away (he was a successor of Hexin Xunsu).
When Faqin returned from Chang’an to Jingshan, after some time, the Prefectural Governor requested that he reside at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou. Faqin...

He subsequently traveled back and forth between these places, choosing no fixed place of residence. On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, he manifested his passing at Longxing Temple.
Three days prior to this, he addressed the assembly, saying: "When I am buried, inter me in the vacant space of the southern courtyard;

do not mound it with earth, nor plant trees, for I fear it might encroach upon the vegetable plots of the monks. He was ninety-two years of age and seventy years since his ordination. How deeply we mourn him!
His vows were vast and profound. To behold him or hear his name was like a child finding its mother. Thus, from the sea and Mount Dai in the east to Long and Shu in the west;

from the depths of Jiaoyang and Guangzhou in the south to the northern reaches of Shuofang—there were no scholars who did not look to him with reverence and admiration. All those who came to receive his instruction regarded him as their own eyes.

It became a mountain of merit, such that devas and nāgas turned toward it in reverence and beings of diverse species sought refuge there. From the earth sprang numinous fungi, and from the sky rained down ambrosia.
Holy lamps appeared at night, and colored clouds shone with radiance at dawn. Fierce beasts took up residence by its side, and flocks of birds gathered in its chambers.
White herons and crows would come to his palms to eat from them. Two white rabbits would prostrate themselves between his staff and sandals.
A rooster constantly followed him to listen to the Dharma and would not eat living creatures; when Huiqin went to Chang’an, it cried out long and loud for three days before dying.
A deer often stayed by his meditation hall and did not wander elsewhere; when Huiqin passed away, it also died after three days.
(Guiyou) Biography of Baizhang Huaihaimen Fa Lingyou. Lingyou was the son of the Zhao family of Changxi.
At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head, received the full precepts, and thoroughly studied the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
He once traveled abroad and arrived at Guoqing Temple, where he encountered Hanshan and Shide walking along the road leading to Songmen; Hanshan let out a tiger’s roar.
Three times he called out, "Sheng! But Huayou had no reply. Heshan said, "Since our parting at Vulture Peak until now, do you still remember me?
Huayou again had no reply. Heshan picked up his staff and said, "What do you call this thing, elder brother?
Huayou again had no reply. Heshan said, "Enough, enough; there is no need to ask him. Since we parted, I have already been reborn as a king for three lifetimes."
He had completely forgotten it all. In the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era, when Huaiyu was twenty-three years old, he traveled to Jiangxi to visit Huaihaim.

Upon seeing him, Huaihaim granted him entry into his inner quarters; consequently, Huaiyu became the foremost among those engaged in study. One day, while standing in attendance, Huaihaim asked, "Who is there?"
Daowu replied, “Lingyu. Guishan asked, “Is there fire in the brazier? Daowu stirred it and said, “There is no fire.

Guishan rose personally, stirred deeply, and finding a small amount of fire, held it up and showed it to him, saying, “You say there is none; what about this? From that moment, Daowu attained awakening.
He prostrated in thanks and set forth his understanding. Guishan said, “This was merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sutra says: ‘If you wish to know...’”

Regarding the meaning of Buddha-nature: one should contemplate the conditions of time and season. Once the time has arrived, it is like suddenly awakening from a delusion or suddenly remembering what was forgotten;
only then does one realize that one’s own property is not obtained from another. Thus the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening;
there is no mind and there is no dharma. It is simply the absence of delusion—the equal mind of ordinary beings and sages, the original mind-dharma, which is fundamentally complete."
"Since you are now thus, protect and maintain yourself well. The following day, he went into the mountains with Hai to perform manual labor.
Hai asked, "Did you bring fire? Huo replied, "I brought it. Hai asked, "Where is it? Huo then picked up a piece of wood.
He blew twice. He gave it to Hai. Hai said, "It is like an insect gnawing through wood.
(Yihai). Chan Master Wuye read the Tripitaka.
After Wuye personally received the mind-seal of Mazu, he went to Caoxi to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa, and then to Mount Lu. Tian... [text fragment]

He traveled extensively to seek out sacred sites, proceeding from Luoyang to Fengyi (the region of Yong). While resting at Ximing Monastery, the monastic community collectively requested that he serve as a Great Virtuous One (*bhadanta*) for both monastic districts.
Daoye said, "This is not my original intention. Upon reaching Shangdang, the Military Governor Li Baozhen attended upon him morning and evening.
Daoye said, "I originally sought to avoid the vast crowds of the capital; now to be troubled again by receiving you, a noble lord—is this truly my heart's desire?"
He then traveled to Qingliang Jinguesi Temple, where he re-examined the Tripitaka, completing the task after eight years.
○ Chan Master Puyuan began teaching at Nanquan in the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era.
While Puyuan was resting at Chiyang, he subsequently opened a Dharma center at Nanquan; this became known throughout all quarters.

Acting as a master carpenter for the city of Jing, he ascended the hall and said: "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, have attained the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
they naturally acquire all meditative concentrations, liberations, and the wondrous functions of supernormal powers, reaching even into all realms of form."
The Universal Manifestation Body (sambhoga-kāya) may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, and entry into nirvana;

it causes immeasurable beings to enter a single pore, where a single phrase of scripture is expounded for immeasurable eons without its meaning being exhausted, thereby teaching and transforming immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Yet this is still called the ignorance regarding the knowable (jñeya-āvaraṇa), the most subtle ignorance regarding the knowable.
This is utterly contrary to the Way; it is a great difficulty, indeed a great difficulty. He further said: "Lately there are too many Chan masters;
one cannot find a person who is dull-witted enough [to be a true vessel]. It is not that they do not exist at all, but they are few among them. If anyone comes forward, I shall deliberate with you."
"Was there any practitioner during the kalpa of emptiness? Whether there was or not—why do you not say?
Usually, those with clever lips and thin tongues, when questioned, all remain silent. Why do you not speak out? Do not discuss matters of the Buddha’s appearance in the world."
When Yuan was staying at the hermitage, a monk arrived. Yuan said to him, "I am going up the mountain to do some work;

wait until mealtime, prepare the food, and after I have eaten it myself, send a portion up here. After a short while, the monk prepared the food, ate it himself, and then smashed all the household utensils at once.
He lay down on the bed. Yuan waited, but seeing that he did not come, he returned to the hermitage. There he saw...
When the monk lay down to sleep, Yuan also went to lie down beside him. The monk then rose and departed.
Yuan remained behind and said, "When I lived in the hermitage in the past, there was a certain keen and talented practitioner; even until now, I have not seen him again."
Biography of Chan Master Puyan Congshen.
Congshen was a native of the Hao family from Haoxiang in Caozhou. Having shaved his head while still a child, he had not yet received full ordination when he followed his own master on a pilgrimage.
Upon reaching Chiyang, he visited Puyan. While his own master was first attending to formalities, Congshen was just beginning his own greetings; at that moment, Puyan was present.
While lying down inside the abbot’s quarters, he saw Xuanzhen coming to pay his respects. He asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Xuanzhen replied, "I have recently departed from Ruixiang.
The Master said, "Did you see the standing Ruixiang statue? Xuanzhen replied, "I did not see the standing Ruixiang; I only saw the reclining Tathāgata."
Yuan then rose from his seat and said, "Are you a *śrāmaṇera* with a master, or a *śrāmaṇera* without a master?
Xian said, "I am a *śrāmaṇera* with a master. Yuan asked, "Who is your master? Xian stepped forward, bowed, and said, "The early spring is still cold;
I humbly wish that the Master’s health be ever blessed. Yuan then called for the *karmadāna*, saying, "This *śrāmaṇera* shall be assigned elsewhere. This was the original [account].
The Master [Nanquan] had already returned home, so Huairang remained to practice under him. One day, Huairang asked, "What is the Way? Huairang said, "The ordinary mind is the Way.
Huairang asked, "Can one still direct oneself toward it? Huairang said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is to deviate from it.

Huairang said, "If one does not intend to direct oneself toward it, how can one know it is the Way? Huairang said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing. Knowing is deluded cognition; not-knowing..."
"This is indeterminate. If one truly penetrates the Way beyond doubt, it is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive. How could one forcibly impose distinctions of right and wrong?
At these words, Xuanzhen attained great enlightenment; he then went to Mount Song to receive the full precepts before returning to Nanquan.

One day, Yuan was about to execute a cat because the monks of the East and West Halls were disputing over it. Holding up the cat, he addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak, I shall save the cat;
if you cannot speak, I shall put it to death. The assembly had no reply, so Yuan immediately killed it.
Xian returned from outside, and Yuan recounted the previous conversation, asking, "What would you have done? Xian took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and—
Xuanzhen said, "If you were here, you could have saved the cat. Yuanwu Changqing said, "At eighteen, I already knew how to make a living.
Xuanzhen said, "At eighteen, I already knew how to ruin a family and scatter a household.
One day, Xuanzhen addressed the assembly, saying, "Mazu of Jiangxi says 'this very mind is Buddha. Old Master Wang does not say so; he says it is not the mind."
"It is not the Buddha; it is not an object. Is there any fault in speaking thus? Xuanze bowed and departed.
At that time, a monk followed him and asked, "The Senior Monk bowed and then left; what was his intention? Xuanze said, "You should ask the Master yourself."
The monk then asked, "What was the meaning of the Venerable Shen’s intention just now?
Yuan said, "He indeed grasped the old monk’s intent. Shen returned to Caozhou to visit his preceptor. When his relatives heard of this, they all wished to come to the meeting.

Upon hearing this, Shen said, "The web of worldly passions has no end; I have already taken leave to enter the monastic life and do not wish to see you again. Thereupon, he departed with [his belongings].
Bingxi traveled extensively throughout all quarters. Jingcen had long relied upon Puyuan; he composed a verse that struck the essential point, saying:
"Today I return home and enter the great gate; Nanquan’s true path pervades heaven and earth. Every dharma is clearly manifest as the patriarchs’ legacy;
Turning my head back, I feel ashamed—what fine descendants! Puyuan said: "Today, do not discuss the matter of striking the essential point; Nanquan did not say it 'pervades' [heaven and earth]."
Heaven and Earth. Returning home is entirely the business of one’s descendants; the grandfather has never left the door.
A monk asked Zen Master Conghui of Tongshan, "How was it after you saw Nanquan? Conghui remained silent. The monk said, "What was it like before you had seen Nanquan?
Conghui replied, "It cannot be that there was anything else. The monk returned and related this to Zen Master Cong.
Cen showed him a verse, saying: "The person who does not move atop the hundred-foot pole, Though they have gained entry, it is not yet the truth.
One must advance further atop the hundred-foot pole; The ten directions of the world are one's entire body. A monk asked, "How does one advance atop the hundred-foot pole?
Cen said, "The mountains of Langzhou, the waters of Lizhou. The monk said, "I do not understand. Cen said, "The four seas and five lakes are the Emperor."
At Huazhi, a monk asked, "How can one turn the mountains, rivers, and lands back into oneself? Ceng said, "How can one turn oneself into the mountains, rivers, and lands?
The monk said, "I do not understand. Ceng showed him this verse: "Who asks about the turning of mountains and rivers?
Into whom would the mountains and rivers turn? Perfect penetration has no two sides; The Dharma-nature fundamentally has no place to return. A monk asked, "Master..."
"Who will succeed you? Ceng said, "I have no one to succeed me. The Master asked, "Do you still engage in study? Ceng said, "I myself continue my study.
The Master asked, "What is your intention, Master? Ceng presented this verse: "The void asks the ten thousand phenomena;
The ten thousand phenomena answer the void. Who can personally hear this? Only the child with hair-ties and wooden combs. Later, Ceng resided at Changsha.
Lu Xeng, courtesy name Jingshan, was a native of Wu Commandery. While serving as the Regional Inspector of Xuanchuan, he visited Baizhang Huaihai (known as Puyuan).
One day, Lu asked, "I have come from the six realms; does my body still exist within the waves? Puyuan replied, "Keep this clearly in mind and present it to a master.
Lu further remarked to Puyuan, "The Master is truly inconceivable; wherever you go, you are in the world..."
He was fully accomplished in all the *dhātus*. Yuan said, "What I have just said was entirely within the scope of your station as a Great Officer.
On another day, he asked, "In my household, I have been raising a gander in a bottle. As the gander grew larger, it could no longer get out of the bottle.
Now, I must not break the bottle, nor may I harm the gander. What skillful means can you suggest, Reverend, to get it out? Yuan called out, "Great Officer!"

Wang Guo (亘) responded with an assent. Yuan said, "This is an emergence. From this, Guo attained awakening. One day he said to Yuan, "I, your disciple, have also gained a slight understanding of the Buddha-dharma.
Yuan then asked, "How do you conduct yourself throughout the twelve periods of the day? Guo replied, "Not a single thread hangs upon me.
Yuan said, "You are still but a man standing at the foot of the steps. Have you not heard it said: 'A sovereign who possesses the Way does not admit those who possess mere cleverness'?"

The official Yuan Huan was a subordinate of [Wang] Zhao. One day he said to Zhao, "Dharma Master Zhaowu is truly extraordinary. He says that all things share the same root as myself, and that heaven and earth are one body with me.
Yuan Huan pointed to the peony flowers in front of his courtyard and said, "Great Officer, when people of this age see even a single stalk of these flowers, it is like being in a dream;
they are utterly unable to fathom it. Yuan Huan took his leave and returned to his administrative seat in Xuancheng. Yuan Huan then questioned [the Master].
The Great Officer said, "I am leaving that place. How will I govern the people there? Yuanwen said, "Govern them with wisdom.
Yuanwen replied, "If that is so, then the living beings there will all fall into misery and ruin. Master Shizu of Zhongnan Mountain went to visit Puyuan.
He asked, "'The mani-jewel no one recognizes; it is personally held within the Tathāgata-garbha. What is this 'garbha'? Puyuan said, "It is right here with you."
"Those who come and go," [Wu]yuan said. "What about those who neither come nor go? [Wuzhuo] said, "They are also thus. The Patriarch asked, "What is the pearl?
Wuyuan invited the Patriarch to enter his room. The Patriarch assented. Wuyuan said, "Go! You do not understand my words. From this point on, the Patriarch entered through faith.
○ Chan Master Baoji preached the Dharma at Panshan Baoji.
Residing at Panshan, a monk asked, "What is the Way? Baoji said, "Hush! The monk said, "I, your student, have not yet grasped the Master’s meaning.
Baoji said, "Go. He ascended the hall and said: "If the mind is free from affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise; when the intellect is severed from the subtle mechanism, even the finest..."

How could dust be established? The Way is fundamentally without substance; it is because of substance that names are established. The Way is fundamentally without name; it is because of names that titles are obtained.
If one says "this very mind is Buddha," at present one has not yet entered the profound mystery. If one says "neither mind nor Buddha," this is still merely pointing toward the ultimate limit.
The path beyond this—where a thousand sages have transmitted nothing—is such that students exhaust their bodies in vain, like a monkey grasping at a reflection in water.
Ying said: "Furthermore, it is said: 'The moon of the mind hangs solitary; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects have vanished, what is this? O Zen masters, it is like throwing a sword into the air: one need not discuss whether it reaches its mark or not.
This is because the empty wheel leaves no trace and the blade of the sword remains unimpaired. If you can act thus, then mind after mind is without cognition."
"The whole mind is Buddha; the whole Buddha is the person. When there is no distinction between person and Buddha, one has begun the Way.
It is further said: "O Virtuous One of Chan, you may study the Way within yourself. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. To be thus is what is called 'leaving home. Therefore, the Guide said: 'The Dharma is fundamentally non-dual...'"
Obstruction. The same applies to the three periods of time. Even for one who is unconditioned and inactive, there remains the difficulty of the golden chain.
Therefore, the spiritual source shines alone; the Way is cut off from arising. Great wisdom is not "bright," and true emptiness leaves no trace.

True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and *nirvāṇa* are both merely figurative designations. Zen practitioners, you must look into yourselves directly; no one can take your place.
It is further said: "The three realms have no dharmas; where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are fundamentally empty; upon what does the Buddha rely to abide?
The celestial sphere is motionless, silent and wordless. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more. Take care.
Huiji studied under Chan Master Yingzhen.
He was the son of the Ye family in Shaozhou. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic order under the monk Buyu Tong.
When he was fourteen, his parents took him back home, intending to arrange a marriage for him. Huiji then cut off two of his fingers and knelt before his parents, vowing to seek the True Dharma.
In response to his laborious service, his parents finally granted permission. Daotong went to him again and was allowed to receive the tonsure.
One day, Daotong ordered Jie to bring a small bed. When Jie had brought it there, Daotong said, "Take it back to its original place.
Jie did as he was told. Daotong asked, "What is that object over there by the bed? Jie replied, "Nothing. Daotong asked, "And what is this object here? Jie replied, "Nothing."
Tongzhao summoned Huiji. Ji replied, "Yes. Tongzhao said, "Go; travel to various places and visit Yingzhen.
Zhen had once said to Ji, "The National Teacher transmitted from the Sixth Patriarch ninety-seven *yuanxiang* (perfect circles).
He bestowed them upon me and said: 'Thirty years after my passing, a novice monk will come from the south and greatly propagate these.'"
The teaching has been transmitted in succession so that it would not be interrupted. I now entrust it to you; you should uphold it. He then gave the original text to Jì (Jìzàng).
Upon receiving it, Jì read it once and then burned it. Zhēn asked one day, "The various signs [of the transmission] previously were very worthy of being cherished in secrecy.
Jì replied, "I read it at the time and then burned it. Zhēn said, "This Dharma-gate of mine..."
"No one can understand this; only the former masters, the various ancestral teachers, and the great sages can fully comprehend it.
Why have you burned it? Ji said, "I, Huiji, understood its meaning upon a single reading. It is simply that one must apply it; one must not cling to the original text.
Zhen said, "Even so, while it may be acceptable for you, future generations will not be able to believe it. Ji said, "..."
"If the Master wishes to have it recorded again, it will not be difficult; I shall immediately compile another copy and present it to you, ensuring nothing is omitted.
Huiji visited Chan Master Hong'en (a Dharma heir of Mazu), who was residing at Zhongyi Mountain. Having received full ordination in Jiangling, Huiji returned to Zhongyi to pay his respects.
The Master [Zhaozhou] received the precepts. He clapped his hands, making a "he-he" sound. He moved silently from west to east, from east to west, and then stood in the center.
Afterward, he took leave of the precepts and withdrew to stand behind. The Master said, "Where did you obtain this samādhi?
He replied, "I brought it out from the seal at Caoxi. The Master said, "Tell me, what did Caoxi use this samādhi to receive?"
A man named Jie Yisuo asked Jique, "Where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? Jique replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Master Mazu.
Jie asked, "How do you understand the principle of seeing the Buddha-nature? Jique said, "Let me give you a simile:
suppose there is a room with six windows, and inside there is a monkey, while outside there is another monkey."
From the east, he called out, "Singing! and the singing-monkey responded. He did this at all six windows; each time he called, there was a response.
Jil bowed in thanks, stood up, and said, "I have now received the Master’s metaphors and understand them all. However, there is one further matter:
if the monkey within has fallen asleep while the monkey without wishes to meet him, how will that be? Yunmen descended from his rope-seat and took hold of [Jil].

Jishou performed a dance and said: "The *xingxing* has met you. It is like a gnat building a nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, crying out at a crossroads: 'The land is vast and the people are few; those who meet are scarce.
Gu-si Heshang (a dharma successor of Mazu) once had Tianran come to stay overnight. The next morning, he boiled some gruel.
When it was cooked, the attendant filled only one bowl for the temple and filled another bowl for himself to eat, showing no concern for the others.
As he was eating the porridge he had filled for himself, the attendant said, "I rose very early at the fifth watch; there are still travelers on the road at night. He then asked why.
The temple official asked, "Why do you not instruct the practitioners? How can they be so lacking in propriety? The Master said, "On pure ground, one should not defile people's sons and daughters.
The temple official replied, "I almost did not question this old fellow about his transgression."
(Guīwèi) Chan Master Wúyè resided at Xīhé in Fénzhōu (a dharma heir of Mázǔ).
Wúyè had lived at Qīngliáng for eight years and subsequently traveled south to Xīhé. The Regional Inspector Dǒng Shūchán invited him to reside at the Kāiyuán Vihāra.
Wúyè said, "My karmic conditions lie here. Thereupon, he rained down the great rain of the Dharma for nearly twenty years.
Throughout Ji, Bing, and Fen, both monastics and laypeople were all drawn toward his transformation. Whenever students came to inquire, he would mostly answer them by saying:

"Do not engage in false conceptualization. Once, a monk asked: "The twelve divisions of the teachings have flowed into this land, and those who have attained the fruits of the Way are not merely one or two.
Why then did the Patriarch come from the West to separately proclaim the Sublime Doctrine, pointing directly to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha? He replied: "..."
As for the eminent monks of past dynasties, they were all thoroughly versed in the nine schools of thought and possessed profound mastery of the Tripiṭaka—such as Sengzhao, Daorong, and Daoyi.
How could it be that they did not understand the Buddha-dharma? Jingye said: "The Buddhas have never appeared in the world, nor have they bestowed a single dharma upon anyone.
It is only by administering remedies according to the ailments of beings that the twelve divisions of the teachings came to exist; it is like exchanging honeyed fruit for bitter gourds."

I wash away the karmic roots of you all; there is no substantial reality whatsoever. As for spiritual powers, transformations, and the hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi—these are used to convert those celestial Māras and heterodox teachers.
The dual adornments of merit and wisdom are intended to shatter the views of clinging to existence and stagnating in emptiness.

If you do not realize the Way and the meaning of the Patriarchs, what does it matter who you discuss—whether it be Daosheng, Sengzhao, Tanyun, or Sengrui? Furthermore, it is said: "It is just like a wild recluse of lofty character..."

There were those who understood the practice of "resting one's head on a flowing stream and rinsing one's mouth with river stones," renouncing honor and emolument, yet still possessed strategies for stabilizing the state and governing the people;
though summoned to office, they did not rise. How much more so is this true for the path of our Chan school?

Furthermore, observe that after the ancients and masters of old attained realization, they dwelt in thatched huts or stone chambers, cooking their meals in broken-legged cauldrons for twenty or thirty years. This is what is called [true practice].

He did not harbor worldly gain in his heart, nor did he fix his thoughts upon wealth and treasures. Utterly forgetting the affairs of the human world, he concealed his traces among the mountain crags and thickets.
Though kings summoned him, he did not come; though feudal lords invited him, he did not attend.

How could he be like his contemporaries, who crave fame and profit, wallowing in the paths of the world like petty merchants who, having small desires, forget the great fruit? Alas! Those who have obtained a human body are as rare as...
The soil upon one's fingernails is like those who have lost their human form; the soil of the great earth is like those who remain. This is truly a matter for lamentation and regret.

Even if one has attained some partial understanding of the principle, if they do not recognize it as the rule within awakening and the gateway for entering the truth, they will claim to be eternally freed from worldly burdens.

Thus, they treat those of superior practice with contempt, causing their mental outflows (*āsrava*) to remain unexhausted and the ground of principle to remain obscure. In the end, they reach old age in vain.

In death, nothing is accomplished; it is merely a vain prolonging of years and months. Furthermore, intelligence and wit cannot withstand birth and death, and dry wisdom does not exempt one from the cycle of saṃsāra.
Let us brothers discuss the reality, not the illusion: this very mouth that eats, this body and mind, are entirely used to deceive the worthy and mislead the sages.
Seeking to obtain [rewards] for the future, when observed with the wisdom-eye that perceives the minds of others, it is like drinking pus and blood;
one must repay them all before it is possible [to attain liberation]. Who, then, possesses the fruits of the Way? It is one who naturally causes the offerings of the faithful to come to them.
A Bodhisattva practicing Prajñā must not deceive themselves; it is like walking upon icebergs or treading on the edge of a sword. At the time of death, [the consequences will manifest]—one...
The emotional and intellectual capacities of ordinary beings and sages alike cannot exhaust it; not even a speck of dust of thought can be forgotten.
Following one's thoughts, one undergoes rebirth, assuming the five aggregates—light or heavy—and taking form within the wombs of donkeys or horses.

After being boiled once in the cauldrons of the hells, all that was previously held in memory, all thoughts and perceptions, and all understanding and wisdom are entirely lost at once. One returns once more to be a mere ant.
Ants! From being [like] mosquitoes and gadflies from the very start, though this may be a good cause, it brings about an evil fruit. What are you trying to achieve?
Brothers, it is simply because greed has become your nature that the twenty-five realms of existence are tied to the soles of your feet; there will be no time of accomplishment.
Seeing that the sentient beings of this land possess the root-nature of the Mahāyāna, the Patriarch transmitted only the Mind-Seal to point the way.
This reveals the deluded state of sentient beings. One who attains it makes no distinction between the ordinary and the sage, nor between the foolish and the wise;
furthermore, much emptiness is not as good as a little reality. A true man of great capacity should, right now, directly cease and rest, suddenly bringing all conditions to a halt.
Wandering through the stream of birth and death, you transcend all conventional norms. Your numinous light shines alone, unbound by the burdens of worldly things.

Majestic and sublime, you walk alone throughout the three realms. Why must one have a body sixteen feet tall with the luster of purple-polished gold, a halo encircling the neck, or the mark of a broad and long tongue?
To see me in terms of form is to follow a deviant path. As for the adornments of a retinue, they are attained spontaneously without seeking.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not obstruct the eye of wisdom; having attained the Great Dharani, one awakens to a thousand truths upon hearing them once.
Such a person does not seek even the price of a single meal. If you all are not like this, then the arrival of the Patriarch in this land will inevitably result in both loss and gain.
As for the gain: among thousands or tens of thousands of people, he will rescue but one or two who are fit to be vessels of the Dharma.

Regarding the "vessel" (the practitioner), those who have impairments have already been explained above. If one follows others in practicing according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, it does not hinder one from attaining the four fruits [of the śrāvaka] or the three stages of the sages [of the bodhisattva];
there remains the possibility of further advancement. Therefore, the masters of old said: "If one has realized [the truth], karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty;
if one has not yet realized it, one must repay past debts."

The marks are quiescent; they encompass virtuous function and include both the internal and external. They are profound and vast, neither existent nor empty, neither arising nor ceasing, without end and without beginning.
One seeks them but cannot find them; one abandons them but cannot leave them behind. If one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), confusion and suffering proliferate;
if one awakens to the true nature, emptiness is luminous and all-pervadingly clear. Although this very mind is the Buddha, it can only be realized through personal verification.
Only then will one truly know. Yet, if there is verification and knowing, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence (*bhava*).
If there is neither illumination nor awakening, the clouds of darkness shroud the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If not a single thought arises, the boundaries of past and future are severed;

the essence of illumination stands alone, and both object and self are equally suchness (*tathatā*). One directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is no wisdom and no attainment, neither grasping nor abandoning. There is nothing...

There is no cultivation regarding this. Nevertheless, delusion and awakening further depend upon the mutual relativity of the true and the false. If one seeks the truth while abandoning the false, it is like abandoning one's shadow while wearying one's body.
If one realizes that the false is itself the true, it is like being within the shade where shadows vanish. If one is mindless and forgets even illumination, then all anxieties are cast aside.
If one allows spontaneous, tranquil knowing to arise, then all practices emerge from this. Be expansive and let go of whether things depart or remain; thus, there is quiet discernment.

Awakening to its source and flow, speech and silence do not lose their profound subtlety; movement and stillness do not depart from the realm of the mind. When words cease, both knowing and stillness are forgotten together;

when discussing contemplation, both stillness and knowing are illuminated together. To speak of realization, it cannot be shown to others; to explain the principle, it cannot be understood without realization.
Therefore, awakening to stillness means there is no stillness; true knowing means there is no knowing. By means of this non-duality of knowing and stillness—
With single-mindedness, one accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are fused as two; there is no dwelling and no attachment, nothing to grasp and nothing to collect.
Right and wrong are both forgotten, and subject and object are both severed. When even this severance is stilled, then *prajñā* manifests before one.

*Prajñā* is not a cognitive nature newly produced outside the mind; rather, it is primordially complete. Yet, although it is fundamentally quiescent, it cannot manifest of its own accord; it truly arises through *prajñā*.

The functions of *prajñā* and the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) mutually complete one another through their reciprocal relationship. Fundamental wisdom and initial cultivation are in truth not two distinct entities.
When both are transcended in realization, there is the perfect clarity of wondrous enlightenment; when the beginning and end are integrated, cause and effect are mutually penetrating.
Mind after mind creates the Buddha; there is not a single thought that is not the Buddha-mind. Everywhere one attains the Way; there is not a single speck of dust that is not a Buddha-land.
Therefore, as for reality and delusion, things and self—by raising up any one, the whole is encompassed. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are, in their entirety, of a single essence.

Thus we know that in delusion, the person follows the dharmas, and though the dharmas differ in ten thousand ways, the persons are likewise diverse. But upon awakening, the dharmas follow the person...
Each person possesses a single wisdom that integrates all myriad phenomena; where words end and paths cease, what is cause and what is effect? Its essence is fundamentally still and solitary;

who is the same and who is different? Only by forgetting the self does one become empty and luminous, where movement and stillness blend in profound harmony—like the reflection of the moon’s brilliance through water.
Empty yet visible, the mindless mirror reflects images; it illuminates while remaining eternally empty.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, where he cut his hair short.

The ox immediately passed by at his voice. He spoke again: "In a previous life you did not uphold the precepts; you have a human face but the heart of a beast.

When Jang Muk Danqu suffered from a headache that no physician could cure, he encountered a Chan master named Fenggan, who said he had come from Tiantai to visit the Prefect.
Danqu informed him of his illness. Fenggan said, "The body is composed of the four great elements; illness arises from illusion. If you wish to eliminate it, you must use pure water.
He requested a vessel, consecrated the water with a mantra, and sprayed it [upon Danqu], whereupon the illness was instantly cured. Danqu marveled at this and requested words of instruction.

This was an omen regarding his future safety or peril. Qian said, "Remember your visit to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
