The old man’s face is revealed. The moon shines on the mountain peak; The wind blows through the valley stream. The ancient mirror is bright and clear; The vast sky is pure and open. If you wish to see the Buddha, Look at the ten thousand forms.
The verse says: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven; standing alone on the peak of ten-thousand-fathom crags, he plunders the bright pearl from beneath the jaws of the black dragon.
With a single word, he exposes Vimalakīrti’s deception. Xianwen struck the desk and praised him as excellent.
While Xingyang Qingpou was lying ill, Dayang Jingxuan asked: "This body is like a bubble or an illusion; yet within bubbles and illusions, things are accomplished. If...
If there is not this bubble-like illusion, there is no way to accomplish the Great Matter. If you wish to accomplish the Great Matter, recognize this bubble-like illusion.
"How so? Huizhao asked. Fenyang said, "This is still a matter of 'this side. Xuedou asked, "What about the matter of 'that side'?
Fenyang said, "The crimson wheel shines across the earth; beneath the sea, no flowers are planted. Xuedou laughed and said, "Are you so very alert? Fenyang shouted.
I thought he had forgotten me; yet, he eventually passed into nirvana (in the year Xinyou).
Regarding the Dharma Master Shengchang’s Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Shengchang, whose courtesy name was Zaowei, was the son of the Yan family of Qiantang. Having left the household life and received full ordination, during the Chunhua era, he resided at Nanzhao.
Admiring the spirit of Mount Lu, he drew blood to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He renamed the Lotus Society as the "Society of Pure Conduct Practitioners," and those eminent officials who joined the assembly were all designated as disciples of the Society of Pure Conduct. Prime Minister Wang Dan was its leader;
at that time, there were one hundred and twenty officials, provincial governors, and local magistrates, along with one thousand bhikṣus. This was in the fourth year of the Tianxi era.
On a day in the first month, he sat upright in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name. After a short while, he called out in a forceful voice, "The Buddha has come!
and passed away peacefully. Those present saw the ground turn entirely golden, and it remained so for some time before fading away. Chuyuan took leave of Xiaocong and traveled to Mount Yang.
Yang Yi sent a letter to Huang Zongdan, the Prefect of Yichun, who subsequently invited Chuyuan to appear in the world at Nan Yuan.
(Renxu) Biography of Chan Master Jingxuan. His Dharma heir was Fayuan.
Fayuan was the son of the Wang family from Puyuan in Zheng. At the age of nineteen, he traveled to Bingzhou and sought the Dharma for transcending the world from Zhi Song.
Song said, "You must shave your head and join the ranks of the Triple Gem; only then will it be possible. Yuan asked, "Is there such a distinction as 'monk' and 'layperson' within the Dharma?"
Song said, "Rather than being a layperson, why not become a monk? For as a monk, one can continue the life-span of the Buddha. Thereupon, he cut his hair and received full ordination.
One day, seeing a monk enter the room, he asked about the karmic conditions regarding Zhaozhou’s "Pine Seeds. Song interrogated that monk, and from this, a profound realization dawned within him.
Later, he visited Shanzhao and returned to reflect upon it; both masters bestowed upon him their seals of approval and instructions. (Recorded during the Tianxi era.)
In the interim, he visited Dayang Jingxuan. Their words and spiritual resonance accorded perfectly. Jingxuan sighed and said, "I am old;
will the lineage of the Dongshan school thus end with no one to carry it on? He showed him the cassock and leather sandals he had worn throughout his life.
Yuan said, "I shall take these robes and sandals and seek someone to whom you may entrust them. Jingxuan replied, "If you truly find such a person in the future, bring forth my verse for him."
As proof, the verse says: "The grass before Mount Yangguang awaits its price through you; where the extraordinary sprouts flourish, the profound and secret spiritual root is firmly established.
Its conclusion states: "One who has attained the Dharma must remain hidden among the masses for ten years before they may propagate it."
(Guihai) Chongxian Chan Master: Chongxian opened the Dharma at Xuedou.
He resided at Cuifeng. At the beginning of the Tiansheng era, Zonghui was guarding Siming and welcomed Chongxian to fill the vacancy at Xuedou.
Once Chongxian had arrived, Zonghui said, "Recently, I have been discussing with Elder Qing the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman. I do not yet know its true meaning."
"Is there a place where one can penetrate this? Xian said, "What did Elder Qing say?
Hui said, "He has gone off in that way again. Xian said, "Let us let Elder Qing off with one stroke for now.
Do you scholars know that the monks of the world cannot escape the trap of this old woman? Hui said, "There is another way to speak of it here. Zhao—

"If the Governor had not scrutinized and resolved the matter regarding the old woman, he would have suffered a lifelong grievance. Xian said, "I have scrutinized and resolved it. Hui laughed heartily.

After Xian resided at Xuedou, his school of Chan flourished greatly; monks from all over the land—both those of noble character and those who had fled from worldly constraints—vied with one another to gather at his seat.
He was titled "The Reviver of Yunmen. A monk asked, "Having distanced yourself from the ancestral seat of Cui峰, you have now arrived at the practice site of Yundou.

I wonder, are these one or two? Xian said, "A horse that lacks the thousand-mile stride need not be pursued for its wind-like speed. The monk said, "If that is so, then when the clouds disperse, every house has the moon.

Xian said, "A fellow who has the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake. Ascending the hall, he said: "For those whose ground is stable and secure, even Buddhas and Patriarchs [cannot reach them]..."
How dare one approach? Why is it that they cannot lift their feet? Those who sport with supernatural powers cannot be fathomed by ghosts or spirits.

Why is it that they cannot set down their feet? Even if one were to move back and forth across the ten directions, striking three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred blows in the evening—none would avail.
Again it is said: "When the world of Abhirati was struck with a mallet and shattered into a hundred fragments, why did those people everywhere know how to hold their alms bowls?
Again it is said: "Those who knew the time and frequently visited the Land of Fragrant Accumulation—why did they lose their eyes upon the tip of their staffs?
Again it is said: "When a single flower blooms, spring comes to the whole world; why did the ancient Buddhas not take advantage of this? If you...
If you can penetrate this, you will take up the legacy of the ancient masters of the world.

Suppose, however, a monk were to come forth and say, "Venerable Sir, save yourself first!"—if you grant him this, he is a golden-maned lion. Again it is said: "In every speck of dust is a Buddha-land;
in every leaf is a Śākyamuni. Why, then, did Deshan set up his signboard in the bustling marketplace? It is also said: "Entering the forest without stirring the grass; entering the water..."
The Wave of Immovability. Why did Touzi [say], "A five-colored rope underfoot"? Those who have passed through the barrier—try to discern this!
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the causal condition of the season? Xian said, "Sleeping fool. The monk then shouted. Xian said:
Feigning alertness, he spoke again: "It is like when the world is destroyed and great waters surge forth.
Amidst them, immeasurable sentient beings—some submerged, some not—are wailing piteously to one another, looking up at the azure heavens and all crying out for rescue.
At that time, a celestial being from the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven sees this and, upon seeing them, cries out in a loud voice: 'Alas, sentient beings! I previously warned you repeatedly.'"
"Up until now, you have refused to listen. Now, what recourse is there? (He claps his hands and says: 'Return to the hall! He speaks again:
'One question and one answer—there is still nothing there at all. Even if it were the heavens and the earth, the grasses, trees, and forests...'"
Suppose all were monks, with one voice and many mouths, each posing hundreds of thousands of difficult questions;

the Elder would not need to snap his fingers once for them all to be answered simultaneously, high and low, universally and without the slightest discrepancy. It is further said: "The ten directions have no walls or enclosures."
The four sides have no gates either. Where did the ancients see the guest? If you can utter a "hand-taking" phrase, I grant you dominion over all under heaven.
[The Master] asked a newly arrived monk, "Where are you from? The monk held up his sitting mat. Xian said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its bucket.
The monk said, "It leaps! Xian struck him. The monk said, "It leaps again! Xian struck him once more. The monk then—
The monk ran off. Xian called him back. The monk bowed and said, "I have offended you, Master. Xian said, "I wanted this very remark to circulate; why did you run away?
The monk said, "It has already spread throughout the world. Xian struck him five more blows. The monk said:
There was another monk present. Xuán said, "Just take the blows! Xuán then called the second monk forward and asked, "Where are you from?
The monk replied, "A man from Dingzhou. Xuán said, "Caught! The monk said, "Under the clear blue sky and bright daylight.
Xuán said, "A double case. The monk said, "Exactly so. Xuán pointed with his staff and said, "You were about to leap away! The monk—
As he was about to speak, Xian also struck him five blows. The head monk said, "This monk has received the staff;
he is not like me. Xian immediately called him forward. The monk, saying "Take care," turned and ran away. Xian followed after him and gave him another blow with his staff.
Attendant Baohua came to visit Xian. Xian asked, "Baohua, how many followers do you have? The attendant replied, "There is no need for the Master to concern himself with such things. Xian—
Xuefeng said, "I will ask you properly: why do you leap about? Xiangyan replied, "I cannot let this pass either. Xuefeng said, "..."
The true lion cub finished drinking his tea. Xian grabbed him and said, "Just now you were so discourteous!

As soon as he hesitated, Xian struck him with a palm and said, "Go back and explain yourself clearly. He reported this to Baohua, who asked Cong Daozhe, "How would you respond when someone has been training for a long time?
Cong said, "Blue sky and bright day. Xian said, "Why are you running about in confusion? Cong then let out a shout.
Xian said, "Eat the staff. Cong was about to raise his hand when Xian struck him with a sitting mat and said, "Look at this blind fellow making a mess!
Regarding the "Portrait of the Head Seat," Xian said, "Since you are the Head Seat, why are there two of you? Cong replied, "There is no point in arguing.
Xian said, "You ask me, and I will tell you. Just as Cong was about to question him, Xian said, "At the gate of Xuedou..."
One day, while Xuansha was walking in the mountains with several monks, he saw a cow raise its head. Xuansha asked, "Why does the cow raise its head?
A monk replied, "It is afraid the Master will pierce it through. Xuansha did not approve and said himself, "Watch it when it enters the grass.
When Chief Seat Zong arrived, just as he was about to offer his greetings, Xuansha called him back, saying, "Since you know Xin’s tactics, you must first pay your respects."
Yunmen bowed in surrender. Xiangqian said, "Today you have failed. Yunmen said, "Before the blade was even applied, the thief’s body was already exposed.
Xiangqian said, "This will kill me with indignation! Yunmen said, "A defeated general is not executed. Xiangqian said, "That is true. Yunmen said, "Prostrate yourself!
Xiangqian said, "After thirty years, someone will bring this up. Yunmen said, "I have already let you pass. One day, as Xiangqian was walking in meditation (caṅkrama), Yunmen...
Zhizhang leaned on his staff as a circle of monks gathered around him. He suddenly asked, "When Yunmen was asked, 'What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall?
he replied, 'The body is revealed in the golden wind. Did Yunmen answer this monk, or did he provide an explanation? A senior monk named Youzong said:
Xian waited, saying, "I shall speak once the old man has attained realization. He looked at Zong intently and said in surprise, "Is this not the Great Uncle Han of Dayang?
Zong replied, "The old man has suddenly awakened. Thereupon, he ordered the drum to be beaten and the assembly to gather.

Xian said, "Great assembly, today’s Venerable Zong of Xuedou is none other than the Great Uncle Han of Dayang from years past. Possessing great wisdom and insight, he has hidden his traces and concealed his brilliance."

"If you wish to propagate the ancestral style, I pray that you will graciously ascend this seat. Zong then ascended the seat. A monk asked, "How is it when the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard?
He replied, "Divine light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox. The monk asked again, "How is it after it has emerged from the scabbard?

He replied, "A thousand soldiers are easy to find; a single general is hard to seek. The monk withdrew. Zong said, "When the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard, divine light shoots..."
“Bullfighting! Though a thousand soldiers are easy to find, a single general is truly difficult to seek.
He then descended from his seat, and the entire assembly was greatly startled.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 35; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 36 (Yu character series).

Jiazi (starting in the second year of the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng of the Sòng dynasty); Rénshēn (the era name was changed to Míngdào); Jiǎxiū (changed to Jǐngyòu); Wùyǐn (changed to Bǎoyuán);
Gēngchén (changed to Kāngdìng); Xīnsì (changed to Qìnglì); Jǐchǒu (changed to Huángyòu); Jiǎwǔ (changed to Zhìhé); Bǐngshēn (changed to Jiāyòu);

Jiǎchén (the first year of the Zhìpíng era of Emperor Yīngzōng); Wùshēn (the first year of the Xīníng era of Emperor Shénzōng); Wǔwǔ (the era name was changed to Yuánfēng); Guǐhài (ending in the sixth year of Yuánfēng).
(Jiazi) Chuyuan visited Chan Master Hongyin.
Chuyuan had resided at Nanyuan for three years when he left to seek out Hongyin. Hongyin was a senior disciple of Shoushan;

among the *nàzǐ* (patch-robed monks), none were as refined or extraordinary as him, and no one dared to enter his gate. He had lived on the mountain for thirty years, and his disciples’ spirit overwhelmed all others.

Yuan arrived from various directions with his hair long and uncut, wearing tattered robes and speaking with a rustic accent. When he announced himself as a "Dharma nephew" and entered the hall, the entire assembly burst into laughter.
Yuan asked a youth sent by Yìn, "Whose successor is this elder? Yuan looked up at the roof and said, "I came directly from seeing Fenyang in person."
Yan Yin took up his staff and went out. Looking back, he saw Yuan standing tall and majestic, and asked, "Is there a 'Lion of the West River' in Fenzhou?
Yuan pointed behind him and cried out, "The house is collapsing! Yan Yin turned back to run, but Yuan sat down on the ground, removed one of his sandals, and looked at him.
Yan Yin, being old, forgot what he had asked and lost sight of where Yuan was. Yuan then slowly...
He rose to adjust his robes and, walking away while speaking, said, "To see the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation. He then departed.
Yìn sent someone to pursue him, but it was to no avail. He sighed and said, "Fenzhou has such a son! As for Master Zōngdào, he received the Dharma from Chóngxiǎn.
He lived with a spirit of total liberation and ease, traveling back and forth between Shu and Qi. By nature he was fond of wine; there was no day that he did not become intoxicated.
The villagers loved and respected him, and they would regularly provide him with fine liquor. One day, while he was in the midst of bathing, a messenger arrived with a wine jar.

He came out to receive it entirely naked. Once the wine was finished, the messenger departed. On another occasion, he went down the mountain with his robes disheveled. A man met him and asked, "What is the Way?"
Regarding family tradition: [Zhao]zong said, "A *kāṣāya* wrapped around straw sandals. [The questioner] asked, "What is the meaning? Zong said, "Barefoot, one descends to Tongcheng.
Chen Guan, courtesy name Yingzhong, style name Liaoweng, was a native of Nanjian. By nature he was leisurely and refined; he did not compete with others.

At first, he studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and made considerable progress. Upon meeting a man of wisdom and inquiring into the fundamental tenets of the Tiantai school, he suddenly attained a profound realization.
While in exile on the sea, he never felt dissatisfied; his only constant thought was of returning to the West [to Amitābha].

Later, he visited Weiqing, clinging to his own views and learning in his quest for understanding. Weiqing said, "If you take your own interpretations as the ultimate principle, when will you ever find harmony? Thereupon, Guàn...

Upon attaining enlightenment, he sent a poem in the *qing* style, saying: "In the study hall, sitting motionless, ten thousand cares cease; The sun is warm and the breeze gentle, the plants and trees are secluded.
Who recognizes the matter of the end of two thousand years? Now it resides right before one's very eyes."
○ Chan Master Shanzhao of Fenzhou Enters Nirvana (The Dharma heir of Shoushan Nian; the sixth generation of Linji).
Shanzhao resided at Fenyang, presiding over gods and men with such gravity that for thirty years his feet did not cross the threshold of the gate.

In the second year of the Tiānshèng era, Lord Lǐ, the Governor of Longdé Prefecture, who shared a long-standing friendship with Shanzhao, dispatched a special envoy to invite him to serve as abbot of Chéngtiān Monastery. The messenger...
The messenger went three times and did not receive him, and was punished for it. He went again and said, "I must have the Master go with me; otherwise, there will be nothing but death.
Huizhao laughed and said, "I am old and ill, and have already decided not to leave the mountain. If you insist on going, we shall simply travel one after the other; why must we go together?

The messenger said, "If the Master agrees, I shall choose whether we go first or last as you prefer. Huizhao then ordered that food be prepared and the journey be readied, and informed [the messenger].
The assembly said, "The old monk is departing; who can follow him? One monk stepped forward and said, "I can follow him.
The Master asked, "How many li do you travel in a day? He replied, "Fifty li. The Master said, "You cannot follow me.
Another monk said, "I travel seventy li a day. The Master said, "You also cannot follow me. The attendant said, "I can follow him," but—
When the Master arrived at his destination, he said, "You have followed me all along. He then looked back at his attendant and said, "I shall go on ahead first.
He set down his chopsticks and passed away; the attendant immediately attained parinirvāṇa standing by his side. His age was seventy-eight.
(Biyu) Chan Master Chuyuan began his teaching at Daowu Dinglin.

The śramaṇa Benyan possessed noble conduct and was highly esteemed and respected by scholars and officials. When Hongyin met Benyan, he remarked that Chuyuan’s insight was capable of reviving the Linji lineage.
Upon learning that the seat at Daowu was vacant, Benyan petitioned the prefect to request [Chuyuan for the position].
Yuanzhu presided over the assembly. He cited the words of the former Baoying: "If you can realize the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and patriarchs.
If you can realize the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to gods and humans. If you can realize the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself."
Daowu, however, is not like this. If you can realize it at the first phrase, you are mixing mud with water. If you realize it at the second phrase, you are binding yourself without a rope.
If you realize it at the third phrase, all four corners touch the ground. Therefore it is said: When he rises, the seas are calm and the rivers clear, and travelers clear the way for him.
When he stays, heaven and earth lose their luster, and the sun and moon have no light. In what direction, then, do you all turn?
He let out a breath. After a long while, he said, "Daowu lets you all out a breath," and then he exhaled once.
He stood up, planting his staff firmly, and said again: "Daowu beats the drum; those in the four great continents participate together. My staff is held crosswise, spanning the heavens and the earth;
my alms bowl is turned upside down, covering the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Now I ask you: where do you all turn?"
To find peace in one’s person and establish one’s life—if you know this, you are eating gruel and rice in the continent of Uttarakuru;
if you do not know it, you are eating gruel and rice on a long bedstead. Guquan of the Great Way returned south from Nan, wandering through Xiang.
Hearing that Yuan was residing at Daowu, he went to pay his respects. Yuan said, "White clouds block the mouth of the valley; where has the man of the Way come from? Guquan stepped to the left.
Turning his head to the right, Nanquan said, "What fire came last night that has burned out the ancient tomb? Yuanwu scolded him, saying, "Not yet!
Speak further! Nanquan then made a tiger’s roar. Yuanwu struck him with his sitting cloth; Nanquan caught it and pushed Yuanwu onto the meditation seat.
Yuan also made the sound of a tiger. Quan laughed heartily and said, "I have encountered more than seventy virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra), but today I have finally met a true master.

On the mountain was a pool where a venomous dragon lay dormant; whenever a falling leaf touched the ripples, thunder and rain would follow, such that those passing by for several days dared not even breathe.
One day, as Quan and Yuan were returning home at dusk, it was still hot from the autumn heat. Quan grabbed Yuan’s robe and said, "We can..."

They were bathing together when Yuan grabbed his elbow and walked straight away. Thereupon, Quan undid his clothes and leaped into the water. A thunderclap followed immediately, accompanied by a stench-filled wind and rain;
the trees and forest shook violently. Yuan crouched among the grass, thinking that Quan must have died. After a short while, the weather cleared and brightened;
suddenly, Quan extended his neck out from between the waves and said, "Qi! (A sound of defiance).
(Canyin) Chan Master Huijue resided at Langye Huijue.
A native of Western Luoyang, while still in his early twenties, he escorted the coffin of his father, who had been the Governor of Hengyang, back to Luoyang.

Passing through Liyang, he visited the ancient monastery of Yaoshan, which felt like his former home; thereupon, he left the household life to become a monk. After traveling to various regions to seek instruction, he received the Dharma from Fenyang.
He was to reside at Mount Langye along the banks of the Chushui River. Ascending the hall, he said: "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all causes of birth and death;
yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are precisely the very root of liberation. It is like a lion turning back upon itself:
it has no fixed direction, whether south, north, east, or west. If you do not understand this, do not fail the Elder Śākyamuni."
Hūṃ hūṃ! Entering the hall: You people here who have spent the summer retreat with me—let me point out five kinds of illnesses for you.
First, do not go to a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass. Second, do not dwell alone on a solitary peak.
Third, do not draw the bow and set the arrow. Fourth, do not seek refuge beyond all things. Fifth, do not stagnate in the cycle of birth and death.
Why is this? If one is obstructed in a single place, it is difficult to save oneself; only when one is unimpeded in all five places can one be called a true guide.
You people, if you travel to various regions and encounter a master of clear vision, send me word. This is so that the ancestral wind may not fall into ruin.
If you meet only ordinary practitioners, then simply let the matter rest. Why? Because to boast of fine finery in a land of naked bodies is to be utterly out of place.

I think you are far too ignorant of the timing. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "I, this mountain monk, while examining the ninth chapter of the *Huayan Jinsi-zizhang* (The Golden Lion Chapter of the Avatamsaka), titled 'The Door of Skillful Accomplishment through the Revolving of the Mind,' saw it further explained thus: 'It is like a one-foot mirror that receives layered reflections and images.
If this is so, then to say 'it exists' is acceptable; to say 'it does not exist' is acceptable; to say 'it is neither' is acceptable; and to say 'it is both' is also acceptable."
"You have attained it. Nevertheless, you must further know that there is a single aperture at the top of this staff.
If you do not understand even this, then the staff will pass through the lanterns, enter the Buddha hall, strike Śākyamuni, and knock over Maitreya.

The pillar will clap its hands and laugh out loud, 'Ha-ha! Now tell me, what is it that he laughs at? He planted his staff on the ground and descended from the seat. Rising for the assembly, he took up his staff.
Zhaozhou said, "Panshan’s way: 'The upward path is slippery. Nanyuan said, 'A thousand-fathom cliff standing upright.
Linji said, 'Stone sparks and lightning flashes are dull. Langye has a phrase that settles heaven and earth. Each of you, look up with high resolve! Look up with high resolve!
He struck his staff and descended from the seat. Jue and Xuedou were contemporaries who sang the Way; at that time, they were called the "Two Ambrosias."
Section on Master Yihuai of Tiexi. (Dingmao year) Master Yihuai of Tiexi began his teaching.
Having long been without news of Yihuai since he took leave of Chongxian, a monk came from the Huai region and said to Chongxian, "Yihuai has appeared in the world."
This is an iron Buddha. Xian was made to recite these words of proclamation: "It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water.
The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no mind to retain the shadow. If one can be thus, only then will one understand how to walk among the heterodox classes.
There is no need to lengthen the ducks or shorten the cranes, nor to level mountains or fill valleys. Let it go—hundreds of deformities, thousands of flaws."
I am clumsy. When gathered together, I appear hunched and humble; yet when employed, I dare to vie in wealth with the Eight Great Dragon Kings.
When not employed, I am not worth even half a coin. Xian Da praised me, considering me his peer, and first sent someone to comfort and encourage me;
only after I had harbored this feeling did I dare to offer the formal greetings of a disciple. Entering the hall: "The skull-bone constantly touches the world; the nostrils rub against—"
Touching upon family customs: the plantain opens at the sound of thunder; the sunflower turns toward the sun. O worthy ones, when the plantain opens at the sound of thunder, does it have ears?
When the sunflower turns toward the sun, does it have eyes? If you can understand this, then the Western Heaven is this very land.
If you do not understand, then seven times nine is sixty-three. [Case] closed. Addressing the assembly, the Ancient said: Five...
A segment of emptiness atop the mountain of the aggregates; entering and exiting through the same gate, they do not meet.

For immeasurable kalpas one has lived in a rented house, yet until the end, fails to recognize the master of the house. An old master took it up, saying: "If you do not recognize him, who did you ask when you first rented?
To take it up in such a way is also far-fetched. Why? One must know that upon the road of the dead, there is life.
The place where people emerge is the road upon which the living travel; there, the dead are innumerable.
Which is the road upon which the dead are innumerable? And which is the place where the living emerge on the road of the dead?
If you can examine this clearly, you will cast off the cap of grease and remove the tattered cloth robe. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one sees..."
"If all marks are non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. Fayuan said, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one does not see the Tathāgata.
Huai said, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, where is the eye? This statement contains two points of defeat.
In the room, he asked a monk: "A handless person can make a fist; a tongueless person understands speech. Suddenly, [the monk] was silent.
A person with hands strikes a person without a tongue. What can a person without a tongue say?
Chan Master Jǐngxuán of Dàyáng entered nirvana (the sixth generation of the Cáo-dòng lineage, successor of Liāngshān Guàn).
Jǐngxuán resided at Dàyáng; for fifty years his feet did not cross the threshold and his ribs did not touch the mat. The *Tiānshèng* year, *Bǐng* [cycle].
On the [blank] day of the seventh month of the Year of the Tiger, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly. Three days later, he sent a verse to Minister Wang Shu, saying:
"My age is eighty-five; Through the cultivation of causes, I have reached this point. If you ask where I am returning, The mark upon my crown can never be seen again.
Having set down his pen, he passed away. Attendant Ping had long been within the chamber of Dayang; although he had fully grasped the Master’s intent, he alone...
Taking the promotion and demotion of others as his own concern, he marginalized his peers and resented anyone who surpassed him.

When Huijiao and Fayuan were among the assembly, Fenyang ordered someone to inquire about the fundamental tenets of Dayang. Fenyang sighed with admiration, saying, "The one who will revive the school of Dongshan is none other than Yuan or Jiao.
The two masters replied, "There is Attendant Ping here. Fenyang pointed to his chest and said, "Ping is right here."
This was not auspicious. Furthermore, he pressed his thumb against the center of his palm and showed it, saying, "If you go in this direction, you shall die here.

When Yanqian later moved to Jici Monastery, he left instructions that his entire body should be buried; for ten years there would be no trouble, at which time an offering should be made for Dayang Mountain.

Later, while staying on the mountain, Ping suddenly said, "The geomancy of my late master’s spirit tower is unfavorable. I shall remove it and burn it. He then opened the stupa, revealing Yan’s remains.

His appearance was as if alive; when the firewood was exhausted, he remained solemnly intact. The assembly was all struck with wonder and marvel. Hui Ping then struck his skull with a mattock and added oil and wood to the pyre, whereupon he was suddenly reduced to ashes.
When the matter was reported to the authorities, Hui Ping was punished for filial impiety and forced to return to secular life, where he went by the name Huang Xiuchou.
He went to visit Huijue. Jue said, "In the past you were Attendant Ping; today you are Scholar Huang.
When I was at Dayang, I saw where you were practicing, so I did not accept you. He then visited Fayuan, who likewise paid him no heed.
Later, at a three-way crossroads, he was devoured by a tiger—truly fulfilling the prediction of the forked road. Chao Jing, style name Mingyuan, served in succession through various offices.

In his third year as a court official, he was posthumously granted the title Wen-yuan (Wen-yuan). During his youth, at the age of twenty, he encountered the eminent scholar Liu Yiwei, who questioned him regarding the matter of birth and death.
Liu said, "A person does not truly die. This greatly startled Daohui. Liu further said, "The physical form dies, but the nature is not extinguished.

At this, Daohui finally attained awakening. From then on, he devoted himself to the practice of Chan meditation. He once remarked: "I have observed that in the *Ratnakūṭa*, at the very end it says: 'If that bhikṣu...'"
Of all phenomena, one should grasp only that single practice which is most profoundly accordant—namely, non-arising. This constitutes the practice of dhyāna.
Having examined these words in detail, it is clear that for those who understand the principles of dhyāna and study the Buddha-dharma, this single category alone is sufficient.
On the first day of the first month of the Dingmao year, I completed the ten fascicles of the *Fazang Suijin Lu*. After retiring from public office, I dwell alone on the path.

He lived in seclusion at the monastery and did not attend to other affairs. He instructed his family members that they must not make requests of him on his behalf. When his son passed the jinshi examination, he changed into his official robes to go and offer his thanks;
however, Yuan Hui paid him no heed. He once wrote a poem that said: "Refining ore into gold yields precious treasure; Refining emotion into nature attains the true.
Among those who encounter this principle and converse upon it, There is not one person in a thousand or ten thousand."
Master Shu-ji opened the Dharma at Cuiyan.
While residing at Dayu, the Prefectural Governor invited him to dwell at Cuiyan on Mount Xishan. Shu-ji rebuked those students who were deficient in learning.
"Content with a little," he said, "Fenyang has the 'Ten Wisdoms Identical to Reality' (*shí zhì tóng zhēn*) Dharma-gate, a forge and tongs for refining Buddhas and patriarchs.
The practitioners of Chan nowadays lack fine character; none have become vessels of the Way. A monk asked, "What are the Ten Wisdoms Identical to Reality?
Zhi replied, "The former master said: 'One who expounds the Dharma must possess the Ten Wisdoms Identical to Reality. If one does not possess these ten...'"
When wisdom is identical to the ultimate truth, one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate between the monastic and the lay.

Unable to serve as eyes for others to discern right from wrong, it is like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or like an arrow shot at a target with a severed string. Because the string is severed, the target is not hit;
because the wings are broken, flight through the sky is impossible. Only when the string is strong and the wings are firm can both the target and the sky be thoroughly penetrated. How so?
Birth is the ten wisdoms being identical with the Truth. As all points are now brought forth: first, identity of substance; second, identity in the Great Matter;
third, collective participation; fourth, identity of true resolve; fifth, identity in universal pervasiveness; sixth, identity in full endowment; seventh, identity in gain and loss.
Eighth, identical birth and killing; ninth, identical sound and roar; tenth, identical attainment and entry. The former master further said: "With what kind of person do you attain entry together?
With whom do you roar with the same voice? What is this identical birth and killing? What thing is it that shares in gain and loss? Which one is it that is fully endowed?
What is it that is identical and all-pervasive? Who is it that shares the same true resolve? Who is able [to realize this]?"
"Everyone is alike; who among you shares in the Great Matter? What thing is of the same substance? Is there anyone who can point it out?
To those who can point it out, I shall not withhold my compassion. Those who cannot point it out have yet to possess the eye of study. You must discern this clearly; you must know right from wrong.
The true face is present right now. Zhi said, "The former master said: 'If you wish to know right from wrong, look at the face.'"

It is clearly present before you. It requires great effort. Later generations and late learners stick their heads into the words and phrases, greedily clinging to their meanings and flavors, like a donkey licking where it has urinated;
they cannot be turned back even when struck with a staff. This is because they do not extensively seek out teachers of knowledge or travel through the various traditions.
For the most part, upon receiving but a single word or half a phrase, they nod their heads and swallow their saliva, claiming they have already attained full realization.
Yet, Elder, there are many things about you that remain unsettled. My late teacher had a song on the styles of fifteen houses of Chan, titled "The Song of Universal Wisdom" (*Guangzhi*), which says:
"The Great Way does not speak of high or low; How could True Emptiness ever involve separation or subtlety? The great ocean swallows all streams as one."

Increase and decrease; the wondrous peaks tower high, all supported by the single foundation. Myriad streams and a thousand brooks all flow into the vast ocean; the seven golden mountains and five sacred peaks are all Mount Sumeru.

After the golden-hued light of the Dharma-lamp was transmitted, those who attained it in two, three, four, or seven lifetimes became universally known. The robe of faith rested, yet the function of the mind was widely opened;
elders from all quarters were free to act as they pleased. To recognize the mind as the source is to speak from the very beginning; to be deluded regarding the mind is to pursue external things.
Wuqie (Wu) became suspicious. Zhi said, "This describes the fundamental principle (zongzhi). Sometimes it is direct pointing; sometimes it is skillful application.
It explains the preceding framework to bring forth the subsequent function. Its essential meaning is as clear as a mirror. The blind, lacking the eye of wisdom, cannot peer into it.

The man of clear eyes perceives its subtle essence; he does not speak of victory or defeat, nor fall into folly. In every thing, they accord with the flowing waters of wisdom. This is the style of our school."
Following the occasion, he pointed out the lineage of the school: "The Buddha as mind, the Buddha not as mind—throughout the ages, it has been ever-luminous, with no separate entity.
This very true mind is my own mind; yet even my own mind emerges from expedient means. Zhi said: "This describes the ancestral lineage of Mazu.
Whether in five ranks or three paths, the arrangements adapt skillfully to the faculties [of practitioners] through mutual interplay. Not touching upon the present moment is the fundamental essence."
The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "Stretching out the hand, one penetrates the profound; there is neither Buddha nor Patriarch. Zhi said: "This describes the lineage of Dongshan.
Sometimes master and servant, sometimes father and son; the vessel may be square or round, yet there is no distinction between self and other.

Noble and commoner, duke and marquis—a single path of equality. Foolish and wise, noble and eminent—the gradual stages are made clear. Zhi said: "This describes the lineage of Shishuang. At times he knocks, at times he sings, following along..."

In the dialogues concerning the faculties, the truths are spoken with precision; in responding to others, how could one ever fail in propriety? Yet those of shallow understanding give rise to slander.

Whether explaining both together or speaking of them singly, the sole aim is to provide sharp, immediate Zen delight. To reveal the provisional teachings is not for the sake of competing in cleverness.

Shuguang merely seeks to distinguish the worthy and the wise. There is the circular mark (*maṇḍala*), and there is silent discourse. Brought from a thousand miles away, it is met with a blink of the eye;

though there be ten thousand kinds of ingenuity, they are all but a single void circle. Śākyamuni’s eye is the penetrating faith. Zhi said: "This describes the lineage of the Miu-Oyang (Wu'an) school.

Whether it be the 'total presentation' (*quan ti*) or the 'total application' (*quan yong*), the myriad phenomena in their dense array are truly not shared [by others]; the green mountains do not obstruct."
"White clouds fly; faintly they pass through the golden phoenix atop the dais. Zhi said, "This describes the lineage of Shitou and Yaoshan.
"The mirror of Xianggu; the moon of Dizang. At Xuansha and Chongshou, the illumination is without flaw. Through a question posed by circumstance, he points back to the source.
The essential meaning is clear and bright for those who come. Zhi said, "This describes the lineage of Xuefeng and Dizang. Or...

"Chengti" (Uplifting) or "nian duo" (Picking up): these are the long-standing exhortations of the本色 (true-color) Chan monk. To clarify human affairs within the words is most refined; a true adept is like using a wedge to drive out a wedge.
Whether raising [the mind] for recommendation or extending the hand in grace, what is essential is that the mind be empty so that the mouth may open easily.
Not recognizing the ancestors' manifestation of great compassion, those who merely manage candles run about illuminating the streets. Zhi said: "This describes the Yunmen school."
The lineage of the school as well. Deshan’s staff, Linji’s shout—standing alone in the vastness of heaven and earth, they sweep away all constraints.
Who cares from the start about such chaotic classifications? This talkative old master cannot speak of it. Seizing the opportunity, snatching it away at the moment of action;

the swift and sharp point of his wit flashes like lightning. Heaven and earth are held within the palm of his hand; the spirits of the bamboo and wood have their skulls split open. Whether as guest or host...
Discernment: Fully unfolding the Zen school’s eye of discernment, the three mysteries and three uses strike the mark; the four propositions and hundred negations are all swept away at once.
I urge my fellow practitioners: do not force an understanding. Those who are precociously clever will remain as obstructed as before.

If you do not know the ancestral lineage, do not be reckless; you will sink forever in the ocean of birth and death. It is difficult to encounter, difficult to meet, and difficult even to hear. Be fierce and resolute in body.
His mind became joyful, clear, and expansive. Zhizhi said, "This describes the lineage of Deshan and Linji.
Regarding the transmission of the Dharma from Chan Master Shouzhi to Wenyue:

Wenyue was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. He was short in stature but possessed a refined and beautiful countenance, as well as keen discernment. When he first left home to become a monk, he traveled on foot, carrying a staff.
Jianghuai was once sitting silently on the meditation platform when he recalled the words of an elder and harbored doubts, saying:
"I have heard that Linji stayed at Huangbo for three years, yet Huangbo did not recognize his potential. It was the Venerable Chen who instructed him, telling him to ask about the Great Meaning;

though he asked three times, he was beaten each time, and I have never heard it said that Huangbo taught him through repeated exhortation. It was only upon reaching Dayu that he attained enlightenment—this is what makes him the founder of the Jiangxi school."
Zong said, "The elders have instructed me, and their intent was not in vain; it is simply that what I wish to hear is different. He then went to visit Shouzhi at Dayu.
He saw that the old monk’s quarters were dilapidated and desolate, like a roadside inn. Shouzhi himself carried his straw rain hat and traveled through the marketplace every day;
in the evening, he returned, closed his door, and lay high upon his pillow with an air of unconcern and detachment. Zong wished to pack his bags and depart, but Shouzhi suddenly ascended the seat.
He said, "When the great assembly gathers to eat a stalk of pickled vegetables, if you call it 'a single stalk of vegetables,' you will enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow.

He then descended from his seat; there were no other words. Yuan was greatly startled and went to the Master’s chamber that night. Zhi asked, "What do you seek by coming here? Yuan replied, "I seek the Buddha-mind Dharma.
Zhi said, "The Wheel of Dharma has not yet turned; the Wheel of Food turns first. You, a person of later generations, possess physical strength—why [do you not use it]?"
"I will not go to beg for alms for the sake of the assembly; I am occupied with enduring hunger. Do I have the leisure to preach the Dharma for you?
Zhiyue did not dare to disobey and immediately requested that he go. Upon their return from Fengchuan, Zhi moved his residence to Cuoyan.

Zhiyue went there again to follow him and visited his quarters one night. Zhi said, "Do you wish to seek the Buddha-mind Dharma? You do not consider that you have only recently settled here and the walls of your dwelling are still drafty."
"Leou is also suffering from the cold and snow. Day and night I have been waiting for you to come so that you might provide charcoal for the assembly;

I can no longer endure the cold. Can you preach the Dharma for me? Yue did not dare to refuse. He entered the city to procure charcoal and returned. At that time, there was a vacancy for the *vina* (steward).
One night, Yue went to the master’s quarters (*zhangsì*), and Zhi said, "The Buddha-dharma does not fear being let to rot. From now on, I entrust the office of Hall Superintendent (*tangsi*) to you."
Fayue was unable to speak and departed. The next day, when the wooden mallet was struck to summon the assembly, he made a firm request [to stay]. Fayue showed a look of distress;

having bowed and risen, he intended to leave, but thinking that his labors had already been long and diligent, he desisted. Nevertheless, he harbored a lingering resentment toward Sengzhi, which did not leave his mind. He sat on the ground behind the rear gallery.
A broken bucket and basin were tied beneath a rack; as they fell from the rack, he suddenly attained awakening and instantly saw that the former uses of Zhì had been right before his eyes.
He rushed to put on his *kāṣāya* and went up to the dormitory hall. Zhì welcomed him with a smile and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, rejoice! Your great matter is now concluded.
Wù bowed twice, perspiring profusely, unable to utter a single word as he departed. He served diligently for eight years until Zhì passed away.

(Wu Chen) On a day in the first month of the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, Fǎzhì (Dharma-Wisdom) knew that the Dharma Master Zhīlǐ (Known-Lite) of the Tiantái School had entered nirvana. On that day, Zhīlǐ summoned the great assembly to preach the Dharma;

he suddenly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha several hundred times and then passed away while sitting upright. His remains were displayed in an open coffin for twenty-one days, yet his countenance remained as if alive, and both his nails and hair had grown.
His tongue remained uncorrupted after cremation, like a blooming lotus; his relics were five-colored and their number was beyond reckoning.
(Jisi year) Zibo visited Chan Master Xiaocong. Zibo was a native of Shouzhou;
he was born into a house of prostitution and had no family name. He left the household life to practice the dhūta austerities, subsisting on coarse food and wearing soiled robes.

As for Fayi: while traveling on pilgrimage, he once stayed overnight as a guest and was harassed by a courtesan. He then yielded his bed to her so she could sleep, while he himself sat upright until dawn.
When day broke, the courtesan demanded payment for the lodging; Fayi gave it to her, then left the door and burned his bedding before departing.
The courtesan told her mother the truth, saying, "He is truly a son of the Buddha. She requested to return home to observe a fast and repent;

later, she received the precepts from her teacher and realized the nature of the mind. Upon reaching Dongshan, she visited Xiaocong. At that time, he was planting pine trees. Xiaocong asked, "Regarding the single phrase for ascending the ridge, how would you say it?
Baoshou replied, "It is enough to kill me with its intensity. Xiaocong leaned on his mattock and scolded him, saying, "From where did you get this?"
This was a case of understanding arising according to the words. When Master Cong was asked about "ascending the ridge," he replied, "It would kill one with its breath.
Consequently, the Buddha-dharma was spread. Baoruo requested that Cong provide another explanation on his behalf. Cong said, "Why not say it would kill one with its panting?
Baoruo asked again, "The ridge is right here; where is the Vajra? Cong pointed and said, "This single pine tree was planted by this old monk himself."
(Gengwu) Zixuan visited Chan Master Huijue. Zixuan was a native of Xiuzhou.
He studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* under Dharma Master Min. When he reached the passage, "The two aspects of movement and stillness are clearly not produced," he said to Min:
"Even striking the air or hitting wood still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare; raising an eye or lifting a brow has already become a calculated act."
[The Master] deliberated: "Only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this principle. Min was startled by this. When Chan Master Huijiao ascended the seat, Min immediately asked:
"If it is fundamentally pure and tranquil, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Jiao replied in a stern voice: "It is fundamentally pure and tranquil."
"How did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly come to be? Xuán attained sudden enlightenment. He intended to remain and succeed him.
Jué said, "Your school has not flourished for a long time; you ought to rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha's kindness.

Later, he resided at Chángshuī. Xiǎocōng resided at Dòngshān. On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, he manifested slight illness. He maintained a fast for seven days and assembled the monastics and laypeople, saying: "The Dharma..."
He instructed Xi Dangling to personally take charge as abbot. Thereupon, he recounted with his disciples the story of "Piercing Through the Dharmakāya" and spoke this verse:

"Do not be in such a hurry when practicing Chan and studying the Way; Question until you have pierced through the Dharmakāya hidden within the Northern Dipper. I am now old and decrepit, exceedingly frail and weak."
"Seeing people who lack the power to deliberate, only the hoe knows my Way. When planting pines, I once again ascend the Diamond [Mount].
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His body was cremated, and five-colored *śarīra* relics were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at Xiezi.
Zizao had been in charge of administrative affairs at Wuzu for some time. One day, the Master was ill; he instructed an attendant to go to the storehouse and fetch fresh ginger to brew [a decoction].

[The Master] Yaoyue was reproached by Baoche. The practitioner informed Jie [of the matter]. Jie ordered him to take the money back and buy [ginger]. Only then did Baoche take some ginger and give it to him.

When Xiaocong passed away, he left a will instructing that Baoche should succeed him on the seat. The Prefectural Governor also sent a letter entrusting Jie with the matter, asking him to appoint someone he knew well.
Jie said, "A man who sells raw ginger can stay. He subsequently emerged into the world at Dongshan. Baoche once composed a eulogy for Bodhidharma.
Preface: The true teacher is remote; his disciples look afar. He is unattached within the three realms. Should you wish to arrange him, know that you are greatly mistaken.
To point him out in vain—where could one ever grasp him? If you wish to recognize the true teacher, heaven and earth are vast and open.

Eulogy: The Teacher’s countenance is rare in this world. The Teacher’s eyebrows hang like gathering storm clouds. The Teacher’s eyes flash with the brilliance of lightning. The Teacher’s nose towers like Mount Sumeru.
The Master has no teeth in his mouth; whose fault is it? If he stays longer at Shaolin, he will depart in shame to the West.
When encountering a monk, one should give him a good beating with a mallet. Although this is so, if he does not understand, there is no use for needles or awls.
Upon seeing this encomium, Huìjué composed a verse, saying: "The Master’s eyes are deep; the Master’s nose is large; the Master’s ears are pierced."
The Master’s tongue was swift; the Master’s body was dark; the Master’s mind was upright. Carrying a single sandal, he returned to the shifting sands.
The stone pagoda at Xiong’er Mountain remains even today. Use this verse alone to test all the monks under heaven.
Yiyu was the son of the Lin family of Zhangzhou. When he first visited Fayuan, Fayuan said to others, "This is a model for future students who travel on pilgrimage."
He went next to visit Guquan. He asked, "Is the Abbot here? Guquan asked, "Who is it? He replied, "A wandering monk. "Doing what?
"To pay my respects to the Abbot. "It happens that the Abbot is not here. "And what about you? "I told you he was not here.
Why speak of 'you' and 'I'? Guquan seized his staff and drove him out. The next day he came again, and Guquan drove him out once more. One day he came again and asked.
"Is the hermitage master here? he asked. "Who is it? [the master] replied. "A traveling monk," [the visitor] said, and he lifted the curtain and entered.
Fayan Quan grabbed him by the chest and pinned him down, saying, "In my place, wolves and tigers run rampant. You bed-wetting ghost, what do you want coming here two or three times?
"The people say the hermitage master has personally seen Fenyang," [the visitor] replied. Quan stripped off his robe and shook it out, saying, "You say I have seen Fenyang?"

"How extraordinary this is! he exclaimed, and upon meeting him, prostrated himself, saying, "What is the master of this hermitage? The Master replied, "One must discern it as soon as one enters the gate.
He asked, "Is it not simply this very thing? The Master said, "How many people have you deceived? He asked, "Where is what was said before?"
He said, "When attending to affairs, one is not true to them; it is like calling a bell a water jar. He said, "When the myriad dharmas are extinguished, the whole body is manifested.
When ruler and subject are in harmony, the deviant is removed from the center. He said, "If this donkey-headed fellow does not understand, he simply leaves. Why such chaotic nonsense?
He said, "If it is truly as the Hermit Master says, with a guest arriving, how will you receive him? He said, "Cloud Gate’s steamed bun and Zhaozhou’s tea. He said, "Thank the Master."
[The guest] offered his respects. [Yunju] said, "I do not even have firewood here yet; why speak of 'thank you' so early? Yuyue then departed and went to visit Beichan Zhixian.
Xian asked, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "Chan’an. Xian asked, "How long is Sida’s nostrils?
He replied, "It is the same as what the Master saw at that time. Xian said, "But tell me, when I saw it, was it long?"
"How much? he asked. Xian replied, "The Master seems as if he has never been to Fuyan. Xian laughed and said, "You are merely a person who parrots the words of others.
He then asked, "When you arrived, was Master Ma doing well? "He was well," [the monk] replied. "What did you say to him? [Xian] asked.

"I told the Master not to be so reckless and disorderly," [the monk] replied. "I spared you because you were a new arrival," [Xian] said. "By meeting you, I have also let the Master pass," [the monk] replied.
After the tea was finished, Xian asked where his hometown was. [Xuefeng] said, "Zhangzhou. Xian asked, "What does Sanping do there?
He replied, "He speaks of Chan and speaks of the Way. Xian asked, "How old is he? He replied, "He is the same age as the pillar. Xian said, "As for the pillar, let it be; but what about him?"

[The Master] said, "As for the candela pillar, how many years has it been? [Yuanwu] replied, "As for the candela pillar, even one year would not be too long. [The Master] said, "At midnight, he released a black chicken;
Yuanwu encountered this and turned his mind to serve him as a disciple."
(Renshen) Chan Master Chuyuan resided at Shishuang during the first year of the Mingdao era.
Chuyuan had previously moved from Daowu to reside at Shishuang. Zanyuan, whose courtesy name was Wanzong, was a native of Yiwu and a distant descendant of Dazhi Fudashi.
Having left home to receive full ordination, he traveled to various regions until arriving at Shishuang, where he went to visit Chuyuan. Chuyuan...
Upon seeing him once, Yuan said, "Excellent! Stay well in the stable. Yuan then proceeded to bray like a donkey. Zhiyuan remarked, "Truly a vessel of the Dharma.
He was then appointed as an attendant to assist with pounding grain and splitting firewood, blending indistinguishably with the community for ten years. Zunshe resided at Ciyun Monastery.
A high-ranking official who had written a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* sought his certification. Zunshe then prepared a blazing fire and said to him, "Now, first you must apply yourself..."
Three questions. If my answers accord with the principle, they shall be circulated; if they do not, I pray you consign them to this fire.
How can one annotate the True, Subtle, Wondrous, Primordial, Pure, and Luminous Mind? "Three times four and four times three turn into twelve;
flowing and transforming through three layers, they become ten, a hundred, and a thousand. What is the meaning of this? It is the Perfect Enlightenment realized by the twenty-five sages.

Tong remarked, "Since it is said that there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, how can Mañjuśrī alone choose Avalokiteśvara? At this, the man was at a loss for words and subsequently burned the text.

On the tenth day of the tenth month of the Ren-shen year, he lit incense and paid homage to the Buddha, vowing that all Buddhas would bear witness as he sought rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
He further addressed Avalokiteśvara, saying: "I observe that Avalokiteśvara does not come from the past nor go to the future;
the Buddhas of the ten directions all dwell together in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). I pray that you abide in this limit of reality and accept this single incense stick from me.
Thereupon, he sat and passed away. People saw a great star fall upon Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Seven days later, he was placed in his coffin; his physical appearance remained as if alive.
(Guiyou) Biography of Chan Master Chuyuan, who Transmitted the Dharma to Fanghui.

Fanghui was the son of the Leng family of Yichun. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted; he did not devote himself to the brush or inkstone. Upon leaving home to become a monk, he studied the Buddhist scriptures.
He immediately attained spiritual realization. He humbled himself to seek instruction from veteran masters. At that time, Chu-yuan had moved from Nan-yuan to Dao-wu and Shi-shuang;
Huai would assist him in overseeing all affairs of the monastery. Although he relied upon him for a long time, he had not yet achieved any awakening or insight.
Whenever he consulted him on this matter, Chu-yuan would say, "The administrative office is busy; go now. On another day, when Huai again requested instruction, Chu-yuan said, "The supervisor..."
"Master, on another day your descendants will be spread throughout the world; why be so anxious? One day Yuan was just about to go out when it suddenly began to rain.
He encountered him on a narrow path, and upon seeing him, he seized him, saying, "You old fellow! Today you must explain this to me."
"I did not say I was going to beat you. Daowei replied, "If the Prior knows such matters, that is enough. Before he had finished speaking, Daohui attained great enlightenment.
He immediately prostrated himself on the ground and asked, "What is it like when we meet on a narrow path? Yunmen said, "You should just get out of the way; I have somewhere else to go.

On his return day, Daohui went to the abbot’s quarters with full ceremonial dignity to offer his thanks. Yuanwu scolded him, saying: [Note: This passage is from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 32, concerning the encounter between Master Yunmen Wenyan and the monk Daohui.]
Yuan was not yet present. After the meal, as they were walking toward Mount Heng, a Zen practitioner asked about the Way, but Yuan did not respond.

When Yuan realized that the monk had not gone far, he immediately struck the drum to assemble the community. Yuan scolded him, saying, "It is too late in the day for you to take charge of the assembly;
where did you get such a rule? The monk replied, "Fenyang used to hold evening sessions. One day, Yuan ascended the hall, and the monk came forward to question him.
The hidden birds warble in soft tones. When they leave the clouds and enter the jumbled peaks, what is it like? Yuan said, "I am walking through the wild weeds; you, too, have entered a deep village.
Yuan asked, "The official will not allow even a needle to pass; may I ask one more question? Yuan then gave a shout. Hui said, "A fine shout!"
Yuan also shouted. Hui also shouted. Yuan shouted twice in succession. Hui prostrated. Yuan said, "This matter can only be taken up by one who is a true person.
Hui shook his sleeves and departed. One day, Yuan asked, "When Mazu saw Master Xiangru, he immediately attained enlightenment.
Tell me, where did his delusion lie? Hui replied, "To attain enlightenment is easy; to remain deluded is difficult."

Zhenke was self-assured, believing that he had personally seen Ciming and that there was no one in the world who could satisfy his mind. When he arrived at Jinkuan, he sat in summer retreat together with Attendant Shan.
Through their conversations, Shan realized that Zhenke’s realization was not yet thorough. One day, while walking in the mountains together, they engaged in a sharp exchange of discourse.
Shan picked up a piece of tile, placed it upon a rock, and said, "If you can utter a turning word regarding this, I will grant that you have personally [realized it]."

When Zhen went to see Laoshi, he looked around left and right as if trying to find a point of correspondence. Laoshi rebuked him sharply, saying, "You stand there with thoughts lingering and mental activity stilled; your emotional consciousness has not yet penetrated it.
When have you ever even dreamed of it? Zhen was deeply ashamed and returned to Shishuang. Yuan saw him coming and rebuked him, saying, "A man of the Way traveling for practice in the true manner."
He must have known the proper timing. There was a matter of great urgency; he had arrived here early while the summer retreat was not yet over.

Zhen wept and said, "My elder brother Shan harbors a poisonous heart that ultimately obstructs others; therefore, I have come to see the Master. Yuanyou suddenly asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
He replied, "Cloudless, clouds arise upon the ridge; the moon exists, yet it sets in the heart of the waves. Yuanyou rebuked him, saying, "Your head is white and your teeth are gone, yet you still—"
Holding such a view, how can one escape birth and death? Zhen was truly struck with awe and sought instruction. Yuan said, "Ask me.

When Zhen asked about the previous words regarding the True Principle, Yuan let out a thunderous shout and said: "Cloudless clouds arise upon the ridge; the moon that exists descends into the heart of the waves.

At these words, Zhen attained great enlightenment. Dao-wu Wuzhen was also a successor of Yuan. One day he brought up [the matter]... *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "一日提" (one day he brought up), which indicates the source material is incomplete.*

Holding a basket of snails, he walked around the monastery courtyard, crying out, "Selling snails! He called upon the assembly to offer a turning word (*gūnyǔ*), but none were in accord with the truth.
An elderly master lifted the curtain, saw him, and looked at Zhen with his eyes; he then threw himself down and lay there. Zhen took the basket and left. Shanxian was a native of Linjiang.
Having left home to travel as a wandering monk, he relied upon Yuanjue Yuan. One day, as Yuan ascended the hall, he looked out and beheld [Shanxian].

The assembly said, "The lion lets out a deep sigh; the elephant king turns his head back. Suddenly, Xian had an awakening. He entered the room to present his realization, and Yuan asked, "How do you understand this?
Xian looked back and said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass. Yuan approved of him. From then on, his spiritual eloquence became swift and sharp;
the Zen community referred to him as "The Layman Xian Who Roams Freely Across the Sea. He also studied under Chongxian, whom Chongxian came to cherish.
Junyi remained at his seat for several years. When [the Master] intended to appoint him to reside at Jinge in Mingzhou, Xian heard of this and wrote a verse on the wall before departing.
[Junyi] entered the world at Kaixian, where he succeeded Yuanyuan; he resided there for eighteen years.
(Gengxu) Chan Master Guquan resided at Baozhen Guquan.
He ascended the summit of Mount Heng and stayed at Lanzan Rock. He moved to Bajiao, and then again to Baozhen—this being a most perilous and remote place in the region of Heng and Xiang.
One night, while sitting on the ground at Mount Zhurong, a great python coiled around him. Guquan untied his sash.
He tied it around his waist. At midnight he was nowhere to be seen. The next day, they searched the mountain everywhere; the sash was found wrapped around a withered pine tree.
He used to carry a large wine gourd on a staff as he came and went through the mountains. When people asked what was inside the gourd, he said, "The elixir of the Great Way.
Shouzhi lived at both Dayu and Cuoyan. Not more than thirty people ever ascended these two mountains, for their buildings were old and dilapidated.
He propped up a leaning wall with a wooden beam; passersby feared it might collapse on them. Carrying his straw hat, he traveled daily through cities, towns, and villages.

The monastery was like a way-station inn, and even the supply of gruel and rice was sometimes interrupted. He once composed a verse on Dongshan’s "Three Pounds of Flax": "With eyes askance, I read Sanskrit characters;
With tongue clicking, I recite mantras. I blow the fire with my long, pointed beak; Wood fills the hearth and smoke rises thick. Furthermore:
Addressing the assembly: "There is no oil in the sand—how pitiful! Cuiyan chews his rice and feeds it to an infant.

When you understand the true nature of good and evil at that time, you will realize for the first time that your face was covered in ashes all along. He entered nirvana in the early years of the Jingyou era.
(Wuyi, the 47th year of the Yuanfeng era; Year of Yi Hai) The Fifth Patriarch, Master Jie, entered nirvana (he was the Dharma heir of Shuangquan Kuan and the third generation of Yunmen).
Dongshan Zibo was a man of refined discipline who strictly upheld the precepts. However, by nature he was fond of reputation and concerned with outward propriety.
Having first received the Dharma from Master Jie, Jie abandoned his assembly in his later years to visit him. Because of this conduct, Zibo’s background fell into public suspicion.

He appeared to be like this, yet he did not perform formal salutations; thus, his precepts eventually led him to great simplicity. Before long, leaning on his staff in front of the Sangha Hall, he passed away with a smile.
The Fifth Patriarch sent someone to retrieve his remains and enshrine them in a stupa.
(Bingzi year) Chan Master Chuyuan resided at Fuyan on Mount Nanyue.
As the seat of Fuyan was vacant, the Prefectural Governor invited Chuyuan to serve as abbot. Huinan was the son of the Zhang family of Yushan;
from childhood he abstained from meat and avoided games. He left home to receive full ordination, always sitting in the full lotus posture and always walking with a steady gaze.

Relying on Letan Cheng, Nan was appointed to share the teaching seat to receive and guide practitioners, and his reputation resounded throughout all quarters. When Wenyue saw him, he sighed in admiration, saying, "Nan possesses the capacity for the Way;
it is only a pity that he has not yet been subjected to the essential tongs and hammer. Later, they traveled together to the Western Mountains.
During a night conversation regarding the Dharma-way of Yunmen, Wenyue said, "Although Master Cheng is a successor of Yunmen, his Dharma-way is different. Nan asked:
This is why they differ. It is said that Yunmen was like nine-refined cinnabar, which can transform iron into gold;
Chenggong was like quicksilver, which may be admired as silver but flows away when subjected to smelting. Nanru threw his pillow at him, and the next day Yue apologized for his transgression.
He said again, "Yunmen’s bearing was like that of a king. Would he have been willing to die for words that are dead? Master Cheng had a Dharma to bestow upon others;

these are dead words. Can dead words bring people to life? He then turned his back and walked away. Yunmen called out from behind, pulling him back, saying, "If it is so, who then accords with your own intention?
He replied, "Shishuang Yuan; his skillful means surpass those of all quarters. You should go see him; you must not let this pass."
Yemo Ji said to himself, "Master Yue likes Cuiyan, so he sent me to see Shishuang. If I gain something from seeing him, what does it matter to Yue? He then set out for Shishuang.
On the way, he heard that Yuan was not diligent in his duties and treated the monastic community with contempt; consequently, he went up Mount Heng to visit Xian of Fuyan.
Xian appointed him as the recorder (*jishi*). Shortly thereafter, Xian passed away, and the Prefectural Governor appointed Yuan to fill the position.
Nanxinti wished to observe the man’s character. Once Yuan arrived, he began to disparage and deconstruct the various schools, enumerating point by point their views as heterodox interpretations;
even the secret instructions and essential teachings of Lestam were included among those rejected.

Nanxinti was reduced to silence, but then recalling what Yuan had said on previous occasions, he suddenly changed his tone and said, "For a great man, how can there be self-doubt or obstruction within the very core of his being?"
He then went to his quarters. Yuan said, "The Secretary has already led his disciples to travel abroad. If you have any doubts, you may sit here and discuss them.
Nan declined, his entreaty becoming even more earnest. Yuan said, "The Secretary studied Yunmen Chan; he must surely be well-versed in its essential meaning."

Regarding the saying that Dongshan’s three blows of the staff were "having a share of receiving the blows" or "not having a share of receiving the blows," [Dongshan] said, "There was a share of receiving the blows.
Yuanse Zhuang said: "If hearing the sound of the three blows of the staff constitutes receiving the blows, then from morning until evening [one would be receiving them]."
"When a magpie caws or a crow caws, everyone should receive a blow of the staff. Yuan then sat upright and received the incense from Nan, performing a prostration.

Yuan asked again, "If you truly understand the meaning of Yunmen’s words, then as for Zhaozhou saying, 'I have thoroughly investigated the old woman of Mount Tai,' where exactly was it that he investigated her through? Nan broke into a cold sweat and was unable to answer.
He hurried out. The next day he went again, but Yuan continued to revile him incessantly. Nan said, "Is reviling the compassionate gift of the Dharma?
Yuan laughed and said, "Do you take this as a reviling? At these words, Nan attained great enlightenment. He cried out involuntarily, "Lectan’s words are indeed dead words!
He then offered this verse: "Standing out from the forest is Zhaozhou; The old woman has seen through him—there is no further cause."
"Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; let not the traveler treat the road as an enemy. Yuan pointed his finger at the characters and submerged them.
"The character for 'South' has been changed to 'Easy. Yuan nodded his head in agreement. He then stayed for over a month before taking his leave. He asked Yuan, "Ultimately, what is the Great Matter?
Yuan scolded him, saying, "Wearing clothes and eating food is not the ultimate. Defecating and urinating is not [the ultimate]."

Bi-jing Yuan-lian, who resided at Guanghui Monastery, on a day in the first month of the third year of the Jingyou era, displayed four circular diagrams (*yuanxiang*), each inscribed with the characters for tiger, dog, rat, and ox.
He hung them upon the door of his quarters. On a day in the ninth month, he passed into *nirvāṇa*. (Recorded by Chenggu).

A native of Xichuan, he was a scholar in his youth and was renowned for his extensive learning. He left the household life to follow Jingxuan and later visited Nanyue Ya, who permitted him to enter the inner circle of disciples.
He traveled to Mount Lu, where he resided at the Hongjue Pagoda Cloister and was known as the "Old Pagoda Master.

Initially, he preached the Dharma at Mount Zhi and became a successor of Yunmen. When Fan Zhongyan was serving as Governor of Rao, in the fourth year of the Jingyou era, he invited Gu to reside at Jianfu Temple.

Fan Zhongyan, style name Xiwen, was a native of Wu Commandery. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he served in successive offices up to the rank of Vice Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shumimi) and Participant in Government Affairs (Canzhizhengshi).

He is regarded as the foremost figure among the personages of the Song dynasty. While he was governing Wu, Huijue came to visit him; after staying for several days, Zhongyan attained realization beneath Huijue’s discourse.
He presented Huijue with this verse: "Throughout the consecutive days we conversed, dissolving the knot of doubt; Who would have thought that of my ephemeral life, half would be spent [in this way]?"
Daily leisure. I simply wish to share this leisure with the Master until we grow old together, fully gathering in our cognitive nature at the profound pivot.
(Wuyin) Chan Master Chuyuan arrives in the capital.
Chuyuan, having moved from Fuyan to reside at Xinghua, addresses the assembly. Striking the meditation seat once with his staff, he says:
"Will the great assembly return? Have you not heard it said: 'In a single blow, all that is known is forgotten; there is no further need for cultivation.
Those who have attained the Way in all quarters say this is the highest capacity.

Xiangyan’s awakening in this manner clearly constitutes the realization of the Tathāgata-dhyāna, yet he has not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna. Now tell me, what excellence does the Patriarchal-dhyāna possess? If one were to..."
To take the words as the standard is to lead later generations astray. Even if one were to respond directly under the staff, one would still be failing the former sages.
All phenomena are fundamentally at ease; it is only people who create their own turmoil. Therefore, when this mountain monk dwells at Fuyan, I see only the realm of Fuyan:
rising late and sleeping early, sometimes clouds arise over the azure peaks, sometimes the moon sinks into the cold pool, and the singing birds fly about and call out.
Before the Prajñā Terrace, scattering *sāla* flower petals beside Mount Zhurong, he sat with his lean staff upon a *pāṇḍaka* rock.
