[Jiazi]: Chan Master Zongben resided at Hui-lin Monastery.
In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree for Zongben to reside at HuiLin Chan Monastery.

The Emperor summoned him for an audience and granted him a seat, instructing him that as the Chan school was newly flourishing, he should provide excellent guidance. After the audience concluded, the Emperor remarked to his attendants, "He is truly a monk of genuine merit and wisdom.
When Fayun Monastery in Bianjing was newly completed, the Emperor issued a decree for Fazhou to serve as its founding abbot and conferred upon him the title "Yuantong."
At that time, Li Bashi Lin was skilled at painting horses. Xiu rebuked him, saying, "You, a scholar's son, have already gained fame for your painting;
moreover, you paint horses. You expect others to praise it as a masterpiece, but even entering the belly of a horse is enough to be feared.

From then on, Lin ceased painting. Xiu urged him to paint an image of Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgression. Huang Tingjian composed flowery verses about this, which people vied with one another to transmit.
Xiu also rebuked him, saying, "Would you truly apply the subtlety of your brush and ink to such a thing? Huijian laughed and said, "Will you then place me within the belly of a horse as well?
Xiu replied, "With your flowery words, you stir the hearts of all people under heaven; your lustful mind knows no bounds."
Fearing that his horse’s belly might sink into the mud, he was terrified of falling into hell. Daojian then received the appointment as the Abbot of Yuanyou.

He was the son of the Wang family of Shangrao and attained enlightenment under Huineng. After Huineng passed away, Daojian traveled to Xiang, where he built a hermitage upon the old foundations of Mazu. Disciples flocked to follow him.

Xie Jingwen, the Governor of Tan, wished to transfer the Chan community to the Vinaya residence at Daolin Temple and invited Daojian to serve as its first patriarch. The sacred images and shrines at Daolin were numerous.
Guān was located west of the Xīng mountains. Huìyòu cleared away the surrounding wilderness and established a spacious hall and meditation chambers there to gather students from all quarters.

When the laborers attempted to dismantle the Buddhist images, Huìyòu himself took a hoe and threw them into the river, saying, "In the past they were originally not created; how can they be destroyed now?"
"In my Dharma, there is not even ordinary sentiment; how could it harbor saintly understanding? Faan was the son of the Xu family of Linchuan.

Having received the essential instructions of Yihuai, he returned to Linchuan and resided at Ruyi Yuan on Mount Huang. His residence consisted of dilapidated buildings and broken walls, barely sufficient to shield him from wind and rain.

Yet within ten years, a great mansion had been transformed there as if by magic. He subsequently abandoned that place and went to stay at Yan'en Temple in Wuning, where he lived in a few rooms of thatched grass huts.

An’s broken bed had no slats, yet he found peace and joy in it. When the Governor sought to reform the wealthy and powerful by planning a new construction project, An laughed and said, “The Dharma is fundamentally for the salvation of people.
To force this upon them now before they have developed the aspiration [for enlightenment] is called ‘worldly activity’;
it is not called ‘Buddhist practice. An was like a brother to Fa-xiu; once, Fa-xiu sent a letter inviting An, but upon reading it, An laughed and said:

"At first, I thought Xiu possessed brilliance; only now do I know his folly. For one who has left the household life, he must attend to the task of liberation between the graves and beneath the trees as if his own hair were on fire.
Yet now, for no reason, he has erected a great mansion at the crossroads of the eightfold thoroughfare."

"To maintain several hundred idle fellows—this is truly to urinate on one's own bed while wide awake. Why should I even deign to converse with them? Yet, from this point on, my school will become increasingly diminished.

In the seventh month of the Jiazi year of the Yuanfeng era, he commanded his disciples to collect the documents of the abbot’s quarters and burn them together, entrusting the affairs of the monastery to a single monk.
In the eighth month, he passed away. Fu Bi, courtesy name Yanguo, was a native of Henan.
When Fan Zhen was governing Bozhou, he heard of the flourishing reputation of Xiu Yong’s Dharma assembly and went there to resolve his doubts. He arrived just as Yong was ascending the seat;

as Yong looked around at the great assembly with his eyes, Fan already gained a subtle understanding. He then assumed the etiquette of a disciple and requested to enter the inner circle of the teaching.
Upon seeing him, Yong immediately said, "The Minister has already come in; Fu Bi is still outside. When Bi heard this, sweat flowed down his body.
He turned his back [and left], but before long he was suddenly enlightened. In his later years, while residing in Luoyang, he invited Sengyong to stay at Zhaoti Monastery.
Once he arrived, [Hui]bi welcomed him to live in the rear garden, where he visited and consulted him morning and evening. Whenever Bi engaged in discussion, Yong invariably considered it incorrect.
One day, he said to Bi, "When this mountain monk nods his head in approval, that shall be it. From then on, whenever Bi had anything to say, Yong would...
He shook his head. One day, in the middle of the night, Bi had a great realization; he hurried to knock on the door, but Yong had already closed the gate and was sleeping.
Hearing the sound, Yong called out, "Sir, rejoice! The great matter is finished.
He did not open the gate again until the following morning when they met. At dawn, Bi went to see him; from afar, Yong saw him and nodded. Bi was overjoyed.

At that time, Zongben was residing at Hui-lin Temple in accordance with an imperial decree. Fǎbì sent him a poem in thanks, which said: "Through meeting Master Yóng, I have realized the profound depth of my awakening;

By successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Old Teacher. Though it is said that the rivers and mountains of the southeast are far away, My eyes face the Ling-guang and Miao-yin [pagodas] directly.
After their parting, he replied to Yóng’s letter, saying: "In your instructions, you state that inquiring into this matter must surely involve a karmic cause from a former life. It is not..."
"It can indeed be accomplished in this life; it is truly so. However, since meeting you, Master, that which has been forgotten since beginningless time was suddenly recognized.
From now on, I must certainly pull myself out from the sea of birth and death; this is no ordinary debt of gratitude.
Though one were to exhaust all one's strength to describe it, one could not express it fully. You have gained many hundreds or thousands of disciples like me—what benefit is there in that?"
Regarding this matter, you have not transcended the human realm. From beneath the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, you have produced nothing more than an old, sickly layman;
what benefit can such a person provide to the Master? You say that you have undergone much refinement and training—this is indeed true.

Yet when I think of the ancient patriarchs, they initially remained with their own teachers for twenty or thirty years, and even those who stayed the least were there for ten or so years, serving them day and night.
I respectfully submit this. Having heard the Way and heard the Dharma, I have finally attained a thorough understanding from top to bottom.
Yet, I reflect that on two occasions I was graced by the Master’s compassionate attention, during which we spent two months together seeking instruction.

Could I have become more intelligent than others, or been capable of applying such great effort, were it not for the Master’s skillful means in exerting himself to extract and reveal the truth? Otherwise, how could I have reached this shore? Although...
Exhausting one's heels and crown, it is difficult to repay such kindness. Sūshì visited Mount Lú and stayed overnight at Dōnglín Monastery.
There, he discussed the "discourse on insentient beings" with Chángzǒng and attained a realization. At dawn, he offered this verse: "The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue;
The color of the mountains is surely the pure and serene body. Last night, eighty-four thousand verses were spoken; How shall I present them to others on another day? Chángzǒng approved.
Shao Yong, courtesy name Yaofu, was a native of Fanyang. He resided in Luoyang for forty years, living in poverty while delighting in the Way.
In winter he used no stove, and in summer he used no fan; there were several years when he did not go to his mat at night. He had a poem on studying Buddhism that says:

"Eating to satiety and wearing fine clothes are not easy to sustain; As the days grow long, what can one do with the seasons of sorrow? Seeking fame in my prime, I threw myself to the Sage of Xuan; Fearing death..."

In old age, one cherishes Śākyamuni, yet in vain seeks to sever attachments; the more one strives, the heavier the bonds become. One prays for the removal of illness, only to find that ailments multiply.
The vast expanse of the Yangtze River is as level as a roll of silk; fortunately, it was windless, yet waves have arisen once more. Fan Zhen, styled Jingren, was a native of Huayang.
He served successively as Hanlin Xueshi (Academician of the Hanlin Academy). Someone asked Zhen why he did not believe in Buddhism. He replied: "You must wait..."
"I joined my palms and prostrated. Then did you believe [me]? Huang Tingjian said: "One day I passed by Zhen. We sat facing each other all day long;
he sat with his body upright and straight, never once looking back, nor did he show any sign of weariness. Zhen said: 'For twenty years now...'"
Not a single thought has ever arisen in my breast. For two or three years, I have not read books much;

when there are no guests, I sit alone all day long and do not sleep until the second watch of the night. Even though my children’s joyful shouts are but a few feet away, I hear none of them. Jian said:
Lord Gong was indeed a master of Buddhist study. Sima Guang initially did not favor Chan; however, after Huo Wenkui asked Master Da Ben about the Dharma, he suddenly attained a realization.
Later, while discussing the characteristics of emptiness with Fan Zhen, he humorously wrote a poem saying: "There is no need for heavenly maidens to scatter flowers;
I have already understood how to stir the Chan mind. He further said: "I, this humble son, realized it long ago; Jingren has now [attained it] once more."

[The Master] said: "Delusion! It is also said: 'Once you have reached the shore, what need is there for a raft? To wield a hoe, one does not require gold. Let the floating clouds come and go as they will;
the bright moon remains in the heart of heaven. Lady Wang, the consort of the Prince of Jing, was devoted to the practice of the Pure Land. One of her maidservants was indolent and disrespectful.

The Lady reprimanded her severely, whereupon the maid repented and became diligent in her practice. Suddenly, she passed away without illness. She appeared in a dream to another maidservant and said: "I have received [the grace of] my Lord..."

The person was instructed. Having already been born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), shortly thereafter the lady also had a dream. She dreamed that she was wandering with her handmaid in a jeweled pond and saw a flower upon which celestial robes fluttered;
inscribed upon it was the name "Yang Jie. On another flower, [a figure] sat in court attire; inscribed upon it was the name "Ma Qian.

Furthermore, they saw a golden platform radiating brilliant light. The handmaid pointed and said, "This is the place where the lady will be reborn. Upon waking, she reflected on this even more deeply.

Jingjin was eighty-one years old. On the morning of his birthday, he held a candle and burned incense, standing before the Hall of Guanyin while his attendants were preparing the ritual offerings for his long life; he then passed away while standing.
○ Qingyuan visited Chan Master Fayen.
Qingyuan was the son of the Li family from Linqiong. Initially, while reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
He questioned his lecturer about this, but the teacher could not answer. Qingyuan sighed and said: "The study of doctrine and its terminology is not what I seek."
Having resolved upon the great matter of birth and death, he traveled south to visit various masters in succession. Upon reaching Taiping, he met Fayan.
He then wandered for alms in Luzhou, where he happened to fall to the ground during a rainstorm. While he was feeling distressed and vexed, he heard two people cursing each other harshly.

One of them advised the other, saying, "You are still suffering from affliction. At these words, Yuan had a sudden realization. When he returned and someone asked him a question, Fayan would immediately say: [The rest of the dialogue follows].
"I am not as good as you; you will surely attain excellence on your own. Or he might say, "I have never done so; I am not as good as you.
Yuan was increasingly suspicious and asked Huayan, "Who among your disciples understands the Master’s way of speaking? Huayan replied, "The Venerable Li understands it.
Yuan then sought a definitive resolution from Yuanli. Yuanli took Yuan by the ear and led him around the brazier several times, walking and speaking as they went.
The Master said, "You understand it well yourself. [Liu] Yuan said, "I hoped you would provide an awakening; why do you mock me so?

The Master said, "In the future, when you attain realization, you will finally understand the twists and turns of today. At that time, Yuan was seventeen years old. After this, Yuan returned to Guizong.
When he moved to Mount Jinshan, he addressed the assembly: "In the past, Yunmen’s preaching was like clouds and rain; he absolutely disliked people recording his words.

Whenever he saw such records, he would scold and drive them away, saying: 'You do not use your own mouths, yet you record my words. At some other time, you will come to trade off my teachings as if they were mere merchandise.'"
The records of his encounters with disciples within the hall were all composed by Xianglin Mingjiao, who used paper as his garment and wrote down whatever he heard immediately.
Later scholars who fish for and hunt through these words and phrases are just like those who blow on a net hoping to fill it; they are either fools or madmen.
At that time, the monasteries of Jiangzhe took texts to be Chan itself, calling this "requesting instruction. Thus, Yuan used this to satirize them.
Zhou Dunyi, courtesy name Maoshu, was a native of Chengleng. While traveling to Mount Lu, he took delight in its secluded beauty and subsequently built a residence there.
He first visited Zu Xin and inquired about the meaning of the "special transmission outside the teachings. Zu Xin said, "It is enough simply to attend to matters within your own house.
Confucius said, 'If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening. Ultimately, what is it that constitutes [the Way]?"
"Is it not acceptable to die this evening? Yanzi did not change his joy; what was the object of his joy?
Simply by reaching the ultimate in this, after a long time, there will naturally be a point of resonance and accord. He then visited Changzong to discuss nature (*xing*).

When the conversation reached the realms of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), and they were seen to penetrate one another, he attained a solitary realization with chilling clarity. Later, he composed the *Taiji tu* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate), every word of which emerged from [this realization].
From the oral instructions of Donglin, at that time Liaoyuan was residing at Luanchi. Yí went there to pay his respects, and they discussed the Way together. Yí asked:
"The *Zhongyong* says, 'That which is mandated by Heaven is called nature; following one's nature is called the Way. Yet in the Chan gate, it is said that 'mindlessness is the Way.

What does this mean? Liaoyuan replied: "If you have doubts, investigate them separately. Yí asked: "If one investigates, it is not non-existent. Ultimately, what constitutes the Way? Liaoyuan replied: "Green mountains filling the eyes."
"Leave it to me to see," he said. Yí was suddenly enlightened. One day, seeing weeds growing before the window, he remarked, "This is just like my own state of mind.
He presented this verse: "In the past there was no delusion, and now there is no awakening;

Mind and object merge, revealing what was hidden. Weeds grow deep outside the window, pines stand by the path; All day long they cause people to look at them without weariness. He then requested [the transmission from] Yuán.

He served as the presiding master of the Qingsong Society, emulating the precedent of the "White Lotus" story. Later, he propagated and clarified the Daoxue (Learning of the Way), and scholars referred to him as Master Liangxi.
He once said of himself: "This wondrous mind of mine was truly inspired by Huanglong and brought to full illumination by Foyin.

However, as for the expansive and penetrating principles of the *Yi*, had it not been for Donglin’s opening, revealing, polishing, and wiping away [obscurations], there would have been no way to manifest them."
The interior was suddenly illuminated. Yang Shi, whose courtesy name was Zhongli and style name Guishan, was a native of Jiangle.
He studied under the two Cheng brothers and once said: "When Weisheng Gao begged some vinegar to give to others, Confucius considered it improper. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:"

"The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When Confucianism and Buddhism reach this point, there is truly no distinction between their principles. He was on friendly terms with Chang Zong;

addressing Zong, he said, "Although your Zen studies are profound, you have not yet attained anything regarding the Way of the Confucians. Zong replied, "As for the essential points of the Confucian Way..."
I also remember a little. But tell me: "The gentleman finds fulfillment in whatever he enters; what is it that he finds? At that time, he remained silent. He once had a poem that said:
"Advancing day by day until every pool is filled—when will it ever cease? Only upon reaching the sea can the myriad streams find rest."
I only fear that Daotuo’s madness has not yet ceased; sitting in restless agitation, he still cherishes his head in the mirror.
(Yichou) Chan Master Kewen resided at Baoning.
Having retired from his post at Dongshan, he traveled east through the Three Wu regions and reached Jinling. At that time, Prime Minister Wang Anshi—
While residing at Dinglin, he heard that Master Wen had arrived; he hurried out to meet him with his shoes on backward, regretting that they had met so late.

He asked why, among all the scriptures, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* alone does not begin by specifying the time and place. [Wen] replied: "That which is expounded in the Sudden Vehicle directly reveals it to sentient beings as manifest in their daily lives;
it does not belong to the present or the past. Right now, the Elder Monk and you, Excellency, have both entered the Great Treasury of Radiance."
In the samādhi of playful mastery, they act as host and guest to one another, regardless of time or place. Again, he asked:

"The sutra states that all sentient beings have already realized perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Yet Guifeng [Zongmi] interprets 'realization' as 'possession. How can this be? He replied:

"If the *Awakening of Faith* could be altered, then the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* could also be altered. Does the *Vimalakīrti* not say: 'Furthermore, one does not realize it by extinguishing sensation'? Now, if one does not extinguish..."
Realizing it through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is identical in meaning to the intent of realizing *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*.
For the ignorance manifesting in the conduct of sentient beings is precisely the fundamental great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) of the Tathāgata. Guifeng’s statement was incorrect.

Anshi was greatly pleased and consequently donated his residence to become a monastery, inviting Wen to be its founding patriarch; thus it was called Baoning. He specifically requested from the court the bestowal of the title Zhenjing, and resided there.

Before long, the days passed without the scholar-officials failing to visit him. Unable to endure the weariness of such constant labor, Wen returned to Gaoyang and built a hermitage at the foot of Jiufeng, naming it "Retiring in Old Age.
Students came to him from afar. Wen Zhun was the son of the Liang family of Xingyuan;
he left home to become a monk at the age of eight. When Fan Gong, the Regional Commander of Shaanxi, wished to take him with him to the west, Zhun said: "To ascend..."

One seeks jade from the mountains; another seeks pearls from the sea. Each person has their own aspiration. My original practice was to study the Way; worldly preferences were never my true intention.

Fan found his words extraordinary and subsequently ordained him as a monk. When he first visited Liangshan Cheng, Cheng said, "You have driven away the crows before you have even received the precepts."
"May I venture to study the Buddha Vehicle? Zhun replied, "Is the ritual site itself the precepts? Or are the three *karmavācanas*, the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and the *ācārya* the precepts?
Cheng was greatly startled. Zhun said, "Even so, how could I dare not receive the instruction? Thereupon, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He traveled extensively among the lecture halls, expounding the essential outlines of various schools. He then departed, saying, "I do not seek a profound understanding. [This refers to] Dharma Master Tanyan.
He patted him and said, "You are a Dharma vessel. In the south there are Great Beings who are like the Sublime Sages:
such as Zhennu of Mount Gui and Zhenjing of Jiufeng. You should go to seek them. Zhun then went to Mount Gui, but there was no accord. He proceeded to Jiufeng and attended under Kewen.
Kewen asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Dayang. [Kewen] asked, "Where did you spend the summer retreat? He replied, "At Dayue. [Kewen] asked, "What..."
He was at Renchu, which is called Xingyuan Prefecture. Wenzhan held out his hand and asked, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? Zhun was at a loss for words.
Wenzhan said, "Just a moment ago, your responses were one by one numinous and clear, one by one truly authentic.

Yet, as soon as you spoke the words, 'How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand,' it immediately became an obstruction. Tell me, where does the sickness lie? Zhun said, "I do not understand. Wenzhan said, "Everything is manifest."

[The practice] was perfected. He further instructed whom else to understand [it]? [They] followed his teachings with devotion and joined the ranks of his disciples. ○ Lü Huíqīng, the Grand Marshal, once studied the *Fǎjièguān* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One day while traveling to Mount Wǔtái, clouds and mist suddenly gathered from all sides, accompanied by a violent wind, thunder, and rain.

The sound shook the forests and ravines. You were struck with terror. After some time, the weather cleared slightly, and you saw a youth clad in hempen garments with his hair disheveled approaching, holding a Sanskrit manuscript in his hand.
He asked, "Official, what do you seek by coming here? You replied, "I wish to see the Great Being. He asked, "For what purpose do you wish to see him?
You said, "I have often perused the *Avataṃsaka* Mahāyāna teachings; their purport is profound and their meaning vast. I hope that the Great Being will grant me an exposition."

Excellent interpretation! I hope this commentary will circulate widely so that those of great resolve may immediately attain awakening. [The author] says: "The sublime intent of the Buddhas is concise, simple, and clear;
it can be understood by paying heed to the insights of the former masters. For instance, the commentary on a single chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* did not exceed a few sheets of paper.

In the present age, however, the commentaries have become as sprawling as weeds, numbering nearly a hundred volumes, yet the sacred intent becomes ever more remote. This is truly what is called 'fragmentation'."
"This is the Great Way. The official said, "A mere youth, yet you dare to scold your seniors? The youth smiled and said, "Official, you are mistaken.
Here, every blade of grass and every tree is none other than the realm of Mañjuśrī. It resides in your daily activities;
when you encounter things without delusion, this is truly Mañjuśrī himself. As soon as the official bowed and rose, the youth manifested the form of a Bodhisattva.
The Lion-Crossing [statue] vanished amidst the clouds and dispersed.
(Bingyin) Chan Master Zongben returned to Wu in the first year of the Yuanyou era.
Zongben requested to return home on account of his old age; once he had left the capital city, princes, dukes, and nobles came to see him off.
Carriages and cavalry followed one after another. Benhuai said, "The months and years cannot be toyed with;
old age and illness do not wait for anyone. Strive only in diligent cultivation without indolence; this is true companionship. Those who heard this were moved without exception.
Huang Tingjian visited Master Zuxin and requested instruction on the direct and swift path. Zuxin said, "It is just as when Zhongni said: 'My disciples think that I am being secretive.'"
"Is it so? I have nothing hidden from you. How could Grand Historian Juyan possibly have reasoned this out? As soon as Juyan opened his mouth, he said, "Not so, not so!
Juyan remained in a state of persistent confusion. One day, while attending Master Xishan on a walk, the mountain cassias were in full bloom.
Xishan asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the wood-camelia? He replied, "I do. Xishan said, "I have nothing hidden from you. Juyan joyfully attained realization.
He immediately bowed and said, "Master, you possess such a compassionate and earnest heart. Xinxiao replied, "I only wish for you to reach home.
Jian, whose courtesy name was Luzhi and whose style name was Shangu, resided at Mount Jiangshan. In the first year of the Yuanyou era, he suddenly said:
"I wish to return to Eastern Wu. He hurriedly prepared his departure, but suddenly passed away. [His body became] pure white. He was the son of the Zhi family of Zizhou; his father was Qian.

Having heard the Dharma from a practitioner on Mount Song, he treated life and death as a play. Though dressed in lay clothes, his practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) was such that none among the monastics or the laity could surpass him.
From his youth, Bai had heard his father’s instructions, which seemed like the ripening of past habituation. One day, while leaping across a stream, he suddenly attained realization. It was not...

Jue lost his composure and laughed. He subsequently shaved his head and received full ordination. He traveled extensively through the lecture halls of Chengdu, mastering both the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Phenomena) schools of Buddhism.
He then departed for a southern journey to visit Huangbo Weisheng. Having attended him for over a year, Weisheng had never once looked at him.

Baizhang served him with even greater diligence. One day, Weisheng suddenly raised his eyes and looked at him; Baizhang shouted, "This old fellow, why can you not hold yourself together? Weisheng was greatly [impressed].
He smiled, thereby providing a seal of certification regarding the mind-ground. At the end of the Yuanfeng era, Changsheng returned to Shu; Baizhang took up his headcloth and alms bowl to follow him.

"To fail to transcend the ocean of nature is the bondage of principle and phenomena; to fail to penetrate the wheel of sound is the bondage of language. Thereupon, he purified [the hall].
The assembly turned toward him in unison, and the lecture hall was left empty. Shanzhou, who had received the essential instructions from Canshui Fang, emerged into the world and resided at Linjiang.
Entering the hall, he said: "A falcon in the vast sky, ten thousand miles of clouds—just this one sudden swoop! What is it? He let out a shout.

Having finished speaking, he sat in *padmāsana* and passed away. Shengquan Shaodeng was the son of the Chen family of Gutian. At his birth, an extraordinary fragrance filled the room, and a purple cap covered his head.

From childhood, he abstained from meat. He received the tonsure and the full precepts, after which he traveled to various regions to study under Weifang. Upon seeing him, he attained realization of the essential meaning.
He then returned to his native village. Suddenly one day, he requested a bath, changed his robes, ascended his seat, and spoke this verse:
"I am fifty-three years old; in going or staying, I have fundamentally no attachment. Facing death, what shall I do? There is no need for idle chatter. He then passed away peacefully and solemnly.
Two days later, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he suddenly awoke again. Thereafter, his four elements were light and at ease, and his body frequently produced *śarīra* relics.
When invited to light lamps during great droughts to pray for rain, every prayer was immediately answered. He moved his residence to Shengquan, where his Dharma path flourished greatly.
Kaiyuan Faming attained the Dharma and returned to his native village. Later, he lived in a state of carefree wandering.
He was very fond of wine. Whenever he played *hulu*, he would become deeply intoxicated and regularly sing several stanzas of Liuchun’s lyrics as his daily custom;
he would refuse when summoned for a vegetarian feast but comply when invited to drink. This continued for over ten years, and everyone called him the "Drunk Monk.
One day, he said to the assembly of monks, "I shall depart tomorrow morning; do not go elsewhere. The assembly laughed to themselves at this. At dawn the following day, he gathered [his things].
He took his seat, called out loudly, "I am departing! Listen to a verse! When the assembly heard this, they rushed to look. Ming then sang:
"Throughout my life, I have stumbled in intoxication; yet even in intoxication, there was discernment.
Tonight, when the wine is sobered, where shall I be—by the willow bank, with the morning breeze and the waning moon? Having finished speaking, he passed away silently.
(Dingmao year) Chan Master Congyue resided at Doushuai Monastery.

From Congyue, he received the essential instructions and secret precepts of Kewen. Later, he stayed at Luyuan. There was an attendant named Qing-su, a native of Min, who had long studied under Chuyuan;
he was eighty years old and had lived in seclusion at Luyuan. Congyue shared a residence with him. Once, while eating lychees preserved in honey, it happened that—
Su Guo entered the gate. Yue called out to him, saying, "This is the local fruit of our village; you may eat it with me.
Su said, "Since the passing of my late teacher, I have not been able to obtain this food for a long time. Yue asked, "Who was your late teacher? Su replied, "Ciming. I am merely his attendant."
"Only thirteen years. Yue was struck with astonishment and said, "To have endured the duties of service for thirteen years—how could this be anything other than having attained the Way?
He then offered him leftover fruit and gradually grew closer to him. Su asked, "Whom did you see? He replied, "Dongshan Wen.
Su asked, "Whom did Wen see? He replied, "Huanglong Nan. Su asked, "Did Nan the junior monk see our former teacher? [He replied,] "No."
The Dharma and the Way had flourished so greatly for a long time that Huiyi was both delighted and struck with wonder. He then placed incense in his sleeve and went to pay his respects to Sengsu.
Sengsu avoided him, saying, "I am of meager merit; my former master gave me a prophecy that I am not permitted to act as a teacher. Huiyi was even more respectful.
Sengsu then said, "Out of pity for your sincerity, I shall violate my former master’s prophecy. Tell me what you have attained throughout your life. Huiyi then fully explained what he had realized.
Jian Su said, "One may only enter the Buddha; one must not enter the Mara. Jian asked, "What do you mean by this? Su replied, "Have you not seen the ancients say:
'The final phrase is where one first arrives at the secure gate'? As Yuan Yue prepared to respond, Su suddenly asked abruptly, "How would you explain 'non-action' (wuwei)?
Yuan Yue again prepared to respond, but Su suddenly laughed loudly. Yuan Yue was suddenly enlightened, and Su then gave him his seal of approval.
He further cautioned him, saying: "The texts shown to you all contain correct knowledge and vision; however, you left them too early and were unable to exhaust their subtlety.
I shall now point them out for you, so that you may attain great mastery in their realization. In the future, by no means should you succeed me.
In the year Dingmao, Yue resided at the Doushuai Monastery in Long’an.
(Wuchen) Chan Master Fayan began teaching at Baiyun on the Wuchen day.
Fayan was about to move to the Haihui Monastery at Baiyun when Qingyuan, having just returned from holding his alms bowl in Feichuan, said with deep regret:
"My affairs have only just begun to be settled; how can I follow him again? We are going to a desolate county—how will I be able to investigate and resolve my own matter?"
He then composed a verse to bid farewell. Yan sent him off with this verse: "When we saw you off before the Baotai Pavilion, The peach blossoms were like brocade and the willows like eyebrows.
On this day next year, leaning against the railing to look, They will still be just two or three green branches as they were.
Yan moved to Haihui Temple and addressed the assembly: "You must affix the two characters 'birth and death' to your foreheads and seek a clear understanding of them."
It is like merely following along with the crowd in a pack, spending one's days in idle clamor.

When the Old Man of Yama settles the account for the price of your food, do not say, "I never told you so. If you are practicing the Way, you must examine yourself at all times and maintain constant mindfulness.
You must discern where you are gaining strength and where you are failing to gain strength; where you are striking [the mark]...

Regarding "losing the point": this refers to those who, as soon as they sit upon their meditation cushions, fall into a daze; when they finally wake up, their minds are filled with random, wandering thoughts;
and as soon as they leave their cushions, they engage in idle chatter. To practice the Way in such a manner is to lose the point.
Even until Maitreya descends to be born, you will not yet have grasped it. You must exert yourself with fierce intensity and hold fast to the *huatou*.
Examine it by day and examine it by night, contending with it head-to-head. You must not sit idly within the armor of "nothingness," nor must you sit rigidly upon your meditation cushion.
If distracting thoughts proliferate ever more, simply let go lightly and walk about once you have descended from your seat.
Having encountered [this realization], he returns once more to his meditation cushion. He opens both eyes, clenches both fists, and straightens his spine.
Raising the *huatou* (critical phrase) as before, he immediately feels a sense of clarity and coolness, like adding a ladle of cold water to a pot of boiling soup.
If one practices in this manner, there will certainly come a time of arriving home. Entering the hall, he said: "All of you, see how the old monk stirs things up."
[He] pursed his lips. Holding up the whisk, he immediately formed a resolute conviction. Yet, when the mountain birds gathered and the ox swished its tail, he treated them as mere trifles.
Little did he know that "the sound of the eaves does not cease from last week's rain; the lightning still connects with the thunder of the coming night. Ascending the hall, [he said]:
"Yesterday, this mountain monk entered the city and saw a stage of puppet plays. I could not help but approach to watch."
At times he saw someone dignified and extraordinary; at other times he saw someone ugly and repulsive.

Whether moving, turning, walking, or sitting—whether blue, yellow, red, or white—he perceived each one clearly. Yet when he looked closely, he realized that there was actually a person behind a green cloth curtain.
Unable to restrain his amusement, the mountain monk asked the High Official his surname. He replied, "Old Monk, you have already seen me; why do you ask what my surname is?"
"Great assembly, when I, this mountain monk, was questioned by him, I was left with no words to respond and no principle to defend.
Is there anyone who can speak for me? Yesterday I fell at that point; today I pull up the roots here. [The Master] thanked the Superintendent of Receipt and ascended the hall.
Regarding the matter of human life and destiny, the first thing required is the ○. To achieve this ○, one must first...
One must be on guard against the "circle" (the trap). If one is a true person of the circle, they will ascend the hall to take their leave of the street-attendant.
Yesterday, the street-attendant took a handful of sand and, upon seeing the old monk, threw it straight in his face.
Fortunately, the old monk saw it coming and shielded himself with the sleeve of his robe; thus, nothing was hindered. Today, I bring this up for the great assembly, not daring to conceal it.
Why? To reward his great audacity, he has managed to deploy such a hand and foot. Suppose someone were to ask Baiyun, "Why did you simply stop there? Have you not heard it said:
"In old age, one does not rely on physical strength for capability"? Although this is so, the roles of guest and host remain distinct.
On the anniversary of Master Duan’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "Last year, at this very time, [it was like] many years ago."
Three matters. This year being exactly like this, it is mostly the seven matters of last year. Among these ten matters, there are many that cannot be counted. Why is this?
If one removes the seven and the three and retains but one matter, then what was said last year is the same as today.

It is as swift as an arrow and as black as lacquer. The wordless child’s mouth flaps and flaps; the footless immortal splits [open]— [Note: The final phrase "劈" (pī) appears to be an incomplete or truncated fragment of a larger expression.]

He kicks out his chest and says, "Intersecting. He descends from the seat. Entering the hall, he preaches the Buddha’s Dharma; he strikes the mallet and raises the whisk—ten thousand miles of white clouds.
Deshan enters the gate and immediately strikes with his staff; Linji enters the gate and immediately shouts—ten thousand miles of white clouds.
Then, it is not permitted to be thus; it is not permitted not to be thus; it is not permitted to be both thus and not thus. Even so...
"White clouds ten thousand miles away. Perhaps someone might come forward and say, "Elder, for you to speak thus is also just 'white clouds ten thousand miles away.
This talk is called 'the short man watching the play,' going up and down along with others; thirty years from now, it will be a source of great laughter.
But tell me, what is there to laugh at? Laughing at "white clouds ten thousand miles away. [The Master] addressed the assembly, citing the Venerable De...
Shan replied to the monk, "In our school, there are no words or phrases. Upon hearing this, Xuefeng attained realization.
Later, Xuefeng said, "At that time, I went with empty hands and returned with empty hands. Yanyou commented, "Today Baoyun speaks for those who have not yet penetrated through."
There was a man who came from Dongjing. When asked where he had come from, he replied, "From Suzhou.
When asked how matters were in Suzhou, he said, "Everything is as usual. Although this may be so, he could not deceive Baiyun.
Why is this? It is simply because their spoken sounds differ. Ultimately, how is it so? "The water chestnuts of Suzhou and the white lotus roots of Shaoyang. To the assembly:
"I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings; when the one flower blooms, the five petals unfold, and the fruiting is accomplished naturally."
Master Dharma came with his feet and spoke with his mouth as he pleased. Yet the descendants of later generations have mostly fallen into calculating deliberation.
Do you wish to understand the place where the flowers bloom and the fruit ripens? Pear trees in Zhengzhou, jujube trees in Qingzhou—among all things, nothing surpasses the excellence of their source.
[He] addressed the assembly: "True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and sentient beings are both merely figurative designations. Or there may be someone...

When someone comes forward and asks, "What about Old Panshan? simply say to them: "Were it not for the early blossoming of flowers along the purple road, how could the yellow oriole descend upon the willow branches?
If they further ask, "What about Old Wuzu? say yourself: "Yes! Be alert! And say again: "Be clear-headed!"
Awakening is the same as non-awakening; returning home, one seeks the old path. One character is one character; one phrase is one phrase.
Since childhood, I have never uttered empty words; at two years of age, I learned to take steps. A lotus grows from the still water; it blooms once every year.

It is further said: "The fellow carrying a shoulder-pole sells his wares at a low price; three catties of hemp for the scale. A hundred or a thousand years of stagnant goods—where can one find a place to set one's whole body?
He utters this remark: "It is like a water buffalo passing through a window frame; its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through, yet its tail remains stuck."
For what reason could his tail not pass through? One day, Yuan held his staff and walked around the corridor, saying, "Is there anyone born under the Ox who would come to ask for a divination?
The assembly remained silent. He then said to himself, "Today Sun Bin has opened his shop, yet not a single person comes to visit.
It is a pity that this three-foot-long dragon-whisker is called nothing more than an ordinary document. In his room, he frequently asked the monks, "I beg you..."
The woman’s soul has departed; which one is the true one? Furthermore, he would often extend his hand and ask a monk, "How do you call this?

[O] Yuanji. A native of the Lin family of Fuzhou, he was a disciple of Master Hui-nan. Having received the secret transmission of the Dharma, he bore the burden of the monastic community, indifferent to cold and heat.
He cleared fields and planted pines, remaining in a single post for ten years without change. Hui-nan praised him as one who had emerged in the true style of the school.
When [Dongshan] Lianchi was appointed to Huanglong, he took Xuanji with him. When the journey ended in the south, Lianchi completed the construction of a stupa and took his leave.
Both Guifeng and Dayue vied to invite him, but he did not go. Zen Master Zuoxin wished for him to succeed to the Dharma seat of Huanglong, but Xuanji shook his head and departed directly.

When someone asked the reason, he said: "My late master instructed me that until I reached the age of fifty, I must not serve as a teacher. At the time he returned to Guizong, he was... (the text ends here).
Forty-eight. Liaoyuan was persuaded by the request of Ying Wen to reside at Cuiyan in Hongzhou (Jisi year).
Zongxian, a native of Chengdu, had been a renowned Jinshi scholar since his youth.
Once, while playing by scooping up mountain stream water during the day, he continued into the night.
He contemplated this, whereupon he suddenly saw a cool radiance filling the room. He wished to draw some up, but it was impossible; yet the dusty world of phenomena became empty of itself.
He exclaimed, "The net of my worldly existence has been torn asunder! He went to rely upon Chunbai (Zhaozhou) to receive the full ordination.

Later, while following the assembly for consultation and inquiry, Chunbai one day asked Xian: "Standing atop the highest peak, walking on the bottom of the deepest sea—how do you understand this? At that, Xian...
Upon hearing these words, he attained sudden enlightenment and said, "My heels have been nailed down!
Bai picked up his whisk and asked, "What about this one? Xian smiled and departed. Yuan You resided at Daolin for six years before leaving to travel to Mount Lu.
King Xu petitioned the Emperor to grant him a purple robe and cassock; Yuan You composed a verse to decline it. When people asked the reason, Yuan You said, "The bestowal of a sovereign..."
"I do not dare decline, for it would bring me near to fame; it is simply that the Dharma has not yet been equalized. Once, Huiman did not accept an invitation for the following day, saying:
"If there were no *saṃgha* in the world, I would accept your offering. What kind of man was Huiman? Wang Anshang once asked Faying about the Dharma.

He remained at Yunju. Daoyou said, "I am taking these bones to return them for burial on the mountain peak. They mounted the carriage and departed. Xianzheng of Nanshan was the son of the Zhang family of Tingzhou.
He studied under Yuanyou at Daolin and received his seal of approval. When Yuanyou moved to Luohan, Xianzheng followed him there.
Nan was the Director of the Hall of the Palm (Zhangtangsi). When Foyu moved to Yunju, Nan succeeded him on the seat. There was a lay practitioner named Zhang Jie who attended upon Nan.
One day, Nan asked him, "How is it? Jie replied, "I do not understand. Nan continued to press him without ceasing, until Jie suddenly grasped the essential meaning.
He offered a verse on the opportune moment, containing the lines: "A body sleeps upon the great ocean with Mount Sumeru as its pillow; the stone sprout shoots forth its branches—how truly marvelous!
Having finished, he took his leave. Nan showed him the verse, saying: "When you reach Mount Lu, Mount Lu will come to you;
who else but you would go to part from Mount Lu? Go out the gate and ask the wind atop the ridge; the Great Way flows freely, having no basis to rely upon. —Shanben Ying.

He was a man from the Han dynasty, a descendant of Dong Zhongshu. He was erudite and lived with pure cultivation, having no desire for official service. Upon arriving at the capital, he became a great monk and took joy in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
One night, he dreamed of a youth resembling Sudhana as depicted in secular paintings, who joined his palms and led him toward the south.
Jue said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have bestowed their grace upon me. Do you wish for me to travel south to seek out my friends?
Thereupon, he traveled to Suzhou to visit Zongben. Once Zongben was seated, he looked specifically at him; Shenjian intuitively grasped the essential meaning of the school's teachings.

He emerged from seclusion at Shuanglin Temple, and in the year Jisi, he moved his residence to Jingci Temple in Qiantang. At that time, he was known as Daoben (Great Ben) and Zongze (Small Ben). — Recorded by Xiang.

Yang Ren abandoned Confucianism to follow the teachings of Śākyamuni. His character and integrity were lofty and far-reaching, and his learning was profound and vast. He studied under Fufu of Changlu in Zhenzhou;

after Fufu passed away, Jize succeeded him. In the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, he organized the "Excellence Assembly of the Lotus" (*padma-viśeṣa-parṣad*), leading a great multitude of practitioners to each recite the name of Amitābha Buddha—whether a hundred times, a thousand times, or even ten thousand times—and dedicated these merits toward their common aspiration to be reborn in that land.
One night, Master Guo dreamed of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, appearing to be about thirty years of age, with a refined and elegant countenance and graceful manners.
The man bowed to Zhe and said, "I wish to enter your assembly for Amitābha; please record my name.

Zhe then took up his brush from the *Shenghui lu* (Record of the Victorious Assembly) and asked, "What is your name? The man replied, "Puhui. Once Zhe had finished writing it down, the man in white robes spoke again.
He said, "My elder brother also mentioned your name. Zé asked, "What is your elder brother’s name? He replied, "Puxian.

As soon as he had finished speaking, he vanished. Huiyuan resided at Chengtian Monastery. In the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, he carried his alms bowl to Lake Hu. The people of the lake said, "A master makes wherever he goes his home;
why do you take such trouble to favor only Gusu? They earnestly entreated him to stay and would not let him return. Consequently, he remained at Baoben Monastery.
(Gengwu) Chan Master Kewen resided at Guizong.
Having occupied Gaoyuan for six years, he moved his residence to Guizong. Zhu Shiying of Xianmu asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Kewen replied: "I am honored by your letter asking about the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha-dharma is supremely wondrous and non-dual; it is simply that [you] have not yet arrived."
Regarding the subtle, there are mutual variations in length; yet once one reaches the subtle, the person who awakens to the mind knows their own mind as it truly is:

ultimately and fundamentally they have attained Buddhahood. They are as they truly are in their sovereignty, as they truly are in their peace and bliss, as they truly are in their liberation, and as they truly are in their purity.
In daily life, they employ only their own mind; as their own mind manifests transformations, they grasp them and use them at will—there is no need for questioning.
Right and wrong—once you attempt to conceive of them through the mind and deliberate upon them, they are already not so. When the mind does not intervene, everything is authentically true;

everything is luminously wondrous; everything is like a lotus flower that remains unstained by water. Therefore, by deluding one's own mind, one becomes a sentient being; by awakening to one's own mind, one becomes a Buddha.
Thus, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, and Buddhas are themselves sentient beings. It is only due to delusion and awakening that there appears this distinction between "self" and "other."

Furthermore, many scholars of today do not believe in their own minds and do not awaken to their own minds; consequently, they fail to attain the luminous and wondrous enjoyment of their own minds, nor do they attain the peace, bliss, and liberation of their own minds.
Instead, they falsely imagine that Chan and the Way exist outside the mind, and they vainly establish various extraordinary and marvelous doctrines.

They give rise to false notions of acceptance and rejection; even if they practice cultivation, they fall into the realms of external paths, the two vehicles, meditative stillness, or nihilistic views.

Fashou presided over Fayun Monastery. On the eighth day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he manifested illness. An imperial edict summoned a medical officer from the Hanlin Academy to attend to him.
When the physician requested to take his pulse, Fashou looked up at him and said, "Who are you? I am ill and shall simply die; what is the use of seeking treatment?"
Therefore, he regarded life as something to be cherished. Regarding the three matters of daily life, birth, and death—dreams—he made no distinction between them and cast them all aside.
He called for his attendant, changed his robes, and sat down peacefully. He spoke this verse: "When coming there was no Buddha; when departing, it is empty.

North, south, east, and west—the affairs are all one and the same. Abiding in the six sense-bases provides no benefit. After a long silence, the Chief Administrator (Jiansi) stepped forward and said, "Master..."
"Furthermore, why do you not speak the final word? Xiu replied, "Be careful, be careful," and having finished speaking, he passed away.
In the second year of the Zhiping era, Huailian submitted a memorial requesting to return home. In the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-one.
(Xinwei) Chan Master Hepan Deput entered nirvana (the ninth generation of Linji, successor of Huanglong Nan).
Deput resided at Hepan for twelve years. On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "When the venerable elders of various regions pass away, the monasteries invariably perform memorial rites. I consider these to be merely empty formalities.

When I die, you should be the first to perform a memorial service for me. He then ordered that preparations for a memorial service be made from this day forward. The assembly, considering him old and fond of humorous speech, [did not take it seriously].
He then asked, "When will the Master pass away? Baizhang replied, "When your offerings cease, I shall depart. Thereupon, he curtained off the main hall and sat in its center.
As the disciples set out the offerings and read the liturgical texts, they knelt and made bows before presenting the food. Baizhang ate his fill with complete composure.

From the chief disciples down to the laborers of the monastery, each took turns performing the rites day by day. When the offerings ceased on the first day of the sixth year, Baizhang said, "Tomorrow it will snow."
Qing then departed. When he arrived there, it suddenly snowed. Once the snow had ceased, Pu’an sat upright, burned incense, and passed away.
In the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, Zhang Shangying was serving as the Transport Commissioner for Jiangxi.

He went to visit Changzong, who gave him his seal of approval and said, "I have a disciple who has attained the Dharma and resides at Yuxi; he is Cigu Jing. You may speak with him. Ying subsequently took up his post in Fuzhou, Fujian. All...

Chan welcomed him. At the outset, he paid his respects with reverence; at the end, he questioned Dou-shuai Cong-yue, saying, "I have heard that you, Master, are quick-witted and skilled in literary composition.
Cong-yue smiled and said, "The Surveillance Commissioner has lost one of his eyes. Cong-yue was the ninth-generation descendant of Linji.
If one were to compare quick wit and literary skill with the Surveillance Commissioner, it would be exactly like the Commissioner comparing Chan with Cong-yue.
Ying silently took note of this. He asked how far Yuxi was from here; [the master] replied, "Thirty li. He asked about Doushuai; [the master] replied, "Five li.

They then passed through Doushuai. Previously, Yue had dreamed that he was boxing with the sun. Upon waking, he said to the Head Seat: "The image of the revolving sun—Transport Commissioner Zhang is about to pass by here;
I shall deeply pierce and painfully prick him. The Head Seat said: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The scholar-officials loathe those who oppose them and may sometimes give rise to separate feuds. Huì said, "Even if it causes me vexation, it will only result in my being driven from this monastery.
As they were conversing, Yīng repeatedly praised Master Zǒng. Huì was not yet convinced of his words.
When the conversation reached a late hour and turned to matters of the Chan school, Huì rose, burned incense, and requested the Buddhas of the ten directions to bear witness, saying: "Dōnglín..."
Having thus granted his seal of approval, [the Master] asked, "Regarding the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, do you have even the slightest doubt?
He replied, "I do. [The Master] asked, "What words do you doubt? He replied, "I doubt the 'One-legged Verse' of Xiangyan and the story of Deshan’s bowl.

[The Master] said, "Since you have doubts regarding these, all else is merely intellectual speculation and conceptual understanding; how could it ever reach the state of great peace and bliss? Furthermore, as for the cliff..."
The Master spoke of the final phrase: "Is it existent? Is it non-existent? Yang replied, "It is existent. The Master laughed heartily and returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him.
That night, Yang could not sleep peacefully; at the fifth watch, he rose from his bed and accidentally knocked over his urinal. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment.

He knocked on the door of the Abbot’s quarters and said, "I have already caught the thief. [The Abbot] asked, "Where are the stolen goods? Ying was speechless. Xue said, "Commissioner, please leave for now;
we shall meet tomorrow. The following morning, Ying then offered this verse: "The drum falls silent and the bell is hushed as he returns with his bowl;
Yantou’s single pressure was like a clap of thunder. Indeed, he could live for only three years; Was it not because he encountered..."
When Taiso arrived, Yue said to him, "The reason one practices Chan is precisely because the life-root has not been severed and one gives rise to understanding based on words.
You have already deeply realized such teachings; however, as for the most subtle and minute points, they cause people to remain unaware and unknowing."
Falling into the mundane world, he then composed a verse as proof, saying: "In the places where one wanders at ease, every step is as it should be.

Though dwelling amidst sound and form, how could one be hindered by existence or non-existence? The single mind is without differentiation; the myriad dharmas are not distinct. Cease dividing essence from function;

do not choose between the refined and the coarse. Unimpeded when facing critical moments, responding to things without constraint. When sentiments of right and wrong are exhausted, both ordinary and sage are eliminated. Who attains, and who is attained?"

Lost! What is near and what is distant? Taking the head for the tail, pointing to reality as if it were empty. Turning one’s back on the realm of demons, turning one’s feet toward the path of the heterodox.

There is no longer anything of "contrary" or "favorable," and one does not violate the practice. Because of an invitation to find joy, he went to Jianchang and composed ten verses to recount these matters.
○ Changzong resided at Donglin; the assembly numbered over seven hundred. Whenever they sat in meditation, the multitude saw [the Master] behind the abbot’s quarters.
A white light and a fragrant celestial incense pervaded the air. On a day in the ninth month of the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, after bathing, he sat peacefully and passed away.
○ Huìyuán resided at Bàoběn Monastery; for thirty years, his side never touched the mat. On a day in the eleventh month of the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, [he passed away].
Ascending the seat, he spoke this verse: "Fifty-five years of a dream-like and illusory body— Who is truly kin among the east, west, south, and north?
When white clouds have dispersed beyond the thousand mountains, A fresh crescent moon shines across ten-thousand-li of autumn sky. Having finished speaking, he passed away. —Yuanjing.
He resided at Upper Tianzhu for a total of seventeen years. During the Yuanfeng era, he took his leave and traveled there again; three years later, he passed away.
Throughout his life, he had diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice. Once, while eating with the monk Xizhong, Xizhong saw a light like a firefly upon [the Master's] pure eyebrows;
when he grasped it, he obtained a *śarīra*. Furthermore, he obtained *śarīra* from the place where the Master slept and rose. On the ninth month of the sixth year of the Yuanyou era.
As he was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he entered the Fangyuan Hermitage and sat in meditation, ceasing all speech and abstaining from food and drink.
He said to Canliao Daoqian, "My pure karma (*śukla-karma*) is about to be perfected; if there are no obstacles for seven days, my vow shall be fulfilled.

On the seventh day, he presented a verse to the assembly and passed away with auspicious signs. When Jing was first born, a piece of flesh rose on his left shoulder like the cord of a *kāṣāya* robe. [He lived] eighty-one years.

The sun then set. When he manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa*, his lifespan was exactly eighty-one years. Following Yue, he resided at Long’an Doushuai. Within his quarters, he would occasionally pose three questions to test his students.
"Those who part the weeds and gaze upon the wind do so only to seek the realization of their nature. Where, then, does the nature of this very person reside?
Only by recognizing one’s own nature can one be liberated from birth and death. [He asked: "At the moment when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, what will you do?"

"How can one be liberated? If one can be liberated from birth and death, one will know the place of departure. When the four elements separate, to what place does one go? Zhang Shangying answered these three questions with a verse:
(1) Deep and shadowy are the summer trees, where the cuckoo cries; The sun pierces the floating clouds, and the universe is clear.
Do not ask Zeng Xi about his father while facing Zeng Shen; From ancient times, a filial son has avoided pronouncing his father’s name. (2) In the human world...
The ghost-messenger arrives with the talisman to take her away; the color of the flower-crown upon her head is already fading.

What a fine moment for a turning! Do not let Old Yama know of it too easily. (3) The drum beats together at East Village; Li’s wife weeps, her tears soaking her robes in the vast wilderness of the west wind.
Upon the southern bank of the Jiangnan, where green reeds and red smartweed grow, she sits instead as Zhang San on the fishing weir. Winter of the sixth year of Yuanyou.
Having finished his bath, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse: "Forty-eight [years], from sage to ordinary person, all have been slain;
if this were not a hero, the path to Long’an would be slippery. Suddenly, he passed away. Shouzhi resided at Yungai for ten years, daily carrying a hoe to tend the vegetable gardens.
He found the Chan forest convenient and comfortable, yet his resolve for the Way grew thin. Those who came to seek instruction, he would shake his head and refuse to admit them. Yuan.

In the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, he retired to the West Hall. When the monastics of Xiangzhong heard that he was receiving visitors, the hall and chambers became filled with them. Cheng Hao responded to questions and engaged in dialogue with an inscrutable alternation of presence and concealment. One day, Su Shi sought an audience in humble attire. Hao asked, "What is the honorable title of your high office? Su replied, "My surname is Chēng (Scale).
