"Leaving my hometown more than forty years ago, I have for a time forgotten the dialect of Shu. When the Chan practitioner returns to Chengdu, He must take care to remember [this]."
He adopted the colloquialisms of Lu. At that time, Bai was still in good health, and Xian attended upon him once again; his reputation became widely renowned.

Qingyuan went to Guizong, but his studies with Kewen were not harmonious. He then spent the summer retreat at Jiangshan, where he happened to meet Weiqing, who said to him, "Recently I have seen the words and phrases of a venerable master in the capital;
you seem to have an affinity with him. Weiqing added, "Master Yan is the foremost patriarch in the world."
"Why did you abandon [your studies] to travel far away? The so-called "one with whom there is a karmic affinity" refers to a teacher whose understanding corresponds to your original aspiration.
Yuan assented. Over a year later, he returned to Haihui (Mount Tiantong). He instructed them to contemplate: "If one kills one's father and mother, one repents before the Buddha;
but if one kills the Buddha and the Patriarchs, where does one repent? Yunmen said: "Exposed. This is that public case.
Later, he ordered his attendant to announce his presence. It was a cold night and he sat alone; as he poked the hearth, he saw a fire the size of a single bean.
Suddenly filled with joy, he said, "Poking deeply, there is something here. My lifelong pursuit has been just like this. He rose abruptly and examined the *Lamp Records* on the desk.
Upon reaching the account of the "Falling Brick from the Hearth," he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse: "Diao-diao! The forest birds cry out; I pull on my robe..."
Sitting through the entire night, he stirred the embers and awakened to his lifelong path. He exhausted the mysteries of the spirit only to return to the state of "broken and fallen.
The matter is as clear as day, yet people remain deluded; who can harmonize with such profound simplicity? Thinking of this, I shall never forget it; the door stands open, yet few pass through.

Kekqin went to visit him in his quarters and tested him with the story of Qinglin carrying firewood, saying, "No one, past or present, has been able to get out of this. How do you understand it? He replied: [The text here implies a response, though the provided excerpt ends abruptly].

"Is there anything particularly difficult about it? [Wumen] said: "Take for instance what he said: 'The Iron Wheel-turning King’s decree within the realm. What is the meaning of this? [Dongshan] said: "I say:
'Within the palace of Śakra, a general amnesty is proclaimed. Qinfeng said to Retreat Master: "How fortunate, Elder Yuan! You now possess a phrase that brings life.
In the Yuanyou era, when Yuanwu was residing at Yunju, he heard that in various quarters it was customary to erect stupas for those who had died. He said: "This mountain..."

The river has its limits, but the deaths of monks are endless. In the future, there will be no space for stupas. Therefore, to the east of the Hongjue Stupa, he built an "egg-shaped" stupa (luantan) and decreed:
"Whenever a *zhuchi* (abbot) dies, unless their physical body remains indestructible or they leave behind śarīra relics after cremation, their bones and flesh shall all be filled here.
To the west, he further built an "egg-shaped" stupa and decreed: "Whenever a monk passes away, their bones and ashes shall all be filled here."
Regarding this, they are called the Three Pagodas. On a day in the seventh month of the second year of the Shaosheng era, he gathered the assembly at night and said:

"The abbots of these three locations have not transmitted a single dharma. The dispersal of the elements of fire and wind is the natural law of things; this is the common understanding of worldly phenomena.

After my passing, you must not follow secular custom by performing a grand burial. You should instead follow the Dharma of our Buddha from Western India: cremate the body and return the remains to the pagoda. He then spoke this verse: "Now..."
At the age of sixty-six, his karmic conditions for the three places were fulfilled. At midnight, as a mountain was engulfed in flames, he leapt into the fire to bathe.

Having finished speaking, he entered nirvana. It was the height of summer, yet his countenance remained as if alive. Upon cremation, five-colored śarīra relics were obtained, which emitted light that swallowed and eclipsed [all else].
○ The Master Huiri of Yongfeng Hermitage received the Dharma from [Fayan] You; at times he dwelt in rocky valleys, or...
While living in the marketplace, he had the local villagers call him "Master Qiu Shibo. Whenever anyone questioned him, he would answer with "I do not know.

Suddenly, he said to the people of the district, "I am going on a walking pilgrimage tomorrow; you all may come to see me off. Thereupon, they gathered in great numbers to provide him with gifts for the road.
He laughed incessantly throughout the day. When the crowd asked for the reason, he immediately wrote this verse: "Master Qiu Shibo does not know. Silent and still."
The light is bright and clear; at noon, he strikes the third watch. Who can strike it to the end? He dropped his brush and passed away.
Huiqin was once conversing with Keqin when he raised the following case: Dongsi asked Yangshan, "Where are you from? Yangshan replied, "I am from Guangnan.
Dongsi said, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Bright Pearl that Subdues the Sea. Have you ever captured one? Yangshan replied, "I have captured one. Dongsi—
[The Master] asked, "What color is the pearl? He replied, "In the bright fortnight it appears; in the dark fortnight it is hidden.
The Master said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk? Yangshan folded his hands and stepped forward, saying, "Yesterday, Huiji went to Mount Mushi and was asked for this pearl.
I was left with no words to answer and no principle to defend. The Master looked at him intently and said, "Since you say you have received it, when he asked for it—"
"Jewel. He continued, "There are no words with which to respond, and no principles to be set forth. What is this? Qín remained silent.
One day, he suddenly said to Qín, "I have a saying regarding the karmic connection between Yangshan and Dongsi.
Dongsi asked for only a single pearl, yet Yangshan poured out an entire wicker basket. Qín deeply approved of this, saying, "Elder brother, you should continue to draw close to him."
The Old Monk departed. On one day, Xuanqin went to the Abbot’s quarters; before he had even spoken, he was reviled by Yan, who scolded him.

Stupefied and crestfallen, he withdrew and returned to his quarters, where he bolted the door and lay down to sleep, harboring an unceasing resentment toward Yan. Xuanqin knew this secretly and immediately went to knock on the door. Xuanqin said:
"Who is it? he asked. "It is I," [the monk] replied. Qín immediately opened the door. Qín said, "How did you find the Old Monk?
He replied, "I originally had no intention of going; I was deceived by you. I have been subjected to this old fellow’s verbal abuse.
Qín laughed heartily and said, "Do you remember the words you spoke the other day? He asked, "What words? Qín said, "You also said that Dongsi only seeks..."
One peck. Yangshan tipped out a *kǎoluǎo* (a large woven basket). Xuanqin was immediately relieved. The two of them then went together to the abbot’s quarters.
As soon as Fayan saw them, he said abruptly, "Brother Xuanqin, congratulations; you have successfully completed the Great Matter. Muzhe resided at Zhihai Chan Monastery.
On the tenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shaosheng era, he spoke a verse without illness, saying: "Last night at the third watch, wind and thunder..."
Suddenly he composed himself; like clouds dispersing across the vast sky, the moon over the front stream set. After a long while, he took leave of the assembly and passed into stillness.
Upon cremation, about one *dou* of *śarīra* were obtained, each as large as a bean. His eyes, teeth, and nails remained uncorrupted. ○ Xingcong was the son of the Wang family from Mianzhou.

He left home to become a monk at a young age. Having passed the scriptural examinations, he received ordination. He traveled south to visit Zongben, but after a long time, he did not attain realization.
Zongben said, "In the past, I had a most extraordinary dream concerning you; if you do not exert yourself, you will die. Cong was bewildered and did not understand what this meant.

He constantly kept in mind the words of Nanyue Huisi: "Mouthfully swallowing the Buddhas of the three periods of time. These words never left his heart. One day, while prostrating before the Saṃgha...
Suddenly, he attained a sudden awakening. He immediately went to the abbot’s quarters to see Yuanwu Keqin and fully recounted what he had realized.
Keqin said, "You have attained it! In the past, I dreamed that you swallowed a world and a razor. What you have now awakened to is exactly as such.

I know that from this day forward, you have truly left the household life. He then ascended the seat to certify him. After a long time, he entered the world at Zhenru Monastery to open the Dharma gate.

He resided at Shengshou Monastery for three years. Later, he left Shengshou and lived in seclusion for ten years, wearing coarse clothing and eating simple food, no different from his days when he first settled on the mountain.
During the Yuanfeng era, Su Che was exiled to Gaoyang; there he associated with Cóng, finding great mutual affinity.
At the end of the Yuanyou era, Su Che was exiled to Gaoyang once more. Cóng went to visit him and said, "This old monk has had a dream: that I would roam the mountains with you."
In the interim, he knew that the Master would surely return. These comings and goings are all matters of past karma; there is nothing to be wondered at.
In the year Yihai of the Shaosheng era, people from Gaoyang flocked to visit Chong, requesting him to reside at Xiaoyao Temple. While Su Shi was in Huizhou, Liao Yuan sent him a letter saying:
"Ziyan passed the highest imperial examination, entered the Golden Gate, and ascended to the Jade Hall, yet has now been exiled far away to these desolate shores."
The powerful minister merely resents that you, Zizhan, might become a prime minister. A human life lasts but a single lifetime, like a white colt passing through a crack;
within thirty or twenty years, fame, achievement, wealth, and honor vanish into emptiness at a glance. Why not simply draw a single stroke to sever them all and seek your own original face?
Within your breast, Zizhan, are ten thousand scrolls of books; when you take up the brush, there is not a speck of dust.
Having reached this stage, one does not know where life and death reside. What is the use of a lifetime of cleverness?

The Buddhas of the three periods were but men of true spirit. If you, Zizhan, can take responsibility for this at your feet, then treat wealth, honor, and fame for twenty or thirty years as lightly as dirt; press forward with effort. Take care.
(Ciming) Chan Master Kewen Resides at Shimen, the Third Year of the Shaosheng Era.
Kewen moved his residence to Shimen. Whenever a monk approached him with questions, he would invariably sit upright with his eyes closed.
Upon seeing a student come to study under him, he would go to tend the vegetable garden. At that time, Wenzhun had been attending him for over ten years; he said to his companions:
"Does this old man have no interest in the Way of the Dharma? One day, Zhun raised his staff and struck a water channel; water splashed onto his robes, and he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He rushed to recount the matter to Wengu, who scolded him, saying, "Is this how you dare to act so recklessly? Fozhao Daogao first visited Yuanji, who raised the following case:
A monk asked Touzi, "When a person who has undergone 'great death' returns to life, what then? Touzi said: [text missing].
"Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive at dawn. What is your intention? Gao replied, "The kindness is so great it is difficult to repay. Ji greatly praised him.
A few days later, he proposed Gao to stand as the presiding monk and wield the whisk. [Gao] was slow and dull in his mental responses, so he laughed heartily upon opening the hall.
Gaō looked ashamed. The following day, he specifically prepared tea for the assembly. He placed the tea service on the table, but by accident he knocked it over;
the ladle fell to the ground and hopped several times. Gaō realized the meaning of the response, its sharp wit being swift and incisive.
He went back to Kewen and, while looking at a patriarch’s verse, read: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. He attained realization.
In the time of empty space, there is neither being nor non-being. A sudden, great awakening. Faqian resided at Jiangshan. In his later years, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Zhihai.
Upon ascending the hall, he asked the assembly: "When departing for Zhihai and remaining at Jiangshan, what is it that is thus?
The assembly did not know how to respond. He then returned to his quarters, took up a brush, and wrote this verse: "Not Buddha, not mind—vain is the deliberation. To obtain the skin..."

"Having attained the marrow, there is nothing more to deliberate upon. Farewell, dear fellow practitioners of Zen; the green mountains outside the gate are bathed in the setting sun. Having spoken thus, he cast aside his brush, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
When the messenger returned to report this, an imperial edict was issued posthumously bestowing upon him the title "Buddha-Wisdom" (Fohui). Huìhóng was a native of the Pēng family in Ruìzhōu.
His courtesy name was Juefan. He left home to become a monk in his youth and could memorize several thousand words a day. At nineteen, he passed the scriptural examination and received ordination.

He traveled to visit Guizong Kewen and later followed Kewen when he moved to Shimen, where he served as head of the secretariat. Kewen was concerned that he suffered from the弊 (shortcomings) of being overly profound in his learning.
Whenever he raised the story of Xuansha’s failure to reach full realization, it would provoke doubt. Whenever Wen gave a response, [Xuansha] would say, "Are you again expounding on principles?
One day, a guest asked Wen, "How is Master Hong practicing Chan? Wen replied, "There are places where he has reached his destination."
There were still points that did not reach his understanding. After the guest had departed, Hong felt uneasy and went immediately to Wen to seek resolution for his doubts.
Wen cited a verse by Fengxue: "A white cat with claws and talons fierce; Raised in the hall, it leaves no trace of insects. This is clearly the method of finding one's place atop a tree;
One must strictly avoid leaving words for one's nephew. He then asked, "And what, pray tell, is this 'method of finding one's place'?"
Hong then gave a shout. Wén said, "This one shout has both places where it reaches and places where it does not reach. Hong suddenly attained realization.
Later, while traveling through Eastern Wu, he stayed at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou. He composed a verse to clarify the meaning of Fēngxué and sent it to Wén, saying:
"A white cat with no seams or cracks; Casually cast out, it strikes fear into people. It turns over and leaps about a hundred times..."
A thousand ways. To look at him in his cold state, he has become a source of talk. Now he too knows how to dabble a bit. Let him rejoice, let him revile;
instead, one laughs at the old uncle on the treetop, who can only climb up but cannot come down.
He also composed a verse on Xuan Sha’s “Not Yet Thorough”: "Lingyun saw it once and did not see it again; on every branch, red and white, no flowers cling. How vexing!
"Enduring the guest on the fishing boat, he returns instead to the level ground to scoop up fish and shrimp. Upon seeing these words, Wenzhien offered him congratulations.
Later, Hong read through the *Recorded Sayings of Fenyang* until he reached the verses on the Three Mysteries (*sanxuan*), at which point he attained realization.

He also once lived in a hermitage beneath Jiufeng in Gaoyang; when a monk asked him about the dialogue concerning "host and guest" from Linji, just as Hong was about to answer the question, he suddenly—
He perceived the essential principles of the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.
(Dingchou year) Chan Master Baoen discussed the Great Essentials of the Three Teachings.

Baoen was a son of the Liu clan from Liyang. Before reaching the age of twenty, he presented strategic plans and was ranked first in the imperial examinations. Later, weary of the mundane world, he requested [to leave secular life].

At court, he requested leave to cast off his official robes and become a monk. The Emperor granted his request, whereupon he devoted himself to the Way of the Patriarchs. Upon reaching Touzi, he studied under Yiqing;
before long, he attained awakening to the essential point of the mind. Yiqing said, "You are one who has returned for a second time; you should protect and uphold it yourself."
Later, he resided at Dahuang Mountain in Suizhou and formed a close friendship with Zhang Shangying. Shangying once sent a letter inquiring about the essential tenets of the Three Teachings.

Zhen'en replied: "The non-Buddhist schools of the Western Regions follow many paths, but when their ultimate convergence is examined, they do not transcend the four views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.
These are known as the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence.
If one does not realize that the single mind is itself the Way, then the Way is not one's own possession; therefore, it is called an "external way" (mārga-bāhya).

If one does not realize that all phenomena are themselves the mind, then phenomena will vary according to one's views; therefore, this is called "false view" (mithyādṛṣṭi). For example, if one says they "exist," then with existence comes non-existence;

if one says they "do not exist," then with non-existence comes existence. When there is both existence and non-existence, views of existence arise in competition; when there is neither existence nor non-existence, views of non-existence likewise arise.
It is the same for the views that things both exist and do not exist, and the view that things neither exist nor do not exist.
Indeed, as long as one cannot free oneself from these various views, there is no way to clarify one's own mind; and without clarifying one's own mind, one cannot know the Right Path.

Therefore, a sutra says: "Those who speak of the Dharma through words and those of small intelligence engage in false discrimination; unable to comprehend their own minds, how can they know the right path?
It further states: "To have a view is itself a defilement; this is not yet true seeing. Only by remaining far removed from all views [does one truly see]."

In this way, one truly beholds the Buddha. Judging by this, the heterodox and the orthodox follow divergent paths; this is precisely because their modes of insight and awakening lead to different realizations.

Thus, Qingliang [Xuanzang] held that the Daoists reckon that the *Dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is spontaneous (*svabhāva*) and can give rise to the myriad things, while the *Yījīng* states that the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) gives birth to the two polarities, and that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Dao.
Taking spontaneity and the Great Ultimate as the cause, and the alternation of Yin and Yang...
To claim that Yang (the active principle) is the Dao and can give birth to the myriad things is to posit a false cause. To calculate it as *xuwu* (non-being or emptiness) is to posit no cause at all.
Let me attempt to discuss this: Now, the three realms are but mind; the myriad conditions are of one essence. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease.
Extending this principle broadly, it encompasses all existence yet is not existent. Synthesizing and unifying it, its ultimate nature is quiescent stillness.

Cessation is not non-existence; non-existence is neither non-existence nor not non-existence. Existence is neither existence nor not existence. Once these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled.
Thus, natural causes and conditions are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); both emptiness and reality are equally provisional designations.

As for the claim that the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) and the Yin and Yang can give rise to the myriad things, or that there is eternal non-existence and eternal existence—these are [the views of] the multitudes.
This is the wondrous gateway. Yin and yang are unfathomable; this is what is called the spirit that has no fixed direction.

Although the sages established their teachings to provide various means for enlightenment, since these differ from the single mind, how could they not be the four views? How can this be clarified? It is because emptiness and non-being constitute the Way.
If the Dao is taken to be non-being—whether as spontaneity (*ziran*), the Great Ultimate (*taiji*), or the alternation of Yin and Yang as the Dao—then the Dao is being.
If it is both constant non-being and constant being, then it is both being and non-being. If Yin and Yang are unfathomable, then it is neither being nor non-being.
Some former scholars have said that that which wondrously transforms all things is called the "Spirit" (*shen*); since it is not a thing, it is likewise non-being.

Therefore, the great masters of India all regarded the existence of phenomena external to the mind as the path of the heterodox (tīrthika), while taking the principle that "the myriad dharmas are mind-only" as the orthodox tradition.
This is because when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all views naturally vanish; though their words may differ, they are not sufficient to constitute a true divergence.
Conversely, when phenomena are held to exist outside the mind, all views compete to arise; though their words may be identical, they are not sufficient to be considered the same.
It is the same. Nevertheless, the sages of Confucianism and Daoism certainly were not unaware of this; they simply set it aside without discussion.
This is because they did not immediately and explicitly designate the single mind as the source of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Even if they occasionally spoke of it, they still did not discuss it.
The non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Heavens are all Great Power Bodhisattvas manifesting through transformation.
Their purpose in displaying various views and exhaustively pursuing heterodox paths is to clarify that the Buddha-dharma alone is the True Path.
This is why it is said that the Way of the Sage takes both the favorable and the adverse as its source; it is beyond the reach of discursive thought. Thus, an ancient said: "By reason of the past..."

Before the True Teaching (Shinshū) had arrived, Confucius merely used it to bind his own mind. Now that we know where the ultimate principle resides, we ought not to continue clinging to provisional teachings.
Yet, to know that a teaching is provisional does not necessarily mean one knows the provisional; only by knowing that the provisional is itself the real does one truly know the provisional.

This is precisely the fundamental intent behind the establishment of teachings and the composition of words by the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi: the great causal nexus of the One Great Matter.
It is that which begins and that which completes all things. Thus, the Three Teachings are one mind; they share the same path yet differ in their tracks.
As for the ultimate principle of the Way, it is fundamentally beyond words and speech. Were it not for the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who could have understood this meaning?
Liu Jingchen, styled Xingchao, served as the Acting Prefect. Initially, he did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, but was subsequently enlightened by Changzong. Thereupon—
His heart was intoxicated with the ancestral Way. Having visited Huilin Chong, he heard a monk ask Xuedou, "What is the original source of all Buddhas?
Xuedou replied, "The cold colors of a thousand peaks. Upon these words, he attained realization. Over a year later, while serving as an official in Luoyang, he visited Shao Shan Gao.
As he was about to depart for his new post, he took leave of Gaofeng. Gaofeng said, "If you apply yourself with such earnestness, why worry that you will not attain awakening?

Hereafter, should there arise extraordinary states or immeasurable joy, you must quickly gather them in. If you can gather them in, you will become a vessel of the Dharma; if you cannot gather them in, you may lose your mind.
Not long after, he again visited Benyi to inquire about the causes and conditions [of his practice]. Benyi said, "In ancient times..."

"The human way: the ordinary mind is the Way. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you emit light and shake the earth; though you do not consciously realize it, you are already aware of it within yourself.
To seek it outwardly is to become increasingly estranged and distant. My doubts remained unresolved.

One night, while entering the inner chamber, I asked Master Póluótí about the words of Venerable Bǎozhì to King Xiāngzhì regarding "seeing one's nature as Buddha. I was unable to answer, and my uncertainty persisted.
"It was profound. He returned to his bed and woke at the fifth watch. While he was reflecting back on the experience, he beheld various extraordinary signs;

his inner and outer being were transparently clear, his six sense faculties trembled, and heaven and earth seemed to spin. It was like clouds parting to reveal the moon, and he could not contain his joy.
Recalling the instructions of Shao Shan, he suppressed the experience. When dawn broke, he reported what he had attained to Yi, who served as a witness and said, "Furthermore..."

"One must actually practice it before one can attain it. [The Emperor] asked, "Do you not require actual cultivation? Yi replied in a sharp voice, "What kind of matter is this? To speak of 'cultivation'!

The subject [Wang Anshi] understood intuitively and subsequently composed six verses on "Elucidating the Mind-Ground" (Famingsin-di-song) as well as the treatise "Elucidating the Way and Admonishing the Confucians" (Mingdao-yuru-pian) to warn the world, saying:
"The elucidation of the Way lies in seeing one's nature. That which I have realized is seeing..."

It is simply nature (*xing*). Mencius said: "The mouth’s desire for flavors, the eyes’ desire for colors, the ears’ desire for sounds, the nose’s desire for odors, and the four limbs’ desire for ease and comfort—these are nature. Yangzi said:
"Sight, hearing, speech, appearance, and thought are what belongs to nature. If one perceives this, one can clarify the Way. One must know the Way.
One is not far removed from humanity. For humans in relation to the Way, it is like fish in water; they have never for a moment been separated from it.

It is only because they delude themselves and pursue external objects that they follow this Way throughout their lives without realizing it. The Buddha calls this "Great Awakening," while the Confucian calls it "Prior Awakening."
It is simply a matter of awakening to this. An ancient person once said: "Past and present should never fall away; it is clearly right before one's eyes. He also said:

"The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet it is difficult to behold while remaining within that very presence. If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, and speech.
Furthermore, he said: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him. Rising and falling..."
Accompanying one another, whether in speech or silence, they dwell together. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech.
This "Buddha" is that which takes speech as its most intimate path. Standing, one sees Him present before oneself; riding in a carriage, one sees Him leaning upon the crossbar.
Looking for Him, He seems to be in front; suddenly, He is behind. Whether turning left or right, one encounters Him everywhere.

This is the original source. Among the words of Confucian scholars regarding the Way, this is the most proximate. Alas, this Way can only be transmitted through the mind; it does not rely on written words.
Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa; when Bodhidharma faced the wall, the essential tenet was entrusted to Huike.
Once the six petals had unfolded, a thousand blossoms vied in their splendor; the schools were divided and the lineages established, each having its own...
Within the gateway of the teaching hall, there are those who blink their eyes or raise their eyebrows; who clench their fists or point their fingers;

who strike with staffs or shout "Ho!"; who brandish fly-whisks or strike the mallet; who draw bows or roll balls; who dance with ritual tablets; who drag stones or carry earth; who beat drums or blow whistles;
or who remain silent or utter a single word, a single sigh, or a single smile—even down to all manner of such expedient means—all of which are direct and intimate acts for the sake of others.
However, precisely because it is so intimate, many people are at a loss for what to do; those who catch even a fleeting glimpse of it find not a hair’s breadth between them and it.

Yet, should one hesitate or linger, the distance becomes ten thousand miles. Those who wish to clarify the Way should not neglect this. Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, it continues unbroken to this day.
It truly embodies what our Confucian tradition calls "being stirred with intensity yet not yet manifesting," and "opening up without contradiction. As for me—
There is attainment; it truly lies within this gate. Reflecting back upon our own Confucianism, we find that this Way has existed there all along.

How excellent were the words of Confucius: "He silently apprehends them and embodies them in one. Thus, the Way exists in the mere glance of the eye, and its meaning is conveyed by pointing at the palm of the hand.
All such instances accord with the wondrous purport of the Chan school and attain the true mechanism beyond formal teaching. Yet, as for Confucius—
The Way was transmitted from [Confucius] to Zisi; Zisi transmitted it to Mencius.

After Mencius passed away, its transmission was lost, and what has been handed down to the world consists merely of the written words. Therefore, in my studies, I must seek personal realization before I can rest.
Fortunately, one night I attained awakening; regarding everything seen by my eyes, heard by my ears, and perceived by my mind...
I reflected: "Whatever is spoken by the mouth or moved by the hands and feet is none other than the Sublime. Having attained this for a long time, it has increasingly manifested before me;
yet whenever I attempted to impart it to others, they were unable to receive it. Only then did I realize that the Sublime Way truly cannot be transmitted through written words. Alas!
This Way is transmitted when there is a worthy person, and perishes when there is no such person. I—
Now that it has been attained, who might resemble it? Whether such a person shall exist for the remainder of my life or not is something that cannot be known.
Therefore, I have composed records, eulogies, songs, and discourses, and have further written this treatise.

He used this to instruct his disciples. ○ Wuxin resided at Cuoyan. Behind the Dharma Hall was a shrine to King Qian’an, where local people prayed for blessings and averted calamities every day without fail.
Wuxin ordered the administrative staff to demolish it; fearing the consequences, they did not dare. He then personally tore down the shrine himself.
He established a hall for the master and prepared a couch for his private quarters. Suddenly, a giant python appeared, coiling and lying down beside him;
though he rebuked it to leave, it returned. This became a nightly occurrence. One night, a deity appeared in a dream and said, "I am a disciple who has been rebuked by you, Master, and find no peace.
I wish to go to Guangnan and request sixty laborers. He granted this request in the dream. Not long after, the laborers died of an epidemic.
According to his count, he once asked a scholar, "Tell me, are there truly ghosts and spirits? When the scholar said "Yes," Xuedou did not strike him dead;
when he said "No," why did Zhuangzi die? None of those who answered were in accord with the truth.
Just then, Yuan, the Head Seat, arrived and replied: "The sweet melon is sweet to its very stem; the bitter gourd is bitter to its very root. Xuedou was greatly pleased by this.
(Wu-yin) Chan Master Liaoyuan of Foyin entered nirvana (the fifth generation successor of Yunmen, heir to Kaixian Xian).
Liaoyuan resided at Yunju. Li Lin painted his portrait; Liaoyuan instructed him to depict a smiling expression. He composed this self-eulogy: "Lord Li is a stone qilin from the heavens;
he has transmitted the true likeness of the Wayman of Yunju. It was not for the sake of the 'Plucking the Flower' that the Great Matter was clarified."
Casually opening one’s mouth to laugh at whom? A clay ox vainly sniffs before the wind. A withered tree unexpectedly finds spring amidst the clouds.
Facing each other in full majesty, both remain unrecognized. In an era of Great Peace, the body is free.

On the fourth day of the first month of the Wuyin year, while conversing with a guest, he laughed heartily and passed away. There was a man from Wu named Zheng Yifu, who had attained the jinshi degree in his youth.
A scholar had an astrologer calculate his lifespan, which was determined to be only thirty-five years; he was deeply distressed by this.

Later, upon hearing that Master Yuan had passed away with a smile during a casual conversation, he said, "I could not attain longevity, but if I can become like Master Yuan, what more would I regret? Thereupon, he began to frequent those who practiced Chan meditation.
Having read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for over a year, he suddenly attained an awakening and said, "I have understood the principle of birth and death. Thereupon, his mind was set at ease.

Subsequently, he came to know in advance the day of his own death. When that time arrived, he bathed and changed his robes, personally supervising his attendants as they swept the gardens and pavilions.
He then burned incense, selected an auspicious hour, and while sketching with his finger, he stood upright and passed away; his hand remained in the posture of drawing with a finger.

Wen Zhun was a dharma-brother of Liang Ya within the gate of the Dharma. Because Ya had composed the *Cen Bencao* (The Pharmacopoeia of Chan), Wen Zhun subsequently authored the *Paozhi Lun* (Treatise on Processing and Refining).
The *Cen Bencao* states: "The flavor of Chan is sweet and its nature is cool. It pacifies the heart organ, dispels noxious vapors, clears obstructions, and circulates the blood vessels.
It clarifies the spirit, benefits the will, preserves the complexion, removes feverish afflictions, eliminates filth and evil, and is skilled at neutralizing all poisons. It is capable of...
Medicines that cure various ailments grow among humans; they differ only in degree regarding skin, flesh, bone, marrow, essence, and coarseness.
Those who obtain the essential ones are excellent; thus, they can treat all beings, whether ordinary or sagely, noble or humble.

The others mostly grow in thickets, where they rustle in the wind and sing with the moon. There are those in the world who, being followers of mere sound, mistake these for medicinal food; this deludes people's nature.

Life is profound in its hidden connections and manifest in its subtleties; none but those who have realized it can know this. Without requiring further cultivation or refinement, a single dose prepared and administered causes one to be liberated from suffering and affliction, as if a bond were suddenly released.
Its efficacy is like that of the divine; it bestows longevity upon people. Therefore, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have used this medicine.
He heals the illnesses of all sentient beings and is titled the Great King of Physicians. He is like a bright lamp for the world, shattering the darkness of all attachments.

Those who are afflicted by delusion, confusion, and deep-seated ignorance; those whose maladies have reached the vital organs (gao-huang); those defiled by false spirits and demons; and those wandering through the cycle of birth and death—these cannot be saved. How tragic!
According to the *Pao-chih lun* (Treatise on Pounding and Roasting), if a person desires to prolong their years, attain longevity, and sever all illnesses, [they must rely upon this method].

First, one must thoroughly examine the "Essentials of Chan" (*Chan bencao*). If one does not consult the "Essentials of Chan," one will not know whether a medicine is warm or mild, nor distinguish between its authenticity and falsity;
furthermore, one will not be familiar with which prefecture or county produces the finest quality.

Since one cannot exhaustively investigate its origins and details, how could one possibly realize the essential nature of the medicine? In recent times, there has been a certain class of people who do not read Chan...

Regarding the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia), they instead take *duloulan* and treat it as the "Mianzhou Aconite. Often, seeing that the facial features resemble one another, they take it to be the real thing.

Alas, alas! Not only do they deceive themselves, but they also deceive others. Consequently, for those who study medicine in later generations, one person transmits the falsehood and ten thousand transmit it as truth;
they are in a state of turmoil, pursuing the superficial branches while remaining ignorant of the source of peace.
Delighting in returning to the source, as days and months passed, a perverse affliction arose. It gradually attacked the four limbs and harmed the essence of perfect clarity and eternal bliss.
From dawn until dusk, one could not rest upon one's mat; eventually reaching the point of no return, many have lost their lives in vain.
This is truly due to the coarse minds of beginners and the haphazard manner in which teachers transmit the instructions, failing to examine the "Pharmacopoeia of Chan."
This is an error. If you wish to rely upon this text to clarify the essential nature of medicine, you must also understand the methods of processing according to the Dharma.

Regarding these methods of processing: first, one must select the purest and most refined ingredients; wash them clean with the flowing water of the Dharma; strip away the leaves of *pudgala* (self) and *ātman* (ego);
remove the roots of ignorance; wield the blade of the eight returns; and crush and mince them upon the anvil of the three equalities, using the reality of emptiness as the [mortar].
Gently warm it over a small fire. Place it in the mortar of the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). Raise the eight vajra-mallets and strike them eighty-four thousand times.

Pass it through the sieve of the thousand hands and eyes of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Only then is the samādhi of every atom (*paramāṇu*) perfected. Refine the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) into a perfect sphere.
Without being restricted by time, boil the soup of "single-minded correspondence" (*ekacitta-saṃprayukta*) and add the three spheres of the former and the three of the latter.
Three pills. With the exception of the eight winds and the two views, there is nothing else to be avoided. The efficacy of this medicine cannot be fully described;
only those who take it will know it. The profound power of this medicine is not recorded in worldly medical texts;
it awaits future scholars of medicine of superior caliber to examine the *Chan-bencao* (Zen Materia Medica) and then, based upon it, to process, compound, and administer it.
His spiritual power was indeed not slight. Having opened his sacred awakening, he studied under Changlu Yingfu for a long time and attained realization.
He traveled extensively through the monastic communities until he arrived at the assembly of Fayan. Fayan asked him: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still but the slaves of others."

"Who is he? [Yuanwu] replied, "The old fellow Zhang San and the dark fellow Li Si. Yuanwu was deeply pleased and told Keqin about it. Keqin said, "I fear this may not be the reality; you must search further. Later, when Yuanwu asked again, [Keqin] still said, "He is that man's slave. "Who is he? Yuanwu asked. Keqin replied, "It is I. Yuanwu laughed heartily. Keqin later said, "I have been deceived by my teacher. Yuanwu said, "You have been deceived by me. Yuanwu then wrote a verse: "The old fellow Zhang San and the dark fellow Li Si / The old fellow Zhang San and the dark fellow Li Si / The old fellow Zhang San and the dark fellow Li Si / The old fellow Zhang San and the dark fellow Li Si. Yuanwu then said, "If you can understand this, you will understand the meaning of 'He is that man's slave. Yuanwu passed away in the spring of the second year of the Shaoxing era (1132). He was seventy-three years old. His remains were enshrined at Mount Tiantong. Emperor Gaozong bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master Universal Enlightenment" (Puzhao Dashi). His dharma heirs numbered one hundred and twenty-four. Among them, the most prominent were Changlu Zongze, Fushan Fayuan, and Xuedou Chongxian. The lineage of the Yunmen school flourished greatly during the Song dynasty, with its influence extending throughout the world. It was only after the Yuan dynasty that the Linji school became predominant. The Yunmen school eventually declined and ceased to exist. Its teachings were compiled into the *Yunmen Kuangzhen Chanshi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen) in ten fascicles, which is extant today. Furthermore, there is the *Yunmen Kuangzhen Chanshi Wenda* (Questions and Answers of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen) in two fascicles, as well as the *Xuedou Chanshi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xuedou), the *Fushan Fayuan Chanshi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushan Fayuan), and the *Changlu Zongze Chanshi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Changlu Zongze). These works are all included in the Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō.
