He asked, "What about 'Hú Zhāngsān' and 'Hēi Lìsì'? The monk replied, "It is not so; it is not so. Jiǎo asked, "Yesterday it was so; why is it not so today?
The monk replied, "Yesterday it was so; today it is not so. Upon hearing this, Jiǎo attained great enlightenment. Later, he entered the world to open a monastery at Kāishèng (Kai-sheng).
Having ascended the hall and received the Dharma-lineage from Chánglú, while he was burning incense, a creature suddenly struck him in the chest. Consequently, a sore developed, and he passed away.

In the second year of the Yuánfú era (1099), during the reign of Emperor Shèngzōng, when the Chan Master Huìqín was residing at Tàipíng Monastery in Shūzhōu, Wéiqīng went to Huánglóng. As the seat at Tàipíng remained vacant, Wéiqīng subsequently recommended Huìqín to the Governor of Shū, who then appointed him to fill the position.
Fǎyǎn had entrusted him with the Dharma robe; Huìqín received it and presented it to the assembly, saying: "In the past, Śākyamuni Buddha..."
Taking the sixteen-foot golden-brocade *kāṣāya* robe, he draped it over the thousand-foot body of Maitreya Buddha; the Buddha’s body was not long, nor was the robe short.
Do you understand? It is simply this pattern and no other. At that moment, the entire assembly was struck with awe and submission. Then, as they were taking their leave...

Yan said: "In general, regarding how to respond to the world, I shall briefly set forth four principles for you. Although these are common worldly sayings, they depend entirely on whether or not one puts them into practice.
First, one's influence must not be exhausted; second, one's merit must not be exhausted;
third, the rules of propriety must not be exhausted; fourth, good words must not be exhausted. Why is this? If good words are exhausted, people will surely treat them with contempt."
When rules and regulations are exhausted, people’s minds become weary of them. When blessings are fully received, one’s conditions will surely become solitary.
When power is fully exerted, calamity will surely arrive. Qín bowed twice more, took the words to heart, and withdrew.

Cíwéi said, “The abbot should carry his staff and pack on his back and hang them from the walls of the abbot’s quarters; when leaving or staying, he should be as light as a monastic. Thus it would be well.”
Chan Master Weiqing resided at Huanglong.

His courtesy name was Juetian, and he styled himself the Elder Lingyuan. He was born in Wuning of Hongzhou into the Chen family. While still a young boy with hair hanging down his forehead, he could recite several thousand words of scripture.
A monk of extraordinary character saw him, took him by the hand, and after gazing at him intently, exclaimed in amazement: "A reed and marsh [hidden treasure]!"
"Does he have such a son? He informed the boy's parents and urged them to let him leave the household life. At the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*).
He first visited Yan'en Fa'an, expressing his wish to remain and study under him. Fa'an said, "In the future, you shall wash the Buddha-sun with light and illuminate the final age."
"The Dharma-boat for crossing the sea of suffering. As for me, I am but a mere ditch and canal. Master Huanglong Xin is your teacher; go now, do not let yourself be detained.
When Qing arrived at Huanglong, he blended indistinguishably with the assembly in their daily activities, yet his questions and answers were utterly bewildered, and he knew nothing of their source.
At night, he made a vow before the Buddhas, saying: "If I should attain awakening, I vow to devote the rest of my life to the Dharma."
Tán, throughout his successive lives, had exerted great effort to propagate the Great Dharma. Initially, while reading the words of Xuansha, he grew weary and leaned against a wall.

Rising to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), he took short steps and left behind his sandals. Bending down to retrieve them, he attained great enlightenment. He reported his realization to Zǔxīn, who said, "Those who enter through conditions will never again suffer loss or regression.
However, those who have newly attained the emptiness of dharmas often experience such joy that it leads to distraction. Have him attend upon you."
This man would sleep soundly in his quarters; his heart was so full of affection that he even forgot he was a teacher. They discussed and deliberated with him as if they were friends.

The various regions called him "Pure Attendant" (Qing Shizhe), much like Zhaozhou Wen’uan or Nanyuan Shoukuo. When he appeared in the world to reside at Taiping Monastery in Shuzhou, students vied with one another to follow him.
Though his regulations were not strict, everyone was naturally disciplined; thus, among the monastic communities (*conglin*) of Jianghuai, he was acclaimed as the foremost.

In the second year of the Yuánfú era, as Zhǔxīn had reached an advanced age, Wáng Huán, the Transport Commissioner of Jiangxī, invited Fǎqīng to return to Huánglóng, wishing for him to succeed Zhǔxīn on the Dharma seat.
Fǎqīng accepted without hesitation and departed. Sànběn resided at Fǎyún Monastery in the Eastern Capital for eight years;
he later returned to Xiàngwǔ Temple in Hángzhōu, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
Master Yuanzhao Zongben’s Rebirth in the Pure Land (The Sixth Generation of Yunmen, successor to Tanyi Huai):

Zongben lived in seclusion at Lingyan Mountain in his old age, remaining withdrawn behind closed doors. Yet, students flocked to him along the path, and the teaching style of Xuedou flourished greatly under him.
While living in ordinary circumstances, he privately cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land. Master Huicai traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and beheld [him there].
There was a single flower, exceptionally beautiful. He asked about it and said, "This is for the High Master Ben, who is to be reborn in the highest grade.

Furthermore, when Master Xi of Zifu arrived at Huilin Temple, he prostrated at [Ben's] feet, gave him gold, and departed. When people asked the reason, he said, "In my meditative concentration, I saw a golden lotus flower; people say it is to await Master Ben.
Moreover, there were countless lotus flowers, which he said were to await those who were to receive ordination. Someone asked him about this.

The Master Ben transmitted the Direct Pointing. Why was he designated by the name "Lotus Realm"? He replied, "Although I belong to the School of the Patriarchs, I have also practiced the Pure Land concurrently.
On the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuánfú era, as he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he bathed and lay down.

His disciples gathered around and requested, saying, "Your Way, Master, has pervaded the world; today you must not be without a verse. We pray that you will exert yourself to rise and sit upright. Ben—
Staring at him intently, he said, "Foolish son! I am usually too lazy even to compose verses; what are you trying to accomplish by making such a special effort today?
When I wish to lie down, I simply lie down; I cannot sit up specially for you today. He took up his brush and wrote five characters in large script:
"The final affairs are entrusted to Shourong. Then he threw down the brush and lay down feigning sleep. When [the disciple] shook him, he had already departed.
(Gengchen) A memorial from Biaozi to Chan Master Keqin.
When Biaozi first attended upon Fayan, he had not yet attained any realization. At that time, Keqin was the head of the assembly, and Fayan ordered him to study closely under Keqin.
Qinjian said to him, "Since you have been practicing together with me, there is no need for you to come here to test my depth. The monk replied, "My own matter is not yet clear;

I venture to hope for your compassion. Qinjian said, "Whenever you have a point of doubt, try telling it to me. [The monk] then cited the occasion when Deshan, during a small-scale sermon, refused to answer questions.
[Zhaozhou] asked, "Thirty blows for one who speaks. [Dongshan] said, "Prostrate yourself; I can act as your teacher. [Zhaozhou] still did not understand the case being cited.
After he had finished prostrating himself, Dongshan urged him to cite the previous dialogue again. Zhaozhou said, "Deshan’s informal sermon does not allow for answers.
Dongshan covered his mouth and said, "Just look at it like this. Zhaozhou came out and said, "Injustice! Injustice! How can there be a public case (gong'an) that merely instructs people..."
He was contemplating the principle of a single phrase when a monk said to him, "Brother, you should not speak in such a manner; the Head Seat must surely have some skillful means.

Thereupon, he sat in quiet meditation and investigated for ten days, whereupon his doubts were suddenly resolved. He went to pay his respects and offer thanks to Fenyang Wude. Fenyang said, "Brother, now you finally know that I did not deceive you.
He then went to the Abbot’s quarters, where Changzheng Fangyan greeted him with a smile. Later, Fenyang was appointed to oversee the general affairs of the monastery.

When [Zhaozhou] was appointed as the head of the community (zuoyuan), he privately told Fayan, "He has only attained a single peg; the Great Dharma is not yet clear to him. He must undergo further refinement;

he will certainly become a vessel for the Dharma. Not long after, Fayan announced, "I request that you establish your own community of monks," truly wishing to stimulate him toward a far-reaching realization.
When Zhaozhou heard this, he felt a profound sense of expectation. One day, while ascending the hall, Fayan looked at Zhaozhou with his eyes and said, "Do not be deluded."

Having had this thought, he descended from his seat. Feeling a sense of unease within himself, he went to Langye. After a long time of diligent practice, Langye took him under his care, and he subsequently attained great enlightenment.
They then returned together to the Fifth Patriarch, who appointed him as the head monk. Shouxun, a native of the Shi family of Anji Prefecture, went to study under Huiqin.

In response to the requests of the assembly, [Zhaozhou] remained distant and entered no state of absorption. He then sealed his bedding, saying, "If I do not attain penetration in this life, I vow never to uncover this.
Thus, for forty-nine days and nights, he stood upon the ground leaning against a pillar, as if mourning a parent’s death.

One day, when Qín ascended the hall, he said: "The myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images are all stamped by the One Dharma. Upon hearing this, Xuàn attained sudden enlightenment. He went to...
Jianqin saw [Linji] and said, "What a pity that this bright pearl has been picked up by this madman.
He then asked, "Lingyun said, 'Since the first time I saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no further doubts. What is it about him that he has no doubts?
Linji replied, "Do not say that Lingyun had no doubts; even now, if you try to find a place where he doubted, you will find nothing at all."
[The Master] said: "Xuansha said, 'It is truly correct, most truly correct; yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate.

Where, then, was his lack of penetration? [Dongshan] said: "I deeply understand the Venerable One’s earnest and compassionate heart. He then bowed in assent. Xun rose from his prostrations and presented a verse, saying:
"Throughout the day I gazed at the sky without raising my head; Only when the peach blossoms were in full bloom did I lift my gaze. Even if you had anything more—"
The net that covers the heavens—once you have passed through this secure barrier, you may immediately rest. He earnestly instructed them to protect and uphold [the Dharma].

That evening, he said to the assembly, "This time, Upādhyāya Xuan will sleep soundly. Kechin doubted that this would actually come to pass and said, "I must first put him to the test before I can be certain.
He then sent someone to summon Xuan and went out for a stroll with him. Upon reaching a mountain pool, he suddenly pushed Xuan into the water.
He asked abruptly, "How was it before Niutou had seen the Fourth Patriarch? He replied, "The waters are deep and the fish gather. He asked, "How was it after he saw him?
He replied, "The tree is tall and it beckons the wind. He asked, "How was it both when he had seen him and when he had not?
He replied, "Stretching out one's legs is within the drawing in of them. Dàqín greatly praised this.
○ Chan Master Huitang Zuxin Enters Nirvana (The ninth generation of the Linji lineage, successor to Huanglong Nan).
Zuxin retired from his duties to live in seclusion, yet those who sought instruction drew closer to him. Once, he replied to the inquiry of Minister Han Zonggu, who said:

"I have received your instruction that in the past you attained awakening and were vast and free of doubt; however, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated since beginningless time have not yet been suddenly exhausted. To this, [Zuxin] replied: [...]

Regarding the statement that "there is no dharma remaining outside the mind": if one does not know what the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) actually are, yet desires to exhaust them, then giving rise to such a thought is, on the contrary, like mistaking a thief for one's own son.
Since the beginning of time, there have been only verbal teachings—even the prescription of medicine according to the specific illness.
Even if afflictions and habitual tendencies exist, they are treated solely by means of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; all of these are [the Buddha's teachings].

These teachings of skillful means and expedient inducements are intended for those who believe that if there were truly habit-energies (*vāsanā*) to be remedied, they could be exhausted by treating them as phenomena existing external to the mind—much like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail through the mud, where every stroke of the brush only creates more tracks.

This may be called "using the mind to employ the mind," which only serves to deepen one's affliction. If one can clearly realize the Mind, there are no phenomena outside the Mind, and no Mind outside of phenomena.

Since the mental dharmas have already ceased to exist, whom else would he wish to instruct so that they might be suddenly exhausted? On the eleventh month of the third year of the Yuánfú era, he entered nirvana.
Hùáng Tíngjiān oversaw the funeral arrangements. During the cremation, the flame held by Línfēng did not continue.
Tíngjiān then looked at Wùxīn and said, "This Master is waiting for you, my elder brother. Wùxīn declined on the grounds of mourning, but Tíngjiān insisted firmly upon it. Thereupon, Wùxīn...
Zhiju said, "It is not that other karmic retributions have accrued to me; my offenses fill the heavens and cannot be pardoned.
Now, with both feet trailing in the air, I shall surely become a donkey rather than an ox. He struck a circular mark with his torch and said, "I shall settle this grievance right here.
As he threw the torch, it ignited upon contact. He was subsequently granted the title Baojue (Treasure Awakening).
(Xinsi) Dharma Master Youyan attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
Youyan resided at Chicheng and studied the Tiantai teachings. In his later years, he thatched a hut beneath a jujube tree and named it Zhuan’an.

Throughout his life, he was devoted to the practice of the Pure Land. In the fourth month of the summer in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, as he was nearing the end of his life, he beheld a treasure...
In the pond were large lotuses, and celestial music played in four rows. Seven days later, he passed away while sitting in the full-lotus posture.

Upon his couch was a light like the moon, which did not disappear until three evenings later. ○ Sūshì was in Dān Prefecture for four years. In the year Gēngchén, he was reinstated as a Cháo-fèng-láng; in Xīnsí, he returned north.
Upon reaching Zhēn Prefecture, the miasmic poison flared up, so he halted at Chángzhōu and subsequently requested retirement, resigning from office with his current rank.

[Su Shi] served [the court]. When he was first exiled to the south, he painted a single scroll of Amitābha and wore it with him as he traveled, saying, "This is my official passport for rebirth in the Western Paradise.
When his illness reached its final stage, Weilin of Mount Jing came to visit him. Su Shi was deaf;
Weilin called out in a loud voice, "Director of Studies, do not forget the West! Su Shi replied, "The West is certainly not non-existent, but one cannot apply effort here [in this state]."
Having finished speaking, he passed away. He once inscribed these words upon his own reflection: "My mind is like wood already reduced to ashes; my body is like an unmoored boat.
When asked about the achievements of my life, there are Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Qiongzhou. Mi Fu, whose courtesy name was Yuanchang, studied Chan Buddhism in his later years and attained realization.
While serving as the Military Commissioner of Huaiyang, he composed a parting poem for his friends and relatives one month before his death.
He wrote: "I shall completely incinerate all the books, paintings, and rare objects I hold dear. I will have a coffin made of fragrant *nán* wood and shall sit, lie, eat, and drink within it.

For the seven days prior [to my passing], I shall abstain from meat, change my clothes, bathe, burn incense, and sit in purity. When the appointed time arrived, he invited his fellow officials throughout the prefecture.
Raising a fly-whisk, he showed it to the assembly and said, "I come from the Land of Universal Fragrance; I go to the Land of Universal Fragrance," and then he cast the whisk down.
He passed away with his palms joined. ○ Weiqing resided at Huanglong. After the Patriarch Xinxin passed away, Qing immediately moved to the Zhaomo Hall.
He sat in meditation in a single room with such profound composure that no one could discern whether he was intimate or distant. Yet, all who saw him found their hearts filled with joy.
When it came to bestowing the hammer and tongs of the Dharma to forge and refine others, there were no seams or gaps; he did not permit students to record his teachings in writing.
Regarding his words, even if one obtains but a single phrase or a solitary sentence, it is like finding a ceremonial jade tablet of full height.
He once said to Huìhóng: "Among scholars today, none have escaped birth and death. Wherein lies their ailment? It is simply that their 'thieving mind' has not yet died.
Yet this is not their fault; it is the fault of those who act as teachers. It is like Emperor Gaozu of Han, who deceived and killed Hàn Xìn; though Xìn was dead,"
Has his mind truly died? Most of the masters of today are much like this. As for the students of antiquity who attained liberation from birth and death beneath a single word, where is the proof?
It lies in the fact that their "thieving mind" has already died. Yet, this was not something they could achieve on their own.

Truly, those who act as teachers possess a subtle and profound mastery of the hammer and tongs. For instance, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty beheld Hou Jing from the great hall, he did not move a muscle or utter a word;
yet Hou Jing broke into a sweat and dared not look up. Retreating, he said to his men, "The celestial majesty of Lord Xiao overwhelms me;
I cannot bear to see him again. Although Hou Jing had not yet died, his heart was already withered and exhausted.
This is the case with others as well. The patriarchs of old were for the most part like this. What is taught by various masters today is not without its beauty;
yet, in essence, it is like Zhao Chang’s paintings of flowers—so lifelike that they are treasured by the world, though they are not real flowers.
(Renwu) Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen entered nirvana (the ninth generation of Linji, successor to Huanglong Nan). Kewen retired to Yun’an.
On a day in the tenth month of the first year of the Chongning era, at midnight, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus position.
When the assembly requested him to preach the Dharma, Kewen smiled and said: "This year I am seventy-eight; the four elements are about to part. Fire and wind..."

Having dispersed, he paused as they were about to depart and further delivered his final instructions. These bequeathed precepts all concern matters of great importance for the School of the Gate (the Chan school). Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully.
During the cremation, flames of five colors arose, and white light ascended into the air; wherever the smoke reached, it produced śarīra relics. Both monastics and laypeople obtained these remains.

He divided [the site] to construct stupas. His sincerity and compassion were natural to him; he treated all people without distinction between kin and stranger, greeting them with a warm countenance and gentle speech, showing equal reverence to each.
In presiding over the monastic community, his regulations were extremely strict; those who violated the rules were punished without pardon.

When he entered the chamber and applied his teachings to the occasion, they were like a copper cliff or an iron wall, impossible to scale or grasp. By nature, he was especially fond of giving; whatever he possessed, he gave away immediately.

Aside from his staff and alms bowl, he did not keep a single coin. For over fifty years, he practiced the Way and preached the Dharma, wearing only coarse cloth and tattered robes while maintaining a serene and self-contained manner.
The people believed in his transformation; every household painted his image, and offerings were made before it whenever they ate or drank. Wen...

I once composed six verses on the Three Contemplations of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which say: Form and emptiness are unimpeded; as one wishes, there is sovereign mastery. Myriad phenomena are arrayed, their reflections appearing within and without.
They emerge and subside, coming and going, in this land and in other realms. The seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*) is vast and open, pervasively penetrating and expansive.
(1) Principle and phenomena are unimpeded; as one wishes, there is sovereign mastery. One holds Mount Sumeru upside down, planting it firmly upon a single speck of dust. Pure and serene...
The Dharmakāya; a perfectly round clod of earth; a single point of light in a mirror-lamp; the ocean-assemblies of the ten directions.
(2) The non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena; sovereign as one wishes; the immovable site of enlightenment; the worlds of the ten directions—rising in the east and sinking in the west;
a thousand differences and myriad wonders; a cricket in the fire swallowing a crab. (3) The non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena; sovereign as one wishes; holding a pig’s head in hand.
Reciting the pure precepts from his mouth, he drives himself out of the brothel; before he has even repaid his wine debts, at the crossroads, he unties the sack.
(4) In every matter there is no obstruction; as one wishes, there is freedom. Picking up a single hair, the entire dharma-realm unfolds;

in a single thought, one enters the boundless oceans of lands—all of it resides right before one’s eyes, sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden. (5) If one does not know each thing for what it is, then form and emptiness...
Who would dare? Affairs of principle and phenomena having ceased, the iron boat descends into the sea; like sparks from flint and a flash of lightning—how lamentable, how unsatisfying!
Transversely grasping the Mo-xie sword, the demons' hearts shatter in fear.
(Guimèi) Chan Master Yuanji resided at Baoning. He later resided at Yuantong.
In the second year of the Chongning era, Zhu Yanfu was the governor of Jinling; it happened that the seat of Baoning was vacant.
Ji moved closer to him. Xu Ji of Xuyang asked to participate in the practice with Ji. Ji said, "Do not hang trivial matters upon your mind. Xu Ji asked, "What is a trivial matter?
Ji replied, "Seeking the Way through Zen meditation is precisely that. At this, Xu Ji attained awakening. After a long while, he said, "The Great Way is exceedingly level and plain;
why use so many words and entangling complications? Ji called to his attendant and had him repeat the previous words.
When he questioned him, the attendant stared blankly and withdrew. Zhiwei said to Huaiji, "Verbal expressions and conceptual entanglements must not be abandoned either.
Zhiwei, detesting those scholars who savor and cling to words, composed a verse: "I do not study literature nor read books;
I remain as I am all day long, like a simpleton. Though I understand nothing of the hundred affairs, Why has this horse ever been called a donkey?"
Huai-zhi resided at the Joyful Hall (Zui-le-tang) in Long’an. On the final day of the sixth month in the first year of the Chongning era, he asked his attendant, "Is it early or late in the day?
The attendant replied, "It is already evening. He smiled and said, "We have met within a dream; I have already awakened from my sleep.

You need only not fail the monastic community, and that is how you repay the Buddha’s kindness. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Hu An-guo, courtesy name Kanghou, was of the Chong... [text continues]
Anren (Peaceful Person) possessed a disposition for transcending the mundane from her youth. She studied under Shangfeng Xiou for a long time and attained the meaning beyond words.
During the Chongning era, while passing through Yaoshan, she encountered a Chan practitioner who raised the story of Nanquan killing the cat and questioned Anren about it.
Anren replied with a verse: "In hand, the pivot of life and death that governs heaven and earth; To deploy it freely or restrict it depends on the moment. The Jade Hall..."
"A hare or a horse is not a dragon or an elephant; the grand function is majestic, yet no one knows it at all.
Furthermore, he sent a letter to Upper Feng, saying: "Mount Zhurong resembles the sky above Ducheng; the mountains and rivers of ten thousand ages are before one’s eyes.

One must believe that Sīxin (Dead Heart) was never dead; last night the autumn moon was once again full. Jingduan resided at Wushan and styled himself Anxian (Peaceful and Leisurely) Worthy. He wore straw sandals.
Carrying a *jiǒng* staff, whenever he encountered a scenic spot by a stream or mountain, he would don his rain cape and straw hat and wander about singing like a fisherman.

At every destination, once his inspiration was spent, he wished to return; even if great lords and high officials offered him gold to stay, he would not linger. When his boat reached Wuxing, eminent officials invariably asked first after his well-being.
He once made two earthenware vessels himself, saying, "When I die, I shall be buried with these. Suddenly, he suffered from a toothache.
He had not recovered for a long time. On the [lunar] day of the twelfth month of the year Guiwei, he said to the assembly, "Tomorrow I shall pass away.

The assembly took this to be a joke and requested that he speak a verse. Zhiyan took up his brush and wrote in large characters: "Master Zhiyan is far too indolent; Before I die, my teeth have already rotted away.
At the two sessions, I accompany the assembly to the hall, Yet I can never manage to get there in time for the gruel and rice. Now, at last, I have attained death."
"It is best for me to sleep long; I shall attend to no affairs whatsoever. First, I will not concern myself with officials; second, I will not concern myself with eating porridge or rice.
Having sung the "Fisherman" song several times, he laughed, adjusted his robes, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. He was seventy-four years old.
He then buried his earthenware vessels beneath Guiyun Hermitage. He once told his disciples, "Sixty years from now, open my tomb.
When his seventh-generation descendant came to request a change of burial site due to geomantic considerations, he gathered workers to excavate the earth;
yet the bricks remained undisturbed and the earthenware vessels were still intact. Upon opening them to look inside, not a single object was to be found.
(Jia-shen) Chan Master Wuzu Fayuan entered nirvana (the Dharma heir of Baiyun Yuan; the tenth generation of the Linji lineage).
Fayuan had appeared in the world for over forty years. In his later years, he resided at Taiping and subsequently moved to Dongshan.
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Chongning era, he took leave of the assembly, saying: "The Venerable Zhaozhou has a final word; how do you understand it?"
Do you understand? Try coming forward and speaking about it. If you can understand it, you will be free and at ease;
if not, how can this good matter be explained? After a long silence, he said: "It has been explained, but it is simply that you all do not know."
"Do you understand? The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few; the poor resent that they have one body too many. Take care!
At that time, there was construction work at the mountain gate, so he went in person to supervise it. He cautioned them, saying, "You all must rest well; I shall not come again.
Upon returning to the abbot’s quarters, he shaved his hair and bathed. On the following morning, he passed away peacefully at the age of over eighty. Previously, the Fifth Patriarch...
The testament states: "After my passing, you may leave my true body [here]. When I lift it with my own hand, I shall emerge once more.
While Fayan was residing on the mountain, he sculpted a hand from clay, which split open in the middle; the gap between the two parts was about seven inches wide. The assembly all marveled at this.

Once, while Fayan was prostrating before the stupa, he pointed with his finger and said: "At that time, I departed with my whole body in this manner; today I have come back again—do you remember? He spoke thus once more.
He asked, "What shall serve as proof? [The other] replied, "This shall serve as proof. He then paid his respects. On the evening of his impending death, mountains collapsed and stones fell;
for forty li around, the cliffs and valleys shook and roared. Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics fell like rain. A stupa was erected to the south of Mount Dongshan.
When Fayan was about to pass away, he left a final instruction to the Prefect, commanding him to appoint Baizhang to succeed him on the seat. At that time, disciples from the four quarters arrived.

He was so preoccupied with responding that he had no leisure for anything else. He himself posted a notice saying: "Dongshan has three phrases; if anyone can speak them, they shall be admitted to the monastery.
The monastics were all disheartened. One day, a monk arrived at the abbot’s quarters carrying his sitting mat and said to him, "I cannot speak the phrases, but I simply wish to be admitted.
Dongshan was greatly pleased and called the *weina* to arrange a place for him beneath the bright window.

Yuanli was a native of Min. Initially, he studied under Fayan at Taiping. Whenever he entered the room for instruction, Fayan would invariably say to him, "Monks of our tradition must clearly distinguish between the black and the white.
Yuanli harbored doubts about this until one day, when Fayan ascended the hall and cited the saying of Shoushan:
"The daughter-in-law rides the donkey, while the mother-in-law leads her. Fayan then asked, "Do you all understand? Do not ask about the daughter-in-law or the mother-in-law."
The Master said, "Enough of troubling yourself on the road with such clamor. When you meet rice, eat rice; when you meet tea, drink tea.

To enter and exit the same gate as one who was an enemy in a past life—under these words, your courtesy is suddenly cleared away. He said, "Today, the distinction between the monastic and the lay is made clear. Yan Qian then became the Fifth Patriarch.
He was ordered to pay his respects and share a seat with [the Master]. After Yan passed away, he went elsewhere. During the Chongning era, he returned once more to Wuzu.
A monk asked, "Where has Wuzu gone since his passing? He replied, "Having eyes but no ears; sitting by the fire in the sixth month.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? He replied, "At home, poverty is still tolerable; on the road, poverty is enough to kill one. [Zong]gao [was from] Xi in Ningguo.
She was the daughter of a certain family. Her mother dreamed of a monk with a dark-complexioned face and a prominent nose, escorted by divine beings, who entered her bedroom.

When asked where he resided, he replied, "To the north of the mountain. Upon waking, she conceived. At the time of her birth, a white light permeated the house; the entire district marveled at this marvel. She reached the age of thirteen.
Upon entering the local school, he sighed and said, "What is the use of reading worldly books? Is it not better to investigate the supramundane Dharma?

In the third year of the Chongning era, at the age of sixteen, he took Huiqi as his master. Previously, when a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha was being sculpted in the monastery, a strange person had said, "Today this image is established;
in the future, there shall emerge a Great Teacher who will greatly propagate the teachings and illuminate this turbid world. One day after this...

Ji was just then about to be born. When the statue encountered a crisis, this man first arrived; that year, there was indeed a theft, as a thief dug into the belly of the statue to take its hidden treasures, and Gao arrived at that very moment.
Consequently, he was named Zonggao. In the third year of the Chongning era, an imperial decree summoned Daokai to reside at Jingyin Temple. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Those who leave the household life do so out of weariness with worldly toil, seeking liberation from birth and death. They must rest their minds, cease their thoughts, and sever [all attachments]."
Grasping at conditions—encountering sounds and forms—is like planting flowers upon a stone; seeing profit and fame is like having grit in one’s eye.
Since beginningless time, you have not failed to experience such things; why must you cling to them with such bitter persistence? If you do not cease now, when will you?
If you can bring this present moment to an end, what further matter remains? If you attain a mind free from affairs, [all is resolved].
Even Buddhas and patriarchs are still kinsmen of resentment. Only when all worldly affairs naturally grow cool and indifferent does one finally accord with that which lies beyond.
Have you not seen how Yinyang, until his death, refused to see anyone; how Zhaozhou, until his death, refused to speak to anyone;
how Biandan gathered acorns for food; how Damei used lotus leaves as clothing; and how the Paper-Robed Ascetic wore nothing but paper?
The Venerable Xuantai wore nothing but coarse cloth; Shishuang established the Hall of Withered Trees where he sat and slept with others, solely intending to cause you to die to your own mind.
Touzi had people prepare rice so that they might cook and eat together, desiring to have you realize the matter for yourself.
Furthermore, the various sages of antiquity set such precedents as these. If there were no merit in it, how could they have endured it? O virtuous ones!
If you investigate this very point, you will certainly not fail others. If you are unwilling to accept it, I fear you will find it difficult in the future.
Kai once went to visit Yang Jie. Jie asked, "How many years has it been since we parted? Kai replied, "Seven years. Jie asked, "Have you been studying the Way, or have you been practicing Chan?
Kai said, "I am not playing these drums and pipes. Jie said, "In that case, you have been wandering idly through mountains and waters."
"I am capable of nothing at all. [The Master] said, "It has not been long since we last met; you are well able to discern this with great insight. Jie laughed heartily.
(Yiyou year) Chan Master Kegan began his teaching at Zhaojue.
Upon returning to Shu, he took up the Dharma at Chengdu’s Zhaojue Temple. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Just this very thing—take it up as your responsibility."
It is attained; it is like the sky universally covering, like the earth universally supporting. There is not even a hair’s breadth lacking, nor is there a second view.
Even if one were to pierce the nostrils of every single atom throughout the boundless seas of fragrant water, at once and all at once, it would still never fall elsewhere.
Should one attempt to deliberate or speculate, there is no connection whatsoever. Therefore it is said: "In a single thought-moment..."

Non-arising, with the severance of the prior and subsequent limits—this is what is called a Buddha. If one engages in deliberation, makes calculations, distinguishes between subject and object, or produces intellectual understanding, then one is separated by thousands and tens of thousands of miles. Under the gate of the Patriarchs, they simply require that you see truly, realize truly, and verify truly. Each and every person possesses a single, numinous, wondrous nature; to speak of it with absolute certainty: [The text continues with the verse: The Great Way is not difficult; It only avoids picking and choosing. If you do not love speech, How could there be right and wrong? If you wish to know the Buddha, Look at the face before your parents were born. If you wish to know the Patriarch, Look at the face before you were born. If you wish to know your own original face, Look at the face before you were born. If you can see this way, Then you have seen the Buddha. If you can hear this way, Then you have heard the Buddha. If you can understand this way, Then you have understood the Buddha. If you can realize this way, Then you have realized the Buddha. If you can verify this way, Then you have verified the Buddha. If you can see, hear, understand, realize, and verify in this manner, then you are a Buddha. If you cannot see, hear, understand, realize, or verify in this manner, then you are not a Buddha. If you are not a Buddha, then you are a sentient being. If you are a sentient being, then you are deluded. If you are deluded, then you are lost. If you are lost, then you wander in birth and death. If you wander in birth and death, then you undergo suffering. If you undergo suffering, then you are far from the Way. Therefore, you must see truly, realize truly, and verify truly. Do not rely on words and phrases; do not rely on intellectual understanding; do not rely on external conditions. Rely solely on your own original mind. This original mind is originally pure, originally bright, and originally free from all defilement. It is not produced by causes and conditions, nor is it created by a creator. It is the true self, the true person, the true Buddha, and the true Dharma. You must see it yourself, hear it yourself, understand it yourself, realize it yourself, and verify it yourself. Do not seek it elsewhere. Seek it within your own body and mind. If you can see it within your own body and mind, then you will know that the Buddha is not outside of yourself. If you know that the Buddha is not outside of yourself, then you will be able to liberate yourself and liberate others. If you can liberate yourself and liberate others, then you will be able to benefit the world and benefit living beings. If you can benefit the world and benefit living beings, then you will be a true successor of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Therefore, I exhort you all: do not waste this precious human life. Strive diligently day and night to see the Buddha, realize the Buddha, and become a Buddha. Do not wait until old age or sickness; do not wait until the end of your life. While you are still young and strong, you must strive to attain realization. Only then will you be able to repay the four debts of gratitude and fulfill the three obligations. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do not doubt it. Do not hesitate. Put it into practice immediately. If you put it into practice, then you will surely attain liberation. If you do not put it into practice, then you will remain in the cycle of birth and death forever. Be careful! Be careful! Do not let this opportunity pass. Amida Butsu! Amida Butsu! Amida Butsu! As soon as one is pressed by circumstances, the feet fluster and the hands go astray. How can one see with intimacy and trust with thorough penetration?

Only when the bottom of the bucket falls away can one be free; yet this is because, from beginningless kalpas, delusive thoughts have been so thick that one remains caught within the realms of the various sense objects.
Originally, one has never stepped upon the local scenery; one must clearly see the original face. If you are a person of true substance, you will directly take it up as your own:
you will realize that birth is fundamentally non-arising, and you will know that death is fundamentally non-dying.
At this place of neither birth nor death, where the thousand sages cannot look with their eyes and the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot lift it up—now, brothers, if...
One is able to reflect back; there is no second person. He addressed the assembly: "The whole body is the eye, yet it cannot see; the whole body is the ear, yet it cannot hear;
the whole body is the mouth, yet it cannot speak; the whole body is the mind, yet it cannot discern.
Setting aside for a moment the idea that 'the whole body is [it],' suppose you were without eyes—how would you see? Without ears—how would you hear? Without a mouth—"
How can one speak? How can one reflect without a mind? If you can find a single thread of the Way here, you will be a fellow student with the ancient Buddhas.
But tell me, whom do you take as your teacher? It is also said: "Rest until you reach the state where not a single thought arises."
This is precisely what it means to penetrate through and be liberated: not falling into the dust of sensory emotions, nor dwelling within conceptual thoughts;
transcending in a manner that is utterly remote and absolute. Thus, one is not hidden anywhere throughout the entire realm; in every object and at every point, the Great Function is fully realized.

Each and every thing flows forth from the very breast of oneself. The ancients called this "operating out" one's own family wealth. Once attained, it is attained forever; how could its enjoyment ever come to an end? Furthermore—

It is said: "This one matter, even if all the Buddhas of the three periods appeared in the world and, with immeasurable knowledge, vision, and skillful means, sought to guide and lead others, would still have its limits.
Even if the ancestral masters of successive generations and the old monks of the world were to provide hundreds or thousands of questions and answers to uphold it, they too would have their limits.
It is better to investigate it beneath one's own feet, from the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda onwards."

The Head Seat gave a shout. An said, "A masterful Head Seat! The Head Seat shouted again. An struck the letter, and as the Head Seat hesitated, An said, "You do not yet understand three, eight, and nine."
He could not help but sigh to himself. He then struck him once with his staff and said, "Jieqin, come to the Dharma Hall with Qingyuan to observe their methods.
Jieqin said in a stern voice, "You are striking my head monk to death! Qingyuan said, "It is like two official horses kicking each other."
"What evidence is there for that? An said, "Do not speak of officials' horses kicking one another; this is precisely the treading of dragons and elephants.
Qín said, "Bring him here! Bring him here! An returned once more to the Dharma Hall. Qín said, "I am the head seat among my five hundred followers."
"Why did you strike him? An said, "Even a monk must take a beating before he is finished. Qinguo looked at Yuan and stuck out his tongue.

the bridge flows, yet the water does not flow'—what is the meaning of this? An bowed low and replied, "This is my offering."

[Both] were indeed speaking the truth. Yuanwu laughed loudly and said, "So, you are originally people of my own house. An then went to the Fifth Patriarch’s [monastery] to present his credentials and submit a letter to the Dharma-kinsmen.

He said, "No one can deceive me. Looking at his attendant, he asked, "Where is that monk from? The attendant replied, "Many people have been suspicious of him.

Sitting in meditation, he stroked the tiger’s whiskers; his realization transcended the mundane world. Not merely beneath a bright window, he arranged and drew them toward the Zen seat to press against the precipice.
Grasping the mallet and raising the whisk, he unleashed his heroic eloquence; its golden resonance and jade-like vibration were like rolling thunder.

For ninety days, he held aloft the essential principles with great clarity, while a multitude of monks hurried forward to receive his influence. His skillful means for untying adhesions and removing fetters were fierce and biting, driving them on.

(Wu-xu year) Chan Master Fuyong Daokai entered nirvana (the eighth generation of the Cao-Dong lineage, successor of Touzi Qing).
Daokai resided at Fuyong Hermitage. On the fourteenth day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Zhenghe era, he requested a brush and wrote this verse: "I..."
At seventy-six years of age, his worldly ties were now exhausted. He did not crave heaven while living, nor did he fear hell when dying.
Casting off his hands and laying down his body beyond the three realms, he wandered freely and spontaneously, unbound by any constraints. After some time, he passed away. How extraordinary!
A native of Chengdu, Qi first visited Longmen. One day, while sitting in meditation, he dozed off. A chorus of frogs suddenly began to croak;
mistaking the sound for the clatter of a shaving board, he hurried toward it. Someone said, "Those are frog calls, not a board.
Startled, Qi went to the abbot’s quarters to disclose his error. Yuan said, "Have you not heard of Rāhula? Qi immediately stopped him, saying, "There is no need for the Master to cite that."
"Wait until I have examined this for myself. Before long, he attained a realization and composed a verse, saying: "In a dream I heard the sound of wooden boards; Upon waking, the frogs croaked.

The frogs and the sound of the boards— All at once, they were equal to the mountains and peaks. From then on, he applied himself even more diligently to his practice, eventually penetrating the profound mysteries.
When Yuan summoned him to share the teaching seat, Qiji firmly declined, saying, "This is no small matter. It is like being pierced by a golden needle."
The eye—if there were even the slightest deviation, the pupil would be destroyed. May you dwell upon the stages of learning in every lifetime and refine yourself therein.
He praised him from afar with these verses: "The Way exists only because one frequently steps back; Humility and gentleness are fundamentally the habit of turning the light inward."
Unaware that he had already ascended to the blue clouds, he still further cast his body into the various repositories.
At the request of a student in his later years, he spoke this verse: "Because all phenomena are empty, my mind is empty; Because my mind is empty, all phenomena are the same.
All phenomena and my mind have no separate essence; They reside only within this present single thought. Tell me, which is that single thought? The assembly was at a loss.
He let out a single "Ki-ha" shout and passed away. Fuyō Hoshun of Fuzhou was the son of the Wen family of Mianzhou. He followed the teachings of Hōen.

Upon hearing Hōen cite the *Mind-King Inscription* by Daisshi (Bodhidharma), he attained realization beneath those words. Later, while contemplating the *Hōzō-kyō* (*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*), he suddenly and fully clarified the Great Dharma.
He presented this verse: "The summit has a unique peak where clouds drift slowly; The source has no separate branches, yet the water flows cool."

He revealed the source of his illness, saying, "In this body of seven feet, where exactly does one receive sickness? When the assembly offered various responses, none were in accord with his intent.
He clapped his hands once, made a sound like vomiting, and said, "What a fine wooden pillow! Thereupon he passed away. His remains were cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were collected.

(Jihai) Zen Master Ming of Tianning Monastery in Ruzhou entered nirvana.
Initially, the Daoist Lin Lingsu had sought an audience with Cai Jing using sorcery. Cai Jing introduced him to the Emperor, who placed his trust in him.

He bestowed upon Lingsu the title "Golden Gate Immortal" and allowed him to style himself "Imperial Preceptor, Lord of the Way. By imperial decree, he ordered that all the great monasteries throughout the realm be renamed.

The Shenxiao and Yuqing Wanshou Palaces changed the Buddhist titles to "Great Enlightened Golden Immortals" (*Dajue Jinxian*); the rest were designated as "Immortals" (*Xianren*) or "Great Beings" (*Dashiren*).

Monks were called "Virtuous Scholars" (*Deshi*), and novices were called "Virtuous Boys" (*Detong*). The Dharma Masters Yongdao and others wept toward one another and said, "When the Buddha-Dharma has reached this state, to be born is as good as being dead.
They immediately went to the government offices to submit their petition. The following day, they prostrated themselves at the foot of the Xuande Gate and presented their grievances.

This was not permitted. The Emperor became greatly enraged and had Dao arrested and sent to the Kaifeng prison, where he was to be branded and sentenced to manual labor at Chongling. One night, the Governor of Chongling dreamed that a Buddhist monk, shackled in fetters, stood beneath the court hall. In the morning, he informed his subordinates, and they all reported having had the same dream. Shortly thereafter, Dao arrived; his appearance matched the vision exactly.

The entire administration was struck with amazement, and consequently, Dao’s labor was commuted. As for Chan Master Ming of Tianning Monastery in Ruozhou: [The text continues: "He was a man from the region of Xiangzhou. His secular surname was Liu, and his given name was Zhi. He was naturally inclined toward the Way from childhood. At twenty-one, he left home to become a monk under Master Huizhao of Mount Zhongnan. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he studied the Vinaya and the Abhidharma-kosa under Master Daoyuan of the Great Xingshan Monastery. He also received instruction in the *Shelun* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) from Master Fashang of the Great Xiangguo Monastery. Subsequently, he went to the Great Xinghua Monastery in Wuzhou to study the *She dasheng lun* (Mahayana-samparigraha-shastra) under Master Huizheng. Thereafter, he visited various masters to inquire about the Dharma. Once, while traveling through Jiangxi, he encountered Master Fayan Wenyi of Mount Donglin. Upon hearing his teaching, he attained great awakening. He remained there for three years, serving as the head of the assembly. Later, he resided at the Great Xinghua Monastery in Wuzhou, where he established the Dharma Hall and propagated the teachings. He passed away in the second year of the Jiayou era of the Shenzong reign."
He changed his name to Deshi (Virtuous Layman). Every day he ascended the seat; after finishing his expression of gratitude, he would say: "The wooden tally is picked up at random by hand;
the sitting mat is set down as the occasion arises. Clouds disperse and waters flow away; the heavens and earth are silent and empty. He closed his eyes and passed away.

Furthermore, there was Tanyuan of Mingyin in Pingjiang Prefecture. He also changed his name to Deshi and entered the practice of *dhūta*. He lived on pine nuts in the mountains to sustain himself, and later relied upon [Master] Ke.

In his quarters, there was only a single low couch; he possessed nothing else of value. In the ninth month of the *gengzi* year, he told the temple monks, "A month from now, I shall no longer remain here.

far-reaching, the Milky Way stretches across the heavens. The dream of the butterfly in the *Nanhua* is still fluttering; who can boast of the brindled tiger of Fenggan? Now, the path traveled from whence has been forgotten;
at twilight, mountains and rivers stretch to the ends of the earth as I watch the wild geese fly away. Written in the winter of the Gengzi year by Jingyin Jicheng. Together with [the author].

Keqin, Fazhen, Huishen, and ten other great Dharma masters, along with a thousand monks from the Chan and Lecture schools, attended a vegetarian feast at the residence of the Grand Marshal Chen Liangbi.

Among them was a master of the Xianshou school who was skilled in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; he addressed the assembly, asking: "Our Buddha established his teachings, ranging from the Small Vehicle to the Perfectly Sudden.
Having first eliminated both emptiness and existence to personally realize true permanence, and only thereafter being adorned with the myriad virtues..."
He is called a Buddha. I have heard that a single shout of the Chan school can transform an ordinary person into a sage; this seems to contradict the various sutras and treatises.
Now, if a single shout can enter our school, then the five teachings are the correct exposition; if it cannot, [they are not].
"This is a heterodox teaching. Chengduo said, "As for the questions posed by the Dharma Master, they do not merit the labor of the three great Chan masters in response.
The junior elder Jingyin alone can ensure that the Dharma Master is free from delusion. Chengduo summoned Zhixian;
Zhixian responded with an assent. Chengduo said, "That which the Dharma Master calls the Hinayana teachings of the Buddha-dharma actually possesses its own principles."
The Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna refers to the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna refers to the meaning of neither being nor not being empty.
The Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna refers to the meaning of being both existent and empty simultaneously.

The Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle refers to the meaning of being existent without being existent, and being empty without being empty. Just as my single shout is not only able to enter these five teachings, but...
He was able to enter into all worldly crafts, arts, and the various schools of thought. He let out a thunderous shout and asked Shan, "Did you hear that?
Shan replied, "I heard it. Linji said, "Since you heard it, this shout has existence; you have entered the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
A moment later, he asked Shan again, "Did you hear that? Shan replied, "I did not hear it. Linji said, "Since you did not hear it..."

Then, as he came, he let out a single shout. This was the "Inability to Enter" (Wunengru) stage of the Initial Teaching (*śikṣā*). He then looked at Shan and said: "When I first gave that one shout, you already said there was a shout.
Long after the sound had faded away, you then said there was no shout. To say there is no [shout] implies that it originally existed; to say there is [a shout] implies that it does not exist now.
Being neither existent nor non-existent allows one to enter the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śikṣā*). When I have that one shout..."
It is not existence; it exists because of non-existence. When there is no single shout, it is not non-existence; it is non-existence because of existence.

When all is exhausted, one must let go in order to possess the freedom of self-mastery. Shenwen (Shen Wen) suddenly grasped its essential meaning upon hearing it. [The Master] struck the drum and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Shen-de has thoroughly realized the Way of the Great Death of the icchantika; later students should rely upon this. Consequently, he was titled "The Old Man of Great Death" (Dasi Weng).

At the Pavilion, he amused himself by blowing an iron flute in the wilds of Qinglong. He spoke this verse of admonition for the assembly: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city:

He reached the very bottom; he trampled down the first peak of Mount Sumeru. A verse on dwelling in the mountains says: "When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one is still separated by delusion;
when form and emptiness are non-dual, a trace of dust still remains. The hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more—who knows who is the person dwelling in the hermitage?
At the beginning of the Jianyan era, Xu Ming rebelled and passed through Wuzhen. The bandits intended to execute Fupin, but Fupin said, "A great man..."

Awakening to my own nature and its wondrous mind, it accords above with the true transformation of all Buddhas and accords below with the ignorance of ordinary beings.
Not a speck of dust stirs; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. How wondrous! Even the sun and moon are not sufficient to match its brilliance.

Heaven and earth are not sufficient to contain his greatness. Magnificent and expansive, he is unimpeded and free from obstruction. He blends his light with the world and mingles with common folk, wandering at ease and in total freedom.

The great assembly earnestly entreated him, and he applied himself diligently to his practice. Not long after he entered the monastery, it was beset by a great bandit raid;

Tánhuá was the son of the Jiang family of Hángméi. From birth, he was extraordinary and outstanding.

He served as an old immortal official. He threw [the staff] down and, holding up his vermilion shoes, said: "Dharma brought back one pair; from this day forth, descendants shall walk barefoot.
