Wrapping his *fàotóu* hat, he travels alone upon the solitary road. Seeking the True to extinguish the False is fundamentally not subtle; realizing the True through the False is entirely an error.
How laughable is that ancient master of Mount Lingyan, who cast down a broken wooden ladle in the midst of the assembly! Raising his fist and letting out a shout was but a slight display of skill;
speaking of right and wrong is merely sinking into the mud. Cut off all manifold distinctions and cease pointing or directing; with a single sound, return to the *luó* flute.
Lao Li was praised from afar for his excellence. He returned to reside at Mount Rui. Tong Sishu (Xingji), whose style name was Jiantang, was the son of the Yang family of Taizhou.
At the age of twenty-five, he abandoned his wife and children to enter the monastic life. Later, he studied under Jingyuan, with whom he attained a profound realization.
He went forth to serve as the abbot of Guanshan, where for seventeen years he lived alone, practicing "sword-plowing and fire-planting. He once composed a verse that said: "The earth..."
The hearth has no fire, the traveler’s pouch is empty; snow like willow blossoms falls as the year draws to a close.
Having gathered scraps of broken hemp to mend his tattered robe, he is unaware that he stands within a world of solitude. He would often say to others, "I am still not yet settled.

One day, while watching a tree being felled and brought to the ground, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. The obstruction that had long weighed upon his chest dissolved completely, like ice melting away. Not long after, he resided at Jiang... [text fragment].
Zhou Yuantong ascended the seat and said: "Yuantong does not open a pharmacy for living medicines; he sells nothing but the heads of dead cats.
I know not which one, free from calculation, will eat it and have cold sweat flow over his entire body. In the winter of the *Chunxi* *bingshen* year, he returned to reside at Pingtian.
In the winter of the third year of *Chunxi*, Emperor Xiaozong summoned Deguang to an audience at Xuande Hall and questioned him.
Regarding the general purport of the Buddha-dharma, he was invited to stay for five nights in the Contemplation Hall within the palace.

The Emperor conferred upon him the title "Buddha-Zhao" (Buddha-Reflection) and asked, "Śākyamuni entered the mountains to practice the Way for six years before achieving success; what was it that he accomplished? Guang replied, "I had thought Your Majesty might have forgotten."
(Dingyou Year) Qian Duolì, the Layman of the Pine Window, entered nirvana.

Qian Duolì’s courtesy name was Chuhe; his style name was Songchuang (Pine Window). He followed Jingyuan and attained realization regarding his own fundamental matter. In the autumn of the Dingyou year, he manifested a slight illness.
He wrote a letter summoning Xingji as well as the presiding monks of Guoqing and Ruiyan, in which he spoke words of parting. Ji...
Accompanied by two monks, he went to the side of the bed; he prostrated, rose, and sat cross-legged. They spoke and laughed for some time, after which he wrote:

"This floating world is illusory; fundamentally, there is no coming or going. The four elements and five aggregates must ultimately reach their end. Though Buddhas and patriarchs possess great majestic virtue,"
Nor can one escape this very point. Among all the elder monks and all the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the world, is there anyone who can leap over it?
It is because earth, water, fire, and wind come together through the conjunction of causes and conditions for a brief moment;
one must not mistakenly take them as belonging to oneself. A great man,磊磊落落 (liě liě luò luò—lofty and unencumbered), should hold fast when acting and stand firm when established.

All is true. It is like sailing with the wind; one may go upstream or downstream as one pleases. Because of this, through the celebration and praise of the *zhāi*, one attains mastery over going and staying.
This is the single path to Great Liberation and the gate to Nirvana opened by all the sages of antiquity.
It is the originally pure and empty-quiescent realm, the Great Way of non-action (*wuwei*). Now that I am thus, how joyful I am! As for the external conditions of worldly toil—

In one moment, he swept everything away. He thanked the various mountains for their visitation and requested that they all bear witness. "I humbly entreat you to take care of yourselves," he said, setting down his brush.

He then turned to Guji and asked, "Is it better for me to go sitting, or is it better to go lying down? Guji replied, "When the Excellency departs, he simply departs; why concern yourself with sitting or lying?
Lili smiled and said, "Dharma brother, you must cherish yourself for the sake of the ancestral path. Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away.
(Gengzi) Chan Master Deguang resided at Ayuwang Deguang and later at Lingyin.
In the seventh year of the Chunxi era, he moved to reside at Ayuwang. ○ Chuming was the son of the Li family of Jiazhou.
Initially, he went to visit Keqin. Keqin asked, "How did the sages of the past receive people? Chuming held up his fist. Keqin—
Ming said, "This is what this old monk uses. What is it that the sages of the past used? Ming then struck him with his fist. Qín also raised his fist;
as their fists met, they laughed and went out. He then visited Zōnggǎo, who asked, "Where have you come from?"
[The monk] said, "Western Sichuan. Daokao said, "Before you have even passed through the Jianmen Pass, I shall give you thirty blows!
[The monk] said, "It was not right for me to disturb the Master. Daokao deeply approved of this. When Foyan Qianhui returned to Shu, Ming followed Anmin and attained great enlightenment.
He left the monastery to reside at Xuedou. In the seventh year of the Chunxi era, Emperor Xiaozong summoned Ming to an audience and asked, "The sages of the Three Teachings are fundamentally..."
It is the same principle. It is said: "For example, in space, there is originally no duality between east, west, south, and north.
It is said: "It is only that the gateways established by the sages differ. Thus, Confucius established his teaching through the Middle Way (Madhyamā-pratipad), saying:

'Without the Middle Way, how could the world be securely established? The *Lotus Sūtra* says: 'Worldly speech, the arts of livelihood, and so forth, are all identical with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*')."
These two are contradictory. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Without destroying the characteristics of the mundane world, one cultivates the supramundane Dharma.
It is said that nowadays many among the scholar-officials who study Confucius are merely skilled in words and language; they do not perceive the Way of the Master.

I do not understand the mind of the Master. It is only the Buddhists who do not teach people by means of written words, but instead point directly to the source of the mind, enabling sudden awakening and entry [into truth], so that one is not disturbed at the moment of death and rebirth; this is what makes them superior.

You say it is not only later scholars who fail to see the mind of the Master; even Yanzi of that time, who was said to have embodied [the Way] completely, exerted his entire life's strength [yet still failed].
They could only say, "Looking for him, he seems to be ahead; looking again, he has suddenly vanished behind.
Or, "He stands there so prominently, as if right before one's eyes," yet they ultimately failed to grasp him. Yet the Sage clearly opened his hands in eight characters, saying to his disciples:
"Do you think, my disciples, that I am hiding anything from you? I hide nothing from you. Judging by this, even at that time the disciples still did not...
"I understand the mind of the Master; how much more so those of the present day! Zhang Shangying said, "It is only after one has studied Buddhism that one can truly know Confucianism.
These words are indeed the ultimate truth. The Emperor said, "My own thought is also like this. The Emperor further asked, "What kind of people were Laozi and Zhuangzi?
[Zhang] replied, "They were merely those below the level of the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna within Buddhism. This is because the Hīnayāna regards the body with such loathing..."
Shackles and fetters! Abandoning wisdom is like discarding a mixture of poisons; it is as if the fire of transformation burns the body to enter the realm of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is just as Zhuangzi said: "The form can certainly be made like withered wood, and the mind can certainly be made like extinguished ashes. Laozi said: "I have a great affliction."
"It is because I possess a body [that I act thus]. Those of the Mahāyāna are not like this; they realize Bodhi only after all sentient beings have been delivered.
This is just as Yi Yin said: 'I am one among the people of Heaven who has awakened first. I shall use this Way to awaken these people.
If there is even one person who does not receive its benefit, it is as if I myself had pushed him into a ditch. The Emperor was greatly pleased."

He was granted the title "Baoyin" (Precious Seal), and on that same day, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Mount Jing. The Emperor once composed the "Discourse on the Origin of the Way" (*Yuandao lun*), in which he stated:

"I have examined Han Yu’s *Yuandao*. Because it speaks of the mutual confusion of Buddhism and Daoism, and the mutual disparagement of the Three Teachings, no one has yet been able to discern the truth.
Furthermore, its prose is verbose and its reasoning circuitous; when measured against the intent of the Sage, it is not yet clearly manifest. Why is this so?"

Thus, the followers of Śākya exclusively investigate the nature and destiny of existence; they cast aside the physical body and do not cling to names or appearances, remaining naturally uninvolved with worldly affairs.
How, then, could they have anything to do with ritual, music, benevolence, or righteousness? Nevertheless, they still establish precepts, saying: "Do not kill; do not engage in sexual misconduct;
do not steal; do not drink intoxicants; do not speak falsely. Now, not killing is benevolence (*ren*); not engaging in sexual misconduct is propriety (*li*); and not stealing is righteousness (*yi*).
"Not drinking wine is wisdom; not speaking falsely is faithfulness. If one acts in this manner, how far is one from Zhongni?
The Master moved with ease along the Middle Way and was a sage. Whatever he did was none other than benevolence and righteousness; how could it be given a specific name?
It is like the movement of Heaven and Earth, the cycle of Yin and Yang without beginning or end—how could there be any deliberate intention regarding spring, summer, autumn, or winter?"
"How distinct they are! These are merely names provisionally applied by the Sage. It is just like the distinctions between ritual, music, benevolence, and righteousness;
these were established to provide instruction and govern the world, and it was unavoidable that they be so. If one examines and seeks the truth behind these provisional names, one finds the Dao.
The Dao is the source of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music; benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music are indeed the functioning of the Dao. Thus said Yang Xiong.

It is said that the Master of the Old Man (Laozi) struck down benevolence and righteousness and extinguished ritual and music. Now, if we examine the traces of the Laozi’s book, those which he treasures are three:

namely, compassion (*ci*), frugality (*jian*), and not daring to take precedence over the world. Confucius said, "Gentleness, kindness, respectfulness, frugality, and yielding," and further held that benevolence (*ren*) is the greatest.
Is what Laozi calls "compassion" not precisely the greatest form of benevolence? As for "not daring [to take precedence]..."
"To be the first in the world—is this not the greatest form of humility? When it comes to realizing the Way, however, [the teachings] are mutually exhaustive.

That which is raised [in these teachings] is purity, stillness, and unity; how could this be fundamentally at odds with the Sage Confucius? This is merely because of the later degenerations of the three teachings."
The ignorant cling to these [distinctions] and consider them inherently different. Now, the Buddha and Laozi advocate for the cessation of thought and non-action;

they merely cultivate the mind and body. Confucius taught the governance of the world; this is simply a difference in application. It is like using a plow and hoe for weaving, or a loom and shuttle for plowing.
Those of later generations have needlessly been mired in confusion and delusion, surely losing the underlying principle. Someone may say: "It should be as follows..."
How can one eliminate such confusion? It is said: "Use Buddhism to cultivate the mind; use Laozi to govern the body; use Confucianism to govern the world. This is sufficient.
Only the sages were able to harmonize them; this must not fail to be discussed.
(Year of the Water Tiger) Master Kequan entered nirvana (Tiantai School).
Kequan resided at Yanqing Monastery and later returned to Zhuan’an at Danghu. On the day of the Water Tiger, he passed away without illness.
His body was cremated; wherever the smoke reached, there were śarīra relics. He was ninety-one years of age and seventy-eight years since his ordination. His dharma heir was Zongyin.
(He was from) Beifeng. A son of the Chen family of Yanguan, he received full ordination at the age of fifteen and studied under Master Zhuan-an, by whom he attained the Way.
He lived in seclusion at Maoshi Hermitage on Leifeng, then resided at Puguang in Huating and Dezang in Xiuzhou, before subsequently moving to Chaoguo in Huating.

From Beichan in Suzhou, he moved to Ling Shan in India. In the sixth year of the Jiading era, while wandering to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at Songjiang on the twelfth month and said to his disciples, "My karmic conditions for transformation are now exhausted. He then passed away in the right lateral recumbent position.
(Gui-mao) Imperial Preface to the Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-śāstra* by Chan Master Chuming of Mount Jing, presented to Emperor Xiaozong.
In the second month of the Gui-mao year, an imperial messenger was dispatched to deliver this preface to Chuming of Mount Jing, ordering its publication.
Chuming offered this verse in tribute: "The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present Share one and the same broad and long tongue. Within the pathless..."
Within the ruts of the path, he opens the way for all things; he parts the clouds across a thousand peaks and releases a single orb of the moon.
He causes all people throughout the great earth to be completely illuminated beneath his words. Awakening is nothing to be perfected; illusion is nothing to be extinguished.
There is not even this "nothingness"—a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace. I bow my head to Buddha after Buddha; in every word, there is no differing teaching. (Having read this above.)

Da Xi (Great Joy), courtesy name Yanzhi, was a native of Liangxi. He passed the jinshi examination and, having heard of the world-transcending Dharma of the Śākya clan, went to visit Chan Master Guizong.
He intended to plan a life of seclusion; however, Zhu Xi sent him a poem which contained the lines: "O Official who flees to Chan, do not be in such haste;

first complete your karmic ties within the mundane world. Later, he was appointed as the Governor of Taizhou. When the Emperor stood at the palace balcony to dispatch him, he asked: "What are the finest sights of the Southern Terrace?"
Gai said, "May there be great peace and abundant blessings; may the state remain pure for ten thousand years.

He continued, "I have heard that Shiqiao Yingzhen is one of the five hundred powerful men who suddenly appears at this time. With what method do you intend to deal with him? Mao clenched his fist and said, "Your servant possesses the Vajra-King Precious Sword.
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the title "The Elder Suichu. Zhao Feng, style name Wenru, styled himself... (text ends).

Huangshan was a native of Dongping. He passed the jinshi examination. By nature he was serene and detached; he studied the Way and attained realization. When the Monk Xian sat in meditation and passed away, Huangshan inscribed this verse for him:
"Having recognized that the primordial enlightened nature is perfect, The single shoe returned to the West with even greater serenity.

Yongjia walked steadily upon the path to Caoxi; Linji thoroughly investigated the Chan of Huangbo. When the bottom of the bucket falls off, there is not a single thing— The faculty [of discernment]..."

In the three mysterious realms of saṃsāra, a single blade of grass remains within the fire. As before, its radiance illuminates the great chiliocosm. (Wushen) Master Chuming retired to Biefeng. While residing at Mount Jing, during the Wushen year of the Chunxi era, he requested retirement; the Emperor granted him a hermitage named Biefeng. *The Three Mysteries* refers to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness. *A single blade of grass* symbolizes the unconditioned nature of the mind. *As before* means that the fundamental essence has never been lost.

*Illuminates the great chiliocosm* signifies that this enlightened wisdom pervades all phenomena. The Wushen year corresponds to 1188 CE. Master Chuming was originally from Chu Prefecture; hence his name, Chuming. He lived at Mount Jing and, upon reaching the age for retirement, was granted a hermitage by imperial decree, which he named Biefeng.
Zhice, styled Tudu, was the son of the Chen family of Tiantai. Having shaved his head in youth, he visited Jishiguang of Guoqing Temple and attained a sudden awakening.
He subsequently visited Dayuan, who asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Tiantai. Dayuan asked, "Have you seen Master Zhizhe?
He replied, "Even now, he is not lacking. Dayuan asked, "Why is he right under your own heels? He replied, "Right before my face."
"You have missed it. [Chuan] said, "The Master has sprouted without weeding; he is straight without being propped up. One day, Chuan took his leave.

Yuan saw him off at the gate, patted the back of his staff, and said, "The treasure house is near; this city is not real. Chuan nodded in agreement. He then traveled to Yuzhang to visit Tianyou. On the way, he passed through Yunju.
The wind and snow were bitter, and he sat by the roadside for forty-two days. At the beginning of the noon hour, the sound of the wooden board rang out.
With a metallic clang, he attained a sudden and vast enlightenment. Upon arriving at the gate, You pointed to his staff and said, "Where have you seen gods or ghosts come from?

He replied, "I heard the sound of the wooden board at Yunju. You asked, "What was that? He replied, "It shattered empty space; it has no handle or rim. You said, "The matter beyond this is not yet settled.
He replied, "The neighbor to the east sits in darkness, while the neighbor to the west curses one another. You said, "This is a towering transcendence."
He was one who produced the Buddhas and Patriarchs; in days to come, he alone would suffice to establish the lineage. In the year Wushen, by imperial decree, he resided at Mount Jing.
(In the year Gengxu), Chan Master Baoyin Chuming entered nirvana (he was a successor of Huazang Minfa and the thirteenth generation of the Linji line).
Chuming retired to a separate peak. In the eleventh month, he arrived at the monastery to see Zhice and took his leave. Zhice asked him:

On the day of his passing, he said, "When the water arrives, the channel will be formed. He returned to Beifeng Peak and requested paper to write the nine characters: "The seventh night of the twelfth month, at the hour of cockcrow.
He passed away according to that schedule. An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title Cibian, and his stupa was named Zhiguang.
(Renzi) Chan Master Tudu Zhice entered nirvana. (He was a dharma successor of Zantang Zun and the eleventh generation of Linji. Zhice resided at Mount Jing.

On the [blank] day of the seventh month in the Renzi year, as he was about to enter nirvana, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly and instructed his disciples to offer a written memorial service.
As they chanted the liturgy, Zhice sat upright and listened intently; when they reached the words "May the offerings be enjoyed" (*shangxiang*), he let out a laugh. Two days later, he bathed.
He changed his robes and assembled the congregation, reciting a verse that said: "The four elements have now parted and flown; smoke and clouds return as they please.
Under the autumn sky, the frosty night moon casts its brilliance across ten thousand li. Suddenly, he passed away in stillness.
(Guichou) Chan Master Deguang resided at Mount Jing. He had previously resided at Mount Aśoka.
On a day in the first month of the fourth year of the Shaohsi era, an imperial decree was issued for him to move to Mount Jing. Deguang declined with all his might.
The Emperor said, "We shall see each other morning and evening. Upon being summoned again to the private hall, he presented the *Zongmen Zhizhi* (Direct Pointing to the Source of the School).
(Bi-mao) Chan Master Deguang returned to Ayuwang Mountain.
Having resided at Mount Jing, in the spring of the first year of the Qingyuan era, he was repeatedly and earnestly entreated to return to Ayuwang Mountain; the imperial decree granted his request.
○ Fan Chong, styled Zhixu, Vice President of the Left, was serving as Governor of Yuzhang after his tenure in the Hanlin Academy when he passed by Yuan Tong Min.
A questioner asked, "Master Chong is nearly old; having fallen among those who wear the purple and gold robes of high office, he has drifted somewhat far from this matter.
Ming called out, "Inner Secretary! Chong responded with a "Yes? Ming said, "How can there be any distance? Chong leaped up in joy and said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction.
Ming said, "It is four stages' journey from here to Hongdu. Chong stood still, lost in thought. Ming said, "If you see it, you see it immediately; do not try to conceptualize it."
As soon as he thought this, his mind cleared and he attained sudden enlightenment. The Imperial Secretary Wu Juhou, returning to Zhongling with his official insignia, visited Chuanming and said:

"One day, when I was going to the provincial examination, I passed through Zhaozhou Pass. I asked the former abbot, Elder Ne, about the matter of 'passing through the pass,' and he replied, 'Go ahead and take up your office.
Now, it has been more than fifty years since then, and I have not realized [the meaning] until now. Chuanming said, "Have you ever truly understood?"
"Did you attain it? [Mingyun] said, "I have passed through eight times, always maintaining this mindfulness, yet I am still not very free and easy.
Mingyun handed him a fan and said, "Please use this fan. Daohou immediately waved the fan. Mingyun said, "Where is there anything that is not free and easy?
Daohou suddenly had an awakening and said, "Please grant me the final word. Mingyun waved the fan twice. Daohou said, "Intimate! Intimate! Mingyun—
He said, "The auspicious barbarian’s tongue extends three thousand li. Jianyi Peng Rulin had handwritten a copy of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and offered it to Master Min.
Min picked it up and asked, "This is the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*; which one is the Jianyi’s sūtra? Rulin replied, "This is what I personally wrote.
Min said, "That which was written are the characters; which one is the sūtra? Rulin laughed and said, "In that case, it is not permissible [to say there is a distinction]."
Yanmin said, "I am presently manifesting in the body of a lay official (zhíguān) to preach the Dharma for you; everyone has their share. Yanmin said, "Do not slander the sutras.
Yanlin asked, "How is it so? Yanmin held up the sutra to show him. Yanlin clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "Ha!"

Mín said, "Furthermore, it cannot be attained through words. Lín bowed. While Zhōngshèng Lú Háng was sitting with Mín by the brazier, Háng asked, "There is no need to labor over the various karmic conditions of the various houses;
I ask the Master for a direct, single phrase of instruction. Mín greeted him with a stern voice, saying, "Look at the fire!
Háng quickly pulled back his robes and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He thanked him, saying, "Truly, the Buddha-dharma is not so complicated."
Master Min shouted, “Put it down! The disciple responded with a firm “Yes, yes. Zuosi Du Xiang asked Master Min, “This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination;
how can one reach it? Min replied, “Enter the mass of fire with your whole body.”
Ming asked, "Ultimately, how do you understand this? Xiang replied, "Go straight ahead. Ming pondered for a moment and said, "Would you like some more tea?
Xiang said, "There is no need. Ming asked, "Why do you not understand it in this way? Xiang attained the essential meaning and said, "I see now that it was originally very close.
Ming said, "It is eighty thousand miles away. Xiang then composed a verse: "Inconceivable! It is a great mass of fire. To go in such a manner— not..."
Ming left the place. Min said, "Eh! There is still this one remaining. Xiang said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction.
Min said, "Just go like this; the cauldron is cast of iron. Xiang bowed his head in thanks.

*Scholar Ye Shi (style name Zhengze, sobriquet Shuixin) once remarked that Buddhist scriptures contain too many categories and that there are not few instances where they contradict one another. He went to inquire:*

Shi Yanlian said: "The Buddha takes precept, concentration, and wisdom as his fundamental principle. When the mind and its objects do not engage with various conditions, the flowing water, blooming flowers, soaring kites, and leaping fish are all the true nature of my own being.
The essential point lies in illuminating the myriad differences as one, so that phenomena and principle are seamlessly integrated."

As days passed and months deepened, the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness naturally sealed his own fundamental mind. If one can withdraw the gaze and turn back the hearing, there is originally no Buddha apart from the mind;

there is no need to inquire into numerous categories, for many words are contradictory. Thus, one spontaneously knows where to return—this is wisdom and integrity. Zhili resided at Huadu Temple in Shangyu.
Initially, he traveled extensively to study under the various schools of the Chan tradition; in his later years, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the Western Paradise.

In the eighth month of autumn in the year of Yimao of the Qinyuan era, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In a dream, I saw Amitābha Buddha preaching the Dharma while surrounded by a great multitude.
The Buddha said: 'All you virtuous people, you must single-mindedly cultivate pure karma so that you may be reborn in my land.'"
"I have seen auspicious signs; my rebirth there is certain. He then wrote a verse: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its reflection sinks into the cold water;
neither extinguished nor born, within the Land of Lotus Flowers. Having finished writing, he turned his body toward the west, formed a mudrā, and passed away.
(Year Ding-si) Chan Master Chongyue resided at Lingyin;
his sobriquet was Songyuan. He was the son of the Wu family of Longquan. At the age of twenty-three, he left home and went to visit Zonggao at Mount Jing.
When Zonggao ascended the seat, he praised Tanhua for being direct and swift in character. Upon hearing this, Chongyue set out before dawn.

Having entered the room, he spent the entire night contemplating the dialogue concerning the dog having no Buddha-nature. Suddenly, he attained realization. He immediately went to knock on Hua’s door;
Hua raised the phrase, "The World-Honored One has a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it. Yue said, "This leaves the Master at a loss."
Huā let out a loud shout. From then on, he visited him morning and evening. Huā was greatly pleased and spoke a verse to encourage him to shave his head.
Once he had received full ordination, he traveled extensively through the old masters of Jiangsu and Zhejiang. Entering Min, he met An Yong. One day he took his leave of Yong. Yong cited the saying:
"A phrase, no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree. Yue said, "I tear it apart! Yong said, "Langya said, 'How wonderful!'"
"Piling up rotten firewood," said Yue. "Adding a point to an arrowhead," replied Yong. They exchanged such repartee several times. Yong said, "My elder brother’s responses, I cannot surpass;
yet they are still not final. In the future, when the fly-whisk handle is in my hands, I shall be unable to guide others, nor will I be able to test others.
Yue said, "One who guides others causes an ordinary person of common ground to leap directly into the realm of the sages."
"It is indeed difficult. To test a person, one strikes before them; without waiting for them to open their mouths, one already knows their very marrow—what difficulty could there be?
Yong said, "I have told you clearly: when the mouth opens, it is not on the tongue; you shall know this for yourself later.
Yue then took his leave and went to Quzhou, where he saw Xianjie. As soon as Xianjie questioned him, Yue answered immediately, and Xianjie smiled.
It is said: Huangyang was merely a Chan practitioner. One day, when Jie entered the room, he asked a monk standing nearby, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
Yue was standing by his side and attained sudden, great enlightenment. He then said, "Today I finally understand why Mudan said, 'Opening the mouth is not a matter for the tongue.
From then on, his spiritual acuity was unassailable. He appeared in the world at Chengzhao in Pingjiang and became a successor of Mi."
An. He frequently moved between famous monasteries. In the third year of the Qingyuan era, the seat at Lingyin was vacant, and Emperor Xiaozong issued an imperial decree for Yue to fill the position.
Anyong, whose style name was Muguan, was the son of the Wu family of Mian County. He studied under Dingxu. One day, while entering the inner quarters for instruction, Dingxu said:

"I do not ask about the word 'having' (you yan), nor do I ask about the word 'non-having' (wu yan). When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, you must not seek understanding from the point where the World-Honored One remained silent."
Thereupon he shouted, and Yong suddenly attained sudden enlightenment. He prostrated himself and said, "Had I not questioned you today, how could I have lost the opportunity before my very eyes?
Xuefeng granted him permission. Later, he resided at Gushan in Fuzhou. Yuancong was the son of the Zhu family of Fuzhou.

Having attained the essential heart of the teachings within Huia’s assembly, the community recognized him as a preeminent disciple. In the third year of the Qingyuan era, he received an imperial decree to depart from Xuefeng.

He moved his residence to Mount Jing. His teacher, Fǎn (later known as Wǔzhǔn), was a native of Zǐtóng and surnamed Yōng. He entered the monastic order at the age of nine; upon merely glancing at the scriptures and books, he could recite them from memory.

When Chengwen was standing by Fan’s side, the burden that had long weighed upon his chest was suddenly cast off. Later, after taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said:

The Three Men Prove the Tortoise to be a Turtle. The Ancestor’s name was Pò’ān (Broken Hut). He was a native of Guǎng’ān and surnamed Wáng. He was a Dharma heir of Mìmān Jié.

You say that Jǐan has come without coming; how shall we meet? Jǐan replied, "In study, one must study truly; in awakening, one must awaken truly. Do not dig up old stumps.
Zhāng said, "Because I struck the fire and the sparks flew apart, I came to know that my eyebrows are arched and my nose is straight. Jǐan said, "..."
"I am separate from this place. [Jian] asked, "How do you manifest this proof? He replied, "The tusks are one piece of bone; the ears are two pieces of skin.
[Jian] said, "I thought there was something else. He replied, "Wrong! Jian shouted, "The grass-robbers are utterly defeated! Chang, go rest for now.

The next day, Chang cited Linji’s statement regarding the simultaneous shouting of the two head seats of the two halls. A monk asked, "Is there still a guest and a host? Linji said: [Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence regarding Linji's response.]
"Guest and host are clearly distinct. How do you understand this? [The monk] said: "I would smash the mirror of the Qin dynasty and sharpen the ancient awl;
when the dragon soars beyond the clouds and mists, what need is there to strike it further with a hammer? [The Master] said: "You have grasped its pivot, but you have not mastered its function."
Jianjian pulled up his meditation seat. Chang said, "The pleasures of the journey do not ultimately lead one home.
Jianjian gave him a slap and said, "A thousand-year-old wild fox spirit; now that you have been seen through, you are not worth a penny. Chang struck with a fly-whisk and said:
"You have only attained its function; you have not attained its essence. Jian stepped forward and said: "The green mountains tower with cold hues; the moon shines upon a stream of clouds.
[The Master] said: "You have only attained its essence; you have not attained its wisdom. Jian said: "The flowing water moves from west to east;
the falling flowers have no front or back. [The Master] said: "Though you are skilled in the samādhi of eloquent speech, it nonetheless has nothing to do with the matter. Jian then held up his staff.
[He made] a fist. He then struck once more, and at that moment the meditation hall shook. Chang said, "So it is, so it is. Jian shook out his sleeves and departed.
The next day, [the Master] appointed him as the Record Keeper (Pal Ji). He further tested him with the "hammer and tongs" of the Ultimate Teaching; Jian’s responses were entirely in accord.
One day, [the Master] said to him, "You have now reached the ground of great peace and bliss. You should protect and maintain it well. I possess the True Dharma of the Tathāgata..."
The Dharma-eye Treasury, the wondrous mind of Nirvana of the Patriarchs, is secretly entrusted to you; do not let it be lost or obscured.
Jian covered his ears and departed, whereupon [the Master] bestowed upon him this verse: Heaven and earth share the same root, with no difference between them;
Where in the home-mountain does one not encounter Him? I now bestow upon you the Seal of the Empty King; All dharmas, in their radiant glory, are entirely as one.
(Wanwei) Chan Master Wansong Xingxiu. [His work] consists of commentaries on the "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" by Tiantong Yuan.
Yili Chuci Jinjing first studied under Sheng’an Cheng, repeatedly questioning him with passages he had obtained from the *Yuanzhong* (Anthology of Ancient Worthies).
Cheng occasionally granted his approval. However, when Jinjing resigned from office, his mind turned toward fame and achievement.

He placed [the scriptures] high upon a shelf. Seeking the Way of the Patriarchs with ever-increasing urgency, he went to visit Sengcheng once more. Sengcheng frequently overturned his cases and did not agree with what he saw.
Jinjing was greatly perplexed. Sengcheng spoke to him composedly, saying: "In the past, you held a position of great importance;

furthermore, many Confucian scholars do not truly believe in Buddhist texts, but merely pluck out phrases and anecdotes to serve as topics for conversation. For this reason, I did not dare to press you too hard."
"Pinch me with tongs and beat me with a hammer! Now, when I fathom your heart, you have indeed come to ask me about matters of your own fundamental nature.
How could I continue to repeat my former errors and fail to offer words that are bitter to the taste? I am old and have never mastered the Confucian classics; I cannot instruct you.

There is an elder named Wansong, who is fully equipped in both Confucianism and Buddhism and is profoundly versed in both the Chan school and the scriptural teachings. You should go see him. Thereupon, he advanced.
When you, [Wang] Qin, visited [Xue] Song, he cut off all human tracks and cast aside all household affairs; for nearly three years, he neglected sleep and forgot to eat.
Only then did Song grant him formal certification (*inka*), naming him the Layman Zhānrán from Yuán.

Thereafter, when you escorted Emperor Yuán to the Western Regions, you sent a letter to Song, requesting that he provide commentaries on the hundred verses of Tiantóng’s *Sònggǔ* (Verses on Ancient Cases) to enlighten future generations.

His studies were arduous; it was not until the seventh year, the *guimǎn* year (1343), that he finally completed them. His name was Haengsu, and he was a successor of Seongyeom Barye of the Caodong school.
(The *gengyin* year [1350]: Chan Master Siman resided at Jingshan.)

Shifan was a direct descendant of the ancestral masters of the Dharma. Later, he successively presided over famous monasteries. In the Gengyin year of the Shaoding era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.

He occupied the abbacy for twenty years, during which his Dharma seat reached its peak of prosperity. Zhiwen, whose courtesy name was Qiyu and style name Quan-yi, was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing other boys. At the age of six, he received the tonsure; at fifteen, he went to study under Wansong. He was profoundly learned...

He recorded [Wen’s] extensive learning and his unimpeded eloquence in debate. Song served as his attendant; whenever he heard a verse or a dharma discourse by Wen, he understood it immediately and subsequently attained the Dharma.
He frequently acted as the attendant to respond to visitors on Wen’s behalf, and his sharp spiritual acumen was inviolable.
Liu Bingzhong, the Grand Guardian, was one year older than Wen; they had been close friends since their youth. Later, Bingzhong grew weary of worldly affairs and desired to study the Way.

He [Wen] exhorted him [Zhong] to become a monk. Later, Zhong was recognized and favored by Emperor Yuan Shizu (Kublai Khan). Zhong recommended Wen for high office, and he was summoned for an audience;

when they conversed, the Emperor was greatly pleased and intended to grant him an official post. Wen declined, saying, "That the Buddha-dharma circulates throughout the world is the wish of this humble monk;
wealth and status are not what I hope for. Emperor Xuanzong appointed Yinjian as the Head of the Buddhist Teachings and issued an edict for its propagation throughout the empire.

He assisted in the Assembly for the Support of the Precepts, interpreting the imperial intent and proclaiming it throughout the empire while aiding its completion. Liu Bingzhong, courtesy name Zhonghui, was a native of Ruizhou.
His great-great-grandfather had served as the Deputy Commandant of Xingzhou, and thus he became a resident of Xing. He possessed an exceptionally refined and extraordinary character;
his aspirations were lofty and spirited, and he was unrestrained by convention. As his family was poor, he served as a clerk in the Commandant’s office to support his parents.
One day, due to some official paperwork, he became dissatisfied. Throwing down his pen, he sighed and said, "For generations my family has maintained the dignity of scholar-officials;
how can I now sink into the life of a mere scribe? If a man of honor finds no fulfillment in this world, he must seek that which transcends it.
He immediately abandoned his post and went into hiding among the cliffs and valleys of Mount Wuchan, clothing himself in grass and subsisting on wood to seek [the Way].
As for his aspirations: Tianning Temple’s Xuzhao invited him to become a monk and appointed him as secretary. Later, while traveling through Yunzhong, he resided at Nantang.
It happened that Yin Jian was summoned to court and passed through Yunzhong; he urged Zhong to accompany him. Upon arriving, they had an audience with Emperor Shizu at Qandi.
His responses were in accord with the Emperor’s wishes. Shizu was divine in prowess and decisive in judgment; whenever he faced the battlefield, no enemy stood firm before him.
Zhong once praised him, saying: "He takes the love of life as the virtue of Heaven and Earth, and compassion for the salvation of beings as the mind of the Buddha.
Through his skillful means of rescue and protection, the number of lives he has preserved and sustained is beyond calculation."
(Xinmao year) Chan Master Yinjian. Chan Master Yinjian preached the Dharma at Daqingshou Monastery.
One day, while walking in the corridor, he encountered several monks. He asked the first monk, "Where are you going?
The monk replied, "I am going to view the flowers. Yinjian struck him immediately. He then asked the second monk, "Where are you going? [The monk replied,] "I am going to pay my respects..."
The Buddha departed. Jian also struck him. He asked the third monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going there. Jian also struck him. He asked the fourth monk, "Where are you going?
The monk remained silent. Jian also struck him. He asked the fifth monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to look for the Master.
Jian said, "Why do you look for him? The monk said, "To give him a beating. Jian said, "With what will you beat him?"
He struck [him] and said, "I will not strike you with the staff. Jianlian struck him four times and said, "You hollow-cheating fellow! The assembly all fled.
Jianlian called out to them, "Venerable elders! The assembly turned their heads back. Jianlian asked, "What is this?"
(Biyu) Chan Master Miaofeng Zhongmao transmitted the Dharma to Zhongmao.
Zhongmao was the son of the Wang family of Luling; he styled himself Youyun. From childhood, he delighted in studying Chan meditation and could not be bound by worldly constraints.
At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order; at nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination; at twenty-two, he traveled to visit various masters. Having heard of Miaofeng...
Fengshan was expounding the Dharma at Lingyin. [Zhao] Yong went to rely upon him, but Fengshan sternly refused him, testing his resolve.
Only after a long time did he gain admission to the hall. Enraged by this, Yong made a vow to himself: "Three 'whites' shall be as one day.

On the day of the Buddha’s Nirvana in the year of Baimu (1235), during the Endianping era, Fengshan ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, said: "The Old Śākyamuni has arrived! Do you all see him? Subtle and pure..."
The Dharmakāya possesses the thirty-two marks. [Dongshan] set down his staff and said, "Seeing that you all do not understand, I am entering nirvāṇa.
At these words, Daomou attained great enlightenment. Yinjian resided at Qingshou Monastery.
Yuan Cuo, who had inherited the title of Yansheng Gong after Confucius, crossed the river to visit Jian and requested the restoration of the ancestral temple rites at Qufu. Jian spoke on his behalf.
Regarding Khudu-hu (Hutuhu), it is said: Confucius was skilled at investigating ancient classics.

Through the Way of Great Centrality and Ultimate Rectitude, the rites of the Three Bonds and Five Constants, the origins of nature, destiny, calamity, and fortune, and the relations between ruler and subject, father and son, and husband and wife, he taught people the fundamental principles for governing the state, regulating the family, and bringing peace to all under heaven, as well as the essentials of rectifying the mind and sincere intention. From Confucius down to this point, the title of Duke has been inherited and conferred.
For fifty-one generations, the ancestral sacrifices have been inherited and maintained without ever being deficient. Khuduhur subsequently ordered that the noble title be restored.

He further decreed that those who transmit the Way of Confucius like Yan Hui and Mencius, as well as those who study the Confucianism of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, shall ensure their descendants do not cease;
these individuals were likewise exempted from corvée labor. The layman Yu was a native of Old Hangzhou, known by the sobriquet Fang.
The layman Niu, during the Chunyou era of the Song dynasty, studied under the master Wumen Kai and attained a sudden, great enlightenment. He once said:

"A person of great intelligence, upon first hearing this matter, immediately attempts to comprehend it through the mind, intellect, and consciousness; for this reason, they mistake a reflection for reality."
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives and your eyes are about to close, you cannot say to Old Yama, "Wait while I settle my mind and collect my thoughts;
I shall go with you then. This is absolutely impossible. You must study urgently and awaken urgently. It is further said: "The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean;
one enters it through its small streams. It is like splitting bamboo: once one node is penetrated, all the rest follow."
It is resolved as if by a sharp blade, without expending further effort. Since my childhood, I have harbored this aspiration:

to travel through the rivers and lakes visiting renowned masters, to engage in a lifelong exchange of "mouth-drums" with practitioners from all quarters, and to declare that the Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this—only then would I lay it all down.
Later, I met Master Wumen K'ai, whose Buddha-eye was such that whenever I opened my mouth, I was immediately cut down by him.
The gateway of his face was completely blocked. He repeatedly said, "It is not so, it is not so. Stepping back to reflect upon it, he thought, "I have spent many years of effort;
how could there not be some place of joy? He had attained various fragmentary realizations, yet he would never submit to Wumen’s "It is not so, it is not so.
Upon meeting Chou'an, he went to question him: "Master, what kind of insight did Wumen possess that you dared [to say such things]?"
Regarding humans and devas, he inverted right and wrong, saying: "Under the seat of Wumen, there is no dharma to be attained and no path to be transmitted;
one can only obtain two words. I asked, "How do you say these two words? He replied, "Not so, not so.
From this, I came to know how the old man Wumen dealt with people: he never lightly sprinkled even a single drop of foul water upon them.
O people! Although I am not clever, I have been dragged before the authorities by the "Stinking Hut" (Chou-an) on a formal charge, and my grievance is no small matter.

Thus, I shall set forth the crux of right and wrong: "Pointing directly at the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood. When one turns the light back upon oneself, there is a total severance of all obstructions.

The moment one attempts to deliberate with the intellect, white clouds stretch for ten thousand miles. To judge people and evaluate character, to apply praise or blame to things, to hold the ancients in high esteem while slighting the present, and to value mere hearsay—[these are the errors].
"Base eyes! Leave it to them to speculate and brood; they have not even dreamed of the point where right and wrong hinge.
How will you penetrate it? Look here! He further said: "The laywoman Shen Dao-po of Anji Prefecture asked, 'Is there cause and effect? I replied, 'There is.

She asked, 'When a student of the Way truly has a place of awakening, why does the teacher deliberately say it is not so? Is there cause and effect or not? I said, 'The Buddha-dharma does not conform [to worldly logic].'"
In human affairs, how could there be no cause and effect? Because Baizhang gave one wrong turning word, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds; since I have no mind at all, what use have I for all dharmas?
[The Master] said: "Regarding this matter of right and wrong, how many phrases are there? [The Disciple] said: "There are four phrases. [The Master] said:
"How do you present these four phrases? [The Disciple] said: "The first phrase: 'To have both right and wrong' is not permissible. The second phrase:

'To have neither right nor wrong' is also not permissible. The third phrase: 'To be both right and wrong' is not permissible. The fourth phrase: 'To be neither right nor wrong' is also not permissible. If...

[The student] said, "If one attains freedom from these four propositions, one finally beholds the natural splendor of the original ground. I asked, "Have you attained such freedom? He replied, "I have not attained it.
I said, "Everyone has their share; why have you not attained it? He asked, "How can I not attain it? I said, "When a hen marries a rooster, she flies after the rooster;
when a dog marries a dog, it follows the dog. He asked, "What is the natural splendor of the original ground? I said, "The crescent moon shines over how many prefectures and how many counties?"
[The Master asked: "Among people, how many are joyful and how many are sorrowful? [The monk] said: "I do not ask about this kind of scenery. [The Master] said:

"Then I ask about that original local scenery. [The monk] said: "It is that which has no marks of male or female. [The Master] said: "Since it has no marks of male or female, what 'gate of right and wrong' could there be to ask about?

[The Master] said: "Is there anything further beyond this? [The monk] said: "There is. [The Master] said: "What is this thing further beyond? [The monk] said: "A horse-leech and a *ding* (a small insect)."
Dwelling at Lüsijiao: "When you ascend to heaven, I shall ascend to heaven.
(Gengzi) Chan Master Daochong resided at Tiantong; his style name was Chijue.
He was the son of Xun of Wuxin. Having grown up studying for the jinshi degree, he renounced it to receive the teachings of Śākyamuni.
Xue traveled to Chengdu to study the sutras and śāstras; however, he grew weary of the obsession with names and characteristics and abandoned his studies.

In the Renzi year of the Shaohui era, he crossed the Gorges and wandered through the Jing and Chu regions. At that time, Chongyue was residing at Jianfu Monastery in Raozhou. Xue went directly to his quarters, but was refused entry due to the famine of the year.
It happened that Cao Yuansheng had recently appeared at Miaoguo Monastery; as soon as Chong entered the gate, he heard a word and attained realization. He then went to attend him.

Chang appointed him to attend to the incense. From morning until evening, he followed and traveled with him; Chang did not spare him even a single old fist or a painful blow. Consequently, much of his lifelong knowledge and views left no trace or influence.
Later, when Cao Yuan moved to Gui Peak, Chang again attended him on his travels. After a long time, he took leave to travel to Zhejiang, offering a verse that said:
"I still have these two hands of a destitute man, which I intend to scratch at the itchy spots throughout all quarters. When he arrived in Hangzhou:
Master Yue presided over Lingyin Monastery; its gates were solemn and its doors steep. For eight months, [Chong] was unable to enter the inner chamber. Someone reported that he had lost a disciple.
Master Yue said, "I have already opened the gates wide for him to stay. He is simply himself; he has missed the mark right before my face.
Upon hearing these words, Chong saw through the source of Cao: that laughter, smiles, scolding, and abuse are all skillful means for the sake of others, transcending the world.
He served at Jiahe Guangxiao, then moved to Jiangshan, and later to Xuefeng. In the gengzi year of the Jiaxi era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Tiantong.
When the seat at Yuyang became vacant, Chong again assumed the duties of abbot. He traveled back and forth between these two mountains, preaching the Dharma.
In the winter of the Jihai year, Hubi-le summoned Chan Master Yinjian to preside over Qingshou Monastery.
In the Renyin year, Hubi-le welcomed him to his encampment and inquired about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Yinjian first demonstrated the causes and effects of gods and humans, and subsequently opened his mind with various essential points of the Dharma.
The King conceived faith and sought to receive the bodhicitta precepts. He further asked, "Within the Buddha-dharma, is there a method for bringing peace to the world?
[The Master] replied, "It encompasses the entire dharma-realm and nurtures the four modes of birth; its provisions are fully complete.
Within the sphere of the Buddha-dharma, these four great continents are like a single mote of dust upon the vast earth—how much more so is a single sea? If one were to discuss..."

The altars of the State depend upon the well-being or distress of the people; their well-being or distress, and their security or peril, depend upon the administration of government. Government does not exist apart from the mind.
As for our Śākyamuni, the Dharma for bringing peace to the world is found in the "Chapter on the Correct Discourse of Royal Law" (*Rājanīti-samyak-vāda-parivarta*);

its principles are inherently clear, being neither difficult nor easy. My only fear is that Your Majesty may be unable to carry them out in full. The King was greatly pleased and received him with the rites due to a teacher. Upon his departure, the King...

Question: Now that the Buddha-Dharma has come here, how should it be received and upheld? Answer: Faith is difficult to produce, yet it has now been produced; a virtuous mind is difficult to arouse, yet it has now been aroused.
One must strive to protect and maintain it with single-mindedness and without forgetfulness. Having originally received the Bodhicitta precepts, do not perceive any faults in the Triple Gem.
Constantly bear in mind the unrest of the common people, comforting them well and clearly administering rewards and punishments. Let those who hold office be free from partiality.
"Appointing the worthy and accepting remonstrance; at all times constantly practicing skillful means—all this is the Buddha-dharma.

After Bianjian had taken his leave, an evil youth spoke with reckless words of slander, claiming that the Buddha-dharma was not to be trusted. The King wished to punish him for his crime and dispatched a special envoy bearing the memorial.

When Bianjian returned, he submitted this petition: "When a bright mirror stands upon its stand, beauty and ugliness appear of themselves. When a divine blade rests in one's hand, rewards [and punishments]..."
Punishment must be impartial. If right mindfulness is manifested before one, it is permissible to slay external demons of false views;
however, a sovereign should maintain a mind of benevolence and forbearance. May Your Majesty be even more reverent in this regard.
(Zimao) Chan Master Zongmao Established a Hermitage at Foding Peak.

Zongmao had previously encountered his spiritual opportunity at Miaofeng Peak; later, when he took his leave to return home, Miaofeng instructed him, saying, "Go and establish a thatched hut deep within the mountains.
In the *guimao* year of the Chunyou era, he ascended Foding Peak on Mount Dongshan. Climbing through the creepers and parting the brambles, he discovered the ancient [remains] of Master Xiu.

He established the foundation of a temple at a site where he cleared away the tracks of tigers, wolves, foxes, and rabbits to dwell. Subsisting on wild fruits and water from mountain streams, he sat upright day and night.
Sometimes, during the cold of snow, there was no fire for the night; he would pass the days eating only a few inches of *chángchǔn* (a type of radish) at a time.

He composed a verse extemporaneously, saying: "The mountain monk has his lot dwelling among the misty vines; Without rice and without money, let him not trouble himself. The waters are like lapis lazuli, the mountains are like jade; Before one's eyes..."
There were already many such [sites]. Subsequently, he slightly diverted a spring and reclaimed wasteland to provide for his own needs.

He personally performed all tasks, from pounding rice and cooking to gathering firewood. After some time, the assembly of students gathered daily; within a few years, it became a towering monastic center.
Following the old name, it was titled Longji Qingliang Temple (Longji Qingliang Monastery). Feng entrusted him with his Dharma robes, along with a self-portrait inscribed by himself, to be passed on.
Mao said: "The solitary peak of the Wondrous Summit has grasses growing thick; horizontally grasping a bamboo staff of three feet of iron, I allow only Foding and Longji to know it.
This true secret instruction is not transmitted from father to son. Mao once wrote this on the gate to await those who would come to study with him, saying:
"Setting aside the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—what is that which is your own self? If you can speak of it, I shall grant you my personal seal of approval."
Upon seeing Longji arrive, if it be not yet so, then dwell outside the gate for a while. Zheng Qingzhi, whose courtesy name was Deyuan, held the position of Chancellor four times.
During the Duānping era, he exerted great influence in summoning and employing upright men.

He once composed a "Treatise on Encouraging the Cultivation of the Pure Land," in which he stated that among those who study Buddhism today—namely Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya—the most ultimate and sudden is Chan.
Those who possess sharp faculties and superior capacity, and who understand through spiritual intuition and mental realization, will still not avoid the error of falling into a stagnant emptiness.
For those who study the Three Vehicles, nothing is equal to the Teaching; yet unless one forgets the trap upon catching the fish, they will not avoid the ailment of poring over old paper.
For those who protect the good and ward off evil, nothing is equal to the Vinaya; yet unless one’s body and mind are pure and the inner and outer are as one, then—
One cannot avoid the suffering of self-entanglement. Viewing the matter as a whole: if one discusses the gateways through which one enters, there are Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;

yet if one considers their ultimate destination, they are Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*). Is it not the single gateway of the Pure Land alone that allows one to attain these precepts, concentration, and wisdom without relying on Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya?
At the very moment of reciting the Buddha’s name, one chants with the mouth and contemplates with the mind, ensuring that no evil is committed—is this not the Precepts?

Binding one’s mindfulness upon the pure realm, where illusory objects and dust alike perish—is this not concentration (*samādhi*)? Contemplating that there is truly no contemplation, while the mind-flower remains serene—is this not wisdom (*prajñā*)?

If a person can set aside all myriad concerns and direct their single intent toward the Western [Pure Land], then without the application of staffs or shouts, they will awaken to the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching;
without reading the Great Canon, they will obtain the Eye of the True Dharma; and without maintaining [the formalities of] the four modes of deportment, they will attain...
Great Sovereignty! Neither defiled nor pure, without dust and without liberation. At such a time, what constitutes precept, concentration, and wisdom?
What constitutes meditation, teaching, and discipline? My own mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction. This is the ultimate realization of the cultivation of the Pure Land.
Wu Qian, courtesy name Yifu, style name Lizhai, served as Chancellor during the reign of Emperor Lizong. He once said to a monk: "In the past..."
Mañjuśrī addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "When I first entered the inconceivable samādhi, I bound my mind to a single object.

As for what is called binding the mind to a single object, it is like the practice of observing the sun, observing the moon, or the tuft of hair between the eyebrows and the white spot on the bridge of the nose.

Although these matters are shallow and mundane, their principle is in fact profound and subtle. It is as Zhaozhou said: 'In the twelve periods of the day, this old monk has nothing to do but the two things of porridge and rice.'"
At that time, this was a matter of employing a mixed mind. Guishan asked Lan’an, “What task do you perform during the twelve periods of the day?
Lan’an replied, “I herd oxen. Guishan asked, “How do you herd them? Lan’an said, “Whenever one enters the grass, I pull it back by the nose.
These were all instances of binding the mind to a single object. Thereafter, the venerable masters further devised skillful and subtle expedients to cause students to train.

This refers to examining the "head phrase" (huatou). Examples include "The dog has Buddha-nature," "Three pounds of flax," "A dried piece of excrement," "The cassock from Qingzhou," and "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
These are all points where the path of logic is blocked. One is instructed to take up one such phrase at random and examine it;
as one looks and looks, doubts arise and persist. Without ever letting go throughout the twelve periods of the day, suddenly—*phut!*—the nostrils spray forth.
The "First Stage" (Diyi) is precisely where one establishes one’s person and sustains one’s life. These are all evidences of fixing the mind upon a single object.
Hidden within the Dharma-gate, he attained great mastery. At the end of his life, he knew in advance that the time had come and said to others, "I am about to depart;
there will surely be thunder and rain tonight. It was exactly as he had said. He composed a poem and passed away while sitting upright.
(Wu-shen year) Chan Master Xiaoweng Miaokan entered nirvana. (A Dharma heir of Wuyongquan. Miaokan resided at Yuwang.
He entered nirvana in the third month of the eighth year of Chunyou. He was seventy-two years old. Initially, Daochong resided at Tiantong.
In the Jiachen year of Chunyou, an imperial decree ordered him to move to Lingyin. Not long after he took up residence there, he beat the drum to bid farewell to the assembly.

He retired to seclusion in Jinling. When the seat at Yuyang Monastery became vacant, the court deliberated that, as Dajue was of a distinguished lineage, he should not be lightly entrusted with the position.
They specifically summoned him from his place of retreat three times, yet he ultimately did not comply with the imperial decree.
(Jiyou) Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan entered nirvana (the sixteenth generation of the Linji lineage, successor to Pō’ān Xian). Shifan resided at Mount Jing.
Emperor Lizong once summoned him for an audience and subsequently issued an edict for him to ascend the seat in the Ciming Hall. The Emperor drew the curtain to listen.
He presented the essential points of the Dharma he had preached to Chen Guiyi, the State Councilor. Guiyi memorialized the Emperor, saying: "It is concise, clear, and direct."
The Emperor decreed: "There is a supplementary holy governance. He then conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Fojian.

Previously, forty *li* from the monastery, Fan had constructed several hundred rooms to receive wandering monks. An imperial plaque was granted naming it Wan'ian Zhengxu. Furthermore, several hundred paces to the west...

He constructed a small hermitage as a place for his retreat. In the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era, he built a dwelling by the Moonlight Pond and inscribed it with the name "Retired Plowman.
He requested retirement from the court, but his chronic illness happened to flare up. On the first day of the third month of the Yisi year, he ascended the hall to address the assembly, saying:
"This mountain monk is both old and ill; I lack the strength to engage in idle chatter with you all here and there. Now..."
On this day, he managed to emerge from his illness. That which he had previously been unable to express to its full extent, he now shook out before everyone with complete sincerity.
He then rose and shook his robes, saying, "How much is there? On the fifteenth day, he gathered the two classes of attendants to arrange his final affairs.
He personally wrote his testament and some dozen letters; his speech and laughter were as harmonious and playful as they had ever been. The physician examined him...
Shi Ci said to Fan, "You have not yet recognized this single lineage. At dawn on the eighteenth day, he asked for a brush and wrote a verse:
"When coming, empty and desolate; when going, bare and naked. If you wish to ask for the ultimate point, there is the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
Within a short while, he passed away. His entire body was buried beside Zhengxu, and his stupa was named Yuanzhao.
Regarding Chan Master Daochong’s residence at Mount Jing:
Daochong lived in seclusion in Jinling. In the Jiyou year of the Chunyou era (1249), Lord Zhao, the Governor of Jingzhao, invited Daochong to found the Fahua Monastery in Wu.
Just as Daochong was about to take charge of that post, an imperial decree arrived appointing him to reside at Mount Jing. Daochong said:
If he did not attend the *Lotus Sūtra* assembly, it would show a lack of faith; if he were to again disobey his lord’s command, it would show a lack of reverence.
Lacking both reverence and faith, how could he serve as a model for future students? Thereupon, he suddenly rose up, left the *Lotus Sūtra*, and within a month ascended Mount Jing.
(Gengxu) Chan Master Chijue Daochong entered nirvana. (The dharma heir of Caoyuan Sheng; the tenth generation of Linji.

In the third month of the Gengxu year, Daochong wrote a hand-lettered inscription for his funerary niche along with a final testament, stating: "The anniversary of Wuzu’s passing falls on the eighteenth day of the third month.
I shall depart on the fifteenth, so I will not be able to prepare incense or perform offerings. He then composed a verse and wrote it down.

The Master praised him, saying, "His laughter and conversation were just as they always were. When an attendant monk requested his final verse, he brushed him away with a gesture of dismissal and paid no heed.

A moment later, he said to the attendant with a smile, "The final word cannot be deliberated upon; it requires that each person directly take it up for themselves. He then took up a brush and wrote his parting words to the assembly.
On the fourteenth day, he ascended the hall and spoke until the late hours of the night. Rising from his seat, he remained there for a short while.
He passed away. His age was eighty-two; his years since ordination were sixty-one. He was cremated, and the relics were of five colors, numbering beyond count.
(Gui-chou year) Chan Master Zuqin resided at Longxing.
Zuqin resided at Longxing in Tanzhou. He recounted his own history: he left home at the age of five and saw his preceptor interacting with guests.
Upon hearing this, he knew that such a matter existed. At sixteen, he became a monk; at eighteen, he set out on pilgrimage.

With a resolute determination to emerge from the world and investigate this matter thoroughly, he stayed under the guidance of Yuanhui of Shuanglin Tiejue. From morning until evening, he did not step outside his quarters.

Even when entering the communal dormitory, he would go to the back hall with his arms folded across his chest, moving slowly and deliberately without looking left or right. His eyes remained fixed ahead.

What was previously seen did not exceed three feet. When first contemplating the saying, "The dog has no Buddha-nature," suddenly, at the very moment a thought arose, I struck it with a turn-back-observation (*pratyavekṣā*) of that single thought. Instantly, it became as cold as ice; it was truly transparent and profoundly still.
Sitting for a day without moving or wavering, it felt like the snap of a finger. I heard not a sound of bells or drums for nineteen days.
I was staying at Lingyin Temple. I met Miaofeng Shan; after Shan passed away, Shitian succeeded him on the seat. Ying Dong-sou was in the Guest Office, while I was in the Hall Monitor’s Office.
There I saw the Secretary from Chuzhou, who said, "Brother Qin, this practice of yours is like stagnant water—it will not serve the purpose.
Stillness and movement are two distinct aspects, yet you treat them as two separate pieces. To study Chan, one must give rise to the 'doubt-mass' (yiqing)."
Great doubt leads to great awakening; small doubt leads to small awakening; no doubt, no awakening. You must harbor doubt regarding the *kōan* before you can succeed.
Since the time of Nanquan, this has been so. Nanquan was the disciple of Songyuan; his words were always upright and correct.
At that moment, I changed my *huatou* (critical phrase) and took up "a dried-up shit-stick. I simply harbored doubt here and there, until it arose before me.
I had completely lost my way. From morning until evening, dullness and agitation attacked me in turn; I could not achieve even a moment of purity.
Hearing that Master Tianning had long served Songyuan and was his true heir, I moved my bedding and went to Jingsi Temple to register as a resident.
There, I joined seven brothers in binding ourselves in seated meditation. For two years we did not spread our mats, and our ribs never touched the ground.
Outside the hall sat the Senior Monk Xiu from Zhangzhou. Every day he remained upon his meditation cushion like an iron stake;
when walking upon the ground, he held his spine erect and kept his arms hanging down with his eyes wide open, appearing just like an iron stake.
I wished to draw near him to converse, but he would go east and come west, or go west and come east. This continued for two years.

He could not attain anything further. One day, he suddenly reflected to himself: "I have sought the Way but have failed to gain entry; my clothes are tattered and worn, and my flesh and skin are withered away.
Unconsciously, tears flowed as he urged himself on with painful resolve, saying: "From antiquity to the present, countless have awakened to the Way.
Could it be that I alone lack the seeds planted in past lives? For now, I shall request leave to return to my hometown. And so he departed.
"This one release releases them all. After two months, he came again to attend to his studies. He once more rectified his practice from the beginning.
One day, while walking in meditation along the corridors, he suddenly encountered Xiu. Gazing at him from afar, he felt a sense of serene self-satisfaction.
He then approached and asked, "Last year I wanted to speak with you, yet you simply avoided me; why was that? Xiu replied, "Truly..."
"A person who correctly practices the Way has no need for the craft of clipping their nails; I have more to say to you.
He then asked, "How is your practice? I recounted it to him from the beginning, saying, "At present, my dullness and agitation cannot be settled."

Xiu said, "What difficulty is there? It is simply that you have not been fierce enough. You must sit firmly upon your meditation cushion and straighten your spine, causing every joint to support one another.
From the three hundred and sixty bones down to the eighty-four thousand pores, unify them all into this single word 'Mu.
When you hold it up in this manner, what room is there for dullness or distraction? As for me..."
Relying on others to practice, he was unaware that drowsiness and distraction had both vanished; his body and mind became one, like a silver mountain or an iron wall.
For three days and nights he did not close his eyes. On the afternoon of the third day, while standing beneath the triple gate, he walked as if sitting.
Suddenly he encountered Xiu, who asked him, "What are you doing here? He replied, "I am practicing the Way. Xiu asked, "What do you call 'the Way'?

At this, he was unable to respond and became increasingly bewildered and distressed. He immediately wished to return to the hall to practice *zazen*, but then saw the Head Seat, who said to him, "Just open your eyes wide and look;
what principle is there? Having been challenged by this single phrase, he was struck speechless.
Even as he withdrew to return to the hall and had just ascended his meditation seat, the space before him suddenly opened up as if the earth were sinking away.
It could not be shown to others; it was beyond all worldly phenomena that could serve as metaphors.

Overcome with joy, he descended from the seat and sought out the practice. He was at his desk by the sutra case when he saw me coming; he immediately joined his palms and said, "How joyful! How joyful!"
He then took his hand and walked once around the willow embankment before the gate.

Looking up and down between heaven and earth, he saw that the myriad phenomena of the forested universe—all things previously detested and discarded, as well as ignorance, afflictions, torpor, and distraction—had originally flowed forth from within his own wondrously luminous true nature. For over half a month, there had been no movement of these appearances.
It does not arise. It is a pity that you did not encounter a great master of vast vision and skill to settle this for you;
otherwise, you would not have remained stuck here, which is called "not being liberated from the ground of views" and obstructing right knowledge and vision.
Every time you fall asleep at midnight and all dreams vanish, you split it into two separate pieces. The ancients spoke of "waking and sleeping being as one," yet you still fail to penetrate this.
[It is] so. "If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams naturally vanish. As for the saying, "If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness," you have completely misunderstood it.
When a *gong'an* has a logical path, one can comprehend it; when it lacks meaning and is difficult to enter, one cannot grasp it at all.
Although you have been under the guidance of our late master Wuzu for many years, every time—
Whenever I entered the room to ascend the seat, not a single word struck home upon my mind.
Neither the sutras nor the recorded sayings contained a single phrase that could resolve this ailment. Thus, this obstruction remained within my breast for another ten years.
One day, while walking before the Buddha hall at Mount Tiem, I suddenly raised my eyes and saw a solitary ancient cypress tree; it touched upon what I had long been seeking.

Attainment! When the boundaries of the objective realm are completely cast down at once, that thing which obstructs the breast disperses with a sudden thud. It is like emerging from a dark room into the bright daylight.
From this point on, one no longer doubts birth, no longer doubts death, no longer doubts the Buddha, and no longer doubts the Patriarchs.
Only then does one begin to see where the Old Man of Jingshan stands. He deserves exactly thirty blows of the staff. Why? If it were otherwise—
For a person of great power and great capacity, where is there so much circuitousness?
When Deshan saw Longtan at the moment the paper candle was blown out, he immediately said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. From that point on, he took up his white staff and shook heaven and earth.

At that place was Master Shuilao of Jinbang. When Mazu gave him a kick, he immediately said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings are all fully realized at the tip of a single hair; one must recognize the source there.

When Gaoting saw Deshan, he beckoned with his hand and then strode away crosswise. You younger practitioners of later generations, if you wish to inquire about or study this matter, you must take a step forward.
To pursue this matter, one must possess this very standard and have this very spirit; only then will it be attained.
If it were something I had spoken myself, you would not be able to remember a single character of it. To commit it to memory would only mislead you for the rest of your life.
Later, when Qin also brought up the koan of Linji’s three blows of the staff, upon reaching the point where [Linji] "pulled the tiger's whiskers," he said: "Linji was struck by Huang..."
Huangbo struck him three times with his staff; the entire world was filled with a whistling wind.

Finally, at the very end, he dealt three punches to Dayu’s ribs—a moment where there was not even space for a hair to enter. This is what is called "transmitting vessel to vessel" and "trading gold for gold. Now tell me:
is this the same as the Second Patriarch standing in the snow until it reached his waist, or the final three prostrations made to Bodhidharma? If [you say they are the same]...

If you turn toward this, you will certainly attain it. It is granted that you understand how a single phrase contains the Three Mysteries (san-xuan), and within each Mystery, there are the Three Essentials (san-yao).

As for when sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not, sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not, sometimes both person and environment are taken away, and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away—this is truly like "the bowl slipping from the hand" (shen-wan-tuo-qiu). Later, he spoke thus:
Master Yun’s verse says: With one punch, he toppled Yellow Crane Tower; With one kick, he overturned Parrot Isle.
When there is spirit, he adds to that spirit; Where there is no elegance, he is nonetheless elegant. Now tell me: does this verse fall on the side of Huangbo or Linji?
If you, all of you, can distinguish the black from the white here, I grant that you have realized the Great [Function].
The Dharma. Should this not yet be so, I, this mountain monk, have a verse as well: The Eastern Lord’s decree does not travel in vain;
Three blows of the black staff are too perilous. When the dragon gains the water, his spirit increases; When the tiger encounters the mountain scenery, his ferocity grows.
(Dingsi) Chan Master Haeun Injeom entered nirvana (the sixteenth generation of Linji, successor of Zhonghe Zhang). Injeom resided at Gyeongsu-sa.
On a day in the intercalary fourth month of the Dingsi year, having finished reciting a verse, he said to the assembly, "Be quiet for a moment;
I wish to rest. An attendant monk hurriedly called the administrative officials to him. Injeom then passed away peacefully and auspiciously.
He was cremated, and countless *śarīra* relics were obtained. He was posthumously titled the Great Master Furi Yuanming (Buddha-Sun Perfectly Radiant).
(Wu-wu year) Yu-miao established limits for the study of Chan;
Yu-miao’s style name was Gao-feng. He was the son of the Xu family of Wujiang. His mother dreamed that a monk boarded her boat to stay overnight before she conceived. As soon as [he was born]...

He left the swaddling clothes as an infant and delighted in sitting in the full-lotus posture. Whenever he encountered a monk entering the gate, he would immediately feel a sense of longing and desire to follow him on his travels.
