At the age of fifteen, he left the household life; he shaved his head, received the full precepts, and studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. At twenty, he changed his robes and entered Jingci Monastery, where he established a three-year limit for himself to practice Chan meditation.
One day, his father and elder brother came searching for him, but he sat there with a dignified air, paying them no heed. (Recorded by Yuan Feisi, year eight of the Tianxi era).

A man from the country of Pāṭaliputra, he could recite one or two thousand verses of secret gāthās from memory upon merely glancing at them. Having consulted all the renowned masters, he became thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka.
During the time when the Great Emperor (Seṅge) was still in obscurity, Pa-si-ba recognized that the true mandate had returned to him;

he dispatched an express courier to travel directly to the Prince’s residence. Seṅge accorded him exceptional honor and respect. In the year Wǔwǔ, the Buddhist and Daoist clergy rectified the *Hu hú jīng* (Sūtra on Converting the Barbarians). [This was during the reign of] Emperor Xiānzōng.
The Emperor summoned Daoists to debate the distinctions between right and wrong. The Daoists were unable to respond and abandoned their own doctrines. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

(In the eighteenth year of Zhizhi [1281], by imperial decree, the spurious scriptures of the Daoist canon were to be burned; with the exception of the *Daode jing*, they were all destroyed. The Elder Linquan Conglun of Ba’en Chan Monastery in Dadu was ordered to set fire to them. As he raised the torch, he said:

"Recall those years in the time of Emperor Ming, when the flames once distinguished the beautiful from the ugly. Now the Son of Heaven of Great Yuan continues the Great Canon, manifesting the orthodox and crushing the heterodox—who does not know this? Alas! The Daoist teachings have secretly corroded Buddhist scriptures from ancient times until now, fabricating errors and forging falsehoods. He then proceeded to burn them.)

I have humbly interpreted the words of the sutras and schemed to inscribe my name upon the *palm-leaf* manuscripts. To slander the Tathāgata and falsely accuse the former sages with such foul language and wicked speech—how can it even be uttered? Such rootless, mad ravings are truly difficult to enumerate in full.

It began with Zhang Ling’s fabrication, who did not follow the profound words of Laozi but falsely composed *zhao* rituals and collated the *Lingbao* scriptures. He fraudulently claimed these were obtained from the void and falsely asserted they were personally transmitted by the Most High (*Taishang*).

Using the demonic arts of the Three Zhangs to delude the ignorant, and devising the divine talismans of the Five Movements to seduce unworthy women—if one observes this, Ge Xiaoxian merely searched for the "essential mysteries," while Tao Hongjing vainly recounted empty rhetoric; Du Guangting was a clever thief who plucked things right from under one's nose, no different from a bandit; and Lu Xiujing was weak within despite his outward pretenses—what kind of man is he, after all?

It is extraordinary! Had it not been for his bitter suffering, how could he have dared to speak ill of others? While the execution of Bǎo Jìng was still tolerable, the retribution incurred by Wáng Fú was no light matter. Fú Yì and Jiāng Bīn are unworthy of mention; as for Zhāng Shēng and Jiāo Lèi, they are hardly worth discussing.

Kòu Qiánzhī’s eloquence flowed like a surging tide as he harmed others to benefit himself; Lín Língsù’s scheming and flattery led to the ruin of the state and the destruction of families. To disparage the ancestors of others is certain to incur disgrace in this lifetime; to destroy the worthy and good will inevitably bring calamity through three lifetimes.

Cause and effect do not err; retribution is precise. Alas! One laments that Fǎlín did not meet with better fortune and suffered demotion; one sighs that Dàoshì, though having risen twice, found it difficult to remain steadfast. This has caused the sons of Śākya to grieve at heart. Fortunately, the August Heaven has opened its eyes. We respectfully acknowledge our Great Yuan...

"Your Majesty, Emperor of the World! You have opened the way for the heterodox to return to the orthodox, and removed the false to preserve the true. Fearing that sentient beings might forever fall into the perilous straits of delusion, you have caused the myriad people to ascend the path of enlightenment. The grievances have now been settled; we thank Your Majesty’s grace, yet even grinding our bones to dust could not repay it.

[He then takes a torch and draws a circle, saying: "O virtuous ones! As for the sacred texts of the Three Caverns (*Sāndòng*), can they still certify this Fire-Light Samādhi? If you can understand it here and now, then the *Beidǒu Jīng* (Dipper Sutra) kept at home is merely a vain teaching that brings unrest to people's mouths.
If you have not yet realized this, then after these ashes fly and the smoke vanishes, go wherever you please to seek the Celestial Honored One, but look with urgent eyes!"
(Jihwei) Yuanmiao visited Chan Master Duanqiao Miaolun (Lun was a successor of Shifan; the seventeenth generation of Linji).
In the year Jihwei, Yuanmiao requested instruction from Duanqiao Miaolun, who instructed him to investigate the koan: "From where does life come? To where does death go?
Thereupon, he did not let his side touch the mat, forgetting both body and mind. Whenever he went to the toilet, he would emerge wearing only his inner robe.
Once, when a letter was opened, its seal and lock were forgotten and left behind. At that time, his fellow practitioner Xian sighed with regret, saying, "I have already failed to fulfill my duties;
why not assist him so that he may achieve success? Thereafter, he attended upon him morning and night with the utmost care and diligence.
(Gengshen) Yu-miao visited Chan Master Zu-qin. Zu-qin was staying at the Beijian Pagoda.
Yu-miao went specifically there to seek an audience. As soon as Yu-miao had offered his greetings and inserted the incense, Zu-qin struck him out and closed the door.
After going back two or three times, he finally managed to approach the master. He then asked about his previous practice. Yu-miao—
Yi-gong said, "Tou-qin, you must now completely eradicate [all thoughts] and contemplate the word 'Wu' (No). From then on, he questioned and investigated daily.
Tou-qin suddenly asked, "Who brought this corpse for you? Before the sound had even faded, Yi-gong struck him.
This occurred countless times, yet Tou-qin’s diligent inquiry became increasingly earnest.
(Year of the Xin You) Master Zuqin Transmits the Dharma to Yuanmiao.
When Zuqin moved to Nanyue in Chuzhou, in the second month of the Xin You year, Yuanmiao returned to his quarters from Mount Jing.

Suddenly, while dreaming, he recalled the koan raised by Duanshao Bridge: “All dharmas return to one; where does that one return? At once, a state of profound doubt (*yiqing*) arose within him. Three...
Day and night his eyes did not blink. On the sixth day, he joined the assembly at the Three Pagodas to chant sutras.
Suddenly, as he raised his head, he beheld the portrait of Master Wuzu Fayan. Seeing the final two lines of the eulogy, which read: "In a hundred years, thirty-six thousand mornings;
turning it over again, it is originally just this fellow," he suddenly shattered the doubt regarding the "dragging of a dead corpse. He then traveled south to Nanming.
Yangqi Qin asked, "Who dragged a corpse here for you? Miaoxin gave a shout. Qin raised his staff;
Miaoxin seized it and said, "Today, I cannot be struck by Yuanmiao. [Yangqi] asked, "Why cannot you be struck? Miaoxin shook his sleeves and went out.
The following day, Yangqi asked, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? Miaoxin replied, "A dog licking a hot oil pan. Yangqi said, "..."
"Where did you learn this pretense? [The Master] said, "I am precisely wishing for the Master to doubt me. Qian then withdrew.
(Guihai year) Chan Master Yǎnxī Guǎngwén entered nirvana (he was a dharma successor of Zhèwēng Yǎn).
Guǎngwén’s courtesy name was Yǎnxī. He was the son of the Lin family of Hòuguān. Having received the tonsure and the full precepts, he traveled to visit various venerable elders.
Later, he visited Tian Tong’s Zhe-weng Yan. Their meeting was as difficult as trying to fit a needle into a grommet, and he realized for himself that he had not yet attained realization.
He went again to Shuangjing, where Yan greeted him with a smile, saying, "Have you come? One night, while sitting by the eaves, he heard the watchman strike the third watch and entered the room.

As he was dragging his sandals, he stumbled and fell, suddenly awakening from a dream-like state. The following morning, he went to the room; Yan brought up Zhaozhou’s story of washing the alms bowl. Upon hearing it...

When he opened his mouth [to speak], Yan suddenly stopped him. All the doubts that had persisted throughout his life were instantly dissolved like ice. In the fifth year of the Shaoding era (1248), he took charge of Xiaojingci Temple.
He successively moved to other famous monasteries, everywhere reforming abuses, supporting what was collapsing, and widely accommodating disciples.

On the [blank] day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Jingding era (1262), he entered nirvana. Zeweng Yan was the son of the Zhou family in Taizhou. From childhood, he was precocious and possessed brilliant intelligence.

Mairen. When the assembly at Stone Bridge on Mount Jing was dispersed, an imperial edict appointed Daoyan to fill the vacancy. He composed a verse in praise of Vimalakīrti, saying: "In Vaiśālī he manifested illness, feigning ignorance;
He added to the suspicions already filling the bellies of the people of his time. Had it not been for Mañjuśrī’s personal investigation and penetration,"
Who knows of these faults? Furthermore, he once wrote the "Chapter on Punishing the Private," which says in brief: "This book is truly a copy of a decree from before the Hall of Old Man Yan.
How can those today who claim to possess the 'Eye of the Way' across various regions know its value?
If one can truly receive and uphold this book, there will be great benefit to be gained in the future. Master Zhe-weng frequently used this work as an example for others.

Master Càn of Yishan also said: "The permanent store of gold and grain, once it is set aside for the purpose of providing for the assembly, is for all intents and purposes like a poison such as *zhēn* (*gall*).
For the abbot and those who manage its income and expenditure, the slightest contact with it causes their entire bodies to rot and溃烂 (*kuìlàn*). This is recorded in detail in the Vinaya texts.
We can see this from the ancients, who would take money to the storehouse to purchase ginger and decoct it into medicine. How much more so for those who occupy the seat [of the abbot] today!"
As for these "measures," they do not merely involve scraping away the contents from the bowls of others to indulge their own appetites; they are also used to cultivate superficial social ties.
At their most extreme, they even involve gouging out precious items to purchase rare curiosities and extensively cultivate such social favors.
I hope you will move to a great monastery; I only fear that one day Old Yan with the Iron Face will settle your account from beginning to end.
The original founder was the son of the Pan family of Tongzhou. He was born with extraordinary marks. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he went to study under Zhe’ung Yan.
Yan asked, “Where are you from? He replied, “From Huai. Yan said, “The Great Sage of Sizhou—why did he appear in Yangzhou? He replied, “Nowadays...”

One day, while in Hangzhou, they encountered each other again. [Hui]yan said, "For now, let us have nothing to do with one another. Zhaorun slowly replied, "I have come from afar to seek your teaching style.
Because Huiyan perceived Zhaorun’s sharp intelligence and wished to stimulate him greatly, he did not allow him to enter the hall.

As soon as he saw him, Huiyan said, "Give me a turning word. Just as Zhaorun was about to open his mouth, Huiyan shouted. Zhaorun then presented a verse, the final line of which read: "Empty teachings turn back."
He looked toward Chang’an. Yan said, "This is where the staff resides. [Fahai] said, "I thank the Master for granting me lodging;
I shall now join the ranks of those who enter the inner chamber. Subsequently, he was appointed to oversee the records. After Yan passed away, Zhaò took up residence at Guangxiao Temple.

He successively moved through famous monasteries until reaching Mount Jing. During years of famine when the monks were few, before long, multi-storied pavilions rose to the clouds and robed practitioners arrived in succession.

○ Zen Master Yudō’s Verses on Mountain Dwelling (Ten Selected Poems) Leaning my staff against a thousand-fathom cliff, I realize that conditioned existence must reach the ultimate state of non-action. Words like these emerge as impurities from the blue sky;
My conduct, failing to accord with the Way, is a flaw upon white jade. How can the metaphor of the horse exhaust the myriad things? The loss of the sheep is but a cause for vain weeping.
Many paths diverge. The traveler on the western road of the sunset mists has eyebrows like snow; as the moon rises, he knocks at the gate to deliver purple *zhī* fungi.

In the human world, the red sun easily slants toward the west; all manner of clever contrivances should never be boasted of. Only when cut open and found flawless is it jade; once drawn with legs, it is no longer a snake.
With fists unclenched, there are ferns in the green forest after the night rain; from the heart, there emerge flowers on the emerald trees in the spring breeze. The world...

One thought melts away, yet remains inexhaustible; the shortcut to fame and office lies within the mists and clouds. Amidst the shadows of white clouds, one laughs heartily; though earth and heaven grow old, one has no further doubts.
On the mountain path, frost awaits as one searches for herbs in the cold; by the stone window, there is no moon, and the sutras are read late.
One pities Su Wu amidst the night snows and his green sheep; one sighs for Li Si in the western wind with his yellow dog. Through the ages, the green scrolls remain.
Throughout the world, who else but you has left behind both fragrance and stench? Moment after moment, thought after thought, the mind finds no rest; why do you harbor anxieties for a hundred years?
Empty space has a substance that must be realized through personal experience; concentration and wisdom have no gate—do not practice them falsely.
When one awakens from sleep, the azure sky holds the sun three spans high; when the poem is finished, a cuckoo calls out from a green tree. The Great Being of the Twin Śāla Trees spoke this clearly.
When you realize that the bridge flows while the water does not, it is no longer involved with any objects; all objects are exhausted. What further matter is there to bring into deliberation?

The river is viewed as unchanged from one’s first year of sight; planting chrysanthemums is hoped for only their fragrance in late autumn. When the smoke warms the deer, they sleep upon the grass of the three paths;
when the night is cold, the geese cry out across the sky filled with frost. Who can tell this to the guests of greed and delusion? Upon the barren mounds, the withered [trees stand].
Skeletons bask in the evening sun; mind after mind has ceased its frantic pursuit. In a paper curtain rolled like clouds, one sleeps in a stone tower.

Birth and death are but the dew upon a hundred-year-old flower; awakening and delusion are but the head reflected in a mirror this very day. People say that one must first see the Way before cultivating it.
I laugh at those who, while riding the ox, still seek the ox; with a single step, they transcend the thousand sages.

Last night, the hundred rivers turned westward. The pure wind of antiquity has long failed to return; the surging currents of this final age are truly pitiable. Plain silk takes on color once it leaves the silkworm’s mouth;
the bright moon is covered in dust once it emerges from the oyster’s womb. How could empty flowers seen by one without illness obscure the eyes? Having doubts is like drawing an arrow.
The shadow sinks by itself; who is it that can die so as to exhaust the thieving mind? Come together to hoe the clouds and plant the plum trees.
Non-action is ultimately non-action; where does ultimate non-action rest? At dawn, the jade rollers open the verses of the Buddhas of the past.
Azure mists clear away the ancient immortal’s altar. Let him cast his seals and melt them down; let you don your caps and then hang them up.
Stride straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags; do not complain that the road is difficult in the human world. I take my own mind and set it at ease;
let confusion and enlightenment have no bearing upon one another. The wooden horse I have nurtured chases the wind with urgency; when released, the mud... [The text is incomplete].

The ox drinks until the sea is dry. When thought arises, ten thousand paths are all obstructed; when principle is exhausted, it is difficult for even a thousand sages to penetrate. Upon the flames of a red furnace, one observes flying snow;

in every land, in every speck of dust, the seas and mountains are cold. To try to stop a child’s crying with yellow leaves— *Note: This is a poetic rendering of the Zen kōan concerning the "Ox-Head" (Niutou) school, illustrating the paradoxical nature of enlightenment where effort and conceptualization fail.*
Scratching my head as the azure sky and crimson sun sink low; The slanderous tongue remains unpolished, sharp as a sword.
A greedy heart is not wine, yet drunk like mud. It is lamentable that no one joins the Western Society; Yet I laugh at the *Nanhua* [Zhuangzi], where all things are made equal.
Outside the gate, peach blossoms form a thousand trees of brocade; Clearly they paint forth the Creek of Wuling.
*Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 39; *Fozu gangmu*, Fascicle 40 (marked with the character "Shuang").

Jiazi (Beginning from the fifth year of Jingding of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty and the first year of Zhizhi of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty). Yichou (The first year of Xianxi of Emperor Duzong of the Song dynasty). Yihai (The [first] year of Gong [of Emperor Gongdi of the Song dynasty]).

Jōdeiu Gannen (Year of the Rat, Bingzi): The first year of Jingyan of Emperor Duanzong of the Song. Gōjin (Year of the Tiger, Wuyin): The first year of Xiangxing of Emperor Bing of the Song. Kōshin (Year of the Dragon, Gengchen): The seventeenth year of Zhizhi of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan. Otsubi (Year of the Sheep, Yiwei): The first year of Yuanzhen of Emperor Chengzong.

Chōtokutei (Year of the Dog, Dingyou): The year was changed to Daide. Goshin (Year of the Monkey, Wushen): The first year of Zhidai of Emperor Wuzong. Jinnishi (Year of the Rat, Renzi): The first year of Huangqing of Emperor Renzong.

Gotatsu (Year of the Tiger, Jiyin): The year was changed to Enyū. Kōshi (Year of the Rooster, Xinyou): The first year of Zhizhi of Emperor Yingzong. Kōgai (Year of the Pig, Guihai): The third year of Zhizhi of Emperor Yingzong of the Yuan (ending here).
(甲子) Chan Master Rujue resided at Mount Jing.
A native of Wuzhou, he studied under Chidun. He once presented this verse: "At Mount Zhong, I braved white blades with my bare body;
Several times I have been nearly buried alive. Since the man was lost and the household destroyed, I have realized there is no station left to arrange."
In the Jǐngdìng Jiǎzǐ year (1264), an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Jìngshān.
(Dīngmǎo year [1267]), Wēn Chánshī entered nirvana (a successor of Wànsōng in the Cáo Dòng school).

Initially, Liú Bǐngzhōng, wearing the informal robes of a śramaṇa, followed Shìzǔ in the prince’s residence and participated in secret deliberations within the inner chambers, thereby determining [the course of governance].

He calculated the affairs of the state and presented Zhiwen to Shizu. When Shizu ascended the throne, Zhong was appointed as Grand Preceptor (Taibao) and participated in the administration of the Zhongshu Sheng.
He was granted a residence in Fengxian Ward and bestowed with the title "Great Chan Master Puan of the Buddha-land. He oversaw the monks and nuns of all regions.
Zhong lived in a vegetarian retreat, remaining serene throughout the day; Zhiwen likewise applied himself with vigor to the protection of the Teachings.

Whenever monastic fields or dwellings were encroached upon by the wealthy or followers of other teachings, he would exert all his strength to restore them. Each year, the government bestowed upon him gold and silk;

yet beyond the maintenance of the temple, he remained as indifferent as if to worldly flavors. Toward the end of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, he submitted his seal of office and resigned from his position.
In the fifth month of the Dingmao year of the Zhizyuan era, he manifested illness. He passed away reclining on his right side facing west. A wondrous fragrance lingered for three days.
Upon cremation, his heart, tongue, and teeth remained uncorrupted; when the multitude excavated the ground several feet deep, they still recovered śarīra relics.
(Jisi) Chan Master Zuqin Resides at Yangshan (Seventeenth Generation of Linji, Dharma Heir of Wuzhun Shanfeng).
Zuqin resided at Yangshan and addressed the assembly: "The decline of the Buddha-dharma has never been more severe than it is now.

We rely entirely upon those of later generations and junior students to give rise to great courage and vigor, to bear great vows and aspirations, to support [the teaching] with bare hands, and to shoulder the burden on single shoulders; do not fail us."
Do not fail the Buddhas and Patriarchs who established this world and bestowed the compassionate grace of the Dharma-milk.
Do not fail the kings and rulers who provide external protection and sustain the land and its waters. Do not fail your parents and teachers who nurtured you and granted you the precepts of tonsure.

Do not fail your own resolve to leave the household life and travel as a mendicant. To consume the offerings of the faithful in vain and to let one’s time pass in emptiness—time does not wait for man; it only turns away.
The eye is precisely the next life. If this body does not attain liberation in this present life, toward what other life shall one turn?

Do not wait until you are on the verge of thirst before digging a well. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, when the light of the eyes is about to fall but has not yet fallen, and one is greedy for life and terrified of death, with hands and feet in a frantic scramble like a crab falling into boiling water—at that time, even if one wishes to turn the light back upon itself, it will be too late.

To practice this Way in order to shatter birth and death—you have already delayed too long! Why not, while you still possess this present body, strike with all your strength and vigor until you penetrate through to the end?
These two words, "Buddha-Dharma," are difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. If you fail to turn yourself around now, you will fall among the various classes of beings;
once there, you shall no longer hear the Buddha-Dharma. You must arouse great courage and advance straight ahead, seizing [the opportunity].
The Vajra-jewel sword sits upon the heads of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it must lie upon the heads of the Buddhas and Patriarchs before one attains it.
(Gengwu) Yuan Miaotong’s Succession Record.
While Yuan Miaotong was at Longxu, one day, because a pillow fell to the ground while he was sleeping with others, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and subsequently mastered [the Way].
The Dharma-succession letter from Zuqin states: "In years past, my failures were personally exposed before the Master.
Today, as I harbor doubts once more, I cannot help but bring them forward from the beginning. At fifteen, I left home; at twenty, I changed my robes and entered Jingci Temple.
Setting a three-year limit for death to study Chan, I then sought instruction from Master Duangqiao, who commanded me to investigate: 'From where does life come? To where does death go?'"
"Where have you been? Your mind has split into two paths and your heart has failed to settle on one.
Look at this; you have been dragging it out for over a year. Every day you are just like a lost traveler.

At that time, being pressed by the three-year deadline, I was in the midst of great distress when I suddenly saw my elder brother Jing from Taizhou, who said that Master Xueyan often asks after your practice and wonders why you have not [made progress]."
After one turn [of the assembly], he joyfully took incense in his sleeve and went to the North Gorge Pagoda to seek further instruction.
Just as he was about to offer greetings and insert the incense, he was struck with a heavy blow of the staff and driven out; the door was then immediately closed.

He returned along the road weeping, and upon reaching the Sangha Hall, he went back the following day after the morning gruel. Only then was he permitted to approach, whereupon he asked about his previous practice. The man related everything in full.
At that moment, he was immediately granted the eradication of the ailments accumulated over his previous days. He was then instructed to contemplate the word "Mu" (無).

From the beginning, he was led through the development of his practice once more, and further ordered to come for instruction every day. This was like a traveler on a journey who must see the progress made each day.
Because [the Master] spoke with such systematic order, [the student] subsequently ceased to inquire about the specific points of practice; he simply entered the gate.
He then asked, "Who brought this corpse here for you to drag? Before the words were finished, he struck him with a painful punch.
Every day he would simply ask in this manner and strike in this manner. While being thus pressured, there was finally some opening.
It happened that the Old Monk was departing for an invitation to Nanming; as he left, he instructed him, saying, "Once I have entered the monastery, send someone to fetch you."
After you had finally ceased all communication, I joined forces with my elder brother Ze from Changzhou and traveled together. Upon reaching our lay relatives' home, we prepared our travel gear;
however, unexpectedly, because they considered us to be young and inexperienced on the road, they confiscated all our luggage and ordination certificates.
We had no choice but to carry our packs and head straight for Mount Jing. On the fifteenth day of the second month, we returned to the Hall. Suddenly, during the following...
On the sixteenth night of the month, while dreaming, he suddenly recalled the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return?
From that moment on, his state of doubt was suddenly ignited, such that he could no longer distinguish east from west or north from south.

On the sixth day, while chanting sutras with the assembly atop the pavilion, he raised his head and suddenly beheld the portrait of Master Wuzu Fayan. At the end of the eulogy, it said: "A hundred years..."
Thirty-six thousand mornings and evenings—it has always been this very person. One day, while handling the phrase about "dragging a corpse," it suddenly shattered;
my soul fled and my heart failed me, and only after death was I revived. This was no less than casting off a burden of one hundred and twenty catties.
It was on the twenty-second day of the third month of the year Xinyou, the anniversary of Shaolin’s founder. That year happened to be—
At twenty-four years of age, having completed the three-year limit, he intended to travel to Nanming to seek a definitive resolution.

However, as the summer retreat was drawing near, he could not be accommodated by the local people. It was only upon the conclusion of the retreat that he reached Nanming, where he suffered a humiliating defeat.

Although he had repeatedly undergone refinement within the master’s room and had come to understand the public cases, and though he could not be deceived by others, when it came time to speak, his mind...
Furthermore, he felt a sense of being weighed down; even in his daily life, he could not attain freedom, as if he were burdened by a debt to another.
He had intended to remain there for the rest of his life to serve him, but did not expect that his fellow practitioner, Brother Ze, would be departing for another mountain.
I abruptly departed from his presence. In the year of Yichou (1205), when the Old Monk hung the plaque at the meditation hall, I was once again able to rely upon him for service and attend him.
Later, while at Tianning Monastery, I was questioned as to whether I could maintain mastery amidst the vast activity of the day.
He replied, "I am the master. He asked again, "In sleep and dreams, are you still the master? He replied, "I am the master.
He asked again, "When one is fast asleep—without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the master?
At this point, he was truly left with no words to respond and no principle to advance. The Master instructed him, saying, "From now on, I do not need you."

Studying the Buddha and studying the Dharma, tracing back to antiquity and extending to the present, is simply this: when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. As soon as one awakens from sleep, shake off the drowsiness and ask:
"Where, ultimately, does this master of mine reside? Where does he establish his dwelling and sustain his life?

Though one may have sufficient faith, alas, my own nature is dull and slow-witted, making it increasingly difficult to see clearly. Thus, I sat upon the dragon’s whisk and [began to] reflect for myself...
I vow: for the rest of my life, I shall act as a simpleton; I must certainly see through this one matter clearly.

After five years had passed, one day while waking from sleep, I was in the midst of doubting this very matter when a fellow practitioner staying with me happened to push his pillow off the bed, making a loud noise.
Suddenly, the knot of doubt was shattered, as if leaping out from within a net. Recalling what I had previously...

Doubt. The enigmatic kōans of the Buddhas and patriarchs, the causes and conditions of distinctions between ancient and modern—these are just like seeing the Great Sage at Sizhou, where a traveler from afar returns to his hometown and finds it is none other than the person of old.

Without changing one’s former way of walking, from this point on the state is settled, the nation is stabilized, and all under heaven enjoys peace. With a single thought of non-action, the ten directions are cut off. As for what has been described above...
Offered with utmost sincerity. I humbly beseech your venerable compassion to deign to examine this in detail.
(Guiyou year) Chiding attended Master Zuqin. Chiding was the son of Wang of the Taihe clan.
From childhood he abstained from meat and pungent vegetables; he was pure, austere, and firm in his resolve, possessing aspirations beyond the mundane world. However—

Worldly conditions deprived him [of his practice]. At the age of thirty-one, he shaved his hair and heard the essential meaning of the Separate Transmission. He went to attend upon Master Qin, who addressed the assembly:
"Brothers, when you apply yourselves to the practice, if for seven days and nights you remain with a single thought without interruption and do not blink your eyes..."

"There is no way to enter," [he said]. "Cut off this old monk's head and make it into a ladle for scooping excrement. Dingmo attained a realization; Qian ordered him to serve as the attendant for purification for the assembly.
On the sixth day of the sixth month of the Guiyou year, the assembly suffered from dysentery. He devoted himself entirely to serving them. Before long, Dingmo himself fell ill.
When his illness became critical and the physicians declared he could not recover, he took a wash-tub, went to a secluded spot, and sat upright upon it.
He abstained from all liquids and food, maintaining right mindfulness alone. For seven days his eyes did not blink.

At midnight on the seventh night, he suddenly perceived that the mountains, rivers, great earth, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the entire realm were like snow. Beneath the bright moon, his single body stood majestic and imposing, such that heaven and earth could not contain it.
After a long while, as if hearing the sound of wood being struck, he was startled awake; his entire body broke into a sweat.

His acute illness also subsided, and he rejoiced in his own recovery. At dawn, he went to the abbot’s quarters and related this to Yuanqin. Yuanqin presented him with a *gong'an* (public case) to interrogate him;
his responses were unhindered. Yuanqin showed him a verse, which said: "What is this luminous, numinous awareness? In the blink of an eye, it has already been missed.
The tally-stick by the latrine emits radiance— Directly beneath, it was always just me."
(Jiaxu) Chan Master Yuanmiao established his teaching at Shuangji Peak.

He lived in seclusion at Longxu for nine years, binding together wood to create a hut that was pierced by the wind and scorched by the sun. Wearing but a single robe through both winter and summer, he used neither fan nor brazier.
Daily, he would pound pine needles to mix with millet, sustaining himself by mere mouthfuls. Once, accumulated snow buried his hut for over ten days; the path—
The smoke and flames were cut off, and everyone said that [Zhaozhou] was dead. When the snow cleared, he sat in meditation as before.
There was a monk named Ruoqiong who burned his monastic documents at Longxu under Miaoxiu. Suddenly, he fell ill. Miaoxiu said, "In the midst of illness, sever all external attachments;
this is precisely the right time to apply yourself to practice. Entrust this stinking skin-bag entirely to me; simply endure it through the sickness, and I will certainly not deceive you. Ruoqiong—
As his illness grew critical, he sought a bath. Looking down at his reflection in the hot water, he attained immediate realization. He laughed with joy as if liberated from a chronic ailment.
After two nights, he wrote: "Thirty-six years of delusion; today, a truly laughable scene. The nostrils born of one's mother are wide open, releasing an unfeathered iron falcon.
Miaoyan asked, "What are the nostrils born of one's mother? Wufeng held up his writing brush. Miaoyan said, "..."
Furthermore, what is called a "hairless iron hawk"? In the year Jiashu (1254), Jue threw down his brush and passed away at Shuangji Peak in Wukang.
Zhiyu, a native of Siming, resided at several famous monasteries; in the year Jiashu, he moved to Mount Jing and addressed the assembly:
Why do those whose own eyes are not yet clear take empty space for trousers to wear? Why do they draw lines on the ground to make a prison?
Why do those who enter the sea to count its sands stand with their feet poised upon the tip of a needle?
(Dingchou year) Chan Master Xuzhou Puduo resided at Mount Jing.
His courtesy name was Xuzhou. A native of Jiangdu, his secular surname was Shi. Having left the household life, he traveled extensively to visit various masters.
Upon reaching Jianfu Temple in Raoyang, he went to call upon Wude. When Wude moved to Fuyan and Huazang, Puduo accompanied him. One day, Wude asked: "Not being with the myriad..."
"Who is it that takes the Dharma as a companion? [The Master] replied, "An iron Kunlun beneath a golden incense burner.
[The monk] said, "I thought this short fellow had some long-reaching insight, yet his understanding was only like this. He then bowed deeply and said, "Thank you, Venerable, for your testimony.
He entered the world at Bānshān in Jīnlíng, where he successively occupied famous monasteries. In the *dingchou* year of the Yuan era (1317), he received an imperial decree to go to Jìngshān.
(Gengchen) Chan Master Xuzhou Pudu entered nirvana (a successor of Wude in the Linji lineage). Pudu resided at Mount Jing.
Encountering the aftermath of a fire, he resolved to restore the monastery; as his efforts were nearing completion, he suddenly manifested a slight ailment.
He requested a brush and wrote in large characters: "Eighty-two years, riding a bottomless boat; I have capsized it and returned—under a single sky of bright moon."

On a day in the fourth month of the Gengchen year of the Zhizhen era, he entered nirvana. Miaogao, whose style name was Yunfeng, was a native of Changxi. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

His mother dreamed of an infant by a pond, sitting with palms joined upon a lotus flower; she reached out her hand and heart to take him up. Upon waking, she gave birth to Gao, who was thus named Mengchi (Dream-Pond).
From childhood, he delighted in books and applied himself to study, especially excelling in his devotion to the Buddhist scriptures. He earnestly requested to leave secular life and become a monk.
Regarding worldly matters, his parents could not bear to deprive him of his aspirations because of his dreams. He left home to receive full ordination and first visited Daochong.
Chong said, "The speech of this youth flows with order; he is a 'hu-lian' vessel of our school. He then visited Shifan, who held him in even greater esteem.

He was about to be appointed to an attendant position, but Gao sighed deeply and said, "To harbor a desire for security ruins one's reputation. I will not stop until I have traveled everywhere to consult with masters of all quarters.
He then went to Yuyuan to see Guangwen, where he entered the inner room and took charge of the treasury keys. One day, Guangwen raised a koan:
"For example, when an ox passes through a window frame, its head, horns, and four hooves all pass through; why is it that the tail cannot pass? At these words, Gao suddenly attained enlightenment.
Xing replied, “The whale swallows the seawater until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches. Wuen remarked, “You have only managed to say half of it.
Later, he appeared in the world at Nanyang Dalu, and after several transfers, he reached Jiangshan, where he remained for thirteen years until the year of Yihai.
The temple was caught in the turmoil of war. Among the soldiers were those who coerced Zhaogao for gold; one soldier pointed a blade at him and threatened him.
Zhaogao extended his neck and said, "If you wish to kill me, then kill me. My head is not a whetstone for your blade. His words and expression were composed and dignified, entirely free from fear.

The soldier was moved by this, cast aside his blade, and departed. On the day of Gengchen, an imperial decree appointed him as the abbot of Jingshan. Previously, when Emperor Shizu first ascended the throne...

He was appointed to this rank, and Bo-this-rgya (Bu-ston) was made State Preceptor (*Gukshi*). In the *Gengwu* year of the Zhizhen era, he was elevated to the title of Imperial Preceptor, the Great Jewel Dharma King (*Dishi Dabao Fawang*), and further granted a jade seal.

He was charged with presiding over the Buddhist teachings of all nations. For the Crown Prince, he expounded the *Tshogs-shes-kyi-bstan-bcos* (*Chos-kyi-dbyings-su-nam-par-mkha’-ba’i-rnam-par-rtog-pa’i-gzhung-lugs-kyi-bstan-bcos*, or *Chakshijie deng zhang suozhi lun*).
He declined the honors and returned to the West. On the [blank] day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year, he entered nirvana.
(Xinsi year) Chan Master Yuanmiao entered the "Gate of Death.
While residing at Shuangji, in the Bingzi year, his disciples fled in all directions to avoid the war. Yuanmiao alone remained, sitting upright with the door closed.

When peace was restored and the area settled, he opened the door to look inside; the *nāga* [statue] was just as it had been before. Consequently, those who came to visit increased, and he could no longer keep up with them.
On a leisurely occasion, he slung his staff across his shoulder and looked left and right, saying, "Does the assembly understand? With my staff slung over my shoulder, I do not look back at people;

I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. In the spring of the Ji-mao year, he packed his belongings in a cloth bag and fled under the cover of night, traveling directly to Mount Tianmu.

On the western peak lies Lion Rock (Sijong-sa), rising a thousand *ren* from the earth with its cliff faces standing like a forest of pillars. Delighted by its wondrous beauty, I felt a desire to spend my final years there.

Before long, however, ants drawn to the bait gathered once more. In the year *Gin-si*, I again constructed a stone cave to the west of the rock, fashioning a small chamber like a boat and inscribing it with the name "Gate of Death" (Sigwan).
Above, water leaked down; below, it was a mire; buffeted by wind and rain, I severed all contact with attendants and cast off my robes.

He did not bathe his body nor shave his hair. He cut open a ceramic jar to serve as a cauldron and ate only once every two days with complete composure. The Cavern (Dong) cannot be ascended without a ladder;
he removed the ladder and severed all ties, so that even his disciples rarely had the opportunity to behold him. He established three "gateless barriers" (san guan yu) to test practitioners, saying:

"A person of great ultimate penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death. Why, then, is their life-root (ming gen) not yet severed? This was the public standard of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Consider this: it is but a single principle; why then is there clarity and lack of clarity? A great practitioner of the Way ought to follow the conduct of the Buddha;
why then do they fail to observe the *vinaya*? If their words do not accord with the truth, they should simply close their door and refuse to receive visitors.
(Guīwèi) The Biography of Chan Master Zǔqīn Transmitting the Dharma to Chídìng.
In the Wùyǐn year of the Zhìyuán era, Zǔqīn ordained Chídìng as a monk and bestowed upon him the robe and verse, saying: "This markless field-of-merit robe..."
"I now entrust this to you. After he awakened to and clarified the ground of his mind, he was like a dragon shedding sweet rain.
From that time on, he followed the great monks back to the hall, never letting his side touch the mat for another six years. One day, hearing Master Qin’s discourse, he cited the case:
"When a deceased monk has died and been cremated, where does he go? [Master Qin] answered on his behalf: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth—these fully reveal the Dharma King."
At these words, his doubts were completely swept away; his body rose up about a zhang into the air.

When the assembly withdrew, he went immediately to the abbot’s quarters and said, "Just now, when the Master expounded upon Prajñā, it startled the stone lion in front of the Dharma Hall so much that it danced with laughter without ceasing."
Yunqin said, "Try and say it. [The monk] replied, "When spring returns beyond the kalpas, all things wither; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are not a single speck of dust.
How can one speak of the Dharmakāya’s transcendence? It makes the blue-eyed barbarian of the Western Heaven laugh to tears.
Yunqin struck the table before him and said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are not a single speck of dust—what is this? He made a gesture as if to overturn it, and Yunqin laughed.
He said, "One color, two prizes. When [Ding] entered the room, he asked, "Speak one phrase regarding the point of intimacy. Ding said, "I will not speak.
The Master asked, "Why will you not speak? Ding picked up the incense box in his hand and said, "This was obtained from here."
"It is not worth even half a coin," said Xingqing. "Talkative fellow! Later, while Xingqing was inspecting the hall, Ding wrapped himself in a paper quilt and fell fast asleep.
Xingqing summoned him to the abbot’s quarters and said in a stern voice, "I am inspecting the hall, yet you are dozing off.
If you can speak a word of Zen, I will let you go; if you cannot, I shall send you packing. Ding replied spontaneously, "The iron ox has no strength."
Too lazy to plow the fields, he slept amidst the snow with his plow and rope still upon his body. The great earth was entirely covered in white silver;
where could Deshan lay down his golden whip? Qian remarked, "What a fine iron ox! and thus it became his title.
(Propylgou) The Biography of Chan Master Yuanyao Liaoyi.

Liaoyi was the son of the Tang family of Deqing. From childhood, he abstained from meat and blood. He first began to speak at the age of six, but followed his mother only in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*;
regarding worldly affairs, he remained utterly ignorant. His physical appearance was imposing, and his will was resolute.
He was waiting for something. At the age of seventeen, a practitioner of Chan passed by him and recited the words from Yuanmiao’s discourse on ascending the hall:
"If you wish to exhaust the view over a thousand li, go up one more story. Yiyu suddenly said, "This is a great *kalyāṇamitra*;
he will surely be able to pull out nails and remove wedges for others. Can you go with me to see him? His mother was greatly astonished and amazed, and so she prepared everything for them.
He provided him with clothing and provisions. When he saw Miaozhuo at the Deadlock (Sigan), Miaozhuo asked, "Why do you carry so much?

He replied, "To prepare for cold and heat. Miaozhuo said, "A student of the Buddha should not be like this. Yiyi immediately distributed all his belongings and was then instructed to contemplate the phrase, "The myriad dharmas return to one.
Consequently, he was named Congyi. On another day, Miaozhuo raised the story of the Ox while addressing the monks.
When Yì heard the story of "Conversing through the Window Lattice," he was suddenly struck with doubt. He investigated it tirelessly.

One day, he said to Miào, "From the celestial palaces above to the depths of the waters below, the entire earth is a single glass bottle. Miào replied, "Do not take this as a realization of holiness."
On another day, while passing by the Basu Pond, he saw snow falling from the pines and attained a realization. He immediately presented a verse, saying:

"Without asking whether it is north, south, east, or west, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are one expanse of snow. Before his voice had even ceased, [Zhaozhou] struck him with a sharp, painful blow of his staff.

Unaware of the blow, [Xuefeng] fell to the bottom of a cliff. The precipice rose up like a sheer wall, and everyone thought he must have died. His fellow student Mingtong reached down, grasped him by the vines, and pulled him back up.
Yuanji used a ladder to rescue him; by then, Yanyi had already reached halfway up the mountain and felt no further distress.
He said, "I am going to Jiangxi to see Master Qin. Baotong said, "You have brought shame upon this old man’s staff! He pulled him back with force.
Yanyi immediately returned to the West Chan Hermitage on the mountain and made a vow, saying, "If I do not realize the truth within seven days, I shall certainly depart. Thereupon...
He fortified his resolve with upright steadfastness, forgetting to sleep or eat. At night he would climb trees and stand in the open air until dawn.
Before he had even reached his destination, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He rushed to Siguan and called out, "Old Monk! Today you shall not deceive me!"
He presented a verse, saying: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow; The moment the sun shines upon them, they leave no trace.
From this point on, I have no doubt regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs; There is no longer north, south, east, or west. Miaoshang ascended the hall and said: "For over twenty years..."
I have spread this all-encompassing net to capture phoenixes and dragons, yet I have never encountered one;
not even a single shrimp or crab has been caught. Today, unexpectedly, a tiny gnat has flown into the net.

Though it is truly unworthy of being looked upon, thirty years from now, atop a solitary peak and at the summit of a precipice, it will raise its voice and cry out loud. But tell me, what does it cry? [He raises his whisk.]

Miaoyan said, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow. Yanyi then seized the whisk and, for the sake of the assembly, proclaimed it, rebuking his fellow students with no lack of severity.
He further remarked, "If there is a single person throughout the entire world who awakens to the true source and returns to the origin, they will know everything from the very beginning.
Miaoyan marveled at his brilliance and quick wit. One day, a monk visited Miaoyan, who sent him to see Yanyi. Yanyi said, "Straight ahead—"
He departed directly. Those who had long been his disciples felt ashamed, fearing for his life as it was as precarious as a thread hanging from above. He subsequently returned to Deqing;
there, his mother sold her hairpins and earrings to provide for him, and he entered Mount Shangbo in Wukang with Yiyi, where they lived in a thatched hut.
No one could fathom their purpose. After five years, he returned to the mountain. Miaoxiu said, "Many people say you are dragging through mud and water. He replied, "Two eyes..."
Regarding his two eyes, he subsequently shaved them off. He changed his name to Liaoyi (Realization of the Meaning). Before long, he shared the teaching seat and expounded the Dharma;

his character was solitary, austere, and stern, and his sharp spiritual acumen was unassailable. When the monastic communities throughout the ten directions heard the name of the Senior Seat-holder Liaoyi, there were none who did not marvel at him.
(Dinghai Year) Chan Master Youyun Zongmao entered nirvana. (A successor of Miaofeng Shanfa and the fifteenth generation of the Linji lineage. Zongmao resided at Foding Peak.
In the seventh month of the Dinghai year of the Zhizheng era, he suddenly manifested illness. On the twenty-seventh day, he gathered the assembly to entrust them with his final affairs.
He then snapped his fingers once and said, "This alone is my parting message to the assembly. His attendant monk requested—
He left behind a verse. Without answering, it reached the night; when the second watch was nearly over, he suddenly sought out a brush and wrote: "A single lamp is within sight;
there is no further speech. The great earth sinks level; empty space bursts asunder. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His age was eighty.
When Yuanmiao entered the barrier of death, Zuzhin sent him a bamboo whisk and a fly-whisk, with the inscription: "Green waters and blue mountains are received as one."

A Record of Dharma Words. Winter of the Dinghai year, the assembly requested that he open the hall. He accordingly entered the Stone Room, offered incense, and preached the Dharma, addressing the assembly:
"To practice Chan, one must possess three essentials. The first essential is to have great roots of faith, clearly understanding this matter as if relying upon Mount Sumeru.
The second essential is to have a great spirit of indignation, like encountering an enemy who has murdered one's father, such that one desires to..."

To cut it in two with a single stroke—this is the third essential. One must possess a great doubt-mind, like having performed a momentous deed in the dark while it is at the point of being revealed but not yet revealed.
If you maintain these three essentials throughout the twelve periods of the day, you will surely achieve success within a set number of days.
Mingben, whose style name was Zhongfeng, was the son of the Sun family of Qiantang. His mother dreamed of the Wayman Wumen (Wumen Kaido).
Carrying a lantern, he went to the man’s house. On the following day, a son was born. The child’s divine appearance was extraordinary, and he possessed the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
As soon as he left the swaddling clothes, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*). He was able to speak and immediately sang praises and chanted *brahman* hymns.

Whenever he played, he invariably performed acts of Buddhist devotion. At the age of fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life. He prostrated before the Buddha and set fire to his own finger, vowing to uphold the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) and daily recite the Dharma.

He devoted himself day and night with unremitting diligence to the *Avataṃsaka*, *Awakening of Faith*, *Vajracchedikā*, and other sutras. When exhausted, he would touch his head against a pillar to rouse himself, vowing not to cease until he had attained realization.
He then proceeded to read the *Transmission of the Lamp* (Jingde Chuandeng Lu), arriving at the kōan concerning the daughter Amalā questioning Mañjuśrī about birth and non-birth.
Having doubts, he resolved to seek a definitive judgment. He went to Tianmu to consult Yuanmiao, whose character was solitary, austere, and severe;
he never once opened his mouth to smile. Only when he saw Ben did he appear joyful, wishing to have him tonsured. Ben, however, did not grant permission because of his father’s command.
Miaofu said, "I shall cite the story of the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin’s renunciation as an analogy for your father; do not let yourself sink into despair.

Before long, while reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage on "shouldering the Tathāgata," and suddenly attained a profound understanding. He had previously believed that his cognitive capacity was merely based on supernatural penetration rather than true awakening.
In the year Dinghai, at the age of twenty-five, he finally shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk, entering the service of the "Gate of Death" (his master).
(Mǐngzǐ) Chan Master Miaogao Elucidated the Zen School. Miaogao resided at Mount Jing.
In the spring of the Wuzi year of the Zhizheng era, there was one who slandered and defamed the Zen school. Upon hearing this, Miaogao sighed and said, "This is a momentous matter for our school;
I shall struggle for it even at the cost of my life. He then hurried to the capital, where an imperial decree was issued to assemble his disciples in the court.
The Emperor asked, "What is the essential principle of Chan? Guoqing said, "As for Chan, its pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its substance is fundamentally empty and still. It cannot be known through seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, nor can it be understood through deliberation or discrimination.
The Emperor asked, "May you recount the lineage of Chan's transmission? Guoqing said, "The lineage of Chan begins with Śākyamuni Buddha."
The World-Honored One, while at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a single flower and showed it universally to the great multitude; only Kāśyapa smiled.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa; I entrust them to Kāśyapa.

From this, the patriarchs transmitted and received [the teaching] through successive generations down to Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma looked toward this land of Zhendan (China) and saw that there was a great...
Riding upon the capacities of sentient beings, he came by sea. He did not rely on words and letters, but pointed directly at the human mind, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha;
this is what constitutes the Chan School. Furthermore, [the Emperor] examined in detail the origins of the six generations and five schools within the Eastern Land, sighing with admiration.

He then summoned Gao Jin to his presence, along with Master Xianlin of the *Bai fa lun* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas), granting them seats and commanding each to present their arguments. Xianlin said: "From the beginning..."
From the Deer Park to the end at the Bahudā River—throughout this entire interval, he never spoke a single word.
Since he did not speak a single word, from where could these five thousand-plus scrolls have come? Linji said, "The temporal teachings of a lifetime are like a finger pointing at the moon;
once you understand what the finger points to, you realize that the finger itself is ultimately not the moon. Baizhang asked, "What is Chan? Baizhang struck him with his hand.
Lín held up a circular diagram and said, "How can you move your hands and feet? Gāo replied, "Even this single circle cannot be penetrated;
what need is there to speak of thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises? Lín was speechless. Thereupon, the Chan school settled back into its former state. (Holding Steadfastly)
Dafu Zuqin, in the year Wuzi, traveled to Xing County in Hengyang. Passing through Taoyuan Mountain, he was struck by its secluded depth and conceived the intention to dwell there in seclusion.
Formerly, this mountain had been home to many fierce and unruly elements who gathered there, taking advantage of its strategic terrain.

Following the upheavals of war, the area was strewn with corpses, and snakes, tigers, ghosts, and demons roamed and appeared at will. Travelers feared it and avoided it; Dafu, however, bound bundles of straw [to ward off evil].
He built a hut and lived there with two or three fellow practitioners of Chan. On evenings when rain and mist made it dark and gloomy, ghosts and beasts surrounded them, howling and crying out.

He would rouse himself from meditative concentration to explain the causes and conditions of delusion and enlightenment to them, whereupon the various monsters would finally subside. The people of Xing were originally unacquainted with Chan studies;

however, the Chancellor Bayan and others led the way into the mountains to inquire about the Way, and subsequently, nobles and wealthy elites prostrated themselves before him, as did those from all quarters who carried their Chan staffs.
He arrived in person. A lay donor offered land for the construction of a monastery, which was named Lingyun (Cloudy Spring). There, he loudly proclaimed the Way of Yunyan.
(Jichou year) Chan Master Yuanmiao transmitted the Dharma to Mingben.

Mingben attended Yuanmiao; in the Wuzi year, he received full ordination. In the Jichou year, while observing flowing water, he attained realization and immediately went to Yuanmiao to seek [instruction].
Zhengmiao struck him and drove him out. Shortly thereafter, a local official asked about a rumor that the government was selecting young boys and girls.
Miao asked him, "Suppose someone were to come and ask the Master for a young boy or girl; what would you do? Miao replied, "I would simply hand him my bamboo staff.
At these words, Ben attained sudden and thorough enlightenment, penetrating to the very source of the Dharma. He remained submerged within the assembly, and no one recognized him.
The Knower. Thereupon, [Yuan] Miao bestowed a true eulogy in exquisite calligraphy, saying: "My own appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot behold it.
I alone grant my unworthy son the permission to see half of its nose. Furthermore, let the assembly of disciples go to the source to seek instruction.
Qu Tingfa, styled Hesha, was a native of Songjiang. He went to attend upon Yuan Miao. Miao held up a bamboo staff and asked, "Official, for what purpose have you come?"

He came to visit the mountain; he had come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma. When [the Master] said, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma," Miaoxian threw down his bamboo staff and asked, "Do you understand?

He replied, "I do not understand. Miaoxian said, "If one does not enter the tiger’s den, how can one seize the tiger’s cub? He then offered two hundred and seventy *qǐng* of manor lands to provide for the assembly of monks.
Miaoxian said, "What is easy in abundance will surely bring difficulty in abundance. My strength is insufficient to overcome this; it must be steadfast."
He refused it. Daofa then proposed the construction of a Chan monastery, naming it Dajue Zhengdeng Chan Si (Great Enlightenment Perfect Equality Chan Monastery).
(In the year Yiwu [1335]), Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao passed away (he was a dharma successor of Xueyan Qin and the eighteenth generation of the Linji lineage).
Yuanmiao had suffered from a stomach ailment for several years. In the eleventh month of Yiwu, at Dajue Temple, Zu Yong of Shizi Yuan...
The head of the monastery, Mingchu, came to visit Miaoguo and was ultimately entrusted with the final affairs.
At dawn on the first day of the twelfth month, he took leave of the assembly, saying: "For thirty years at West Peak, I have vainly discoursed upon Prajñā;
my offenses fill the heavens. Yet, in this final phrase, I dare not involve ordinary people; I shall take it upon myself alone. Does anyone among the great assembly know where it lands?"
"Ma. After a long silence, he said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth; heaven and earth are as far apart. He then spoke a verse:
Coming, one does not enter the Gate of Death; Going, one does not exit the Gate of Death. An iron snake drills into the sea, Toppling Mount Sumeru. Then, all was still and silent.
The coffin remained open for seven days; he sat upright as if alive. His entire body was enshrined at Siguan.
He was a wondrous man, profoundly compassionate and diligent in instructing others, speaking with kindness and gentle ease, sometimes continuing his teachings with tears.

When entering the hall to carry out the patriarchal command, he spurred on the dragons and elephants, scrutinizing them with all his heart and leaving no room for even a grain of error. He once cautioned his students: "People today carry only a fragment of knowledge..."

[The Master] said: "They do not understand thoroughly. When questioned by a student, they are at a loss, unable to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. As phrases come and go, it is like a hand wrestling with a child;

this is because their realization is superficial and muddled. One must achieve great penetration, seeing for oneself and realizing for oneself, and clearly attain the wisdom of differentiation (*vibhāga-jñāna*), before one can examine and discern between killing and giving life.
Its functional application is steep and perilous, and cannot be approached by mere intellectual calculation. Thus it is.
He was particularly meticulous in his minor conduct and revered the precepts. Although he founded two monasteries, his eyes never beheld them;
yet the lay devotee Quan Congjin obtained some of his shorn hair, which he venerated morning and night. His *śarīra* relics were so numerous they appeared like strung pearls.
Everyone in the world, whether acquainted with him or not, marveled and praised him, saying: "The Ancient Buddha of Gaofeng."
(Gengzi) Chan Master Mingben established a hermitage at Yuanmiao in Pingjiang, where Miaoshi passed away.
Because Da Jue was assigned to Mingben, Ben declined the appointment with great vigor and recommended Zu Yong to preside over it.
Mingben traveled back and forth between the Three Wu regions, carrying his bundle to Shuzhou; after traveling to Mount Lu and returning, he rested at Changmen in the winter of the Jihai year.
On the western slope, he saw pines and cypresses growing in a lush, verdant forest. When he asked the local inhabitants for its name, they replied, "This is Yandang.
Benxi said, "In Yongjia there is Mount Yandang, a place where the *ārhat* Nāgarāja manifested himself; the names are identical.
Could this be the time when his Prajñā is to flourish? He then bound together three thatched huts to live in, inscribing them with the following:

At Qiyun Hermitage, those who came to seek the Way arrived in a continuous stream. In the year Gengzi, he established a precinct for spiritual cultivation and named the hermitage "Huanzhu" (Abiding in Illusion).
He further remarked: "The World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One, renounced his royal throne and lay amidst the deep snow;

at night, beholding the morning star, he simultaneously entered the illusory samādhi together with boundless sentient beings. Alas! Sentient beings have reached this day [still wandering in ignorance]."

They are steeped in emotional delusions and do not realize it themselves. Although we who have left the household life dwell in reliance upon this "Illusory Samādhi," there are still those among us who have not yet awakened to it.
Thereupon, wherever he went, he established hermitages, one of which was named Huanzhu (Abiding in Illusion).

The śramaṇa Xuanchan of Yunshan had long been well-versed in both the teachings and contemplative practice; he would often say, "I have heard that there is a Chan school in the Great Tang. I wish to examine whether this is indeed so."
"I shall follow his teachings; if they prove inappropriate, I will change their fundamental tenets so that they may advance toward the contemplation of the Dharma.

Consequently, he went with his disciples to visit Mingben, who suddenly attained great enlightenment upon hearing a single word. Later, he traveled throughout the land to propagate the Way and passed away in Zhongwu.
When Yan’s disciples painted a portrait of him and returned home, the fourfold assembly welcomed the image into the city, and a wondrous light emanated from it.
It illuminated the heavens; ten thousand eyes looked up at it with eager devotion and profound faith. From this time forth, the Chan school was established, and he was honored as the First Patriarch.
Xingduan, style name Yuansou, was the son of the He family of Linhai. From childhood, he abstained from meat and possessed a transcendent aspiration to leave the mundane world.
Having received the tonsure and the full precepts, he went to study under Zangsou Shanzen. Shanzen asked, "Who are you? He replied, "A person from Tai."
Dongzhou Zhen gave a shout. Baizhang Dun unfolded his sitting mat. Zhen shouted again. Dun folded his sitting mat back up.
Zhen said, "I spare you thirty blows; go to the hall for practice. At these words, Baizhang attained sudden enlightenment. One day, Zhen said, "There are no monks in my land of Quannan."
Duan said, "What about the Master? Zhen immediately struck him with his staff. Duan caught it and said, "Do not say there is no good monk here.

Zhen nodded his head in approval and immediately invited him into the position of Attendant. When Zhen entered nirvana, Duan went to visit Zuqin. Zuqin asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Two Zhe regions."
[Daowei] said, "Why is it that their voices differ? [Dongshan] said, "Shut your stinking mouth. [Daowei] said, "The Tadaping Bridge is high; the Jiyun Peak is steep.
I do not yet know where the record of this is kept. Dongshan clapped his hands and said, "A duck swallowing a snail—its eyes bulge out!
Qianxi laughed and looked at his attendant, saying, "Bring some fine tea here. Dongshan said, "It is unnecessary. When Qianxi passed away, Dongshan returned to the region of Zhejiang.
In the *gengzi* year, he appeared in the world at Zifu Temple in Huzhou.
(In the *xinchou* year,) Chan Master Wenzan transmitted the Dharma to Qinggong.
Qinggong’s courtesy name was Shiwu; he was the son of the Wen family of Changshu. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he later traveled to various regions to study under Yuanmiao.
Miaofeng asked, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I wish to seek the Great Dharma. Miaofeng said, "Is the Great Dharma so easily sought?
You must burn a finger as an offering of incense. He replied, "Today, Xiong has personally seen the Great Dharma of the Master; how could there be anything hidden? Miaofeng took him on as a disciple.
Having served him diligently for three years, he suddenly took his leave to go elsewhere. Miaoxian said, "There is a blind donkey at Wenshu and Ji’an at Huai;
you should go to see them. Upon arriving at Jianyang, he met Ji’an. Ji’an asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Tianmu. Ji’an asked, "What instructions did you receive there?"
[The Master] said, "All dharmas return to the One. [Jingqing] said, "This is a dead word. What is it that harms those with fever?

(Year of the Renyin) Yuan-chang visited Chan Master Mingben.

Yuan-chang’s courtesy name was Wuming; he was also known as Qianyan. He was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan. At the age of seven, he could recite from memory any scripture he saw upon reading it.
His conduct in daily life followed the rules and standards of propriety as if he were already an adult. His father said with joy, "This son..."
"Shall I uphold my lineage through literary conduct? At the age of seventeen, he followed his paternal uncle, Tanfang, and studied the teachings of the Nine Schools and the Hundred Masters.
After some time, he remarked, "This is not the Dharma for transcending the world. He then returned to his teacher of secular classics to study the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," he immediately asked: "If it is as stated regarding Bhaiṣajyarāja, why did his two arms reappear in their original form?"
"Is it the body? The Master marveled at this. He shaved his head and received full ordination. He went to Wulin to study the Vinaya.
A Vinaya Master asked him, "The eight methods of interaction are entirely free of contradiction; what does this mean? He replied, "Why do you not ask about the ninth method? The Vinaya Master said:

When asked about the Vinaya, he answered with Chan; he was truly a vessel for the Mahayana Dharma. Once, when the Chancellor Zhang Huixing was hosting a meal for the monastic community, Zhang Chang followed the assembly into the hall.
At that time, Mingben was also seated there. Seeing him from afar, Mingben said to him, "How do you spend your daily life?

Zhang replied, "I do nothing but recite the Buddha's name. Mingben asked, "Where is the Buddha now? As Zhang was about to deliberate on how to respond, Mingben rebuked him with a stern voice. Zhang then suddenly—

(Gui-mao year) Chan Master Chiding entered nirvana (the dharma successor of Xueyan Qin; the eighteenth generation of the Linji lineage).
While residing at Taoyuan, in the winter of the Ren-yin year, he wrote a long verse by hand to instruct the assembly. Its conclusion read: "The mundane world is not..."
For a long time, through the daily erosion and monthly polishing of years, a single stream from the Peach Blossom Spring has flowed forth after thirty years.
A flute without holes has sounded the song of Great Peace. On the first day of the first month of the Gui-mao year, he sat peacefully and passed away.
(Gengxu) Chan Master Cheonggong established a hermitage on Mount Hae-mu.
Having received the imperial decree and instructions, he ascended Mount Hae-mu and established a hut named Tianhu. His Way was harmonized with both the monastic and lay communities.

Visitors arrived in great numbers even during the New Year and festival periods, and whatever he required came to him spontaneously without his seeking it. As for the labor of gathering firewood and vegetables, he performed it all with his own hands.
In his leisure from meditation, he delighted in composing "Mountain Dweller's Verses. Yuan Gong harbored the ambition to spend the remainder of his life on this mountain.
(Guichou) Biography of Chan Master Mingben’s Dharma Heir, Yuanchang.
After receiving instruction from Mingben, Yuanchang went on to thatch a hut in the mountains of Lingyin. Xueting summoned him to serve as the head of the inner records.
Suddenly, he abandoned this position to return to his dharma lineage and follow worldly conditions for nearly ten years. One day, he suddenly sighed:
However, he said, "Throughout my life, my spirit and ambition have filled the heavens and earth; how can I now become a vinegar-worm in a jar?

He went again to Lingyin Temple and sat in *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) meditation, his side never touching the mat for three years. While traveling to Wangting, he heard the cry of a magpie and attained realization.
When he presented himself to Master Ben and fully recounted the cause of his awakening, Ben again rejected him. Long remained indignant and returned home. Toward the end of the night...

Ji was suddenly startled when a mouse turned to eat from the cat’s bowl; as it fell to the ground, it made a sound. In that instant, he attained sudden enlightenment. He felt his body leap several *zhang* into the air, like a cicada shedding its husk from amidst filth and floating within the profound void. Heaven and earth appeared all at once clear and bright. He put on his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to consult his teacher, Ben. Ben asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? Ji replied: "I was startled by a mouse eating from the cat's bowl; as it fell to the ground, it made a sound. Suddenly I attained awakening. I felt my body leap several *zhang* upward, like a cicada shedding its skin from within impurity and floating in the midst of the profound mystery. Heaven and earth were simultaneously clear and bright. Ben asked, "What did you understand? Ji said, "I understood that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, no Patriarchs, and no sentient beings. Ben said, "If so, who is it that has attained this? Ji remained silent. Ben struck him and said, "This fellow has fallen into a pit of emptiness! Ji bowed and departed. Later, he went to visit Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou asked, "Where have you come from? Ji said, "From Master Ben. Zhaozhou asked, "What did Ben say? Ji recounted the previous events. Zhaozhou said, "Ben is a man of great capacity; he would surely not let you fall into a pit of emptiness. Ji said, "He struck me and said, 'This fellow has fallen into a pit of emptiness! Zhaozhou laughed heartily and said, "Ben has indeed let you fall into a pit of emptiness! Ji then bowed and left. That night, he dreamed that he was climbing a mountain. Upon reaching the summit, he looked down and saw the entire world. He then leapt off the cliff and awoke. From that time forth, he never spoke of this again. It is said that after this, Ji’s realization became even more profound. One day, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered a tiger. Without fear, he stepped forward and sat cross-legged before it. The tiger merely growled and moved away. Later, while crossing a river, he met a woman washing clothes.
