(Zi-yin) Chan Master Zudeng resided at Upper Yunfeng. His courtesy name was Wujin.
He was the son of Wang Haoqian of the Ming family in Siming. His father had once transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and five-colored śarīra were seen emerging from the tips of his brush.
When Zudeng was still young, he sighed and said, "The manifestation of Prajñā reaches such an extent!"

Yes. At the age of fourteen, he left the household life, received ordination, and attained full precepts. Later, he attended upon Rixing Yongyong, who appointed him as the keeper of the treasury keys.
One day, when Yongyong ascended the seat, Deng went forth and asked: "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift. I beg the Master for instruction. Yongyong said:
"Throughout the twelve periods of the day, investigate this closely and secretly. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again. Deng—
He raised his voice, saying, "Impermanence is swift; the matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, Yong gave a shout, and Deng suddenly prostrated himself.
Yong asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself so? Deng replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Yong nodded in approval.
Deng served [his teacher] diligently for several years and subsequently traveled to visit other renowned and virtuous masters; his realization was essentially no different from that of Yongyun.
Having attained the Way, Deng desired to remain in seclusion to preserve it, and thus he planted his staff atop Mount Tiantai at Yunfeng Peak. The scenery of Yunfeng Peak is exceptionally sublime.
During the Five Dynasties period, the Great Being (Bodhisattva) Yong’an of Dong’ou came to reside there, where he composed commentaries and exegeses on the sutras and śāstras.
The collection reached over one hundred scrolls. Those who took refuge [in the Dharma] increased by the day. Consequently, land was cleared to establish a great monastery.

King Qian Zhongyi bestowed upon it the name "Zhengdao" (Realizing the Way). Over the course of three hundred years, it suffered successive destructions by fire, until only broken foundation stones remained amidst slanting sunlight and desolate smoke.
Master Deng was grieved; surveying the old site, he sighed and said, "This is the dharma successor of the Great Being, National Teacher Shao."
"How could I not follow these bequeathed tracks? In the year Jiayin of the Yanyou era, I bound grass to construct a thatched hut and sat in meditation within it.
Tigers, wolves, snakes, and boars were unable to inflict harm upon me. Dadong, whose courtesy name was Yiyun and style name Bie Feng, was the son of the Wang family of Shangyu.
At the time of his birth, his father saw a monk with a long white beard walking along while shaking a mendicant’s staff. He asked the monk, "From where have you come?"
He said, "To Mount Kunlun. He then pushed open the door and entered. His father hurriedly pursued him, but found him silent and nowhere to be seen.

Upon hearing his son’s voice crying out, the father laughed and said, "Was my son not a Buddhist monk (*buddha*) just now? He subsequently received ordination and full precepts; later, he met Chengyugu at Chunning.
Jingtong went to study under Jingde. When Jingde ascended to Baolin Monastery, he summoned Jingtong and said to him, "Your learning is both refined and extensive;
I fear it may become stagnant within your mind, leading to coarse attachments. Why not devote yourself to contemplation and cultivate it to sweep away these impurities?
Jingtong immediately departed for Qiantang to study under Yuanxi. He cast aside everything he had previously memorized, retaining nothing at all. Only...
Tongxun preserved his solitary brilliance, illuminating himself with a steady, flickering light. In this manner, six cycles of summer and winter passed. Suddenly, he went to attend upon Mingben.
Tongxun intended to remain for a long time, but Mingben said, "The school of Xianshou is becoming increasingly distant and its teachings ever more obscure.
Your capacity is sufficient to expand and propagate it; do not linger here for long. He then composed a eulogy for the image of Qingliang and sent Tongxun on his way. Tongxun joyfully remarked:
"Only now do I realize that the myriad dharmas are all fundamentally rooted in the one mind. I did not know which was Chan and which was the Teaching;
from this point on, both internal and external [distinctions] are empty. He then hurried back to Baolin Temple to see Yu, and related what had occurred.

Yu said, "It is well," and subsequently ordered him to lecture separately on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the Profound Gate (*Xuánmén*). At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he emerged from seclusion at Jingtusì Temple in Xiaoshan.

Tanne (d. 1037), whose courtesy name was Wumeng, was the son of the Wang family of Cixi. His family had been an official lineage for generations. At his mother’s command, he attended the local school and studied under Master Youji;

as he grew up, he exhaustively examined the Confucian classics and thoroughly penetrated their essential meaning. Later, however, he experienced a profound spiritual awakening and, snapping his fingers in sigh, exclaimed:
"Toiling over books and refining rhetoric—these are merely worldly phenomena. Why not seek the Dharma that transcends the world? Thereupon, he informed [his parents].

His mother had entered the monastic order. He devoted himself day and night to the study and refinement of all the Śākya sūtras as well as the various texts of the Tiantai, Jiaxiang, Xianshou, and Cien schools, remaining unaware of hunger, thirst, cold, or heat. Thereafter, he sighed again, saying: "The characteristics of the teachings are like the ocean;

if one clings to them without turning back, it is like finding a rope with which to bind oneself. Why not seek instead to clarify the fundamental mind? Thereupon, he applied himself with earnest intent.
After practicing *dhyāna* contemplation for a long time, Xueting Chuan resided at Lingyin Monastery. Yuanwu went to serve him. When Chuan passed away, Xingduan came to fill his position.

Du’an’s conduct and standards were stern and rigorous; none who were not of long-standing study dared to venture through his gate. Yet Yuanwu went straight forward to inquire and seek instruction, entirely without fear.
As their spiritual sparks met and struck one another, the paths of conceptual thought were severed. Inner and outer became as one without interval, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of separation.
Suddenly, after one turn, he reached the sixth or seventh [turn], and his speech became increasingly clear and forceful. Duān joyfully nodded in agreement.

At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, Ling of Xugou from Mount Jingshan invited him to serve as Secretary. Zhao Mengfu, whose courtesy name was Ziyang and sobriquet Songxue, was a member of the imperial clan of the Song dynasty.
At the age of twelve, he was already fond of copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When conversing with monks, he treated them with the intimacy of a close kinsman.

Whenever he received a copy of the *Mingben* (Bright Root) text, he would invariably burn incense and bow toward it in worship. When he served as the Superintendent of Confucian Studies in Jiangzhe, he once inquired about the essential points of the fundamental mind;

Mingben explained for him the principle of guarding the emotions to restore one's true nature. Later, when he entered the Hanlin Academy, he sent someone to ask about the general meaning of *prajñā*; Mingben replied that he possessed [a vision of] the Pure Land.
There were one hundred and eight verses, for which he subsequently composed one hundred and eight eulogies, which he transcribed by hand and bestowed upon him.

Feng Zizhen, styled Haishu, once visited Dao Mingben. Mingben replied in a letter, saying: "Among the talented and accomplished men of both ancient and modern times, there are none who do not know that the three realms are a great house of dreams.
However, if one has never experienced a single moment of intimate and profound awakening, then this knowledge [of theirs] is no different from..."
The mind [of such attachment] falls entirely into the realm of dreams; hence it is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Although Your Excellency’s roots of faith in our Way have never been anything but deep, you alone have not yet seen that within the sphere of faith one can cast off all that is known and transcend the floating lights and illusory shadows of the mundane world.
How much longer can this last? As for the humble verse I previously composed, it contains the lines: "Clad in robes, sitting all day in a thatched hall..."
...these words. I have long been honored by Your Excellency’s promise to fulfill them today; it is, as it were, a poor man seeking the repayment of an old debt.
Hu Changru, courtesy name Jizhong, was a native of Tiantai. He stood apart from the crowd and lived with singular integrity, devoting his heart to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures).
He once composed the "Treatise on Great Unity" (*Dàtóng lùn*), which states: "One thousand four hundred years after the passing of Mencius, Zhouzi appeared. As for the transmission of Zhouzi..."
This originated with Chan Master Shouyaya of Beigù. Both Chengzi and Zhuzi received it from Zhouzi;
after Zhuzi, he obtained Zhang Qinfu, who investigated this Way until he suddenly attained liberation. He realized that this matter is ten times more similar to Chan Buddhism than previously thought.
Scholars do not understand Chan, and Chan practitioners do not understand scholarship; they attack one another, yet neither ever strikes the mark.
This state of illness is truly laughable. ○ Zheng Suonan, also known as Sishao, was a native of Lianjiang.
He passed the Song dynasty’s examination for "Broad Learning and Grand Prose" (Bóxué Hóngcí). He lived in seclusion in the region of Wu; whenever he sat, he invariably faced south.

On the seasonal festivals of Fu and La, he would gaze toward the southern fields and wail, returning only after performing two prostrations. He vowed never to associate with courtiers. He was on good terms with Mingben. One day, they met at...
The filial son Mei Yingfa’s family [was present]. The two men pointed at each other and remained silent. Ben asked, "Why does Suonan not preach the Dharma?

Xiao replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes—there is no Dharma that can be preached. He abandoned his residence and did not live there anymore, instead lodging at the two monasteries of Wanshou and Juebao south of the city.
He had fields, which he gave entirely to various monasteries. ○ Meng Gong, whose courtesy name was Poyu and style name was Wuan...

A native of Gui'an. During the reign of Emperor Lizong, he served as a Regional Commander (Zhizhi). He died posthumously with the title Zhongxiang. He was fond of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) and was particularly profound in his study of Buddhist doctrine.

When advancing into battle, he gauged the enemy and devised stratagems, wielding his blade upon the field. When retreating, he swept the ground and burned incense, sitting upright and contemplative with his elbows resting on a low table.
He distanced himself from wealth and beauty and renounced rich flavors. His own eulogy read: "This old fool loves to play; amidst the bustle, I let loose my folly."
"Han! At this very moment, there is nowhere to see Wuan. His verse at the time of death says: "Where there is birth, there must be extinction;
Wuan has nothing to say. He kicks over Mount Kunlun, And at midnight, the red sun rises."
(Wu-wu) In Japan, there was Zen Master In-gen, whose courtesy name was Ku-sen.
He was a native of Japan. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he traveled extensively through the gates and courtyards of various masters, yet found no realization among them.
He sighed with regret, saying: "The Middle Kingdom is the very source and repository of the Buddha-dharma; why not go there to seek it? At that time—
He was thus inspired and set out southward on his travels. He first visited Master Xiandu at Mount Huading, who said to him, "Your karmic affinity does not lie here.
The Venerable Ben of Zhongfeng is a foremost disciple of Gaofeng; he currently preaches the Dharma at Tiantu Mountain in Hangzhou.
His forge is glowing red, and disciples from near and far have none who do not undergo his refinement. He is truly your teacher; you should go to him."
Hastening away, Yuan immediately left through the brush and went to see Ben. As soon as Ben saw him, he abruptly ordered an attendant to stand by his side.
Yuan repeatedly presented his insights, but Ben rebuked him, saying, "If the roots and objects of perception are not severed, what is the use of such entanglement?
Yuan withdrew and wept with grief; even his eating and drinking were abandoned. Moved by his sincerity, Ben said to him, "This mind..."
It encompasses all phenomena. To be deluded is birth and death; to awaken is nirvana. The delusion of birth and death is indeed not easily dispelled;
the awakening of nirvana remains like a speck of gold-dust entering the eye. One should know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire.
To draw near [to this state] is to risk having one's head scorched and forehead blistered; one must simply maintain a single thought of non-retrogression. Whether born, one is born together with it;
whether dying, one dies together with it. Thus, one naturally accords with the Way. Even if one has not yet attained awakening, there are thousands of Śākyamunis and tens of thousands of Maitreyas.
The great waters of the four seas poured forth and entered your faculty of hearing; these were all empty, false, and wearying defilements, none of which were ultimate matters.
Upon first hearing this, I was unconsciously moved to perspiration all over my body. Day and night, I never for a moment ceased [this practice].
After accumulating it for a long time, one day suddenly I attained an awakening: the present realm became a boundless expanse of white. I hurried toward the master...
Shishuang told Yuanben, "Originally, you entered through silver mountains and iron walls. Yuanben asked, "Since I have already entered the silver mountains and iron walls, why have I come here?
Yuanben attained realization with transcendent ease and took his leave. Shishuang instructed him, saying, "Guard and maintain this well for yourself."
Originally, he traveled extensively to visit various regions, and all regarded him as a "lion cub" of the monastic groves.
(In the year Jiwu [1359]), Chan Master Huiji Yuexi entered nirvana (he was the sixteenth-generation successor of Linji in the lineage of Wuchu Guanfa).
Yuexi’s courtesy name was Huiji; he was the son of the Tang family of Yuzhang, whose family had been Confucian scholars for generations. Yuexi and his elder brother Yuanling both...
Later, he pursued the studies for the jinshi degree. Once he had passed the examinations at the age of nineteen, Huixi left the household life to travel as a wandering monk.

His mother, pitying him, privately prepared silver to provide for his journey. Huixi, believing that wealth was sufficient to ruin one’s resolve, took his leave of his mother with polite words and set out without carrying a single coin.
Hearing that Wuchu was expounding the Dharma at Yujiji, he went to rely upon him. For ten years no one recognized him; it happened that he—
The secretary Qingmo spoke [of this]. Mo was greatly astonished and informed Guan. Guan interrogated him, and it proved to be true.
He retained him in his service, consulting him morning and evening until all its secrets were revealed. Guan named him Huiji and composed a verse to entrust him with [the teachings].
Yang Lianzhenga, who presided over the Buddhist teachings, invited Xi to accompany him to the capital. Xi declined, saying: "I have an aged..."
After the war, his mother’s whereabouts became unknown. He subsequently returned to Jiangxi, where Yuanling was serving as the Prefectural Administrator of Linjiang;

having followed Wen Tianxiang in raising an army, Yuanling died in battle. Only his mother remained at home, and Xi served her with such filial piety that he became renowned for it. In the year of Bingshen—
He succeeded Baizhang in the world of men and moved to Jingci for seven years; after three months there, he moved to Jingshan. After three months, he returned to Nanping carrying his staff.

Scholars from Jiangxi led the way to welcome him back to Yangshan. In the intercalary eighth month of the year Jiwu (1279), as he was about to pass away, he wrote by hand letters of thanks to those with whom he had corresponded, composed a verse for the assembly, and cast aside his brush to enter nirvana. He was eighty-two years old.
(Gengshen) Chan Master Yongning resided at Shixiang Temple in Guangde.
His courtesy name was Yiyuan. He was a native of Tongzhou and surnamed Zhu. His family had been a lineage of officials for generations. At the age of six, he entered the local school;

he was able to memorize the classics and their commentaries by heart and could grasp their general meaning. However, this was not what his nature delighted in. When he heard people mention... [text continues]
Regarding the Buddha’s name, he immediately focused his ears and listened intently. At the age of nine, he earnestly requested to leave secular life, but his parents would not grant him permission.
He then refused to eat for several days, which led them to allow him to become a monk at Lihé Monastery. Lihé was a renowned monastery in the prefecture;

during the Song dynasty, Chan Master Zhào had preached the Dharma there to save sentient beings. On the eve of Ning’s arrival, the monastic community collectively dreamed of welcoming Master Zhào, and on the following day, Ning arrived.

Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he traveled west of the Zhejiang River carrying a basket on his back. He met various senior masters, but their responses did not accord with his understanding.

He entered Qionglong Mountain to pay his respects to Keweng Shao, who appointed him to manage the library. After a long time, he went to Pilu Mountain in Wuling and made an agreement with Mingji Cai to practice meditative concentration at Jiaozishan.
Whenever he fell into slight drowsiness, he would carry sand on his head or transport bricks, and he sat suspended from a wooden board.
"Empty. Thus it was for five years. Ning said, "The Master’s understanding has reached its limit; I should go to consult another teacher. He then went to Lake Tai to visit Wuyong Kuan.
Kuan’s gate was stern and severe; Ning could not even enter the doorway. Kuan shouted at him with a harsh voice and drove him out.
Ning performed a prostration outside the gate and stood there with palms joined. After a long time, Kuan finally permitted him to enter. Kuan asked, "Where are you from? Ning replied:
Tongzhou asked, "What has been the state of the sea of Huaihai lately—full or empty? Wu said, "It floods the sun and rises to the heavens;

not even a drop has leaked away. Tongzhou said, "You have not yet hit the mark. Wu said, "Please, Master, speak for me. Wakuan gave a shout. Ning withdrew and retired to his meditation chamber, remaining awake throughout the entire night.
One day, hearing Wuakuan cite Yunmen’s words, "A single thought does not arise," his realization occurred before the sound had even faded.
He hurried into the hall. Yuanwu struck him. Ning realized that he had attained sudden enlightenment and was instructed to compose a verse on Zhaozhou’s “Mu.
Ning composed it on the spot, saying: “Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; The myriad phenomena all beg for their lives. A bottomless basket holds dead snakes;
Adding much or reducing little leaves nothing remaining. Yuanwu let out a hearty laugh and then recited the *Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way).
Question: A flash of lightning strikes from afar; with no regard for one’s entire body, in the mere interval of a thought, there is no path for the holy or the mundane.

Speak quickly! Speak quickly! How could one say, "The sparks fly like shooting stars"? What room is there for deliberation? To face the adversary directly at the critical moment—this is neither "is" nor "is not."
Kuan-zhen let out a shout of awe. Ning asked, "What was that shout for? He replied, "Before the mountain of melons, he swallowed the flat yoke;

○ Chan Master Xuansou Xingduan Enters Nirvana (Dharma Heir of Zangsou Zhen; 16th Generation of Linji) Xingduan resided at Mount Jing.
On the fourth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Zhizheng era, he passed away while sitting upright.
He was eighty-eight years old. His entire body was interred in the Jizhao Pagoda Courtyard. He possessed a flat crown and an ancient countenance; his eyes shone with brilliance, and beneath his chin—

Counting his beard hairs, they stood bristling and solemn, like a solitary pine after a snowfall. When sitting, he was upright and imposing; when walking, he did not look back. His heroic spirit overwhelmed those around him.
When accompanied by friends, he never spoke of the trivial affairs of the world. Setting aside the Great Dharma, he would not utter a single word.
From the time he became a monk until his passing, there was not a single night he slept without his robes on. As he returned from Nanping...
While receiving the scriptures at Huacheng (City of Transformation), he lay down to rest one summer evening with the window open.

Suddenly, a Brahma-monk arrived, flying along with his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), and conversed with him on the essential points of the *Prajñāpāramitā* without ceasing. After a short while, the monk ascended into the air and departed.

When [the Master] was about to pass away, he left behind the nails and hair he had clipped to be interred in the Huacheng Hermitage. Upon opening them to examine the remains, *śarīra* relics were found growing there in profusion.
(Renwu) Chan Master Weize resided at Puti Zhengzong Temple. Mingben passed away.

Although various famous mountains repeatedly invited Weize to preside over their monasteries, he firmly declined and did not go. He lived in seclusion north of Huating City, about two li from the city walls. In the Xinsi year of the Zhizhi era, he traveled to Wumen and stayed at Huanzhu.

Without contrivance and without discrimination, if you directly realize this, it is the correspondence of a single thought; it is the attainment of that which is sought.

Songyin’s name was Mao. His courtesy name was Zishian. He was the son of Zheng of Fenghua. From his youth, he often spent the middle of the night...

As there were many *āraṇyakas* (forest hermitages) in the village, on an auspicious day he wandered among them with a group of children, lingering there in deep affection and longing. At last—

"I can spare you; shall I not allow you to fulfill your ambition? He then had him tonsured and receive full ordination. [The novice] immediately said with deep emotion:
"I study the Buddha-dharma in order to clarify the mind. Without a teacher, there is no way to demonstrate the subtle nuances of the mind.

Liang immediately went to attend upon Xun. During their dialogue, blows from the staff and shouts were exchanged; in a single kṣaṇa, his ordinary delusions were instantly cast away.
After some time, he finally attained realization of the mind-dharma. In the Renwu year of the Zhizheng era, he emerged into the world at Shengshou Monastery in Jiaxing.
(Guīwèi) Chan Master Yongning retired to Longchi. Yongning had resided at Tianning.
In the Guīwèi year, he retired to Longchi. ○ Huìrì, styled Dōngmíng, was the son of the Jiā family of Tiantái.
He left home to follow Zītíng’s instruction and studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantái school. Zītíng sighed and said: "It is like casting a ball down a steep slope."
The slope was insufficient to contain his swiftness. On the path of the Northern Peak, will he not rely upon it for great prosperity?
One day, while taking a brief nap, he had a dream of both Upper and Lower Tianzhu. Not long after, he emerged from the world at Wushan and moved to reside at Lower Tianzhu;
in the third year of the Zhizheng era, he moved again to Upper Tianzhu.
(Jia Shen) Chan Master Zhidu returned to Folin. His style name was Baiyun.
He was the son of the Wu family of Chuzhou. At the age of fifteen, he felt a profound sense of renunciation and a desire to transcend the mundane world.

He wished to pursue the study of the Buddha-dharma, but his parents would not permit it. Fadu fasted for several days, refusing to eat food cooked with fire, until they finally allowed him to leave the household life.

He shaved his head and received full ordination, then applied himself deeply to dhyāna-concentration. Every time he sat in the lotus posture, he remained awake until dawn; he continued in this manner for three or four years.
Thereafter, he sighed and said, "The Great Universe is as vast as this; how can one remain listlessly confined to a single room? Thus, he departed.

He traveled through the seven prefectures of Min, visiting all the mountains, yet found no resonance with them. He returned once more to Mount Baimu in the commandery, where he built the Folin Monastery as a place of rest.
Daily, he took up the commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, reading them thoroughly.
Having done so, he sighed again, saying: "To be fettered by the literal words is like oil soaking into flour; there is no end in sight. Deshan—
"It is truly not false to say that 'exhausting all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void. Why not cast them aside?
He then traveled to Western Zhejiang, where he visited Lingshi Zhi and ascended Mount Tianmu to study under Duannaya Yi. At that time, Wu Jian was first to witness [the Master's arrival];
he was preaching at the summit of Mount Fahua, and Du went there again to pay his respects. He asked about the secret meaning of the West—whether it had been fully realized or not.
"How is it? asked Xuedou. "Wait until Mount Sāla nods its head, and then I shall speak to you. As Fodu attempted to answer by waving his hand, Xuedou suddenly shouted.
Fodu said, "Upon the summit of Mount Sāla, white waves surge to the heavens; flowers bloom after芒種 (Mángzhòng), and leaves fall before立秋 (Lìqiū).
Xuedou said, "In my house, there is no leftover soup or stale rice. Fodu replied, "This is not leftover soup."
“‘What is this leftover rice? [Dongshan] looked at him. Having served him diligently for several years, as he was about to take his leave and return home, Dongshan instructed him, saying:
‘In the past, Nan Yue left home at fifteen and received a prediction from Da Jian. Later, he obtained the mind-dharma from Mazu;
it was like a needle meeting its eye—how could it have been through many words? Do not wag your three-inch tongue to deceive people; you must establish a truly authentic insight.’”
Only by practicing in this way can one truly repay the profound kindness of the Buddha. Du [Dudu? received these instructions and did not dare forget them.

In the fourth year of the Zhizheng era, he returned to Fulin Temple, where he and Duzhong, Tan Cheng, and Shan Qin exhorted one another with mutual diligence, as if fearing they might lose [the teachings].
Da Yin resided at Longxiang for fourteen years; on the fifth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Zhizheng era, he passed away into nirvana.
In the year Yiyou, Chan Master Huixin presided over Tiantong;
he also resided at Putuo. In Renwu, he ascended to preside over Zhongtianzhi; in Yiyou, he was transferred to Tiantong.
(Cǐngxū) Chan Master Shìyú presided over Shíxī.
He resided at Wūshí, where his reputation was exceedingly great. In the sixth year of the Zhìzhèng era, he was transferred to serve as the abbot of Xīnglóng Chán Monastery at Shíxī in Guǎngdé.
The flourishing of those who turned toward his transformation did not fall short of the time he was at Wūshí.

his dharma heirs were Wuneng and Jiaofa. Shuisheng resided at Miaoguo Temple on West Lake. Not long after, he returned to his former hermitage at Nanchao. Those who looked up to him became even more numerous.

From childhood he abstained from meat; as he grew older, he mastered the *Zuo Zhuan* and took particular delight in the Buddhist scriptures.
Having shaved his head, taken the dyed robes, and received full ordination, he traveled through various regions, but found no one with whom he could reach accord.

Maudgalyāyana then asked: "What is the Dharma-eye treasury? Śāriputra called out, "Maudgalyāyana! Maudgalyāyana responded, "Yes? Śāriputra said, "The mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind. At these words, Maudgalyāyana was greatly enlightened. This is why he said: "The mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind. If you can see this, then you will understand the meaning of the Buddha’s words. If you cannot see it, then you should look at the following story. When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was about to pass away, he entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, saying: "After I am gone, you must protect and uphold the Dharma-eye treasury. Ānanda then asked: "What is the Dharma-eye treasury? Kāśyapa called
Xinxin said, "I have a question to ask you, sir; please try to answer it. Once we have both been burned to a single heap of ashes, where will we meet?
Guishan was at a loss. Later, he went to attend Huichang, who showed him the meaning of the single phrase: "Is there anything that you do not reveal to me? (Analects 1.17).

Hearing the fragrance of the osmanthus, one breaks through the lacquer bucket; their nostrils reach toward the heavens. A man of great character who wishes to accomplish this matter must have his own appointed time.
Although the mountain valley is a single piece of refined gold, it must enter the furnace and bellows of a master such as Sishin Huidang;
only then will it be forged by the fierce tongs and hammers. If this lot of fellows were to arrive at the gate of Wuming, [they would find...]
Furthermore, you must examine each point one by one. Why? Because "one who is not a master of the tide should not enter the surging waves.
As for this arbitrary fabrication by the Mountain Hermit, what do you, my attendants, think of it?
(Wuzi) Chan Master Baogin arrived in Yanjing. His style name was Bifeng; his surname was Shi.
He was born into a distinguished lineage in Yongshou County, Qianzhou. His father, Tongfu, was known among people as a "Venerable One" (*zhǎngzhě*).
His mother, Zhang, was likewise tireless in her devotion to goodness. There was a *śramaṇa* who, carrying his alms bowl, went begging for food.

He bestowed an image of Avalokiteśvara upon Zhang and instructed him, saying, "Serve this with diligence; you shall give birth to a son of wisdom. Before long, a son was born named Jin. A white light illuminated the room.
From childhood, he was frequently ill, remaining confined to his bedding for long periods. His parents wondered, "This child was born as a result of auspicious omens;
would it not be fitting to entrust him to the Śākya clan? At the age of six, he left the household life and shaved his head.

Having received full ordination, he traveled extensively to lecture halls to exhaustively study the teachings on the nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. Eventually, he struck his thigh and sighed, saying:

"The texts of the Tripiṭaka are all like fingers pointing at the moon. Even the ancestral masters of old, when preaching the Dharma, caused heavenly flowers to fall in profusion and golden lotuses to emerge;
yet they were still unable to transcend birth and death—how much less so for someone as mediocre as myself? Thereupon, he changed his robes and entered a Zen monastery.
At that time, Sengzhen was like an ocean; he erected the banner of the True Dharma amidst the Yunshan Mountains of the Jin dynasty. Huijin went to visit him repeatedly.

Zhen showed him the essentials of the Way, and Jin gave rise to a great state of doubt. For two or three years, he neglected both sleep and food. Once, he happened to be carrying a basket while following Zhen.
While gathering vegetables in the garden, [Wuzhuo] suddenly sat down and remained motionless. After three periods (nine hours) had passed, he finally awoke.
Zhen asked, "Did you enter meditative absorption? Jin replied, "Yes. Zhen asked, "What did you perceive? Jin replied, "I have attained some realization. Zhen said, "Just speak of it.
Jin held up his basket to show him, but Zhen rejected this. Jin set the basket on the ground and stood with his hands folded; Zhen again rejected this.

Jin let out a single stern shout. Zhen lunged forward and struck him in the chest, demanding that he speak quickly. Jin pinned Zhen to the ground with his chest and threw him down, yet Zhen still would not grant it.
He laughed and said, "The afflictions of the mundane world have been briefly stilled, but your power of meditative concentration has not yet reached depth.

Only when the paths of the mind are severed and you have penetrated the Patriarchal Barrier can the Great Dharma be clarified. Upon hearing this, Jin became even more diligent and unremitting in his practice.

He then departed to visit various masters and stayed at Mount Emei, where he vowed never again to eat grain. Each day he gathered pine and cypress needles to consume, remaining without his side touching the mat for another three years.
A single thought did not arise; the past and future were severed, and he stood alone, illuminated by the essence of reality.
He realized that both things and self are identical to suchness (*tathatā*). From then on, he entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), sometimes remaining seated for several days without arising.

Once, while he was sitting cross-legged beneath a great tree, a mountain stream overflowed its banks; people thought that Sengjin had been drowned. After seven days, when the water receded, they hurried to look at him;
Sengjin was sitting in meditation as usual, with only his robes dampened. One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, sweat poured from his entire body like rain.
He sighed and said, "Miaoxi has had eighteen great awakenings and countless minor ones; how could he deceive me?

Regarding the state prior to birth, only today do I finally know its true nature. He hurried to seek verification from Zhen, engaging in a forceful exchange of arguments and cross-examinations until he dragged the meditation seat over and walked out.
Zhen said, "This is indeed so. We shall re-examine it tomorrow. The following day, they investigated it again.
When the appointed time arrived, Zhizhen drew a circle on the ground. Jinguang brushed it away with his sleeve. Zhizhen drew another circle;
Jinguang added a stroke across its center and brushed that away as well. Zhizhen drew again as before, and Jinguang added another stroke, forming a cross, which he then brushed away.
Zhizhen looked at him without speaking and drew yet another circle as before. Jinguang—
A cross with four corners forms the *svastika* symbol; then he swept it away. In truth, he had drawn thirty circular marks in total.
Jin answered each one individually. The Master said, "Only now do you realize that the Dharma is so vast and supreme.
Among those who have studied and attained realization over the past hundred-odd years, surely there were none in the world? Yet how many could truly clarify its great functional power?"
The Master Wuyong once said, "Under my seat shall emerge three tigers and one leopard. Is it not you who are that 'one leopard'?
You should go to the north; there your Way shall flourish greatly. Wuyong was indeed the master of Zhuanzhen.
Prior to this, while in a state of meditative concentration, Jing saw a mountain that was exceedingly beautiful, with multi-storied pavilions and magnificent halls shimmering in gold and azure.
Within it, various Buddhas and fifty-two bodhisattvas were practicing the Way. One of them beckoned to Jing and said, "This is Mount Wutai, the Secret Demon Rock (Bimoyan).
You practiced the Way here in a previous life; your sacred remains are still there. Why have you forgotten this? Once [he had seen this],...

Jingwu then traveled to Mount Wutai. On the road, he encountered a woman with disheveled hair, wearing tattered garments of five colors and walking barefoot at a slow pace, followed by a black mastiff.
Jingwu asked her where she was going; she replied, "I am entering the mountains. He asked, "What will you do there?"
He replied, "I do nothing at all. After a long while, he vanished. When they knocked, his companions could not see him anywhere.
Some said that he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī. Consequently, Jin established the Lingjiu Hermitage on the mountain; hearing of this, people from all directions came from as far as a thousand li.
Every day he carried provisions to offer as tribute, and he stored all the gold there to provide food for more than a thousand itinerant monks who came to study.
In the winter of the Wuzi year of the Zhizheng era, Emperor Shun of the Yuan dynasty summoned him to the capital of Yan, where he was granted the utmost consolation and favor.

A monk from India named Zhikong had long resided in Yan; it was rumored that he possessed the power of precognition and was said to be three hundred years old. Jin went to visit and engage him in discussion.
Kong stared blankly at him without answering. When [the Master] came out, Kong sighed and said, "This is truly one who possesses the Way.
One winter evening, amidst a heavy snowfall, a crimson light rose from within the golden chamber, reaching up to touch the Milky Way. The Emperor was struck with wonder and sighed in admiration.
(Ji-chou) Chan Master Shiyu returned to Mount Wushi. He resided at Guangde for three years.
The community of Mount Wushi, mindful that Shiyu had been gone for a long time, exerted great effort from their local villages to welcome him back.
Shiyu once said to the Dharma Master Shanjiang of Wutai: "Even if Mañjuśrī were to emit golden light..."
The Buddha stroked your head; the Lion was ridden by you. Guanyin manifested a thousand hands and eyes; the Parrot was captured by you.
All of these were merely following forms and sounds. What benefit have they brought to your own self?

If you wish to clarify the great matter of your own person and break through the sturdy barrier of birth and death, you must first sever all the false views and understandings of both the holy and the ordinary. 10.
During these two periods, turn the light back upon itself and reflect inwardly; simply look into what is neither mind, nor matter, nor Buddha—what is it?

Do not seek it outward at all. Should you possess even a hair’s breadth of Buddhist dharma, supernatural powers, or noble understanding, no matter how small it may be—even the size of a grain of millet—it is entirely self-deception.
It is nothing but slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma. You must investigate until you reach the state of total liberation.

Without reliance; there is not even a hair’s breadth of a place to stand upon. If you can gain a single eye of insight, you will immediately see that the "Cheongju cloth robe" and the "Jinzhou radish" are both things for your own use;
there is no need to seek elsewhere for supernatural powers or sacred understanding. Huixin resided at Tiantong.
In the tenth month of winter in the year Jichou, he moved his residence to Longxiang in Jinling. Some said, "As for Longxiang..."
At the beginning of his administration, he slightly displayed a majestic demeanor to punish the habit of arrogance.
(Gengyin) Chan Master Shougui resided at Tianlong.
His courtesy name was Wuyong, and his style name was Shui’an. He was the son of the Zhen family of Pujiang. His family’s occupation was farming and wood-gathering; whenever they were sent...
While he was performing his duties delivering food to the fields, Kōshi found no joy in it. Consequently, he followed a local youth to study under a teacher.

At the age of eighteen, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk; at twenty, he began traveling to seek instruction. Upon reaching Ryūge, he visited Genchō, who bestowed upon him the "one stroke" that points directly upward.
Kōshi practiced in private and investigated in silence until, suddenly, there was a realization. At the neighboring temple of Tenryū, there was one named Dōdō Hei, who invited him...

In the first month of the spring of the *dingmao* year, Xiaoyin reported Chang’s virtuous conduct to the Xingxuanzhengyuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs), intending to have him emerge from seclusion to preside over a great Chan monastery.
Chang, however, ultimately fled and evaded the messengers; crossing the Taohang River by night, he went into hiding at Mount Fulong, where Gui accompanied him.
On that mountain was a ruined temple called Shengshou, which Chang renovated entirely and commissioned [Gui] to...
Guì led his disciples. Guì had previously gone to consult with Duānyá Yì and Liángshān Kuān; their repeated exchanges and responses were no different from when he had studied under Jiàncháng.
He then sighed and said, "Though a thousand rivers differ, the bright moon remains one. From this day forward, I have no further doubts.
In the summer of the Wùzǐ year, he retired to Jiāxīng and built an *ān* (hermitage) as a plan for his leisure in old age. In the autumn of the Gēngyǐn year, the seventh month...
On the tenth day of the month, he dreamed that Daodao Ping arrived. Daoping said, "I have already abandoned the world of men. Daogui was greatly startled;
he hurriedly took his boat to go see him, only to find that Daoping had indeed passed away. From then on, he resided at Tianlong Temple. [Daogui].
Zhutianlong sent a letter to Yuanchang. Chang’s reply was brief, stating: "It is unnecessary.
Since you have become the master of this region, you are no longer the same as when you lived alone in the past. Why is this?
In ancient times, those who practiced Chan and sought the Way—whether living in solitude or among a community—regarded only the two matters of birth and death as their urgent priority."

"Save your head from the fire. After breaking the lacquer bucket, day and night you must polish and refine your body and mind until they are as utterly empty as a vast expanse, free from even the slightest fault or affliction.
After a long time, its radiance cannot be concealed; it will naturally be revealed.
Forced by circumstances, you will be placed upon a seat by others. Because your realization is secure and profound, and your application is precise and correct, with every movement—
Whether in stillness or in speech and silence, one may serve as a model for others; hence there is the doctrine of the *zhuchi* (abbot).
Now, the *zhuchi* dwells in a place where there is nothing to dwell in, and upholds a Dharma that cannot be upheld.

To benefit and deliver all beings and transmit this infinitely—how could this be possible for those of inferior roots and limited capacity? This is truly a great [task] for both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
He is a powerful Great Man and a great spiritual friend (mahā-kalyāṇamitra). Thus, those with eyes see him, and those with ears hear him.
It is like a state having a sovereign and a family having a father; the sovereign is sagely and the ministers are worthy, the father is compassionate and the son is filial.
The multitude take one person as their master, and that one person takes the multitude as his guests. The roles of guest and host are clearly defined, and the influence spreads like the wind.

The grass bends; there is order without words—this is fundamentally rooted in this. Moreover, [the Master] possesses great vision upon his brow, distinguishing dragons from snakes and differentiating tigers from rhinoceroses.
He opens the great furnace and bellows, wielding the great tongs and hammer to melt away ordinary beings and sages, and to refine Buddhas and patriarchs.
From among thousands and tens of thousands, he selects one person to emerge as the true successor of Vulture Peak and the foundational seedling of Shaolin, like a lamp.
It is like a lamp illuminating another; it is like water meeting water. Thus, there is the teaching of the Dharma-heir.

How could there be the current state of clamor, where people vie for power and profit, compete through notions of self and other, deceive one another with fraud, and seize from one another with cruelty?
It even reaches the point of engaging in lawsuits and killing one another out of malice. Yet, often before laypeople, they wag their tails and beg for pity—iron-faced living Yamas.
These people, who beg for their lives at the hands of King Yama, are as numerous as millet seeds or hemp seeds.
They perform the karma of hell and are called "hell-dregs. Can they be called *chuzhi* (abbot)? Can they be called *fasu* (dharma-heir)? How bitter! How grievous!
The single school of Baizhang and Linji has been swept away and utterly destroyed.
(Xinmao year) Chan Master Mingde resided at Dongchan Mingde in Songjiang;
his style name was Gufeng. He was the son of the Zhu family of Mingzhou. His father had been friends with the Putuo monk Jie, who had entered the Way upon hearing the crowing of a cock.
Whenever he preached the Dharma, he would invariably flap his wings and crow like a cock. Although Jie had been deceased for some time, his mother dreamed of him.
He came to seek lodging; upon waking, she found herself pregnant. After fourteen months had passed, he was born. As a child, he took no pleasure in play;
instead, he would frequently sit cross-legged, motionless. The temple administrator, Huiming, scolded him, saying, "This boy does not know how to recite poetry or read books."
Sitting in ignorance, what does one seek? De said, "I wish to study seated meditation (zazen) to seek the state of Buddhahood. Ming was amazed by this.

He took him to Jinge-ō-in Temple in Yinkun and assigned him to the duties of sweeping and cleaning. At that time, he was twelve years old. After five years had passed, he received the tonsure and the full precepts (upasaṃpadā).
With a resolute determination to seek the Way, he set out with his monk’s staff and first visited Zhuxi Tan at Tianping Temple.
Tongtan asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "I have come from Mount Jingē. He asked, "How high is Mount Jingē?
He replied, "One cannot see its summit. Tongan rebuked him. Dede redoubled his self-exertion, vowing that he would not rest until he had attained realization.

One day, Tongtan ascended the seat and raised the koan of the World-Honored One holding up a flower. Hearing this among the assembly, Dede suddenly felt as though he had an understanding. He immediately—
He composed a verse and presented it to Tan, who nodded his approval. Yet, De still did not consider himself to have attained realization. He went again to Jingci to see Huiji Xi;
when Xi saw that De had arrived, he asked, "What kind of person comes like this? De replied, "The Hu Zhangsan and the Hei Lisisi.
Xi asked again, "From morning until evening, wearing clothes and eating food—do you recognize your own self? De again replied, "The Hu..."
Zhang San-hei Li Si [was present]. Xi raised his staff, intending to strike him, but De shook his sleeves and departed. He arrived at Shuanglin, where he met Mingji Jun.
When Japan invited Jun to serve as National Teacher, De escorted him to the seashore. At that time, Zhutian Lin also came from Xuedou;
seeing that De’s bearing was extraordinary, he invited him back to the mountains to reside in the position of First Seat. Lin ascended [the seat].
In the Hall, [Zhao] De raised the koan of Yishan’s “Mud Ox Entering the Sea” and exhorted him with repeated and earnest guidance.

Zhao De was unconsciously moved by a sense of joy and liberation, and his many doubts were instantly resolved. He then presented a verse to Zhonglin, who sighed and said, "The eyes and mind of humanity and heaven remain vividly present.

From then on, he invited Zhongfang Lun to establish a hermitage in the Peach Blossom Gully, where they together engaged in vigorous debate and exegesis. In their leisure time, they would peruse the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He did not step beyond the threshold of his door, yet his reputation grew daily. The Xuanzheng Yuan (Office for the Propagation of the Teaching) requested that he reside at Dongchan Temple in Songjiang.
Ming-sou Chang went to Fulong to study under Yuan-chang; Yuan-chang, pitying his earnestness in seeking the Way, showed him this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The mountain peak is high and cold, the snow has not yet melted. Why has the Master come, enduring such freezing? Do not stand in the courtyard with your waist buried in snow;
wait for the sky to clear and the warmth to return naturally. After Chang Zun had practiced this, he suddenly attained realization, and Chang [Changsha] gave him formal approval (*inka*).
(1392) Master Lansi Xing resided at Qingyin Hermitage.
He received the Dharma from Yuanchang. In the *Renchen* year of the Zhizheng era, he traveled with his fellow practitioner Gudao You to Qingyin in Jinhua.
Initially, about three *li* west of the city, there was a local resident, Liu Qiubiao, who lived in seclusion.
This Qiao, whose courtesy name was Ziyuan, was extremely filial toward his parents. Although his family was poor, he applied himself diligently to his studies and gathered disciples to support them;

he would not accept even a grain of anything that did not accord with the Way and righteousness. His integrity and conduct were praised by the people of the land. One hundred and seventy years later...
When Xingyou arrived, he subsequently established a monastic community (conglin) at this very site, naming it Qingyin.
Once, Deyan visited Qinggong, who told him: "After you leave me, the place where you will seek a retreat must surely be Huating in Songjiang.
The people of Huating are wealthy and inclined toward goodness; being wealthy, they delight in giving. Inclined toward...

If you are virtuous, you may be transformed by the Way of our Buddha; there must surely be a place for you. He wrote the two characters "Pine Seclusion" (Sōngin) and gave them to him to carry with him.
Upon reaching the north of Guohui in Huating, he suddenly recalled the prophetic prediction and consequently built a thatched hut to dwell within it.
Once his work was completed, he took the calligraphy written by Shi Wushan and named it "Pine Seclusion. — Qinggong.

While living in seclusion at Tianhu, on a day in the seventh month of the *wuchen* year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. Two days later, in the middle of the night, he took leave of the assembly.
His disciples asked, "How shall the Master's funeral arrangements be handled? He then requested a brush and wrote this verse: "The green mountains do not harbor a stinking corpse;
once dead, why need one dig into the earth to bury it? Looking back, I have no fire of *samādhi*; [the light]..."
He said, "I have cut off what was before; here is a pile of firewood. He threw down his brush and passed away. His body was cremated, and relics of five colors emerged, brilliant and beyond counting.
He was eighty-one years old and fifty-four years since his ordination. At that time, there was one named Wei, whose style name was Wanfeng. He was the son of the Jin family of Leqing.
His mother dreamed that a śramaṇa entered her chamber; upon waking, she gave birth. Just then, a light illuminated the room, and the mother, being afraid, wished to abandon [the child].

Her aunt raised her. While still in her swaddling clothes, whenever she saw a monk, she would smile and make gestures of joining her palms in homage. She left the household life and received full ordination under Chan Master Zhicheng.
Cheng said, "For what reason do those who practice Chan fail to awaken to their true nature? Day after day they busily engage in idle clamor;
sometimes in groups of three or five they discuss how this elder is this way, or in groups of three or five they discuss the monasteries."
Lin Hao-chou had been exclusively failing to apply himself to his own practice. If he wished to awaken to the Supreme Vehicle, it was essential that he engage in genuine inquiry and authentic study.
Consequently, [the Master] presented him with the "Three Are Not" kōan of Nanquan for investigation.

Wei then departed separately for Mount Dapeng in Mingzhou, where he pursued the matter until he reached its ultimate resolution, to the point of forgetting both sleep and food. One day, the temple master recounted this to him.
Regarding the story of Guishan kicking over the water pitcher: it triggered a state of doubt, and before he knew it, there was a "clunk" sound from the floor.
He immediately spoke a verse: "The old Nanquan is topsy-turvy; He has caused my practice to be delayed for half a year.
If one could personally realize this right now, Why would he not strike me with a fist to the chest? Thereupon, he went to Huading to visit Wujiandu. Du asked, "From where have you come?"
“Where have you come from? He replied, “From Hangzhou. “Have you met anyone there? He replied, “Master Zhuyan.
“What instructions did he give you? He replied, “Nanquan’s ‘Three Nots. “I do not ask about Nanquan’s ‘Three Nots’ here,” [the Master] said.
"What is it that 'all dharmas return to one'? He replied, "From birth until death, there is not even one. He asked, "What is this 'one,' and where does it return?
Weiyin stepped forward, joined his palms, and said, "I do not presume to know. He asked again, "What is the Way? He replied, "The Way cannot be spoken of.
He asked, "If you do not speak of it, what is it that you do not speak of? He replied, "I specifically want the Master to have doubts about it. He asked, "Doubt? He replied, "Doubt."

Dongguo said, "To 'cling' is an error. To say 'I do not doubt' is also an error. He saw [Yunwei] and shouted; Yunwei also shouted. Dongguo shouted again; Yunwei also shouted. Shaking his sleeves, he departed.
Dongguo said, "Although you have realized the true nature, you are still young in years; it is not yet time for formal certification."
"You stay in the mountains for ten or twenty years; I shall personally send someone to fetch you.
At the age of twenty-six, he returned to Dapeng and lived in solitude for ten years. Suddenly hearing that Zhiyan had passed away, he went to sweep the stupa.
Once, while staying overnight at Lingyin Monastery, a monk recited a verse by Yuan Chang that contained these lines: "The two wheels of sun and moon pass like a comb;
the entire universe seems to turn busily like a grindstone. I send word to all students of the various quarters: do not let this fine time slip away.
Upon hearing this, Wei immediately went with the monk directly to see Yuan Chang at Fulong. Chang asked, "What will you bring to me, old man?"
When the monks met, Weir raised his fist and said, "I meet the Master here. The Master said, "Once dead and burned, where will you establish your body and life?
Weir replied, "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, yet the water remains; the wind ceases and the waves subside, and the moon reflects in the pool.
The Master said, "Do you not wish to request instruction or receive the precepts? Weir immediately covered his ears and departed. One day, on the Buddha’s birthday, [the Master asked him again].
Ascending the Hall for a Long Sermon: Today there are three auspicious matters. First, the World-Honored One’s birthday; second, clear skies in the heavens;

third, a donor has prepared a vegetarian feast. If you can recognize, upon these three auspicious matters, where this old monk’s tongue falls, you will be able to consume ten thousand taels of gold daily. Wei goes from west to east, pointing with one finger.
Tianyi pointed to the ground and said, "The Heaven among Heavens, the Middle Heaven of Heavens; who comes first, Śākyamuni or Maitreya?
Chang replied, "The Great Lion’s Roar has already passed; is there still a Little Lion?

On another day, while ascending the hall, he cited the saying, "When the lotus leaf moves without wind, there must be a fish swimming. Weir came forward from the assembly, let out a thunderous shout, and brushed his sleeves.
He traveled on. Longshi presented him with a verse: "Thick yellow chrysanthemums fill the eyes; autumn is here. Baizhang sits upright atop the green peak.

Lightly bringing forth the 'no guest, no host' phrase— A single shout makes the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward. Not long after, Wuyue returned to Dapeng and subsequently moved to Mount Song, where he spent nine years.
Longshi sent a handwritten letter inviting him to share the seat [of the abbot]. He soon returned to Mount Song. In the *Renchen* year, Zhuo...
He traveled to Mount Dengwei in Suzhou and established a monastic center, naming it Sheng’en. Students gathered there like clouds. Ascending the hall, he said:
"A man of great capacity who can carry his burden beyond the empty kalpa prior to King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras—where would there be so many complications?
Have you not seen how Linji, while under Huangbo, asked about the Buddha-dharma?"
This is the general meaning. He asked three times and received three severe blows. Later, he went to Dayu, who gave him a single thrust with his staff.
At that moment, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, exclaiming, "It turns out Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not so very much!

Dayu said, "Just now you asked whether you had committed an offense or not, and you immediately said the Buddha-dharma is not so very much. After all, how much is there? Speak quickly! Linji [replied].
Daoyu struck him three times under the ribs with his fist. Upon reaching this point, not a single atom could be hidden from him.
Thereafter, he manifested great capacity and exercised great function; he opened the eyes of the human and celestial realms and revealed the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
His sharp wit was like the flash of a stone flint or a bolt of lightning; truly difficult to approach. Whenever he saw a student enter the gate, he would immediately shout. Great!
Assembly: Suppose, as in the assembly of Linji, the two head monks of the two halls simultaneously let out a shout. Now tell me, which shout is the host, and which is the guest?
If you can see through this point thoroughly, you will see where the old man Linji stands;
you will see where you yourself and all sentient beings in the great earth stand. Concealed within is the mirror of wisdom; the mirror precedes the stimulus. It is revealed.

It manifests great function; this function transcends the conventional. Thus, one knows that the ladle-handle of the eastern neighbor is long and that of the western neighbor is short—there is nothing not known.
Yet today, the high-minded scholars who study in the monastic groves do not clarify this matter until their death.

What is the cause of this ailment? It is truly lamentable. These students deludedly grasp at dharmas as being the illness, using one illness to attack another, thereby causing their Buddha-nature to become ever more obscured.

The further one seeks, the more distant it becomes; the more urgently one strives, the slower the progress. A person of keen intelligence turns the light back upon themselves and realizes their error in this very moment.
When medicine and illness are both forgotten, the eyes protrude, piercing through mountains, rivers, and the great earth, illuminating billions of Mount Sumerus.
Fully rolling up and fully unfolding, fully killing and fully giving life, they capture and defeat the gateway of Deshan and see through the family style of Linji. This is—
It is so. To see Deshan is easy; to see Songshan is difficult. Why?
You must know that within dead words there are living words, and within living words there are dead words; within dead words there are dead words, and within living words there are living words.
Do you understand? "When Shancai reached this point, there was no path to travel; yet it exists within the mere snap of his fingers."
(Guisi) Ziyuan, a Chan Master who built a hermitage at an ancient temple, styled himself Huitang.

He was the son of the Chen family of Linhai. His mother conceived him after experiencing a wondrous dream; from birth, his physical bearing was extraordinary, and he possessed a serene air of transcendence from the mundane world.
Whenever he entered a temple and beheld a sacred image or a Buddhist scripture, he would invariably kneel in the *hu-gui* posture with palms joined.
Zhao. His father said to his mother, "This child is like a blue lotus flower; water cannot wet it, so how could the secular world submerge him? He then ordered him to leave the household life.
Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he sat in meditation in a single room, making the practice of *bandha-dhyāna* (bound sitting) his daily task.

Later, he returned to Tiantai to attend upon Rixing Yong. Upon seeing him, Yong was immediately pleased and ordered him to serve at his side. When Yong moved to Jingci, [Zhao] followed due to their karmic affinity.

He followed his path and consulted on the essential points of the resolute determination. Suddenly, he attained a profound realization. After some time, Huiyuan returned to the imperial court and his father’s residence. On the way, he passed through Ninghai;
the sun had already set, and a mournful wind howled through the wilds. Huiyuan hurried along in great haste.

Having traveled about three li by night, he encountered the master of an inn—a single dilapidated room that could not shield one from the wind and rain. Huiyuan stayed there throughout the entire night.

He fell asleep. At dawn, he pointed toward the heavens and swore an oath, saying: "If I am unable to establish a hermitage to provide lodging for those passing through the day, may I be as guilty as the sun itself.
In the village there was an ancient temple, Miaoxiang, whose two corridors were desolate. Following his travels, he went there to inspect it and said with joy:
"This is sufficient to fulfill my aspirations. He informed the presiding monk and borrowed the western wing; he cleared away the weeds and filth and prepared a bed.
The bedding and mats were prepared in such numbers that none were not neat and clean. On the east side of the county, at Taoyuan Bridge, there was formerly the Yuantong Pavilion;

because [the image] had been moved there, the Huayan Pavilion was constructed to its south. Furthermore, the Amitābha Pavilion was built, depicting the sixteen contemplations of the Pure Land, so that those who behold them might give rise to practice and awaken the true cause for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
(Year Jiawu) Chan Master Fuliang resided at Tiantong.
He had been in the world at Shengshou Monastery in Jiaxing for thirteen years; in the year Jiawu of the Zhizheng era, he was transferred to Tiantong.
(Yiwei) Chan Master Huizhao resided at Baota during the Yiwei year of the Zhizheng era.
Regarding Huizhao’s relocation to Baota: previously, the temple had been abandoned due to a legal dispute. Huizhao said:
When disputes arose due to excessive contention, he would settle them all with broad compassion and never engage in comparison or argument.
He would say, "Our Buddha attained the Samādhi of Non-contention; it is for this reason that he transcends all other beings. As a son of the Buddha, how could I not follow his teachings?
The assembly submitted to his transformation. Puren (字: De-yin), a native of the Zhao family of Lanxi, shaved his head and received the precepts.
He was fully endowed with a profound sense of regret and a resolve to seek the Way. Sitting upright until dawn, he vowed to cease all delusive conditions.
Daoliangyi, as a son of great eloquence, vigorously revitalized the Linji school’s tradition. When Ren went to visit him, they engaged in a dialogue within the inner chamber;

their exchange of wits was like a flash of lightning or a crash of thunder. Daoliangyi then charged Ren with the duty of attending to the incense. After a long time, he traveled abroad to Fuzhou, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, and Hunan, visiting all those of renown.
Wherever he traveled, he invariably sought out venerable elders to verify his realizations; there was none whom he did not honor with a changed countenance and prostrations.
When Nan-chu of Shuangjing requested him to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, he recommended Gu Ding to come and fill that position.
Nan-chu further extolled Ren’s virtue, remarking that they had met too late. Yet Ren himself remained humble and unsatisfied, quickly traveling to Siming to see Yuejiang.

Yin Yunwaixiu engaged him in debate every day without fail. They examined the karmic conditions of the Chan school, encompassing everything from the vastness of the *sahasra-lokadhātu* to the minute detail of a single hair-tip, leaving nothing uncollected.
In the year of Yiwei, he emerged into the world at Jingtu Temple in Jinhua.
(Bingshen year) Chan Master Huizhao resided at Ayuwang Temple and later at Baoduo Temple.
One day, a monk dreamed of a divine being whose robes and cap were most magnificent, who came flying through the air.
The monks paid their respects and questioned him. The spirit said, "I have come from Mount Aśoka; I wish to invite the Great Teacher Dàqiān to attend a sacrificial offering.
Not long after, the Xingxuan Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) appointed Zhào to reside on this mountain.

Zhào, lamenting that the Great Dharma was declining, exhorted and guided others with tireless effort. He once set forth three "gateless barriers" to test those who came to study under him. The first said: "Within the mountains..."
1. A fierce tiger takes flesh as its life; for what reason does it not eat its own offspring? 2. Space has no front or back;
by what cause do there exist north, south, east, and west? 3. One has drunk milk equal to the four great oceans, and the accumulated bones are like Mount Vipula;
who among these were your original parents? At that time, there was none who could penetrate his intent. (Huidan)

At first he went to Mount Niutou in the world; then he moved to Guanghui, and later to Baoning. In the year Bingshen, when the Imperial Preceptor established Jianye, Tán went to pay his respects at the imperial camp.
Upon seeing Tán’s appearance and demeanor, which were extraordinary, the Emperor sighed and said, "This is a monk of great merit.
He then commanded him to preside over Jiangshan Taiping Xingguo Chan Monastery. At that time, it was a year of famine, and Tán transformed food through his spiritual power.
He provided for his followers so that none lacked anything. The farmers in the valleys below the mountain wished to enroll in the military registers;
Fataṃ feared the temple fields would fall into ruin, so he petitioned the Emperor and returned them [to the temple]. Furthermore, the timber forests of the mountain had been cut down by woodcutters.
Tán again submitted a memorial. The Emperor bestowed a single sword upon him, saying: "Whoever dares to fell these trees shall be executed.
To this day, the forest remains lush and verdant. Yuán Jìng, whose courtesy name was Tiānjìng and pen-name Pǔyǐn, was the son of the Ni clan of Kuàijī.
His appearance was imposing and dignified, and his disposition was as warm and radiant as spring. He was entirely ignorant of the worldly arts of traps, snares, and the closing of gates.
Wu shaved his head and received full ordination; he was strikingly dignified and possessed far-reaching aspirations. He followed Tian'an to study the Tiantai *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation).

Later, he went to Shuangjing to visit Xingduan. When Jing entered the gate, Duān let out a single shout with a stern voice. Jing felt as if he had heard the roar of thunder; all his attachments and fetters were completely cast off.
He immediately prostrated himself in homage. Duān asked, "What have you truly seen? He then engaged in four rounds of question and answer.

He underwent the threefold turning [of the Dharma wheel] and in each case satisfied Yuan-duan’s expectations. Yuan-duan looked to his left and right and said, "This is one of those in the stage of Prajñā.

He then ordered him to return to the office of attendants; shortly thereafter, he was appointed to oversee the secretarial records. At that time, he was twenty-seven years old. In the year Bingshen, he took up residence at Changqing in Kuaiji.
He ascended to Tianyi Wanshou Monastery. Those from the four quarters who sought the Way heard of his reputation and came to take refuge in him.
(Year Dingyou) Chan Master Lijin resided at Ruiguang Lijin;
his style name was Baitan. He was the son of the Yao family of Wu Prefecture. His mother dreamed of a monk with a thick, bushy beard who walked straight into her chamber.
She waved her hand and drove him away without retreating. Startled by this, she woke up and subsequently became pregnant. Once the child was born, a fragrant aroma filled the courtyard.

When she reached the age of five or six, she had a square forehead and a round brow; her complexion was as white and pure as jade. All who saw her felt nothing but pity and affection. At seven years of age, she began to read;
whatever she saw once, she could recite from memory. Whenever she beheld a Buddhist image, she would immediately prostrate herself on the ground. One day, she requested of her mother, saying:
"The boy was troubled by the fact that worldly phenomena arise and perish without constancy, and he asked, 'Is it possible to seek the supramundane Dharma?

His mother said, 'Leaving the household life is extremely arduous. You are still young; how could you possibly endure it? He replied, 'My heart finds joy in it myself; I imagine there is no suffering.

As he entreated her repeatedly without ceasing, she finally allowed him to leave the household life. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he studied the teachings of the Vehicle with great diligence. Suddenly, he sighed deeply and said:"
"I have gained a rough acquaintance with the study of names and signs; why not cast aside all external conditions and ascend the path to enlightenment?
He then changed his robes and entered the Tiger Forest (Hulin), where he visited Guding Ming at Shuangjing. Ming showed him the dialogue between Deshan and Longtan.
Jin Fenshun leaped with vigor and directly struck the essential point, whereupon they reached a profound accord. Jin was appointed to serve as the head of the secretariat (zhǎng jìshì).
Before long, he was invited to share the seat and preach the Dharma. In the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era, he emerged from seclusion to preside over Rui Guang Temple in Suzhou.

On a day in the sixth month of the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era (1357), Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang entered nirvana. He was a dharma successor of Zhongfeng Benmo, representing the twentieth generation of the Linji lineage.
When Yuanchang manifested slight illness, he requested a bath and changed his robes. Summoning the assembly, he wrote a verse which said:
"Throughout my life I have been loquacious; today I am exposed in my failure. One phrase roars through the heavens—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. Thereupon, he cast down his brush.
He passed away. Ryōryō traveled extensively to study under various masters, yet for a long time he was unable to attain realization.

He went to visit Gennō Shōichi, who, seeing Ryōryō’s sincerity and integrity, deemed him fit for further cultivation and frequently exhorted him with words of admonition. Subsequently, Gennō appointed him as the keeper of the storehouse, instructing him to read the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka daily.
After some time, Ryōryō ascended to the position of First Seat (Dai-ichiza). He once presented this verse: "Ignorance is the Buddha-dharma."
"I have no children. A single dose of arsenic medicine kills a man. Wait until your coffin has opened its eyes, and then I shall cause you to turn over upon the edge of a sword.
One day he said to Liang, "The true nature of suchness transcends the sense organs and their objects. When auspicious light manifests, it illuminates heaven and earth.
Without the profound merit of severing all thoughts, one cannot transcend birth and death and enter [the Way]."
"This is the realm of eternal stillness. Why do you not bind some thatched grass among the deep mountains and dense forests to investigate and clarify it?

Zhi Liang sprang up with joy and descended the mountain that very day. In the spring of the Dingyou year, he traveled to Longyou County; to the north was a mountain called Bao’ai (Precious Canopy), whereupon he halted his staff.

Within three or four years, a monastery was established there, named Jishi Chanju (The Meditation Retreat of Reality). — By Shanji (Zhang Shangying). Character: 繼 (Jì) (Note: The character "繼" (jì) is provided as the signature or authorial mark at the end.)
Juezong was the son of the Lou family of Zhujia. His mother dreamed that a divine being bestowed upon her a white lotus flower before he was born.

When he first began to speak, seeing his mother recite the names of the Buddha, he joined his palms and chanted along with her. As he grew older, he read the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) and sighed deeply, saying:
"The *Chunqiu* is but a mundane teaching. If one seeks the supramundane, whom can one rely upon other than the followers of Śākyamuni? This body is unreal; [existence]..."
Like a plantain tree, even if one attains high office and noble rank through the study of books, how long can such status last?

He subsequently shaved his head and received full ordination, studying the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. He then traveled to India to follow Zhantang Cheng, who said, "In the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, I hope for you, my son, in the future.
He presided over three monasteries during his tenure as an abbot, after which he suddenly retired from public affairs.

He returned to the East and diligently cultivated pure practice. On a day in the seventh month of the Dingyou year, he gathered the assembly and said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs propagate the teaching by relying on the preciousness of timing and conditions.
When conditions conflict with the timing, how can the transformation proceed? I am about to depart. He then sought out a brush and wrote a verse, after which he passed away.

Upon cremation, his teeth and tongue remained uncorrupted, and *śarīra* relics lay strewn across the ground like a multitude of pearls. [This concludes the entry for] Huixin. He resided at... (text ends).
Longxiang. When the troops of the Great Ming descended upon Jinling, the monks all dispersed; Xìn alone sat in meditative equipoise with his legs crossed.
Soldiers stood before him in full force, yet every one of them cast down their weapons and prostrated. The Emperor once visited the temple and listened to Xìn’s preaching of the Dharma;
admiring Xìn’s pure sincerity, he specifically renamed Longxiang as the Great Tianjie Temple. The temple’s outstanding grain taxes remained with the common people.

Recently, an official was dispatched to verify these matters. On a day in the eighth month of the year Dingyou, he rose at dawn, sought a bath with fragrant water, and after bathing and changing his robes, sat in the lotus posture.
He said to those around him, "I am about to depart. You should resolve to uphold the Dharma and exert yourselves with diligent progress.
Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes. His attendants shook him and called out to him, repeatedly requesting a verse of farewell. Xìn [the official] took hold of him...
He wrote in calligraphy: "Throughout my life, I have harbored a rebellious spirit; for seventy-eight years it has leaked forth. This morning, casting off my hands, I depart.

Ten thousand li of clear sky, a single flake of snow. Having finished writing, he closed his eyes again. He was cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were as large as beans and hemp seeds, brilliant in five colors.
Even in places reached by the smoke, they grew in clusters. They were stored in a precious vase, which emitted light.

Externally, she was known for her extreme diligence in lifelong spiritual cultivation. From her youth until her old age, she would silently recite one volume of the *Lotus Sūtra* every day without fail.
On several occasions, she experienced the fragrance of lotuses filling the courtyard, its scent exceptionally rich and pervasive. On the day before her death...

The Emperor was stationed with his troops at Jiangyin when he fell asleep during the day. He dreamed that the Master arrived wearing a brownish-brown dhyāna robe and said to him, "For what purpose have you come, Master?
The Master replied, "I am about to return to the West; therefore, I have come to bid you farewell.

Upon returning, the Emperor heard that the Master had passed away and that his robes were identical to those seen in the dream. Greatly delighted, he issued an imperial decree to provide silk and fabrics from the Inner Treasury.
He assisted with the funeral arrangements. On the evening the coffin was carried out, the Emperor personally presented offerings and escorted it beyond the city gates.
(Wuxu year) Chan Master Zuming of Guding, a descendant of the seventeenth generation of the Linji lineage (the dharma heir of Yuansou Duan), resided at Mount Jing.
On the first day of the New Year, while he was offering prayers for the state, three paths of white light appeared before the headquarters of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration. The Chancellor...
Kangli saw him and felt increased reverence. Furthermore, Kangli enshrined the Avalokiteśvara image that Ming had praised in the Ziwai Pavilion.

That evening, an auspicious light shone brilliantly. He invited it to Yunju Temple in the prefectural city. At that time, Ming frequently visited [Kangli] to inquire about the profound principles of the Chan school.

One day, while [Ming] was reading the scriptures, he asked the Elder, "Why do you not read the scriptures? Ming said, "Is it by tracing the lines and counting the characters that one reads the scriptures?
The Elder remained silent. Ming turned the pages of the scripture and said, "The old monk is going to read the scriptures.
The Elder covered the scripture with his hand and said, "Please explain this for me. Ming said, "Who were Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? In the year of Wuxu (1358), when he was about to...
He passed away in peace. He wrote a letter entrusting his inner and outer protectors. On a day in the first month, he said to his disciples, "The lotus pedestal of Avalokiteśvara has arrived.
He then requested a brush and wrote this verse: "Life and death are pure truth; the great void is perfectly full. Seventy-nine years [have passed]."
The cradle-cord snapped; he cast down his brush and passed away. Fuliang presided over Tiantong for four years before moving to Zhong Tianzhu.
At that time, the realm was in great turmoil and the ravages of war continued incessantly. All the monasteries of the two mountains, north and south, were consumed by raging flames.
Lingyin, anciently renowned as a field of supreme awakening, was left with only cool smoke and white grasses, shrouded in desolation under the evening sun.
