In the interim, those who passed by sighed with lamentation. Prime Minister Kengri selected an excellent dwelling for him.

Upon arriving there, he thatched a hut with reeds to provide shelter for scholars from all quarters. Even during this autumn of decline, he instructed his disciples with words that were particularly fervent and urgent.
He once said: "The single school of Bodhidharma has nearly fallen into ruin; you must exert yourselves as if your very heads were on fire."
Nevertheless, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings can all be fully known upon the tip of a single hair.
If one knows them thus, one may transform the great earth into gold and accept it without hesitation; otherwise, one will incur the shame of eating in vain.
Time flows like lightning. Regarding matters of the upward path, you all must urgently cultivate yourselves.
Among those who study through inquiry, many have attained awakening and entry by means of these words. ○ Shao Da resided at Mount Jinhua for eighteen years.
In the year Wuxu, he moved his residence to Baolin Chan Temple on Mount Yunhuang in Yiwu. ○ Yang Yuzhen, whose courtesy name was Wushi, was from Jin... [text ends]
To the east of the county, at a distance of approximately fifty-five *li*, there is an earthen mound extending for several *li*.
It is called Luohan Mountain (*Lohan Shan*). Previously, during the Yuanfeng era of the Song dynasty, the local virtuous man Zheng Kexun and his younger brother Keming—
Iron was smelted on that site to cast five hundred and eighteen statues of arhats; the mountain derived its name from this.

More than two hundred years later, Yunzhen resided by the side of the mountain. Together with his wife, Lady Wang Benjing, he went to Mount Fulong to pay his respects to Lansi Xing, where they received the Mahayana Threefold Pure Precepts (Tri-skandhaka-śīla). He thereafter devoted himself to the practice of bound meditation (bandhana-dhyāna).

One night, he dreamed of a strange monk who appeared to have come from the Western Regions and told him, "You should build the Yongning Hermitage on Luohan Mountain to cultivate meditative concentration.
Upon waking, he marveled at this, and immediately constructed a Buddhist dwelling on that very site.
He personally planted pine trees that grew into a lush forest, and he also constructed a gate tower.
(Jihai) The Dharma Master Bicai, whose courtesy name was Dayong, was the son of Qu of Linhai.
At the age of twelve, he studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school and received the tonsure.
He received full ordination and traveled to Hu-lin, where he visited Zhan-tang Cheng. At that time, Yu-gang Run was serving as the First Seat (Dharma-seat leader).

As soon as [the Master] took up his scriptures and entered the inner chamber, he did not step beyond the threshold for ten years. Run sighed and said, "If this man had not already cultivated his practice during the assembly at Vulture Peak, how could he have attained such a state?
He later appeared in the world at Dang-hu in Hai-yen. This was the year of Gui-wei in the Zhizheng era.
On the day of the third month in the year Jihai, while presiding over the Yanfu Monastery, he summoned his disciples and said, "The conditions for my life are nearing their end.

He then burned incense, sat facing west, and called out the name of the Buddha of the Western Paradise in a resolute voice. For six periods of the day and night, his voice did not cease for even a moment.
On the following day, he spoke again, saying, "Do not say that your practice yields no results; my karmic affinity for the Pure Land is mature, and samādhi has manifested before me."
"I shall now depart. He then prepared his bath and changed his robes. He wrote a letter of parting for those he knew, and further composed a verse of farewell to this world.
When the coffin was carried to the pyre, a five-colored divine light radiated from within it.

Once the fire had subsided, his tongue was like a red lotus, his teeth and gums like white jade or shells, and śarīra relics the size of soybeans filled the ground. The multitude vied with one another to collect them from the ashes.
They all vanished simultaneously. Those who arrived later dug the earth for over a foot and likewise found them. Fanchi presided over Benjue Temple in Jiaxing.

In the year Dingyou, he moved to Tianning Temple in his native district. In Jihai, he built a dwelling to the west of Tianning Temple in Haiyan to reside in, calling himself the "Elder of the Western Study.
He devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of Pure Land. Once, he beheld a great lotus flower filling the entire world.

Amitābha is in the center, surrounded by the assembly of sages. He composed a poem on cherishing the Pure Land to exhort his fellow practitioners and members of the same society, so that all who possess a mind might be led to recite the Buddha’s name. Yunruo (字:
Jiheng), surnamed Xiangli, left the household life and received full ordination under Fohai Cheng. He studied together with Tian'an Ji, Wuan Wu, and Yuting Han. All were...
He possessed great renown; people called him one of the Four Heavenly Kings within the Buddha’s assembly. He resided in India and later retired to Yunmen.
During a time when the world was in great turmoil and weapons were brandished in chaos, he encountered a band of soldiers who threatened him with drawn blades.
When he refused to submit, he was consequently killed; white milk overflowed from his body, and when the troops withdrew, his body was cremated, yielding countless *śarīra* relics.
(Gengzi) Chan Master Chong resided at Yuantong Chong.
He received the heart-seal (*citta-mudrā*) from Da Xin and remained in his service for over ten years. When Chief Minister Zhang Qiyuan asked Xin, he said:
"Within this field for selecting Buddhas, the monks are so numerous; are there any among them who do not contradict Prajñā?"
He said, "His precepts and discipline were refined and strict; his words and deeds did not contradict one another. He revered the Buddha alone.
Since receiving ordination, he has not let his side touch the mat for thirty years. Yan Shen praised him all the more. Not long after, he emerged into the world at Guangxiao Temple in Taiping.
One day, he ordered plasterers to coat the walls. In the middle of a wall, there was a protrusion as if there were an object contained within. He scraped it away.

He obtained a statue of Prince Siddhārtha, which had been carved from a Buddha’s tooth. He summoned artisans to gild it with gold, but the gold cracked and splintered, and śarīra (relics) surged forth from within.
He carved a small incense pavilion and enshrined the image therein. Donations from near and far increased day by day and month by month.
Soon after, he moved to Yuantong Monastery in Jiuyang. At the beginning of the Song dynasty, there was a divine monk named Yuande who, as he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, repeatedly...

The stupa was made of blue stone. He said to his disciples, "If this stupa turns red, it shall mean that I have returned. When Yuanji Min arrived to preside over the Dharma seat, the stupa indeed became red in color.
At the time of Min’s passing, he again left a prophetic record, containing an omen that Buddhist affairs would flourish greatly after three hundred years.
When [the current abbot] entered the monastery, the assembly of monks dreamed that Min had arrived, and the stupa shone with a brilliant light.
This lasted for a full month. Those who understood him remarked that from the time of Emperor Min (Emperor Wen of Liang) until this point, exactly three hundred years had passed.

Xuánzàng was styled Gūtíng. Born into the Mǎ family, he left the household life and received full ordination. He devoted himself to the masters of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to exhaustively study their doctrines, yet for a long time he made no significant progress.
At that time, Bǎojiào Jiǎn was lecturing on the sutras at Cáo-xī; Xuánzàng followed him there. Jiǎn said to his disciples: "Xuán..."
"Superior man," one might say, "your reputation truly accords with your reality. If you disciples can emulate his virtue, our school may well be restored to its former glory.

From that time on, his fame spread rapidly. He went forth to Jianfu Temple in Kunshan, but after two years he left it behind and returned to Donglin, where he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure karma.
Addressing his fellow practitioners, he said, "I have observed that the *Ciyun Jingtusanchan Yi* (The Ritual for Repentance for the Pure Land by Ciyun) is clear and lucid..."
In brief: the various texts concerning the five repentances all originate from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. I wish to rely upon them to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
(Xin-chou year) Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan entered nirvana. (He was a successor of Luguling and served under Linji [Luohan].
Zhengyuan’s courtesy name was Zhuyuan. He was a descendant of Ouyang Xiu and resided in Nankang. His mother dreamed that a foreign monk entered her room.

He was born [into the lineage]. Having received full ordination, he traveled as a wandering monk and visited Xugu Ling. Ling questioned him using the words from "The Dragon Pond Extinguishes the Paper Torch.
Yuan said, "A scorched stone can break through layers of ice. Ling asked, "What is it like after it has been broken? Yuan replied, "One must explore to know. Ling asked, "What is that which is known?
As Yuan was about to respond, Ling raised his staff and struck him. Startled, Yuan attained silent realization. He entered the world and resided at Guan.
Yinxing, Shengdaochang, Lingyin, and Jingshan—these five great monasteries—once exhorted people to recite the Buddha’s name, saying:
"Shigong drew his bow; Sanping set his arrow. Master Huiyuan urged swift and direct practice: recite one phrase of Amitābha with no other thought."
In the year of Xinchou during the Zhizheng era, he announced the date of his passing. On the [blank] day of the sixth month, he wrote a verse and entered parinirvāṇa.
His entire body was enshrined in a stūpa at Mount Jing; his disciples separately buried his fingernails and hair, from which śarīra relics emerged in profusion.
○ Shougui, residing at Tiantong Mountain, on a day in the eighth month of Xinchou, composed this one verse to bid farewell to the Chancellor Da-shi-ti-mu-er. The next day, he departed.
He bathed, then took up his brush and wrote this verse: "A single stinking snail-shell, filthy within and without; casting it aside, he goes forth, ringing the bell in the void.

The dragon and the deva point with a finger—today is just as it was yesterday. Having cast down his brush, he passed away. He valued his life's conduct, and his observance of the precepts was exceedingly strict.
Once he lost a tooth; his attendants enshrined it in a casket, where a *śarīra* (relic) was produced within it, shimmering with five colors and growing larger day by day.

Zhi Ji served him from Longjiao, then moved to Puci, and later to Jingci. In the autumn of the *xinchou* year, he moved to Jingshan, where his reputation stirred the four quarters and those who examined his virtue increased ever more.
(Gengzi) Chan Master Yongning resided at Cihui.
(Jiaxu) Yongning took charge of Shanquan and recruited ten thousand people for the "Ten Thousand Good Deeds Return to One Source" assembly (*Wanshan Tonggui Hui*) over two days and nights.
Furthermore, they buried the skeletal remains from after the war, which reached no fewer than ten thousand. (Renyin) He again retired back to Longchi. (Guiyou) Guangde.
There was a great drought. Hui-ning established an altar and recited mantras; before the Buddhist chants had even concluded, a heavy rain poured down like a torrent.
The assembly then urged Ning to remain at the Cihui Chan Hermitage on Mount Macheng.
(Jiachen) Chan Master Songyin Miao entered nirvana.

Having resided at Qingliang for fifteen years, he retired to Dongtang, where he remained in seclusion without venturing beyond the mountains. On a day in the eighth month of the Jiachen year, he passed away.
He manifested a slight illness. When his attendants requested a verse, Daomao pointed to his heart and said, "Within this, all is vast and empty;

what need is there for a verse? The following day, he summoned the bhikṣus to bid them farewell. He then sat upright, leaning against a couch, clenched his right hand into a fist, and rested his forehead upon it before passing away.
Seven days later, his countenance remained bright and radiant; when they felt the crown of his head, it was still warm. Upon cremation, [relics were obtained].

Śāriputra, those who resemble pearls and gems are indeed numerous. He lived to the age of eighty-five and had seventy years of monastic seniority. Initially, he studied the *Prajñāpāramitā* and then withdrew to Mount Laṅkā.
In the year Jiachen (1904), he moved his residence to Puci Temple at Longquan.
In the year Yisi, Chan Master Mingde resided at Jingci.
He then lived at Dongchan in Songjiang and was subsequently transferred to Baoning in Jiqing, where he stayed for fifteen summer retreats.
Having moved three times among the great monasteries of the Lake region, in the year Yisi, Chancellor Keng-li invited him to reside at Jingci.
(Dingwei) Chan Master Yunqing established the Fahai Hermitage.
Yunqing, whose courtesy name was Youyuan, was the son of the Wang family of Jinhua. He left home to study under Yuan Chang, never letting his mat touch the floor for ten years.
One day, he entered the inner chamber, and as their spiritual sparks clashed and met, their depths could not be fathomed. Yuan Chang nodded with evident delight.
He then instructed him to travel among the regions of Min, Zhe, and Huai to seek formal certification (*yinke*). Qing saw that the various masters were not at all different from himself;

for a long time he remained in seclusion on his home mountain, where his literary brilliance was naturally revealed. He subsequently emerged into the world at Zihu and later moved to Yushan. In the year Dingwei, he...
Feng traveled to Lanxi Longyan, where he was delighted by its climate and environment and took up residence there.
He then sighed, saying, "In such a sacred land, how could one not establish a site for Prajñā? He subsequently went to Nanzhou and built the Fahai Vihāra.
Huaiwei received the Dharma from Da Xin; as Xin approached his death, he called Wei to him and said, "I have occupied the position of the Master for over forty years, receiving people..."
"It is not that there are not many others, but as for those who can propagate the Way of Great Wisdom and ensure it does not fall into ruin, there are none but you and Zongle.
You must exert yourself! After Xun passed away, Wei appeared in the world at Baoxiang Temple, then moved to Baoguo Temple, and later to Daochang Temple.

Even during a period when military conflict and destruction were continuous, he sought out followers for the sake of the Dharma without the slightest retreat. At the end of the Yuan Zhizheng era, he fled to Kuang...
At Lu, some fierce soldiers came to demand gold and silk. Wei glared at them and rebuked them, saying, "How could a Buddhist monk possess such things?

The soldiers grew angry and drew their swords to kill him. Wei extended his neck toward the blades, and the soldiers sighed in admiration and departed. Huitan resided at Jiangshan. In the year Dingyou, he moved to Tianjie.
In the first year of the Wu era, when the new imperial palace was completed, an edict was issued summoning Huitan to lead a thousand [monks].
A gathering of two hundred people perused the Tripitaka. As Tan ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, the Emperor personally led his ministers to attend and observe him.
Tan’s Dharma voice was grand and resonant, wondrously harmonizing with the Imperial mind. The Emperor then released silk from the inner treasury to bestow upon those near and far.
Disciples, hearing the news, flocked to the hall and its courtyards until there was no room to accommodate them.
Tánbèi implemented all the regulations of the ancestral temple, such that the onlookers sighed in admiration, saying, "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties could not surpass this.

Initially, the monastic halls, quarters, and storehouses had been temporarily used by officials to store military equipment, which remained there for a long time without being returned. The Emperor then commanded the Chancellor Lǐ Shànzhǎng to remove it.
Furthermore, the Emperor personally inscribed the six great characters "The World’s First Zen Forest" (Tiānxià dìyī chánlín) and suspended them at the triple gate.
[In the year] Jizuō, he resided at Puci. In the year Yisi, he moved to Maoshan; in the year Wufeng, he relocated to Wufeng Peak. In the year Dingwei, he returned once more to seclusion at Chenlou.
(Wushen) In the first year of the Hongwu era, the Seng-shih Yuan was established.
Huitan resided at Tianjie. In the third month of spring in the Wushen year, the Seng-shih Yuan was opened;

Huitan was specially invested as the Great Chan Master of Pure Virtue, Benefiting the State, and Exalting the Teaching, and appointed as the Abbot of the Great Tianjie Temple, presiding over all mountain monasteries of the Buddhist teachings.

At that time, those from the state who were intent upon the ancestral altars and those recluses dwelling in the mountains and forests who embraced the Way emerged one after another, all residing in famous mountains and great monasteries.
Since ancient times, the veneration of the Dharma gate has reached its peak here.

Yet, scholars in their ceremonial robes claimed that the followers of Śākyamuni were a parasitic blemish upon the world and petitioned for their eradication. The Emperor showed this memorial to Tán, who said:
Confucius regarded the Buddha as a sage of the West. From this, we know that a true Confucian will certainly not disparage Buddhism;
one who disparages Buddhism is certainly not a true Confucian. The Emperor likewise [recognized] the Buddhist teachings as providing secret support for the imperial order, yet he refused to listen.
The Emperor heard that many of the monks at the temple were practicing unlawful acts and ordered strict measures to suppress them. However, Fatan only sought to lead them with kind words.

Although the various groups of śramaṇas were defiled by worldly customs and truly violated the monastic precepts, some urged that they be severely punished. Fatan said, "There is a proverb that says:"
"In the great forest there are trees of no use. Can they be completely removed? They would only serve to increase the burden upon the Śākya school.
As for those whose deeds have been exposed, you must not show them leniency. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The spring breeze blows vast and wide; the spring days linger on.
The yellow oriole sings among the branches of the myriad flowers. Within this, there is boundless meaning—whose message can it be known by? Before he had finished speaking, a monk suddenly asked:
[The monk] asked, "What is it like when mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed? Tanyan shouted back, "Who is there to suppress?
In his room, Tanyan said to the monks, "During the twelve periods of the day and night, there is no portion for you to chew upon, nor any portion for you to pursue. Do you understand?"
The monks were at a loss. Tan said, "If you do not understand 'three, eight, and nine,' you cannot avoid sinking into deep reflection.
Because Yuanzhen resided at Ba’en Chan Monastery, when political chaos broke out at the end of the Yuan dynasty and military forces stirred upon the sea, the smoke and flames rose to the heavens.

The three pavilions and the temple were all reduced to fields of overgrown weeds. Yuanzhen was deeply pained by this; taking the restoration of the monastery as his own responsibility, he went forth with his alms bowl.
While traveling to transform those in the villages, he established assemblies for the transmission of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* according to each location and expounded upon cause and effect.

Butchers and wine-sellers changed their occupations accordingly. Thereupon, donors gathered from the four quarters; thus, at the two embankments flanking the river in Taoyuan, he established the site.

He lined the foundation with stone and constructed a pavilion; not long after the work was finished, he grew weary of the world. On a certain morning in the third month of the Wushen year of the Hongwu era, he rose as usual without any illness.
He requested a bath, changed his robes, and exhorted his disciples, saying that the realization of one's nature must be made the priority.

Furthermore, he said, "I shall pass away tomorrow. When the appointed time arrived, he took up a brush and wrote a verse, then serenely submitted to the natural order. His remains were enshrined in a stupa.
Seven days passed; his countenance remained as if alive. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained. Weizé, whose courtesy name was Tiānzhēn, was of the Fèi clan and a native of Wǔxīng.
His mother dreamed of a strange monk and subsequently conceived. At his birth, a wondrous fragrance permeated the air, so he was named Sēngbǎo.
He left home at the age of seven and received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). He traveled to various regions to visit Chùshí Qí, Qiānyán Cháng, and Wújiàn.
Du saw that [the masters] Wuyong, Kuan, and eighteen others all failed to accord with the Dharma. Later, he heard that Wujiyuan of Mount Kuanglu was the Dharma heir of Xueyan Qin.
Qin had once instructed Yuan, saying, "Your merit is thin; it is not fitting for you to appear in the world to save others.
Though he was already a hundred years old, he sat alone in a thatched hut, remaining silent all day long. Du went directly to visit him, but Yuan offered no further instruction.
Later, he encountered Huairang while the latter was on the latrine. He hurried forward and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Huairang seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! At these words, he attained great enlightenment; he simply shook his hand. Huairang asked, "Have you gained something?
He immediately replied, "How could there be anything to gain? Huairang asked, "Are you applying intellectual reasoning? He then brushed his sleeves and departed.

He departed from there. From this point on, his sharp intellectual edge (*jīfēng*) was inviolable. Having served him with diligence for over a month, [the Master’s teachings] grew increasingly profound and mysterious;

those from all quarters came to revere and submit to him. After a long time, he took charge of the treasury keys at Lingyin Monastery. Later, hearing that his preceptor was aged and ill, he returned to attend upon him.

He had a vow never to involve himself in worldly affairs. Scholars from the four quarters flocked to his gate daily. At the request of the assembly, he opened the gateway to the ocean of Dharma, surrounded by a thousand fingers [of disciples].
His reputation for the Way grew ever more renowned. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, when all eminent monks of the empire were summoned to the capital, he was the foremost candidate for selection.
Suddenly, due to an ailment of the foot, he was granted leave to return to the sea. In the spring of the Guiyou year, he manifested a slight illness, which one day worsened.
At dawn, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I am departing. When his attendant requested a verse, he replied in a stern voice, "Is what I have been saying all along not sufficient?
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained; his cranial bone, teeth, and tongue remained uncorrupted. Chongfu resided at Yuan Tong.
In the first year of the Hongwu era, he was transferred to serve as the abbot of Ayuwang Monastery, which was among the Five Mountains (*wushan*).

This was the first instance. Those who had presided over the affairs of the temple were all men of renowned virtue at once; thus, it was difficult to find a successor worthy of the position. Upon hearing that [Master] Dao’an was approaching, both the young and the old rejoiced.
Those who came from afar to welcome him with incense and flowers lined the roads one after another. It was the middle of winter, yet the wind was calm and the sun was bright.

Celestial music was heard from all four directions, and ten thousand voices offered hymns of praise, everyone vying to say they had witnessed something unprecedented. As for his manner of guiding and receiving others...

"Unawakened" refers exclusively to the practice of single-mindedly upholding the upward-pointing function [of the Way], where staff and shouts are deployed with such mastery that those who encounter them are struck with terror.
(Jiyou Year) Zen Master Mujin Zudeng entered nirvana. (He was a Dharma heir of Rikkyu Ei.
Zudeng resided at Unpō on Mount Tiantai, where he lived together with his disciples practicing asceticism to provide for their own needs. In winter, one...

In winter he wore a fur robe and in summer a single hempen garment; for breakfast and dinner he took but a single bowl of rice. He did not venture beyond the mountains for over fifty years, and many were transformed by his example.
Regarding diligent practice as his primary concern, whenever anyone offered him land or fields as a gift, he declined, saying: [...]* *Note: The original text appears to be incomplete at this point.*
"The Buddhas of the past took begging for alms as their primary task; what need have I for this? In the first month of spring in the year of Jǐyǒu, he suddenly manifested a slight illness.
He summoned his disciple Pùráo to succeed him on the Dharma seat. On the eighth day of the second month, he again wrote a letter bidding farewell to his fellow practitioners.
At the half-hour before midnight, he looked to those around him and asked, "Is it nearly dawn? They replied, "Not yet. He said, "The Master [the Buddha] was precisely at this time..."

"What is this state like? asked [the assembly]. Deng broke into a smile and said, "In the past, when an ancient worthy was sitting in illness, someone asked him, 'Is there anyone who does not fall ill?
He replied, 'There is. The questioner asked, 'What is it that does not fall ill? He replied, 'Father! Father!

Having uttered these words, Deng remained silent for a long while, and then said again, "If one calls this being ill, would that be correct? The assembly remained speechless. Deng offered his blessing.

He said, "The physical body is impermanent; seek realization early. The time has come and I shall depart. The attendant held out paper and requested a verse. Yunmen said, "I will certainly not die without a verse; would you rather I not pass away?

When the attendant’s request remained firm, he then wrote: The mountain is high, the path is steep; One step forward, ten thousand miles behind. If you wish to know where I am going, Look at the footprints on the snow.
Arising and ceasing, coming and going—these are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. It crushes the five Sumeru mountains; vast and empty, it has no front or back.
He set down his brush, sat upright, and passed away. His body was cremated, and a wondrous fragrance permeated the air;

the śarīra relics were beyond counting. Yongning resided at Maceng Mountain. In the year Wushen, he again retired to Longchi. In the sixth month of the summer of Jiyou, he manifested a slight illness.

He entrusted [his affairs] to his disciples. He had paper cut and fashioned inner and outer robes, saying, "I am about to depart. At dawn on the seventeenth day, he rose, bathed, and donned the paper garments.
He wrote a verse, which said: "For seventy-eight years I have guarded my simplicity; Clearly, it has all been one great failure. The clay ox turns over in the depths of the sea;
In the midst of the blazing heat of June, snow falls. Having finished writing, he lay on his side and passed away. [His body was] preserved...
He was enshrined in a niche for seven days; his countenance remained as if alive. Upon cremation, light of five colors appeared.
His teeth, jaw, tongue, and rosary were all unharmed. The *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. When the smoke reached the middle forest, they too emerged in profusion.

People vied with one another to break off branches to collect them, and even from the ashes and soil, many obtained them by sifting through it. His disciples each divided the remaining bones among themselves.
As for those who did not perish: [the relics] were enshrined in five pagodas constructed at Longchi Monastery. Huitan presided over Tianjie Monastery.

Having encountered a prosperous era, he received abundant imperial favor. While all those holding rank among the ministers were invariably addressed by their given names when summoned, Huitan alone was always addressed in imperial edicts as "Grand Chan Master," a distinction unprecedented in history.
In the winter of the second year of the Hongwu era, Huitan suddenly fell ill.

He suffered from a speech impediment and consequently resigned from his monastic duties. In the first year of the Hongwu era, the Shanshi Yuan (Court for the Propagation of Goodness) was first established to select monks of realized virtue to preside over famous mountains throughout the empire.
When the seat at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou became vacant, everyone wished to appoint Tianning Monastery’s master from Jiaxing to fill it.
Gong Jin was appointed as the Abbot. Gong Jin declined the honor and retired to Tonggui Hermitage, where he welcomed his mother there to support her.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued for Gong Jin to reside at Dajianjie Temple. Upon arriving at the palace, Gong Jin had an audience with the Sovereign in the Outer Court;

the Emperor’s consolations were most generous, and he immediately ordered an inner court official to escort him into the monastery. Gong Jin was thoroughly versed in the scriptures of Western India as well as the various texts of Eastern Lu. Together with...
In the discussions of the gentry, his words fell like fine snow, as if scattering jade shavings. Yet when it came to examining students, he insisted on pointing directly to the source of the mind.
He practiced both the doctrinal teachings and their realization, with their respective functions alternating and unfolding, causing those who listened to revere him without ceasing.
(Gengxu) Chan Master Baiyun Zhidu entered nirvana (the successor to Wujian Ding in the lineage of Linji). Zhidu resided at Huading.
In the second month of spring in the Gengxu year, he manifested a slight illness; with a vast resolve, he set his mind on returning home.
Although the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to remain, Zhidu said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; this is my wish. He then returned to Fulin in Chuzhou. It had been barely five...

On the third day of the third month, he suddenly bathed and changed his robes. He sought out a brush and wrote a verse, saying: "There is no world from which to take leave; there is a multitude with whom to part.
In the great void of space, why need one drive in a stake? He then threw down the brush and passed away.
His body was cremated, and five-colored *śarīra* relics, as well as his teeth and a rosary, were recovered and interred to the west of the monastery. ○ Shanxue resided at Guangfu on Huxi.
On the gengxu day, a monk of the monastery was to be exiled to Qianzhou for failing to meet a deadline on government levies.

The authorities, knowing that the Master Xue was solely devoted to teaching the Way, wished to debate the matter with him. Xue said, "I am the presiding abbot; by law, I must take responsibility for this. How could I dare involve others?
He then resolutely requested to go in his stead. When someone asked the reason for this, Xue said, "My past karma is already fixed; it cannot be avoided. (Gengxu 4)
In the month of [the first lunar month], he arrived at Madang Mountain in Chiyang and passed away while manifesting illness. ○ Baogin resided at Wutai.
In the year Jiyou, the capital of Yan was pacified. In the year Gengxu, an imperial edict summoned Jin to Nanjing; he had an audience with the Emperor in the Fengtian Hall and spoke as follows:
"I have long heard of the Master's reputation. Because the central plains are bitterly cold, I specifically invited the Master to reside in the south. He was subsequently lodged at Dàtiānjiè Temple.
At that time, the Emperor summoned him to inquire about the Buddha-dharma and the nature of ghosts and spirits. [The people of the world were deluded.
While residing at Wūshí, in the twelfth month of winter in the third year of the Hongwǔ era, he manifested slight signs of illness. He summoned his disciples and exhorted them...
He entered the path with diligent effort. Taking up his brush, he wrote a verse: "Birth is fundamentally non-birth; cessation is fundamentally non-cessation.
Casting off my hands, I go forth; under the bright moon of the single sky. He threw down his brush and passed away.
(Xinhai) Chan Master Jie’an Fuliang entered nirvana (the 18th generation of the Linji lineage, successor to Guangzhi Xun). Fuliang resided at Lingyin Monastery.

When his period of propagating the Dharma had come to an end, on a day in the first month of the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he personally drafted a document entrusting his robes and assets to the monastery’s public treasury.
Having settled matters regarding his social relations as well as the funeral rites and enshrinement, he looked toward those around him and said: "The next day..."
At that time, I was about to depart this life. When the appointed hour arrived, I bathed, sat upright, wrote a verse, and passed away.

Upon cremation, my teeth and jawbones were firm and clean, and my tongue was red and moist; none of these were damaged. When the fire was extinguished, the various *śarīra* relics were as round as pearls and as bright as jade, nearly filling a pint.

The fourfold assembly scrambled for them until the ashes and embers were completely exhausted. The bones were interred within the Return-to-Clouds Stūpa. Initially, I had not informed [the disciples] of this.
At the time of his passing, he entrusted his final affairs to his fellow disciple Zongle in a letter, saying: "My end has arrived.

You should return at once; if you delay even slightly, we shall not meet again. At that time, Zongle was staying in Gusu, thinking that since Zhiliang’s spirit was still strong, how could it have reached its end so suddenly?
He packed his belongings and returned home, only to find that Zhiliang had already been cremated for several days.
His goodness was truly remarkable. He propagated the Great Dharma without concern for external embellishments, and thus the essential intent of the West naturally became clear.
Furthermore, he took the contemplation gates of the Pure Land as a vessel for crossing the sea of suffering, practicing them concurrently at all times without ever slackening for even a moment.
○ Chan Master Chushi Fanqi Enters Nirvana (The 17th Generation of Linji, Successor of Yuansou Duan).

In the autumn of the fourth year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor, considering that the principles of ghosts and spirits are profoundly mysterious, intended to seek out the wondrous and established teachings of the former Buddhas.
He selected those among the monks who were proficient in the Tripitaka to question them. Fanqi and Mengtang E, among others, responded to the summons.
He was summoned and arrived. He was lodged at Tianjie Monastery, where he consulted the sutras and śāstras to compose a treatise.

Just as he was about to present it to the Emperor, on the twenty-second day of the seventh month, Yuanqi suddenly manifested a slight illness. On the twenty-sixth day, he requested a bath and changed his robes; sitting in the full lotus posture, he wrote a verse which said:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death. A wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west. Having set down his brush, he passed away.
Wuo said, "Elder brother, I am going. Wuo asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to the West. Wuo said, "There is a Buddha in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?
Qi let out a thunderous roar and passed away in stillness. When the Emperor heard of this, he expressed deep sorrow and lamentation.

At that time, cremation was prohibited by law; however, because of [Fahai] Qi, a special edict was issued to open the tomb. Among the remains, his teeth, tongue, and prayer beads were not destroyed by the fire.

His *śarīra* were five-colored and adhered to his bones, clustering like pearls. His disciples took the bones and the indestructible relics back to Haiyan, where they erected a stupa at Tianning Monastery to enshrine them.
He was seventy-five years old and had been a monk for sixty-three years. (From the *Zonglin*).

Le resided at Mount Jing. In the spring of the fourth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to assemble ten eminent monks of the three schools along with two thousand of their disciples to establish a Great Memorial Dharma Assembly on Mount Zhong. He commanded Li Jin of Tianjie Temple to oversee the ritual matters.
Jin declined on the grounds that his mother was elderly, and proposed Le as his substitute. Le returned once more to his mountain hermitage, and subsequently took up residence at Tianjie Temple.
Initially, Huìtán presided over the Tianjie Monastery. He resigned from his duties due to illness. In the second month of spring in the year Gēngxū, his illness was completely cured.

In the sixth month of summer, the Western Regions had not yet submitted to the court. Since that realm highly esteemed the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), the Emperor specially commissioned Huìtán to go there.
Having received the command, Huìtán set out on his journey that very day. Traveling by sea from Zhejiang and Fujian, he propagated the teachings in all the kingdoms and cities he passed through.

The majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven were such that there was no one who did not hear of them and come to submit. On the *xinhai* day, in the seventh month of autumn, his journey brought him to rest in the kingdom of Siṃhala.
The king was overjoyed and provided him with lodging at the Buddhaśaila Monastery. At the hour of the tiger, he paid his respects;

he then ordered all the ministers and citizens of the realm to be able to behold and worship him. Dharmatāta guided them according to their capacities, and all received the benefit of the Dharma. In the ninth month, he manifested a slight illness.
Before long, he bathed and changed his robes, then called to those around him, saying, "I shall no longer return to life. He sat upright in the full lotus posture.
At midnight, he asked, "Is the sun about to rise? They replied, "No. He asked again after a while, and so it continued three or four times.
Finally, he said, "The sun has risen," and passed away with a serene expression. Five days later, his countenance remained as if alive. The King was greatly amazed and sighed in admiration.

An altar was constructed for the cremation. The king and his hundred officials escorted him to the foot of the altar and commanded more than a thousand bhikṣus to circumambulate him while reciting various dhāraṇīs.
At that time, a column of white smoke rose up, illuminating the heavens. When the fuel was exhausted and the fire extinguished, the śarīras were beyond counting;
the tongue, roots, teeth, and jaw remained unharmed. Thereupon, the sacred bones were collected and interred alongside the stūpa of a pratyekabuddha in that kingdom.
Previously, that Buddha had once issued a prophecy regarding today’s opening and enshrinement ceremony; it now perfectly accords with his words.

(Renzi) In the fifth year of Hongwu—the fourth year since the founding emperor ascended the throne—he again reflected upon the military upheavals at the end of the Yuan dynasty and the fierce struggles for supremacy throughout the empire that affected all living beings.
Their kindred could not provide for their final rites with a righteous livelihood; tens of millions of wandering spirits were agitated and writhing, filling the space above and below.
No one came to offer condolences or funeral offerings, leaving them solitary and without support. On nights of dark, rainy dampness, their cries could sometimes be heard as shrill whimpers.

The Emperor’s heart was as if burdened by affliction; he further believed that to cleanse the dark and repress the spirit and ascend toward the bright and luminous, only the teaching of the Great Hero (the Buddha) could achieve this.
Consequently, in the twelfth month of winter, he issued an edict summoning ten Buddhist monks of realized virtue from Jiangnan.
He proceeded to the Southern Capital, where he established a grand memorial Dharma assembly at Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple on Mount Jiangshan.
The Emperor stayed in the fasting quarters for one month, abstaining from meat and strong flavors.

On the thirteenth day of the first month of the spring in the fifth year, the Renzi year, at the break of dawn, the Emperor donned his *pibian* ceremonial cap and ascended the Fengtian Hall to present the imperial composition of the petition. He then conferred [it upon the assembly].
Tao Kai, Minister of Rites, carried [the image] out through the Wumen Gate and placed it within the dragon carriage. It was escorted to Mount Jiangshan.
Suddenly, the Imperial Carriage arrived for an imperial visit; from the clouds, five-colored seeds like beans rained down.

On the fifteenth day, as the ceremony was about to conclude, the Sovereign donned his *pibian* cap and held a jade *gui* tablet. Ascending the hall, he faced the Great Hero (Buddha) and stood facing north to personally welcome the Buddha.

Upon reaching the time for the fire offering (*liao*), there was nothing in which his utmost sincerity and reverence were not fully manifested. The music consisted of eight performances: first, the "Song of Benefiting the World" (*Shanshi qu*);

second, the "Song of Manifesting Faith" (*Zhaoxin qu*); third, the "Song of Extending Compassion" (*Yanci qu*); fourth, the "Song of Dharma Joy" (*Faxi qu*); fifth, the "Song of Zen Delight" (*Chanye qu*);

sixth, the "Song of Responding to Leakage" (*Leying qu*); seventh, the "Song of Sublime Salvation" (*Miaoji qu*); and eighth, the "Song of Perfect Accomplishment" (*Shancheng qu*). When the rite concluded, the ministers hurried out and returned.
At that time, as the Buddha’s light followed the five paths of existence, it emerged from the northeast, piercing the moon and illuminating the heavens; after a long while, it vanished.
Mingde presided over Jingci Temple during the chaotic period of the late Yuan dynasty when warhorses were rampant.

Upon the entry of the Sacred Dynasty (the Ming), Mingde retired due to his advanced age and returned to Zhulin Hermitage on the temple grounds. On a day in the second month of the Renzi year, he manifested a slight illness and exhorted his disciples.

He said: "Though my body is humble, my single true, perfect nature is equal to that of the Tathāgata. The arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena are no different from sparks struck from stone or flashes of lightning.
Practice diligently day and night; do not give rise to regression. After my death, you must follow the Buddha's regulations and commit me to cremation;
do not allow the fourfold assembly to wear hempen garments and wail. Having finished speaking, he asked for a brush and wrote a verse. He then passed away.

He then entered *parinirvāṇa*. His age was seventy-nine and his *dharma-śrāmaṇera* years were sixty-two. After his cremation, his cranial bone remained intact and his *śarīra* relics lay in profusion amidst the ashes.
Zhi-shun, style name Yichuan, was the son of the Chen family of Rui’an. His grandparents had cultivated pure deeds with great diligence;
after they passed away, lotus flowers appeared upon the door and screen. His father married into the Lou family, and she frequently wept for her deceased son out of deep emotion.
Unable to bear her grief, she fashioned a statue of the Great Master Zhi and served it with devotion. One night, she dreamed that the statue’s head was encircled by a halo;

it traveled upstream against the current and called out to Lady Lou, saying, "I shall become your son. Upon waking, she found herself pregnant. When the child was born, his noble qualities were evident from birth.
However, from his youth, he took no pleasure in wearing hair; he lived with a carefree air, as if beyond the mundane world. At the age of seven...
He left the household life. Upon reaching maturity, he received full ordination. He studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for three months until he could recite its text from memory.

Traveling to various regions, he practiced the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. After a long time, he sighed and said: "While scholastic study is beneficial for increasing one's learning, it is difficult to resist birth and death.
To resist birth and death, what else can be clarified if one sets aside one's own nature? Thereupon, he changed his robes to enter meditative practice and went to Mount Tiānbǎo to visit Tiě.
Guanshu transmitted the essential points of his heart-mind to Shun, who wished to remain under Guanshu’s guidance.

Guanshu rebuked him, saying, "A man of worth does not confine himself within this narrow shell of a snail, competing with others in a great forest. He then swept his sleeves and entered [the inner quarters].

After some time, [Dongshan] sat on the seat of honor to preach the Dharma. When Shu passed away, Shun succeeded him in the affairs of the monastery. Subsequently, he returned to Zhejiang, and soon after, he returned home again.
In Yongjia, he resided at Ba’en; subsequently, he entered Min to reside at Dongchan, then moved to Xuefeng. Returning to Wenzhou, he lived in seclusion among the forests and springs.
In the year Renzi, Huaiwei, the abbot of Jingci, proposed Shun to succeed him. Initially, Shun did not comply, but later he sighed and said:
What is most esteemed in the practice of a śramaṇa is to respond to the world in accordance with conditions; what room, then, is there for the mind to dwell upon it?

Thus he struck his *śikya* staff and departed for Baojin, remaining in the celestial realm. On the first full moon of the first month of spring in the year of Renzi, His Majesty personally performed the rites of offering to the Buddha.

At the hour of midnight, he issued an imperial decree bestowing *mōtúójiā* (modaka) and *hù* (droṇa) measures of dharma-food. When the ceremony was concluded, the Emperor’s gracious rewards were most abundant.
In the fifth month of summer, he sold all his clothing and bowls to provide funds for seven days of Buddhist services. He then manifested slight illness.

The Emperor, becoming aware of this, personally took up brush and ink to bestow a twelve-line poem upon him, which contained the words: "The profound gate is fully realized; you have already attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, his illness was critical, and he was unable to go to the palace to offer his thanks. On the fourth day of the sixth month, he bathed, changed his robes, and—

The fourfold assembly spoke among themselves, straightening their robes and sitting upright; their eyes were nearly closed. A disciple requested, saying, "Master, you are about to pass away, yet you have left behind not a single word.
How shall you manifest yourself to future generations? Jing said, "Even the Three Pitakas of the Dharma-treasure are but old paper;
what more could my words accomplish? He then passed away with serene composure. Three days later, his body was cremated, and relics of five colors were obtained.
The relics, teeth, tongue, and rosary remained undamaged; people scrambled for them in a chaotic frenzy until the ashes and soil were exhausted.
(Gui-chou year) Chan Master Tan’uo passed away.
Tan’uo had lived in seclusion in a separate chamber at Rui Long Monastery on Mount Xiang. In the third year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to summon those of talent from Jiangnan.

The monk Dao’er was among those present. He was lodged at Tianjie Temple. After he had presented himself before the Emperor, His Majesty took pity on his advanced age and granted him permission to return to the mountains.
In the second month of the sixth year, when Dao’er was eighty-nine years old, he suddenly became free of ailment;

one day, without illness, he unexpectedly bathed, changed his robes, and brought out his utensils to distribute as gifts to his friends throughout the monastic community. He instructed his disciples, saying: "The three realms are empty."
Flowers [vanish] like smoke swept away by the wind; the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects are like snow melted by boiling water.
From antiquity to the present, only this single nature remains alone. My illusory body shall now enter extinction. After my passing, I shall undergo cremation, and my bones shall be reduced to dust.
Do not erect a stupa to burden future generations. Listen to my verse: "I have an object that has neither head nor face. If you wish to obtain it..."
"Clearly! Look after my parinirvāṇa. Having spoken these words, he closed his eyes and sat upright until he passed away.
Keshou resided at Longhua for thirteen springs in a single term. In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, he was transferred to Central India.

As he traveled to the banks of the Qiantang River, the veteran monks of Jingci Monastery deliberated, saying, "This great spiritual teacher—how could we let him go? While Central India may be difficult to reach, he can still be brought here."
"Are we alone unable to do so? He led the assembly to take up his position there. Zhi-shun went to Jingci Monastery, intending to carry out great works of service;
however, monks who were in arrears with government taxes filled the courtyard in chains. Shun wept for them and paid their debts in full on their behalf.
In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, he arrived at Nanjing. After only four months, he bathed, wrote a verse of farewell, and passed away. The *sha*... [funeral rites were performed].
Having obtained immeasurable śarīra relics, his wisdom shone forth. He resided at Ayuwang (Aśoka) for nine years, then retired to Miaoxi.

On the banks of a spring, he built a dwelling called Meng’an (Dream Hermitage). He remained there in solitary seclusion behind closed doors; though layers of dust accumulated upon his mats, he took no heed of them.
On the first day of the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of the Hongwu era, he summoned his disciples and said: "I am about to return to the West. Any of you who are away should hasten back."
Upon his return, seven days later, he entrusted his final affairs to the abbot Chongji. He bathed, changed his robes, and requested paper to write a verse.
Having finished writing, he passed away peacefully. He was eighty-five years old and had spent seventy summer retreats. His body was cremated;
his teeth, eyes, and prayer beads remained unburnt, while the rest became śarīra relics, brilliant in five colors. [End of] *Liji Jingui*, "Retirement from Office" (Tonggui).

In the winter of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, a Dharma assembly was convened once again. The Imperial Carriage arrived in person, and an edict was issued for Jin Chanyang to expound upon the First Noble Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
From the dukes and marquises down to the common officials, all gathered in a circle to listen; there was none who did not submit with joy and conviction.
On a day in the twelfth month of the sixth year, he suddenly addressed his disciples, saying: "I have a karmic debt from former lives that remains unsettled; I must surely repay it."
"Do not constrain me with worldly appearances. Not long after, he manifested a slight illness and declined medical treatment, medicine, and food.

He wrote a verse by hand and passed away in accordance with the natural course of things. His coffin remained for sixty days before the cremation was performed; his countenance was observed to be as if alive.
His prayer beads and teeth remained unbroken, and his *śarīra* relics were beyond counting; those who beheld him vied with one another to take them away.
(Jia-yin) Chan Master Yin-yuan entered nirvana. (Zhongfeng was the dharma successor of Benmo; this was the twentieth generation of Linji.

Jōtetsu was about to enter Japan to establish the banner of the Dharma. He originally sent En-gen to Siming.
Jōtetsu said, "If you can return with me to assist me in completing my mission? En-gen replied, "The traces of a wandering monk have no fixed dwelling and no fixed mind;

what could there be that is not possible? Thereupon, he gathered his robes and boarded the ship. Subsequently, all those who were able to spread the transformative teachings far and wide were due to En-gen’s efforts. En-gen.

He returned to Japan and presided over various famous monasteries. On the first day of the first month in the spring of the Jia-yin year of the Hongwu era, at the half-hour of the night, he summoned his disciples and said to them:
"I shall pass away today. You must immediately enshrine me in a coffin and bury me; do not follow worldly customs by performing rites of memorial or sacrifice.
Furthermore, you must inform all my former disciples at the various monasteries to strictly observe the instructions I have given throughout my life, so that the Dharma..."
"It may be that the wheel [of the Dharma] shall turn forever. At dawn, friends and associates came to inquire after his well-being, and he received them as usual.
At noon, he called to his attendant, saying, "The time has come. Bring me my brush and inkstone. When they arrived, he spoke again: "My stupa is now complete."
Only the plaque had not yet been inscribed. [He] wrote the two characters "Heart Seal" (Xinyin) in large script. Entering his room, he sat upright and entered nirvana with serene composure.
○ Li Yuanzheng, style name Dayou, was a native of Gushu. His mother, née Tao, had no offspring; she prayed day and night to the Buddha Avalokiteśvara.
One night she dreamed of a bhikṣuṇī riding in a white-deer carriage and holding an infant, who said to her: "This is a child of merit and wisdom."
She also took good care of her. Later, she became pregnant; not more than a month after the child was born, the boy’s body suddenly became feverish like fire, and he would not take nourishment.
His mother again dreamed of the aforementioned bhikṣuṇī, who held several chestnuts and chewed them. Upon waking from the dream, the boy’s sweat poured down like rain, and he was immediately cured.
When he was four years old, while playing at his father’s knee, his father gave him a primer for learning characters. The boy said:

"What is the meaning of this? What is the purpose of reading it? His father was greatly astonished. [The boy] then took the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing*) and could recite it from memory after a single reading.

As he grew older, his brilliance and development became extraordinary beyond the norm. His father once personally transcribed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).

[The boy] read them one volume at a time and earnestly petitioned his parents for permission to leave the household life. He shaved his head, received full ordination, and after a long time, traveling with his monk’s staff, came to the south.
He went to the capital and paid his respects to Huitan at Tianjie Temple. Huitan appointed him as an attendant and said to him, "Your talent is exceptionally sharp;

you should apply yourself to literature. In the future, I expect you to propagate our school and uphold its teachings. Thereupon, he sat alone in a single room, exhaustively investigating the texts of both India and China.
Subsequently, he was appointed to oversee the temple records. In the year Wushen, he entered the world at Suixi Temple in Jiaxing. In the year Geng...

In the year Wuxu, he moved to Daochang Monastery in Wuxing. Not long after, he retired to the mountains of Wukang and composed the *Neiwai pian* (Inner and Outer Chapters) of the *Guanhuanzi*, intended to harmonize the profound unity of Confucianism and Buddhism.
In the winter of the Gui-chou year, he returned to Tianjie Monastery. At that time, Song Lian was attending the Emperor at the Shangsheng Lou;
looking out toward the Chan forest, the Emperor asked Lian, "Is there a virtuous monk within? Lian replied, "Recently there has been..."
Two monks arrived from the region of Wu-Yue; both were proficient in literary composition. The Emperor asked, "What are their names?

They replied, "One is Yuan-Zheng, and the other is Zheng-Chuan. The Emperor said, "Bring them forward so I may examine their work. Zhu Xi (Lian) consequently presented a volume of Zheng-Chuan’s writings.
The Emperor read it personally and, upon reaching the end of the scroll, remarked, "This is perhaps something even Confucian scholars have not attained. He then questioned Yuan-Zheng.

The Emperor examined the documents presented. It was stated that Zhang Ding, the Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, possessed a correspondence concerning the debate on human nature (*xing*).

Thereupon, an imperial eunuch was dispatched to summon Ding, who arrived bringing the certified documents. The Emperor reviewed them once more as before and said with delight, "The arguments are most profound; he is truly one who stands out like tempered steel.
The following day, Ding was summoned to the Jinshen Hall for an audience, where he received the Emperor’s utmost consolation and favor. An edict was then issued:
The two monks from the Ministry of Personnel were both appointed as Attendants for the Provisioning of Texts at the Hanlin Academy.

They were granted residences at Taiping Gate, along with two wives and concubines each, and ordered by the Imperial Library to be provided with books. They were to remain shut in their chambers for study;

after three months, once their hair had grown long enough to wear the ceremonial cap, they were then to take up their official duties. Three months later, Zheng fell ill. Messengers from the imperial court came and went incessantly on the roads to inquire after his health, yet in the end—
When he was rising [from his seat], as his illness was about to turn fatal, he looked upward and said, "I shall die;

what I regret is that, having received the profound grace of the Sovereign, I am unable to repay it. He then orally dictated a letter of thanks to a friend. Before the letter was finished, he passed away.
During the first watch of the night, [the Emperor] dreamed that Sengzheng came to express his gratitude; he was wearing a loose garment of coarse cloth, and his headcloth was slightly tilted.

When the Emperor questioned his attendants, their description of the attire matched exactly. Consequently, he moved the coffin and shook the headcloth, finding it indeed not straight. The Emperor marveled at this even more.

This was in the second month of spring in the year Jia-yin. [Seng]zheng’s age was thirty-seven. Zhenglue is the same person as Guo Zhenglue, whose courtesy name was Wenyuan; he was a native of Kuaiji and was a contemporary of Sengzheng.

He was summoned. Later, he was promoted to the post of Director of the Bureau of the Record of Rites and Ceremonies (*Qiju Zhu*), and subsequently transferred to the position of Director of the Office of Merit (*Kaogong Jianling*).
One day, the Emperor said to Liǎo: "You stated that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is the scripture for transmitting the mind of the Dharma Master Bodhidharma.

Upon reading it, I find this to be true. The mind is the most difficult thing for a person to maintain. It moves upon contact with external objects; it plunges into the abyss or soars to the heavens, shifting according to every thought—like frozen ice or a parching fire."
The scripture speaks of the way to maintain [the mind] and subdue [the passions]; this is truly no different from what the Confucians say.

If the feudal lords, high ministers, and great officers were all to know this, then even if they could not yet align themselves with the Buddha’s wisdom, they would at least restrain their depraved thoughts and sever their greedy desires, so that they would not fail to become virtuous men and gentlemen. Lian replied: "It is indeed as Your Majesty has commanded. However, as for its text..."
The style is concise and archaic, and its meaning is profound and subtle; it was only the Song official Su Shi who frequently complained that it was difficult to read.

The Emperor said, "This is merely the fault of scholars being entangled and obscured by the literal meanings of the text. Within the palace, I have glanced through it several times and already fully grasped its main purport.
He then commanded the Palace Attendant to fetch the scripture and show it to Lian, personally reciting it with punctuation as he went: "As for the Buddha..."

The First Fascicle of the Chapter on Mind and Speech states: All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravṛtti*) and arising as a phenomenal characteristic (*nimitta*).
They have two kinds of abiding, namely, abiding as a continuous flow and abiding as a phenomenal characteristic. They have two kinds of cessation, namely, cessation as a continuous flow...
And their mutual cessation. These three characteristics are most subtle and hidden; only a Buddha can fully explain them. As stated in the fourth fascicle:
"The false imaginings of one's own mind have no inherent nature. Through the observation of wisdom, one does not fall into the two extremes.

One attains a state that is progressively superior from previous bodies and is indestructible—the self-realized noble path. This is the Prajñāpāramitā. This refers to the six perfections and the myriad practices.
The practices mutually integrate and encompass one another to form the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), all of which are established through *prajñā*; this is especially profound.

Both the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* are connected to the study of the mind; they must be studied and practiced. He was able to transmit [the teachings].
Having received the Dharma from Yuanchang, he went to reside at Fanli Rock. There was a tiger on the rock, which fled one night.
In Renhe County of Hangzhou, five *li* east of the city, the land had been a zone of warfare during the end of the Yuan dynasty and was desolate, with no inhabitants.

When it returned to our Ming dynasty, the surviving people gradually gathered there; they were often fond of violence and greed for profit, establishing butcher shops where they slaughtered sheep and pigs.
Master Chuan took pity on them and traveled through the area begging for alms to propagate his teachings. Among them were Chu Daozhen and Jin Xiang, who were the first [to follow him].
To welcome him with ceremony, it was previously reported that a strange monk had appeared at his hermitage in a dream, presenting him with a verse as a gift.
Upon meeting Zhuan, he found him to be exactly as in the dream, without any difference. Consequently, Zhen provided incense for him and daily offered alms-food to Zhuan;

furthermore, he requested a prominent family to jointly construct a vihāra, which was completed in the seventh month of the year Jiayin. He named the hermitage Yuanying (Perfect Response). Puren resided there.

The wise man [Zhao] resided at Chan Temple for fifteen summer retreats in a single sitting. He constructed a separate hermitage on the western slope called Qian’an, intending to spend the remainder of his life there.
In the Wushen year of the Hongwu era, he was invited from Zhongzhu to serve as the abbot; Ren was about to accept the appointment.
The District Magistrate asked with composure, "In the Buddha-dharma, are there degrees of gravity? Ren replied, "No.

The Magistrate said, "If in the Buddha-dharma there are no degrees of gravity, how can there be high or low status for a Master? Ren smiled and ceased speaking. In the year Jiayin, the seat at Jingci Monastery was vacant;
messengers came from Wulin three times. Ren then rose to accept the invitation. On the day he began his teaching, the monastics and laypeople gathered in a circle to listen.
...a thousand people. Each drew deeply from the source and drank the rich essence, departing with sighs of praise and verses of admiration.
Initially, Wumen was resentful when he visited Master Zhu Yuandao and inquired about the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan. As soon as he opened his mouth, he was met with a shout from Yuandao;
Wumen was greatly enlightened, and sweat poured down his entire body. He then presented this verse: "The dog has no Buddha-nature. The spring colors fill the imperial capital. Zhaozhou’s East..."
In the monastery, a gourd was hanging on the wall. Dao laughed and said, "Even if you understand it this way, how could it suffice?
He then angrily brushed out his sleeves and departed. He once told his fellow practitioners, "This matter is like a fish drinking water;

its coldness or warmth is known by itself. It certainly does not reside in words or written characters. Had we not encountered this old monk, we would have nearly been trapped by intellectual understanding."
A lifetime of toil has been spent in obscurity. Even if you gentlemen were to take a mere thatch roof for shelter, you should not forget your origins.
He left the world to reside at Lingyan in Mingzhou, and later moved to Ruiyan in Taizhou. Addressing the assembly, he said: "One sits steadily within the ancestral hall;
why, then, does the master of the house remain unrecognized? One overturns the great ocean and shatters Mount Sumeru; yet on level ground, why is it that one cannot even lift a foot? His eyes—
His radiance shone so brightly that it shattered the four continents; yet his own eyebrows fell away entirely. Why was it that he could not see what was before or behind him?
Most who offered words of response failed to accord with the truth, and the students merely followed along in admiration. Eventually, he retired from affairs and entered Songyan.
